en: May there be prosperity.
The Necklace of Jewel-Ornaments; repeated salutations to the glorious Hayavadana, the Supreme Brahman.
Salutations to Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Brahman.

Having obtained the commentary marked with the *cakra* from the venerable Vāsabrahmatantra, the best of scriptures which crushes the Kali age, and having surrendered his own burden to the venerable Vāsa, the lord of teachers and guru who crushes the Kali age, [he received it] from the fourth teacher, the lord of teachers who conquers the Kali age, from Raṅgendra, the foremost among those who know the Brahma-tantra.
We take refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the supreme goal of the Brahma-tantra and the most excellent among those who know the meaning of the subsequent time-periods.
May my speech recognize Him of wondrous form, who adorns the peak of the glorious Veṅkaṭa mountain—the most sublime auspiciousness for all the worlds. (1)
Here, by the word "alaṅkāra," it is indicated that this treatise has as its subject matter the field of poetics (alaṅkāra).
May the glory of Hayagrīva and Nārāyaṇa adorn the region of my heart—those two who, as the King and the Crown Prince, reside within the boundaries of the kingdom of the supreme abode of Kāla.
With reverence, I bow my head to Hari, the supreme primordial being, who manifested here on Vedagiri, who is beloved by the Lotus-born Brahmā, and whose splendor is as delightful as camphor.

On the mountain of the Vedas, Veṅkaṭādri—since its names are listed as "Vedādri" and "Garuḍādri"—I bow my head with devotion to Hari, the Abode of Śrī (Śrīnivāsa), who is the primordial cause of the universe and therefore supreme above all; who has manifested, being made manifest from the lotus-born Śrī, according to the Mahābhārata statement, "I, indeed, was born in the lotus"; who is beloved and dear; and who is like the finest of clouds (ghanasāra)—for Amara states, "Sāra [is used] for strength, the firm part, and what is just; it is neuter, but in the sense of 'excellent,' it is masculine. I bow to that one of radiant splendor.

In this context, *sarojabhū* refers to Brahmā; *dayitaḥ* means that compassion arose for him from Him [Viṣṇu]. [The suffix] *-itac* is applied here according to the rule beginning with *tārakādi*. Thus it is said. Therefore, He was respectful toward the Vedas (*vedagiri*), which are the speech of the scriptures (*nigamavāci*).

Consequently, at that moment, O King, the Lord Hari, assuming the form of Hayagrīva, appeared before the lotus-seated one—who was despondent because the Vedas had been stolen by Madhu and Kaiṭabha—and took back all the Vedas that had gone to the subterranean realm (*rasātala*).

The meaning is that he has taken incarnation for the purpose of recovering the Vedas, according to the manner described in the *Hayaśīrṣopākhyāna*. "Ghanasāra" means camphor; as Amara states: "Now, *karpūra* is neuter; [it is also] *ghanasāra*. Like that [camphor], he possesses a "sarasabhāsa"—that is, a charming, clear, and beautiful luster. "Ādyam" refers to Hari in his form as Hayaśīrṣa (the horse-headed one). The instrumental case here is used in the sense of "characterized by such a state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe*). I bow most deeply (*param*) to him.
Here, there is a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between Śrīnivāsa and the horse-faced one, both of whom are presented as objects of salutation. || 3 ||
May that eternal couple, mutually harmonious, ever-expanding, radiant, charming, and most sweet, the ornament of the entire universe, shine forever within my heart. (4)

May that eternal couple, in the form of Śrī and Śrīnivāsa—the supreme ornament of the universe, the adornment of all the worlds—shine within my heart; they who are most sweet through their graceful charms (*lalita*), which are mutually harmonious, exceedingly radiant, and full of joy. Alternatively, the word may be analyzed as a separate term meaning "that which possesses a mutual, harmonious, and exceedingly radiant splendor. May that eternally existing pair shine in my heart.

In this context, it is so described because it contains these ornaments (*alaṅkāra*): mutual compatibility, excessive expansion, and brilliance. By means of the ornament named *lalita*, the entire world is most sweetly adorned; that is to say, the entire science of poetics (*alaṅkāra-śāstra*). Alternatively, the construction is: "the couple whose nature is such that all ornaments exist within it through the relationship of subject and object. The rest is clear.
This elaborate play on words (*śleṣa*) is intended to indicate what is about to be expressed. (4)

I honor my teachers, who are jewels of speech adorned with logic, vivid descriptions, diverse and mature expressions, and illustrations; they are profoundly deep and possess the methods for meditative absorption along with their auxiliary components. 5.

By means of the illustration—that is, the manifestation—of mature and bold utterances that are diverse and wondrous through the application and reasoning of logical arguments, [he refers to those] whose method of meditative absorption (samādhi-vidhi)—accompanied by its requisites such as the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama)—is exceedingly profound; this means they are constantly devoted to the meditation upon the Supreme Brahman. By these two qualifiers, it is indicated that they are recipients of the knowledge of both the higher and the lower, as stated in the passage: "Two sciences are to be known."
I compose—that is, I praise—by means of my speech those who are artificial gems, the most excellent among the learned, beginning with Lakṣmīnātha and ending with our own teacher.

In the alternative sense (pakṣe), they are the most eminent teachers who are exceedingly profound due to specific ornaments such as *yukti*, *ullekha*, *vicitra*, *prauḍhokti*, and *nidarśana*; they are so called because they exist together with the ornaments *parikara*, *samādhi*, and *vidhi*. These "ornament-gems" (*alaṅkṛtimaṇayaḥ*) are like gems that serve as ornaments; I compose them, meaning I string them together by means of my words. Here, the intended meaning is indicated through a pun (*śleṣa*). || 5 ||

With firm devotion, I approach the Enemy of the Wicked, whose ornaments are *vakula* and *sarāla* flowers, who is the balm for the entire burden of the diseases of worldly existence, and who is to be served by those with guileless hearts.

One whose devotion is firm is "dṛḍhabhaktiḥ. Here, the word *dṛḍha* does not undergo the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) because the word *bhakti*, being listed among the "priyādi" group, is excluded by the rule "apūraṇīpriyādiṣu" from the application of the masculine substitution prescribed by the rule "striyāḥ puṃvat. Furthermore, the word "ornament" (*alaṃkāra*) here serves as an indication of what will be explained [later]. (6)
I fully honor Nāthamuni—the venerable one among those who perform sacred rites and knowers of Brahman—whose range of simile and poetic fancy has removed all discordant and contradictory examples. 7.

"Beyond the scope of simile and poetic fancy"—that is, beyond the reach of the imagination of similarity, meaning incomparable. "By whom the ends of those who have been uprooted"—meaning those whose conclusions or certainties have been eradicated by opponents and proponents of rival doctrines—"the examples or scriptures of such [opponents] are seen": this means he is one by whom all the established tenets of opposing views have been cast out. According to the *Ratnamālā*, "end" (*anta*) is used in the senses of certainty, destruction, essential nature, front, proximity, and interior; according to Amara, "examples" (*dṛṣṭānta*) refers to both scripture and illustration.

In one sense, it is that in which the two figures of speech, Simile (upamā) and Poetic Fancy (utprekṣā), are the objects to be established; and in another sense, it is that by which the figures of speech known as the Unequal (viṣama), the Contrary (pratīpa), and the Exemplification (dṛṣṭānta) have been extracted and set forth. It is worthy of honor for those who perform actions with full sufficiency—those who are characterized by the performance of deeds whose fruits are not sought after, and who are therefore knowers of Brahman. By this, the Muṇḍaka Śruti is made to resound: "This performer of action is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman."

In this context, for those who possess poetic ornaments—that is, for the *ālaṅkārikas*—the rest is easy to understand. Here too, by the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), that which is intended has been indicated. || 7 ||

I address the lordly sage Yāmuna with a slighting tone toward those who have well-composed works of little substance, employing a crooked speech (vakrokti) that is confrontational and replete with double-entendres.

The word *sādhu* means "properly. It refers to one by whom contempt—that is, disregard—has been cultivated toward those [scriptures] of little substance, namely the first part of the Veda (*pūrvabhāga*) which prescribes rituals for attaining worldly fruits; the meaning is that he has abandoned what is of little substance according to the principle stated: "One should discard the worthless and the slightly substantial, and retain the substantial and the most substantial. By this, his disregard for the external scriptures of false views (*kudṛṣṭi*), which are themselves worthless, is established through the logic of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (a fortiori).

This is an elliptical expression for both the disregard for the portion of the Veda that establishes results pertaining to the next world, and the even greater disregard for that part characterized by the means for attaining the Self. By this very fact, as stated in the maxim, “One should resort to the most essential [portion] in the scripture, like nectar from the ocean of jewels,” devotion to the most essential portion of the Veda—which consists of those sections establishing the means for attaining the Supreme Self—is established by implication.

By those clever and skillful sayings—whether they be "interwoven" (*parigranthitāḥ*), "obstructed" (*bādhitāḥ*), or "overcome" (*krāntāḥ*)—there are "crooked expressions" (*vakroktayaḥ*), meaning indirect modes of speech accompanied by censure (*sākṣepāḥ*), belonging to opponents (*pratyanīkānām*), that is, those who propound rival views; he by whom these are [employed] is so described. Regarding the word *granthitam*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The term *granthita* is used in three genders for 'interwoven' (*gumbhite*), 'overcome' (*krānte*), and 'harmed' (*hiṃsite*)."

I shall meditate upon the Lord of Yāmunamuni, who has fashioned (kalita) this work so that it is excellent in its parts (*pakṣe*), being adorned by "little essence" (*alpasāra*) and "disregard" (*avajñā*); who is woven together (*parigranthita*), meaning composed and blended with the ornament named *chekokti*; who is accompanied by "objection" (*sākṣepa*), meaning existing along with the ornament of that name; and who is likewise characterized by the ornaments of "counter-attack" (*pratyanīka*) and "indirect speech" (*vakrokti*).

The root *man* means "to understand"; it is in the imperative mood, first person singular. The indication [of the meter] is as before. May I worship this author of the Commentary, who, having assumed the state of a sage to protect the Vedas, became the foremost among those whose eye is the Śruti, and who is the Lord of the Eye and the Śruti. 9.

The Lord of Sight and Hearing (Śeṣa), in order to protect the Vedas both in meaning and in word, assumed the state of sages—namely, the state of the sage Rāmānuja and the state of the sage Patañjali—and became the foremost among those who possess the eye of the Śruti, that is, the knowers of the Vedas. The sense is that the distinction lies simply in this: initially he was the Lord of Sight and Hearing, and in his state as a sage he became the foremost among those with the eye of the Śruti. May I worship the author of the Bhāṣya, the author of the Śrībhāṣya, and the author of the Mahābhāṣya. || 9 ||
May the jewel-like Vedāntadeśika, who shines forth amidst the union of memory, doubt, error, intoxication, inconsistency, and conceptual construction, bestow joy upon the world as its ornament. 10.

In the *Smṛtis*, such as the *Dharma-saṃhitās* of Manu and others, there exist "unconnected" (*asaṅgatayaḥ*)—meaning incoherent or irrelevant—speculations belonging to those possessed of doubt and delusion, or those of uncertain origin. The [work] shines forth (*ullāsī*) through the gathering—that is, the refutation—of those alternatives. Alternatively, it is so called because it contains the seven poetic ornaments beginning with *Smṛti* and ending with *Ullāsa*. This is an elliptical expression for its possession of all poetic ornaments. || 10 ||
I meditate in my heart upon all those most noble ones—the preeminent pillars of the court of the venerable Brahmatantra-kali-ripu-guru—who are like necklaces of jewels that adorn the earth. 11.

By the phrase "a necklace of jewels that is an ornament of the earth" (*vasudhālaṅkāramaṇihāra*), the intended title of the work is indicated. May that great Parakālamuni, the crest-jewel of my lineage and my guru, be victorious—he whose extraordinary and boundless devotion toward the Lord of Śrī was witnessed by all people! (12)

That teacher whose devotion toward the Blessed Lord Śrī Śeṣa is *atimātrā*—exceeding all measure, exceeding bounds, and overflowing—whether that devotion be *pratipatti* (reverence), *prabodha* (awakening), or *pravṛtti* (active engagement);

and whether it be displayed in *prāgalbhya* (boldness), in *gaurava* (gravity), in *saṃprāpti* (attainment), in *prabodha* (enlightenment), or in the attainment of the supreme state (*padaprāpti*). (Note: The verse concludes with a list of contexts in which such devotion may manifest: in boldness, in gravity, in attainment, in enlightenment, and in the attainment of the [highest] station, as well as in the presence of women.)

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), that in which the mere *ti*—the syllable *ti* alone—is absent, is *prapatti*, meaning the surrendering of one’s burden (*bharanyasana*). This is because when the syllables *ti* are removed from the word *pratipatti*, it results in the form *prapatti*; here, the identity of word and meaning (*tādātmya*) serves as the basis. Being wonderful (*adbhutā*) and bringing amazement, she was beheld by people. The meaning is that the Lord’s majesty, knowledge, and the act of taking refuge (*prapadana*) were seen by people as being exceedingly marvelous.

The wonder of this surrender (*prapadana*) is clearly evident in works such as the *Tadvaibhavaprakāśikā*, because this very teacher, having performed the surrender while being afflicted by extreme distress, attained the sovereignty of liberation at the very moment he had desired. By the word "was seen" (*dadṛśe*), it is shown that such a surrender was witnessed by all the world. He is called "the crest-jewel of my lineage" (*madanvayasya śekharaḥ*) both by virtue of his spiritual knowledge and his birth; for he belongs to the lineages of both Śrīśaila and Ghanagiri (Appalārya). 12.
May that teacher Śrī Vāsabrahmatantraparakāla be victorious—he by whom the arguments of those with false views were quelled, like adverse winds by a rain-cloud. 13.

The word *dāvāḥ* means "forest fires," which are those things that have attained *pratilomatām*, i.e., a contrary or adverse state. This plurality residing in the meaning is superimposed upon the word. By that Teacher, the arguments of the evil-seers (*kudṛśām*), which had attained a contrary state—that is, hostility—were quelled. The rest is clear. || 13 ||
May he who removes the fear of rebirth for those who have come for refuge be victorious for me—he who bears the titles Śrīvāsadeśikendra and is the leader of the ascetics of the Śrībrahmatantra. 14.

May that Śrī Raṅgendra Kaliripuyatīndra, by whom—through his single [state]—the nature of a Buddha, of a Guru, and of a poet was revealed as being free from all taints, pacify the affliction caused by the difficult-to-grasp Kali age. 15.

By whom, as the Moon alone, moonliness was shaken off—meaning that in his other [aspect], it was not shaken off, nor moved, nor subject to the influence of others; yet his state as Mercury (Budhatā), his gentleness and wisdom, his state as Jupiter (Gurutā), his mastery of speech and status as a teacher, his state as Kavi (Kavitā) and as Bhārgava (Bhārgavatā), and his authorship of poetry were displayed. May he pacify the affliction of evil planets (durgrahabādhā)—the torment of malefic planets such as Mars and the rest, as well as the obsession with stubborn attachments.

The sense is that because this one alone possesses the forms of auspicious planets such as the Moon and Mercury, he possesses the power to pacify the afflictions of evil planets. The rest is easy to understand. ||15||
May my mind cling excessively to the pair of lotus feet of my venerable Guru, the noble-souled Ārya, whether it be contrary or favorable [to his will]. 16.
The meaning is that the mind is "pratiloma" (contrary). The suffix *ac* is applied to the words *pratiloma* and *anuloma* by the rule: *ac-pratyanvava-pūrva-utsa-āma-lomnaḥ*. 16.

Kṛṣṇa, the son of Kṛṣṇambā—who is the guide from the ninefold miseries and born into the lineage of Śrīśaila—has composed this *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. (17) We worship the incomparable Śrī Śrīnivāsa, the ornament of the entire world through all manner of similes and the like; may He make our desire for ornaments fruitful. (18)
This clever man exerts himself under the guise of describing extensive ornaments, in order to express even a mere fraction of the Blessed One’s essential nature, form, majesty, qualities, and power.

This work is composed solely to fulfill the purpose of speech by causing it to proclaim the virtues of Hari; if, through its elegance, it should be of benefit to the young, may it be of great service.
I have composed this work using only my own definitions and illustrations; for what would the Lord of Yakṣas, who possesses the nine treasures, take from others like a beggar? 21.
With the Ānuṣṭubh meter for its definition and the Āryā-jāti for its illustrations, I compose this work; by this effort, may the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śiva) be pleased.

May the Lord of Śrī, whose abode is the Mountain of Serpents, cause this jewel-necklace of ornaments—consisting of both definitions and illustrations composed by myself—to attain the highest state of heart-pleasing beauty.

May this necklace of jewels of ornaments, which conforms to the *devacchandas* (the will of the Lord), which possesses hundreds of streams of aesthetic flavor such as simile (*upamā*) and the like, and which is charming in the heart of the Beloved of Lakṣmī, shine forth. [Commentary: "Conforming to the *devacchandas*" means conforming to the *chandas*—that is, the will (*abhilāṣa*)—of Śrīnivāsa. Amara states that the word *chandas* has various meanings ending in a nasal, including "verse" and "will. Thus, the meaning is "suitable for the pleasure of Śrīnivāsa. In the alternative sense [of the word *anuguṇa*], it is "conforming by virtue of its quality" (*guṇena anugataḥ anuguṇaḥ*), according to the rule for compounds beginning with *ava-* and others when used with the third case in the sense of "reproached" and so forth.

It is so called because it possesses a hundred "saras"—that is, poetic figures such as *upamā* (simile) and others—which are themselves "saras" (full of aesthetic flavor) and "yaṣṭis" (beautiful stalks). As it is said: "The words *latikā*, *laḍikā*, and *yaṣṭi* are synonymous; likewise, *sarā* and *sarī*. For this very reason, it is named *Devacchandas*, according to the rule: "That which has a hundred *yaṣṭis* is *Devacchandas*. It is the composition titled *Lalita-alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
In the alternative sense, may this necklace of jewels in the form of poetic figures shine—be manifest—in the heart, the mind, and the chest of the Beloved of Lakṣmī. || 24 ||
Churning our book with his mind as if it were the ocean with a churning-stick, may the Lord of the Wise, casting aside faults like poison, take up its virtues like a jewel. (25)

Thus ends the introduction to the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*, a treatise on poetic figures. May that Supreme Brahman, who dwells upon the mountain of the bull (Śrī-Vṛṣādri), who protects the three worlds, who is most generous, and whose chest is characterized by ornaments, be victorious! (1)

That which has on its chest the ornament—the characteristic mark consisting of the Śrīvatsa sign—is [the Lord]. By this, it is indicated that this composition in the Anuṣṭubh meter possesses the nature of an ornament (alaṅkāra). This is the opening verse concerning the commencement of the definition of ornaments.
Now begins the chapter on the figure of speech *Upamā* (Simile).
Where the glory of similarity between two things shines forth, that is *Upamā*.

In a poetic work where the splendor of resemblance—the beautiful likeness, so to speak—between both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), which delights the hearts of connoisseurs, shines forth as something manifest and most vivid without being merely suggested (*vyaṅgya*), and gleams as something not subject to negation; there, the meaning is, the figure of speech *Upamā* resides.

In this context, if one were to state merely that "where the similarity between two things is described, there is the figure of speech *upamā*," then an unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *upamā* would arise in such cases as "I string together the moon of poetry, which has rays of extensive meaning. This is because, in that instance, a perception of similarity occurs through the commonality of the quality of "delighting the hearts of connoisseurs" shared by the "poetry-moon" and its "meaning-rays. Therefore, it is specified that [the similarity must be between] the "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) and the "object of comparison" (*upameya*). The meaning is: those things which, by virtue of poetic convention, are fit to stand in the roles of standard and object of comparison.

For there is no fitness for the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) between poetry and the moon; thus, there is no fault. Although the relationship of standard and object of comparison exists in such cases as "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," this does not constitute the figure of speech *upamā*. To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such instances, the phrase "delighting the hearts of the connoisseurs" (*sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādinī*) is included. This qualifying attribute—being "delightful to the hearts of the connoisseurs"—follows as a requirement for the definition of all figures of speech.

Therefore, they say that in cases such as "The Vāhīka is a cow," there is no *rūpaka* (metaphor); in "Is it a post or a man? there is no *saṃdeha* (doubt); in "This is silver" there is no *bhrāntimān* (illusion); and in "This is not silver, but mother-of-pearl," there is no *apahnuti* (concealment), and so forth. [The word] "manifested" (*udbhūta*) is used for the purpose of excluding the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) simile:
"The minds of men who see you mounted upon the field of battle do not yearn to behold the Lord Śiva enraged at the end of an aeon."

In such passages as this, since there is the cognition that "for one who has seen you in such a state, there arose a vision of existence (bhava) in such a state," there is the figure of speech *viśeṣālaṅkāra*, which consists in the production of another impossible thing by one who is performing some [other] action. And by means of that, the simile (*upamā*) is suggested: "At that time, you stood like Bhava himself. Here, because the suggested simile is predominant, it possesses the status of being the object of embellishment (*alaṅkārya*), and not the status of being an embellishment itself. Therefore, since the term "emergent" (*udbhūta*) results in the exclusion of what is not suggested, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of this definition to the case of a suggested simile.

By intending [the definition] as "not being the counter-correlate of a negation," the possibility of a negative (vyatireka) relation is excluded. Consequently, what is intended here as the definition is simply this: "similarity that is not explicitly expressed (*avyaṅgya*), while bestowing delight upon the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*). It is not necessary to include the phrase "between two things capable of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)," because in cases such as "I compose the moon of poetry" (*grathnāmi kāvyaśaśinam*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) since there is an absence of beauty (*cārutva*) itself. For this very reason, it was stated simply as "the splendor of the similarity between both"; even that was for the purpose of eliminating over-extension in the case of *ananvaya* (self-simile).

Even so, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definitions to the figures of "reciprocal simile" (*upameyopamā*) and "inversion" (*pratīpa*), because it is accepted that these two are included within the figure of "simile" (*upamā*) due to the presence of the description of the aforementioned similarity. Furthermore, they are stated separately from "simile" precisely because they possess an additional result: the exclusion of a third similar object and the excellence of the well-known subject of comparison (*upameya*) achieved by way of contrast with the well-known standard of comparison (*upamāna*). This is because in "reciprocal simile," the form consists of two similes—one concerning the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) and one concerning that which is not at hand (*aprakṛta*)—whereas in "inversion," it pertains solely to that which is not at hand.

Because it is so perceived; otherwise, even the recollection of an irrelevant object resulting from the recollection of the relevant object would result in its being classified as a separate figure of speech. For this very reason, it was explicitly stated in the *Citrāmīmāṃsā*, during the occasion of refining the definition of *upamā*, that "both *pratīpa* and *upameyopamā* must indeed be included, and thus the failure to encompass them is not a defect of the definition."

However, some maintain that what is intended by the definition of *upamā* (simile) is "a beautiful similarity that has become the object of a poet’s creative effort (*kavisaṃrambha*) directed solely toward the cognition of that similarity. According to this view, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the cases of *ananvaya* (self-simile), *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), or *pratīpa* (counter-simile). This is because in those instances, the similarity serves to highlight the incomparability [of the subject], to exclude a third similar entity, or to enhance the excellence of the subject; thus, it does not fall within the scope of the poet’s effort aimed merely at the cognition of similarity. This is in accordance with the author of the *Kuvalayānanda*. However, according to the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, the definition is as follows:
That similarity which embellishes the meaning of a sentence and is beautiful is *upamā* (simile). || 2 ||

Similarity (*sādṛśya*) that is beautiful and serves as an embellishment for the meaning of the sentence is the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). Beauty (*cārutva*) consists in the capacity to produce aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), and this wonder is a particular kind of bliss witnessed by the hearts of sensitive connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*). In cases of non-repetition (*ananvaya*) such as "the ocean is like the ocean," the similarity is employed merely to exclude a second counterpart; because it does not establish itself independently, it lacks aesthetic wonder. For this very reason, they designate it as *ananvaya* (non-repetition) due to the absence of a correlative connection (*anvaya*).

In such instances of *vyatireka* (poetic contrast) as "How can the moon bear comparison with the beauty of Your face, O Lord?", the description of the similarity (*sādṛśya*)—which serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the striking negation—is itself devoid of aesthetic charm (*acamatkāra*).

Likewise, even among figures where non-difference (*abheda*) is predominant, such as *rūpaka*, *apahnuti*, *pariṇāma*, *bhrāntimad*, and *ullekha*, and among those where difference (*bheda*) is predominant, such as *dṛṣṭānta*, *prativastūpamā*, *dīpaka*, and *tulyayogitā*, although similarity exists as the constituent factor that brings about each of these effects, they do not possess the status of the figure of speech *upamā* because of their lack of aesthetic charm.

In the case of *pratīpa* (the "counter-simile"), such as "The moon is like the face," and in the case of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), such as "The face is like the moon; the moon is like the face," one need not fear the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the similarity in these instances possesses aesthetic charm (*camatkāritva*) and is therefore intended to be included [within the definition].

If it is argued that in such instances as “O wrath appears upon you like fire upon the moon,” because the object of comparison is so utterly impossible, one cannot even apprehend a mere similarity—let alone the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) which would be even more remote—the answer is this: for a poet who has brought the individual word-meanings to mind, there is no obstacle to imagining fire as residing in the moon according to his own desire through a form of possibility, and then conceiving a similarity with that [imagined fire]. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Nor should it be argued that a similarity based on an imagined non-existent thing cannot produce aesthetic wonder; for we observe that the embrace of a woman standing before one through the power of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*)—even though she is a most delicate and beautiful golden image—is full of delight. Since the definition of simile does not require the actual existence of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, there is not even a scent of fault here. Therefore:
"The curling lock of hair falling upon the expanse of her breast shines like a serpent hanging from Mount Meru down from the orb of the moon."
Thus, there is no inconsistency even in such cases as these.

Others, however, maintain that this "imagined simile" (kalpitopamā) constitutes a distinct figure of speech because it results in the absence of any other standard of comparison. This is not correct; for since similarity possesses aesthetic charm, its inclusion within the scope of *upamā* is more appropriate. Furthermore, the condition of being "defined by another" is not included in the definition [of *upamā*]. Indeed, the fact that it results in the absence of another standard of comparison serves as a proof for its being a specific variety of *upamā*, rather than a reason for its exclusion from *upamā* altogether.

Those who know the essence of poetic figures have declared that simile (upamā) is of two kinds: complete (pūrṇā) and elliptical (luptā). When these four elements—the object of comparison (upamāna), the subject of comparison (upameya), the common attribute (dharma), and the word of comparison (vācaka)—are all present, it is considered a complete simile.
Just as that ancient, radiant jewel shines within the celestial palace named Ānandanilaya, so does that dark-hued, eternal effulgence triumph, like a sapphire set within a golden casket. 26.

Here, because of the employment of these four—the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the object compared (*upameya*), the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing the comparison (*upamāvācaka*)—namely "the dark gem" (*śyāmalaṃ ratnam*), "an ancient treasure" (*ciratnam*), "shining radiance" (*vibhāsamānaṃ dhāma*), and the word "as if" (*ivaśabdaḥ*)—this is a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*). This is an illustration according to the *Kuvalayānanda*.
According to the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however:

"O jewel of the mountain by the shore, when will you indeed release these wretched ones, who are ensnared in the net of delusion, just as one might release fish caught in a vast net out of compassion? (27)

Here, the suggested simile (pratīyamānopamā) is an ornament (alaṅkāra) by virtue of its function as an embellishment for the entire meaning of the sentence, acting as an enhancement for the sentiment of tranquility (śāntarasa) through the mediation of the suggested thought.

When there is the non-employment of one, two, or all three of the following—the object of comparison, the standard of comparison, the common attribute, and the word expressing comparison—there arises the eightfold elliptical simile (luptopamā). || 4 ||

The object of description is the *upameya*. When one, two, or all three of the elements beginning with the *upameya* are not mentioned, it is an *elliptical simile* (*luptopamā*). That [elliptical simile] is of eight kinds.

In this context, when there is the elision of the property (*dharma*), or likewise the elision of both the property and the expressive word (*vācaka*), or the elision of both the object of description (*varṇya*) and the expressive word, these are indeed the various types of elided similes (*luptopamā*). (5)
When the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is omitted, it is known as the fifth type,
"omitted [comparison]," while when the denoter (*vācaka*) and the standard of comparison are both omitted, it is called the sixth type by the learned.

Another [type] is the *dharmopamā* (quality simile) when both the quality and the object of comparison are elided; the eighth is when the quality, the object of comparison, and the word expressing them are all elided. (7)

He analyzes that very [simile] here: when any of the [eight] components—the denoter (*vācaka*) and so forth—are omitted, they are called "elliptical" (*luptā*) according to what has been dropped. Thus, there is the elliptical omission of the denoter (*vācakaluptā*), the elliptical omission of the attribute (*dharmaluptā*), the elliptical omission of both the attribute and the denoter (*dharmavācakaluptā*), and the elliptical omission of the object of comparison (*upameyavācakaluptā*). These are the four varieties excluding the omission of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Then there are the four varieties including the omission of the standard of comparison: the elliptical omission of the standard of comparison (*upamānaluptā*), the elliptical omission of both the denoter and the standard of comparison (*vācakopamānaluptā*), the elliptical omission of both the attribute and the standard of comparison (*dharmopamānaluptā*), and the elliptical omission of both the attribute, the standard of comparison, and the denoter (*dharmopamānavācakaluptā*). Thus, there are eight types of elliptical simile (*luptopamā*).
Among these, an example of the elision of the expressive word (*vācakaluptā*) is as follows:

"May that Abode, whose forehead is radiant with moonlight, who is as dark as a beautiful autumn cloud, and whose dwelling is the cave of the king of mountains—the Mandara-bearing mountain—dwell indeed within my heart. (28)

In this instance, there is an elision of the expressive word (*vācakalopa*) in both cases: "the forehead is as radiant as the moon" and "it is as dark-blue as a beautiful monsoon cloud. This is based on the rule governing compound formation—"upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ"—which prescribes a compound in the sense of "radiant like the moon" and "dark-blue like a monsoon cloud."

May that multitude of splendors—which possesses a face like the autumn moon, which has made its abode on the king of mountains (Giriśa) who wears the shimmering moon, and whose teeth resemble jasmine blossoms—dispel the ruin of fear. 29.

“Bhayakadanaṃ” means the crushing of the fear of worldly existence; “kadanaṃ” [is used] in the sense of crushing or evil, according to the *Viśva* lexicon. Here, in both instances—“one whose face resembles the autumnal moon” (*śaradindusadṛśavadanaṃ*) and “one whose teeth resemble kunda flowers” (*kundasumopamaradanaṃ*)—there is an omission of the common property (*dharmalopa*). This is optional (*aicchika*), not prescribed by the scriptures, because it can equally be said that [the face is like the moon] due to its delightfulness and so forth. Or, for example:
“O Lord of the Mountain, we have no confidence at all in beauty which is like a flower, in youth which is like the rush of a river’s current, or in life which is like a fire in grass. (30)
In this context, the common properties—namely, rapid withering, instability in one place, and immediate extinction—are not explicitly mentioned.
An example of the elision of the indicator of the property (*dharmavācaka-luptā*) is as follows:
"May the curved glance of the Lord of the Serpent-Mountain (Śeṣa), which flows like a beautiful breeze moving through the caves of Mount Candana, dispel my fever. (31)

In the phrase *gandhavāhaśābanti*, there is an elision of the expressive property (*dharmaluptā*). This is because the suffix *kvip*—which is prescribed in the sense of "acting like the breeze from the sandalwood tree" (*gandhavāhaśāba ivācaranti*) and which signifies an action consisting of providing joy—is elided along with the word *iva*. Here, the elision of the property is optional (*aicchika*), since it is also possible to employ that [suffix] by stating "they act like the breeze from the sandalwood tree by way of providing joy. [The form] *bhintām* means "let her pierce"; it is the imperative (*loṭ*) in the middle voice (*taṅ*) of the root *bhid* belonging to the *raudhādika* class, due to its being marked with a circumflex accent (*svaritet*). || 31 ||
An example of the elision of the word expressing the object of comparison (*upameyavācakaluptā*) is as follows:

"Who indeed would not delight in the supreme abode of the Lord of the Serpents (Śrī Śeṣaśailam), which is beyond even the minds of sages, which is sufficient in the essence of the Upaniṣads within its own sacred grove, and which possesses the splendors of the highest state? (32)
When Śrīnivāsa, who is determined to be the very essence of the Upaniṣads,
sports according to his own will, the illusory one (Māyāvī), abandoning supreme bliss, rejoices with Ramā on the banks of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī at the highest Vaikuṇṭha.

The meaning is: "while [the Self] is sporting within itself" in the manner described above. In the phrase *paramapadīyati*, there is an elision of both the denoter (*vācaka*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*); this is because the object of comparison, namely *ātmānam* (the Self), is not mentioned together with the word expressing the comparison.

Nor should it be argued: "Since the suffix *kyac* is prescribed after a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the sense of 'behaving like' (Pāṇini 3.1.10), even though the meaning 'he behaves like the supreme state' is understood, how can it be determined that the object is 'himself' (*ātmānam*), as it is possible for another [object] to be so as well? This is because that determination is reached through the force of the qualification that behaving in conformity with the supreme state consists in the employment of one's own powers (*vibhava*); for in such behavior, since the powers are spontaneous, they are understood to belong to oneself. Furthermore, this elision [of the object] is optional, since it is also possible to employ the thing being compared (*upameya*) by saying, "He makes himself into the supreme state" (*svātmānaṃ paramapadīyati*). || 32 ||

The *upamānaluptā* (omission of the object of comparison) and the *vācakopamānaluptā* (omission of both the word and the object of comparison) are as follows: "I praise Hari, the subduer of enemies, whose gait is like that of an elephant, whose fortitude is as heavy as the divine mountain [Meru], who pacifies all fear, whose abode is on the mountain of the double-tongued [serpent Śeṣa], and who is beloved by Indirā. (33)

In the first quarter, in the phrase *dviradasamālasagamanam*, there is an elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānaluptā*), because the standard of comparison, namely "the gait of an elephant" (*dviradagamana*), is not mentioned. In the second quarter, in the phrase *suragirigurudhairyam*, there is an elision of both the expressive particle and the standard of comparison (*vācakopamānaluptā*), because the expressive particle such as *iva* and the standard of comparison, namely "the firmness of the divine mountain" (*suragiridhairya*), are both not mentioned.
Examples where both the object of comparison and the word expressing the comparison are omitted (dharmopamānaluptā and dharmopamānavācakaluptā) are as follows:

"I perceive in his heart a depth like that of the ocean, a magnanimity as vast as the arrival of the Kalpa-ending fire, an irresistible majesty in which Śeṣa finds refuge, and a beauty that captivates the heart of the Daughter of the Ocean. (34)

The word *saundaryam* (beauty) here is a separate term; the meaning is that the Blessed One, Śrīnivāsa, is determined as being [identical] with beauty in its true nature (*tattvena*). In this verse, regarding the phrase "possessing a depth like the ocean," because the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*)—limitlessness—and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), namely the ocean's depth, are not explicitly mentioned, it is a case of "omission of the attribute and the standard of comparison" (*dharmopamānaluptā*).

In the analysis of the compound *kalpakāgamasyaudāryamivaudāryaṃ yasya* ("that which has a magnanimity like the magnanimity of the Kalpa-scripture"), because the property (*dharma*) of fulfilling all desired objects without exception, the object of comparison (*upamāna*)—namely the magnanimity of the Kalpa-scripture—and the expressive word (*vācaka*) such as *iva*, are not employed, it is a case of elision of the property, the object of comparison, and the expressive word (*dharmopamānavācakaluptā*). Other types will be discussed further on.
Thus has simile been explained according to the method of the *Kuvalayānanda*; now, its classification according to the opinion of the ancients is set forth in detail.
Furthermore, that [offering] is of two kinds for those two, distinguished as "full" (pūrṇā) and "omitted" (luptā).

The complete (*pūrṇā*) simile is of two kinds—verbal (*śrautī*) and objective (*ārthī*). Each of these two may further be threefold: residing in a sentence (*vākyagā*), residing in a compound (*samāsagā*), or residing in a secondary derivative (*taddhitagā*). Thus, according to the view of the ancient rhetoricians, the complete simile becomes sixfold. This means that between the two types—the complete and the elliptical (*luptā*)—the complete is divided into the verbal and the objective; both of these two (the verbal and objective) are each further divided into three: residing in a sentence, residing in a compound, and residing in a secondary derivative. Thus, the complete simile is of six varieties.
The experts in the scriptures say that when words such as *yathā* and *iva*, which directly express similarity, are employed, it is a *śrautī* (verbal) simile.

Those words such as *sadṛś* (similar) and *nibha* (resembling), which establish similarity by means of an intervening substratum (*dharmin*), have their [simile] application based on the meaning (*ārthī*) according to usage. || 10 ||

He characterizes the *śrautī* (verbal) and *ārthī* (implied) [simile] with the words beginning "yathā" (as), and so forth. When words such as *yathā*, *iva*, and others—which directly express similarity—are employed, it is *śrautī*, because the similarity is conveyed through direct expression (*śruti*). By the word "and others" (*ādi*), the suffix *vat* prescribed by the rule "tatra tasyeva" is included, since that suffix is prescribed in the sense of *iva*. When words such as *tulya*, *sadṛśa*, *sadṛk*, *nibha*, *saṅkāśa*, and others—which extend to the substratum (*dharmī*) qualified by similarity—are employed, it is *ārthī*, because the similarity is established through the sense (*artha*).

In the phrase "nibhādi" and so forth, the word "ādi" (and so on) includes the suffix *vat* prescribed by the rule *tena tulyam*. This is because that suffix is prescribed in the sense of similarity (*tulyārtha*). Although words such as *yathā*, *iva*, and others—when employed after words like *candra* (moon)—are qualifiers of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) since they cause the cognition of the status of a standard of comparison for that object (such as the moon), and they serve as the cause for the cognition of the status of a standard of comparison for the object with which they are co-referential, they do not, however, serve as the cause for the cognition of the status of an object of comparison (*upameya*) for the face and so forth.

Nevertheless, just as in the case of "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), although the genitive case serves as the cause for the cognition that the king—who is the meaning of the nominal stem co-occurring with it—is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the relation that constitutes its own referent, yet when there is co-occurrence with the word "man," the cognition of him being the substratum (*anuyogin*) of that relation also arises through the power of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*); likewise, when there is co-occurrence with "face" and so on, the cognition of the face and so on being the substratum of that relation is also possible.

By this, the objection that in the expression "the face is like a lotus" there would arise the cognition "the face is the similarity to a lotus," rather than "the face is similar to a lotus," is refuted. Just as in the case of "the king's man," although the base word (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and the word "man" individually convey the notions of "king," "relation," and "man," yet by virtue of their co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), the cognition arises that "the man is related to the king"—for such is the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*)—so too here, the ancient teachers say, the cognition of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭapratīti*) is logically established.

In reality, however, the meaning of *iva* is similarity (*sādṛśya*) alone. And that [similarity] is not a qualifier of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as the moon; rather, it is the standard of comparison—the moon and so forth—that qualifies [the similarity] by means of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). Furthermore, the similarity qualified by the moon and so forth connects with the face and so forth by means of the relation of sub-correlativity (*anuyogitā*). It should be understood that in expressions such as "the face is like the moon," the cognition takes the form: "the face is the sub-correlate of a similarity whose counter-correlate is the moon."

Among these, the *śrautī* (explicit) simile is of three kinds, as follows: "The sky shines dark-blue like the heart of the Lord of Serpents and the Lord of Mountains; the necklace of pearls shines like a row of stars, and the splendor of the Kaustubha gem is like that of [the goddess] Ārdrā. (35)

In this context, from the words "just as the sky" (*yathā gaganaṃ*) up to "deep blue" (*vinīlam*), there is a complete *śrautī* simile in a sentence (*vākya-pūrṇā-śrautī*), because there is the employment of the particle "just as" (*yathā*) as the uninflected indicator (*vācaka*), "the sky" (*gagana*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), "the heart of the Lord of Serpents and the Lord of Mountains" (*phaṇīśvara-nagapati-hṛdayam*) as the object of comparison (*upameya*), and "deep blue" (*vinīla*) as the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*). In the compound "a necklace like a row of stars" (*tārāvalir iva hārāvaliḥ*), there is a complete *śrautī* simile in a compound (*samāsa-pūrṇā-śrautī*), because of the rule: "There is a compound with the word 'iva', and there is no elision of the case-ending," which prescribes both the compounding and the non-elision of the case-ending when joined with the word "iva."

And because of the employment of all four [types of words], such as the expressive word (*vācaka*), etc.: in the example “there is beauty like that of the *ārdrā* [constellation] in the *kaustubha* gem,” there is a full simile (*pūrṇopamā*) based on a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). This is because the expressive word *vati*—prescribed by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116) in the sense of *iva*—and the other three [types of words] are employed. The analysis (*vigraha*) is *ārdrāyām iva* (like in the *ārdrā*), resulting in *ārdrāvat*. However, in the reading “the beauty of the *kaustubha* is like that of the *ārdrā*,” the analysis is *ārdrāyā iva*, since the suffix *vati* is prescribed by that same rule even when following a word in the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhīsamartha*). || 35 ||

The *ārthī* [simile] is of three kinds. The *pūrṇā* (complete) *ārthī* is as follows: "Equal to the orb of the moon in its whiteness, resembling a cluster of jasmine blossoms, this conch of Hari shines within the palm of his hand like a white lotus. (36) In the phrase "equal to the orb of the moon in its whiteness," the *ārthī* simile is complete (*pūrṇā*) within the sentence; here, the term "in its whiteness" (*viśadatayā*) connects with every [comparison]. In the phrase "resembling a cluster of jasmine blossoms," the *ārthī* simile is complete within the compound (*samāsa*).

In the example "like a white lotus" (*dhavalasaroruhavat*), the *pūrṇopamā* occurs in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), because of the employment of the suffix *vati*, which is prescribed in the sense of similarity by the rule "when there is an action equal to that [standard], the suffix *vati* is used. Thus, the sixfold *pūrṇopamā* has been briefly illustrated.
Now, he classifies the *luptā* (elliptical) [simile] in general:

it may be of three kinds—*ekaluptā* (omission of one), *dviluptā* (omission of two)—which is fourfold, and *ekarūpā triluptā* (omission of three with identical form); thus, in general, the *luptā* is eightfold. (11)

When there is the omission of the object of comparison (*dharma*), the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), or the expressive word (*vācaka*), it is "omitted in one" (*ekaluptā*) in three ways; however, it is "omitted in two" (*dviluptā*) in four ways. (12)

Likewise, [the simile is complete] when there is the elision of both the property and the indicator; similarly when there is the elision of both the property and the object of comparison; and likewise when there is the elision of both the subject of description and its indicator, as well as when there is the elision of both the indicator and the subject of description. (13)
But the *triluptā* (the elided type) is of one kind, due to the omission of both the expressed property (*dharma*) and the suffix (*vācaka*).

The *ekaluptā* (single-elided) simile is of three kinds: elision of the quality (*dharmaluptā*), elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānaluptā*), and elision of the word denoting comparison (*vācakaluptā*). The *dviluptā* (double-elided) is of four kinds: elision of the quality and the word (*dharmavācakaluptā*), elision of the quality and the standard of comparison (*dharmopamānaluptā*), elision of the object of comparison and the word (*upameyavācakaluptā*), and elision of the word and the standard of comparison (*vācakopamānaluptā*). The *triluptā* (triple-elided) is of one kind: elision of the quality, the word, and the standard of comparison (*dharmavācakopamānaluptā*). Thus, in general, the elided simile is of eight varieties.

O Lord with eyes like blue lotuses, you are like a treasure-trove; there is no one equal to you. Your virtuous conduct is peerless, and though possessing the profound depth of the ocean, you make friends with those who bow before you. (37) In the phrase "you are like a treasure-trove" (*nidhiriva*), because qualities such as being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) are not mentioned, it is a case of *dharmaluptopamā* (simile with elision of the common attributes). (1) In the phrase "there is no one equal to you," because the negation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is made in a general sense, it is a case of *upamānaluptopamā* (simile with elision of the standard of comparison). (2) In the phrase "blue like a cloud" (*jaladanīla*), because the expressive word "like" (*iva*) is not employed, it is a case of *vācakaluptopamā* (simile with elision of the expresser). (3)

In the example *jalajākṣī* ("lotus-eyed"), because the property [of being like a lotus], such as clarity, and its expressive word are not mentioned—[the compound meaning] "one whose eyes are like lotuses"—it is a case of elision of both the property and its expressive word (*dharmavācakaluptā*). (4) In the example *tava sauśīlyamatulyam* ("your good character is incomparable"), because the property [of being extraordinary], such as world-transcendence, and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) are not mentioned through the negation "incomparable" (*atulyam*), it is a case of elision of the property and the standard of comparison (*dharmopamānaluptā*). (5) In the example *mitrīyasi natajane* ("you act as a friend toward those who bow before you"), because the object of comparison (*upameya*), namely the self (*ātman*), and its expressive word are not mentioned—[the sense being] "you behave like a friend"—it is a case of elision of the object of comparison and its expressive word (*upameyavācakaluptā*). (6)

The *vācakaluptā* (omission of the word expressing comparison) and the *upamānaluptā* (omission of the object of comparison) will be illustrated further on. In the example "ocean-deepness" (*abdhigāmbhīrya*), since there is no mention of the ocean's depth, nor of the word expressing the comparison, nor of the common attribute (*dharma*)—in the sense that "his depth is like the depth of the ocean"—this is an instance of the *dharmavācakopamānaluptā*. Thus, the seven types of elliptical similes (*luptopamā*) have been summarized in general.
Now, the classification [of the types] beginning with *dharmalupta* is demonstrated in sequence. (14)
Even when the property is omitted, it may be twofold: based on the literal word (*śrautī*) or based on the sense (*ārthī*), just as in the case of *pūrṇā*.

In that regard, the metaphorical expression based on direct denotation (śrautī) cannot occur when a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is used, because the connection [of the primary meaning] would be lost.

The *śrauti* (expressed by the suffix) *dharmaluptā* (omission of the quality), like the *pūrṇā* (complete), is of two kinds: *ārthī* (implied) and *śrautī*. It occurs in a sentence (*vākya*), a compound (*samāsa*), and a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Among these, the *śrauti dharmaluptā* cannot occur in a *taddhita* [derivative], because there is no facility of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) without the mention of the quality (*dharma*) for the suffix *vat*, which is prescribed after bases ending in the genitive or locative case. Indeed, in expressions such as "the wall in Pāṭaliputra is like that of Mathurā" (*madhurāvat pāṭaliputre prākāraḥ*) or "the wall of Pāṭaliputra is like that of Mathurā" (*madhurāvat pāṭaliputrasya prākāraḥ*), there is no facility of syntactic connection without the mention of the quality.

Even in the case of the use of suffixes such as *kalpa* and *deśya*, which are prescribed under the heading of *taddhita* (secondary nominal derivation)—as in examples like *kṛṣṇakalpaḥ* ("almost Kṛṣṇa") and *kṛṣṇadeśyaḥ* ("bordering on Kṛṣṇa")—there is the perception of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substantive (*dharmin*). Therefore, since the verbal form of ellipsis (*śrautī*) is impossible here, that [elliptical simile] is indeed of five kinds alone.

If it is argued that, under the governing rule *ive pratikṛtau* (Pāṇini 5.3.96), since words ending in suffixes such as *cha* prescribed in the sense of *iva*—such as in the expressions *kuśāgrīyā buddhiḥ* ("an intellect sharp as the tip of a blade of kuśa grass") and *śaileyaṃ dadhi* ("curd like a mountain-plant")—possess a state of semantic completeness (*nairākāṅkṣya*) even without the explicit mention of the common property (*dharmopādāna*), a *śrautī dharmaluptā* (verbal simile with the property omitted) is indeed possible; we say no. This is because one must necessarily accept that the suffixes prescribed under the governing rule *ive pratikṛtau* are ordained specifically in the sense of "equality" (*tulyārtha*).

Otherwise, since those [words] would not terminate in the substratum qualified by similarity (*sādṛśyaviśiṣṭadharmiparyantatva*), it would be impossible for them to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object of comparison (*upameya*), such as in the expression "an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass" (*kuśāgrīyā buddhiḥ*). Therefore, they maintain that even the prescription of similarity ultimately results in [the application of] the word *sadṛśa* (similar), and thus the inclusion of the term *iva* in the Sūtra is not contradictory.
An example of *śrautī dharmaluptā* (omission of the common property through words) in a sentence is as follows:
"O celestial beings, as the cloud is, so are you here; as the peacock is, so are you. O men, as the ocean is, so are you; as the mountain torrents are, so are you. (38)

In this context, the address "O Blessed One" is understood by implication. In examples such as "just as a rain-cloud [is to] the peacock," because the word *yathā* is used without being compounded, there is a *śrautī* (verbal) *dharmaluptā* (omission of the common attribute) in the sentence, due respectively to the manifestation of the quality of bringing joy and so forth, and the quality of exultation and so forth. Similarly, in cases such as "just as the ocean [is to... and "like men [are to...]," there is an omission of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), because qualities such as being attainable and so forth, or being devoted to that [object] and so forth, are not explicitly mentioned.

An example of *dharmaluptā* (omission of the common property) based on a *śruti* (direct expression) within a compound is as follows: "O Hari, all men have so far taken refuge in you—who sport upon the mountain that bears the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and who are the ruler of the world—just as they would in the wish-fulfilling gem itself. (39) In this instance, because the common properties such as "the bestower of desired objects" are not mentioned, it is a *dharmaluptā* based on a *śruti* within the compound "like the wish-fulfilling gem" (*cintāmaṇimiva*). We have already stated that this [type of simile] is not possible when [the comparison] occurs through a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). Furthermore, "Cintāmaṇidharaṇībhṛt" is simply another name for the Veṅkaṭa mountain; thus it is said in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:

"But those who contemplate this truth shall succeed; they know this to be the mountain Cintāmaṇi. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Veṅkaṭādrimāhātmya* contained within the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*, beginning with the words, "The sacred field named Śrī Veṅkaṭagiri is [famous] upon the earth," it continues:
"Añjanādri, Vṛṣādri, Vedādri, and Garuḍācala..."
Tīrthādri, Śrīnivāsādri, Cintāmaṇigiri,
Vṛṣabhādri, Varāhādri, Jñānādri, Kanakācala,
Ānandādri, Nīlādri, Krīḍādri, and Puṣkarācala.
And Siṃhācala, Śrīśaila, as well as Nārāyaṇācala.
"Vaikuṇṭhādri, Śeṣaśaila"—these are the twenty names. Thus [it is said].
The *ārthī* (implied) [metaphor] with the elision of the common property (*dharmaluptā*) occurs in sentences, compounds, and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), as follows:

"The enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) is like the earth supporting the peak of the bull-horned mountain (Mount Kailāsa), and the lotus-pool is like a mirror resembling the tilaka-mark made of musk on the jewel among women. (40)

In this instance, there is the *arthī dharmaluptā* (elliptical simile based on meaning) occurring in a sentence in the phrase "of the jewel among women" (*ramaṇīmaṇeḥ*), occurring in a compound in the phrase "resembling a tilaka of musk" (*mṛgamadatilakanikāśaḥ*), and occurring in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the phrase "like a mirror" (*darpaṇīkalpā*); for the attributes such as loveliness, blackness, and purity have not been explicitly mentioned.

The authors of the *Citramīmāṃsā* maintain that even when there is reduplication—as in "paṭu-paṭu" and so forth—the *dharmaluptopamā* (simile with the attribute omitted) is observed. An example of this is as follows: "It shines, sweet beyond sweetness; the fruit of heaven and such is never truly sweet. O people, worship for a long time that which bears the burden of the earth, the bearer of serpents—[the Lord] who is eternally sweet. (41)

Here, because the rule "of a quality-word [used] in the sense of manner" prescribes reduplication in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), this word *madhura*—denoting that which is by its very nature not sweet but appears sweet at first sight—functions in the sense of something similar to sweet; thus, this is an implied (*ārthī*) *dharmaluptā* (elliptical simile). Furthermore, this does not occur in a sentence or a compound, because *madhuramadhuram* constitutes a single word.

The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, maintains that since even the denotative word (*vācaka*) is not employed in examples such as *paṭupaṭuḥ* and so forth, it is appropriate to point out this excess within the *vācakadharmaluptā* (the elision of the denotative word and its attribute), and not within the *dharmaluptā* (the elision of the attribute). This is because by the term *dharmaluptā*, they intend only the elision of the attribute alone. Otherwise, if the two-fold elisions and the three-fold elision were included under the category of "single elision" (*ekaluptā*), their separate mention would be entirely incoherent.

And it cannot be argued that there is no elision here because only the reduplication (*dvirbhāva*) exists [as the expressive element] and not the property (*dharma*) alone; for the *Bhāṣya*, *Kaiyaṭa*, and others accept that reduplication merely indicates similarity (*sādṛśya*), and thus its status as a direct denoter (*vācakatā*) is impossible—so he stated.
The elliptical simile (luptopamā) is of two kinds: that occurring in a sentence (vākyagā) and that occurring in a compound (samāsagā).
An example of a sentence-occurring simile with the object of comparison omitted (luptopamānā) is as follows:
"Even if the entire world were searched, surely no place equal to the illustrious Veṅkaṭādri could be found—whether it has already been born or is currently being born. (42)

Here, because of the negation of similarity, there is an elision of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) within the sentence. In this regard, one should recall the statement: “There is no place whatsoever in the universe equal to the Veṅkaṭādri mountain. Nor should it be argued that this is not merely an elision of the *upamāna* but rather a distinct figure of speech altogether, on the grounds that the absence of the standard of comparison results here in the absence of similarity, and since the presence of similarity is the very lifeblood of the simile (*upamā*). [The reason for this is: Even though the absence of the standard of comparison results in the absence of similarity, the intended meaning does not terminate in that mere absence; rather, it culminates in the affirmation of a superior excellence. Therefore, because the intended sense is the establishment of a specific quality, it is indeed a case of the elision of the *upamāna*. This is illustrated by the following example: “O King, your fame is not white like the moon, nor red like the lotus, nor black like collyrium; rather, it is white, red, and black [simultaneously]! In this instance, the negation of the similarity with the moon and so forth serves as a means to establish the fact that the king’s fame possesses all those qualities simultaneously. Thus, it is established that this is an instance of the elision of the *upamāna*. Furthermore, this is not a case of the figure *Vyatireka* (Distinction), because the intended meaning is not the superiority of the object of description (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), but rather the simultaneous possession of multiple attributes. Moreover, since the negation of similarity is expressed through words, it cannot be classified as *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description). Consequently, it remains a distinct figure of speech known as the elision of the *upamāna*. It is said: “Where the similarity is negated by words, it is called *Upamānaluptā* (Elision of the Standard of Comparison); where it is negated by implication, it is *Arthopamānaluptā* (Elision of the Standard of Comparison by Implication). An example of the latter is: “The sky is not blue like the ocean,” which implies that the sky is blue in its own right. Here, the negation of similarity with the ocean is understood through the force of the sentence. However, this is not a case of *Vyatireka*, because the intended meaning is not the excellence of the subject over the standard, but rather the independent blueness of the sky. Nor is it *Aprastutapraśaṃsā*, because the description of the subject is not subordinate to the praise of something else. Therefore, it is a distinct figure of speech. It is said: “Where the similarity is negated by implication, it is *Arthopamānaluptā*; however, this is not *Vyatireka*, because the excellence of the subject is not intended. This concludes the discussion on the elision of the *upamāna*. Now follows the section on the elision of the common property (*dharmaluptā*). Therein, when the common property is elided, there are two types: elision of the common property through words and elision of the common property through implication. An example of the former is: “The face is not like the moon. Here, the common property of beauty is elided by the word “not. An example of the latter is: “The face is not the moon. Here, the common property is elided by the force of the sentence. This is not *Vyatireka*, because the excellence of the subject is not intended. Nor is it *Aprastutapraśaṃsā*, because the description of the subject is not subordinate to anything else. Therefore, it is a distinct figure of speech. It is said: “When the common property is negated by words, it is *Śabdadharmluptā*; when it is negated by implication, it is *Arthadharmluptā*. An example of the latter is: “The sky is not blue like the ocean,” which implies the sky’s inherent blueness. Here, the negation of similarity with the ocean is understood through the power of the sentence. However, this is not *Vyatireka*, because the intended meaning is not the superiority of the subject over the standard, but rather the independent blueness of the sky. Nor is it *Aprastutapraśaṃsā*,

Since it is stated that "one who is born or being born shall not find a place equal to Veṅkaṭādri," there is a culmination in similarity—namely, that no one yet to be born will find any place comparable to this; therefore, it is appropriate to say that this is simply an *upamā* (simile) with the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) omitted, and not a separate figure of speech.
An example of the compound-occurring *upamānaluptā* (where the standard of comparison is omitted) is as follows:

"We know that there is no object here in this world as fortunate as musk; for the face of the Lord of the Mountain-dweller [Śiva], the ornament of the three worlds, is indeed marked by this [musk]. (43)
Here, because of the negation of similarity, there is an elision of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) within a compound.
The elision of the agent (*vādiluptā*) occurs in a compound, in the *karmadhāraya* and *ādhāra-kyac* formations, in the *ky-aṅ* formation,
in the *ṇamul* formation where the agent is the object, in the *ṇini* suffix, in the *kvip* suffix, and in *taddhita* suffixes.
Thus, this [mantra] which elides the designator should be known as having nine varieties. (17)

He analyzes *vācakaluptā* (the elision of the word expressing comparison). It is [elided] when the word expressing comparison (*upamānavācaka*)—such as *yathā*, *iva*, and so on—is omitted in the following cases: in a compound; in *karmakyac* prescribed by the rule *upamānād ācāre*; in *adhikaraṇakyac* prescribed by the rule *adhikaraṇācca*; in *kartṛkyaṅ* prescribed by the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*; in *karmaṇamul* prescribed by the rule *upamāne karmaṇi ca* (and also in *kartṛṇamul* due to the word *ca*); in *ṇini* prescribed by the rule *kartary upamāne*; and in *kvip* prescribed for the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*) by the rule *sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kvib vā vaktavyaḥ*.

And when occurring in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it becomes ninefold. Here, an example of *vācakaluptā* (where the denotative word is elided) occurring within a compound (*samāsagā*) is as follows:

"May I repeatedly contemplate in my heart some indescribable love (*śṛṅgāra*), which rests upon the mountain of Mahi, dark-blue like a fragment of the finest sapphire from the shattered chest of the enemy of Bala, and ever-smiling. (44)
In this instance, in the compound *śakalavinīlam*, there is an elision of the expressive word (*vācakalopa*). Furthermore, *candiraruciraniṭālam*, though cited previously, is also an example of this.
An example of *vācakaluptā* (the elision of the expressive word) with the suffix *kyac* is as follows:
"Resting upon his lap, Kamalā makes that lofty one recline; she makes his arm—tender as the coils of a serpent—serve as a pillow. (45)

In the expressions *paryaṅkīyati* and *upadhānīyati*, the sense is "he acts like a couch" (*paryaṅkam ivācarati*) and "he acts like a pillow" (*upadhānam ivācarati*). Here, by the rule for the suffix *kyac* after an object, the common attribute is that both the couch and the pillow are "high" and "tender as the coils of a serpent. In *paryaṅkīyati* and so forth, the suffix *kyac* is applied according to the rule *upamānād ācāre* ("after a word denoting a standard of comparison, [the suffix *kyac* is added] in the sense of behaving [like that]") to the object in its inflected form (*subanta*), and the vowel *a* is changed to *ī* by the rule *kyaci ca*.

In the sentence "He behaves as if toward a couch marked with a lion," two objects are introduced; however, because the object of comparison is included within that [action], the verbal root is considered intransitive (*akarmaka*) in relation to it. As it has been said:

"An action is intransitive due to the occurrence of the root in a different sense, due to the inclusion [of the object] within the meaning of the root, due to common usage, or due to the lack of intention to express the object."

Thus [it is said]. However, with respect to other actions, it is indeed transitive (*sakarmaka*). As the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* stated: "For here there are two actions: the action of the standard of comparison (*upamāna-karman*) and the action of the object of comparison (*upameya-karman*). Since the action of the object of comparison is included within the action of the standard of comparison, it becomes transitive by virtue of that action of the object of comparison. This should be understood in other instances as well.
For example:

"Those glances of yours act like Indra; those people whom they touch are intensely enriched with splendors. Those quarters of the sky act like the moon through the radiance of your fame, owing to their vast and clear expanse. (46)

This *karma-kyac* is also an example of the elision of the expressive suffix (*vācakaluptā*). In both cases—*indrīyanti* and *candrīyanti*—the sense is "they act like Indra" and "they act like the moon," respectively; thus, there is a *karma-kyac*. In the phrase "by the splendors of Indra and of the *viśas*," the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) is [splendor]; in the phrase "of the moon and of the directions," the common attribute is "vast clarity. The word *viśaḥ* means "human beings. As Amarasimha states: "The two *viśau* are the Vaiśya and the human being."

In the second quarter, regarding the phrase *bhṛśaṃ vibhavaiḥ*, if one composes it as *bhṛśam udārāḥ*; and in the fourth quarter, if one composes it as *yaśaḥprakāśāstu kāśanīkāśāḥ* or *śeṣaśailendoḥ*, then in both cases, because even the attribute (*dharma*) is not mentioned, this [type of ellipsis] will also be an "elliptical [metaphor] where the word expressing the attribute is omitted" (*dharmavācakaluptā*). This is what should be understood. Thus, it should be noted that in this instance, the mention or non-mention of the attribute is optional. This is the only distinction between this and the previous examples.
An example of the elision of the expressive suffix (*vācakaluptā*) when the suffix *kyac* denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is as follows:

"Kamalā (the Goddess Lakṣmī) dwells in the ocean as if in a birth-house; she dwells in the lotus as if in a pleasure-house; and she dwells upon the spotless, expansive chest of the Lord of Veṅkaṭa as if in a palace. (Verse 47) The word "manojñe" (in the lovely one) should be supplied here after "jaladhau" (in the ocean) as well. In this verse, through the suffix *kyac* denoting the locus in "jaladhau jananagṛhīyati" and so forth, the common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) are established: between the ocean and the birth-house, and between the lotus and the pleasure-house, the quality is "lovely" (*manojña*); and between the Lord’s chest and the palace, the quality is "spotless" (*amala*).

If the word *manojñe* were not connected with the word *jaladhau*, this would serve as an example of the elision of the word expressing the property (*dharmavācakaluptā*); the other case would be an example of the elision of the word expressing the substratum (*itaravācakaluptā*). Thus, it should be understood that here too, the inclusion or non-inclusion of the property is merely a matter of intention (*vaivakṣika*).
An example of the elision of the verbal suffix (*vācakaluptā*) when the agent (*kartṛ*) is also elided in the *kyaṅ* affix is as follows:
"O Blessed One, the life-story of Your Lordship dispels the fever of those men who are tormented by worldly existence;

for those who possess the knowledge of its flavor, it flows with boundless sweetness. In this verse, the agent is elided because the verb *madhūyate* (it becomes sweet) is used impersonally, and the *kyaṅ* affix is elided in the sense of "becoming like that" (*tad-bhāve kyaṅ*). Thus, both the agent and the suffix are absent from the expression.

The construction is as follows: for those people who possess the knowledge of this [flavor]—that is, those who know the flavor connected to this life-story of the Blessed One—the word "of" (sambandha) in the genitive case denotes a general relationship; thus, "the limitless (asīmam), that is, boundless (anavadhikam), conduct of the Blessed One is sweetened (madhūyate) by the tongues (rasanā) of those who possess the knowledge of that flavor. Here, in the sense of "it acts like the moon" (vidhur ivācarati) and "it acts like honey" (madhv ivācarati), the forms *vidhūyate* and *madhūyate* are derived using the suffix *kyaṅ*. Consequently, the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) shared between the conduct of the Blessed One and the moon or honey is the act of behaving [like them], and that property is explicitly mentioned.

According to the view that the suffixes *kyac* and *kyaṅ* denote merely the act (*ācāra*) itself, and that the similarity to their respective meanings is understood through the inherent power (*prakṛti*) of the base via indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is a case of "elision of the denoter" (*vācakaluptā*) because there is no word expressing the similarity. Even according to the view that the entire complex form such as *paryaṅkīyati* possesses the capacity to denote an agent who performs an action that causes similarity to a bed (*paryaṅka*) and so forth, it is still a case of "elision of the denoter," because there is no word expressing either the similarity alone or that which is qualified by the similarity.
O Lord of Vṛṣagiri, O Supreme Person, it is precisely because of beholding you, whose form surpasses that of Kāma, that beautiful women act like Rādhās, and men act like Brahmās.

The meaning is "precisely from that beholding. The distinction is that in the first instance [the word *rādhā*] is in the genitive case used for the object (*karma*), whereas in the second it is in the ablative case used for the agent (*kartṛ*). Here too, in the sense of "they act like Rādhā" or "they act like Brahmā," the forms *rādhāyante* and *vedhāyante* are derived by means of the suffix *ky-aṅ*. Thus, the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) is the conduct of Bhāmā and the men respectively. The vocative "O you of surpassingly beautiful form" (*kāmādhikarūpe*) is appropriate for the women's imitation of Rādhā, while "O Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*) is appropriate for the men's imitation of Brahmā.

In the example *vedhāyate*, the specific feature is the elision of the *s* of the suffix *kyaṅ* according to the rule *kartuḥ kyaṅ salopaśca*. However, these two examples are cited according to the view of the ancient grammarians (*prācām*), who maintain that the nature of conduct (*ācāra*) possesses common characteristics [with the agent].

However, conduct (*ācāra*) in the sense of the suffix *kyac* and so forth is not a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), because conduct in its mere form as "duty" lacks the capacity to function as the basis for a simile. This is because, in examples such as "The enemy army, beholding his graceful movements while sword in hand, behaves like a woman (*nārīyate*) on the battlefield," it is the conduct—which is determined as non-different from qualities such as cowardice revealed through other modes of expression—that brings about the simile.

Furthermore, if mere conduct (*ācāramātra*) were the producer of the simile for the meaning of *kyac* and other suffixes, then in such instances as “*triviṣṭapaṃ tatkhalu bhāratāyate*,” the figure of speech of simile (*upamālaṅkṛti*) would not be produced even though conduct is presented in a general sense; conversely, when a different verse-quarter is composed as “*suparvabhiśśobhitamantarāśritaiḥ*,” that same figure would not be produced. Therefore, although the meaning of *kyac* and so forth is common [to both], it does not bring about a simile by way of a form that delimits its capacity to produce a simile (*upamāprayojakatāvacchedakarūpeṇa*).

Because the word *dharmalopa* (omission of the common attribute) denotes precisely the emptiness (*śūnyatva*) of the expression of the common attribute, otherwise—lest there be the consequence of a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) in cases such as "This face-like object is like a blooming lotus"—those who do not accept mere conduct (*ācāra*) as a common attribute hold that this cannot be an example of the "omission of the denoter alone" (*vācakamātraluptā*), since in their view the attribute itself is also omitted; rather, it must be something else entirely.
