"Just as those who gaze without blinking at you, the Lord, shining on the Mahendra mountain with a splendor that captivates the three worlds—even though they possess eyelids, they do not act like gods. Here, the quality of "blinkingless gazing" is stated as a common attribute shared by both gods and men; thus, it should be understood that there is an elision of the mere expressive word [of the agent] in the case of the single agent (*kartṛky-aṅ*).
An example of the elision of the expressive suffixes *karmaṇi* (accusative) and *kartari* (agentive) in the *ṇamul* construction is as follows:

"O lotus-eyed one, dark blue as a dense rain-cloud, you place the worlds—which have no other refuge—within your womb, and thus, while protecting your own mother, you protect [the worlds]. In this verse, the suffix *ṇamul* is used after the root *dhā* (to place), which governs two objects (*dvikarmaka*). The first object, *garbham*, is expressed by the accusative case ending (*-am*), while the second object, *bhuvanāni*, is not expressed by its own case ending but is instead conveyed by the accusative-like function of the *ṇamul*-formed word *nidhāyam*. Thus, both the agentive and the objective expressives are elided.

Here, in the sense of "placing as if they were embryos," the term *garbhanidhāyam* is formed with the suffix *karmaṇi-mul*. The common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) is that both the embryos and the worlds share the state of being placed [within] and having no other refuge. Even if the second quarter were read as "at the time of the dissolution of the ages, the worlds [were placed] in the womb," the act of placing (*nidhānam*) remains the common attribute.

In the sense of "protecting like a mother," the form *jananīrakṣam* is derived from the root *rakṣ* with the suffix *ṇamul* [denoting the agent]. The act of protecting is a quality common to both the Lord and His mother. By the rule *upamāne karmaṇi ca*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied; and by the rule *kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ*, there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the verbal root that serves as the base for the *ṇamul*.

An example of *vācakaluptopamā* (simile with the word of comparison omitted) in the locative case is as follows: "The lover, who walks like an elephant sweet with rut, who speaks like a swan intoxicated with passion,
and whose arms are like the coils of the serpent Kāliya, bestowed his splendor upon a certain manifestation of the ocean."

The meaning is: regarding a certain manifestation of the ocean—namely, Lakṣmī—who is superimposed as such; [there dwells] the Lord, a lover, whose voice is like that of a rutting swan, according to the statement in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "He was a youth with the voice of a mad swan. He is described as having arms (*doṣaḥ*) which are *āpīnāḥ*, meaning excessively thick or stout. Here, in both the terms *dvipagāmī* (going like an elephant) and *haṃsālāpī* (speaking like a swan), the suffix *ṇin* prescribed by the rule *kartaryupamāne* (Pāṇini 3.2.79)—meaning "when the agent is the object of comparison"—is elided from the expressive word (*vācakaluptā*).

Going and speaking share the same grammatical property (*samānadharmatva*). However, some scholars do not favor the separate mention of the suffix *ṇini* in the classification of elided expressers (*vācakalupta*), on the grounds that in instances such as *kokilālāpinī*, the compound exists by virtue of the rule *upapadam atiṅ*; thus, it is already included within the enumeration of compounds itself. ||52||
In the case of the *kvip* suffix, there is elision of the expressive element (*vācakaluptā*), as in:

"O you whose soul is restless with the desire to sport upon the crest of the Blue Mountain, your blue garland of luster constantly acts like a bee, like a young emerald, like a mass of clouds, and like a thicket of *tamāla* trees. (53)
"Nīlācala" is indeed another name for Veṅkaṭādri, because the monkey-lord Nala dwells there eternally;
therefore, the great sages call it by the name Nīlācala.

Thus it is stated in the *Vārāhīya-veṅkaṭācalamāhātmya*. Here, in the phrase "alibālati" and so forth, the sense is "acting like a young bee" (*alibāla*); by means of the *kvip* suffix, "blueness" (*nīlatva*) is the common attribute shared by the garland of the Lord’s favor and those [bees]. The word *ātmann* is a separate term, serving as an address to the Blessed One: "O Supreme Self" (*paramātman*).
An example of the elision of the expressive [element] in a secondary derivative (taddhita) is as follows:
"That impure man who never has a desire for service at the lotus feet of Veṅkaṭapati, but always wanders among evil objects—he is a donkey-stable. (54)

A *kharakuṭī* is a specific type of place that is extremely small and a harsh dwelling. Here, in the sense of "a man like a *kharakuṭī*," the suffix *kan* prescribed by the rule *ive pratikṛtau* is elided in the sense of a human being according to the rule *lummanuṣye*. Thus, in the word *kharakuṭī*, there is an elision of the expressive element (*vācakalopa*) within the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). By the principle *lupi yuktavadvyaktivacane*, through the status of being like the original base (*yuktavadbhāva*), the gender of the base is maintained. Impurity is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).

In the formulation of the fourth quarter [of the verse], “*varvarti sa eṣa kharakuṭīmanujaḥ*,” the omission of the word denoting the property (*dharmavācakalopa*) occurs here because that [word] is not employed. Furthermore, in the *Kāśikā* and other works, under the rule *lummanuṣye*, *kharakuṭī* is cited as an example, just like *cañcā*.
But the elision of the word expressing the property (dharmavācaka) is described as occurring in the case of the suffix *kvip* and in compounds (*samāsa*). || 18 ||

Just as that row of side-glances was not merely a garland upon your heart, it was indeed a supreme garland; for you, O preeminent among gods, are the father, the mother, and the brother to those who bow before you.

In your heart and on your chest, Lakṣmī did not shine (*alāsīt*); however, her line of side-glances (*apāṅgāliḥ*) shone exceedingly (*amālāsīt*), meaning she acted like a garland (*mālā*), becoming equal to a garland. [Grammatical note: From the word *mālā*, in the sense of "acting like," with the suffix *kvip* and the *luṅ* tense, the *sic* affix is applied; then by the rule *yamaramanamātāṃ sak ca*, the augment *iṭ* and the suffix *sak* are added. You act like a father, you are a father (*pitarasi*). Other examples are to be understood likewise. Here, the Vedic scripture beginning with "Mother, Father, Brother... is to be kept in mind.

In this context, in expressions such as *mālevācarīt* ("he acted like a garland") or *pitrivācarasīti* ("you act like a father"), words such as *mālā* and *pitṛ* become verbal roots (*dhātu*) when the suffix *kvip* has been elided in forms like *amālāsīt* ("he was not a garland") or *pitarasi* ("you are a father"). In that case, the words *mālā* and so on convey the similarity to a garland and the like through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). According to the view that even an elided *kvip*, when remembered, conveys the sense of "acting like," the loss of the expressive property (*vācakadharma-lopa*) is quite evident.

Even in the view that words such as *mālā* (garland) themselves, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), convey an activity (*ācāra*) that is non-different from similarity (*sādṛśya*), they maintain that since there is no word to express the property (*dharma*) itself—just as there is none for the similarity—it is indeed a case of elision (*lopa*). In the compound *devaḥ puṅgava iva* ("the king is like a bull"), there is both the elision of the expressive word (*vācakalopa*) and the non-employment of the common property (*sādhāraṇadharmāprayoga*); thus, it is an instance of "elision of the property-expresser" (*dharmavācakaluptā*). Furthermore, we have already stated that this type of elision is possible even in the case of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), such as in *kharakuṭī*, where the suffixes *kyac* (expressing the object or locus) or *kyaṅ* are used and the property is not expressed.
But the loss of the standard of comparison occurs in a sentence, in a compound, and in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).
The meaning is "in a compound" (vṛttau).
An example of the *dharmopamānaluptā* (omission of both the common property and the standard of comparison) in a sentence:
"O abode of Śrī, O ocean of compassion, by no one anywhere has anyone been seen equal to me; therefore, even by me, I pray for the great glory of liberation. (56)

Here, because no specific object of comparison is mentioned—expressed by the phrase "equal to whom I have not seen in the world of men"—and because the common attribute (*dharma*) is also not mentioned, this is a case of the elision of both the attribute and the object of comparison (*dharmopamānaluptā*) within the sentence.
An example of the elision of both the object of comparison (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) within a compound is as follows:

"Somewhere, no one equal to Sudarśana has been seen, is being seen, nor will ever be seen—by whom, in former times, the garland-wearer (Kṛṣṇa) crushed the head of Mālin like the flower-cluster of a *māla* tree. (57)

Here, by the phrase "nowhere was anyone seen equal to Sudarśana," etc., there is a case of *dharmopamānaluptā* (omission of both the common attribute and the standard of comparison) occurring within a compound, because the standard of comparison situated in the compound is negated. The word *draṣṭā* is the agentive form of the future passive participle (*luṭ*) used in the sense of the object. That [head] refers to the head of the asura named Mālin, who is well-known for his difficult-to-sever nature. It is also understood that *sumālivat* means "like a row of flowers" (*sumānāṃ āliḥ*), and thus "like the head of the asura Sumālin. The verb *alāvīt* means "he cut off. And in these two cases, it is not merely the essential nature of the standard of comparison that is negated.

However, one should not mistake this for the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison) because of the mention of the "perception of the standard of comparison" (*upamānadarśana*). Nor is it appropriate to suspect the fourth type of *pratīpa* (contrariety) that will be described later; for while that consists in the non-achievement of a comparison between the subject of description and another due to its strikingness, this differs from it because it is striking precisely through the negation of the perception of the standard of comparison. This is the general direction [of the argument]. An example of the elision of both the attribute and the standard of comparison in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is as follows:
"If there were a meeting here in Mucukunda’s cave with Mukunda, or even the attainment of a boon from Him—then I consider this [cave] to be a *vartakī* for Andhaka. (58)

The term *andhakavartakīyam* is cited in the *Kāśikā* on the sūtra "asamāsācca tadviṣayāt" as being equivalent to the expression *kākatālīya*. A *vartaka* is a particular species of bird; this is established by the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana* (Amara-kośa), which begins with "Their varieties are the hārīta, the madgu, the kāraṇḍava, and the plava," and continues with "the vartaka, the vartikā, and so forth," among the names for specific birds. In this instance, within the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), both the quality and the standard of comparison are elided.

For instance, in the expression *andhakavartakīyam*, the words *andhaka* and *vartaka*—which, though not forming a compound themselves, reside within the action inherent to them—form a compound in the sense of "like" (*iva*), according to the rule *asamāsācca tadviṣayāt* (Pāṇini 5.3.106) as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), or by the rule *sup supā*. In both cases, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is, respectively, Mucukunda’s staying somewhere in the cave and Mukunda’s going to that very place.

Thus, the meeting between Mucukunda and Mukunda results in being like the meeting between Andhaka and Vartaka. Then, as in the case of *andhakavartaka*, the suffix *cha* (forming *āndhakavārtakīya*) is applied according to the rule *asamāsācca tadviṣayāt* within the governing context of *ive pratikṛtau*.

Thus, it follows that just as a quail arriving unexpectedly was caught by Andhaka who was inactive, so too Mukunda, arriving by chance, was caught by Mucukunda who was sleeping motionlessly. Accordingly, here, in the simile based on the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), there is an omission of the common attribute (*dharma*) and the object of comparison (*upamāna*), because the object of comparison—consisting of the quail seized by Andhaka—and its shared quality are not mentioned. This omission of the attribute is optional. Herein lies the conjunction of Mukunda and Mucukunda within the cave, which arises from this [simile].
This acquisition of a boon is merely accidental, like that of the blind man and the sparrow.

However, if this verse were composed in another manner by adopting the attribute of "occurrence by chance" (*yādṛcchikatva*), then for the *pratyayārthopamā* (simile based on the meaning of a suffix), this very example would also serve as an illustration of the elision of the *upamāna* alone in a *taddhita* formation. But in the case of a *samāsārthopamā* (simile based on the meaning of a compound)—such as "like the staying of Andhaka" and "like the arrival of Vartaka"—there is an elision of the *upamāna*, because the meeting of the *upamānas* (the staying of Andhaka and the arrival of Vartaka) which are to be compared with the meeting of Mucukunda’s staying and Mukunda’s arrival has not been mentioned.

Likewise, due to the force of compounding (samāsa), there is the elision of the expressive word (vācaka), and due to the non-mention of the attribute (dharma), there is the elision of the attribute; thus, students should carefully consider that this very same example will also serve as an illustration for the elision of the attribute, the expressive word, and the standard of comparison (upamāna).
In some cases, it is also accepted as being elided even by both the expressive word (*vācaka*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*).
For example:

"Having reached his abode on the Vṛṣa mountain, everyone behaves like Śrī [Viṣṇu]; for their blackness, produced by a luster equal to the *atasī* flower, has indeed completely transcended all bounds. (59)

Every person, having reached and entered the divine abode—the residence of that Śrīnivāsa—on Mount Vṛṣa, acts like Śrīnivāsa (śrīvāsīyati), meaning they behave like him due to their dark-blue color; for they become possessed of a boundless and limitless blackness (kālimā) produced by the lovely luster of that Śrīnivāsa, which is like the hue of the flax flower (atasī-suma).

Here, because it is understood through the force of the context that "one behaves toward oneself as if toward Śrīnivāsa," there is an elision of both the expressive word (*vācaka*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), since neither the self (as the object of comparison) nor its designator is explicitly mentioned. In this case, the elision of the object of comparison—even the mention of "oneself" (*ātmānam*)—is intentional, as it could easily have been stated. Nor should it be argued that there is no elision of the object of comparison because the word "all" (*sarva*) serves as its designator; for, lacking an accusative case ending, "all" cannot function as the designator of the object of comparison in the phrase "behaves like Śrīnivāsa."

Furthermore, on this basis, it is not tenable to assume a coordination of case endings in the expression *śrīvāsīyati* by interpreting it as "he acts like *śrīvāsa*," because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for the suffix *kyac* to denote the agent [of the comparison]. This is the general direction of the argument.
In some cases, there may be a compound itself that expresses the meaning while omitting the vowels of the denotative words.

The standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not explicitly mentioned. The meaning is that the *vācakopamānaluptā* (the type where the word for comparison and the standard of comparison are omitted) occurs only in a compound.
Just as the secret union with the beauties of Vraja and their enjoyment were for Śauri, so too has this lotus and its bee arrived by chance.

In the expression *lolambāmburuhīyam*, the analysis (*vigraha*) is similar to that of *kākatālīyam*. To explain: in the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), the words *lolamba* (bumblebee) and *amburuha* (lotus) denote the actions pertaining to them. Thus, following the method previously stated, the compound *lolambāmburuham* is formed as "the arrival of the bumblebee" and "the blooming of the lotus. In both cases, the object of comparison (*upameya*) is, respectively, the Lord’s movement to some secluded spot and the stationing of a beautiful woman from Vraja in that very same place.

In this case, because the final meaning of the compound results in the simile: "The union of Śauri with the beauties of Vraja is like the union of a bee with a lotus," there is an elision of both the denoter and the object of comparison (*upamāna*). This is because the arrival of the bee (the object of comparison) and the blooming of the lotus (the object of comparison) are not explicitly mentioned within the compound, and because the denoter [of the simile] is absent in the compound. However, since the property (*dharma*)—expressed by the word *yadṛcchayā* (by chance)—is present, there is no elision of that property. That which lacks the property, the denoter, and the object of comparison is a simile residing in a compound (*samāsagā*). Specifically, a simile residing in a compound occurs when the property, the denoter, and the object of comparison are all elided; here, "object of comparison" refers to that which is not being praised (*avarṇya*).

May that indescribable, most excellent youth—the abode of the heart of the Lord of the Vṛṣa Mountain, possessing the loveliness of dense lightning, and the refuge for the rows of bowed gods, asuras, and men—shine forth forever. 61.

*Tāruṇyam* is a separate word; its meaning is "beauty (śrī) determined as being youth. Here, in the sense of "one whose beauty shines intensely like the beauty of lightning," the term *vidyullāvaṇyam* is taught [by the grammatical rule], wherein there is an elision (*lopa*) of the words denoting the quality (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). This entire elision is prescribed by the rule *saptamyupamāna*. We have stated previously that this threefold elision also occurs in the case of a compound-based simile (*samāsārthopamā*), such as in the phrase *yanmelanaṃ guhāyām*.

Furthermore, it should be understood that when there is a threefold elision (*trilopa*), the elision of the property (*dharmalopa*) may sometimes even be optional. Now, one might object: "In this case, if the analysis (*vigraha*) is 'that which possesses a splendor shining intensely like the loveliness (*lāvaṇya*) of lightning,' then in the compound, why could there not be an elision of the word *lāvaṇya* itself, which serves as the object of comparison (*upameya*)? Thus, let this be considered a case where both the expressive word and the object of comparison are elided (*vācakopameyaluptā*), rather than a case where the property and the expressive word of the standard of comparison are elided (*dharmavācakopamānaluptā*)? To this, some reply: "Even in the elision of the object of comparison, there is no loss of the status of being a threefold elision."

In reality, however, in accordance with the *bhāṣya* and *vārttika* on the rule *anekamanyapadārthe*, which states "there is elision of the final member [of a compound] when the first member contains a locative case-ending or a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*"), it is more appropriate here for the word expressing the standard of comparison alone to be elided.

For this is the meaning of the *vārttika*: in the expression "that whose prior member contains a locative or a word denoting a standard of comparison" (*saptamyupamānapūrvapadasya*), the term *saptamī* refers to a locative case-ending such as "in the throat" (*kaṇṭhe*) which constitutes a part of a compound like *kaṇṭhestha*; and the term *upamāna* refers either to the word "camel" (*uṣṭra*) etc., which forms part of a word such as *uṣṭramukha*, or to the standard of comparison itself. Thus, the compound *saptamyupamānapūrvapada* is a *bahuvrīhi*.

In this case, a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed with the word [ending] in the locative case as the final member (*padāntara*), and it must be stated that there is an elision (*lopa*) of both the word *stha*, which constitutes the final constituent of the preceding compound, and the word *mukha*. Thus, the *Bhāṣya* on that point says: “A *bahuvrīhi* should be prescribed for a word ending in the locative case and for one preceded by a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Furthermore, the elision of the final member should be prescribed. For example: ‘He whose blackness resides in his throat (*kaṇṭhe-sthaḥ kālaḥ*) is *kaṇṭhekālaḥ*; he whose face is like the face of a camel (*uṣṭra-mukham iva mukham asya*) is *uṣṭramukhaḥ*.’”

In this *vārttika*, by the word "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*), the camel—the substratum of the camel's face which serves as the primary standard of comparison—is indicated. Otherwise, the compound *uṣṭramukham* would not possess the status of being preceded by a standard of comparison. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, taking the introductory phrase from the *bhāṣya* on the example of the aforementioned *vārttika*—namely, "his face is like a camel's face, thus he is 'camel-faced' (*uṣṭramukhaḥ*)"—explained: "Because a whole is designated by means of a property of its part, the camel functions as the standard of comparison; therefore, the word *uṣṭramukha* is preceded by a standard of comparison."

And thus, in this context, just as in the *bahuvrīhi* compound "one whose throat has Time (Death) upon it" (*kaṇṭhasthakālaḥ*), there is the elision of the word *stha* following the word *kaṇṭha*; or just as in the expression "a face like a camel's face" (*uṣṭramukhamiva mukham*), there is the elision of the word *mukha* which constitutes the final member of the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound; likewise, in the *bahuvrīhi* "one whose loveliness is like the loveliness of dense lightning" (*ghanavidyullāvaṇyamiva lāvaṇyaṃ yasya*), there is the elision of the word *lāvaṇya* itself—the primary term denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) following the word *vidyut*—and not the word *lāvaṇya* which denotes the object of comparison (*upameya*).

This should be understood as an illustration specifically of the *dharmavācaka-upamānaluptā* (the elision of both the word expressing the quality and the standard of comparison). All of this has been explained by us in the commentary on the phrase "kalpākārām" in the opening verse of the *Haṃsasandeśa-rasāsvādinī*.

Some earlier scholars, however, maintain that in the example "the villain is *āyaśśūlika* (one who uses an iron stake)," where one seeks one's own interest through cruel conduct resembling an iron stake, there can also be a threefold elision (*trilopa*)—namely, the elision of the common property (*dharma*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the word expressing the comparison (*vācaka*)—because the common property such as sharpness, the object of comparison, and the word *iva* are not employed. This is not correct; for by means of the word *ayaśśūla*, the cruel conduct is swallowed up through identification (*adhyavasāna*), and by this hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), the object of comparison is actually presented, so there is no elision of the object of comparison (*upameyalopa*) therein.

They say: regarding the term *āyaśśūlika*, under the governing rule *pārśvenānvicchati* (Pāṇini 4.4.27), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ayaśśūladaṇḍājinābhyāṃ ṭhakṭhañau* (Pāṇini 4.4.19) in the sense of "one who seeks" (*anvicchati*). Thus, *ayaśśūlam* means a sharp expedient; the meaning is "one who seeks [his livelihood] by means of that. In this way, they maintain that this division of elided case-endings (*luptavibhāga*), being restricted to specific domains such as sentences, compounds, and suffixes, serves merely to demonstrate proficiency in the technical analysis of grammar (*śabdaśāstra-vyutpatti*) and does not deserve to be explained at great length in the science of poetics (*alaṅkāraśāstra*).
Thus, the eight types of elided [words] have been described according to the tradition of the ancients. ||20||

Thus, although many varieties such as the garland simile (mālopamā), the necklace simile (raśanopamā), the simile with parts (sāvayavopamā), and the simile without parts (niravayavopamā) are possible, they need not be defined separately because they are already included within the varieties already mentioned. Nevertheless, we shall define some of them here:
"When a single object of comparison (upameya) has multiple objects of comparison (upamāna), the wise call this the 'garland simile' (mālopamā). (21)

Just as in a garland (*mālā*) one flower is strung together with another, so too, because of the mutual connection between the objects of comparison (*upamāna*), this is designated as "garland-like simile" (*mālopamā*). Accordingly, Daṇḍin states: "As the sun's heat [bestows] beauty upon the day, as the day [bestows it] upon the sun, and as the day [bestows it] upon the sky—so does your valor bestow fortune upon you; this is considered *mālopamā*."
Such is this variety; however, when there is an abundance of similes, it is simply the "many similes" (bahūpamā) which will be described later.

Just as she shines like a female serpent, like Kālī, and like the full moon; she possesses the luster of the nails of the Lord of the Golden Mountain, and she is like camphor and like the flood of the Ganges.

Vyālīśa is Śeṣa; Kālīśa is Śambhu; Kanakanageśa is Veṅkaṭādrīśa. Here, because multiple standards of comparison (upamānas) such as Vyālīśa and others are employed in the form of a garland for a single object of comparison (upameya)—namely, the luster of the nails of Śrīnivāsa—this is a "garland simile" (mālopamā). In this regard, the verse previously cited as an example of the "omission of the word of comparison" (vācakalupta), beginning with "alibālati harinīlati," is also an illustration; the distinction there lies in the inclusion of the attribute "blue" (nīla).
Furthermore, when the attribute serving as the ground for similarity is mentioned, this mālopamā occurs whether that attribute is identical or different [in each case].
In that regard, regarding the identity of their nature (*dharmaikya*), it is as follows:

just as a streak of gold shines upon a touchstone, or as a coral creeper gleams in the ocean, so does Kamalā reside within the heart of the Lord of the Añjana mountain like the filament-tips of a blue lotus. (63)
Just as a king shines by the glory of his kingdom, a king of poets by his most intense brilliance, and spring by its abundance of flowers, so does a person shine through devotion to Mādhava. 64.

Like the beauty of the lotus at dawn, like the moonlight during the bright fortnight, or like the splendor of the night-lily at evening—fortune generally shines upon one who has taken refuge in the Lord of Fortune.

O Giver of Boons, at the sight of you, the abundance of suffering vanishes like the winter frost at the arrival of spring, like the light of the moon at its setting, and like the appearance of clouds at the onset of autumn. 66.
O Illustrious Lord, those who are averse to You among men are like shriveled grain among crops, like female gnats among birds, and like mosquitoes among insects. (67)

In these five examples, since multiple standards of comparison (*upamāna*) such as Kanakarekhā and others are employed for each single object of comparison (*upameya*) such as Lakṣmī and so forth, this is a "garland simile" (*mālopamā*). The distinction from the previous examples lies in the fact that the common attribute (*dharma*) is indicated both through the relationship of image and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) by the phrase "like a touchstone," etc., and through its recurrence (*anugāmitā*) by the phrase "shining," etc. The word *vaśikāḥ* means "insignificant" (*tucchāḥ*); according to Amarasimha, "the word *vaśika* [denotes] the insignificant and the empty. Furthermore, in the first three examples here, the objects of comparison are praiseworthy.

In the final two examples, it should be understood that the distinction lies in the fact that the objects of comparison (*upameya*) are censurable. This very same *stabakopamā* (cluster simile) takes the form of a series (*mālārūpā*). As Daṇḍin has stated:
"The similarity of multiple pairs of objects is the *stabakopamā*; for example:
'I have taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, just as a bee [rests] upon a lotus.'"

Thus it is said. Nor should one suspect that a difference in gender—as in "like the moon" (*vidhubhāsī*) or "like a small bird" (*pataṅgikā*)—is a defect of simile (*upamā-doṣa*). For such a discrepancy is not a defect, as it does not cause distress to the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*). As Daṇḍin has stated:
"A difference in gender or number, nor even inferiority or superiority [of qualities], is not sufficient to constitute a defect in simile, provided that it causes no distress to the wise."
This eunuch walks like a woman; this woman speaks like a man;
he is as dear to me as my own life-breaths; he is like knowledge and wealth acquired.
O Great King, like you, the Lord of the Gods shines resplendent;
by his splendor, this king is fully capable of ascending to the rank of the Sun.
Such good fortune as this never indeed forsakes him at any time;
yet there is also a certain agitation in the performance, as is known by those skilled in speech.
The moon is white like a female swan; the sky is stainless like a lake;
a man devoted to his master shines like a dog; and a firefly glows like the sun.
"Such [faults] are avoided by the virtuous; let the reason for this be considered. Thus it is said.
Regarding the distinction of qualities:
"May the wives of Hari—profound as the ocean, exceedingly delicate like the petals of a lotus, and noble as the arrival of the Kalpa—bring about our welfare. (68)

In all the previous examples cited, the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) was one and the same; here, however, it is different in each case. Furthermore, whereas in the former instances the complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*) was contained within a compound (*samāsagā*) or a sentence (*vākyagā*), here it is contained within a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhitagā*); this is the distinction. As for its being in the form of a garland (*mālārūpatva*), that remains exactly the same.

Rudraṭa, however, maintains that the *mālōpamā* (garland simile) exists only when there is a distinction in attributes (*dharmabheda*). Thus, in his *Kāvyālaṃkāra*, he states: "This is the *mālōpamā* where a single object, possessing multiple commonalities, is compared with several objects of comparison that each possess a single commonality."
Thus he spoke:
"She, slender as a dark vine, as utterly pure as the crescent moon,
and with a sweet voice like a female swan— she steals away my consciousness like sleep."
But when this [simile] is accepted, examples such as "like the ocean" and so forth should be understood as illustrations of the *mālā-upamā* (garland simile).
Bharata, moreover, says:
"That [activity] may be performed by one with one, or again by one with many;
likewise, it may be performed by one with many, or by many together with many."

Thus he has demonstrated the fourfold nature of *upamā* (simile). That is the meaning of *sā upamā*. Among these, the first variety, consisting of the comparison of one thing with another, is to be seen in the previously cited verses such as: “The sky is like the heart of the Lord of Serpents [Śeṣa] and the Lord of Mountains [Himālaya].”
The second type of simile, consisting of one [object] compared to many, has been demonstrated by him as follows: for instance,
that which might be expressed as "having eyes like those of a hawk, a peacock, and a vulture."
That is proclaimed as a simile (upamā) because of the similarity of one thing with many.
Thus [it is said]. And Daṇḍin has employed this very same type [of simile] as "the many-simile" (*bahūpamā*). As it is stated in the *Kāvyādarśa*:
"The touch of yours is cool like sandalwood water, moonbeams, moonstones, and so forth"—this, making known an excellence (*atiśaya*), is the many-simile.

Thus, this example is given in accordance with that [rule]: "May Acyuta, whose beautiful luster is like that of the blue water-lily, the rain-cloud, the Yamunā, and the tamāla tree, and whose feet are companions to the lotus bud and coral, be my refuge. (69)

In this context, the words *sabrahmacārin* and *sahacara* function as terms of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus it is said: "The words *iva*, *vat*, *vā*, and *yathā*, as well as *samāna*, *nibha*, *sannibha*, *tulya*, *saṃkāśa*, *nīkāśa*, *prakāśa*, and *pratirūpaka* [are used in the sense of 'like']."
Antagonists, adversaries, opposites, and contraries;
similar, resembling, concordant, homogeneous, and counterparts.
Reflected image, counterpart, similar, equal, commensurate;
possessing characteristics, resembling, appearing like, having the same side, and compared—these are the synonyms for "comparison" (upamā).

Words such as *kalpadeśīya* and *deśya*, as well as those that are well-known synonyms or substitutes, and words that denote a similar meaning or are equivalent in quality, or those whose meanings are not inferior [to the original], [are also used].
And the compound *bahuvrīhi* in expressions such as "moon-faced" (*śaśāṅkavadanā*) [is used when it] rivals,
conquers, hates, harms, or roars back [at its object].
He reviles, despises, torments, and censures;
he mocks, imprisons, laughs at, envies, and finds fault.
It consumes his good fortune and robs him of his splendor.
He contends with him and enters into a comparison with him.
He occupies the same station as that person, enters his very sphere,
whether he be a kinsman, a thief, a friend, an adversary, a fellow student, or a companion.
The words "follows" (anveti), "binds" (anubadhnāti), "prohibits that conduct" (tacchīlaṃ tanniṣedhati),
or "imitates him" (tasya vānukaroti) are indicators of similarity (sādharmya).
"These [similes] have been declared by poets to provide delight to the intellect. Thus [it is said].

In this context, in the expression "it imitates that" (*tasya vānukaroti*), the word *iti* denotes a manner; the meaning is that words of this kind indicate similarity (*sādharmya*). By this, it is established that terms such as *sagotra*, *sabrahmacārin*, and *dāyāda* also function as indicators of comparison (*upamāna*). Here, *iva* and others are particles (*nipāta*). The suffix *vat*—prescribed in the sense of "like" (*iva*) and "equal to" (*tulya*)—is included in the term *vadi*. The suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes; although these are prescribed in the sense of "slight incompleteness," they nevertheless possess the very same meaning of "equality."

Because even "slight incompleteness" (*īṣadasamāpti*) results in a sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*). As Kaiyaṭa has stated: “*Guḍakalpā* means grape that is slightly incomplete [in its sweetness] like molasses (*guḍa*). Although the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless, by implication, there exists the relationship of the standard and the object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*). In that regard, the suffixes are employed only after the standard of comparison, because that alone serves as their base (*prakṛti*). As for words such as *nibha*, however, starting from the rule “*vācyaliṅgāḥ samastulyaḥ*,” it is said: “These [words] occur when they are the final member of a compound (*uttarapada*).”

Because of the grammatical rule stating that "nibha, saṅkāśa, nīkāśa, pratīkāśa, upama," and so forth, form the domain of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), the analytical expansion (*vigraha*) for "candranibham" (moon-like) must be shown as "candreṇa samam" (equal to the moon), rather than using separate words. This was stated by Kṣīrasvāmin: "Since it is specified [by the rule] that this occurs 'in the final member' (*uttarapade*), the form *candreṇa nibham* does not occur. Words denoting enemies or friends which signify similarity [form such compounds]. In examples such as *śaśāṅkavadanā* (moon-faced woman), there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the object of comparison (*upamāna*) as the prior member.

Expressions such as "the reflection vies [with the original]" and so forth imply similarity; enough of this digression. Let us return to the subject at hand. Bharata himself has demonstrated a third variety, in which many things share a single object of comparison, as follows:
"The best of the twice-born, possessing light, shine forth like the moon.
This is proclaimed as the simile of many [things] by means of one.
In this regard, there is this illustration:

Established in the maintenance of the world, renowned for the gaze of a kinsman to the nectar-filled realm, and bearing true prosperity within their hearts, the devotees of the Lord shine forth like the Blessed One himself. (70)

The "world consisting of nectar" (amṛtamayaloka) means the non-material world (aprākṛtaloka), that is to say, the supreme state (paramaṃ pada). Those for whom there is "vision" (dṛṣṭi)—meaning knowledge or insight—into that [state] are so described; that is, they are renowned as possessing the fullness of knowledge which is the primary cause for bestowing ultimate liberation (niśśreyasa), or alternatively, they are renowned as having such a vision.

The phrase "he whose eyes (dṛṣṭī) are those very two—the moon consisting of nectar (amṛtamaya) during the fortnight (pakṣe), and the sun who is the kinsman of the world (lokabāndhava)" should be construed by modifying the word order as "thus celebrated. Regarding the term *sthiti*: it refers to the stability of the world, that is, the boundaries of dharma such as the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramādi*); as the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *sthiti* is used in the feminine sense of 'abiding,' 'boundary,' and 'limit' (*maryādā*)."

The meaning is that they are those who, having placed their trust in that [Veda], protect the boundaries of the world through their own practice and so forth—starting from the words “For the non-subversion of the dharmas and for the establishment of the limits” and ending with the statement “A wise man should not transgress Vedic conduct even in thought. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), they are those who have placed their trust in the maintenance and protection of the worlds.
O highly wise one, apart from Hari, the Lord of All, who remains established in the maintenance [of the world], no other whatsoever possesses the power to sustain it.
This eternal creator creates the world, and he protects it during its maintenance.

Because of this statement: "The Śrī of the virtuous" means the *sat-śrī*, which refers to the three Vedas (*trayī*), according to the Vedic revelation: "The Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus—she is indeed the immortal Śrī of the virtuous. "Bearing [her]" means possessing all the Vedas and their meanings within the heart. In the alternative sense, it means "bearing the virtuous Śrī," that is, Lakṣmī. Thus, the Bhāgavatas, who are equal to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), shine forth. Here, for many Bhāgavatas, the single Blessed Lord alone serves as the point of comparison; the common attribute is rooted in *śleṣa* (punning wordplay).

It should be understood that in the expression "equal to the Blessed One" (*bhagavattulyā*), because the case-ending of the word expressing the standard of comparison (*upamānavācipada*) is elided in its grammatical function (*vṛttiluptatayā*), it does not cause aversion; thus, there is no fault characterized by a discrepancy in number (*bhinnavacanatā*). It should further be noted that this [type of comparison] occurs only when the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is singular, because the standard of comparison is one.
The fourth type, consisting of many [illustrations] for many [objects], is to be seen in the previously cited examples such as "like the shriveled grains among the rice."
If each preceding object of comparison becomes the standard of comparison for each succeeding one, this is called the "girdle simile" (raśanopamā) by poets. (22)

The meaning is that when that which is the object of comparison (*upameya*) in the first simile becomes the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the subsequent simile, it is called a "girdle-simile" (*raśanopamā*). For example: "O Lord of the mountain of Śruti (the Vedas), your heart is captivating like your face; your speech gives joy like your face; and your eye, with its charming syllables, is like your speech. (71)

Here, since the face and so forth, which are presented as the objects of comparison (*upameya*) in relation to each preceding element, are presented as the standards of comparison (*upamāna*) in relation to each succeeding one—and since each subsequent element is linked to the preceding ones like a chain—this is a *raśanopamā* (girdle simile). Furthermore, the common attribute (*samānadharmā*) consists of two meanings embraced within the word *hārī*: namely, "possessing a necklace" (*hāravat-tva*) and "charming" (*manoharatva*), [which apply respectively] to the heart and the face.

In this way, for speech and eyes as well, the term *lalitavarṇam* (possessing charming phonemes) functions through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of two meanings: the quality of having sweet syllables and the quality of being beautiful and clear. However, one should note the distinction that for the face and speech, [the term] *ānandadāyī* (bestowing bliss) functions as a common attribute (*anugāmitayā*). This is the *raśanopamā* (girdle-simile) based on a difference in attributes (*dharmabheda*).

Just as sovereignty is to stability, stability to magnanimity, magnanimity to the irresistible valor of the serpent, the mountain, and the celestial tree, and valor to profound depth—alas, such is the unity of his virtues! (72)
In this case, "unpreventable" (avārya) is a single property alone; likewise, examples may be cited even when there is an omission of a property.

This *upamā* (simile), like *rūpaka* (metaphor), is of eight kinds: the simple (*kevala*) and partless (*niravayava*), the partless in the form of a garland (*mālārūpa-niravayava*), the whole-object-based with parts (*samastavastuviṣaya-sāvayava*), the partially-manifested with parts (*ekadeśavivarti-sāvayava*), the simple and based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*) and successive (*paramparita*), the garland-form based on paronomasia and successive, the simple and pure (*śuddha*) successive, and the garland-form pure successive. Among these, "simplicity" (*kevalatva*) means not being included within a garland, and "partlessness" (*niravayavatva*) means independence from other similes. This has already been illustrated in many ways previously.

Even that which is partless in the form of a garland has already been illustrated in such examples as: "It acts like a young bee, it acts like a sapphire, it acts like a female serpent, it acts like a dark goddess."

Having as its object all things, possessing parts, and rising beautifully from the peak of Mount Kalinda like the splendor of Lord Mukunda emerging from the mountain, this [poem]—like a river with waves of exquisite beauty—removes intense suffering, as a torrent washes away sin. (73)

O ornament of the lordly mountain Kuṇḍala, I perceive your heart to be like the pool of the Yamunā, and I know this Kaustubha gem within it to be like a lotus; these necklaces of yours appear like its foam. (74)

The meaning of "having all things as its object" (*samastavastuviṣayā*) is that it has as its objects both the whole (*avayavin*) and its parts (*avayava*). Here, in both of these two verses, because the wholes and the parts—which serve as the points of comparison (*upamāna*)—are mentioned in their entirety by means of words alone, this [simile] possesses the quality of having all things as its object; and because it is produced by the comparison of the parts, it also possesses the quality of being "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatā*). The distinction here is that in the first verse there is the mention of a common attribute (*dharma*), whereas in the second there is not. Daṇḍin maintains that this is a "sentence-meaning simile" (*vākyārthopamā*) involving multiple instances of the word *iva*. As stated by him in the *Kāvyādarśa*:
If a certain meaning of a sentence is compared with another meaning of a sentence,
that is *vākyārthopamā* (simile of sentence-meaning), which is of two kinds depending on whether there is one or more instances of the word *iva*.
Your face, with its steady eyes and the radiance of visible teeth,
shines like a lotus with hovering bees and discernible filaments.
Like a bee repeatedly drinking from a lotus, I took delight in repeatedly drinking in the face of that slender-limbed woman, which was like a lotus belonging to a lotus-pond.
Thus [it is said]. The simile consisting of the meaning of a sentence expressed by the word *eva* alone will be demonstrated further on.

O Lord, that primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which possesses parts and exists in a single location, has indeed brought forth [the universe] like a female swan that has conceived; from her, O Śrīśa, the Egg of Brahmā was produced like a sheath, and from that Egg was born the Mother of the Creator. (75)
In this regard,
O Bhārata, my womb is the Great Brahman; therein I place the seed,
and from that the birth of all beings occurs.
"O son of Kuntī, whatever forms arise in all wombs, their great womb is Brahman; I am the seed-bestowing father.

Thus is the meaning of the verse from the Gītā summarized. "That which is my Great Brahman, which is the womb of the entire universe—that which is my *prakṛti*—into that I place the embryo. This refers to the supreme *prakṛti*, described as "know my other, higher *prakṛti*, which has become the individual soul (*jīva*)" and which consists of a mass of insentient matter; it is here called by the word "embryo" because it serves as the seed for all living beings.

The meaning is this: in that great, insentient Brahman which serves as the womb, I place the embryo in the form of an aggregate of sentient beings; that is, by means of the insentient *prakṛti*, which has become the field of experience, I unite it with the sentient *prakṛti*, which constitutes the aggregate of the class of experiencers. From that—namely, from that conjunction of the two *prakṛtis* brought about by my resolve—there arises the birth of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

"In all wombs—namely, the wombs of gods, gandharvas, and so forth—the great Brahman is the womb, that is, the cause, of those various forms that come into being; the meaning is that *prakṛti* (primordial nature), in which the group of conscious beings has been joined by Me, and which exists in states ranging from the *mahat* down to the specific elements (*viśeṣa*), is the cause. I am the seed-bestowing father; the meaning is that I am the one who joins the group of conscious beings in each respective case according to their corresponding karma. This is the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Regarding the word "kośa," it means like an egg; as Amara states: "A *peśī*, a *kośa*, and *dvihīna* [egg] refer to an egg (*aṇḍa*)."

Here, in the latter half [of the verse], in the phrase *vidhātṛkādamba*, there is only a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison), because the identity (*tādātmya*) understood through a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (adjectival compound) is of no use in the present context; furthermore, this is due to its inclusion in a section primarily consisting of comparisons. However, if the fourth quarter were read as *śrīśa tato’jani marāla iva dhātā*, the simile would be explicit. In this case, although the Lord’s comparison to a *kalahaṃsa* (swan) is not directly expressed by a word, it is apprehended as being suggested by the comparisons of his limbs; thus, this is a *ekadeśavivartinī* (partially manifesting) simile.

It should be understood that [the figure] is called *ekadeśavivartinī* (occurring in one part) because it functions specifically as something to be expressed in only one part of the whole and its parts (*avayava-avayavin*). Here, by describing the birth of the four-faced Brahmā—the source of the aggregate of individual souls (*jīva-samaṣṭi*)—in the phrase "the mother of the Creator" (*vidhātṛkādamba*), the birth of others is also established by implication; thus, this does not contradict the statement in the cited verse, "the source of all beings" (*saṃbhavaḥ sarvabhūtānām*), which speaks of the origin of all beings. This being so, [it is consistent with the following]:
"In the beginning, he created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant like the thousand-rayed sun."
"In that [egg], Brahmā himself, the grandfather of all the worlds, was born"—
thus it should be understood that this statement of Manu is also consistent [with our position].
An example of the purely "clinging" (śliṣṭa) type of "successive" (paraṃparita) metaphor is as follows:
"Like the dawn of the rising sun, the glorious Lord, whose abode is Śeṣagiri, shines forth, possessing a dense radiance and bestowing an abundance of light. (76)

The "rising" (*abhyudaya*) of the Āditya gods and of the Āditya Sun refers to their sovereignty and their appearance. Here, the rising of the Sun is compared to the rising of the gods, which is brought forth through *śleṣa* (punning). This constitutes a *kevala-śliṣṭa-paraṃparita* (purely punning, successive) metaphor, because "successiveness" (*paraṃparitatva*) is defined here as the state of being a mutual means for one another, and because it lacks the nature of a *mālā* (garland-like) structure.
An example of a purely serial *śleṣa* (pun) in the form of a chain (*mālārūpa*) is as follows:
"O lotus-eyed one, O moon of the golden-peaked mountain, you shine like the Himalaya for *sattva*, like the monsoon cloud for *rajas*, and like the ocean, the treasury of lights, for *tamas*. (77)

Regarding the term *sattvasya*: it refers both to the quality of *sattva* and to the multitude of living beings such as deer; the singular number is used with the intention of denoting the genus. Just as the Himālaya—the snowy mountain—is foremost among those who nourish all living beings (*sattva*), so too this Blessed One is foremost among those who nourish the *sattva* of those who take refuge in him; for it is heard in scripture: "The Great Puruṣa is indeed the Lord, the impeller of *sattva*. Regarding *rajasaḥ*: the sense is that he is the extinguisher of the quality of *rajas* and of dust, just like a monsoon cloud.

The sense is that, like a treasury of light for darkness—that is, for the quality of *tamas* and for physical gloom—it brings about their total cessation. Here, the means for the comparison of the Lord with the Himalaya, the monsoon cloud, and the sun are the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which are evoked through paronomasia (*śleṣa*) by means of "living beings," "dust," and "darkness. Now, one might ask: how can such a comparison—as between "living beings, dust, and darkness" and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—be easily understood?

If it is argued that this is because the words for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are not perceived separately, [the reply is: in the case of *śleṣa* (punning), since they are conveyed by a single word, just as the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāna*) occurs through that form, it is equally easy to state the determination of similarity (*sādṛśyādhyavasāna*) through that very same common property (*sādharmya*). For that [determination of similarity] alone serves as the means (*upāya*) for the simile (*upamā*) to be employed in the present context; so they say.
Or rather, as Mādhava is to the delight of the Śākhi trees, so are you, O abode of the serpent-king Mādhava; as a great poet is to his few verses, so are you, like a rain-cloud, to the worlds. 78.

"O Mādhava, abode of the serpent-king, Śrīnivāsa Mādhava!"—this is another name for Śrīnivāsa, as stated in the *Bhagavat-śāstra*: "Mādhava on Veṅkaṭagiri. Those who possess branches (*śākhā*) are "branch-bearers" (*śākhinaḥ*): both trees and the twice-born who study the various divisions of the Vedas. They are the "fragrances" (*āmodāḥ*)—meaning perfumes and joys—of that lineage. According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *śākhā* refers to a different side, an arm, a division of the Veda, and a part of a tree. The sense is that [the Lord] is the one who causes them to flourish, like the spring season (*vasanta*), which is itself called *Mādhava*.

The sense is that he is, like a skilled poet (*sukavi*), the source of numerous verses (*śloka*), poetic compositions (*padya*), and glories (*yaśas*). This is based on the Vedic text: "His name is great glory" (*tasya nāma mahadyaśaḥ*). According to Amara, "the word *śloka* denotes both a verse and glory. Furthermore, the sense is that he is, like a cloud (*ghana*), the support of the worlds (*bhuvana*)—meaning both waters and the universe. Here, through the double meanings (*śleṣa*) revealed by the trees (*taru*), the fragrance (*kulaparimala*), the verses (*padya*), and the waters (*jala*), there are similes for the assemblies of Vedic scholars (*vaidikapariṣad*), their joy, their fame, and the world; and through the spring (*vasanta*), the skilled poet (*sukavi*), and the rain-cloud (*ghanaghana*), there are the means for the comparison with the Blessed Lord.
Or rather, O illustrious one, you cause the pure twice-born to rejoice at will, like the arrival of autumn; O Infinite One, you are the support of great auspiciousness, like Mount Sumeru. (79)

"O Bhūman, O Blessed One! That wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman)," according to the Śruti. [He addresses] the pure twice-born ones, the *haṃsas*. In this context, he who is pure in his purpose is indeed pure; one who is merely pure through clay and water is not truly pure. The supreme purification of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is held to arise from the knowledge of the Lord.

For a Brahmin possessing all kinds of purity in the manner described, there is the employment of two similes for the auspicious and golden Brahmin—*kalyāṇam* meaning gold and *maṅgala* (Hemacandra)—and two similes for the Lord, namely the arrival of autumn and Mount Sumeru. Here, the means [of comparison] are the swan and gold brought forth by *śleṣa* (paronomasia). The distinction is that in the previous examples the common attribute (*dharma*) was unstated, whereas here it is stated. Although in the first example, "of the being" (*sattvasya*), the common attribute appears as if conveyed by the word "shining" (*bhāsī*).

Nevertheless, it should be understood that in this case, the commonality (*sāmānyadharma*) of nourishing, extinguishing, and completely removing—which alone were intended to be expressed—is not what is meant here; for while such a commonality would arise naturally (*svārasika*), its mere appearance [without these specific actions] would lack aesthetic charm (*acamatkāritva*). Furthermore, the distinction is that in the two previous examples the figures take the form of a "garland" (*mālā*) involving many elements, whereas in the final example there are only two. The difference between the first two examples as well will become clear immediately below.
The purely pure-sequential [ornament] is as follows:
on the heart of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), who is the Lord of Mountains, a garland composed of *tulasī* leaves shines like a swarm of bees upon a laughing, shimmering, dark blue lotus. 80.

In the word *prahasita*, the suffix *kta* denotes the state of being (*bhāve*). Thus, *prahasitena lasite asitāmbuje* means "in the blue lotus (*indīvare*) shining with a smile—that is, with expansion. The comparison of the swarm of bees to the garland of *tulasī* leaves serves to enhance the comparison of the Lord’s chest to the blue lotus; thus, both comparisons form a continuous series (*saṃjātaparaṃparā*).

The pure *paraṃparita* (successive) type in the form of a single string (*kevalā mālārūpā*) is as follows: "O bull-like one, formerly you acted toward the women of Nanda’s cowherd settlement who were acting like cows; O elephant-like one, [you acted] toward those acting like female elephants; O sandalwood tree, [you acted] toward the fair-toothed women who were acting like climbing vines. (81) "Formerly" (*purā*): "you acted like a bull" (*puṃgavasi*). Because of the connection with the word *purā*, the present tense (*laṭ*) is used for the past according to the rule *puri luṅ cāsme*. "Acting like cows" (*gavantyaḥ*): those who act like cows. "You acted like an elephant" (*kareṇavasi*); "acting like female elephants" (*kariṇayantyaḥ*): those who act like female elephants. "Acting like climbing vines" (*vallayantyaḥ*): those who act like climbing vines.

The suffix *kvip* is used here in the sense of "conduct" (*ācāra*). In this context, the comparison of the cowherd women to cows and so forth serves as the means for the comparison of the Blessed One to a bull and so forth; thus, these comparisons form a continuous series in the shape of a garland (*mālā*), being purely simple (*śuddha*) similes.

Just as one who has bowed down to you, O Kṛṣṇa, becomes like Indra— the lord of the gods whose mental power extends even to the celestial beings— so too does he become a guide on the path through the dense thicket of logic and a churner of the ocean of supreme knowledge.

"O Kṛṣṇa, the person who bows to you [is such that] policy (*naya*) is like a scripture (*śāstra*), which is as difficult to fathom as a dense forest; thus, 'the density of policy' (*nayagahana*) is a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison), because the word *pathin* (path) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). It is not, however, a *mayūravyaṃsakādi* compound, for that would be inappropriate here. In this case, *pathīnati* means 'he acts like a path' (*panthā ivācarati*); the suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule *upamānādācāre*. The lengthening of the penultimate vowel occurs by the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*. The same applies in the following cases."

By this, his status as a proponent of the "lower knowledge" (aparavidyā)—as described in the passage beginning with "Therein, another is the Rigveda"—is indicated. "Higher knowledge" (paravidyā) refers to the knowledge of Brahman, as described in the passage: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained. The compound *jaladhiriva* is to be understood as before (i.e., a *karmadhāraya*). He acts like a churning-stick (*manthā*) for that [ocean of knowledge]; by this, his role as the one who churns out the entire essence of the knowledge of Brahman is indicated. For this very reason, he acts like *Ṛbhukṣan*—the lord of the vast assembly of those whose minds are perfected through wisdom, like gods in heaven; thus, he is called *ṛbhukṣīṇati*.

In this instance, for those whose minds are fashioned by the science of policy (*nīti*), the means [of success] are likened to the gods who dwell in the deep ocean; and for those who have bowed to the Blessed One, they are likened to the path, the earth, and Indra. These similes are, as before, *paraṃparita* (successive), *mālārūpa* (in the form of a garland), and *śuddha* (pure). Here, because the meanings of the words "path," "earth," and "Indra"—as prescribed by the rule *pathimathyṛbhukṣām*—are employed in succession as the objects of comparison, there is a commingling with the *ratnāvalī* ornament to be described later; this is the distinction from the previous example.
Thus, when there is mutual compatibility between the two similes and the two objects of comparison, this status as a means has been described for the two objects of comparison.

Just as one who is scorched by the great forest fire of the summer heat always finds relief in a cloud, so too this lordly elephant among mountains is a constant remedy for the host of calamities that afflict the race of bipeds. (83)

He acts like a forest fire during the summer heat toward the great calamities belonging to men, the best of bipeds; yet he acts like a rain-cloud toward those calamities. Śeṣādri, the preeminent mountain that is like a serpent (pṛdāku), is his lordly elephant of pride; the meaning is that Śrīnivāsa is determined to be his very essence. Here, although there is a mutual opposition between the two points of comparison—the forest fire and the rain-cloud—and their respective objects of comparison—the human calamity and the lord of the serpent-mountain—the very fact of the comparison exists because the two comparisons themselves are mutually compatible.
This [type of *śleṣa*] occurs even in the form of a garland (*mālā*). For example:

"O Śauri, you are the protector of the great ones; you are the crowning crest of those who have allies; you are the scorcher of the enemies of the gods; you are the one who brings coldness here; and you are the king over those devoid of darkness. (84)

You act like Sutrāman; you are Sutrāman. From the word *sutrāman*, by the rule “*kvip* may optionally be added after all nominal stems,” the suffix *kvip* is applied; then, by the rule “*anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*,” there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel. The same applies in cases such as *śikharīṇatām*. [The compound] *sapakṣaśikharīṇantaḥ* means those who act like mountain peaks (*śikharin*) that possess wings (*sapakṣa*); [the form] *teṣām* is derived from that [stem] with the addition of the suffix *śatṛ* after a *kṛt* suffix ending in *kvip*. You act like Pūṣan; you are Pūṣan. Those who act like snow (*himānī*) are called *himantaḥ*; [the form] *teṣām* refers to them.

"You act like a king, you act like the moon; you are a king, [and those who] act like darkness are *tamasantaḥ*—of them. All the words ending in the genitive case are qualifiers of the term "enemies of the gods" (*suradviṣām*). Thus, in the example of the *mālā-upamā* (garland simile) consisting solely of *śliṣṭa-paraṃparita* (conjoined and successive) type, such as "like the Himālaya of *sattva*" in the first verse, and "you [are] like the monsoon cloud of *rajas*" and so forth, the means [of the comparison] should be seen as being in opposition (*prātikūlya*). And thus, it is established that this [simile] is mixed with both favorability (*ānukūlya*) and opposition.
Furthermore, other distinctions as well should be discerned by themselves by those of keen intellect; therefore, for fear of prolixity, we shall desist.

In this regard, when the simile (*upamā*) is complete, the common property (*dharma*) is sometimes indicated as merely following along; sometimes it has attained the state of a mere reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*); sometimes it has attained the state of reflection and reflection through being interspersed with the relation of object and counter-object (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*); sometimes it has attained the state of a pure object and counter-object; sometimes it is figuratively applied even though non-existent; sometimes it consists of words, which is precisely what constitutes *śleṣa* (paronomasia); sometimes it is rooted in the employment of different compound forms;
and sometimes it occurs through the mixing of these [varieties] as far as possible.

Therein, I shall ever place my mind upon the two Buddhas, the parents of the worlds, who are exceedingly easy to cross over, who possess great splendor, and who, like the moon and its light, dwell together upon the peak of the Bull Mountain (Śrīparvata), remaining eternally united. 85.

Here, because of the simultaneous mention of the two as "ever-connected," there is a common, recurring attribute shared by both moonlight and the moon, as well as by Śrī and Śrīnivāsa. Or, for example:
"Like a dark cloud-mass, fond of wandering through the caves of the serpent’s mountain (Garuḍa-hill), this certain great and wondrous deity gladdens the world. (86)
Here, because of the single mention of both "dark blue" and "refreshing," there is a recurring common attribute shared by the Supreme Deity and the cloud-bank.

Or rather, who indeed would become utterly dejected after having enjoyed that lotus-eyed one—who is like a treasure-trove without limit, whose feet are placed upon the mountain of the serpent-king (Śeṣa), who bestows welfare, and who has shaken off all calamities? 87.
A beneficial word is that which brings about benefit; here, the property of being a beneficial word and so forth is the recurring factor.
Or rather,
those who ever desire service to Your pair of lotus feet are born for their own destruction alone, like bubbles from the ocean of Śrī’s fame.

Or rather, those who, though born with eyes capable of seeing well, do not bow even once to the Lord of Ramā; having failed to perform what is beneficial, they perish in vain like worms that have been born but for a moment. 89.

Those who are blind from birth (*januṣāndhāḥ*)—meaning those who are blind by nature regarding the object that is the sight of merit (*puṇyadarśana*), which is the vision of well-performed deeds (*sukṛtekṣaṇa*)—are devoid of the discernment born of virtuous action. Here, because the intent lies solely in censuring those who do not bow to the Blessed One, the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not a fault; on the contrary, it is indeed a merit. In both cases, "destruction" is the common property (*anugāmī-dharma*).

May that Reality, which has entered into a state of mere identity between the original image and its reflection—wonderful in its manner of being embraced on all sides by the pair of lotus-like arms—and which resembles an emerald set in a circle of golden pins, abide in my mind. 90.

That wondrous being, Śrīnivāsa, who has been honored by and has received an embrace from all sides—a complete union—with the pair of Kamalā’s arms; here, the common attribute consists of the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), such as the golden rod [of her arms] and so forth.

If it is asked, "How can there be a simile (*upamā*) given that the pair of arms of Kamalā and other such attributes are unique (*asādhāraṇa*)?", they reply here: the establishment of the simile occurs because even those attributes residing in the object of comparison (*upameya*) and those residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), though unique, are conceived as common through a superimposition of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on similarity. Nor should it be argued: "How can an absolute non-existence of identity—arising from a cognition of non-difference that is illusory (*bhrama-ātmaka*) and forced (*āhārya*)—be capable of establishing the commonality of things like the pair of arms and the golden rod, which are in reality distinct? For it is impossible for an object to be established by means of an illusion. This is not to be said.

It should be understood that just as in examples such as “Your anger appears like fire in the moon,” where the similarity between the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is established through mere imagination despite being utterly non-existent, so too is the case here with the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*). For this very reason, the ancients define the relationship of the prototype and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) as: "the dual presentation of two attributes that are in fact distinct, but which are determined to be non-different due to their mutual resemblance."

When constituted by the relationship of *vastu* (the object) and *prativastu* (its counterpart), having attained the state of an image and its reflection, the *dharma* (the subject) is of three kinds: [it may consist] of two qualifiers alone, two qualificands alone, or the pair of those two, each being constituted by the relationship of *vastu* and *prativastu*. Among these, the first is as follows:
"Your face, resembling a lotus with a swarm of bees hovering above it, like the moon atop the peak of Mount Vṛṣabha, with locks of hair moving above—[it is] the abode of all worldly prosperity. (91)

In this case, although being "above" (*uparicara*) and "moving above" (*upariṣṭāccala*) are in reality of one kind, they are designated by two distinct words; thus, there is the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (subject and counter-subject). Furthermore, the two qualifiers, "the swarm of bees" and "the potter," stand in the relation of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection). Thus, the attribute (*dharma*) is composed of these elements.
The second [verse] is as follows:
"Our mind licks, as it were, the lower lip of the Lord of the Serpent-Mountains, which is softened by the luster of a smile, like coral slick with the charming waves of the Ocean of Milk. (92)

Here, although smoothness (*masṛṇatva*) and oiliness (*snigdhatva*) are in reality of one and the same nature, because they are expressed by two distinct words, there is the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding entities). Since these two possess as their qualifiers the smiles and the radiance of the milk-ocean’s charming waves, there is the relation of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection). Thus, this common attribute is composed of those [two relations].
Or like the Jambu tree shining eternally upon the peak of Mount Jambūnada, I praise that indescribable mass of auspiciousness gleaming on the summit of the mountain named Kanaka. 93.

Here, there is the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding subject and predicate) between the qualities of "shining" (*cakāsattva*) and "illuminating" (*kanattva*). Furthermore, the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) between the "peak of Mount Jāmbūnada" and the "summit of the mountain named Kanaka"—which serve as the qualifiers (*viśeṣya*) for those two qualities—is also included within that [figure]. The mountain named Kanaka is the Vaikaṭa mountain. Here, the Lord is identified (*adhyavasāna*) with a mass of splendor. Or, for example:

"O King, your body, a creeper of beauty variegated by the spreading luster of a necklace of diamonds and rubies, is like the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā), made multicolored by the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī. (94)

Here too, there is the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding object) between the qualities of variegation and being adorned; and since the objects qualified by these—namely, the brilliance of diamonds and *kuruvinda* gems on the one hand, and the luster of the necklace and the currents of the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī on the other—stand in the relation of prototype (*bimba*) and reflection (*pratibimba*), this [figure] is likewise based upon that [relation].
The third example is as follows:
"Just as this wife of the Lord of Mountains, who bears the moon-crested crown, is beautiful with the most cooling water, so too is she sweet with the essence of exceedingly cool compassion. (95)

Here, through the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding objects) between the two qualifiers—extreme coolness and extreme cold—and the two qualificands—loveliness and sweetness—the waters and the sentiment of compassion (*karuṇā-rasa*), which are mutually enclosed, stand in the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*); thus, this [figure] is also indeed a variety of that [simile].
Or rather, O Lord, your row of teeth shines forth, situated between the pair of your lovely lips, like a string of pearls within a casket made of beautiful kuruvinda gems. 96.

Here too, there is the *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) relationship between the two qualifiers—*sundaratva* (loveliness) and *mañjulatva* (charm)—and the two qualificands—*antasthatva* (being within) and *madhyagatatva* (being situated in the middle)—which are joined together on both sides by way of the *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding object) relation; this [simile] is also based upon that [same principle]. Or, for example: "Victorious is the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), who, like a *tamāla* tree, bears smooth branches with dark blossoms, while the Lord of the Serpent-Mountain (Garuḍa) bears arms thick with dark jewels. (97)

Here, between the qualities of "blackness" and "blueness" as qualifiers of "flowers" and "jewels," and their respective qualificands, "smoothness" and "density"; likewise, between "smoothness" and "glossiness" which have become qualifiers of "palaces" and "arms," and their respective qualificands, "bearing" and "possessing"—there exists a bimba-pratibimba (original and reflection) relationship between the flowers, jewels, palaces, and arms, encapsulated on both sides by this very state of vastu-prativastu-bhāva (correspondence of things). Thus, this too is indeed composed of vastu-prativastu-bhāva.

The distinction here is that whereas in the previous instance there was a single relationship of image and reflection joined together, here there are two. *Śālāḥ* refers to trunk-branches; as Amara states: "The words *skandha*, *śākhā*, and *śālā* [are synonyms for branch]. A trunk-branch (*skandhaśākhā*) is a branch issuing from the trunk; a *skandha* is the main stem of a tree extending from the root to the branches, as Amara says: "The word *prakāṇḍa* is not feminine; it may be called *skandha*, referring to the main stem of a tree from the root up to the branches. Both the words *skandhaśākhā* and *śālā* denote the aforementioned branches.

This is the third variety mentioned by the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhar*. In the *Citramīmāṃsā*, however, only the two previously mentioned varieties are shown. As it is stated there: “The *vastuprativastubhāva* (the relation of thing and its counterpart) consists in the twofold employment of one and the same attribute due to a difference in its correlates. But that [simple relation] does not occur in its pure form; rather, in every case, it is permeated by the *bimbapratibimbabhāva* (the relation of prototype and reflection), whether as a qualifier or as a qualificand.
Thus, they maintain that an attribute existing in a purely *vastuprativastubhāva* relation is impossible.

The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, has stated that in the verse “Her face is stainless, like the spotless moon,” if there exists the capacity to produce a simile between "stainlessness" (*vaimalya*) and "spotlessness" (*niṣkalaṅkatva*)—which are in fact identical in nature and which, being devoid of the relation of reflection (*bimbapratibimba*), have attained the status of "thing-to-thing-correspondence" (*vastuprativastubhāva*)—then this is indeed a sixth attribute characterized by a pure "thing-to-thing-correspondence.
It is in accordance with this very intention that we have also enumerated below the variety consisting of a pure "thing-to-thing-correspondence."

Just as your two stainless eyes resemble white autumn lotuses in full bloom, so too do they belong to you, the sovereign lord of the mountain king who sports with the one called the king of beasts. 98.

O wife of the Lord of the city called Mṛgarāja, the sovereign of Śrī Veṅkaṭādri, your two pure eyes—spotless, bright, and clear—behave like autumnal blossomed lotuses; they act as "autumnal blossomed lotuses" (*viśada-śarad-vikasitāmbujāyete*). This is the first person dual present tense (*laṭ*) from the denominative root (*kyaṅanta*).

Here, it should be understood that the quality [of the eyes] attains the state of *vastuprativastubhāva* (correspondence of things), being free from the relation of *bimbapratibimba* (original and reflection) because the qualities of purity (*vimalatva*) and brightness (*viśadatva*) are in fact of one and the same nature. Thus, there is the presence of a pure *vastuprativastubhāva* of the attribute.

Furthermore, in such instances as "the embrace all around, bent by the pair of lotus-arms," where there is a comparison between the emerald and the Lord, one must necessarily admit a relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) between the pair of lotus-arms and the golden rods—specifically between their qualities of being embraced and being encircled—because no other common attribute (*dharmāntara*) is perceived. However, in the present case, such a relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding objects) does not exist; for since the common attribute of "charmingness" is already perceived in both the eyes and the lotuses, there is no dependence on any further attribute.

This must be stated: if that were so, then even in the verse by Bhavabhūti, “*yāntyā muhurvalitakandharamānanaṃ tadāvṛttavṛntaśatapatranibhaṃ vahantyā*,” the acceptance by all rhetoricians of the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) between the neck and the stalk, and the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding things) between the qualities of being bent (*valita*) and turned back (*āvṛtta*), would be contradicted—since the comparison could be sustained by the common property of beauty alone, which is what is actually perceived. Therefore, the matter remains exactly as it was originally stated.

Even though they do not exist [in reality], they are figuratively attributed [to you]: "Alas! O lotus-eyed one, even the greatness of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the gods sink, as it were, into the ocean of your greatness like the principal mountain ranges. (99)
In this context, "immersion" (majjana) is a property of material substances metaphorically attributed to greatness (mahiman).

Or rather, O Lord, though Your deceitful heart has been forcibly entered by me during my daily practice, it does not melt at all—just as iron, even when cast into the ocean, remains exceedingly hard. 100.

The word "samudre" (in the ocean) also connects with the latter half of the phrase "prasabhaṃ praveśitam" (forcibly entered). "Ghanataram" means as if it were solid iron, like black metal (*kāla-ayas*). Here, because entering and melting are attributes of material substances, they are metaphorically attributed (*upacāra*) to the heart.
An example of that which consists of *śleṣa* (punning):

"Possessing the splendor of a most beautiful *tāla* tree, resting upon the heart of the Lord of the Earth who is like the *añjana* mountain, and spreading with fragrance, she is like a wonderful forest garland (*vanamālā*). (101)

She whose true and praised glory (*śrī*) consists of beautiful *tamāla* and *tāpiñcha* trees; alternatively, the compound is analyzed as "she whose splendor (*śrī*) is exceedingly lovely (*mañjulatama*) and radiant (*lasat*)," meaning she is most charming.
