She has reached the heart—the central region and the chest—of the Lord of the mountain bearing collyrium (the great mountain named Añjana); alternatively, she has reached the heart of the Blessed Lord, the Master of Veṅkaṭādri.

She whose fragrance—a particular kind of sweet scent—is spreading and diffusing; elsewhere, she in whom there is the intense joy (*āmoda*) of *sṛmara* deer, that is, great yak-like antelopes (*mahācamarī*). According to Amara, "sṛmara," "gavaya," and "śaśa" are names for specific types of deer. Like a forest garland—that is, like a row of woods—the Vaijayantī [garland] is variegated and wondrous with its birds (*vibhiḥ*).

In the alternative view, the meaning is that [the row of trees] is variegated by virtue of having five colors, according to the manner stated in the verse: "The Vaijayantī garland of the Wielder of the Mace indeed possesses five colors. Here, the common attribute is established through the pun (*śleṣa*) between the "row of forest trees" and the "Vaijayantī [garland]. Others maintain that because there is no single object residing in both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the common attribute is the word itself.

Just as the rainy season— resplendent with peacocks that sing of its own majestic power and possessing the lofty brilliance of thick clouds— appeases the thirst of the world, so too does this friend of Ramā, whose intense luster is exalted by the peacock-like sages who sing of the greatness of his own sovereign majesty, pacify the cravings of the worlds.

He is so described because he has as his singers (*gāyakāḥ*) the *mayus* (peacocks) and *kinnaras*, who proclaim the greatness of his own majesty (*nijavibhavamahima*). According to Amara: “The *kinnara*, *kiṃpuruṣa*, and *turaṅgavadana* are called *mayu*. He is radiant like the sun (*ravibhrāṭ*), shining like the sun. In the case of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), he is one whose splendor (*tejaḥ*) is noble (*udātta*), excellent (*śreṣṭha*), dense (*ghana*), and thick (*sāndra*). However, in the case of the rainy season (*varṣāsamaya*), he is radiant (*vibhrāṭ*), that is, shining, through those peacocks who are the singers of the greatness of its own majesty by means of their cries of *kekā*.

He is described as one in whom the splendor of the clouds is exalted; he pacifies thirst, the quarters of the sky, and the desire for water. Here too, there is a common attribute produced by *śleṣa* (paronomasia). An example of a property based on the employment of different types of compounds is as follows:

"O Śauri, your body—with its fleshy [or prominent] conch-shell, beautiful eyes [or Sudarśana discus], and the whorls of hair [or the curls of a swan]—is like the Yamunā river, which possesses thick conch-shells, beautiful lotuses, and lotus-stalks, and has calmed the immeasurable waves of worldly existence. (103)

"Plump and broad, with beautiful conch-like [shoulders] and beautiful swan-like whorls"—thus it is described as having beautiful conch-like [shoulders] and beautiful swan-like whorls. In another sense, the compound means "whorls like those of a swan, resembling beautiful conchs. It is further described as "possessing a lotus-stalk together with the navel" (*nābhernālīkaṃ tena saha vartate*). In another sense, the compound means "lotuses (*nālīkāni*) which exist together with the central pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the navel. Or alternatively, the compound means "possessing a lotus-stalk (*nālīka*) equal to the navel, together with that."

"Bhava is like Damunā, like Agni"—in this alternative, the compound is analyzed as "one who is similar to Bhava and is Damunā. Thus, by resorting to different types of compounds, there is a common attribute (*samānadharmatā*). Some do not regard this common attribute as distinct, because they achieve the state of being a single attribute through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on *śleṣa* (punning coalescence) between the two meanings produced by the different compounds. Their intention is that even this [type of comparison] is included within the common attribute itself when it consists of *śleṣa*.

Regarding the blending [of figures], it is the combination of two properties that have entered into the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) while being mutually pervasive, as follows:

"In this world, a person devoted to the Lotus-Eyed One is praiseworthy—like a tree laden with fruit, like a pool of the Ganges filled with water, and like a sovereign of the earth possessed of power. (104)

In this instance, the qualities of "being devoted to the Lord" and "possessing fruitfulness," which have entered into the relationship of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), abide as non-different from the common, accompanying quality (*anugāmī dharma*) of "praiseworthiness. Or, for example: "Even those born of the *sumanas* lineage, if they are mere *kheṭas* (flies) ignorant of the excellence of Your greatness, are to be shunned from afar like insects, even though they too are born of the *sumanas* lineage. (105) [Note: In the first case, the two specific qualities are reflected in the general quality of praiseworthiness; in the second, the word *sumanas* (flower/devotee) is used twice with different meanings, while the word *kheṭa* (fly/ignorant person) serves as the common ground.]

In the lineage of the wise, within the second half of the cluster of flowers belonging to the *sumanaḥ* (jasmine) family, are born "wretches" (*kheṭāḥ*), meaning contemptible persons; for Amara states: "The words *kupūya*, *kutsita*, *avadya*, *kheṭa*, *garhya*, and *aṇaka* are synonyms. Here, the common property of being fit to be shunned from afar—which belongs both to the contemptible people who are ignorant of the perfection of the Lord’s majesty and to insects—is established by means of the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) between their respective qualities of being born in a lineage of the wise and being produced from a cluster of flowers.

Just as a great mountain-king among birds is difficult for men to reach due to its height and lack of fruit, yet easy to access because of its level peaks; so too, O Protector, you are difficult to attain through others' lack of virtue, yet easy to approach because of your own sublime conduct. (106)

In this instance, the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharma*)—which consists of being difficult to attain and being easy to understand, respectively, and which exists by virtue of the relationship between original and reflection regarding loftiness and fruitfulness—is a pervasive one that follows both [the subjects] through their qualities of supreme nobility (*paratva*) and excellent character (*sauśīlya*). The distinction here is that the first [example] takes the form of a *mālā* (garland), while the second is mixed with *yamaka* (rhyme), and the third is mixed with *yathāsaṅkhya* (correspondence).

O Infinite One, just as kings who are not bowed down before an emperor yet do not overstep their bounds, so too do those whose faces are like the lotus-seated Brahmā bear Your command upon their heads. 107.

The word *samrāj* (emperor) is a term ending in the genitive case. Here, it should be understood that qualities such as "not bowing down" (*anamratva*) and so forth—though they are general attributes—derive their existence by depending on the relationship between the Lord and the Emperor as original image and reflection.
Or, for example:
O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents, the region of Your heart shines like the ocean reflecting the moon and stars, with its excellent pearls and gems polished smooth by the waves. (108)

The *maṇivara* is the Kaustubha gem. Thus, the blending (*miśraṇa*) should also be observed in the verse previously cited, "ānandanilaya" (the abode of bliss). This is the blending of two elements that follow the relationship of pure *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflected image).

The blending of two dharmas—the state of being a reflected image and its counterpart, which are interwoven through the qualities of following and the relationship between object and its correspondence—is as follows:
"O Supreme Self, you are approached by people through devotion to your knowledge and dispassion, appearing like a tree resplendent with flowers, fruits, and sprouts."

"Abhyuditaḥ" means having attained exaltation (*abhyudaya*). Here, there is a relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (original object and its counterpart) between "being risen" (*abhyuditatva*) and "being radiant" (*samullasitatva*). Furthermore, there is a relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and its reflection) between the Lord’s knowledge, devotion, and dispassion—characterized by those [qualities]—and the flowers, fruits, and sprouts. Thus, this quality (*dharma*), consisting of those [elements], attains non-difference with the accompanying quality (*anugāmin dharma*) that follows upon the approach.

"O Hari, just as an elephant sinks when caught in a thicket of reeds or becomes stuck in the mouth of a crocodile, who other than you could bring me security from my desire? (110)" The address "O Hari" is intended to signify the granting of boons to the king of elephants, since it was in an incarnation as Hari that the Lord liberated Gajendra. Here, there is a relationship of *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (correspondence of things) between "sinking" (*vinimagna*) and "being stuck" (*lagna*); furthermore, there is a relationship of *bimba-pratibimba-bhāva* (original and reflection) between the "thicket of reeds" (*vṛjinavraja*) and the "mouth of the crocodile" (*makaramukha*), which serve as the respective qualifiers for those two states.

The mixing of these two—“I sink by leaning upon that” and “having attained existence”—is as follows: nor should it be argued that because the states of being submerged and being attached are distinct, the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (correspondence between the primary object and its counterpart) is impossible; for since immersion in a mass of sins is impossible, what is intended there is merely the state of connection, and thus the two possess a single form.

Just as a king of bees is captivated by a cluster of flowers with dense petals, so too does Hari, resting upon the crest of the serpent whose hoods are composed of thick, cool sapphire gems, steal the heart of the mind. 111.

Here, although "uninterruptedness" (*avirala*) and "denseness" (*ghana*) are in reality of a single nature, because they are expressed by two distinct words, there is the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding object and counter-object). This applies to the petals and the rays which possess those respective qualifiers. Likewise, there is the relation of *vastu-prativastu* between "stillness" (*stimitatva*) and "dissolution" (*vilīnatva*).

There is a relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) between the two subjects (*viśeṣya*), namely the flower-cluster and the sapphire mountain; thus, this attribute, being interwoven with them, remains in a state of non-difference from the accompanying attribute that effects the enchantment. This constitutes their "mixture" (*miśraṇa*). In the two previous examples, there was a *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (correspondence of things) between the subjects; here, however, there is a twofold *vastu-prativastu-bhāva*—between the subject and the qualifier—which is the distinction.

In some cases, there is a causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*), as in the following example: "The lotus-eyed Lord, the source of accessibility, should be resorted to by all men, just as a cluster of lotuses, the birthplace of fragrance, is sought by swarms of bees. Here, "source of accessibility" (*janisthāna*) and "birthplace of fragrance" (*janmabhūmi*) stand in the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (original and counterpart). Their respective qualifiers, "accessibility" (*saulabhya*) and "fragrance" (*saurabhya*), stand in the relation of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflection). The common property of being "resorted to" (*sevyatva*) by both the lotus-eyed Lord and the cluster of lotuses serves as the cause (*hetu*). It should be noted that this type of "blending" (*miśraṇa*) occurs even when there is a pure *bimba-pratibimba* relationship.
An example of the blending of *anugāmitva* (pervasive correspondence) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:
"This excellent mountain Narasiṃha, bearing upon its peak the orb of the moon filled with beautiful digits, bestows joy upon all the worlds, like the Mountain of Sunrise bearing the lunar disc. (113)

"Filled with all the arts (sakalābhipūrṇa) through the placement of the mantra and the Lord of Mantras, she too possesses the embodiment of the six attributes (ṣāḍguṇyavigrahā)"—according to this stated method, the meaning in the context of the image of the Blessed Lord is that it is completely filled with all the arts. In other cases, however, it is quite clear: "The lunar orb, the image of Śrīnivāsa, and the six attributes surpassing all others reside in both the mantra and the image.
Therefore, the Blessed Lord is to be worshipped directly [in them], never with the thought that they are merely ritual accessories."

Thus, the words of the Blessed One’s scriptures should be considered here. Elsewhere, the meaning is "the lunar disc. Here, by relying on the pun (*śleṣa*) on the words "the full moon's disc" (*sukalābhipūrṇavidhubimba*), the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) that follows is the bestowing of joy upon all the worlds, which has attained its own established state.

Just as a person of demonic character does not attain clear knowledge even when well-instructed—just as charcoal, O Acyuta, remains of a soiled nature even when polished on a whetstone—so too is the mixture of *śleṣa*, *vastu-prativastu-bhāva*, and *bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*.
This creation of beings is of two kinds: the divine and the demonic.
One who is devoted to Viṣṇu is divine, while one who is the opposite is demoniac.

The meaning is that, in the manner described above, he is of an asura nature. Even though he has been thoroughly instructed—that is, properly taught—the knowledge of Brahman, which is called "that knowledge which leads to liberation," he does not attain clarity, which is the realization of the supreme reality.
As it is said: "Whatever intellect was cultivated by a living being in thousands of previous births, to that very same one he resorts; instruction is useless."

The meaning is that they are incapable of understanding because of such statements as "those of an asura-nature are not able to comprehend. In the secondary sense (pakṣe), "clarity" (*vaiśadya*) means whiteness; the rest is easy to understand. Here, there is a relationship of reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) based on the arrangement of *vastu* and *prativastu* between the states of being "asura-like in character" and "having a dark nature. This is because "character" (*śīla*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*), which are in reality identical, are designated by two different words; and because "asura" and "dark," which are in reality non-different, are identified as one through their similarity (*sārūpya*) despite having those [two terms] as their respective qualifiers.

Between the state of being thoroughly trained in knowledge and the state of being polished on a whetstone, there exists merely the relationship of original and reflection. It should be understood that the common attribute—namely, the failure to attain clarity—is applied through a pun (*śliṣṭa*) and is thus intensified by those two [qualities].
An example of the blending of paronomasia (śleṣa), metaphorical treatment (upacāra), the relation of original and reflection (bimba-pratibimba-bhāva), and intermixture (miśraṇa) is as follows:
"Like learning, this Śrī, who is like the Supreme Brahman himself to the discerning man, shines forth in the heart-lotus of Vṛṣagiri, the lord of mountains."

Just as learning—such as the knowledge of poetry, prosody, grammar, and so forth—is present in a discerning person endowed with wisdom, so too is Śrī, that is, Lakṣmī, present in the Supreme Brahman, Śrīnivāsa, who is directly before us; she dwells in his heart (*hṛdayasthā*), meaning she is held within his mind and is not stale. [The suffix] *yat* is applied to the word *hṛdaya* in the sense of "being in" (bhavārtha), because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. In the other sense, she is "beloved of the heart" (*hṛdayapriyā*), where *yat* is applied according to the rule "that which is dear to the heart. In both cases, the substitution of *hṛd* for *hṛdaya* occurs by the rule "in place of *hṛdaya*, there is *hṛt* when followed by *lekha*, *ya*, *aṇ*, or *lāsa*."
"Cetohṛt" means captivating or heart-stealing; "padya," "śloka," and "kāvya" have the same meaning. It "illuminates" (ujjvalayati), which is to say, it causes [the truth] to proceed.

In the auspicious interpretation (*śrīpakṣe*), the division [of the verse] is into three words: *itaḥ*, *hṛt*, and *iti*. The word *ca* (and) is displaced in its position. *Itaḥ* is the suffix *tasi* used in all case-endings; its meaning is "of this Śrīnivāsa. *Hṛt* means the chest. *Padyam* means that which is visible (*dṛśyam*) on the foot (*pade*); the meaning is that it is marked by the soles of his own feet smeared with red lac (*yāvaka*). Alternatively, it means "in such a way that it is visible on the foot. The suffix *yat* is used in the sense already stated, derived from the word *pada* according to the rule: "The suffix *yat* occurs when something is visible on this [foot]."

The meaning is that it "makes [it] blaze," which is to say, it illuminates it as being superior to the Kaustubha gem and others. The short vowel [in *ujjvalayati*] occurs because the root *jval* takes the suffix *ṇic*, followed by the present tense marker (*laṭ*), and is subject to the *mit* designation due to its inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group. In this context, one should consider such verses as: “The full splendor flashes forth, mingled with the lac-dye of Your feet. Here, there is the relationship of original and reflection between the wise observer and the Supreme Brahman. There is a pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *hṛdya*, meaning both "pleasing" and "the lotus of the heart," and there is a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) in the sense of "making [it] blaze"; these elements are thus blended.

O Śrīparibṛḍha, your followers wander throughout the entire world like lamps of exquisite beauty—treasuries of great luster and repositories of noble fame—who possess a continuous flow of union between the original and the reflection, the substance and the counterpart, and the intermingling of forms and their reflections, as if they were the very embodiments of existence itself. (116)

The construction is as follows: "Your noble [disciples], being repositories of brilliant splendor like lamps and treasuries of good fame, wander through the worlds as if through their own homes. Here, "noble" (*abhirūpa*) means both "charming" and "learned. As Amarasimha states: "The words *prāptarūpa*, *surūpa*, and *abhirūpa* denote one who is wise and pleasing."

In this passage, there is a mere relationship of reflection (bimba-pratibimba) between the house and the celestial realm; a relationship of object and counter-object (vastu-prativastu) between the treasure and the hoard; and a relationship of reflection between the splendor and the fame that qualify those two subjects. This is combined with a pun (śleṣa) on the word *abhirūpa* (beautiful/attractive) which incorporates those elements, and with the pervasive quality (anugāmitva) of the word *saṃcaranti* (they move about); thus, there is a blending of these figures.

An example of the mixture of the figures *anugāmitva* (pervasive similarity), *śleṣa* (paronomasia), *bimba-pratibimba-bhāva* (the relation of prototype and reflection), and *upacāra* (metaphorical identification) is as follows:
"O Enemy of Mura, people drink your conduct—which is celebrated everywhere in the world and arises from your expansive eloquence—as if it were nectar; they drink it like gods. (117)

*Sārasvatam* means that which has come from Sarasvatī; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* in the sense of "come from that" (*tata āgataḥ*). *Uditam* means that whose rising (*udayaḥ*) is its manifestation (*āvirbhāvaḥ*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which is both extensive (*pravitatam*) and *sārasvatoditam*," meaning it is vast and produced from the ocean of milk. Alternatively, *sārasvatāni* refers to those scriptures (*śāstrāṇi*) which are manifestations of Sarasvatī, as seen in such usage as "the ocean of milk of the *Sārasvata*" (*yatsārasvatadugdhasāgara*). By these [scriptures], it is *uditam*, i.e., proclaimed (*udīritam*).

Here, "spread everywhere" (*samantātprathitatva*) is the common property (*anugāmī*); "proclaimed by the far-reaching Sarasvatī" (*pravitatasārasvatodita*) is the *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) one; and "those who drink" (*pibanti*), which has entered into the relationship of prototype and reflection between the nectar and the conduct, is the metaphorical (*upacarita*) common property—thus there is a blending (*miśraṇa*) of these. In this way, other mixtures should also be inferred by the wise; because this subject is vast, we have provided only a mere indication (*diṅmātra*). As it is said in the *Kāvyāloka*: "Since the wise provide a conceptualization that serves as the basis for both metaphor and simile, only a mere indication has been shown; what was not mentioned should be inferred."

"These varieties of *dharmabheda* exist only when [the common property] is explicit (*pūrṇā*). However, when it is elided (*luptā*), such varieties do not exist, because in that case there is a rule that the common property must be pervasive (*anugāmitva*)," so says the author of the *Citramīmāṃsā*. But the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* does not accept this restriction. Thus states his text: "As for what was said by Appayadīkṣita—that 'in the case of the elided [common property], however, there are no such varieties, because in that case there is a rule that the common property must be pervasive'..."

Therefore, in the verse "In the world, Pāṇḍu was like the Malaya mountain; Dhṛtarāṣṭra was like an anthill upon the earth," since there is no cognition of a common property (*anugāmidharma*), one understands only the relationship of original and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) between the sandalwood trees and the Pāṇḍavas, and between the serpents and Duryodhana and his kin. Furthermore, it is not appropriate for the learned to insist that being expressed by words (*śabdopāttatva*) is the sole determinant for the relationship of original and reflection, because it is proper that this relationship exists in two forms: as one based on direct verbal expression (*śrauta*) and one based on implied meaning (*ārtha*).

For this very reason, he stated: “In figures such as Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant), the comparison between the contextual and non-contextual sentence-meanings—which is based on the relationship between a whole and its reflection—is logically consistent. Furthermore, there is this distinction here: when only the reflection is mentioned between the two, the defect of the “loss of attributes” (*dharmahāni*) applies to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because the attributes corresponding to that [reflection] are not stated there. However, when only the original object (*bimba*) is mentioned, the defect of the “excess of attributes” (*dharmādhikya*) applies to the standard of comparison, because the attributes corresponding to that [original object] are not stated in the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Therefore, they say that the truth is this: it is intended that both [the original and the reflection], having entered into the state of being the prototype (bimba) and the reflection (pratibimba), are either both verbal or both objective; it is not the case that one is verbal while the other is objective. And thus, it is established that in some instances, even a property understood through the meaning may exist in the form of a prototype and its reflection.

Just as the grounds of the Nandana forest belong to Indra, so too is this land of bliss the domain of the Lord; like the beloved of the mountain of serpents, he is preeminent like the noble Himālaya. 118

Since "Ānandabhūmidhara" and "Śeṣādri" are recorded among its names as "Ānandādri," the statement [is justified] by the verse cited below from the twenty-ninth chapter: "In the Cintāmaṇidharaṇībhṛt. Here, because no other common attributes such as "followers" are perceived between the Nandana forest and the Śeṣādri mountain on one hand, and the Himācala and Śrīnivāsa on the other, the relationship between the Kalpataru and Śrīnivāsa, and between the Gaṅgā and Dayā, is understood solely as that of the original and its reflection; thus, a simile (upamā) is established. As for example: [The verse follows: *yathāvā*... [rest of the verse omitted].

This very goddess, who dwells upon the mountain peak frequented by those who subsist on air, is like the treasury-chamber of the Lord of Wealth; she is like a mine, and she is the supreme deity who is the beloved of the Daughter of the Ocean. 119.

The supreme deity Śrīnivāsa is the one who possesses love for the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī); this is the meaning. Here, since no other shared attributes—such as being a follower—are perceived between the two primary subjects, namely the summit of Śeṣācala and the treasury-house of Kubera, as well as between the Lord and the treasure, it should be understood that the simile is established solely through the relationship of the original object and its reflection between the Lord’s qualities and the jewels.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on Simile (Upamā), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now, the Figure of Speech of Reciprocal Simile (Upameyopamā):
Reciprocal Simile occurs when there is a mutual relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.
If the reverse of the two preceding [cases] is stated again subsequently, [it is a repetition]. || 23 ||

The meaning of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile) is that where, in the first comparison, the object of comparison (*upameya*) serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the second, and the standard of comparison therein serves as the object of comparison.

Just as the forest-garland (vanamālā), like the young maiden of the forest-treasure (the Earth), shines while moving upon the heart of Śrī Vāsudeva; so too does the young maiden of the forest-treasure, possessing a radiant web of virtues, shine forth like the forest-garland. In this verse, the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is described through the distinction between two sentences for the "young maiden of the forest-treasure" and the "forest-garland. In the first sentence, the status of the standard of comparison belongs to Śrī and the status of the object of comparison to the forest-garland; in the second, however, it is the reverse. Thus, the definition [of *pratīpam*] is fully applicable.

When the similarity of Lakṣmī and Vanamālā is stated by one person with respect to another, the similarity of that [second person] with yet another is established by implication; however, when this is explicitly stated in words, it results in the exclusion of a third similar object. In this example, the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is conceived between two subjects alone; yet, as established in the *Kuvalayānanda*, this figure is possible even between a subject and a non-subject.
In this regard, there is this example:
"This lord of the world shines like Kubera, and this Kubera shines like the lord of the world;
this Lakṣmī is as fickle as lightning, and even lightning gleams like Lakṣmī. (121)

The Lord of the World is the Blessed One, and *capalā* is lightning. Here, both the Lord of the World and Kamalā constitute the *prakṛti* (the subject), as indicated by the demonstrative pronouns "this" (*eṣaḥ*) and "this" (*eṣā*). Furthermore, this [type of simile] is of two kinds: that whose attributes are explicitly stated (*uktadharma*) and that whose attributes are suggested (*vyaṅgyadharma*). First, the type with explicitly stated attributes is manifold through the previously mentioned attributes such as "corresponding" (*anugāmī*) and so forth. Among these, the corresponding attribute has already been illustrated in the immediately preceding example by the words "shines" (*lasati*) and "blazes" (*cakāsti*).

May he who has attained the state of being both the original object and its reflection—like the king of jars [the moon] amidst the waves of the ocean enveloped by autumn clouds; like Mount Mandara bearing serpents, yet appearing like Mandara bearing serpents—shine forth. 122.

The suffix *liṅ* in "vibhāyāt" is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). Here, the attribute consisting of the autumnal cloud, the water-jar, and the ocean wave—which has attained the state of mutual reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*)—is embellished by two qualifying attributes, "being enveloped" (*parivītatva*) and "being situated in the middle" (*madhyagatatva*), which have entered into a relationship of mutual correspondence (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*).
It consists merely of the relationship between a thing and its counterpart (*vastu-prativastu*), as for example:

"The two cheeks of the one whose abode is the lotus are stainless and like mirrors of polished diamond; the two mirrors of polished diamond resemble the stainless cheeks of the one whose abode is the lotus. (123)
In this instance, there is merely the relationship of object and counter-object between purity and extreme smoothness.

Just as the rays of the moon, when honored, clarify the world, so too do the feet of the devotees of Madhumathana; and just as the rays of the moon are cool and smooth, so too are the feet of the devotees of Madhumathana.

Here, the phrase "cool and smooth" (śiśirimamasṛṇāḥ) should also be construed with the first half of the verse. Furthermore, the expression "making [them] clear" (viśadayanti) is used figuratively. In the term *bhaktacaraṇāḥ*, the word *caraṇa* denotes one worthy of reverence, as in expressions such as *gurucaraṇāḥ*.
An example of that which consists of *śleṣa* (punning):

"Is she an elephant-mate, whose own luster is rippled by the spray of the far-spreading nectar from her blossoming trunk-tips; or is she a lotus-pool, whose beauty is rippled by the spray of the far-spreading nectar from its blossoming lotuses? Like an elephant-mate dwelling on a mountain of sandalwood, she is like a lotus-pool. (125)

The lotus-pond situated on the Ahiśaila mountain is like a female elephant (kariṇī); here, the word "vā" functions as a term of comparison. It is that whose own luster, radiance, and sweetness are exceedingly enhanced—made wavy, as it were—by the spray of nectar and droplets of water spreading forth from the blossomed *puṣkaras*, which are lotuses; elsewhere, [the same applies] to the blossomed *puṣkara* which is the tip of the trunk. Herein lies the common attribute shared by the lotus-pond (*puṣkariṇī*) and the female elephant (*kariṇī*), expressed through the figure of *śleṣa* (punning paronomasia) in the word "blossomed" (*vikasita*) and so forth.
The suggested qualities are as follows:

the daughter of the ocean is like the wish-fulfilling creeper, and alas, the wish-fulfilling creeper is like her; Kṛṣṇa’s heart is like the Nandana grove, and the Nandana grove is like his heart. (126)

This very same [type of simile] is also of the "successive" (paramparita) form; likewise in the verse previously cited beginning with "like Ghanapati. All of these have been elaborated upon where the difference in sentence structure is manifest.
But when there is a difference in meaning within the sentence, as for example:
"Whatever is the fortune of the Venkata mountain and whatever is the excellence of the milk of the Sindhu cow—that couple manifests in this abode with mutual splendors that rival one another."

Here, regarding the "mutual comparison of sovereignty," from the concise statement, two explanatory sentences emerge: namely, that "this person's sovereignty is similar to that person's sovereignty" and "that person's sovereignty is similar to this person's sovereignty. In the expression *saubhāgyaṃ daugdhasaindhavam*, there is a vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) of both members of the compound according to the rule *hṛdbhagasindhvante*. Likewise, almost all varieties of this [type of simile], such as the complete (*pūrṇā*) and the elided (*luptā*), are possible, just as they are for the standard simile (*upamā*).
In this regard, a mere illustration is given:
as is discipline, so too is policy; O Acyuta, for people, renown is like prosperity, and prosperity is likewise like renown.
The regard for the future is equal to the present, and likewise the future is to be regarded as equal to the present; depression is similar to elevation, and elevation is also similar to depression.
O Lord of the Earth, King of Serpents, your fortitude triumphs like your intellect, and your intellect like your fortitude; such is this abundant prosperity—could it ever have been yours before? 130.

These three verses constitute a *viśeṣaka* because they form a single syntactical unit, according to the definition: "A *yugma* is said to consist of two [verses], while a *viśeṣaka* consists of three verses. The phrase "is victorious" (*vijayate*), found in the final verse, connects with all the preceding statements by virtue of being a common attribute.

In this regard, the fivefold *pūrṇopameyopamā*—both *śrautī* (expressed by a word) and *ārthī* (implied by sense)—is to be understood as follows: in the first half-verse, there is the *śrautī* expressed by a derivative suffix (*taddhitagā*); in the second half-verse, there is the *śrautī* expressed by a sentence (*vākyagā*), because the rule for compounding with the particle *iva* is prescribed; in the third half-verse, there is the *ārthī* expressed by a sentence; in the fourth half-verse, there is the *ārthī* expressed by a compound (*samāsagā*); and in the fifth [half-verse], there is the *ārthī* expressed by a derivative suffix. Thus, the five varieties of the *pūrṇopameyopamā* are to be observed.

In this very context, if the first half of the third verse were read as "O Lord of the Serpent Mountain, even the intellect is like fortitude, and fortitude is like the intellect," then because the attribute (*dharma*) is not explicitly mentioned, all five types [of *vācakaluptā*] would become cases where the expressive word is elided. Furthermore, we have already stated that a *śrautī* type of *dharmaluptā* is impossible when occurring in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

The Veṅkaṭādri indeed acts as Meru; Śrīveṅkaṭādri fulfills all desires; the celestial Gaṅgā (Abhragaṅgā) acts like the Gaṅgā; and the Gaṅgā acts like the celestial Gaṅgā. By the two terms "Abhragaṅgā" and "Surapathagaṅgā," the celestial Gaṅgā located on Veṅkaṭādri is meant, according to the statement in the *Brahma-purāṇa*: "The Svāmipuṣkariṇī itself, and thereafter the Viyadgaṅgā. Here, with the suffixes *kvip* and *kyaṅ*, there is a *dharmavācakaluptopamā* (elliptical simile where the common property is expressed).
Following this very method, other varieties of this [simile] should be inferred by those possessed of creative intuition (*pratibhā*) as far as possible.
Thus ends the second lake, on the Simile of the Compared with the Comparer, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the lake on Non-Comparison (*ananvaya*):
non-comparison occurs when a single thing serves as both the standard of comparison and the object compared.

Where the relationship of both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is attributed to one and the same thing, there is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence). This is based on the etymological derivation that even when being described, its own similarity with itself does not correspond. Just as in the *arthavāda* passages concerning Rudra’s weeping or the cutting off of his arms, the composition of an unreal matter—which serves as praise or censure—is employed for the sake of praise or censure; likewise, the description of a thing’s similarity with itself, though lacking correspondence, is employed to illuminate its incomparability by excluding any second peer.

Thus, it is concluded that *ananvaya* (self-comparison) is a similarity where there is a single object of comparison and a single subject of comparison, which is the subject of a description whose result is the exclusion of any second similar thing. And this [similarity] is an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) when it serves as an embellishment for something else; otherwise, however, it rests merely in its own distinctiveness. The same applies to other ornaments as well.
While the Blessed One wanders nearby, the summit of Mount Mecakīma-vṛṣa shines as if strewn with clouds swelling forth in the rainy season.

In this context, the peak of the serpent-mountain (Śeṣa), which is made to bristle with joy by its delight in the divine form of Śrīnivāsa, is compared by the poet himself to a mountain covered in blue clouds during the rainy season. To preclude such a comparison, the epithet "consisting of the elements" (*bhūtānta*) is employed; for here, the purpose of describing similarity is not the exclusion of a second peer (*sabrahmacārī*), as no such counterpart is perceived.
In the face of Hari, whose abode is the mountain Pṛdāku, the radiance of his smile shines like the dense moonlight upon a night-lotus blossomed by the rays of the autumnal sun. 133.

Thus, in order to prevent an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding this type of simile where the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is imagined, it is specified that there must be "one and the same" object of comparison and subject of comparison. Here, because the non-existent object of comparison is made existent through imagination, there arises the cognition of an exclusion of a second similar thing, based on the fact that a real object of comparison exists. An example: "O Blessed One, let the Veda describe you as being beyond the three kinds of limits; let it describe you as peerless. Yet, upon careful reflection, there is indeed no simile for you—indeed, you alone [are the standard]. (134)

The Veda declares You—who are described as such because Your threefold limitation (avadhi) regarding space, time, and substance has been shaken off—to be "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" according to the Śruti; and that You are "unequaled," meaning devoid of a second object similar to You, according to the Śruti: "No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen. The sense is "resembling a comparison" (upamāsadṛśa), for Amara states: "A likeness, resemblance, or comparison shall be called a pratikṛti, upamā, or upamāna. There is also the usage: "O mango tree, no comparison for You was found by the bee in this world."

Or rather, just as you have searched the entire world and even understood the true nature of those [who dwell within it], O Lord of the Mountain, you alone are the source for granting the desires of supplicants; there is none equal to you. 135.

*Tīrthagiri* is merely another name for Śeṣādri; for its etymology is given in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*: "Because it consists of all sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), the wise call it Tīrthādri. The distinction is that in the preceding verse, the quality of being "supremely excellent" was the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) persistent attribute, whereas here, the act of "granting the desires of those who seek them" is the expressed (*vācya*) one. In both cases, however, this is an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) because it serves to embellish the love directed toward the Lord.

However, there is no property here that has entered into the state of being both the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). And if such a property existed, then because there would be no sublation to the connection of a self-identity characterized by some property with itself as characterized by another property, and because there would be no comprehension of the exclusion of other similar things, *ananvaya* (non-concomitance) would not even exist. This *ananvaya* is of two kinds: complete (*pūrṇa*) and elliptical (*lupta*). The complete type, moreover, can be of six varieties, just like the simile (*upamā*).
Just as Śrī is Fortune, so is she of profound compassion; like Kamalā, she is full of auspiciousness. The Lord is equal to Acyuta and is indeed Acyuta himself; Hari is dear to him and is like Hari.

Just as the Lord of Śrī Veṅkaṭādri is our supreme goal, so too is the Lord of Śrī Veṅkaṭādri alone; just as devotion to the feet of Śrī Śrīnivāsa is our [goal], so too is the state of Śrīnivāsa alone.

In this pair [of verses], in the first quarter, there is a complete, scripturally based (śrauta) *ananvaya* residing in a sentence. In the second quarter, there is a complete, scripturally based *ananvaya* residing in a compound (*samāsaga*), because of the rule prescribing a compound with the word *iva*. From "O Lord" (*nātha*) up to "indeed Acyuta" (*evācyuta*), there is a complete, meaning-based (*ārtha*) *ananvaya* residing in a compound. In the remaining fourth quarter, beginning with "Hari," there is a complete, meaning-based *ananvaya* residing in a compound. In the first half of the second verse, because the suffix *vati* is present in the phrase "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*), there is a complete, meaning-based *ananvaya* residing in a secondary derivative (*taddhitaga*).

It should be understood that in the second half of that [verse], because the suffix *vat* exists in the phrase "tatra tasyeva," it is a complete simile based on the suffix (*taddhitaga*). Even when [the words] are elided, all five types of elided similes (*dharmalupta*) are possible; these will occur through the substitution of other words in the manner of "kamalā yathaiva kamaletyādi," by removing the word expressing the common attribute (*dharmavācakapada*) from the two verses mentioned previously.
The *vācakalupta* (omission of the word) also occurs in this way:
"This great Veṅkaṭabhūmidhara acts like Veṅkaṭabhūmidhara; the Lord dwelling there, resplendent with the Lord who dwells there, is victorious."
In this [verse], there is the elision of the expressive element (*vācakalupta*) in both the *kyac* and the compound:
"Beholding the Lord of the Vṛṣabha Mountain, seeing the Lord of the Vṛṣabha Mountain before me, with tears of widespread joy, I rejoice constantly in my own joy.

(139) Seeing the "Vṛṣabhādrināthadarśa" as if he were the Lord of the Vṛṣabha Mountain himself, I rejoice in my own joy (*sannanda*), just as [the Lord] rejoices. Here, there is the elision of the expressive element in both the *namul* suffix and the object-agentive construction.

On the chest of the Lord who dwells on the mountain of the serpent-king, this gem is Kaustubha because it shines like Kaustubha; the mark is Lakṣma because it possesses Lakṣmī; the necklace is Hāra because it takes away (removes) weariness; and the daughter of the ocean is Sindhuduhitarati because she delights in the Ocean’s daughter.
In this case, there is the elision of both the object and the word expressing it. This very same [figure], when consisting of a series, is also called *ananvaya* (non-correspondence).

How many gods are there who do not compare themselves to the ocean in depth? Yet this Lord of Śeṣagiri possesses a depth that follows [surpasses] that of Śeṣagiri itself. (141) In this instance, there is an elision of the expressive word (*vācaka*), the quality (*dharma*), and the object of comparison (*upamāna*). Furthermore, other varieties such as the elision of the object of comparison (*upamānalupta*) have not been illustrated here because they are either impossible or lack aesthetic appeal (*acārutva*).

First, this much should be noted here: generally, when a poetic figure such as simile (*upamā*) is suggested as the primary element by means of an entire sentence, it is then designated as "suggestion" (*dhvani*), while the status of being a mere poetic figure is set aside. And in this case, the designation of a "poetic figure" is based merely on contact with the properties belonging to ornaments like necklaces and so forth—which are themselves currently not functioning as ornaments—just as necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings are designated as such even when placed inside a casket or similar container. Among these, first, the suggestion of simile (*upamā-dhvani*) should be illustrated.

And this simile is, in some cases, the domain of resonance rooted in the power of words (śabdaśaktimūla-anudhvani), and in other cases, the domain of resonance rooted in the power of meaning (arthaśaktimūla-anudhvani).
Among these, the first is as follows:

Like a *puṃnāga* tree radiant with its golden bracelets, its great fortune enhanced by the presence of Gandharvas, the mountain-crest jewel possesses the splendor of the abode of Śrī, which is not small.

It is so described because it possesses brilliant *punnāga* trees—a specific species of tree—and *puṃgaja* trees upon its ridges (*kaṭaka*), plateaus (*sānu*), and capital cities (*rājadhānī*). According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *kaṭaka* denotes a bracelet, a plateau, a capital city, and a mountain slope. It bears the state of being the abode of non-trivial prosperity and wealth—that is, the state of being the residence of great fortune—since it is the crest-jewel of the Gandharvas (a specific class of divine beings) and horses, and the crest-jewel of the mountains and kings, wherein resides the non-trivial Śrīnivāsa.

Or just as certain birds, afflicted by excessive heat and with their vision obscured by darkness, remain for some time, yet rejoice exceedingly when, by chance, the moon rises; so too are those who, intensely distressed by internal and external sufferings as well as the heat [of the sun], and whose insight—both knowledge and sight—is cast down and destroyed by the quality of *tamas* (darkness) and gloom, remain for a while. (143) [Note: *Nikāmam* means excessively; *tāpaiḥ* refers to spiritual and worldly sufferings as well as those produced by the sun's heat; *tamasā* refers to the *tamas* guṇa and physical darkness; *pratyasta* means cast down or removed; *dṛṣṭi* here signifies both wisdom and the eye.]

By fate—that is, through a particular stroke of fortune—when there occurs the manifestation of the Lord Moon as a direct perception rooted in constant meditation; or, in the alternative sense, when the moon (vidhu) appears, only a few twice-born ones (dvija)—meaning only fortunate Brahmins and others, and no others who are far removed from fortune—[perceive it]. This is the intended meaning.

In the [other] case, it is only specific birds such as the *cakora* that rejoice. In these two examples, although the scope of the expressive power (*śakti*) of words with multiple meanings has been restricted by the context, one must ensure that the expression of the unintended, extraneous meaning—whether in the form of a great king or a specific bird—which is perceived through suggestion (*dhvanana*) based on that restriction, does not undesirably follow. Therefore, the relationship of simile (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between the relevant and the irrelevant is postulated as the primary meaning of the sentence.

In this case, because words such as *kaṭaka* (bracelet) and others, being homonymous (*śliṣṭa*), cannot tolerate a shift toward meanings such as *nitamba* (hip), this simile is the domain of resonance (*anudhvani*) rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
An example of the scope of suggestion rooted in the power of the literal meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) is as follows:
“O cloud (*ghanāghana*), your pride that ‘I possess an incomparable luster’ is indeed great; yet you have not approached even slightly the crest of the mountain of the serpent-king. (144)

Or rather, O Ocean, abandon with effort the pride that you are a "mine of jewels" (ratnākara) at my word; for you do not move even a step from your place—have you not seen the treasury-chamber of Śrīnivāsa? 145.

In this case, because words such as "foolish" (*mūḍha*) are not employed and because feelings such as envy (*asūyā*) are not perceived, it is primarily through the power of the meaning (*artha-śakti*) that the simile alone is suggested (*dhvanita*). Thus:
"Why do you wish to go to the Gaṅgā? O dear one, freely embrace this spreading [stream]—this torrent of compassion from the beautiful peak of Mount Vṛṣācala. (146)
Thus, here too, the suggestion of a simile based on the power of the meaning (arthaśaktimūlopamādhvani) is to be observed.
An example of the suggestion of simile (*upamādhvani*) through ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"Beholding Hari shining upon the mountain of serpents (*phaṇiśikhariṇi*), embraced by Ramā, the flocks of peacocks felt a despondency like that of seeing a flickering rain-cloud. (147)

Here, although there is no actual connection between the peacocks and their longing to gaze at the clouds accompanied by lightning, the suggestion of the Lord Śrīnivāsa’s similarity to them is conveyed through the figure of hyperbole (atiśayokti), which consists in describing that non-existent connection as if it were real; thus has the direction for the suggestion of simile (upamādhvani) been illustrated.
Now, an illustration of the direction of suggestion (*dhvani*) through the figure of "simile upon simile" (*upameyopamā*) is given:
"For this Sudarśana of the Enemy of Mura is like the autumnal sun; and likewise, the autumnal sun is like the Sudarśana of the Enemy of Mura. (148)
In this case, because the word "second" lacks a primary denotative power (śakti) for that which is qualified by similarity, it is merely an indication (vyakti).
If, however, it is *lakṣaṇā* (indication), then this is the example:

"The lines of the nails on the pair of feet of Hari and the crescent of the nectar-rayed moon risen in autumn—these two vie intensely within one another to teach each other excellence of beauty. In this case, since the mutual teaching performed by the agents—the nail-lines on the pair of Hari’s feet and so forth—is sublated (*bādha*), it must be understood that the purpose of the specific transfer of beauty, which is apprehended through *lakṣaṇā*, is the establishment of a mutual relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) brought about by themselves.
Now, the suggestion of non-concomitance (*ananvaya-dhvani*) is illustrated:

"Having repeatedly observed and repeatedly reflected upon him today, I have attained rest; for I have not perceived any likeness to the leader of the serpents (Śeṣa) or to the leader of the gods (Indra) in his distinctness."
Here, by the statement "the scale did not perceive [them] as distinct," it is suggested that it *did* perceive them as non-distinct.
Or how many mountains are there not? Which one was held by Acyuta at his final step? And which one did he bring forth the Kamala from, so that others might become equal to Mandara? (151)

In this context, what other mountain besides Mandara was held by the Blessed One as his final limb? Or who else brought forth the Goddess Śrī from the ocean, such that other mountains might be considered equal to Mandara? By the power of the word "anya" (other), the figure of *ananvaya* (non-comparison)—which culminates in the incomparability of Mandara—is suggested: namely, that since he alone was held by the Blessed One as his final limb and alone brought forth Śrī, he alone is truly equal to himself. Thus, through the greatness of the word "anya," the sense that no other is like him is revealed.
Thus, even having abandoned the supreme state, he dwelt for a long time on the peak of a certain mountain, O serpent-bearer; we know no comparison for him other than that supreme mountain itself.

In this case as well, a suggestion of non-connection (ananvaya-dhvani) is to be observed; here, the sense beginning with “the magician, having abandoned supreme bliss and the highest Vaikuṇṭha,” is intended.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on the *Ananvaya* (Non-Comparison) Ornament, in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the *Asama* (Unequal) Ornament:
"The absolute negation of comparison in every respect is called *asama*. (24)

The complete negation of comparison is the figure of speech known as *asamā* (the peerless). This, even when suggested (*vyaṅgya*) in *ananvaya* (self-comparison), does not—by virtue of being conducive to that same aesthetic charm—attain the status of a distinct figure of speech like *rūpaka* (metaphor) or *dīpaka* (illumination), just as comparison itself [does not become distinct] in those cases. However, when it is expressed directly (*vācyatā*), it possesses its own independent charm and thus receives a separate designation.

O Hari, just as no fellow practitioner of the holy life is more capable than you of perceiving Brahman— even the slightest— so too, the Śruti declares without doubt that you possess the state of being beyond all comparison.

Or rather, O Blessed One, by virtue of qualities such as sovereignty, heroism, fortitude, steadfastness, and magnanimity—who could ever be imagined as fit for comparison with You, and when or where could such a thing possibly occur? O Lord, in the creation of Brahmā, there has never been, nor is there now, any being equal to You; even in the beginning, before this creation, was that [equality] obtainable, just as it is now? 155.
The Creator of the Universe has never created, does not create, nor will he ever create such an object, wherein even a trace of the scent of a mere fragment of a comparison to you might sprout.

Or, if a fool were to say, "There exists something common to Śauri," let them both reply: "Where or what could he find that which is common? Even if he were to wander through the worlds, what would he find? (157)

That fool, even while wandering through all the worlds, where or how could he find any proof (*māna*) for the existence of an entity equal to the Blessed One? The meaning is that he would find none at all. Alternatively, "would he receive honor (*māna*)?"—the sense is that for one who asserts a similarity between the Blessed One and anything else, there could never be honor anywhere. In the other sense (of the pun), the meaning is that this fool would not fail to find some object (*vastu*) similar to or equal to the Blessed One, wherever or however.
Herein lies the charm of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), which distinguishes it from the previous examples.

Or rather, although you indeed create, protect, and will destroy the world as one accompanied by a second—O Lotus-eyed One, the Śruti nevertheless declares you to be truly without a second! (158) The term *sadvitīyaḥ* means "accompanied by a second," that is, characterized by both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). It may also mean "accompanied by Śrī, his co-consort. Since he who is qualified by Śrī alone is the cause of the creation and other states of the world, the statement "you create [the world] as one accompanied by a second" and so forth is made.
Nevertheless, the Śruti says, "One only, without a second"; the actual meaning is that it is "without a second," meaning devoid of a second entity, and thus peerless.

Just as a person might be greeted with joy when saying of you, "He is unlike [any other]," yet be censured by people for saying, "There is one who is like you," it is a marvel that you are praised when called "unlike" and criticized when called "like. (159)

O Blessed One! When a person says that you are incomparable (*asadṛśa*), they are saying what is comparable, appropriate, and fitting; thus they are praised by people. The sense is that this is because they have correctly stated your actual state of incomparability. When a person says that there exists one who is your equal (*sadṛk*), such a person is not "comparable" (*sadṛk*)—that is, not fit or worthy—because they have spoken of an object that is not truly analogous. Furthermore, the term *sadṛk* (meaning "possessing sight") implies one who is not blind; the meaning is that [the speaker] is indeed devoid of knowledge.

The sense is that if he had truly possessed such vision, he would never have said, "There is one who resembles you. Thus he is censured by people; the point is that this statement is marvelous (*citram*)—it is astonishing because it describes one who speaks of similarity as speaking of dissimilarity, and one who speaks of dissimilarity as speaking of similarity. In these two examples, it should be understood that their distinction from the previous ones lies in their being mixed with a contradiction rooted in *śleṣa* (punning).

Thus, there has never been, nor is there now, nor will there ever be anything equal to the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, wherein the sun, the moon, and fire appear like mere sparks. (160) In the entire creation of the Creator, there has never been, nor is there now, nor will there ever be anyone like me anywhere; for while you—the marketplace for auspicious virtues—exist, I am a miserable soul who would wish to bargain away my merits elsewhere. (161)

In such instances as these, one should also observe the commingling with figures such as *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason). In all these examples, because there is an absolute negation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the figure is *asamālaṃkāra* (the unequal). The occasional negation of a similar object is the province of the *upamānaluptā* (omission of the standard of comparison) variety of simile; however, since this [figure] involves an absolute negation of similarity, it does not serve the same purpose as *upamānaluptopamā*. Because similarity cannot be established when the standard of comparison is negated in its entirety, there is not even a scent of simile here.

If it is asked, "Since the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is established simply by the suggestion (*dhvanana*) of the *asamālaṃkāra* (the 'unequal' ornament), how can *ananvaya* (self-comparison) be considered a distinct ornament?", the answer is true; however, the same objection applies: if the charm in *dīpaka* and other figures is also established solely through the manifestation of a simile (*upamā*), then how can they be considered distinct ornaments? Nor should it be argued that there is a difference because, while in *dīpaka* and others the simile is suggested, it remains subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), whereas in the present case, the *asamālaṃkāra* itself is primarily suggested by the extreme disparagement of one's own similarity to oneself. For even if the simile is suggested, it is subordinated in *dīpaka*, etc., while here the *asamālaṃkāra* is the primary element. This distinction is not tenable.

For just as in cases such as *dīpaka* (the illuminator) and *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), the status of being an ornament (*alaṃkāratva*) is not lost even when there is the presence of a subordinate suggested meaning (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), so too in the case of *ananvaya* (non-comparison), there is nothing contradictory even when there is a predominant suggested meaning. Since the mere similarity that constitutes the body of *ananvaya* is expressed by the words, its designation as a "verbal ornament" (*vācyālaṃkāra*) is indeed primary. As for poetry containing ornaments such as *dīpaka*, let it be called "subordinate-suggested" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) because of the presence of a subordinate suggestion.

If it is argued that the nature of *dhvani* (suggestive poetry) has never been observed anywhere in an alaṅkāra-kāvya (poetry based on figures of speech), [the reply is] that this is not so, because the status of *dhvani* is clearly evident in such works as *paryāyokta*, *sādṛśyamūla-aprastutapraśaṃsā*, and others; thus they say.
The ancients do not consider this to be a separate figure of speech at all.

This "ornament of incomparability" (asamālaṅkāra) is possible even when it is being suggested, as in: "O Lord of Śrī, although the Lord of the Mountains is omniscient, he desires to describe some object comparable to you; yet, due to his failure to do so, even today he does not abandon his state of being a mere pillar (sthāṇutā). (162)

In this regard, even the omniscient Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), desiring to praise you, remained as motionless as a pillar for such a long time due to the lack of any object comparable to you; he would remain exactly the same even now. Since there is no evidence for any change in this state, it is understood that there is absolutely no object whatsoever equal to you. Thus, although the figure of speech *asamālaṅkāra* (the incomparable) is suggested here, it is indeed an ornament because it serves to enhance the excellence of the primary theme: the praise of the Blessed One.
Primarily suggested [by implication], it is as follows:

"O Lord whose crest is the mountain of the hooded serpent, every word was made meaningful by You; yet, alas, Your word that expresses the same thing has not been meaningful even throughout the three periods of time!"

By you, every word—consisting of nominal and verbal suffixes, as well as the stations of Indra and other deities—was fashioned as meaningful, possessed of a denotable object, and endowed with power. Yet it is a marvel that a word expressing the same name as yours, expressing a similar meaning, is not meaningful, nor wealthy, nor possessed of a denotable object, even throughout the three periods of time; why is this so? This is truly astonishing.
Or rather, just as among figures of serpents,
great mountains, and leading bulls drawn in the sky, or among painted men, that man alone is to be counted as truly worthy who could serve as a likeness even for you, O Lāvaka.

In these two examples, the inequality [of the subject and the object] is primarily manifested: in one case through the negation of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and in the other through the direct negation of the comparison itself. Of these, the first has been demonstrated. An example of the second is as follows:
"O Lord of Kamalā, this entire world is filled by you alone, both within and without. O Lord of the World, where could it find a place upon the scale to equal you? (165)

O Lord of the World! Where could Your likeness—that which acts as a comparison—find a place? Since You alone completely fill the entire universe both internally and externally, the sense is that there is not even space for the setting down of a footstep of Your comparison.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the figure of speech *Asamā* (Incomparable). Now begins the chapter on the figure of speech *Udāharaṇa* (Illustration),
which is easy to understand because it defines only one aspect [of the general definition].
When the relationship of part and whole between those two has been stated, the illustrative example follows. || 25 ||

The figure of speech called *udāhṛti* (illustration) or *udāharaṇa* (example) consists in describing a specific part of a matter that has been defined in general terms, for the sake of easy comprehension, and then stating the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) between that specific part and the general matter. The word "stated" (*ukte*) is used here to exclude the figure *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration). In poetry, this statement is clearly expressed through such terms as *iva*, *yathā*, *nidarśana*, *dṛṣṭānta*, *pramāṇa*, *udāharaṇa*, *sākṣin*, and so forth; for in *arthāntaranyāsa*, the relationship of part and whole is merely suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

Nor should it be said that the words *iva* and *yathā*, which denote similarity, have no application in the relation of part and whole (*avayava-avayavibhāva*) consisting of the particular and the universal; for the scope of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is all-pervasive. Otherwise, even the capacity to convey poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) would be difficult to establish. It should be noted that in this ornament, the qualifiers of the particular and the universal are indicated either separately or simultaneously. For example: "Even though it is dark, an object attains honor in a high position by the power of its quality, just as musk, due to its fragrance, does so upon the surface of the forehead of the Lord. (166)

Furthermore, a comparison between a soiled object and musk cannot be stated here, because no similarity arises between them due to their relationship as general and particular. If that were the case, words such as "like" (*sadṛśa*) would be used in this ornament just as the word "as if" (*iva*) is. In this instance, the faces of the Blessed One—which possess the greatness of the qualities of soiled objects—are particulars [of the general category]. In this verse, the word *iva* expresses the relationship between the part and the whole.

Or just as someone here, even by association with the great, is cherished by the Omniscient One himself— just as in ancient times the flood of the Gaṅgā was cherished by the Enemy of Cities (Śiva) through contact with the feet of the one whose banner bears Garuḍa (Viṣṇu).

In this context, "contact with the feet of one who has Garuḍa as his banner" and so forth are specific instances of "association with the great" and other such qualities. Here, the term "yathā" (as) expresses the relationship between part and whole.

Or just as a single supramundane object, when carried [by many], attains great exaltation in the world— bearing here the Lord of the World (Lokeśa) as its illustration— is the king of mountains, the belly of the serpent Kākodara.

The word "object" (*padārtha*) should be supplied as the predicate for the word "one" (*eka*); likewise, it should be supplied for the word "someone" (*kaścit*) in the preceding verse. Here, this is indicated by the word "illustration" (*nidarśana*).

Or rather, wherever one may be born, if one is radiant, one becomes a great ornament for the noble; the Kaustubha gem, born from the ocean yet remaining on the chest of the Lord of Śrī, is the illustrative example here. (169)

In this case, there is no distinction between the ocean and the Kaustubha gem, or between fire and that which is born from it; the same should be understood for what follows hereafter. Here, by the word "illustration" (dṛṣṭānta), [the point is made].
Or,

just as someone attains the status of Lord of the Mountain by receiving the excellence bestowed through reliance on a supreme consciousness, so too the Mahendra mountain here is a proof of wonder, for it possesses such a state despite being insentient.

"Uttamacetanaḥ" means the supreme living being; elsewhere, it means the Blessed Lord. "Girīśatām" means lordship over speech; elsewhere, it means the state of being the king of mountains. "Avidyamānā cetanā" means that in which consciousness or knowledge is absent; its abstract state is "ajñatvam" (ignorance). Elsewhere, it means being distinct from consciousness, because a mountain is insentient. Here, by the word "pramāṇa"— [The verse continues: *Śrīkaṇṭhena vinā kṛtaṃ na hi paraṃ vastu svayaṃ vetti yaḥ | sa kathaṃ paravastuṣu pramitidātā syād girīśo 'pi hi ||* "Indeed, he who does not himself know the supreme reality apart from Śrīkaṇṭha—how could even Girīśa be a giver of valid cognition regarding other things? [The commentary continues: In this [verse], the word "girīśa" is used as a synonym for "parameśvara" (the Supreme Lord). By the word "vastu," the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is intended. By the word "para," the distinction between the object and the subject (*grāhya-grāhaka-vibhāga*) is indicated. By the word "svayam," the self-luminous nature (*svaprakāśatva*) of the subject is shown. By the word "na vetti," the absence of the activity of knowing is expressed. By the word "hi," the reason is stated. By the word "katham," the impossibility of the means of knowledge is indicated. By the word "paravastuṣu," the objects of knowledge are specified. By the word "pramiti," the result of knowledge is meant. By the word "dātā," the capacity to produce that result is signified. By the word "syāt," the possibility of such a capacity is denied. By the word "girīśa," the subject of the sentence is presented. By the word "api," the inclusion of others is implied. By the word "hi," the certainty of the statement is affirmed. Thus, the meaning is: "How can even Girīśa be a giver of valid cognition regarding other things? This is because he lacks the capacity to perceive the supreme reality, which is distinct from himself. Therefore, the conclusion is that he cannot be a giver of valid cognition. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "girīśa" is used here as a synonym for "parameśvara. By the word "vastu," the object of knowledge is intended. By the word "para," the distinction between the object and the subject is indicated. By the word "svayam," the self-luminous nature of the subject is shown. By the word "na vetti," the absence of the activity of knowing is expressed. By the word "hi," the reason is stated. By the word "katham," the impossibility of the means of knowledge is indicated. By the word "paravastuṣu," the objects of knowledge are specified. By the word "pramiti," the result of knowledge is meant. By the word "dātā," the capacity to produce that result is signified. By the word "syāt," the possibility of such a capacity is denied. By the word "girīśa," the subject of the sentence is presented. By the word "api," the inclusion of others is implied. By the word "hi," the certainty of the statement is affirmed. Thus, the meaning is: "How can even Girīśa be a giver of valid cognition regarding other things? This is because he lacks the capacity to perceive the supreme reality, which is distinct from himself. Therefore, the conclusion is that he cannot be a giver of valid cognition. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "girīśa" is used here as a synonym for "parameśvara. By the word "vastu," the object of knowledge is intended. By the word "para," the distinction between the object and the subject is indicated. By the word "svayam," the self-luminous nature of the subject is shown. By the word "na vetti," the absence of the activity of knowing is expressed. By the word "hi," the reason is stated. Or, for example, even a common bird becomes radiant when it holds you within its breast; here, the orb of the sun, the friend of the multitude of lotuses, may serve as an illustration.

*Kheṭaḥ* means "contemptible"; as Amarasimha states: "The words *kupūya*, *kutsita*, *avadya*, *kheṭa*, *garhya*, and *aṇaka* are synonyms. In another sense, it is a *kheṭa* because it "moves in the sky" (*khe aṭati*), meaning it is a sky-walker; the elision of the suffix is according to the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti*. Here, by the word "example" (*udāharaṇa*), the relationship between the part and the whole is expressed.
Or again, just as one who takes from many objects accepts only that which is suitable to himself—Mādhava is the witness here, who, among those born of the ocean, accepted only Kamalā. || 172 ||

O Beloved of Hari, even if an object initially possesses a quality of darkness (tāmasa), if it takes refuge in you, it will eventually become full of aesthetic flavor (rasavat); the lotus flower is the witness to this.

In the first instance, although it initially bestows benefit upon those characterized by *tamas*, the meaning is that it subsequently assumes association with the two syllables *ta* and *ma*. At the end, it is "possessing essence" (*rasavat*), like the experience of Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as "He is indeed essence" (*raso vai saḥ*); here the word *rasa* refers to Brahman. In the alternative sense, at the final part, it is joined by the two letters *ra* and *sa*. In both of these verses, the word "witness" (*sākṣin*) expresses the relationship between a whole and its parts.

When words such as *ivādi* (‘like,’ etc. are employed, there is a predominance of the general meaning and unity of the sentence. However, when words such as *nidarśana* (illustration) or *dṛṣṭānta* (example) are employed, the distinction is that there is a predominance of the particular meaning and a division of the sentence. The earlier scholars, however, maintain: “This is not a distinct figure of speech, as its purpose is already served by *upamā* (simile). Nor should it be argued that this cannot be called *upamā* because no similarity is manifested between the general and the particular; for [it is said] ‘the general does not exist without particulars,’ since a general property cannot function as the subject of discourse without some particular instance.”

They say: "Since there is no obstacle to the manifestation of similarity between one particularity and another by taking such a particularity as a basis, the relationship of general and particular—though initially perceived by proponents [of the view]—ultimately rests upon similarity alone."

Now, it must be said that if the *udāharaṇa* (illustration) were accepted as a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), then the support of a general statement by a particular instance could not constitute a variety of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), because its purpose would already have been fulfilled by this [new figure] alone.

If it is argued that, because the absence of the use of words such as *iva*, *vā*, *yathā*, and so forth constitutes a distinction between these two, even so, since there is an absence of a denotative word (*vācaka*), this should be considered merely the figure of speech *udāharaṇa* (exemplification) and not a variety of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), we reply: there is indeed this distinction between the two. For the particular statement that supports a general meaning has two possible modes: one is that the particularity resides only in the portion being restated (*anuvādya*), while the portion to be enjoined (*vidheya*) remains within the general sense; the other is that the particularity resides in both the portion being restated and the portion to be enjoined.

Among these, the first is the province of the figure of speech *udāharaṇa* (illustration), while the second belongs to a variety of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration). Thus, in the case of the specific instance within the *udāharaṇa* figure, such as "the musk-deer's navel, by virtue of its fragrance, [is placed] upon the boundary of the Lord’s forehead-slab," the action—conceived in the form already mentioned—is to be predicated only of the general object belonging to the ancients, thereby attaining the status of being worthy of respect.

When the fourth quarter is read as “it bears the nature of a tilaka-mark upon the face of the Blessed One,” then, because it has attained the status of an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth), it exists in the form of a distinct, separately stated particularity (*viśeṣa*). Likewise, in the illustrative verses of the *alaṅkāra* [text] such as “Wherever there is a luminous object, it becomes a great ornament for the great,” one should understand the distinction between the example and the particularity of the *arthāntaranyāsa* when the second half of the verse is read as: “O Acyuta, that this Kaustubha gem, possessing birth, shines within the ocean and within your heart. Thus, the difference between the example and the particularity of the *arthāntaranyāsa* is to be understood.

If this slight distinction does not suffice to establish that the figure *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) is a distinct figure of speech from the figure *udāharaṇa* (exemplification), but rather is said to be merely a variety thereof, then one could equally well say that the figure *udāharaṇa* is a variety of *arthāntaranyāsa*, *prativastūpamā* a variety of *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), *atiśayokti* a variety of *rūpaka* (metaphor), and even that the figures *smaraṇa* (recollection), *bhrāntimat* (error), and *sandeha* (doubt) are nothing but metaphor in its figurative sense (*ārthī upamā*), since the distinction in those cases as well is equally slight.

Considering this matter already understood through the simile alone, the ancients, however, maintain that one should not attempt to enter elsewhere except where the support of a general principle (*sāmānya*) by means of a particular instance (*viśeṣa*), known as *arthāntaranyāsa*, is required; such is the direction of their view.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Illustration (*udāharaṇālaṅkāra*), in the *Alaṃkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on the Ornament of Contrast (*pratīpālaṅkāra*):
"Contrast (*pratīpa*) occurs when that which is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) becomes the object of description (*upameya*). (26)

*Pratīpa* (the inverse) is a comparison described through the inversion of well-known conventions. This inversion occurs by conceiving of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) as being respectively the object of comparison and the standard of comparison. Here, the result is the perception of superiority, because that which was the object of comparison in a conventional comparison is now treated as the standard; and the perception of inferiority, because that which was the standard is now treated as the object of comparison. This very point is the seed for the distinction between this figure and the *upamā* (simile) ornament, despite there being no difference in the nature of the comparison itself.

Now, one might ask: even though the similarity is common to both the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya), from what does this arise when the superiority of one and the inferiority of the other are perceived? Listen: it is universally accepted that the connection with the common attribute is restated (anūdya) in relation to the standard of comparison and enjoined (vidhīyate) in relation to the object of comparison. Furthermore, injunction and restatement are characterized respectively by being something to be accomplished (sādhya) and being already established (siddha). These two, in turn, bring about the inferiority and superiority of the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, respectively.

In the world as well, it is perfectly clear that one whose status as king is certain is honored, whereas one whose status as king is uncertain is not. Furthermore, since the states of being "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) and "that which is already accomplished" (*siddha*) depend upon the speaker’s intention, there is no fault here. Regarding the five types of *pratīpa* (the inverse) to be described, the process of comparison (*upamiti*) is complete in the first three; however, in the others, it is not—this is the distinction.
Let the aged cow bellow as much as she will: even if it were heated pure gold, it might only come to resemble your color after a very long time—provided that it were truly beloved by its refuge. 174.

The term *jaradgavī* refers to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*), and it is also understood as "an old cow.
