[In the phrase] *śucitaptam*, it means performing penance in the midst of five fires during the summer; alternatively, *śuci* may be a separate word, meaning "pure" (*śuddha*) and "ascetic" (*tapasvin*). However, the intended sense is that it has been purified by the process of *puṭapāka* (enclosing in clay and heating) in fire. Here, the second half of the verse sets aside the excellence of the golden color—understood through the simile in the first half—which was prompted by its status as a point of comparison, and instead conveys a contrasting excellence of the color of the Goddess Lakṣmī, prompted by her status as the object of comparison.

By these two verses—"Without heat, even opposition is difficult to find; but as for a simile, it is cast far away even in a dream"—it is understood that [the Goddess] speaks like an old cow. "O Thou who art most dear to the one worthy of refuge" is an address to Śrī. Or, for example:
"O Mother of the World, let the independent Veda proclaim Your solar radiance; yet if the splendor of the great heat were to arise, it would be merely the color of Your feet. (175)

The Śruti says: "Born from the heat [tapas] of the sun-like color. This means that even if that Sun—described as such because he possesses the great splendor of penance (tapas-śrī) and the splendor of heat (ātapa-śrī)—were to rise, or were to attain exaltation and manifestation, even then his color would remain only like the color of your feet, that is, possessing a color like a fourth part of your own; the sense is that it would not be your color in its full perfection. However, the intended meaning is that it would be the reddish color of your feet.

Here too, having set aside the excess of the sun’s color—which is understood through the simile in the first half-verse by virtue of its being the standard of comparison—the second half-verse conveys a *pratīpa* (inversion) wherein the excess of the Mother of the World’s complexion is attributed to her being the standard of comparison. This is understood from the phrase "let the independent Veda declare," implying that without her being risen along with the glory of great austerity (*mahātapaśrī*), even the *pratīpa* would be difficult to establish, let alone the possibility of a simile. Furthermore, the pun (*śleṣa*) contained in the words "only the color of your feet" embellishes this very meaning.

The disparagement of the subject of description (the *varṇya*) through the acquisition of the non-subject of comparison (the *upamāna*); and the disregard for others through the acquisition of the subject of description as the object of comparison—these constitute another [type of *vyatireka*]. (27)

The second type of *pratīpa* (contrary simile) is even more distinguished than the first: it consists in showing some object as a standard of comparison (*upameya*) for that which is being described as possessing matchless qualities and is unable to tolerate similarity with anything else, thereby eclipsing it. The third type of *pratīpa* is the reverse of the first: it consists in designating the subject of description (*varṇya*) itself as the object of comparison (*upameya*) for that which, due to its extreme excellence, cannot bear the status of a standard of comparison anywhere, thereby eclipsing it.

O Daughter of the Ocean, do not be arrogant, thinking, "I alone am the protectress of the worlds"; for in the heart of the Lord of the Hill of Serpents resides your compassion, which is like that of a mother and bestows auspiciousness.
O treasure-house of splendor, abandon this pride that "I am the ornament upon the heart of Ananta"; do you not consider placing a gem upon the chest of Veṅkaṭanātha, who is your equal? 177.

In the first example here, although the act of comparison is accomplished by the phrase "similar to you," the disregard for the described Lakṣmī is expressed through making compassion the object of comparison (*upameya*). In the second example, however, the disregard for the Kaustubha gem on the chest of Śrīnivāsa—the abode of splendor—is stated by imagining it as the *upameya*, since that unpraised treasure of light is incapable of being an object of comparison anywhere due to its being an infinite and heart-pleasing ornament.

This verse is embellished by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as it is both "beloved of the infinite sky" (*anantagaganasya śrīnivāsasya*) and "beloved of Śrīnivāsa" (*śrīnivāsasya hṛdyam*), while also being "situated in the heart" (*hṛdayastham*) and "an ornament" (*bhūṣaṇam*). Since the result of these two distinctions is self-evident, there is no need for further analysis.

In some cases, even when there is no perception of disregard [for the object of comparison], *pratīpa* (the inverse) is observed through the mere conceptualization of the object of comparison as the standard of comparison. For example:
"O Supreme Person, the lotus is similar to your hands, feet, and eyes; yet Kamalā (Lakṣmī) makes it her hand-ornament, takes it up, holds it, and rests upon it. (178)

Here, by virtue of its redness, fragrance, softness, and other qualities, the lotus—which is well-known as a standard of comparison—is stated merely to be the object of comparison (*upameya*); there is no disregard for it. Just as in the case of *upamā*, the various types such as the complete (*pūrṇā*) and the elliptical (*luptā*) are possible here as well, and should be inferred by the intelligent. Furthermore, the non-attainment of the comparison may occur either through the object of description itself or through another.

In the phrase "by means of the subject of description" (*varṇyena*), the meaning of the instrumental case is "being defined by" (*nirūpitatva*). The fourth type of *pratīpa* consists in the statement that the simile of another non-subject (*avarṇya*) as defined by the subject of description does not come to fruition. In the first two [types], there is a non-fruition of the act of comparison through the conceptualization of the non-subject as the object of comparison (*upameya*), and in the third, through the conceptualization of the subject as the object of comparison; however, in this [fourth type], that [non-fruition] does not exist, and thus it possesses superiority over the preceding ones.
O Lord of the Mountain and Serpents, the lotus might indeed serve as a metaphor for Your eyes; yet I consider the Vedic revelation audacious in stating that "the lotus is like [Your eyes]. (179)

"O Lord of the Uraga Mountain, even the lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) might serve as a comparison for Your eyes"—this is the rhetorical question (*kāku*). By the word "even" (*api*), the occasional fading and lack of beauty of the lotus is implied. If so, how is it that the *Antarāditya-vidyā* scripture states, "His eyes are like a lotus with petals like those of a monkey," thus asserting a similarity between the Lord’s eyes and a lotus? To this, he replies: "It is audacious."

The scriptural passage beginning with "As his [face] is like the seat of a monkey" (*kapyāsa*) which speaks of similarity to a lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), I consider to be rash (*sāhasikī*). It is called *sāhasikī* because it acts with rashness (*sahasā vartate*); the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "ojas-sahas-ambhaso vartate," and the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. The sense is that she speaks while closing her eyes. Here, by the phrase "even a lotus might be a simile for the eyes," it is understood that a simile is not possible. The word *sāhasikī* in the latter half of the verse reinforces this very point.

They know the fifth [type of] *pratīpa* (the inverse) to be the uselessness (*kaimarthya*) of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). "Of what purpose" (*kaḥ arthaḥ*) means "what is its aim or utility" (*kimarthaḥ*); the state of that is "uselessness" (*kaimarthya*), which is pointlessness. Because the object of comparison (*upameya*) alone bears the burden of the function of the standard of comparison, this "uselessness of the standard of comparison" is the fifth *pratīpa*, due to its opposition to the standard of comparison.
Just as the virtuous,

dwelling in the Lord of the Serpents— who is the Supreme Brahman through mastery over all qualities and who is the source of wondrous bliss— surely consider even the highest heaven (*paramavyoman*) to be of no account.
Or, for example:
While taking Padmāvatī’s hand in marriage, the Lord of the Mountain who bears hooded serpents cast aside even his play-lotus; why did he do this without concern? (181)

In this sequence, the futility of the two points of comparison—the supreme sky and the play-lotus—is stated, since they serve as mere analogues for the hands of Padmāvatī and the mountain of serpents (Śeṣa), which alone bear the burden of performing such tasks as bestowing unsurpassed bliss.

Thus, five types of *pratīpa* (the inverse) have been described here in accordance with the views of earlier authorities. In reality, however, the first three are merely varieties included within *upamā* (simile). The fourth, moreover, is included in *vyatireka* (contrast), where the point of difference (*vaidharmya*) is not explicitly stated. As for the fifth, it is considered by some to be a form of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis). For instance, similarity that is either being brought about or is beautiful constitutes *upamā*. Indeed, in the first type of *pratīpa*, such as "The lotus is like the face," there is neither a failure to produce similarity nor an absence of beauty, by which it might be excluded from the category of *upamā*.

For you yourself have admitted a specific excellence [of beauty]; and a specific quality does not preclude the general category. Nor is there any Vedic injunction stating that similarity consisting solely of a well-known counter-correlate, such as a lotus, constitutes the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). Furthermore, it cannot be asserted on the mere authority of the word *pratīpa*—which denotes something contrary to *upamā*—that such a form of similarity is indeed *upamā*. This is because that word can be explained as denoting a specific variety of *upamā* that is contrary to [the standard] *upamā*. Thus, the first type of *pratīpa* is itself a specific variety of *upamā*, just like the well-known *upamā*.

For this very reason, the second and third varieties are also indeed specific types of simile (*upamā*); the disparagement of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) serves to differentiate them from other similes, but not to exclude them from the general category of simile itself, since they are perceived precisely as being permeated by that [simile]. For sugar, though distinct from other earthly substances due to its excellence of sweetness, does not thereby cease to be earthly. Furthermore, if the disparagement of the *upamāna* and *upameya* were the determinant of their status as a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), then their glorification would likewise be so.
O wicked ones, do not harbor remorse, thinking, "Alas, we are sinners! For how many others like you have there not been in this age who forgot the serpent-girded Lord of Mountains? 182.

In this case, the result of demonstrating the comparison is not the subordination of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because its pride and so forth are not intended to be expressed. Rather, it is the pacification of that [pride] through remorse; and thus, by asserting that it constitutes a distinct figure of speech merely on account of the difference in its result, one would have to admit either that this [figure] is indeed an *alaṅkāra* or that it is a sixth variety of *pratīpa*.

Furthermore, even the various sub-types of *pratīpa* (the "contrary") that you have mentioned would each constitute a separate figure of speech due to their mutual distinctness, rather than being sub-types of *pratīpa*, because there is no general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) common to all its varieties. Moreover, the property of being "any one of these" (*anyatamatva*) cannot serve as a definition at all, as it is swallowed up by a thousand flaws. However, the definition of *upamā* (simile) is indeed universal. As for the fifth variety, let it be considered a figure of speech according to the opinion of those for whom it is *ākṣepa* (paralipsis); but as for the fourth, the solution has already been stated.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ornament of Contrast (*pratīpa*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*. Now, as for Metaphor (*rūpaka*):
it is the coloring of the subject by means of the form of the correlate.
The wise know that metaphor (rūpaka) is determined by the non-difference and the identity of such a kind. || 29 ||

The *viṣayin* (the object of comparison) is that which serves as the standard of comparison, such as the moon; the *viṣaya* (the subject of comparison) is that which is being described, such as the face, which is the object of that comparison. The "coloring" (*uparañjana*) of the *viṣaya* by means of the form of the *viṣayin*—that is, coloring it as it were, meaning its being made the object of a cognition colored by itself—is what constitutes *rūpaka* (metaphor), because it brings about the possession of a form through the form of another. This [metaphor] in some cases culminates in the non-difference of the well-known *viṣayin*, while in other cases it culminates merely in the superimposition of its attributes, even while difference remains perceived.
Furthermore, *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) is of two kinds: *abhedarūpaka* (identification by non-difference) and *tādrūpyarūpaka* (identification by resemblance). This is stated as follows:
"When there is superimposition (*āropa*), if there is non-difference, it is called *abhedarūpaka*;
if there is resemblance (*tādrūpya*), it would be *tādrūpyarūpaka*. (30)

If that superimposition (*āropa*) were of the nature of identity (*tādrūpya*), then it would be *tādrūpyarūpaka*; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the superimposition of non-difference (*abhedāropa*)—as in "The face is the moon" (*mukhaṃ candraḥ*)—is a voluntary (*āhārya*) ascertainment of non-difference with the moon. However, in the case of the superimposition of identity, as in "The face is another moon" (*mukham aparaś candraḥ*), because the distinction is made explicit by the word "another," a superimposition of non-difference with the moon is impossible; therefore, there is a voluntary ascertainment of identity consisting in the capacity to perform the functions of the moon. Nor should it be asked: "Since that [capacity] exists in the face, how can it be called a superimposition?"

This is because the quality of "producing an effect similar to the effect of the moon" exists specifically in the face. Although, in accordance with the requirement for non-difference (abheda) in the relation between the word and its referent, here too the face is construed as non-different from that which is indicated by the word "moon"—namely, that which produces its effects—therefore it is indeed a *rūpaka* of non-difference; nevertheless, they say that it is a *rūpaka* of non-difference only when there is a manifestation of non-difference through the form that delimits the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), whereas when there is a manifestation of non-difference through such forms as "producing its effects," it is a *rūpaka* of identity (*tādrūpya-rūpaka*).
And that pair [of causes] is threefold, through expressions of superiority, inferiority, and neither.

Each of the two types of *rūpaka* (metaphor) is again threefold: by describing the excellence of the object of superimposition (*viṣayi*), by describing its deficiency, and by stating the absence of both excellence and deficiency. Thus, *rūpaka* is sixfold. Among the varieties of non-difference metaphors (*abheda-rūpaka*), he defines the "excellent non-difference metaphor" (*adhika-abheda-rūpaka*) as follows: "The description of the excellence of that which is being superimposed over its previous state constitutes the excellent non-difference metaphor, provided that the state being described is indeed superior. (32)

Just as the nectar that rose from the ocean—the lord of serpents, shaken by the conflict between the Asuras and the Asuras—bestows upon those who follow it immeasurable freedom from old age and death, so does this smile bestow the same. (184)

Here, by establishing the non-difference of Śrīnivāsa from the ocean through the phrase "the lord of the ocean, the king of serpents," and by the qualifying epithet "agitated by demons and asuras" [applied] to the ocean; and likewise, by establishing the identity of the smile being described with nectar through the phrase "the smile is nectar," and by stating that it bestows immeasurable, ageless, and deathless status—thereby manifesting the excellence of the nectar over its previous state—there is a pair of *adhikābhedarūpaka* (metaphors of superior non-difference) based on a *paraṃparita* (successive) structure.
The distinction here is that the first is a complete (samasta) metaphor, whereas the second is a partial (vyasta) one.
If there is a deficiency compared to the prior state, it is a "metaphor of deficient identity" (nyūnābhedopamā).

Just as poetry, polished by the weight of the qualities of the jewel on the mountain of the incomparable Lord of Serpents, being like the three Vedas personified, shakes off evil and extends immeasurable happiness. (185)

Here, by revealing the identity of the modern poetry concerning the qualities of the Blessed One—which is the subject of description—with the well-known Triad (the three Vedas), the author establishes that it lacks the quality of being non-human (apauruṣeya). This constitutes a *nyūnābheda-rūpaka* (metaphor of inferior non-difference). The term *pauruṣeyī* means "composed by a person. According to the rule *sarvapuruṣābhyāṃ ṇaḍhañau*, and specifically the supplementary statement *puruṣādvadhavikārasamūhatenakṛteṣviti vaktavyam*, the suffix *ḍhañ* is applied; subsequently, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*. Thus, it is derived as follows: *puruṣeṇa kṛtā* = *pauruṣeyī*.

The inclusion of the word *tena* within the compound due to the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya is striking, as even the demonstration of deficiency serves to strengthen the sense of non-difference.
When there is an absence of both superiority and inferiority, it is the "Metaphor of Non-difference through Neither" (anubhayābhedārūpaka). || 34 ||

Just as I perceive the lotus— the abode of the rising nectar, marked with lines of pollen, and celebrated by the songs of bees— to be the very refuge of Śrī, I behold it as the manifest foot of the Lord of Ramā.

It was sung with the "six-footed mantra"—that jewel of mantras described as "this six-footed one consists of two parts"—because therein the feet of the Blessed One are established as the means (*upāya*). Elsewhere, it was sung with the mantras of the six-footed ones, that is, the humming of bees. It is accompanied by lotus-designs, meaning it possesses lines in the shape of lotuses or rows of lotuses; and it is the birthplace (*udayaniketa*) of the earth (*rasā*), for the Veda states, "From his feet came the earth."

Elsewhere, it is the abode of the rising of *maranda*—the essence of nectar—and the refuge and birthplace of *śrī*, meaning both the goddess Śrī and the splendor of delicacy and other such qualities. Here, by means of the qualifier "directly" (*sākṣāt*), the identity of the Lord’s foot with the lotus is established; then, through qualifiers such as "sung by bees," since there is no description of either superiority or inferiority relative to its previous state, this is a *niravayava-abheda-rūpaka* (non-limited identity metaphor).
In this way, the wise should infer that there are likewise three varieties even in the *tādrūpya-rūpaka* (metaphor of identity).
Among these, an example of the *adhika-tādrūpya-rūpaka* (metaphor of excessive identity) is as follows:

"The ocean of the wise [the Buddha] reigns supreme; though he possesses the beauty of the river of his own mind, he never undergoes the agitation caused by the serpent-mountain [Mount Mandara], nor does he delight the ignorant. (187)

The lover of the river (the ocean) never experiences even the slightest agitation, fear, or extreme disturbance caused by Mandara—the mountain that serves as the churning rod—within his heart; for while this lover of the river of his heart reigns supreme, the well-known Sindhu (ocean) does not delight the wise (the gods or scholars), because it lacks such [tranquility]. This is the intended meaning.

In this context, in the phrase "the beloved of the river of his own mind" (*svāntasaritkānta*), the term *saritkānta* (beloved of the river) refers merely to the performance of the functions of the ocean; for what is intended is a distinction from the well-known ocean, as expressed by the fact that [this beloved] does not delight the wise (*budha*). Thus, by stating that he does not undergo the agitation caused by the supreme Mandara mountain, the excellence of the "beloved of the river of his own mind" is established; since the contrast with the well-known ocean is thereby made clear, the superiority is described—this is therefore the figure of speech known as *adhikatādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of superior identity).
Just as the rain-cloud, thundering with a cool and darkened face, bestows poison, so too does the rain-cloud that is the Lord of the Hill of Serpents bestow even nectar with the very greatest ease.

*Parjanya* is *śītaka*, meaning "one who makes cold," hence *śītaka*; [the suffix] *kan* is applied according to the rule *śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi*. Amara states: "*ālasyaḥ śītako 'lasaḥ*" (the lazy one is *śītaka*). In another sense, the analysis of the compound is: "he whose water (*ka*) is cold (*śīta*). He has a face (*mukha*)—meaning the countenance or the front part—which is *malina*, i.e., soiled by being defiled with anger; in the other sense, it is naturally dark blue (*nīla*). He roars and threatens; in the other sense, he thunders. He bestows poison (*viṣa*), which is both venom and water.

In this way, one who is indolent and whose face is stained by anger, even when thundering, ultimately bestows only poison and not a thing worthy of being accepted. But the rain-cloud that is the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents (Śrī Śeṣa) bestows even nectar—the supreme ambrosia—and even the highest liberation (niḥśreyasa), with ease and joy, being untiring, with a stainless face, and without any exertion; such is the meaning. [The word *sudhām* becomes *sūdha*] because of the doubling [of the final vowel] according to the rule "akṛchre priyasukhayoranyatarasyām," which results in the elision of the case-ending (*subluk*) as if it were a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Here, the superiority of the rain-cloud that is the Blessed Lord over the well-known rain-cloud has been stated.
An example of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) characterized by deficiency (*nyūnatādrūpya*) is as follows:
"Those who bow to, worship, praise, and circumambulate the Beloved of the Lord of Serpents (Śrī Śeṣādri)—those devotees of the Blessed One are liberated; others born of the earth are not. (189)

Here, because of the qualification "another among those who are liberated," which reveals the distinction of the Lord’s devotees from the well-known liberated ones, and because it demonstrates a deficiency in the form of being produced on [lower] planes, this is a *nyūnatādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of inferiority).
An example of a metaphor that is neither [based on] identity nor difference (*anubhayatādrūpyarūpakam*) is as follows:
"We know this ocean—the abode of the moon’s rays, skilled in bestowing nectar upon the gods, and the heart of the crest-jewel of the serpent-king—to be something other [than the actual ocean]. (190)

Skilled in bestowing nectar (*amṛta*), ambrosia (*sudhā*), and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) upon the wise (*vibudha*)—both gods and scholars—he is the birthplace and abode of the moon, which possesses the rays of Hari. This is because of the well-known fact that the ocean rises at the moon's appearance; in the alternative sense, it is because of the Vedic revelation: "The moon was born from the mind."

Here, by revealing the distinction of this "other ocean" from the well-known ocean and by describing only its performance of the functions of the well-known ocean—without describing either superiority or inferiority—there is the *anubhayatādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of neither identity nor difference). Thus, following the opinion of the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda*, the two-fold nature of metaphor has been described, as well as the three-fold variety of each of those types therein.

The ancient authors, such as Maṅkha, Mammaṭa, Bhāmaha, and others, however, recognized only *abhedarūpaka* (metaphor of identity) and not *tādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of resemblance). Their intention may be inferred as follows: the division into *abhedarūpaka* and *tādrūpyarūpaka* is untenable, because even in instances such as "the face is another moon," only *abhedarūpaka* is possible.

Furthermore, it must be stated that a *rūpaka* based on identity occurs only when there is the manifestation of non-difference (*abhedabhāna*) between the object and the standard of comparison as delimited by their respective delimiters (*upamānatāvacchedakāvacchinna*). In the example cited, since the word "other" (*apara*) brings about the cognition of the very difference from the moon (*candrabheda*), the manifestation of non-difference from the moon is impossible; how, then, could this be an *abhedarūpaka*? Therefore, one must accept that this is indeed a *tādrūpyarūpaka*, because the word "moon" (*candra*) is taken there to refer to that which performs the functions of the moon (*candrakāryakāritva*), and through the superimposition (*āropa*) of that nature, the identity of form is established.

In such contexts, there is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby a word beginning with *apara* (e.g., *apara-candra*) conveys merely a difference from some particular individual that serves as the locus of the property delimiting the relation of the word's own referent; thus, even though a difference from the well-known individual moon (*prasiddha-candra-vyakty-bheda*) appears, a difference from the universal moon (*candra-sāmānya-bheda*) does not appear. Consequently, it is possible for there to be an appearance of non-difference delimited by "moon-ness" (*candratva-avacchinna-abheda*) in the face and so forth, based on the error of perceiving two moons.

Otherwise, even if the word *candra* here refers to that which performs the function of the moon, the defect remains as it was; for one must admit that there is an appearance of non-difference from the well-known individual moon (*prasiddha-candravyakti*) by way of its unique form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*), namely, the performance of the moon's function. Furthermore, if the performance of the moon's function were common to things other than the well-known moon, then the superimposition (*āropa*) of that [function] upon the face would not be necessary, and thus the metaphor (*rūpaka*) itself would fail to arise.

In this way, there would also be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [classifying] expressions such as "the face performs the function of the moon" as *tādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of identity). Therefore, metaphor (*rūpaka*) consists solely in the superimposition of non-difference (*abheda*), and not in the superimposition of identity (*tādrūpya*). However, if one insists that a classification into *abhedarūpaka* and *tādrūpyarūpaka* is necessary, then one must simply adopt the following distinction: *abhedarūpaka* occurs when there is a superimposition of the object characterized by the delimiting property of the standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedakāvacchinnāropa*), whereas *tādrūpyarūpaka* occurs when there is a superimposition of the attribute that serves as the delimiting property of the standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedakadharmāropa*).

An example of the first [type] is "The face is the moon; the face is another moon," and so forth; indeed, every instance where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words denoting the object of comparison and the standard of comparison falls under this category. However, it should be understood that an example of the second type is "The state of being the full moon resides in the face," and the like. Furthermore, even within that [first type], *abhedopacāra-rūpaka* (metaphor based on identity) is of two kinds: one in which identity functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*), and the other in which identity functions as a word-meaning (*padārtha*).

O lotus-eyed one, you are like a wish-fulfilling gem to those who worship you, or like a tree that provides shade; your body has attained a non-duality with the sapphire, or else a complete identity with the *tamāla* tree.

The sense is that the non-duality of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and the sapphire (*harinīla*), as well as the identity (*tādātmya*) of the *saṃtāna* tree and the *tamāla* tree, are both wonders. Here, "you are the wish-fulfilling gem" or "you are the *saṃtāna* tree" serves as an example of the first [type]. For in this case, the non-difference (*abheda*) takes the form of a relation (*saṃsarga*). But for the second [type], it is "your body attains the non-duality of the sapphire and the *tamāla*, or identity with the *tamāla*. For here, the non-difference takes the form of the word-meaning itself (*padārtha-rūpa*).

Thus, in cases such as "the face is the moon" (*mukhaṃ candraḥ*) and even in cases such as "he attains identity with the moon" (*candrādvaitam eti*), one should observe that non-difference (*abheda*) functions both as a relation (*saṃsarga*) and as the very nature of the word-meaning (*padārtha*). Furthermore, between these two—non-difference and the metaphor of identity (*tādrūpya-rūpaka*)—there can also exist a relationship of the established and the establisher (*upapādyopapādakabhāva*).
O lotus-eyed one, since your streams of rain are like necklaces and the brilliance of lightning is like a golden sash, we certainly know that you are truly a cloud. 192.

"O Acyuta, in your gentle smile there is the nature of nectar, and in your sidelong glance the nature of the mandāra flower; on your forehead, the nature of the crescent moon shines. Therefore, you are non-different from that ocean [of beauty]. In the first verse, the *abheda-rūpaka* (metaphor of identity) is the means of proof (*upapādaka*), while the *tādrūpya-rūpaka* (metaphor of similarity) is what is to be proven (*upapādya*). In the second verse, however, it is the reverse. Furthermore, within those two examples, the distinction is that in the first instance, the identity in the metaphor which serves as the means of proof is of the nature of a relation (*saṃsarga-rūpa*), whereas in the second, in the metaphor which is the object to be proven, it is of the nature of a category (*padārtha-rūpa*).

Thus, even though the classification of *rūpaka* (metaphor) as presented by the authors of the *Kuvalayānanda* has been reconciled, the verses they cited—such as "While your face-moon exists, that another moon should shine forth; this is another virtuous Lakṣmī"—are not actually examples of *tādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of identity). Enough of this prolixity.
In the opinion of the Easterners (Prācīnas), the varieties of *rūpaka* are also described;
this [rūpaka] is of three kinds: with parts (*sāṅga*), without parts (*niraṅga*), and the "successive" (*paraṃparita*). (36)
"Thus, *sāvayava-rūpaka* (metaphor with parts) is also of two kinds: that which has all things as its object (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and that which is partial (*ekadeśavivarti*).

In this regard, *rūpaka* is threefold: *sāṅga* (with limbs), which is *sāvayava*; *niraṅga* (without limbs), which is *niravayava*; and *paraṃparita* (successive). Among those three types of *rūpaka* mentioned, *sāvayava-rūpaka* is of two kinds: that which has all things as its object and that which is partial."
He defines the *sāvayava* (composite) [simile]: that which is composed of figures whose production is mutually dependent;
for a collection of figures indeed constitutes a *sāvayava*.
The meaning is that a "composite metaphor" (sāvayavarūpaka) is a collection of figures (rūpakas) whose production is mutually dependent upon one another.
There too, in the investigation [of the object], it characterizes that which exists in all things as having parts; for, in terms of verbal expression, both the whole and its parts are [perceived].
Indeed, that which has parts must have all things as its object. (39)

The meaning is that *sāvayavarūpaka* (metaphor with parts) is that where all the constituent parts and the whole, being superimposed, are expressed by words; thus, it has as its object all the constituent things.
Just as within the cage of Hari’s heart, amidst a lattice of necklaces of fresh pearl gems, the sovereign Kaustubha jewel is fixed like a pomegranate fruit for the sake of the Śrīvatsa mark.

In this case, although in reality all the constituent parts of the whole—which consists of a composite form—possess an equal relationship of mutual capacity and capacity-bearer (*samarthya-samarthaka-bhāva*), it is understood that because the poet intends only the pomegranate fruit to function as the object supported (*samarthya*) within the metaphor, the other parts are presented as the supporting factors (*samarthaka*).

This being the case, although the metaphors (*rūpaka*) that constitute the supporting elements (*samarthaka*) are subordinate (*anuvādya*) because no separate case-ending is heard for their subject and object (*viṣaya-viṣayin*), the metaphor consisting of the Kaustubha gem and the pomegranate (*dāḍima*) is primary (*vidheya*) because a separate case-ending is heard for its subject and object. Taking this into account, it is designated here as a "composite" (*saṃghātātmaka*) or "part-based" (*sāvayava*) metaphor, which is itself primary.

Just as when a certain principal warrior within a host of soldiers wins or loses, the entire host of soldiers is said to have won or lost; yet, in such cases [as those previously mentioned], it is not possible to speak of a suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the non-difference [between the object and the attribute] is being definitely ascertained. If there were *utprekṣā*, there would have to be a state of mere possibility (*saṃbhāvyamānatā*). Otherwise, by the consequence that even in instances such as "The face is the moon" there would be a suggested *utprekṣā*, the very destruction of the figure of speech known as *rūpaka* (metaphor) would follow.
Or rather,

I cherish in my heart the great sapphire of Śauri, which is like a dark lightning-flash born from the lion upon the crest of the lion-bearing mountain [the Vindhya], and which is set within the gold of his radiant beauty— just as in such expressions as "a gem set in gold," the word *upacita* is seen to carry that specific sense of being inlaid or set.

"Siṃhaladharādharaśekharaḥ" refers to Śeṣādri, the best of mountains; he is indeed Siṃhala, a specific island. Regarding that, it is said by Agastya: "Those [gems] produced from the mines of Siṃhala are known as Mahānīlas. "Hṛdaye" means in the mind and on the chest. This is a *sāvayava-rūpaka* (compound metaphor) which functions solely as an *anuvādya* (the subject of description), because no separate case endings are heard for the object (*viṣaya*) and the superimposed object (*viṣayin*). In both examples, since the whole objects and their parts—the things being superimposed—are expressed through words, it is a *samastavastuviṣaya-sāvayava-rūpaka*.
It defines the *sāvayava* (composite) variety known as *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest):
"When that which is being superimposed is verbal in some instances and non-verbal (implied) in others, this is known by the name *ekadeśavivartin*, and it is called *sāvayava*. (40)

In whatever part [of a whole], that which is being superimposed is either expressed by words or implied by the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*), that is called *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) because it "turns" (*vivartanāt*)—that is, it exists by concealing its own nature and appearing otherwise—in a part whose object is not expressed by words. Alternatively, it is called *ekadeśavivartin* because it "turns" specifically as the denoted meaning in a part whose object is expressed.
For example: [Example omitted as per instructions]

This world crosses over the exceedingly vast ocean of existence, which is turbulent with the rivers of various great latent impressions (vāsanā), by resorting to the compassion of the Lord of the Mountain of Kākoda. 196.

Here, through the metaphors of the ocean and so forth applied to existence (*bhava*) and the like, the nature of a boat is implied in relation to compassion; thus, this is an *ekadeśavivarti* (partially developed) metaphor. Or, for example:

"Victorious is the jewel-sun upon the crest of the serpent-king, which, spreading its rays of auspicious virtues, bestows joy upon the world of virtuous birds, and brings about the blossoming of the face of the Daughter of the Earth. (197)

In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*, within the *Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya*, it is well known that the daughter of the Earth (Dharaṇisutā), named Padmāvatī—who was obtained from the surface of the earth by Ākāśarāja while he was clearing the ground for a sacrifice, given into the hand of his own queen named Dharaṇī, reared by her, and married by the Lord Śrīnivāsa—is none other than Lakṣmī herself. In the preceding example, there is a negation (*ākṣepa*) of the metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting of the superimposition of "mercy" upon the poet’s intended skill.

In this case, however, the distinction is that there is an *ākṣepa* (implication) of the lotus-metaphor (*padmarūpaka*) located on the face of the daughter of the Earth, which is intended as the "supporter" (*samarthaka*). Thus, one should not insist that there is an *ākṣepa* only of the metaphor that is supported (*samarthyarūpaka*) and not of the metaphor that supports (*samarthakarūpaka*), for it has been illustrated exactly so in the *Rasagaṅgādhara* and other works. For this very reason, the designation "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*) is also appropriate for this; for its meaning is that it "manifests" (*vivartate*) either in a single part—the supported metaphor as the whole—or in the supporting metaphor as the constituent part.
The author of the Vimarsinī states that this [type of *śleṣa*], which possesses constituent parts, is seen to be of two kinds, even when it is *śliṣṭa*.
Among these, an example of a *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) metaphor that applies to all parts of the object and possesses constituent members is as follows:

"Adorned with a thousand heads made of jewels, with many feet well-guarded by the virtuous, and spreading forth a multitude of tongues in the form of jewel-rays, the serpent-king shines like a mountain."

"Maṇimayaśirassahasra" means having a thousand jewel-encrusted heads; "uttuṅga" means lofty because of that. He is so described because he possesses many "pādas"—meaning foothills—which are well-guarded, protected, and hidden. Alternatively, "bahupāda" refers to one who has many feet (legs); as Amara states: "Kuṇḍalī is gūḍhapāt. The term "phaṇabhṛddharaṇīdharādre" refers to Śeṣa, the serpent-bearer of the earth.
Here, words such as "śiras" are used with double meaning (śleṣa); as the Ratnamālā states: "Śiras [is used] for the chief, the front of an army, the top of a tree, and the head."

Or rather, as I am being dragged along the treacherous path of the dense thicket of sense objects for the sake of robbing me of my true nature, O Sole Controller of all, bind this housebreaker within my heart to Your lotus feet. 199.

On the difficult path through the dense forest of evil objects, on the painful and treacherous road of the sense-objects of the wicked senses, and indeed on that wretched track through desolate regions and wildernesses—[where] "object" (*viṣaya*) means a field of perception, a place, or a region; and "dense" (*gahana*) means a forest or suffering—[this path exists] for the very purpose of "stealing one's own nature" (*svarūpaharaṇāya*), that is, for the alteration or the removal of one's true nature whose sole essence is its subservience to the Lord. It is for the theft of one's excellent wealth; for "excellent" (*praśasta*) refers to one's own true nature (*sva-svarūpa*). The suffix *-rūpa* is applied here according to the rule *praśaṃsāyāṃ rūpap*.

Bind me—me who am dragging away your very heart—to your lotus-like feet (*abje pade*), which are like lotuses situated in water, that is to say, in the midst of the ocean; or rather, bind me to your station, which is like a prison (*kārāgāra*). Here, “binding” (*nigalaya*) means making one motionless, as if providing the state of being shackled. [Note on grammar: The word *aikāgārika* is grammatically correct due to the rule of *nipātana* (irregular formation) stating “*aikāgārika-ṭcora*” [Pāṇini 3.1.48]. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: for this thief (*mumupiṣoḥ*) whose sole purpose (*prayojanam*) is the solitary house (*ekam asahāyam agāram*), he is an *aikāgārika*. Thus, it refers to a housebreaker. Bind me to your feet, which are like lotuses, within the ocean—that is, in the middle of the sea—or in your place, which is like a prison. In this context, making [the heart] motionless is itself the production of the state of being shackled.

The vocative “O Ruler of All” (nikhilaniyantaḥ) intends to convey His sovereignty over such acts of restraint and grace; here too, words such as “durviṣaya” and others are used with double meaning (śleṣa).
He defines the partless metaphor (*niravayavarūpaka*):

the wise know that to be "partless" which is the metaphorization of the subject alone. According to the opinion of the virtuous, it is of two kinds: simple (*kevala*) and in the form of a garland (*mālārūpa*).
"Without parts" means devoid of components; [it refers to] that which consists merely of parts, that is, that which consists merely of a whole.

Therein, that which is absolute, partless, as vast as the wind-nourished mountain-born [ocean], abundant wealth, the refuge of all, pure, renowned, and praised by the Lord of Wealth—when meditated upon, it whitens the multitude of heart-lotuses. (200)

The Blessed One is determined [by the devotee] through his possession of abundant wealth; he "whitens"—that is, gladdens—the heart-lotus, meaning the lotus of the heart. Here, the figure of speech *hṛtsarojātam* (heart-lotus) is a *niravayava* (non-composite) metaphor, because it lacks the nature of being a collection of dependent metaphors (*sāpekṣarūpaka*). It is *kevala* (simple), as it lacks the quality of being a *mālā* (garland).

I bow to Him who is partless, whose form is beyond all taint, the root-source of all beauty, the sandalwood tree that brings bliss to Mucukunda, the celestial *mandāra* flower for the hosts of gods who prostrate before Him, and the moon upon the mountain of serpents.

Because it consists of the superimposition of various objects upon a single subject, this is of the nature of a *mālā* (garland); because it lacks mutual dependence [between its parts], it is partless (*niravayava*).

The author of the *Vimarśinī*, however, states that even when there is a superimposition of multiple word-meanings upon multiple objects, this "partless" (*niravayava*) series simile (*mālārūpaka*) is seen to exist through the distinction between the *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) and *aśliṣṭa* (non-pun-based).
Among these, an example of the non-pun-based superimposition of multiple [meanings] upon multiple objects is as follows:

"Your eyes are lotuses; your face is the abode of Lakṣmī; your smile is nectar; your two cheeks are fragments of mirrors; your two earrings are the tips of the trunk of Airāvata and the sun. (202) In this instance, there is a non-pun-based superimposition of multiple meanings upon the multiple objects, namely the eyes and so forth.
Superimposition of multiple [identities] based on a pun (śleṣa) is as follows:

"Your face is indeed a lotus, your heart is a mine of jewels, and your luster is the river Kṛṣṇā; destroying the heat of the heart, O Lord of the Mountain, you are a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) through your very glance. (203)

We have already stated that *Tīrthagiri* is indeed another name for Veṅkaṭādri. Here, because many scholars assert that the words *puṣkara*, *ratnākara*, *kṛṣṇa*, and *hṛttāpanāśinī* are *śliṣṭa* (double-entendre), there are numerous superimpositions (*āropa*) based on multiple meanings such as "mouth" and so forth. Thus, this is a *śliṣṭārtha-rūpaka-mālā* (a series of metaphors with double-entendre meanings). *Puṣkara* refers both to a lotus and a well-known sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). *Ratnākara* refers both to the source or abode of jewels such as the Kaustubha and the ocean. *Kṛṣṇa* refers both to the color black/blue and a specific river.

It means that she is the destroyer of heart-burning and the remover of mental anguish, and she is a particular sacred site (tīrtha) located in the Vīkṣāraṇya forest. Indeed, among her names it is recited: "She whose essence is all sacred sites, who takes the form of all planetary influences."

Just as your eye is a white lotus, your smile a night-lotus, and the radiance of your gaze the collyrium, yet your conduct is universal— I know you to be the very soul of the world-elephant of the quarters.

Here too, the words *puṇḍarīka*, *kumuda*, *añjana*, and *sārvabhauma* signify both white lotuses and so forth, as well as the elephants of the quarters (*diggaja*). Thus, since there are multiple punned terms applied to the eyes and other features as elephants of the quarters, this is a "garland of metaphors based on punned meanings" (*śliṣṭārtha-rūpaka-mālā*). As Amarasimha states: "Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the quarters."

*Sārvabhauma* means "known throughout the entire earth. Under the governing rule *tatra viditaḥ* ("known therein"), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *sarvabhūmipṛthivībhyāmaṇañau*. Due to its inclusion in the *anuśatikādi* group, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both syllables. In another sense, it means a particular type of world-elephant (*diggaja*).

When one object belonging to a certain domain is described as being connected with another object belonging to a different domain, through a relationship of cause and effect, that is then called *paraṃparita* (transferred) metaphor. (42)

If the object of superimposition (*viṣayī*), which is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) standing in the relation of cause and effect, is connected through identity with another object of superimposition associated with a single [primary] superimposition upon the subject (*viṣaya*), that is *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor of succession).

O Lord, best of gods, just as the entire multitude of people was made to rest by you— the moon who holds the ocean of existence— so indeed has this abundance of intense heat produced by the austerity consisting of such worldly existence been pacified.

*Tārānātha* is the moon; *tapaḥ* is the summer season. Here, in the phrase "the moon that is the ocean for the mass of people who are entirely submissive," between the two metaphors (*rūpaka*)—that of the ocean and that of the moon—which stand in a relationship of cause and effect, the metaphorical form of the moon (*tārānātha*), which is the superimposed object (*āropyabhūta*) and is already connected with the ocean, is then established through identity (*tādātmya*) with the Lord, who is the substratum (*viṣaya*).

Since the intended representation is specifically as the Lord of Stars (the Moon) related to the ocean, there is here a *paraṃparitarūpaka* (successive metaphor). Because of the qualification that the superimposed object (*viṣayin*) is connected with another superimposed object, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a *sāvayavarūpaka* (metaphor with parts), such as in the verse: "I cherish in my heart the great sapphire Śauri, who is born from the lion-like crest of the mountain [the moon], who is a dark flash of lightning, and who is enriched by the gold of the beauty of Lakṣmī."

For in that case, although there exists a cause-and-effect relationship between the metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) of Śauri as "Mahānīla" and the metaphorical identification of the mountain Siṃhadharādharā and so forth as "Siṃhala" and so forth, there is no over-extension [of the definition], because the superimposed Mahānīla lacks a connection with the superimposed Siṃhala and so forth which have entered into another metaphorical identification. In that instance, Śauri is identified solely by way of being Mahānīla, and not by way of being the Mahānīla belonging to Siṃhala and so forth.
By this [definition], "that which is a superimposition upon another by means of a fixed superimposition is 'paramparita' (metaphorical transference)."

Thus, the aforementioned definition suffers from the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases of *sāvayava-rūpaka* (compound metaphor), such as "white with the smearing of moonlight-ashes" and the like; for even there, it is possible to maintain that the representation of [her] as ashes and so forth necessarily serves as the cause for the representation of her as a *kāpālikī* (female ascetic).

For just as in examples such as “the swan of the learned man’s mind” (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), the metaphorical representation of the king as a swan is not possible without the simultaneous metaphorical representation of the "mind of the learned" (*vidvanmānasa*) as the Mānasa lake, so too the metaphorical representation of the night as a female skull-bearer (*kapālikī*) is not possible without the metaphorical representation of the moonlight and so forth as ashes and the like; this is because of their similarity. As for the claim that in examples such as “the swan of the learned man’s mind” alone, a single metaphor is necessarily dependent on another metaphor while this is not the case elsewhere, that is refuted by the fact that such a distinction can only be established through a mere oath.

This is because it is accepted that such a definition ultimately reduces to the very definition we have presented; for in a case where there is the superimposition of one thing upon another, one superimposition invariably becomes the cause of the other superimposition, and thus the reduction of that definition to such [a state] is possible.

By this, the statement of certain scholars—that "the *paramparita* (transferred) metaphor terminates in merely two superimpositions (*āropa*), whereas the *sāvayava* (composite) metaphor is not like that"—is to be disregarded. For, in cases such as the *paramparita-rūpaka* cited by [Appaya Dīkṣita] beginning with "O swan of the learned man’s mind" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), there exists a plurality of superimpositions; thus, their definition would result in the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*). Nor can it be argued that there is no under-extension here because each part of the verse—such as "swan of the learned man’s mind"—consists of merely two superimpositions.

Therefore, it must be stated that this verse is cited as an example of a "garland-like" (*mālārūpa*) successive metaphor (*paraṃparita-rūpaka*) precisely because of its abundance of such metaphors. If this were the case, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur even in the verse beginning with *jyotsnābhasma*, since in the portion *bibhratī tārakāsthīni, rātrikāpālikīyam*, there is the possibility of only two metaphors. Nor can the definition of a successive metaphor be restricted merely to two metaphors standing in a cause-and-effect relationship while being independent of any other metaphor.

And thus, just as in the *kāpālika*-metaphor in the verse beginning with "moonlight-ash" (*jyotsnābhasma*), there is a dependence on the metaphor of "stars-bones" (*tārakāsthīni*), so too, because there is a dependence on the metaphor of "moonlight-ash" and so forth, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition. Furthermore, it should be stated that in cases such as "O swan of the mind of the learned" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), in the metaphor of the swan and so on, there is indeed a dependence on each individual metaphor, such as the metaphor of the Mānasa lake; thus, the consistency of the definition is maintained.

Even so, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as that cited in the *Kāvyadarpaṇa*: “‘In this way, while the glory of King Sūrya, the son of the lord of the earth, remains as a mere remnant, he [the sun], the companion of the beauty of the sky, sleeps’”—wherein the metaphor of the "companion of the beauty of the sky" depends upon the metaphor of the "remnant. Nor is it appropriate to accept this as a desired conclusion, because it is not accepted by the authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others who define the "chain metaphor" (*paraṃparita-rūpaka*) as: "That wherein the non-superimposition of one thing serves as the fixed means for the superimposition of another."

Even if one does not conceive of fame as having the status of a remainder (*śeṣa*), it is possible to establish the metaphor of "the companion of Śrī" through the reading of the verse: "Under the pretext of fame, the companion of Śrī sleeps while remaining as a remainder. This is because, in that case, a fixed relationship of cause and effect between the two metaphors is impossible. Nor should it be argued that, this being so, the definition should be refined by incorporating only the state of having become a fixed relationship of cause and effect into the two metaphors.

Even so, in cases such as "the root-tuber of the fourteen world-vines," there would be the undesirable consequence of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding the *paraṃparita* (transferred) type, which is accepted by [some] as consisting of a series beginning with "light" (*prakāśa*). For even there, since it is possible to construe the composition either as "the cause of the fourteen world-vines" or as "the root-tuber of the fourteen worlds," it is difficult to establish a fixed relationship between cause and effect. Therefore, the definition of *paraṃparitarūpaka* must be accepted as being simply: "another metaphor whose object is connected to the object of a preceding metaphor of a single form."

In all the examples of *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor by metaphor) found in venerable earlier treatises such as the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and the *Sarvasva*, the word expressing the object (*viṣaya*) in the subsequent metaphor is seen to be uncomposed (uncompounded) with the word expressing the superimposed object (*viṣayin*). Consequently, in that case, the superimposition belonging to the subsequent metaphor occurs in the object of the former metaphor only after it has already been connected [with that object].

Thus, we take refuge in Him whose feet are the crest-jewel of the maiden of the City of the Immortals, who possesses compassion that ferries one across the ocean of existence, and who is the mountain-adornment dark blue as a rain-cloud. 206.

In such examples of *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (successive metaphor), although in the two subsequent metaphors the words expressing the objects (*viṣaya*)—namely "feet" (*caraṇa*) and "compassion" (*karuṇā*)—are seen in a compound with the words expressing the superimposed objects (*viṣayin*)—namely "ornament" (*vataṃsa*) and "sun" (*taraṇi*), the connection of the two superimposed objects, namely the "ornament" and the "sun," occurs precisely through their connection with the respective objects of the preceding metaphor, namely the "feet" and "compassion."

Likewise, in the case of those instances of *sāvayavarūpaka* where [the parts] are themselves superimposed, there is nowhere a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) between the object of one superimposition and the object of another superimposition that would be conducive to their syntactic connection; thus, there is no room for the suspicion of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor should it be argued that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of the *Rasagaṅgādharah* example of "successive metaphor" (*paraṃparita-rūpaka*), namely: "Your sword is a serpent, with a smooth luster fed on the milk of the lives of bewildered enemies," because the superimposition of the prior metaphor cannot be construed with the object of the subsequent metaphor—the serpent—due to the intervention of words such as "feeding on milk. This is not so, because we have included in our definition the property of being "conjoined with the object of superimposition" (*āropya-anvitatva*) in a manner common to both direct and indirect relations.
Indeed, this being so,
having plunged into the cool Gaṅgā of the compassion of the Lord of the Mountain-Kings— the serpent-king who is an ocean of vast and auspicious qualities— men never again engage in talk of suffering.

If it is argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) here because the prior metaphorical superimposition (*pūrvarūpaka*) upon this ocean and the posterior metaphorical superimposition (*uttararūpaka*) upon the Gaṅgā could occur in succession (*paraṃparayā*), we say no; for that is excluded precisely by including the qualification "being related as cause and effect" (*hetuhetumadbhāvāpannatva*) within the definition of the two metaphors. For in this case, there is no relationship of cause and effect between the two metaphors shown.

Although the verse "paryaṅko rājalakṣmyāḥ" is cited as an example of a *mālā-paraṃparita* (chain-like successive) metaphor, there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in such a case of *ekadeśavivarti-paraṃparita-rūpaka* (successive metaphor with partial transformation), because the author of the *Sarvasva* states that in the phrase "kṣmāsauvidallaḥ," even though it is a *paraṃparita*, it is an *ekadeśavivartin*. This is because the superimposition (*āropa*) of the "king's wife" upon the "earth" is for the sake of the meaning; thus, the queen—who is the object of superimposition in the preceding metaphor—cannot be construed with the "chamberlain" (*sauvidalla*), who is the object of superimposition in the subsequent metaphor.

Nevertheless, the status of being a "partial metaphor" (*ekadeśavivartin*) does not apply to the "successive" (*paraṃparita*) type according to the author’s own intention; for that would contradict his own previous classification. For in that [classification], by the passage beginning with “But this is partless,” the partial metaphor is counted as a sub-variety of the "possessing parts" (*sāvayava*) type alone, and not even as a sub-variety of the "successive" type.

However, the statement in this verse that "the entire essence [of the figure] has been demonstrated" must somehow be reconciled by taking the phrase *'kṣmāsauvidallaḥ'* as a single-part concealing metaphor (*ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka*) which stands in grammatical apposition with a chain of metaphors (*paraṃparita-mālā-rūpaka*) beginning with *'paryaṅkaḥ'*.

Otherwise, if one were to accept a mere pair of metaphors produced by implied metaphors (*ākṣipta-rūpaka*), there would arise a contradiction with the statement in the section on *samāsokti* (speech of compendium) which aims to establish the single-part concealing metaphor in the verse *'nirīkṣya vidyunnayanaiḥ'*.

For this very reason, it is logical that the variety known as *ekadeśavivartin* (partial metaphor) is not enumerated among the types of *paraṃparita* (metaphor in a series) in earlier treatises on poetics such as the *Prakāśa*, nor in later works such as the *Rasagaṅgādhara*.

In reality, even if one accepts a *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (compound metaphor) based on the metaphor of the "Queen" (*rājamahiṣī*)—which is obtained through implication—in the expression "the chamberlain of the earth" (*kṣmāsauvidallaḥ*), there is no risk of our proposed definition being too narrow (*avyāpti*) in that case. This is because we accept that from the word "chamberlain of the earth," there arises through the assistance of implication a verbal cognition of the form "the chamberlain of the Queen of the Earth"; thus, the property of being connected with the superimposition of the first metaphor remains unimpeded in the superimposition of the second metaphor.

It is well-established in the tradition of the Tantrikas—who accept the theory of generic power (*jāti-śakti*) and so forth—that even a meaning obtained through implication (*ākṣepalabhya*) appears in verbal cognition alongside the meaning of the word actually uttered.

And thus, one must necessarily rely on the fact that the analytical statement (*vibhāga-vākya*) composed by the author of the *Sarvasva* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Otherwise, the demonstration by the commentator Vimarsinīkāra—of the two types, *śliṣṭa* and *aśliṣṭa*, which were shown by him [the Sarvasvakāra] only in the case of *paramparita* [metaphor], as occurring even in *sāvayava* [metaphor]—would be contradicted; for instance, in the example: “The king is the chamberlain (*sauvidalla*) of the earth,” where it is stated: “This is also a *paramparita* [metaphor] that is *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest).”

The statement by the author of the *Sarvasva*, “Other varieties such as these have also been indicated even briefly,” as well as the statement by the author of the *Vimarśinī*—taking up the phrase “such as these” (*evamādayaḥ*)—“these types include even the *paraparita* (metaphor of succession) where there is a partial transformation (*ekadeśavivartin*),” would not naturally be consistent [if the former were not meant to include the latter].

Furthermore, this does not conflict with the passage from the *Kāvyapradīpa* which, on the occasion of defining "closely connected" (*śliṣṭa*) and "successively connected" (*paraṃparita*) [metaphors], cites the verse "O swan of the mind of the learned" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*) and states: "For this is also called 'partially transformative' (*ekadeśavivartin*). Taking up the phrase "for this," the text continues: "In the root text, the construction is 'this also. Even though there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the specific lake (*sarovisheṣa*) presented by a single word, there is no superimposition (*āropa*) of one upon the other; for that [superimposition] requires the indication of a distinct object."

"Otherwise, since that [superimposition] would also follow in the case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which consists in the swallowing up of the object (*viṣayanigaraṇa*), this superimposition must be understood as purely semantic (*ārtha*). Therefore, it is appropriate here as well for it to be 'subsisting in a single part' (*ekadeśavivartin*). This is the explanation provided by Prabhākara. Consequently, there is no harm in accepting the statement from his own work, "The earth's *sauvidalla* (eunuch)," etc., which—according to its literal sense—conveys that even a *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor with a chain) can be subsisting in a single part. Thus, even if one asserts this, there is no defect.
But surely, if one accepts that even a metaphorical expression based on a series (paraṃparita) is a type of partial metaphor (ekadeśavivartin), then consider this:
"She is a river of beauty, a surge of joy for the excellence of youth, a magical spell for loveliness, and the dwelling place for the blossoming of playful words."

She is knowledge that realizes the boundless mastery of the Creator who fashions crooked speech; she is the life-breath of the five-arrowed god of love; she is the crest-jewel of women; she is my beloved.

If this were so, the statement in the *Citramīmāṃsā* that this verse serves as an example of a "garland" (*mālā*) and "non-component" (*niravayava*) metaphor would be inconsistent. For in such cases as "a river of beauty" (*saundaryasya taraṅgiṇī*), since the superimposition of the nature of water upon beauty and the like occurs prior to the superimposition of the nature of a river, and because the superimposed object in the form of water—obtained through implication—is connected with the superimposed subject in the form of a river, the status of "transferred" (*paraṃparita*) metaphor remains unimpeded. To this, we reply: true.

There is no fault in this, for [the examples] such as "the *kārmaṇa*-action of her beauty" (*kānteḥ kārmaṇakarma*) cited by others are instances of the *mālā-niravayava-rūpaka* (garland-like non-limbed metaphor). For in that case, only the *kārmaṇa*-action and so forth are superimposed upon the beloved, but nothing at all is superimposed upon her beauty and the rest. Thus, it should be understood that this *mālā-niravayava-rūpaka* is indeed a type of *paraṃparita-saṃkīrṇa* (successive mixed metaphor). Indeed, even in the primary examples of a single figure of speech, a mixture with other figures of speech is observed.

For example, in the illustration of the "qualified metaphor" (*sāvayavarūpaka*) such as "moonlight-ash," there is a commingling with "concealment by pretext" (*kaitavāpahnuti*) and other figures, as seen in the phrase "under the guise of the [moon's] mark."
This, however, is an example of a pure *mālā* (garland) compound consisting of indivisible members:

"I take refuge in the foot of Hari, which is the crest-jewel for the ears of those who hear his deeds; [the foot] upon which rest the lotuses sportively held by the tips of the hands of Lakṣmī and the Earth, and which is bowed to by the crowns of the prostrating gods. (208)

The form of Hari—whose enchantment is like that of a blue lotus, whose magical power is like a dark rain-cloud, whose splendor is like the tamāla tree, and who is intent on the playful delight of sporting upon the mountain of serpents—removes all suffering.

*Saṃvanana* means the act of subjugation (*vaśakriyā*). *Kārmaṇa* refers to *mūlakarma* (root-rites); as Amara states: "Subjugation is *saṃvanana*, while *mūlakarma* is *kārmaṇa*. *Śrī* means prosperity or excellence. In the first example, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) solely of the crown, the play-lotus, and the ear-ornament upon the feet of Hari as the object. In the second, however, there is a superimposition solely of the blue lotus, the subjugating power, the dark cloud, the *kārmaṇa* rite, and the *tamāla* tree upon the form of Hari; thus, this is a pure, partless (*niravayava*) *mālā* [metaphor].

In the same way, even in cases of superimposition based on grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), such as "the double appearance of the Flower-Arrowed God [Kāma] is the redundancy of the celestial trees," it should be understood that there is pure *mālā* (garland) and no subordinate members (*niravayavatva*). Enough of this prolixity.
And he divides that transposed [metaphor] by the distinction between the "coalescent" (śliṣṭa) and the "non-coalescent" (aśliṣṭa): "That transposed [metaphor] is of two kinds."
And the *mālikā*; thus that [metaphor] becomes twofold.
In this way, according to the opinion of the ancients, metaphor (*rūpaka*) is held to be of eight kinds. (43)

That *paraṃparita* (successive) [metaphor] is of two kinds. Among these, when the intended superimposition (*āropa*) functions as the means of justification (*samarthaka*) and is rooted in *śleṣa* (punning), it is *śliṣṭa-paraṃparita*. Both of these are further divided into two types: simple and in the form of a garland (*mālārūpa*). Regarding this *paraṃparita-rūpaka*, Maṅkhuka and others maintain that the subsequent metaphor serves as the cause for the preceding metaphor.

Their intention is this: in such instances as "O swan of the learned mind" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), since the king and so forth are the subjects of description and thus appear first, there is first an imposition (*āropa*) of the nature of a swan and so on upon him; subsequently, through *śleṣa* (pun), there is an imposition of the nature of a particular lake and so on upon that which is not the subject of description, namely the "learned mind" (*vidvanmānasa*). This is also the case in non-*śliṣṭa* (non-pun-based) *paramparita-rūpaka*. However, Mammaṭa and others maintain that the preceding *rūpaka* serves as the cause for the subsequent *rūpaka*, as they say: "Thus, the imposition of the nature of a swan and so on is caused by the [prior] imposition."

Their position is as follows: in examples such as "vidvanmānasahaṃsa" ("the swan of the minds of the learned"), because the *śleṣa* (punning) in "mānasa" and so on occurs first, it is logical that the *rūpaka* (metaphor), which depends upon the identification of two meanings rooted in that *śleṣa*, should—by virtue of its initial cognition—serve as the cause for the subsequent cognition of the *rūpaka*. Thus, under our definition of *paramparita-rūpaka* (metaphor by succession)—namely, that it consists in the state of having another object as its correlate, while being associated with a single subject that has entered into a relationship of cause and effect—the inclusion of both views will be achieved.
In that regard, an example of the purely *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) *paraṃparita* (metaphorical chain) is as follows:
"O heart, worship that ancient Person who has exerted effort, the crest-jewel upon the head of the Lord of Serpents; for what could be more novel than even that? (210)

In this case, although the relationship of the supported (*samarthya*) and the support (*samarthaka*) between the two superimpositions (*āropa*) is in fact equal, the poet’s intention is that the superimposition of the identity with the crest-jewel upon the Blessed One is to be supported by the superimposition based on *śleṣa* (punning) in which the mountain (*bhūmibhṛt*, literally "earth-bearer") is itself the king (*rājā*, also "earth-bearer"). For this very reason, the rejection of other ornaments mentioned in the fourth quarter of the verse is also consistent.
O lotus-eyed one, you who delight in the vast abode of the broad lower lip of the queen of the great serpents, you are like a restless cloud that repeatedly increases the splendor of the waters.

O lotus-eyed one, you who take delight in dwelling upon the vast ground of that Śeṣādri—the mountain-like Śeṣa whose lower lip is as expansive as the king of serpents—you are a cloud for the lightning of Lakṣmī; for according to the *Medinī* lexicon, "the word *capalā* refers to Lakṣmī, lightning, a wanton woman, and long pepper. You repeatedly increase the beauty of the waters, the abundance of the liquid; in the alternative sense, you increase the splendor and fortune of *bahuśasta*, which is an auspicious destiny (*ayaḥ*).

Alternatively, there is the analysis *bahuśastaḥ yaḥ śriyam* (the one highly praised who [bestows] prosperity). Or, it may be construed through a syntactical split as: "O you who are *capalāvalāhakaḥ* (a restless cloud), you who increase (*samedhayase*) prosperity (*śriyam*), that is, wealth. In this case, because the word *yat* (who) occurs in the subsequent clause, there is no necessity of employing the word *tat* (he/that) in the preceding clause.

Although there is an equality in the relationship between the mutual support and the supported in both these superimpositions (*āropa*), the poet’s intention is that the superimposition of identity with a cloud (*balāhaka*) upon the Blessed One is to be supported by the superimposition based on *śleṣa* (punning wordplay), namely, "the fickle Lakṣmī is herself the fickle lightning. For this very reason, it is also appropriate that the abundant increase of the beauty of water, indicated by the *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* (split-pun) occurring in the fourth quarter [of the verse], serves as its support.

In both examples, there are two metaphors (*rūpaka*) which, because they are linked through a causal relationship, constitute a "successive" (*paraṃparita*) metaphor; they are based on punning words (*śliṣṭa-śabda-nibandhana*), and because they lack the form of a series (*mālā-rūpa*), they are simple (*kevala*).

May that very form, which is like a garland—possessing all flowers as its springtime, possessing a dense mass of lightning as its thunderclouds, and possessing the goddess Sarasvatī as its line of bees—take refuge in my heart, for it is the beloved of the Mountain (Himavat). 212.

The heart—the agent—is [the locus] of that pearl necklace, which is a row (*āli*) or a series of pearls; these pearls being like all flowers (*sakalasumanas*), like all the learned (*samastavidvas*), like a cluster of virtuous men (*sādhukadamba*), like a grove of trees beloved by noble people (*sajjananivaha*), and like those liberated from their natural bonds (*muktā*). Its heart is the subject.

I bow upon this earth to the lotus-eyed one, who is like an ocean for the family of the unblinking [gods], whose bodily form is the limit of the abundance of dense majesty and splendor, and who is a mountain of snow for the supreme frost of worldly existence.

I bow to that lotus-eyed one on earth—whose multitude of fish is like a host of deities with unblinking eyes; whose dense and thick mass of opulent splendor is like the supreme excellence of the ocean's majesty; who is the Himālaya mountain of excessive snow, as it were, through his supreme greatness, at the end of the summer heat, which is the season of the rains. Having suddenly prostrated before Kṛṣṇa upon the dusty ground, one becomes instantly free from sin by the mere decoration of dust upon the forehead.

The statement "bowing upon the earth" (*bhuvi namānī*) is based on the investigation of such authorities [as grammatical rules]. It is the first person singular imperative form of the root *nam*. Here, because the intended superimposition (*āropa*) of "being springtime" and so forth upon Śrīnivāsa—based on a superimposition rooted in *śleṣa* (punning) such as "the springtime of the well-minded" (*sumanasām vasantam*)—is supported by being composed in many ways, this is a case of *śliṣṭamālāparaṃparita* (a chain of punning superimpositions).

Regarding this, some say that in examples such as "O swan of the learned man’s mind" (*vidvanmānasahaṃsa*), because the nature of a swan and so forth is superimposed upon the object of description, the superimposition of the nature of a lake and so forth upon the mind and other things is understood by implication; therefore, they claim this is merely *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest) metaphor. In reality, however, because it possesses the certainty of a specific aesthetic charm consisting of a superimposition of non-difference based on the use of punning words (*śliṣṭaśabda*), it is indeed distinct from that [type of metaphor]. This is the general direction [of the argument].
In this very way,
I salute the elephant of the Vṛṣācala mountain— the auspicious Malaya mountain, which is a divine cow bestowing the play of the Śrīvatsa mark, a source of joy for the swans, and the granter of boons.

In this case as well, a "conjoined metaphorical succession" (śliṣṭa-paramparita-rūpaka) is to be understood. *Bhadraśrī* refers to auspicious prosperity itself, as well as the sandalwood tree named Bhadraśrī. *Śrīvatsa* refers to the mark on Viṣṇu’s chest, as well as a calf endowed with beauty (*śrī*). *Haṃsa*s refer to the wise, as well as swans.

O Hari, who dwells in the lotus-born Brahmā, you alone performed this pure, traditional, and absolute act: for the destruction of the forest-like multitude of your enemies and for the protection of the worlds, you built a dwelling upon the mountain that sustains itself on the wind.

"Bhāvana" means manifestation. In the phrase "śritābjabhuvana," the superimposition of the nature of water upon the Blessed One is intended as the basis for the superimposition of the nature of a lotus upon those who have taken refuge; thus, it is a "paramparita" (transferred) metaphor. Furthermore, because it lacks both a "mālā" (garland) and "śleṣa" (punning), it is purely "śuddha" (simple).
In this very form as a garland— just as the earth,
the peacock, the cloud, the full moon, Lakṣmī, the blue-lotus pond, the sun, the lotus, and the lord of the world— I shall worship the Lord of the World on Śeṣādri.

In this case, since the numerous superimpositions (āropa) of "cloud" and so forth upon Śrīnivāsa—the Lord of the World—await the superimposition of "peacock" and so forth upon the earth and other objects, it is a pure *mālā-paraṃparita-rūpaka* (garlanded chain metaphor). We have already stated that this can also be a *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest), as for example:
"May we contemplate within our hearts the divine-limbed abode, which is a stage for the dance of beauty, a lofty inner apartment of tranquility, and a chariot of forgiveness for the Destroyer."

In this verse, through the metaphorical representations of the Blessed One as a dance stage and so forth, the metaphors of a dancer, a queen, and a lotus-lady are perceived in relation to her radiance, tranquility, and forbearance; thus, this is a pure *mālā-paraṃparita-rūpaka* (a series of metaphors) that is partially developed (*ekadeśavivartin*).

O my heart, [fix upon] that certain pinnacle of auspiciousness residing on the mountain of the serpent-king (Śrīparvata), which is the support of the worlds, the refuge of all lights, and the cause of the glory of the Śākhi lineage. 218.

Here, through paronomastic metaphors (*śliṣṭarūpaka*)—where "worlds" (*bhuvana*) refers to the oceans, "lights" (*bhā*) to the stars, and the "lineage of branches" (*śākhikula*) to the multitude of Vedic reciters as well as a cluster of trees—the metaphors of the Lord as the ocean, the moon, and the spring are implied; thus, this is an example of a "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*) "paronomastic chain metaphor" (*śliṣṭaparaṃparita*). This is the general direction [of the analysis].

Knowledge is the wealth of the wise; splendor is the great wealth of the illustrious here on earth; honey is the wealth of bees; and truly, the Lord of the Serpent Mountain is the wealth for those who bow before him. 219.

In this case, the mere arrangement of a series of objects (*viṣayamālā*) does not produce any particular aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*); therefore, it is not counted as a separate variety in the enumeration of types. However, a series of superimposed objects (*āropyamāṇamālā*) is indeed counted, because it possesses a specific aesthetic charm. Now, one might ask: how can there be a relationship where one superimposition serves as the cause for another superimposition in a *śliṣṭaparaṃparita* (based on paronomasia) example, such as "the crest-jewel of the mountain-king of the serpent-lords" (*bhujagādhipabhūmibhṛcchiroratnam*) or "the spring of all flowers" (*sakalasumanovasantam*)? For, through the paronomasia (*śleṣa*), only the identity between the mountain and the king, and between the learned men and the flowers, is perceived here; there is no superimposition of one thing upon another, since such a superimposition requires the mention of a distinct, independent locus (*svatantraviṣaya*).
