In the definition, the two mentions of the "subject" (*dharmi*) are for the purpose of excluding *mīlita* (the concealment of a specific quality) and *sāmānyatadguṇa* (the assumption of common qualities). The term "non-artificial" (*anāhārya*) is for the purpose of excluding the cognition of *rūpaka* (poetic metaphor); alternatively, one may say "residing in someone other than the poet. The term "certainty" (*niścaya*) is for the purpose of excluding doubt; and the term "wonderful" (*camatkārī*) is for the purpose of excluding a cognition such as "this is silver," which has a piece of mother-of-pearl as its qualificandum. The meaning is "produced by the poet’s creative intuition" (*pratibhā*). Since the cognition "silver in the mother-of-pearl" is merely worldly, it is not produced by the poet’s creative intuition. For example: [Example omitted] In this case, the identification of the moon with a lotus is not produced by the poet’s creative intuition, because it is based on a worldly convention. However, the identification of the face with the moon is produced by the poet’s creative intuition, because it is not established in the world. Therefore, the definition is faultless. During the sport in the water, seeing their own reflections in every wave, the fish, mistaking them for large sharks, flee far away, agitated by fear.

"Large-scaled great fish"—through this delusion, all [the waters] are "sakalāḥ," meaning complete; as Amara states: "The words *samagra*, *sakala*, *akhaṇḍa*, *pūrṇa*, and others are used for that which is not deficient. "Śakulāḥ" means small fish; the sense is that they are tiny. Here, the figure of speech is *bhrānti* (delusion), as the error residing in the fish serves to intensify the agitation caused by the fear of the *śakula*.
Or, for example:

"The side-glance of the Lord of the Golden Mountain (Śiva), resting upon the surface of Lakṣmī’s cheek, bestowed beauty upon her by creating the illusion of a drop of collyrium applied to ward off defects of vision. (288)

Here, because it is stated without qualification, the figure of speech is *bhrāntimān* (error) as it pertains to all beings, such as gods and humans; however, the scope of the figure *bhrāntimān* is restricted solely to error caused by resemblance, not that which is occasioned by other causes.

Just as I know that there is nothing here that is not You, who have become the inner self of all— whosoever wanders in error regarding this truth wanders for a long time in existence, O Lord of the Serpent Mountain.

O Lord of the Mountain! "In you" here means that no diversity exists; the meaning is that you alone are the Supreme Brahman. The reason for this is expressed in the words beginning with "I know. I know you to be the inner self of all—that which constitutes the inner self of all objects existing throughout all space and time. He who wanders, who becomes deluded regarding this truth, wanders for a long time in *bhava*, that is, in *saṃsāra*.
By this [scriptural passage] it is meant: "What is here is there, and what is there is here.
One goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity."
This must be attained by the mind alone; there is nothing whatsoever diverse here.
He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death.

Thus the meaning of the scriptural passage has been considered. Here, because error is based on dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*), it does not constitute a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*). Even when error is caused by similarity (*sādṛśya*), it is accepted as a figure only when it is brought forth by the flash of a poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*) for the sake of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*), as in the verse cited immediately below beginning with “*jalavihṛtau*. It is not brought forth by its own inherent nature, like the [erroneous perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Thus, because it is caused by similarity, properties such as the "corresponding" (*anugāmin*) and others may serve as its common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) as the case may allow. Among these, an example of a corresponding property (*anugāmidharma*) is as follows:

Out of fickleness, Lakṣmī approaches the Lord of Mountains, who is like a serpent, to embrace him; meanwhile, the Sun, thinking it to be the Kaustubha gem, covers that radiant jewel with both his hands.
In this instance, the attribute "possessing compassion" is indicated as a pervasive quality.

Just as bees, perceiving the Kaustubha gem resting upon the peak of the line of hair on his chest as a lotus with its stalk, suddenly alight from the white water-lily used as an ear-ornament by Lakṣmī, who has become like a reflected image of him.

*Jhagiti* means "instantly" or "in a flash. In this manner, other instances should also be inferred by the intelligent. Sometimes, there is a striking charm (*camatkāra*) arising from the successive expansion of an error (*bhrānti*), as in: "O Śauri, your playful parrots mistake the emerald crest-jewel for a parrot, and then the ruby crown for a pomegranate; having thus completely stripped it [of its true nature], they perceive it as a pomegranate. (292)

O Śrī, the parrots that are the playful ornaments of Śauri perceive the crest-jewel of the Lord—which is emerald in form—as a parrot; immediately thereafter, they perceive His crown, which is composed of red gems and studded with rubies, as a pomegranate fruit whose seeds have been extracted by that very parrot through the pecking of its beak-tip, such that the rows of seeds are revealed on the outside.

Regarding the term *niṣkulākṛtam*, it is derived from the rule *niṣkulānniṣkoṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 5.4.62), where the *bahuvrīhi* compound *niṣkulaḥ*—meaning "that from which the *kula* (the collection of internal parts) has gone out"—takes the suffix *ḍāc*.
In some cases, a particular striking effect arises from the basis of a mutual confusion regarding each other's objects, as in:
"Seeing peacocks, the female swans are terrified, mistaking them for fresh clouds; and they too, seeing the geese, perceive them as autumnal rain-clouds in the forest of Mount Vṛṣādri. (293)
Then,

O Śauri, as the young elephant-faced one bows down, he sees the reflections of Your feet in every wave of the river that flows from the crown of Śiva who is prostrate before You; seeing them, he extends his trunk.
Here, the illusion of lotuses is suggested within the reflections of the Blessed One’s feet.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Chapter on Error (*bhrānti*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Doubt (*sandeha*):
"The charming [figure] is distinct from both probability (*sambhāvanā*) and certainty (*niścaya*)."
The figure of speech known as Sandeha (Doubt) is considered to be a cognition caused by resemblance. || 47 ||

The figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt) is a delightful cognition (*dhī*) caused by resemblance, which is distinct from either probability (*saṃbhāvanā*) or certainty (*niścaya*). Probability is a doubt in which one alternative is predominant. Certainty, however, is merely a state of knowledge that does not have another contradictory alternative as its qualifier; it is not, however, defined as being distinct from a cognition that has two contradictory alternatives as its qualifiers, because there is no purpose in including such a qualification. The qualifying term "probability" and so forth is intended to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to figures such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *rūpaka* (metaphor).

The term "charming" (*ramaṇīyā*) is used to exclude ordinary worldly doubt, such as "Is it a post or a person?"; its meaning is "wonderful. Furthermore, this qualification is already implied by the general definition of poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*). It should be understood that the same applies to its quality of being an embellishment (*upaskārakatva*). This figure of speech, Doubt (*saṃdeha*), is of three kinds: pure (*śuddha*), containing a resolution within itself (*niścayagarbha*), and ending with a resolution (*niścayānta*). Among these, the "pure" is that in which the conclusion remains as doubt alone.

"Is this perhaps a downpour of snow, or camphor, or even the essence of nectar? For it pacifies this exhaustion"—thus did people speculate regarding the objects of Hari’s glances. (Verse 295) *Ghaśaḥ* refers to the sidelong glance (*kaṭākṣa*). *Idam* is used as a neuter pronoun in its general sense to refer to Hari’s glance. *Samaśāyi* means they were in doubt.

"Is she a portion of the essence of the stars, or is she the splendor of a mass of shimmering lightning vines? Thus did the people deliberate upon seeing the Daughter of the Ocean dwelling within the heart of the Enemy of Mura.

Furthermore, this *saṃdeha* (doubt) occurs sometimes when there is doubt only regarding the objects (*viṣayiṇaḥ*), and sometimes it becomes an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) involving both the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). This is because the general definition is understood to apply in both cases; for *saṃdeha* is a deliberation that rests upon two indefinite aspects. In the two examples [previously] cited, doubt was stated to concern the subjects alone; for here, since the two primary elements—the Lord’s glance and Lakṣmī—are excluded from being the poles of doubt, the doubt belongs only to the subjects, namely the showers of frost, the showers of stars, and so forth.
Is this the circle of light from his claws, or a wreath of flames from the splendor of his arms? This incomparable discus, possessing a ruddy luster, shines upon the lotus-hand of Hari. (297)
In this case, the object (viṣaya), namely the wheel, like the circle of light from the nails of the subject (viṣayin), also occupies a position within the scope of doubt.
Or, for example:

"Did Hari study from the mountain, or did the mountain [attain] this great loftiness from Hari? In total elevation, both the serpent and the mountain, along with their respective lords, are equal. (298)
The *niścayagarbha* (interior certainty) is that which begins with doubt, has certainty in the middle, and ends with doubt. For example:
"Could this be the Gaṅgā emerging from the mouth of Hari, or could it be moonlight? It is exactly like that," so people wonder upon beholding the smile of the Lord of Śrī. (299)
The meaning is that even that moonlight would likewise not exist upon the face of Hari; here, from the beginning to the conclusion, there is only doubt.
Resolution as the conclusion (*niścayānta*) is that where there is an initial doubt and a finality in resolution.
For example:
"Is she lightning clinging to a cloud, or is she a digit of the moon wandering in the sky? Having thus doubted, Hari, smiling, resolves in his heart that she is Ramā. (300)
The word "lagna" (attached) from the preceding verse "gaganabhramāt" (due to the wandering in the sky) is also to be supplied here.
In some cases, doubt is observed because the objects being superimposed reside in different substrata, as for example:

"Have all the mountains been turned into *tamāla* trees? Or have the birds been turned into peacocks? Or have the quarters of the sky been turned into clouds by the spreading mass of Acyuta’s splendor? (301) In this instance, the quality of being a *tamāla* tree and so forth is superimposed upon the subject of the superimposition—the mass of Acyuta’s splendor—by virtue of its location in objects distinct from the mountains and other things. "Mountains" (*naga*) here means trees. In these examples, because doubt alone is predominant and does not serve as a subordinate embellishment for anything else, the designation of a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*) is applied figuratively (*gauṇa*) based merely on its suitability, as in the case of the bracelets and other items found in the *saṃpuṭa* and similar ornaments. And thus...

O Blessed One, those who even doubt your status as the Lord of the World, though you possess unsurpassed majesty—even those people, whose sole wealth is their virtue, doubt the very existence of such beings. (302)

In this case as well, although there is a sense of wonder (*camatkāra*), because it lacks a basis in similarity (*sādṛśyamūlakatva*), the doubt does not constitute a poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*). While those people who are doubting exist, regarding the object of excellence (*prāśastya*) inherent in qualities such as Brahminhood, the *sāttvika* (pure-hearted) people, whose sole wealth is their essential being (*sattva*), doubt to the highest possible degree.
Even if one is a knower of the meaning of all the scriptures, if he is devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, he does not possess the status of a Brāhmaṇa; let the origin of such a person be investigated.

The meaning is that they entertain doubt in the manner described above. Thus, the author of the *Sarvasva* maintains that this figure of speech, *saṃdehālaṅkāra*, is rooted in superimposition (*āropa*) and occurs even when based on identification (*adhyavasāna*). Furthermore, the author of the *Vimarśinī* holds that it is threefold, according to whether the nature, the cause, or the effect is the object of doubt.
In this regard, an example of doubt concerning the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is as follows:

"Was the interior of the temple on the peak of the serpent-king filled by floods of emerald luster, or was it smeared by the splendors of sapphires? Victorious is the radiance of Hari, which gives rise to such doubt! (303) And this doubt, by way of nourishing the poet’s internal passion directed toward the radiance of Hari, receives the designation of a primary poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*), just like the bracelets worn upon the hands of a woman. Furthermore, when the intended object—the radiance of Hari—is being discerned, the doubt culminates in alternatives such as "floods of emerald luster" and so forth.

And this is not a superimposition (*sāropa*), because one does not observe case-endings corresponding to those [of] the object and the subject; therefore, by means of the quality of being a mass of emerald luster and so forth, the green light—which possesses the property of being doubted—is determined as the subject.

The doubt regarding the cause is as follows: "O Master, why do you smile? Is it because of reflecting upon my conduct, or perhaps because of obtaining such a person worthy of protection, or due to my exertion toward a desired goal that is difficult to attain? (304)
Here, regarding the cause of smiling—namely, the state of unsurpassed bliss—the poet has identified three causes, such as the contemplation of his own past deeds, among them.

To indicate that there is no doubt regarding the fruit—that this very state alone bestows happiness—and to declare, "What indeed is this supreme state?", the Lord of Serpents and the Lord of Mountains have bowed down this hand. (305)

The meaning is that this hand—the right hand—is bent down by Hari Śrīnivāsa for the purpose of granting boons. Or rather, is it bent down to indicate that this very foot, his own, is the source of happiness for people? That is to say, is it bent down to suggest—or rather to reveal—that this very spot is the supreme abode (*paramapada*)? The construction is: "Is it bent down? Here, the fruit of the bending of the hand—namely, the granting of boons—is figuratively identified with the fruit of the indication [of the supreme abode].

However, some maintain that in such instances—just as with words like *iva*—terms such as *nu*, *kim*, and so forth, indicate probability (*saṃbhāvanā*) and thus constitute *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, on the other hand, considers that in such cases the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is not possible.

According to his view, this is what is investigated here: in the verse beginning "Is it by floods of emerald luster...?", a doubt is perceived through the words, having as its locus the interior of the Lord’s temple situated on the mountain of serpents, and as its alternative possibilities (*koṭi*) the state of being filled by means of floods of emerald luster and so forth.

And regarding that doubt—whether this might be a flood of emerald luster or perhaps the radiance of a sapphire—a further doubt concerning the quality of "green light" (haritejodharma) provides the necessary compatibility. Just as when there is a doubt before one's eyes as to whether a bull is a post or a man, there arises a doubt as to whether the ground itself possesses a post or possesses a man. Thus, this subordinate doubt concerning the quality of green light, being apprehended through suggestion (vyañjanā), does not require the use of case-endings concordant with the imposition (āropa) of the object and the subject.

And since it depends directly on being cognizable through words, how could doubt have its root in conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)? By this, the statement of those who attempt to define doubt as having its root in conceptual determination is refuted.
"Is this gaze anointed with collyrium, or is this body smeared with musk-paste?"—may the splendor of Acyuta, creating such doubt among the people, dispel all inauspiciousness. (306)

This should also be observed in cases of doubt rooted in the determination of diverse substrata (*vibhinnāśrayādhyavasāya*), such as those mentioned above. In this type of doubt, among the various alternatives (*koṭi*), sometimes there is only a single common property (*samānadharmā*), and sometimes they are distinct. Furthermore, that [property] is sometimes pervasive (*anugāmī*), sometimes it has attained the state of a mere reflection and its original (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), sometimes it has attained the state of reflection and its original as manifested through the relationship of thing and counter-thing (*vastuprativastubhāva*), and sometimes it is unspecified, and sometimes it is specified.

In that regard, concerning the verse previously cited—“Is this Gaṅgā not [the smile] of Hari?”—whiteness is the single common property (*anugāmī dharma*) belonging to both poles: the Blessed One’s gentle smile as the subject (*dharmin*), and the Gaṅgā and moonlight. Because it is understood through implication, it is unexpressed (*anirdiṣṭa*). The same applies to the verse beginning with “clinging by mistaking [her] for a cloud. However, in the very same verse previously cited, “Did the mountain study the quarters?”, greatness is the common property, and it is expressed (*nirdiṣṭa*).

The substrata—the Lord’s majesty, the limit of another [entity], and the height of the mountain—are directly specified. Furthermore, the separate specification of the property (*dharma*) is seen in the verse previously cited: “Is it the circle of the luster of his claws that is blazing? For there, the blazing nature of the circle of the luster of the claws and the reddish luster of the circle of the flame-like splendor of the arms are common properties that accompany the discus separately.
In this very instance, if the two qualifiers “blazing” and “reddish luster” were not employed, that [common property] would remain unspecified.

Having beheld the mountain that supports the serpent-king as having become the locus of both the original object and its reflection— just as the peak of the emerald mountain with the sun reflected upon it and Hari together with the Kaustubha gem— the sages stood upon the earth, uncertain whether they were to bow to the mountain itself or to the Lord.

In this instance, the attribute consisting of the state of being a reflected image of the sun and the state of possessing the Kaustubha gem has entered into a relationship of the original (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba).

Was it the lightning-bearing cloud accompanied by lightning? Or was it the sun-gem atop a peak of emerald? Thus was the moon upon the king of serpents, adorned with a crown of gems and surrounded by lotuses, mistaken for one or the other.

In this context, lightning and the sun are mentioned separately as the two objects of comparison for the reflections of Lakṣmī and the crown respectively. The word *śikhara* exists in the masculine gender as well, according to the rule of Amarasimha: “*śikharaṃ vā nā*” (the word *śikhara* is either neuter or masculine). Furthermore, there is the usage by Murāri: “*alagitavato vindhyaśikharān*” (having clung to the peaks of the Vindhya mountains). Then, having beheld the interior of the palace of King Ākāśarāja, people wondered: "Is this the belly of the ocean, or the summit of the Golden Mountain? (309)

In this instance, by the force of the contextual context, the word *tadā* (then) implies the locus (*dharmin*) of the city of Ākāśarājagṛha; and the gem—which is common to both [possibilities] and is implied by the two alternatives of doubt regarding whether the Blessed Lady Padmāvatī has descended at that time from the womb of the ocean or elsewhere—serves as the reflection. Although these two are not explicitly designated as the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), they are perceived as such and establish a similarity. By this, it is refuted by others who claim that only the "concomitant attribute" (*anugāmī dharma*) can be elided, but never the "reflected object" (*bimbita*).

And this [doubt] is sometimes non-artificial (anāhārya) and sometimes artificial (āhārya). For where a doubt residing in another person is depicted by the poet, there it is generally non-artificial, as in the previously cited verses beginning with "Is it perhaps a shower of snow? and so forth.
Who indeed did not suspect that Lakṣmī, seated upon the heart of Hari, was either a ray of the sun clinging to a cloud, or a sprout of ruby set within a sapphire? 310.

Here too, the doubt is indeed non-artificial (*anāhārya*), because for the person who is doubting, there is no determination of what is to be grasped. Furthermore, the distinction here is that between "fixed" (*lagnā*) and "inlaid" (*khacitā*), as well as "gone" (*gatā*), there exists the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding object and counterpart), while the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflection) pertains to the two thick sapphire gems and the heart of Hari.

And where doubt is established as residing solely within the speaker himself, there it is *āhārya* (artificial or assumed). This occurs, for example, in the verses previously cited such as "Did the mountains study the Vedas? (*harito’dhyaiṣṭa giri kim*). Or, for instance:

"Is this the peak of an emerald, its luster softened by the rays of the sun? Or is it the supreme Brahman, beautiful with the splendor of Lakṣmī, dark-brown like Kṛṣṇa, upon this mountain that is the serpent-king? (311)

That is to say, this object seen before one, which is black and tawny—of a dark-brown color—is a compound according to the rule *varṇo varṇena*. Here, the Vedic text "the man who is black-and-tawny" (*puruṣaṃ kṛṣṇapiṅgalam*) is called to mind. In this case, because the poet-speaker is a knower of reality, his doubt is merely feigned (*āhārya*). Here, one should observe the relationship of image and reflection between the rays of the sun and the luster of the lotuses; the relationship of primary object and its counterpart (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*) between their own smooth and beautiful splendors; and the pervasive recurrence (*anugāmitā*) of the term "black-and-tawny."

"O Śauri, even though this dharma is characterized by ambiguity, poets remain in great doubt upon beholding you: 'Is this a great sapphire produced in the Siṃhala mines of the same lineage, or is it the Blessed Lord? (312)

Regarding the term *mahānīla* (the great sapphire): in the case of the gemstone, it refers to that whose origin (*bhavana*) is in the mine (*ākara*), which is a celebrated and praiseworthy land (*gotrā bhūḥ*) belonging to Siṃhala, that is, the island of Siṃhala. This is in accordance with the statement of Agastya: "Those [gems] produced from the mine of Siṃhala are known as *mahānīlas*. In the case of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), *siṃha* means shining or manifesting; *gotra* means a mountain, thus *siṃhādri* refers to Śeṣagiri (the Hill of Śeṣa).
That which has its origin—the divine abode (*divyālaya*) or its very existence (*sattā*)—in that very mine or support is so described.

This figure of speech is indeed a doubt based on similarity between the subject and the object, or between two objects, and not mere doubt alone. Thus, when Kṛṣṇa said, "I wish to touch this [face] which is beautifully smiling due to its contact with the beauty of the moon," Rādhā hesitated, wondering whether he would touch her face or her two breasts. (313)

Thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition] here. For in this case, the act of touching—having as its objects the face and the two breasts—is itself the subject of doubt, as it has not yet entered into the relationship of object and subject. "By the contact (*vyatikara*) with the auspicious beauty of the moon (*vidhu*)," that is, by its connection with the lovely splendor of the moon; hence, "shining brightly" (*susmera*), meaning smiling, and thus "moon-like. Elsewhere, however, it means "shining brightly" through the contact—that is, the application—as an ointment of camphor (*vidhu*) and sandalwood (*bhadraśrī*). As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *vidhu* refers to the moon and to camphor."
"Bhadraśrī is sandalwood in the feminine," according to Amara; the rest is clear.
This [confusion] can also arise through a traditional succession, as in the following example:
"Is this a forest fire in the groves of the Vedas, or is it the crest-fire of the rainy season for Lakṣmī? As people observed it to be a 'mountain-jewel' (a cobra), they were filled with doubt. (314)

In this case, the "successive nature" (paraṃparitatva) of the doubt consists in its being preceded by a successive metaphor (paraṃparitarūpaka), and not in its being a doubt caused by a doubt; for it should be understood that the literal sense (śruti) and other factors do not serve as the objects of the doubt regarding [the forest] being a forest and so forth.

In some instances, even a doubt residing in another person, when described by a poet, becomes an "assumed" (āhārya) one, as in the previously cited verse: “Is it lightning clinging there through a mistake for a cloud? In that case, the doubt of the omniscient Lord is indeed assumed. Furthermore, regarding the two alternatives—“Is it lightning clinging there through a mistake for a cloud, or is it a digit of the moon clinging there through a mistake for the sky?”—the quality of "clinging through a mistake," although non-existent, is superimposed upon the subject (dharmin), who is the beloved (Ramā) fixed in his heart, in order to strengthen the similarity [between her and the objects of the doubt].
Other varieties such as these may also be inferred. In the examples mentioned above, this figure of speech, *saṃdeha* (doubt), is expressed (*vācya*), because it is cognizable through its own words.

Just as the heart of the Lord of Vyāla mountains wavered at the moment of taking her hand—while he gazed upon the lotus from the playful lake held in the hand of the immovable maiden—so too does it waver for me. (315)

At the occasion of taking the hand of Padmāvatī—born from the womb of the Earth, steadfast and youthful—at the moment of the ritual pressing of the hands; here, by means of a metaphorical sequence, because of her resemblance to a swing due to being suspended from two ends, the word "swing" (*dolā*) indicates a state of suspense.
An example of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is as follows:
"During a festival, the lotus-eyed Lord, the sovereign of his own mountain, suddenly touched his chest upon beholding the rising sun. (316)

In this case, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is the doubt: "Is it the Kaustubha gem that was already there which has fallen from its place due to the Lord’s sudden touch of his chest, or is it something else seen before us?"
Or, for example:

"The pair of eyes of Lakṣmī’s friend, eager to behold her own face adorned with a tilaka mark, grew weary from the constant coming and going between the mirror and the surface of Kamalā’s cheek. (317)

Here, the doubt residing in the pair of the Lord’s eyes—“Is this a mirror, or is it this?”—which has as its qualifiers two objects present before him and which consists of non-difference through a relation of inherence, is what is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). In this context, there is a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the Lord’s doubt onto the pair of his eyes. Nor should it be argued that the cognition of non-difference with the mirror is useless because it is required merely as a means for the operation of the pair of eyes; for [the cognition of non-difference] serves a purpose.

Since the cognition of one object as having the property of another object serves as the cause for the realization of the non-difference of that other object from the first, there arises—due to the sovereign power of the realization of non-difference with the mirror—the form of doubt: "Is mirror-ness resident in this [object], or is it resident in that [mirror]? This is the suggestion (dhvani) of doubt.
Is she a likeness of molten gold, or a form of a whirling flash of lightning; is she a streak of ruby, or the lotus-dweller within the heart of Mukunda?

Although here too, due to the non-employment of a denotative word, there is a doubt that it must be a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), nevertheless, because it has been stated clearly through the definition of its object, it is not a cause for the designation "suggestion" (*dhvani*), but rather for the designation of a specific variety of "subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Chapter on Doubt (*sandehasara*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Concealment (*apahnutisara*):

"If there is a negation of a perceived identity—whether brought about by external means (*āhārya*) or not—that constitutes concealment (*apahnuti*), provided it is either a subordinate element (*aṅga*) or the principal element (*aṅgin*) [of a poetic figure]."
This they call the ornament known as Apahnuti (concealment) in its general form.

The general definition of the figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment) is: the state of being a negation that possesses either the status of a subordinate (*aṅga*) or a principal (*aṅgin*), as determined by a cognition of identity (*abhedapratipatti*) that is superimposed (*āhārya*). This negation is expressed (*vācya*) when particles such as *nañ* are employed; however, in some cases, due to their absence, it is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) through words such as *kaitava* (deceit) or *chala* (pretext), or by the presentation of another's true nature. Furthermore, the distinction is that in some instances this negation is co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the cognition of identity, while in others it is non-co-referential (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Likewise, in some cases the identity is something superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*), whereas in others it is natural (*svābhāvika*).

It should be understood that the apprehension of that [identity] also occurs, in some cases, through suggestion (*vyañjanā*), but for the most part through the expressed function (*vācyavṛtti*) alone. If it were stated merely that "Apahnuti is a negation," there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of speech *Pratiṣedha* (Negation), which consists of the restatement of a well-known negation, such as: "O gambler, this is not gambling; it is play with sharp arrows. Therefore, the qualification beginning with "defined by the apprehension of non-difference" has been included.

For in that case, regarding a gambler engaged in battle, the absence of gambling in battle—though already known—is stated explicitly for the purpose of mockery, as in "your skill lies only in gambling, not in battle," and not as a means to establish the non-difference between battle and gambling; because that [non-difference] is established even without such a statement. Nor is it a corroborative instance (*aṅga*), since when something is already known, there is no need for such a means.

If one merely asserts that the status of being the primary element (*aṅgitva*) is defined by the cognition of non-difference (*abheda*), there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the cases of *śuddhāpahnuti*, *hetvapahnuti*, *paryastāpahnuti*, and *kaitavāpahnuti*. This is because in all those instances, the negation—such as "this is not the moon"—serves the purpose of establishing the non-difference with the celestial Ganges-lotus and so forth; thus, as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to that [non-difference], it lacks the status of being the primary element (*aṅgitva*).

If one were to state only that the nature of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is defined by the cognition of non-difference (*abhedapratipatti*), there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the cases of *bhrāntāpahnuti* (denial based on error) and *che kāpahnuti* (clever denial), because in those two, the negation—which consists in warding off the suspicion of error—is predominant, and thus lacks the status of being an auxiliary to the cognition of non-difference. Therefore, the inclusion of "being either of these" (*tadanyataratva*) is necessary. As they say: "That in which there is a denial for the sake of similarity should be known as *apahnuti*;
likewise, that in which there is a similarity for the sake of denial is also *apahnuti*."

Thus, all of this will become clear during the occasion of explaining those examples. In such cases as “Kāma is not five-arrowed, but rather one whose arrows are innumerable,” the qualification that the cognition must have non-difference as its object is added to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For here, no superimposition of non-difference is made upon anything denotable by the word “one with innumerable arrows,” since no such entity is established anywhere.

Nor can it be maintained that there is a superimposition (samāropa) by way of identity upon an object not previously established elsewhere—such as in the case of "aṅkaṃ kepi" and so forth—but rather imagined here alone; for in such a conception, the poet has no intention (asaṃrambha). Therefore, since the word "asaṃkhyaśilīmukha" (countless-arrowed) intends Kāma himself, one must accept that while the state of having five arrows is well-known of Kāma as the subject, that state of having countless arrows is superimposed by way of difference (bheda) upon his very attribute.

Thus, in this context, the negation is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) only for the intended cognition of difference-cum-connection, and not for the cognition of non-difference; this serves to prevent an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, in examples such as "This is not the moon," which are all instances of Apahnuti (concealment), the definition remains consistent because what is intended to be cognized as non-different with respect to the subject—such as the celestial Ganges or a sky-lotus—is that very substratum (*dharmin*) characterized by those respective attributes, whether it be well-known elsewhere or imagined by the poet.

In the opinion of Daṇḍin—who, disregarding the view that *apahnuti* consists in a cognition whose object is non-difference, defines *apahnuti* as "the attribution of another meaning after having concealed something"—there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even in the example cited, namely, "He is not the five-arrowed one. This is because, in his definition, *apahnuti* is simply the superimposition of another meaning preceded by concealment (*kevalāpahnutipūrvakānyārthāropa*). Thus, the verse "na pañcaviśikhaḥ" does not fall under this definition.

Whose animal in this world has turned this sun into the moon— he who, with rays as piercing as glowing coals, devours the orb of the universe and instantly makes the darkness of the sky manifest through the fissure of his gaping center, which was torn open by the many lords of the earth who came before him on the field of battle?

In such instances as the speech of a person suffering from separation—where the implied sense is that "this is not the moon, but rather the sun with a hole"—the negation of the moon is merely an auxiliary factor for the cognition of its identity with the sun. Therefore, to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in such cases, the qualification "voluntary" (*āhārya*) is added to the term "cognition of identity. In this context, however, the superimposition (*āropa*) of the sun is not voluntary, as it is produced by a specific defect [of perception].

For this very reason, the statement of the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*—that "here there is merely a semblance of concealment (*apahnava*), but not the figure of speech *Apahnuti*, because the cognition thereof is not voluntary (*anāhārya*) since it is produced by a specific defect [of the senses], but rather it is simply the figure of speech *Bhrānti* (Error)"—is consistent. Furthermore, the secret point is that if this [verse] were not the speech of a person separated from their beloved, but were instead produced solely from the creative imagination of the poet, then it would indeed serve as an example of pure *Apahnuti*.

For this very reason, the status of the verse "The moon is not intense, nor is the sun at night; this is the submarine fire risen from the ocean" as an example of *hetvapahnuti* (denial based on a reason) becomes consistent. Otherwise, if it were intended merely as the speech of a person suffering from separation (*virahijanavacana*), it would result in its falling outside the scope of the figure [of speech], and the inconsistency of the examples provided by earlier authorities would be evident.

Nor can it be argued that even with this general definition, the inclusion of the qualification "artificial" (āhārya) is improper, because it would result in the fault of under-extension (avyāpti) in cases of the concealment of error (bhrāntāpahnuti). For in such instances as, "O friend, does not love cause a feverish heat accompanied by trembling?", there is no absence of artificiality in the cognition of identity with real love; thus [the definition] must be stated. This is because the term "artificiality" must be understood as being restricted to the absence of both non-artificiality and the state of being an erroneous cognition, thereby warding off all defects.

In the case of *bhrāntāpahnuti* (denial based on error), although the cognition of non-difference is not "artificially induced" (*anāhārya*), the definition is consistent because, due to the absence of erroneousness (*bhramatva*), the principle that "when one exists, the other two do not" applies; thus, by the power of the qualifier "absence of both," the definition holds. In the other varieties of *apahnuti*, however, even though the cognition of non-difference is erroneous, the absence of both is easily established precisely because of the lack of being "non-artificially induced"; therefore, the consistency with the definition applies there as well.

However, since the non-difference from the sun (*mārtaṇḍa*) is perceived in the statement of the person separated [from his beloved], and because that perception is both non-artificial (*anāhārya*) and a form of error produced by a specific defect, both of these [conditions] are present; thus, the absence of both is impossible, and there is no room for the suspicion of the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, the general definition of the figure *apahnava* (concealment) is: being a negation (*pratiṣedhatva*) qualified by a cognition whose object is a perception of non-difference that possesses the absence of both non-artificiality and erroneousness.

It should be understood that, regarding comprehension, the specific character of such comprehension [is established] by way of either the relation of possessing the state of being the principal (aṅgin) as defined by the state of being a subordinate (aṅga) residing in itself, or the relation of possessing the state of being a subordinate as defined by the state of being the principal residing in itself. As for the qualification "specific charm" (cārutva-viśeṣaṇa), since it is already obtained through the governing context (adhikāra), it need not be explicitly mentioned here; enough of this prolixity.

Thus has the general definition of *apahnuti* (concealment) been stated. Now, desiring to define its varieties, the author first defines *śuddhāpahnuti* (pure concealment): "When there is a denial of a property in the subject for the purpose of superimposing something else upon it, this figure of speech is called *śuddhāpahnuti*. (49)

The figure of speech known as *śuddhāpahnuti* (pure concealment) consists in the denial of a quality belonging to the subject under description (*prakṛta*), with the result of superimposing upon that subject a quality belonging to something else (*aprakṛta*). Thus, the definition is ultimately established as follows: *śuddhāpahnuti* is the negation of what is intended to be regarded as a quality of the object of comparison (*upameya*), with the purpose of superimposing the nature of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) upon it. Furthermore, this negation must be qualified by being "unmotivated" (*anuktanimitta*) and not being suggested by words such as *kaitava* (deceit) or *chala* (pretext). By this qualification, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the figures of *hetvapahnuti* (concealment based on a reason) and *kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment through deceit).

In the case of *chekāpahnuti* (verbal concealment), as in the example “Is it not lovely? Indeed, it is an anklet,” there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because the negation of the quality of loveliness—which belongs to the object of comparison (*upameya*)—is present. To prevent this, the first qualification [“the negation of which is not intended”] is included. For in that instance, the negation of loveliness does not result in the superimposition (*āropa*) of the anklet; rather, it is the superimposition of the anklet itself that results in the negation of the suspected loveliness. Thus, that case is excluded. The phrase “belonging to the object of comparison” is stated to exclude *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment).

In that case, since there is a negation of the very attribute of the object of comparison (upamāna), such as its being the "moon" and so forth, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Furthermore, in this context, there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of the concealment (*nihnava*) and the superimposition (*āropa*); for the definition merely states that the concealment of an attribute results in the superimposition of another.

Indeed, we have not formulated the definition here as "if, having concealed an attribute in the object, another is superimposed," which would necessitate that the gerund suffix (*ktvā*) restrict the concealment to a strictly prior time; therefore, there is no lack of extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of the *apahnuti* preceded by superimposition (*āropapūrvakāpahnuti*) which will be discussed later.

Daṇḍin, however, in his definition—"Apahnuti is the concealment of something and the superimposition of another meaning"—defined *apahnuti* as merely the superimposition of some attribute preceded by the concealment of something else, regardless of whether that superimposition is based on similarity or involves the denial of attributes in the subject at hand. According to his view, even the verses to be cited hereafter are indeed examples of *apahnuti*. In this context, the sense of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word "apahnutya" (having concealed) does not intend to emphasize the temporal sequence of the negation; thus, the forthcoming examples will be consistent with this definition. For example:

O Śauri, having approached to conquer your splendor, the cloud—though possessing a thick bow whose string was severed by you—was bound by that very [splendor]; therefore, it is not merely a "jīmūta" (cloud), but a "jyāmūta" (one bound by the string).

The cloud (ghana), having approached with its bow in order to conquer your luster, had its string severed by you; yet, bound by that very same string—*mūta* being derived from the root *mūṅ* in the sense of "binding" (as Amara states: "that which is bound or tied is called *mūta*")—this cloud is therefore fit to be designated as *jyāmūta* ("string-bound"), but not as *jīmūta* ("water-born"). This is the meaning.

Or rather, O Lord, it is fitting that Nārada—who at first was not respectful toward the essence of your life-story—should now have become one who bestows [wisdom] upon the worlds, for he is indeed "Sārada" (the giver of the essence). 321.

The sage is not one who is untrustworthy, thus he is "not-untrustworthy" (*anāpta*). Regarding this, Vāmana states: "Two negations serve to negate the possibility of a negation. The meaning is that he is the most supremely trustworthy (*atyāptatama*), such that even the possibility of his being untrustworthy does not arise. This qualification is included for the purpose of indicating the authoritative character (*prāmāṇikatā*) of what he has spoken.

Being full of reverence, with the thought that these worlds, exhausted by the coming and going on the path of existence, might be revived, he first [bestowed his favor] upon Vālmīki and others; the sense is that even their comprehension of the essence of the Lord’s deeds was rooted in him. O Lord! He gave the essence of your life-story to the worlds. This is not merely Nārada;
for it has been said that you always give *nāram*—meaning water—to his ancestors, and therefore your name shall be Nārada.
Thus,
because he split apart the assembly of men (nara-saṃghāta) through quarrel itself,
that sage became renowned in the world by the name Nārada.

Or rather, he is not to be designated by the etymological word *Nārada*, but it is more appropriate to call him *Sārada*. The sense is that, according to the reasoning already established, he possesses the essence (*sāra*) of the Lord’s deeds. Here, the word *nārada* is first (*ādau*), meaning initially unjoined with the phoneme *nā* (i.e., having abandoned the form *nā*). Then it becomes *sādara*: one who has reverence (*ādara*) for that very same phoneme *sā*. That is to say, it is initially composed of the phoneme *sā*.
If this is so, the word *nārada* results in *sārada*; thus, a poetic ingenuity (*vaicitrya*) is embedded within it.
Or, for example:

"Though you should be called 'Sphītāmbarā' (Possessing Abundant Garments) because of your gift of vast cloth to Kṛṣṇā, those incapable of pronouncing syllables with great breath-force called you 'Pītāmbarā' (Wearing Yellow Garments). (322)

Some, who were incapable of pronouncing consonants with *mahāprāṇa* (aspirated) breath and were unable to utter sounds requiring great effort, addressed you as "Pītāmbara. They took the two words *sphītāmbara* and *pītāmbara* as a single compound of address (*saṃbuddhi*). For in the word *sphītāmbara*, the letters *s* and *ph* are indeed *mahāprāṇa*, while the others are *alpaprāṇa* (unaspirated). This is according to the rule: "The first, third, and fifth letters of each varga, the *yama* sounds following the first and third letters, and the letters *ya, ra, la, va* are *alpaprāṇa*; the rest are *mahāprāṇa*."

In these verses, the concealment (*nihnava*) of the states of being a cloud, Nārada, and one clad in yellow garments—which serves as the basis for the superimposition (*āropa*) of the states of being a bowstring, the essence of truth, and the vast sky—is not rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*).

"Thus, having bound the sun with its rays, Śauri (Viṣṇu) makes it move as one who steals the burden of the wealth of the Kaustubha jewel; he does so to manifest [his nature], but not to measure time here. In this case as well, one should understand that the basis is dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*). In the previous examples, the concealment of a quality was for the purpose of superimposing another quality; here, however, the denial of the result—measuring time—is for the purpose of superimposing the result consisting in the manifestation of the state of being a thief. This is the distinction.
Surely this dark spot upon the orb of the moon is not a blemish; rather, it is the dart of fear held within his heart because he has been defeated by the radiance of your face.

Here, the concealment of the spot's status as a "spot" (kalaṅka) is established with the result of superimposing upon it the state of having the dart of fear held in the heart, based on its being surpassed by the luster of the Blessed One’s face—despite the fact that this [status] is not actually the subject under discussion.
O Mother, thus a single ray of the moon, desiring to attain superiority over your smile, was struck down in the middle and became inferior; they call that mark a "spot" (*aṅka*).

In this case as well, there is the concealment of the "spot" (*kalaṅka*), which results in the superimposition of "ray-ness" (*kiraṇatva*) upon that very spot which is not the subject under discussion. O Mother! The sense is that one particular ray of the moon—the most essential—remains situated in the middle. Desiring a state beyond, or an excellence (*utkarṣa*), even over your smile (the genitive in *tava* is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyaya-niṣṭhā-khal-artha-tṛṇām*, as it functions as the object); therefore, it was struck down in the very interval between the desire and the attainment of its fruit by your smile. Consequently, having reached a state of inferiority or lack of excellence, it became a scar (*kiṇa*).

They say that this very *kiraṇa* (ray) is a *kiṇa* (scar); the sense is that this is indeed a scar and not a mark (*aṅka*). Here, the word *kiraṇa* has its middle syllable struck out; thus, having become "other"—that is, having lost its *repha* (the letter *ra*)—it became *kiṇa*. The meaning that the word *kiraṇa*, upon the removal of the *repha*, results in *kiṇa*, is also strikingly beautiful.

However, this is not an example of the definition of "pure negation" (*śuddhāpahnuti*) as presented by us—which follows the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other such works; rather, it should be understood that this very instance will be defined later. Furthermore, in this [figure], when the negation of the subject matter is conveyed either directly through particles such as *nañ*, or indirectly through the introduction of another's opinion and so forth, there is generally a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). But when the negation is conveyed through words such as *iṣat*, *chala*, *chadma*, *kapaṭa*, *vyāja*, and others which result in the falsity of the subject matter, or through words such as *rūpa*, *vapuh*, *nāman*, *ātma-bhaṅgi*, and so on, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

In some cases, there is a prior negation; in others, a prior superimposition; in some, one element—either the non-contextual identity with the subject or the negation of the subject—is expressed verbally while the other is implied; in some, both are verbal, or both are implied; and there are various other possibilities such as being the predicate or the subject of a restatement. Although these many varieties are possible, they are not worth enumerating because they do not produce any particular aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*). Nevertheless, a mere indication is provided here by way of example.
This face is not an ocean of loveliness, nor is this lower lip a sprout; these teeth are not pearls, nor is this pair of eyes, O Lord, a pair of fish. 326.

"he īśa" is the vocative address; "te" (of you) is connected to every word in the sentence. Furthermore, this [sentence] is composite in nature, consisting of a collection of parts that have entered into a relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary. In this regard, both [negation and affirmation] are preceded by concealment (*apahnava*), both are expressed through words (*śābda*), both are things to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and there is a division of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
Or again,

while the ignorant here might say that these two dark and joyful eyebrows upon your face are a pair of sprouts, O Lord, we declare them to be the first two leaves emerging from the stalk of your nose.

This [negation] is partless (*niravayavā*). Here, because the speaker’s lack of knowledge is stated, the comprehension of the negation is mediated by the comprehension of his error; thus, the negation is "implied" (*ārtha*), whereas the identity [of the object with its predicate] is "verbal" (*śābda*). The qualities of being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*), the absence of sentence-split (*vākya-bheda*), and the denial [of the literal sense] are exactly as before. Or, for example: "Some may call the conch placed in Hari’s hand a swan, others a white lotus; let them say so. But we declare that what dwelt in Vraja is fresh butter—even now it remains as such. (328)

This too is partless. Here, as well, there is superimposition preceded by negation; however, the negation is mediated by the presentation of the opponent's position, which serves as its implied context.

Or rather, just as the Yamunā shines when its waters are struck by the rays of a jeweled crown, so does this [darkness] shine upon Your face; yet the simple-minded call it the musk-tilaka from the forehead of the king of beasts on the peak of the best of mountains. 329.

Or rather, the wise know that for those whose minds are averse to the feet of Hari, his abode is indeed hell; yet, out of a lack of revulsion, they call it "nilaya" (abode), relying on the identity between the letters *ra* and *la*.

In both of these two examples, the *apahnuti* (concealment) is indeed "without parts" (*niravayava*). The distinction is that the concealment is preceded by a superimposition (*āropa*). As before, the identity (*tādrūpya*) is expressed by the words, while the negation is implied; furthermore, there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because [the negation] functions as the thing to be predicated (*vidheya*). Regarding the verse: "The virtuous know the abode of those whose minds are turned away from the feet of Hari to be nothing but hell (*niraya*)," one might ask: "If that is so, why do they not simply use the term 'hell' (*niraya*)? To this, he says: "Because of the non-difference between *ra* and *la*" (*ralayoḥ*). The meaning is that, relying on the non-distinction between the sounds *ra* and *la*, they speak of the abode itself as "hell."

To the question "Why even that?", he says: "so as not to cause agitation. The sense is that, because of the prohibition—"One should not utter that speech by which one is agitated, for it does not lead to the world of light"—people say "nilaya" (abode) instead of saying "niraya" (hell), lest these people become agitated.

Thus, O Mother, this very Svātī constellation is firmly embraced by the moon of your face; the rumor among the simple-minded is that this Rohiṇī, who possesses the luster of your lower lip, has been released from the nose [of the bull]. 331.

In this case as well, one should observe that [the process] begins with superimposition (āropa). Because the constellation Svātī has the color of a ruby, there is a superimposition of that [color]. Rohiṇī is "red" (rohitā). According to the rule *varṇādanudāttātopadhāt to naḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied; by virtue of its association (*sanniyoga*), the substitution of *na* occurs, and from that, the substitution of *ṇa*.

The author of the *Vimarśinī* maintains that because this [figure] contains an imposition (*āropa*), it arises either from similarity (*sādṛśya*) or from another relation; even in the case of similarity, its common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) are to be understood as they are in a simile (*upamā*). Among these, the recurring attribute (*anugāmī dharma*) is indicated in the previously cited verse beginning with, “This is certainly not a dark spot on the moon’s orb, for it is blue... and so forth.

Just as the pure universal form [of gold] is not the tawny hue upon the body of the Lord of the Vṛṣagiri mountain, nor is it a golden garment; rather, it is the deep orange pollen clinging to the lotus that is the mind of the sages.
In this instance, the qualities of "tawny" and "reddish-brown" possess the nature of pure universals; this indeed constitutes the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding objects).
And because it follows [the original] through the state of being formed by the correspondence of object and counterpart, like the relationship between an image and its reflection—for example:

"Just as this Supreme Person shines within the golden celestial mansion, so does the most excellent of bees shine clinging within the interior of the golden lotus on the peak of the mountain of serpents. (333)

Here, the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding objects) exists between the refined gold (*tapanīya*) and the golden (*kanaka*), as well as between the interior of the belly (*antarjaṭhara*) and the interior of the womb; furthermore, it should be observed that the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and its reflection) exists between the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and the lotus (*saroruha*) formed by those [objects], and that the word "shining" (*kanat*) functions as a pervasive common attribute (*anugāmitva*).

Just as the manifestation of the Blessed One on the mountain of serpents is not perceived by the sages through any other relationship, but rather as the disappearance of the demoness of inauspiciousness for the worlds that bow down to him; so too [is the case here]. (334)

Here, by the negation of the cause—the manifestation of the Blessed Lord—there is the affirmation of the effect—the disappearance of the inauspicious demoness. Thus, the type based on superimposition (*āropa*) has been demonstrated in detail. Now, the type based on identification (*adhyavasāna*) is further illustrated: "O Lord of the Bull Hill, the Sun is not worshipped during the twilights because he is the embodiment of the Vedas, nor because of his brilliance, nor because he is the friend of the world; rather, it is because he is the jewel in the heart of the Lord. (335)

The Kaustubha gem is the heart-jewel of the Lord of Vṛṣādri; [the sun is so called] because of its servitude to it, that is to say, because its splendor follows that of the gem. Here, regarding the worshipfulness of the sun, the cause consisting of its majesty as revealed by scriptural authorities such as "meditating upon the sun as it rises and as it sets" is suppressed (nigīrya), and another cause is instead predicated (adhyavasita) of it.

Or rather, this fresh rain-cloud is not to be welcomed by the people because of its extreme coolness, nor because of its softness, nor even because of its fickleness; [it is so] because of its likeness to you, O Hari. (336)
Here, having suppressed the fact that the quality of being worthy of praise is caused by such things as the granting of life, another cause is superimposed upon it.

Or rather, just as the Kaustubha jewel on his chest does not wear it for the sake of ornamentation, but because it is his own property; so too does the Lord of the Mountain, the bearer of the serpent-king, hold Lakṣmī and her co-born [Brahmā] out of great respect.
In this context, regarding the wearing of the Kaustubha jewel upon his heart:
"The Blessed Lord Hari bears the very nature of the Kaustubha gem, [which represents] himself, as being untainted, free from qualities, and stainless for this world."

Thus, having swallowed the result—namely, the state of being a true instrument caused by the conceit of identifying with the principle of the individual soul (jīvatattva)—an identification with a different result has been made.
"The author of the Rasagaṅgādhara observes that this [superimposition] is also seen as one involving parts."
This autumn season, clarifying the lake-like hearts of the wise and making the moon-like face of Lakṣmī beautifully radiant, does not, however, possess the luster of the side-glances of Hari.
He himself has stated that if the means consists merely of superimposition, this [designation] can also be understood as figurative (paraṃparita).

While those of superior intellect may call this [the moon] your foot that crushes the pride of the fresh sprouts, I shall declare it, O Hari, to be a fresh parasol for warding off the fierce heat of worldly existence.
In this way, even in the verse previously cited, "The sun of the jeweled crown," the *paraṃparita* (successive) [metaphor] is to be understood.
And its suggestion (*dhvani*) is as follows:
"This is certainly not the city of Vaijayantī shining there; nor is this the daughter of the ocean, but rather a flash of lightning has burst forth. (340)

In this case, by the preceding and following [verses], two apahnutis (denials) are clearly indicated: "This is not indeed the Vaijayantī banner, but rather a rainbow-creeper," and "This is not Lakṣmī, but rather a flash of lightning. Through these two, a third apahnuti—"This is not the Blessed Lord, but rather a rain-cloud of the monsoon"—is primarily conveyed through suggestion (*vyañjanā*), because it is logical that the denial and the superimposition of one thing serve as the indicators of the denial and the superimposition of that very thing.
Now, the concealment of a cause (*hetvapahnuti*):
if that same concealment is preceded by a logical argument, it is *hetvapahnuti*. (50)

"Just as this Fortune does not dwell eternally upon the chest of Hari, for she is fickle; rather, she is like the steady streak of a kuruvinda gem-lamp within the palace of Hari’s heart. Here, by means of a logical argument (*yukti*) consisting of the impossibility of eternal residence caused by her fickleness, there is a concealment of Lakṣmī’s true nature as Lakṣmī, for the purpose of superimposing upon her the nature of a "steady kuruvinda gem-lamp streak."

Or rather, this mark upon the chest of Śauri is not natural, because he is by nature stainless; it is undoubtedly a drop of collyrium from the eyes of Kamalā as she slept from the fatigue of love-making. (342)

Here, by means of the reasoning that the Blessed One is free from blemish, the negation of the status of being a "mark" (aṅka) upon the mark (aṅka) is intended for the purpose of superimposing the nature of a "collyrium drop."
Now, as for *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment):

*paryastāpahnuti* occurs when there is a denial of a certain attribute in some [other] object, provided that it is described as having the purpose of superimposing that [denied] attribute onto the subject being described. (51)

When the denial of a certain attribute in some object is described for the purpose of attributing that same attribute to the object being described, it is called *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment).

Just as they declare that place beyond the *rajas* region to be the "Supreme Abode" (*parama-pada*), that cannot indeed be the Supreme Abode; rather, it is only the mountain of the Lord of Serpents [Śeṣa]. Or again, just as a gem produced in Siṃhala is not a great sapphire, whereas Hari is the Great Sapphire; for while the former merely turns a small amount of milk blue, this one, residing in the Ocean of Milk, turns the entire ocean blue.

That [gem] is the *siṃhalasaṃbhūta-maṇi* (the gem produced in Siṃhala). This is the illustrious Hari; he resides therein, as does the milk, and he dwells in the midst of the Ocean of Milk. Regarding this, it is traditionally taught: "Those great sapphires (*mahānīla*) which originate from the mines of Siṃhala, if one were to cast a sapphire into the midst of milk, the milk would turn blue."
The gem known as mahānīla is exceedingly rare;
thus has the meaning of the treatise on gems been summarized.
Or rather:

"Just as the moon is the leader of the good, so too is the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva) the leader of the fallen; tell me, who among these two could be the leader of the virtuous—one who bestows joy upon those weary of the cycle of existence, or the other? 345.
For the wheel of truth, for the assembly of noble beings, and for the ruddy goose, the moon brings weariness, whereas the Blessed One brings joy.

Just as the dawn’s rays are not the sun, nor is the ocean the refuge of the serpent-bearing mountain; yet that very sun crosses over the ocean of worldly existence, while this mountain carries the worlds across it. 346.

*Taraṇi* means the sun, a jewel, and a boat; as the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *taraṇi* is masculine when meaning the sun, and feminine when meaning a young girl or a boat. He has crossed over and causes others to cross; this is formed from the root *tṛ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the imperfect tense (*laṅ*) with *caṅ*. That [sun] is the ray of dawn; this one is the one whose abode is Veṅkaṭagiri.

Or rather, O Hari, just as the ocean— the repository of rivers— is not disturbed when a river flows into it, so too this [ocean] does not suffer even a single wave of distress when you, who are the refuge of all rivers, resort to it with your face turned toward every direction in agitation.

In the compound *nadīna*, it is a contraction with the word *na*. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "not non-lowly" (*adīnaḥ na*), but rather the meaning is "indeed lowly" (*dīna eva*). The actual state of affairs is that he is the lord (*ina*) of rivers (*nadīnām*). One who has taken refuge in the Blessed One alone is not lowly (*adīnaḥ*) among the lords of rivers. He is the "storehouse of waters" (*apāṃ nidhiḥ*). Due to defeat on all sides—meaning from being turned back in every direction (or, in the alternative sense, from water-waves)—he suffers a "defeat" (*bhaṅgam*); for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "Defeat (*bhaṅga*) occurs in the reversal of victory; [it is used] for division, disease, and waves."

Here, in the first example, "If here [is] beyond," the denial of the status of the "Supreme Abode" (paramapada) to the place beyond the *rajas* is for the purpose of superimposing that status upon the Śeṣādri mountain, which is the subject of description. In the other three examples, beginning with "Siṃhala," the denial of being a great sapphire and so forth is for the purpose of superimposing those qualities upon the Lord who is the subject at hand. In the first example, no reason for the denial is stated; in the second and subsequent examples, the reason is stated.

In that regard, in the second verse beginning with *siṃhala*, it is pure; in the third and fourth verses, it is mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia). In the fifth verse, “*nāpāṃnidhiḥ*,” the concealment of the ocean’s status as the lord of rivers (*nadīnata*) is for the purpose of superimposing that status upon the subjects at hand—the devotees of the Lord. As for the mention of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, it is exactly as before. Consequently, one should understand that here too there are two varieties, just as in the case of pure *apahnuti*. This variety of *apahnuti* has been stated in accordance with the *Kuvalayānanda*.

In the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, having cited the verse: “And that [figure] is *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment), for the purpose of superimposing it upon something else,” [the author] states: “It is not proper to say that this is a variety of *apahnuti* (concealment), because it is not encompassed by the general definition of *apahnuti*. For instance, the definition stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*—‘*Apahnuti* is that wherein the subject (*prakṛta*) is denied and something else is established,’ or ‘*Apahnuti* is that wherein the object of comparison (*upameya*) is rendered unreal and the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is established as real’—clearly excludes this [case].”

Thus, even the definition of *apahnuti* (concealment) stated in the *Alaṃkārasarvasva*—namely, "it is the concealment of the object [of comparison] when another thing is perceived"—does not apply here.

When, by means of the negation of the subject at hand, something else is postulated on account of similarity, that is *apahnuti* (concealment); it is of two kinds, according to whether there is a difference or non-difference of the sentences.

Thus, the definition found in the *Citramīmāṃsā* is likewise [applicable]. Therefore, in the verse “This is not the moon; rather, it is the moon—the face of my beloved,” there must be *rūpaka* (metaphor) with firm superimposition (*dṛḍhāropa*), and not *apahnuti* (concealment). This is because the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the delimiters of the object of comparison (*upameyatāvacchedaka*) and the delimiter of the standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedaka*) is perceived without obstacle.

As it is stated in the *Vimarśinī*: “They say that poison is not poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison. Here, since poison is superimposed upon the property of a Brahmin after being negated, it is indeed *rūpaka* with firm superimposition, and not *apahnuti*.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be such mutually contradictory assertions among those who have been initiated [into the tradition]," listen: there is no contradiction, for the definition of *citramīmāṃsā* follows the view of the ancients, whereas this [present work] follows the view of the *Ratnākara* and others.
Now, the figure of speech *bhrāntyapahnuti* (denial of error):
*bhrāntyapahnuti* occurs when, upon the prevention of an error, there arises a suspicion of something else.

When there is a disclosure of the truth (*tattvākhyāna*) for the purpose of dispelling another's error, it is "the concealment of error" (*bhrāntyapahnuti*). They also call this "the concealment of the erroneous" (*bhrāntāpahnuti*). In that case, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), meaning "that which is erroneous" (*bhrāntam*); the concealment of that is the result. Thus, the definition should be understood as: the denial of the object of an error caused by the statement of the truth is "the concealment of error. For example:

"What is it that cools my heart—is it camphor (*ghanasāra*) or sandalwood (*gandhasāra*)? No, no! Friend, it is the Lord of the Serpent Mountain (Śiva) who has suddenly been brought before my memory. (348)

In this passage, when the Lord’s account—"Here my heart is cooled"—is told, there arises through the superimposition (adhyavasāya) of non-difference based on the pun (*śleṣa*) between the two meanings of the word *hṛdaya*—namely, "mind" and "chest"—a situation where it is common to both camphor (*ghanasāra*) and other substances. Consequently, a certain friend, whose mind is inclined solely toward external objects, asks: "Is it camphor (*ghanasāra*) or is it sandalwood paste (*gandhasāra*)? In response, with the words "No, no," etc., the removal of the error is effected. This is an example of *bhrāntāpahnuti* (concealment by means of an error) preceded by a possible error.

"This is not a mass of clouds preceded by imagined delusions; this is not lightning, but this parting of the hair shines forth. "O Kṛṣṇa, why do you prepare yourself for the bearing of mountains? Thus Śrī spoke to the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śeṣa). 349.

*Sīmanta* refers to the parting of the hair; as the *Vaijayantī* states: "The *sīmanta* is not feminine; it is the line situated in the middle of the hair of women. Regarding *śailadhṛtau*, this means "in the upholding of Govardhana," which is precisely why he is addressed as "Kṛṣṇa" (the Uplifter). It also refers to the grasping of her breasts, which are superimposed upon the nature of mountains. Here, there is a constructed error (*kalpitā bhrāntiḥ*), which is inferred solely from the negation in the words "not a mass of clouds" and so forth, because—as before—there is an absence of a question. Daṇḍin, however, considered such a case to be a variety of simile called "simile of the statement of reality" (*tattvākhyānopamā*). As he says: "This is not a leaf; this is indeed a face. These are not two bees; these are two eyes."
Thus, because of the clearly manifest similarity, this is considered a simile that declares the true nature [of the object].

Thus [it is said]. In reality, however, because there is an absence here of words such as *iva* that indicate a simile (*upamā*), a variety of simile is not appropriate. If one were to accept a simile even in the absence of such [words], it would follow that even a metaphor (*rūpaka*) would be a simile.
For example:
"This is not lightning, but the daughter of the ocean; this is not the mountain of Śeṣa, but its leader. O swan of the mind, why do you despair? Tell me, does he not bring joy to the swans? (350)

Here too, the imagined error is to be inferred from the mere negation due to the absence of a question. In the negation "not possessing lightning," the statement of the reason is "bestowing joy upon the swan"; furthermore, the presence of the metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*) as "the swan of the mind" constitutes its distinction from the preceding [verse].
Chekāpahnuti (Artful Concealment):
Chekāpahnuti occurs when there is the concealment of a fact due to the suspicion that it might be something else. || 53 ||

The meaning is as follows: when someone is speaking a secret to another, and that other person hears it, they conceal the truth by imagining a different intention behind the speaker's words; this is *chekāpahnuti* (the clever denial). Hemacandra states: "The word *cheke* means 'clever' (*vidagdha*) or 'trustworthy' (*viśvasta*). Thus, the definition of the term is: a denial of a suspected real object caused by the reinterpretation of a sentence.
It is designated as being caused by the suspicion of another—meaning it must be removed by that suspicion—just as one says "he eats food because of hunger" (*kṣudhānnamatti*). And in this case:
Whose anger would not be aroused at the wounded lip of his beloved?
For even now, though forbidden by me, you have smelled the lotus together with the bee.

Thus, the first qualification is provided in the definition of *vyājokti* (disguised speech) to prevent over-extension [of the term]; for it will be stated later: "The distinction between this [figure] and *chekāpahnuti* (clever concealment) is that in the latter there is a denial by taking the statement in another sense, whereas in this [figure] there is a hiding of the outward appearance by describing it as being due to some other cause."
"Does the Lord of the Collyrium Mountain, with his dark luster, sport constantly in my heart? "No, indeed, no! It is the jewel of the best of gods," the clever Padmāvatī said to her friend. (351)

In this context, when Padmāvatī’s playful companion informs her of the account of her own beloved Śrīnivāsa—saying, "The one with dark luster (nīlaruci) plays within my heart"—and upon hearing that, [Padmāvatī] suspects another [woman] might be referring to the Lord of Añjana Hill, she replies to her, "No, no, it is the jewel of the best of gods (the Sun)," which is a denial of the very truth.
Or rather, O friend, has not the moon, marked with the Śrīvatsa, surely caused me to thrill intensely throughout the night as it approached and touched me with its hand of nectar-cool rays? 352.

With that hand, which was as cool as frost and like nectar to nectar itself, he caused [her] to rejoice throughout the night—both by his rays and by his hand. [This is expressed by] *adhiniśam ajīhṛṣat*, using the periphrastic aorist (*luṅ*) with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) of the root *hṛṣ*. Here too, while some woman from Vraja is reporting news of the Son of Nanda to her playmate, saying "approaching her face-to-face" and so forth, another woman, having heard this, wonders "What is this? regarding the one marked with the Śrīvatsa; thus, there is a denial (*apahnava*) of the very truth by saying "it is not the moon."

These two examples are given for the purpose of concealing the truth through the application of meaning (*arthayojanā*). In reality, however, the second example will become an illustration of *apahnuti* (concealment) through the application of both word and meaning (*śabdārthobhayayojanā*), according to the method that is about to be described.

*Apahnuti* (concealment) by means of the connection of meaning (*arthayojanā*) is the denial of a fact intended to be expressed—which is common to both the intended and unintended meanings—by describing it as being connected with the unintended meaning. By contrast, that [same figure] through the connection of words (*śabdayojanā*) is the denial of such a fact by describing it as connected [to the unintended meaning] merely through a pun (*śleṣa*).
When Nīlā said with vehemence, "I meditate upon your two large lotus-like eyes," Śauri describes his devotion to her as she becomes angry. (353)

Here, although there is a difference in meaning between the two words *kamale* and *vipule*, there is a concealment of the truth (*tatthyanihnava*) through an alternative construction based merely on word-play (*śabdaśleṣa*). It may be construed as: "O *kamale* (Lakṣmī)! O *vipule* (Vast One)! I meditate upon your two eyes," or alternatively: "O *vipule* (Earth)! I meditate upon your two eyes, which are like lotuses (*kamala*). This applies to each [address] individually. If, however, *nīla* is taken as an adjective, then the vocative "O *nīle* (Blue One! is obtained by implication. In that case, the construction is: "I meditate upon your two eyes, which are both lotuses (*kamale*) and vast (*vipule*)."

In this case, the sentence-meaning is not one that has *Ramā* (Lakṣmī) and *Bhūmi* (the Earth) as its objects of address, consisting of meditation on their eyes; rather, it is one that has *you* as its object of address, consisting of meditation on your eyes which are like vast lotuses. That Śauri (Viṣṇu) intends this [other] meaning by means of concealment (*apahnava*) is what is revealed by the word "it" (*tat*). This refers to the aforementioned speech. Furthermore, the meaning here is not unique to Lakṣmī and Bhūmi; rather, it is merely the employment of words with double meanings (*śliṣṭa*) regarding gender and number, namely "in the lotus" (*kamale*) and "vast" (*vipule*).

Or as I, sleeping at night on the heart of my beloved, charming and fortunate, perceived nothing at all; did I not, having pressed her many times against my chest, experience the pleasure of lying upon her? (354)

"O captivating one, O wearer of pearl necklaces, O fortunate one, O beautiful one, [reside] in the heart—the chest—of my beloved, the Blessed One, the Delight of Nanda. In the alternative sense: "O captivating one, O charming one! O you whose heart is dear [to me]—that is to say, she who acts for my pleasure! O fortunate one, O you endowed with good fortune! These are the vocatives addressed to the female friend. "Is it Śauri? is the question of the neutral bystander. "No, indeed," and so forth, is the heroine's truthful yet evasive reply.

Here too, although there is a difference in meaning for phrases such as "in the heart of the beloved" (*priyahṛdaye*), the denial of the truth is achieved through a different construction based merely on word-play (*śabdaśleṣa*). The use of the third person (*na viveda*) is due to being overwhelmed by bliss, just as in the expression "he spoke much" (*bahu jagada*).
Did not Śauri, greatly delighted, awaken you—who were closing your eyes in the darkness of night—by touching your heart with his hand, just as the moon awakens the night-lily? 355.
