In this instance as well, the concealment of reality is to be understood through the application of wordplay (*śabdayojanā*). "At night" (*niśi*) means in the darkness of the night; "closing" (*nimīlantīm*) refers to one who has fallen asleep, and by extension, to the closing of the night-lotuses (*kumuda*). "Touching the heart" (*hṛdispṛśā*) means touching the chest; in the alternative sense, it means "heart-pleasing" or "causing to blossom. The absence of the elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending is according to the rule *hṛdyubhyāṃ ca*. "With his own hand" (*svena kareṇa*) refers to his own hand, or in the other sense, to his ray (*kiraṇa*); the singular number is used for the genus (*jātāv ekavacanam*).

"Bhṛśamuditaḥ" means being exceedingly joyful; in the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word division is "bhṛśam uditaḥ," meaning having attained its rise. The word "bhṛśam" connects with the word "unnidrām. "Unnidrām" means one whose sleep has departed, i.e., abandoned sleep; in the alternative sense, it means "blossomed," according to Amara’s lexicon: "likewise, 'puṣpita' and 'unnidra' [mean blossomed]. The phrase "samatānīt" describes the heroine’s narration to her playful friend (narmasakhī) during the night of the amorous pastimes performed by her beloved. "Kiṃ śauristvām" is the question of a bystander. "Kumudinīm induḥ" is the heroine’s truthful yet evasive reply.
Through the conjunction of both word and meaning, as follows:

"O friend, this mass of snow nearby wounds my lower lip and especially causes trembling in my body during the night; is it not the great power of cold, O friend, that acts as Śauri [the enemy of Mura]? (356)

In the phrase "asau himānī," it should be understood that there is a concealment (*nihnava*) through the application of words (*śabdayojanā*), whereas elsewhere it occurs through the application of meanings (*arthayojanā*). For in the case of the true meaning, the word division is *asau hi mānī*, whereas in the alternative of concealment, *himānī* is a single word. The term *asau* is common to both masculine and feminine genders. Here, because the word previously indicated in the masculine gender—referring to Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) in the phrase *asau hi mānī*—is now described as referring to Himānī (the Snowy Mountain Range) in the feminine gender in the phrase *asau himānī*, this constitutes a concealment through the application of words.

In the word *mahaddhimaṃ* (great snow), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would have been applicable by the rule *indravaruṇa* (*Pāṇini 4.1.49*) and which is taught as being conditioned by the addition of the augment *ān* in the rule *himāraṇyayormahattve* (*Pāṇini 5.4.104*)—is restricted [to its absence].
Or, for example:
"Come, friend Satyabhāmā; you, Rukmiṇī, are my beloved"—when these words were spoken by force, Śauri propitiates the enraged Rādhā by performing that very [act] toward her. (357)

The construction is as follows: "O Rādhā-parā (one devoted to Rādhā)! O virtuous one! O Satyabhāmā (O Abhāmā, O one without anger)! O Rukmiṇī (so called because she possesses *rukma*, meaning gold; that is, one adorned with golden ornaments)! O friend! You alone are my beloved. One should understand that this constitutes an *apahnuti* (concealment) by means of the verbal connection in the phrases "Satyabhāmā" and "Rukmiṇī," and by the semantic connection in the phrase "friend, [you are] the beloved. This is achieved by arranging his own previously spoken words so as to refer to someone other than himself—namely, to Rādhā.

All of this is an illustration for the application [of the figure] when there is a difference in objects. However, even when the object is the same, as in the case of an application based on a difference in state, consider the following:

"A certain rogue, while saying to his wife, 'Kṛṣṇa is my beloved,' was then addressed by her—mistaking him for a friend—as follows: 'O friend, what did you say? Realizing it was he, he completed the sentence: 'I [am Kṛṣṇa], from a dream. (358)

In this context, the intended meaning concerns the account of the passion directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa: a certain cowherd girl, while lying on the same bed as her husband during a state of sleep-interspersed-with-waking, spoke out due to the delusion that he was a friend; immediately upon realizing it was her husband, she became agitated with fear. To the words of his which were intent upon that very account, she—being in a state of dreaming—attributed the meaning of a dream-event by completing the sentence with "O friend, what did you say in a dream?"; for even there, [the word] "jagada" (you said) is used.

This is further clarified by the use of the first person optative (*liṅ-uttama*) expressing something out of sight. Here, the concealment of the fact that the heroine’s intended account of her passion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa actually occurred during her waking state is established by the sense of the passage; thus, one must apply the definition of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). In the word *jagade*, there is no vowel lengthening of the penultimate syllable because the *ṇit*-status is optional according to the rule *ṇaluttamo vā*. In *apūrī*, the *ciṇ* suffix is optional in the *luṅ* tense when used in the active voice, according to the rule *dīpajanabudhapūri* etc.; the meaning is "she fulfilled."

Or, for example, when a certain young bride, out of carelessness, said before her elders, "As we two were talking freely, I and Śauri," she completed the sentence by saying, "It was the uninhibited talk of childhood. (359)

"Who is this bride? I am a cowherd’s daughter-in-law, and Śauri and I have been sporting at our own will"—this is the first person dual imperfect (*laṅ*) of the root *vi-hṛ* (to sport). In the presence of elders—that is, in the vicinity of her mother-in-law and other senior relatives—she spoke these words out of negligence or lack of attention. "Childishness" means the actions of a child; the sense is that it refers to an unintentional activity performed by children.
The meaning is that in the case of such childish conduct, there can be no insistence as to what must or must not be done according to one's desire. Thus she completed [the sentence].

By a certain woman of Vraja, whose inner heart was single-mindedly intent on the uninterrupted savoring of the elixir of unrestrained enjoyment in the Nandana grove experienced not long ago, the account of how she had spoken freely in the presence of her elders due to that very same latent impression (saṃskāra) and through negligence, is clarified by completing the sense with the phrase "the unrestrainedness of childhood," as its subject matter concerns events such as the dust-play performed with Śrī Kṛṣṇa during the stage of infancy. In the previous example, the application was by way of a distinction in the state of dreaming;
here, however, the distinction lies in the state of childhood.

Or, as Śauri once called out to me while I was bathing with dust on my body, saying, "Come and eat together"; having spoken thus involuntarily in my childhood, she said, "For friendship is indeed unfabricated. 360.

In this instance, having inadvertently uttered before her elders the literal meaning of a sentence—"the invitation made by Śauri for the purpose of eating together with him as the fruit of his own action after bathing at the end of her menstrual period"—a certain clever heroine, awakened by that alone, remarked, "Friendship in childhood is indeed unfeigned. She then reinterpreted that very sentence as meaning something else: namely, that it was an immediate invitation made by Śauri for the purpose of the act of eating together with him as the fruit of his own action of bathing caused by the fact of being soiled by dust during childhood play.

Here too, the application according to the different stages is exactly as before; however, the distinction is that it is embellished by *śleṣa* (paronomasia). In the interpretation of the primary meaning, "Sarajaskā" refers to her who is accompanied by *rajas* (menstrual flow), while elsewhere it means "accompanied by dust. Furthermore, this occurs after the menstrual period (*ārtava*) and after the smearing with dust (*dhūlī*).

"To enjoy me"—that is, to consume me as one who has bathed, in mutual conformity, that is, for the sake of eating together; for it is well known that even during their stage as young students (*māṇavaka*), men eat at will with girls. Having said "I called" (meaning he had summoned her) out of necessity or inadvertence, he spoke—that is, he declared—of his friendship (*maitrī*) or camaraderie (*sakhya*) from childhood (*bālya*), meaning from infancy (*śaiśava*), as being uncontrived and sincere. The statement "friendship from childhood" and so forth is intended to illuminate that the matter he has spoken of was established during his youth.
If a concealment is expressed through words such as *kaitava* (deceit),
*chalacchadma* (fraudulent disguise), *nibha* (resembling), and so forth, or through terms like *vapus* (body) and *ātman* (self), that is indeed *kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment by pretense).

The distinction here is that words such as *chala* (deceit) and so forth establish the unreality of the object, whereas words such as *vapuḥ* (form) and so forth result in the same conclusion regarding the unreality of the object. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in *chalādi*, terms such as *kapaṭa* (guile), *kaitava* (fraud), *vyāja* (pretext), *miṣa* (disguise), *apadeśa* (excuse), *upadhi* (artifice), and *dambha* (hypocrisy) are included. It should be understood that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in *vapurātmādi*, terms such as *rūpa* (appearance), *nāma* (name), *rīti* (convention), and *bhaṅgī* (artifice) are intended.

May this false musk of Hari, placed upon the tips of the breasts—which are like the peaks of mountains under the guise of the earth-supporting jewel-bearing serpent—remove our dullness here by its own quality. 361.

By its own qualities—such as the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and compassion (*vātsalya*), etc.—may it remove and dispel elsewhere dullness (*jaḍatām*) and coldness (*śaityam*), which are synonymous with ignorance (*ajñatā*). For it is well known that Hari possesses the quality of removing ignorance, and musk (*mṛganābhi*) possesses the quality of removing coldness. Here, because the words *nibha*, *chala*, and *kaitava*—which establish the unreality of the object—convey a negation such as "this is not the earth, but rather a beautiful woman," there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatvam*). Furthermore, the negation and the resemblance (*tadrūpya*) are both implied (*ārthatva*), and the latter is the predicate (*vidheyatva*), since the removal of dullness is what is being predicated.
And this [white light] possesses parts, because it consists of a collection of parts that have entered into a relationship of the benefactor and the benefited. Or, for example:

"Even though it is black, the sun spreads its white radiance upon the pair of feet of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), which are like the moon, by means of the form of a pair of jeweled anklets on the serpent-king. (362)

In this instance, by the force of the word *dvijamarāja* (the king of the twice-born), a negation is perceived—one whose essence culminates in the untrue—conveying that "this is not a pair of jeweled anklets, but rather the sun itself manifesting the kingship of the twice-born. The unity of the sentence and other such features are as explained previously. This [figure] is also *niravayavā* (without parts). The meaning of *dvijanmarājatvam* is *dvijarājatvam* (the kingship of the twice-born). For, according to the Vedic revelation, "Soma alone is our king," so the moon possesses the status of being the king of the twice-born (*dvijarāja*).

In the word *rājattvam*, the doubling of the letter *t* occurs according to the rule *anaci ca* for the sake of conforming to a different meaning (*arthāntara*). In one sense, *rājattvam* means "the state of being a king" (*rājato bhāvaḥ*); in another, it refers to the two types of birth (*dvividhe janmanī*), which are the "twice-born" (*dvijanmanī*). Through the pun (*śleṣa*) on these two meanings—"kingship" and "manifestness through those two births"—there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*).

The author of the *Vimarśinī*, however, stated that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "deception and so forth," even the third [type of *chala*] sometimes conveys untruth. Regarding this, he gave the following example:
"When the moon of Madhumathana (Viṣṇu) rose from the eastern mountain of Phaṇigiri (Śrīraṅgam), the ocean in the guise of the forest on its slopes foamed with masses of flowers. (363)

"It emits foam; it foams. Here, by means of the *vārttika* "it should be stated that [the suffix] *kyaṅ* occurs after the word 'phena' in the sense of emitting," the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied in the sense of vomiting. In this context, by the use of the instrumental case in the phrase "by masses of flowers" (*kusumaughaiḥ*), there is a basis for concealment (*apahnava*), as it implies: "This is not a mass of flowers, but rather foam itself."

Although in such instances—as in "to the one crowned by the river" (*anadyā śekhariṇe*) and others—it is more appropriate to consider this as a metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting of a superimposition (*āropa*) through grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), nevertheless, in accordance with the initial presentation of concealment (*apahnava*), it has been stated that concealment is also expressed at the end by means of the instrumental case, following the authority of the author of the *Vimarśinī*. In reality, however, this will be a non-co-referential metaphor (*vyadhikaraṇa-rūpaka*) animated by concealed denial (*kaitavāpahnuti*).
For this very reason, it should be noted that even the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, though following the *Vimarśinī*-author, has disregarded this position.

This [type of superimposition] also takes the form of a garland (*mālārūpa*). Regarding that as well, the authors of the *Kaustubha* and others maintain that there are two varieties: when many [attributes] are negated and one is superimposed, and when one [attribute] is negated and many are superimposed.
Among these, the first is as follows:

"O Lord who reclines upon the serpent, by means of the pretext of the crest-jewel on the mountain of jewels [on earth], by the pretext of the serpent's hood-jewels in the netherworld (Pātāla), and by the pretext of the sun-gem in the path of the gods, Your mass of majesty has manifested its descent. (364)
Sumeru has jewel-peaks. "Reclining on the hood of a serpent" is an address to the Blessed One. The rest is easy to understand.
Your majesty shone upon the ocean under the guise of coral, in the celestial river under the guise of golden lotuses, and upon the heads of your enemies under the guise of clusters of rubies. 365.

*Kaladhauta* means gold; as Amara states: *kaladhautaṃ rūpyahemnoḥ*. The presence of golden lotuses in the Mandākinī is well known. *Prabhāva* means majesty (*pratāpa*); as Amara states: *syāt pratāpaḥ prabhāvaśca*. Here, it should be noted that the description of the Golden Mountain (Meru) and the like—which are renowned for their yellow color—and coral and the like—which are renowned for their redness—as being similar to majesty by virtue of their very redness, is established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). This is because the non-difference between the colors yellow and red is also established by poetic convention. Thus it has been said in the *Alaṃkāraśekhara*:
In the case of Kamalā and Saṃpat, Kṛṣṇa and Hari, nāga and sarpa,
yellow and red, and gold-dust and flames of fire, and so forth;

"In the case of the moon, the hare and the deer; and in the case of the banner of Kāma, the sea-monster and the fish—the identity of the Dānavas, Asuras, and Daityas is intended [to be expressed]. Thus it is said.

O Lord, your renowned glories shine forth: in heaven under the guise of the cool-rayed moon, on earth under the guise of the river of the immortals flowing from the snowy mountain, and in the netherworld under the guise of Śeṣa.
Śītādri is the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya). Animiṣadhunī is the Gaṅgā. By their "miṣāt" means by way of a pretext or guise. O Vibhu, O Blessed One!

O Blessed One, O Infinite One, your splendor shines forth, divided and distinct on all sides: above in the guise of the vault of heaven, below in the guise of the surface of the earth, and all around in the guise of the ocean.

It should be understood that the blueness of the surface of the earth is established by the description, "the orb of the earth has the tender luster of a blue lotus," which accords with the Vedic scripture stating, "that which is black is [the essence] of food."

In some places here your great, blazing light shines in the form of emeralds, in some places like a cloud, in some places like a tamāla tree, and in some places it has the splendor of a blue lotus; thus your majesty shines throughout the world.

In this context, the word *nibha* signifies a pretext, as Medinī states: "The word *nibha* is said to mean a pretext (*vyāja*). Here, the description of the Lord’s splendor—which is renowned for its dark-blue color—as being comparable to an emerald of greenish-yellow (*harit*) hue is justified by the previously cited authority which establishes the non-difference between blue and greenish-yellow colors. "O Mother, under the guise of earrings they shine upon Your neck; under the guise of a necklace, O Mother, they shine upon Your throat; under the guise of a garland, they shine in Your braided hair; and the fragments of Hari’s radiant smile shine forth, stainless. (369)
In these examples, having negated many things such as Mount Sumeru and others, there is the superimposition of a single quality, such as majesty, upon that [subject].
The second verse is as follows:

"O Mother, you bear the four manifestations of the Lord (bhagavad-vyūha) under the guise of your arms—the Vedas, the human goals (puruṣārtha) they expound, the men who worship them for those ends, and the four [goals] themselves. (370)

The term "fourfold" (*catura*) is an adjective qualifying all three: the Vedas, the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), and the manifestations (*vyūha*) of the Blessed Lord. The Vedas are those known as Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharva; the goals of human life are those known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; and the manifestations of the Blessed Lord are those known as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. Here, after first negating the possession of arms by Lakṣmī, there is a superimposition of unity upon the many elements, such as the Vedas and the rest.

O Lord, Sun of the Mountain of Serpents, having placed the three worlds, or the three Vedas, or the primordial nature consisting of the three qualities within Your belly, You protect them under the guise of the three continuous folds [of Your waist].

The *trayī* refers to the three Vedas beginning with the *Ṛgveda*; as Amarasimha states: "The *Ṛk*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* are feminine; the three Vedas are called *trayī*. It is composed of the three qualities (*triguṇā*), consisting of the attributes of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Here too, following the negation of the three folds [of her waist], there is a superimposition of the unity of many things—such as the three worlds and so forth—upon that [triple quality].
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Chapter on Apahnava (Concealment), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Utprekṣā (Poetic Fancy):
"The imagining of one thing as being another due to its connection with the attributes of that other."
This suggested hyperbole (utprekṣā) is said to be threefold, consisting of the nature of a thing, a cause, and a result.
Poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding an object is considered to be of two kinds, according to whether its locus is explicitly stated or unstated.
Fancy regarding a cause (hetūtprekṣā) and fancy regarding an effect (phalotprekṣā) are distinguished by whether their locus is established or unestablished.

The meaning is as follows: when there is a property belonging to one subject (*viṣayin*), and based on that property’s relation [to another], there arises in respect to another [subject] a conjecture of its being something else—that is, a conceiving of it as other; this is a conceiving of the subject as being identical with [the property of] the first subject. The genitive case in "of another" (*anyasya*) signifies a state of being an object (*viṣayatā*) in the form of being a locus (*dharmitā*); whereas the genitive case in "of the subject" (*viṣayiṇaḥ*) signifies a state of being an object in the form of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*). Furthermore, the mention of "as something else" (*anyatvena*) is intended to indicate that the conceiving is an artificial or voluntary mental construction (*āhāryatā*).

Thus, the final definition is that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is a voluntary mental attribution (*āhārya-saṃbhāvanā*) which has the object as its locus, is prompted by a connection with a property residing in the subject, and has the subject as its predicate through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). The refined essence (*niṣkarṣa*), however, is: "voluntary attribution of that [subject] prompted by a connection with a property residing in it. The remaining parts of the definition serve merely to state its essential nature, as they do not function to exclude other cases.

In the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "I consider the face to be the moon," there exists a superimposition (*āhārya*) of the moon upon the face, brought about by the connection with qualities such as the power to delight residing in the moon; thus, it conforms to the definition [of *utprekṣā*]. However, since the superimposition of the moon and so forth upon the face and other objects that arises when there is no state of contradiction (*bādhā*) and the like is not considered *utprekṣā*, the term "superimposed" (*āhārya*) is used to exclude such cases.

"By this, the entire expanse of the quarters became resonant with the tumultuous sound of kettledrums and cymbals; I believe that the Lord who adorns the peak of Phaṇigiri has immediately set out on a triumphal procession. In this instance, although there is a superimposition upon the Lord—based on the connection with the attributes of embarking on a triumphal procession, such as the pervasion of the quarters by the clamor of kettledrums and so forth—there is no over-extension [of the definition], because that [superimposition] is not involuntary (*anāhārya*). For the scope of the figure of speech *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy) is defined as: "Poetic fancy is a conjecture (*ūha*) of the form 'if it were thus,' for the sake of establishing something else. Since this [superimposition in the verse] is not of that nature, it does not fall under that category.

If the ocean were devoid of water, if Mount Meru were made of common gold, and if the crest-jewel of the mountain range were to abandon his vow of protection, then only would I believe it possible. (373)

The phrase "employed" (*prayukta*) is used in such instances to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*); for here, in the case of a supposition such as "if the ocean were waterless," there is an absence of being caused by a relation to a property residing in the object of the supposition (*viṣayin*).
I consider this Kākodaragiri to possess a world-transcending beauty, since Mukunda dwells here together with Śrī, even while abandoning his supreme abode. (374)

In order to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in such cases, the phrase "residing in that" (*tanniṣṭha*) is used as a qualification of the attribute (*dharma*), meaning it must be something whose occurrence is possible [in the subject]. In this context, the attribute consisting of wandering together with Śrī, preceded by the abandonment of the Supreme Abode (*paramapada*), resides in Mukunda; however, since it is not merely "possible to occur," there is no over-extension. If it is objected that this would fail to include figures of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on other types of relations, we say no. This is because the statement was made in accordance with the view of the ancients, who maintain that in all cases of *utprekṣā*, the imagination occurs solely through identity (*abheda*).
It should be noted that the inclusion of the term "identity" (*tādātmya*) in the definition is precisely for the purpose of indicating this.

And that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is threefold, according to its scope as having the nature of a thing (*vastu*), a cause (*hetu*), or a result (*phala*). The nature of a thing, cause, or result consists in the identification (*tādātmya*) with another thing, cause, or result. Here, the first type is the fancy of a thing (*vastūtprekṣā*), which is the imagining of some thing as being identical with another thing; this very same [type] is called the fancy of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*). The fancy of a non-cause as a cause and of a non-result as a result is called the fancy of cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) and the fancy of result (*phalotprekṣā*). Among these, the first—the fancy of essential nature—is twofold, according to whether its locus (*āspada*) is expressed or unexpressed.

The term *āspada* means "object" (*viṣaya*). The meaning is that [poetic fancy] is of two kinds: that which has an expressed object and that which has an unexpressed object. Furthermore, both *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy based on a cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (fancy based on a result) are each of two kinds: those with a realized object and those with an unrealized object.
In order:

"May the great crown, which desires to attain a supreme superiority over the lord of serpents who bears the mountain [of Mandara], and which shines upon the head of Hari like the young mountain of the gods [Meru] upon the head of Hari, protect [you]. (375)

Here, by means of the cause consisting in the connection with attributes such as being composed of gold and jewels, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the identity of the great crown with the peak of Mount Sumeru; because the object [of the fancy], the great crown, is explicitly mentioned, it is a "stated object" (uktaviṣaya) fancy regarding the essential nature (svarūpotprekṣā).
Or,

like the beloved of the Lord of the Serpent Mountain, whose body is encircled by the mass of her own spreading radiance, she seems to manifest her own status as having a golden rampart, as proclaimed in the scriptures.

Here, by means of the suggested cause—the tawny color and so forth—there arises a poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) identifying the circle of light from Lakṣmī’s body with a golden rampart. However, it should be noted that since the act of manifestation itself is primarily indicated here, this will be an example of a "fancy regarding the nature of an action" (*kriyāsvarūpotprekṣā*), according to the method to be explained later. Other matters will be defined further on. In this instance, the meaning of the Vedic text, “Hiraṇyaprākārām ārdrām,” has been kept in mind.
Poetic fancy regarding an object whose subject matter has not been explicitly stated (*anuktaviṣaya-vastūtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"This lord of mountains, the king of serpents, seems to consecrate me with nectars; he seems to anoint the eyes of wretched me with divine collyriums. (377)

Here, based on the understood grounds such as "causing nourishment" (*āpyāyakatva*), there is a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) whose object is unstated: namely, a fancy identifying the Lord’s act of causing bliss with His act of performing an immersion in nectar (*amṛtābhiṣeka*), and a fancy identifying [the Lord] with the application of divine collyrium (*divyāñjana*). This occurs because the agent, presented by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), is construed as identical with the Lord; that agent is then construed with the meaning of the verbal root—namely, the act of immersing and the act of applying collyrium—and this agent is further construed with the sense of "as if" (*iva*), which signifies a possibility, and that possibility is construed as the objective domain (*viṣaya*) within the act of causing bliss.

This is because the sentence-meaning culminates in the cognition that "the act of gladdening" is the object of the possibility of being consecrated and anointed by the Blessed One through logical connection (anvaya); furthermore, in both cases, the gladdening which serves as the object is not expressed by anything other than the two words denoting the subjects, namely *abhiṣiñcati* and *añjati*.

Now, one might argue that here, having accepted the connection of the two verbal roots *abhiṣiñcati* (he sprinkles) and *añjati* (he anoints)—whose meanings are sprinkling and anointing—as qualifiers with the agent denoted by the verb, one should instead conceive of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting in the identity of the agent with the sense of the particle *iva*, namely, the possibility [of being] the agent of sprinkling and anointing.

Furthermore, since the status of being the aforementioned object is attained by taking the Blessed One as the [grammatical] object (*viṣaya*), it follows that the cognition in which the Blessed One—presented by the word ending in the nominative case—is the primary qualificandum (*mukhya-viśeṣya*) is established as a view accepted by the experts in the system (*tāntrika*); thus, let both of these two hypotheses have the aforementioned object as their scope.

If it is argued that this is not so because—due to the rule of non-occurrence of two simultaneous functions (*yugapadvṛttidvayavirodha*)—it is impossible for the roots *abhiṣiñcati* (he consecrates) and *añjati* (he anoints), when uttered only once, to bring about both consecration and anointing through a secondary indicative function (*sādhyavasānalakṣaṇā*) based on their capacity (*śakti*), by way of presenting a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and joy (*ānandana*) [as the object of the transfer]; we say: not so. For, according to the rule *‘laḥ karmaṇi ca’*, since a verbal suffix possesses the power to denote the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, even though the agent is presented by the verbal suffixes *abhiṣiñcati* and *añjati* in the present context, [the principle] *‘bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam’* [remains applicable].

According to the traditional teaching of Yāska, the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the primary element (*pradhāna*), that which is to be qualified (*viśeṣya*); thus, the sense of a verb (*ākhyāta*) is that whose qualificand is the action denoted by the root. Consequently, since the agent—who is construed as subordinate to the two actions of "anointing" (*abhiṣecana*) and "applying collyrium" (*añjana*)—cannot be the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), it is impossible for him to be connected with the "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*) expressed by words such as *iva*. In this way, precisely because the verb is subordinate to the action, even this verse: "Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium," is largely consistent with the definition of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
In some cases, a misconception regarding a simile arises here due to hearing the word "iva" (like),
even while disregarding the authoritative statement that there can be no simile with a finite verb.

By these and other such arguments, Daṇḍin—refuting the possible misconception of some who perceive a simile (*upamā*) in the locus of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), as in the verse "He seems to smear" (*limpatīva*)—states:
"If the agent were the object of comparison (*upamāna*), he would be subordinated in the verbal expression;
being preoccupied with accomplishing his own action, he is not capable of attending to another."

Thus, the possibility of the agent being construed as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) within a simile has also been refuted. To explain: the meaning of the verse is introduced as a response to the following doubt: "In the phrase 'as if smearing' (*limpatīva*), since it is possible for the agent of the act of smearing to be construed as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in relation to the meaning of the word 'as if'—which denotes similarity—why should this not be considered a simile? This verse is presented as the answer to that doubt. If the agent were indeed the standard of comparison, then such a doubt would be appropriate; however, this is not possible. The reason for this is stated in the words "subordinate" (*nyagbhūta*) and so forth. The meaning is that this agent is "subordinate" (*nyagbhūta*)—that is, made subservient to the action—within the verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) of the finite verb.
The verbal root is traditionally held to denote both the result and the operation, while the personal endings (tiṅ) denote the locus [of these].
Among them, the result is the primary element, whereas the operation—the meaning of the personal ending—is a qualifier.

This is because of the aforementioned statement. He establishes this very state of subordination (*nyagbhūtatā*) with the second half of the verse, beginning with "sva-": "This agent, intent (*vyagra*)—that is, occupied—with the accomplishment of his own action, such as the act of smearing and so forth, is not capable (*nālam*), that is, not able, to expect (*vyapekṣitum*), that is, to desire or to accomplish, anything else other than his own action to be achieved."

Just as one who is dependent on another cannot accomplish a task for someone else, so too an agent who is dependent as a qualifier of one action cannot attain the status of being a qualifier of another [action] in the form of a standard of comparison; for that which is presented as a qualifier of one thing cannot be construed as a qualifier of another. Therefore, the status of the agent as a standard of comparison is not tenable here.

Thus, whether the meaning of the word *iva* be "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*) or "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), in either case the agent cannot be construed with it; therefore, the view that this is a simile (*upamā*) is untenable. Consequently, the opinion that the agency of smearing in darkness is to be regarded as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is indeed unacceptable, because that agent would merely be a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, by distinguishing what is intended to be expressed, it is the act of smearing itself that must be the object of the poetic fancy.

Thus, it is established that in the verse cited above, the very possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) regarding the primary acts of consecration and the application of collyrium has swallowed up the object of joy (*ānanda*). Nor is there the fault of contradiction due to the simultaneous occurrence of two functions (*vṛtti*), for such [simultaneity] is not admitted.

However, some say that in the verse, "Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs; the sky, as it were, rains collyrium," there is a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy on the nature of the thing itself) regarding the attributes of smearing and raining, which belong to the subjects—darkness and the sky—and are performed by them. According to their view, *svarūpotprekṣā* is divided into two types: *dharmyutprekṣā* (fancy on the subject) and *dharmotprekṣā* (fancy on the attribute). In that case, there is the difficulty of construing darkness and the sky twice each—as the agents and as the subjects.

Likewise, there is the *dharmyutprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the substratum); however, while the *dharmyutprekṣā* is prompted by similarity (*sādharmya*), the *dharmotprekṣā* is prompted by the connection with a property that coexists with it. Thus, there is a lack of conformity (*ananugama*) in the definition. Nor should it be argued that this lack of conformity is avoided by defining "property" as being either residing in that [subject] or having a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it; for since poetic fancy occurs everywhere only on the basis of similarity, the superfluous complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the inclusion of the term "either-or" (*anyataratva*) and so forth is not to be adopted—so they say.
Or, for example:

"O Goddess, Mother of the World, having seen Your pair of eyes—fickle at the corners of Your ears—with pearls attached to the ends of Your ear-lobes, they seem to laugh loudly. (378) In this case as well, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) identifying the light belonging to the pearls of the ear-ornaments with the laughter performed by them; it is an "unexpressed-object" (*anukta-viṣaya*) fancy, because the object of the fancy—the light—is swallowed up [into the subject]. This is how it should be understood.
An example of a "established-object" (*siddha-viṣaya*) causal fancy (*hetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:

On Mount Añjanaśikhara, which is densely covered with clusters of gems possessing a charming luster that shatters the strength of the *khañjana* bird’s brilliance, this dark Hari is surely [dark] because he is constantly attached to it. 379.

It is called *khañjana* because it causes one to limp, making the gait defective (*gativikala*). "Of the luster of a *khañjana*" means possessing the brilliance of the bird known as the *khañjarīṭa*; the sense is that its blackness exceeds even that of the *khañjana*. Amara states: "The *khañjarīṭa* is the *khañjana*; one who limps is *khañja*. It refers to that which has a "nicula"—meaning a *nicola* or covering—consisting of a beautiful mass of luster from "balabhañjana-maṇis," which are sapphire gems (*indranīla-ratna*). Viśva states: "The *nicula* is a *nicolaka* (a cloak or covering)."

The term *nicola* refers to a coverlet, as seen in Murāri’s usage: *vinayaniculitaiḥ*. Here, regarding the Lord’s natural dark complexion (*śyāmaliman*), the constant application of collyrium from the Añjana mountain is not actually the cause; nevertheless, the attribution of causality to that which is not a cause constitutes a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of cause). Since the constant application of collyrium from the Añjana mountain is treated as established, this is a *siddhaviṣayā* (having a proven object) fancy. It is based on the superimposition of identity (*abhedādhyavasāya*) founded upon the pun (*śleṣa*) inherent in the word *añjana*, for the blueness of collyrium is well-known.
An example of poetic fancy (*hetūtprekṣā*) whose object is unestablished (*asiddha-viṣaya*) is as follows:

"O Hari, you who wear the Śrīvatsa mark, O you who are the ornament at the hem of the garment of the mountain-like excellent chamberlain [the moon], why do you display some small mark upon your heart, the abode of Ramā, as if out of affection? (380)

Śrīvatsa is the son of Lakṣmī; according to the *Medinī*, "vatsa" means "son" and so forth, as well as "year"; and according to the *Ratnamālā*, "vatsa" [means] "son" and so forth, or "calf," and is used in three genders. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), Śrīvatsa is the name of a mark. You honor (*añcasi*), that is, you worship or respect. Here, "worship" refers to showing respect, as in such passages as "he is to be honored just as I am" and "they are to be honored and cherished. In the alternative sense, the meaning is "you obtain."

Here, in the case of the one whose chest—the locus of the golden region that is the abode of Ramā—is marked by the auspicious Śrīvatsa, the affection resulting from being the father of Lakṣmī is not the cause [of his holding the discus]. Thus, the attribution of causality to that which is not a cause and is unestablished constitutes a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of a cause) regarding an unestablished object, enlivened by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Or, for example:

"As the lightning, as if conquered by the shimmering luster of the jewels in the earrings of the wives of the serpent-king and the mountain-lord, undergoes a transformation upon her face—namely, a state of exhaustion and a dark blue hue in the midst of its brilliance. (381)

The lightning, as if conquered here and there by the splendor and radiance of Lakṣmī—the jewel upon the young wife of the Lord of Mountains and Queen of the Serpents—engages in a battle by seizing her at every lock of hair; thus vanquished, it undergoes a transformation in its face: a loss of color, a paleness that marks defeat, exhaustion, and languor, while seeking concealment and remaining invisible deep within some mountain cave or in the midst of the sky.

In the word *dyumat*, the substitution of *u* for the final syllable of the word *dyu* ending in *v* occurs by the rule *diva ut*. Alternatively, *dyu* is an indeclinable denoting the sky, according to the lexicographical authority of Medinī: “*dyu* is neuter in the sense of day and sky.”

The actual meaning is as follows: in the word *vidyut*, at the beginning (*mukhe*) there is the syllable *vi* (in the form of *vi*), which ends in *t* (the state of ending in the letter *t*); the cluster of phonemes *dyu* is situated dissolved (*līnaḥ*) between those two letters, *vi* and *t*. The state of being such—that is, the state of having the quality of being dissolved in the middle of *dyu* (*dyumadhyalīnātva*)—is to be observed in the word *vidyut* through its possession of the initial modification (*mukhavikāravattva*), its ending in *t* (*tāntatva*), and its being dissolved in the middle of *dyu* (*dyumadhyalīnātva*).

Because the word *dyumadhyalīnāśabda* is a compound (*samasta*), it is not a quality-word (*aguṇavacana*); therefore, by the rule *tvatalorguṇavacanasya*, there is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Here, the term "quality-word" (*guṇavacana*) refers to a word other than a technical name (*saṃjñā*), a genus-term (*jāti*), a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix, a compound, a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), or a numeral (*saṃkhyā*). This is because that very meaning is obtained from the Bhāṣya on the *ākaḍāra* sūtra. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ekataddhite ca*, having raised the objection that "the form *ekatvam* is established through the application of the masculine form," it is stated: "It is not established; this has already been explained."

It has been stated [in the *Śabdakaustubha*] that "for a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* [are applied]. The intention behind this is that in the case of the word *eka*, the technical designation *sarvanāman* (pronoun) supersedes the designation *guṇavacana*. This is clear in the *Sūtraśekhara* on the rule "tvataloḥ. Here, since the lightning possesses natural qualities such as facial contortions and the like, its being "averse to Lakṣmī’s luster" is not the actual cause; rather, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of it being a cause constitutes "causal fancy" (*hetūtprekṣā*). Since, in reality, there is an absence of such aversion, the subject matter is unestablished (*asiddhaviṣayā*), and it is reinforced by paronomasia (*śleṣa*).

In the previous example, the causality of "out of affection" (*vātsalyāt*) was indeed indicated by the ablative case itself; here, however, because "conquered" (*jita*) functions as an attribute of the subject (*dharmī*), the causality of the victory is implied (*ārtha*). This is just as in expressions such as "he is pleased when honored" (*pūjitastuṣyati*), where the act of honoring and so forth serves as the cause.

If it is asked: "How can the quality of possessing the phonemes *vi*, *pra*, and so on, which resides in the word 'lightning' (*vidyut*), possibly exist in the object denoted by that word, such that the stated meaning could be established through the assumption of identity based on the supported *śleṣa* (paronomasia)?"—then understand that this is due to the sovereign power of the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*).

For thus the grammarians (śābdika), on the occasion of defining the power of words, cite the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*: "The convention (*saṃketa*), however, consists in the mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) between word and object; it is of the nature of memory, such that 'whatever is the word, that is the object; whatever is the object, that is the word. They maintain that the relation between word and object is indeed a distinct relation called "power" (*śakti*), which is synonymous with "the state of being signifier and signified" (*vācyavācakabhāva*). And its grasper is identity (*tādātmya*) rooted in mutual superimposition; that alone is the relation.

This is because the terms "object" (*artha*) and "word" (*pada*) are conventionally used to mean "that which possesses identity as determined by both. Furthermore, regarding that identity, the object intended as the determiner (*nirūpaka*) is the "denotable" (*śakya*), while the word intended as the locus (*āśraya*) is the "denotative" (*śakta*).

Precisely because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between word and meaning, there is the common usage that "one speaks the meaning" while hearing the verse. Furthermore, there is the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) in the context of Vedic revelation and traditional law (*śruti-smṛti*) which convey linguistic capacity (*śakti*), such as: "The single-syllable Brahman is *Ām*; the two-syllable name is *Rāma*, [which is] the shatterer of the pride of the Wielder of the Pināka bow; *Vṛddhi* consists of *ĀT* and *aiC*. This identity consists in being perceived as non-different from that [meaning] while remaining distinct from it; thus, it is co-extensive with both difference and non-difference. And since non-difference is superimposed (*adhyasta*), there is no contradiction between the two.

The detailed exposition is found in the *Mañjūṣā* and other works. Therefore, by relying on the identity between word and meaning, the possession of phonemes such as *vi*, *pra*, and so forth—which belong to the word "lightning" (*vidyut*)—is established as being equally unrestricted with respect to its meaning; thus, the point already demonstrated is confirmed, and there is no difficulty whatsoever. Intelligent persons should understand other cases in this very same way.

Or rather, it is as if the earth, unable to endure the oppression of those seeking wealth, has surely gone to the great mountain; for where else, O lotus-eyed one, could these throngs of supplicants find life when they approach a generous man? 382.

"Unable to endure the afflictions of supplicants"—the word *asāsahiḥ* is correctly formed from the root *sah* with the suffix *yaṅ* (intensive) followed by the suffix *kvip*, according to the rule "sāsahi-vāvahi," etc., functioning here as if it were *asahiṣṇuḥ*. The genitive case in *pīḍanānām* is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). The phrase *ahimahīdhram* refers to Śeṣa, the mountain; it is also understood to mean a mountain consisting of venomous serpents. By this, his inaccessibility to others due to extreme dreadfulness is illuminated. *Agāḥ* means you went or reached.

O lotus-eyed one! The sense is that these throngs of supplicants, not considering even slightly the great danger [to you], are solely miserable for their own sake. There is a common proverb: "Where do the multitudes of seekers keep a generous man—one whose nature is to give preceded by kind words—alive? The implication is that they would surely not fail to afflict him, even if he were stationed in a place most difficult to access.

In this case, the attribution of the cause—the Lord’s inability to endure the suffering of those who seek Him—to the effect—the Lord’s attainment of the mountain that supports the serpents—is an instance of *asiddhaviṣayā* (unestablished subject) poetic fancy, because such an inability to endure is unestablished [in reality]. Here too, as in the previous examples, the cause is implied (*ārtha*). The distinction is that while the two preceding examples were intermingled with *śleṣa* (paronomasia), this one is pure (*śuddha*). An example of *siddhaviṣayā phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding an established subject with respect to its result) is as follows:

"O Śauri, it is said that you bear upon your chest the Kaustubha gem, which possesses auspicious rays and resembles a thousand sunbeams, for the purpose of dispelling the darkness of the people who bow before you. (383)

In this passage, there is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) concerning the wearing of the Kaustubha gem; for although the dispelling of darkness is not the actual result of that act, it is here imagined as such with respect to an established object.
[This is illustrated by: "Abiding within their very self, out of compassion for them, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge."
Because, in the manner thus stated, the Lord's destruction of darkness is established by its very nature.
An *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) whose object is unestablished (*asiddha-viṣaya*) with respect to its result (*phala*) is as follows:
"To fulfill the curiosity of his constant, affectionate cohabitation with the nectar of his sister, the Lord of the Kākodara Mountain (Śeṣa) indeed reveals the nectar of his smile unto Kamalā. (384)

The particle *kila* is an indicator of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). Here, the fancy regarding Lakṣmī—that the fulfillment of her curiosity for constant, respectful, and intimate cohabitation with the nectar of the Blessed One’s smile is not the actual result [of that smile], but rather that she herself, who is like a sky-lotus, becomes the result—is a fancy of result (*phalotprekṣā*) whose object is unestablished (*asiddha-viṣaya*).

Or rather, O Blessed One, as if to suggest that even I have been conquered by her—saying "Delight me"—you indeed bind upon your own heart, which is her abode, the Vaijayantī garland; for *vaijayantī* refers both to a banner of victory and to the forest-garland.

In this instance, the binding of the Vaijayantī banner—which is designated by that term because it is identified with the forest garland (vanamālā) upon the Lord’s own heart, which is the abode of Lakṣmī—is not itself the result; rather, it serves as a manifestation of his own defeat by Śrī. Since this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) regarding a result that is not actually established, it is an "unestablished-subject" (asiddha-viṣaya) conceit of result. This [conceit] is supported by both metaphor (rūpaka) and paronomasia (śleṣa). The former [type of conceit], however, was mixed with metaphor; this is the distinction between them.
Or rather, O lotus-eyed one, you surely bind this many-colored Vaijayantī garland upon yourself in order to manifest that your own chest is the abode of the victory of Lakṣmī. (386)

O lotus-eyed one! [He has made] his own chest the "standard" (*ketana*) of Lakṣmī—that is, the banner-staff (*dhvajayaṣṭi*) of victory; here the word *ketana* denotes a banner-staff. In another sense, it means the "house of victory. As Ajaya states: "The word *ketana* refers to a banner, a task, an invitation, and a dwelling."

To clearly manifest [your victory] upon that very spot on your chest which serves as the banner of triumph, you surely fasten a Vaijayantī—a multicolored and variegated garland; in another sense, the Vaijayantī-flag, whose colors are described as "the Vaijayantī garland of the Wielder of the Mace (Viṣṇu) consists of five colors. Here, the word *vaijayantī* denotes the cloth of a banner (*dhvajapaṭī*). Although in lexicons such as the *Sudhā*, all four terms—*patākā*, *vaijayantī*, *ketana*, and *dhvaja*—are explained as synonyms for a banner (*dhvaja*), [in this context it refers specifically to the garland].

Nevertheless, one must necessarily accept that the words *patākā* and *vaijayantī* denote the cloth of the banner, while the words *ketana* and *dhvaja* denote the staff of the banner, precisely because this is how they are well-known in common usage.

Otherwise, the co-occurrence of the words *patākā*, *dhvaja*, and so forth in many passages of the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Māghakāvya*, and other works—such as in "adorned with flags and banners" (*apatākādhvajamālinam*), "with the banner of a restless snake grasped by the tip of its beak" (*cañcvagradaṣṭacaṭulāhipatākayā*), and "the Vaijayantī banners of the manifesting standard" (*prabhāvanīketanavaijayantīḥ*)—would be contradicted. For indeed, the co-occurrence of synonymous terms such as *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa* is neither observed nor accepted.

Furthermore, in the verse from the *Māghakāvya* cited above, the metaphorical representation of the serpent as a "flag-cloth" (*dhvajapaṭī*) in the phrase *caṭulāhipatākayā* is precisely what corresponds to the expression *uragāśanaketuyaṣṭyā*. For this very reason, the metaphorical representation of the flag-staff as the staff carried by an ascetic in the *Campūbhārata* verse—“The chariot’s flag-staff, with its severed head and hand, possessing pure bones for teeth and wearing the blood-pool as a silken garment”—is appropriate; likewise, the metaphorical representation of the Mandākinī as a "flag of virtuous conduct" in the verse of Murārimiśra—“This celestial river is the flag of your ancestors' good deeds”—is also fitting.

The statement from the *Pādma-saṃhitā* found in the section on the hoisting of the flag—“one should likewise paint a banner equal in size to half the flag”—is also favorable to this very point. Here, the meaning of the suffix *-tumun* (in *viśadayitum*) is the result (*phala*). This is also the case in the example to be cited later. In the preceding examples, however, the meaning of the dative case is the result.

Here, the Blessed One’s binding of the Vaijayantī garland upon his own chest—which serves to manifest that his chest is the banner for the conquest of Lakṣmī—is imagined as being fruitless while simultaneously being treated as its very fruit; thus, this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result). Its specific distinction is that it has an unestablished object (*asiddhaviṣayā*), because such a manifestation is not actually established, and it is animated by a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of two meanings—namely, the house-flag and the forest-garland—conveyed by the words *ketana* and *vaijayantī*, through the device of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Or,

just as the lord of the mountain of collyrium (Añjanabhūdhara) manifests his own nature as Mādhava (the Spring), he brought to the grove-rows a heart-pleasing fragrance and the beauty of exceedingly tender creepers.

As if to manifest his own nature as Mādhava, as the month of Madhu (spring), and as the Lord of Śrī—[the word] *mādhava* being defined by the *Medinī* lexicon as "Mādhava [is used] for the month of Madhu and for Rādhā"—the Lord, who is dear to the heart (*hṛdyā*) and resides upon the chest, [manifested himself] near the grove of forest rows and near the Vaijayantī banner, like the lord of the Añjana mountains.

And those creepers were exceedingly tender; their "splendor" (*śrī*)—meaning their abundance—was such that, in another sense, it was Lakṣmī herself, whose "excessive tenderness" (*ati-mṛdu-latā*) is her delicacy, who was made to attain "fragrance" (*āmoda*)—meaning both scent and joy. Here, the Blessed One himself attains the fragrance of excessive tenderness by his very nature, yet it is not for the sake of manifesting his own identity as Mādhava. Thus, there is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result), wherein the manifestation of that identity—which is actually fruitless—is imagined as having a result. Since such a manifestation is unestablished, this is an *asiddhaviṣaya* (unestablished-subject) poetic fancy.
This [example] is supported by *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* (pun with word-splitting), whereas the former was by *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (pun without word-splitting); such is the distinction between them.

Just as lotuses, in order to attain a state of being full of nectar (or: full of affection), abandon their innate state of being merely red lotuses (*tāmarasa*), so too, O Lord of the mountain of the best of serpents, do these lotuses (*sarasija*) attain the status of a garland upon Your chest. 388.

In order to attain "sarasahitatām"—meaning either "the state of being beneficial to those who possess aesthetic flavor (rasika)" or "the state of possessing aesthetic flavor (sarasatā)"—[the lotus] attains that very "arasatām," meaning "the state of lacking aesthetic flavor" or, alternatively, the compound *tāmarasatām* may be taken as a single word, meaning "the state of being a lotus (*tāmarasa*). Here, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the fruit—which consists in the attainment of the state of being a lotus by the lotus itself—is one whose object is unestablished (*asiddha-viṣaya*), since the attainment of "beneficialness to the flavorful" is as impossible as a hare's horn; yet it is presented as a fruit. It should be noted that this, too, is assisted by a broken pun (*sabhaṅga-śleṣa*), just as in the previous example.
Or as you descended in haste from the city of Akṛtaka to set foot upon the Mahendra mountain, O Acyuta, you placed your hand here, it is said, merely to steady your waist which had become agitated.

Here, there is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result), wherein the act of carrying—performed by the Lord, consisting in the supporting of His own arm which serves as the locus for the agitation induced by the descent of Satī from the limit of the supreme ether—is fancied as having the status of a result, even though it is not actually a result, namely the placing [of the arm] in His own natural left hand. This is an *asiddhaviṣayā* (having an unrealized subject) because the subject of the fancy, the act of carrying, is itself unestablished. The distinction is that this is pure (*śuddhā*), whereas the previous one was mixed (*saṃkīrṇā*).

In this regard, the mode of understanding is as follows: in the example of *vastūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a real object), such as "The great crown is like the child of the mountain of the gods," the term "child of the mountain of the gods" (suragiriśiśu) is construed as the qualifier (*prakāra*) within the sense of "likeness" (*iva*), which here signifies a poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*). Furthermore, this fancy is construed with the "great crown" (*mahākirīṭa*) by way of the relation of being its object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "The great crown is the object of a poetic fancy whose qualifier is 'the child of the mountain of the gods'."

The imaginative identification (*saṃbhāvanā*) has as its object the Great Diadem (*mahākirīṭa*) and is qualified by the state of being the peak of the divine mountain (*suragiriśiśu*), precisely through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), because it is so experienced and because there exists no other relation that could serve as the basis for the resulting aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*). However, it is not so [qualified] when the state of being the peak of the divine mountain is the subordinate element, since that [state] is merely an adjunct to the divine mountain’s peak. The same should be understood in cases of co-utterance with words such as *dhruvam* (certainly) or *nūnam* (surely).

In cases such as “I consider the face to be the moon,” the cognition is that there is a mental attribution (saṃbhāvanā) having as its object a face non-different from the moon, because of the grammatical rule regarding the non-difference relation between the meanings of two nouns. It should be understood that the same applies to expressions such as “I imagine the face to be the moon” or “I conjecture [it to be] the moon.”

In the example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) where the object [of the fancy] is not explicitly stated, as in "He seems to sprinkle [me]," the verb "sprinkles" (*abhiṣiñcati*)—through a metaphorical indication (*sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā*)—brings to mind a state of "gladdening" (*ānandana*) that is common to both sprinkling and gladdening by virtue of its nature as a nourishing agent (*āpyāyakatva*). Since the fancy of "sprinkling" is construed with this gladdening, the resulting cognition is: "The object of the fancy is a mode of sprinkling performed by the Blessed One upon oneself, which is a source of nourishment. This should be understood similarly in cases such as "He seems to anoint [me]" (*anaktīva*). Regarding the verse "Darkness seems to smear the limbs," the author of the *Kāvyapradīpa* maintains that the fancy is construed with "pervasion" (*vyāpana*), which is brought to mind through suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

In the example of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause), namely “*añjanaśikhariṇi satatāsañjanato nūnam asito eṣa hariḥ*” (“Surely this Hari is black because of his constant non-contact with the mountain of collyrium”), the meaning of the suffix *tasi* in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is that of a cause (*hetu*). Therein, the word-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) is construed [with the suffix] by way of identity (*abheda*), and the cause is construed with the property of being black (*asitatva*)—which is qualified [by the non-contact]—by way of the relation of being produced by itself (*svaprayojyatā*). This is because when the qualifier is produced by something, the qualified whole is also unimpededly produced by that same thing. Alternatively, there is a construal by way of the relation of having a locus produced by itself (*svaprayojyāśrayatva*).

Its connection is with the act of *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy) through the relation of *prakāratā* (the state of being a qualifier), and that [act] is connected to Śiva (*hari*) by way of being its object (*viṣayatā*). Thus, the resulting cognition is: "Śiva is the object of a poetic fancy whose qualifier is 'white,' which has as its cause something non-different from a continuous application located on the Añjana mountain. It should not be argued that this cannot be considered *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy regarding a cause) because it lacks the status of having a cause as its predicate (*vidheya*) through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Rather, it must be said that this is simply a *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the essential nature) of such a white form through the relation of identity.

Because, through the discernment of what is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣitavivecana*), the non-difference from the cause is to be imagined for the constant application of collyrium; thus, even though the cause is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the constant application, it is accepted as being the predicate (*vidheya*). Furthermore, just as in the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "the moon-like face," by accepting that the non-difference of the face—which serves as the correlate (*anuyogin*)—is the relation (*saṃsarga*) for the constant application, the manifestation of the non-difference from the cause is possible with respect to that constant application.

Although a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) characterized by a cause is directly perceived [in the verse], it is designated specifically as a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a cause) by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). This should be understood as being like the case of the injunction “one offers with curd” (*dadhnā juhoti*), where, although there is a direct perception of an oblation qualified by curd, the designation “the injunction of curd for the oblation” is applied through a discernment based on what is intended to be expressed.

Nor should it be argued that one should simply accept the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) of a property in the form of the cause—either through the relation of being prompted by itself or through the relation of having an abode prompted by itself—with respect to the object "asita" (black), rather than undergoing such strenuous conceptualization; for the refutation of accepting a conceit of a property has already been stated previously.

For this very reason, even the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, in citing the following as an example of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause): “O you of graceful form, I believe the beauty of the lotus has become attached to your feet out of joy,” intended that the fancied identity with the cause—joy—is predicated of the natural attachment itself. However, according to our own method, the fancied identity with the cause—joy—as residing in the subject (*viṣaya*), namely the beauty of the lotus, is what is intended; for if the attachment were merely a subordinate element of the substratum (*dharmyupasarjanatvena*) within the fancy, its connection to the fancy would be untenable. This is the general direction of the argument.

The same should be understood regarding the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) whose cause (*hetu*) has an unrealized object (*asiddha-viṣaya*), because there is no difference in the cognition [of the fancy] whether the object is realized or unrealized; enough of this.

In the example of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) given as "vinatānāṃ janatānām" [of the people of Vinatā], the result—namely, "for the destruction of darknesses" (*tamasāmavasādanāya*)—is expressed in the dative case. Therein, the connection with the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) occurs through identity (*abheda*), just as in the case of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the cause). Furthermore, the result is connected to the wearing of the Kaustubha gem by way of being its motivator (*prayojakatā-saṃsarga*), either directly in the act of wearing, or in its substratum (*tadāśraya*) by way of the relation of being the locus of its own motivator (*svaprayojakāśrayatā-saṃbandha*). This [result] exists as the object (*viṣayatā*) of the imaginative probability (*saṃbhāvanā*) whose relation is identity with that [wearing].

And thus, the cognition is that Śauri (Viṣṇu) is the locus for the imaginative identification (*saṃbhāvanā*) with the bearer of the Kaustubha gem, whose fruit is non-different from the destruction of darkness. Similarly, in instances involving the suffix *tumun*, the fruit is the meaning of *tumun*; however, the resulting cognition remains exactly the same. Furthermore, the status of this as "poetic fancy regarding the fruit" (*phalotprekṣā*) is to be established according to the method already stated. This is the general direction. Thus, the sixfold nature of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) has been demonstrated in accordance with the *Kuvalayānanda*.

According to the view of the Easterners (*prācām*), however, *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is twofold: expressed (*vācyā*) and implied (*pratīyamānā*). Where the collection of conditions for a supposition is accompanied by words that express it—such as *iva*, *nūnam*, *śaṅke*, *saṃbhāvayāmi*, *manye*, *jāne*, *tarkaye*, *ūhe*, *utprekṣe*, *avaimi*, *pratyemi*, *vedmi*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, *kila*, and so forth—the *utprekṣā* is expressed. And where there is merely the collection of conditions without words that express it, there it is implied.

Where there is merely the expressive word devoid of that complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there there is only mere poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) and not *utprekṣā*. That [fancy] is also threefold each: fancy regarding the essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*), fancy regarding the cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), and fancy regarding the result (*phalotprekṣā*).

In that regard, *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy of essential nature) is the imagining (*utprekṣaṇa*)—as far as possible—of objects consisting of genus, quality, action, or substance, whether they exist through identity or other relations, by means of causes (*nimitta*) that consist of genus, quality, action, or substance; these causes may be individual or combined, expressed or unexpressed, accomplished or to be accomplished, and may pertain to objects consisting of genus, quality, action, or substance. This applies to both positive entities and those whose nature is the absence of such categories.

In that regard, *dharmisvarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy on the nature of the subject) is said to occur through non-difference (*abheda*) as the relation of connection (*saṃsarga*), while *dharmasvarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy on the nature of the attribute) occurs through another type of relation. Among the categories of objects mentioned above, the imagining (*saṃbhāvanā*) of previously described types of objects—by means of similar causes—as being either the cause or the effect according to their possibility, is called *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy on the cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (fancy on the effect). These result in numerous variations, such as those whose forms are already complete and those whose forms are yet to be produced.

A mere indication of that [topic] is now presented. Among these, an example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature of a genus (*jāti*) caused by the sign of an appropriated genus (*upāttajātinimitta*) is as follows: "O Mother, I consider your face to be the lotus-habitat for the Goddess of Fortune who resides in the glances of the Lord of the Bull-mountain, because of the swarm of bees hovering intensely above it. (390)

The splendor (*śrī*) of the side-glance is itself *Śrī*, that is, Lakṣmī; [the word] "of her" refers to her. The "bees" (*bhramarakāḥ*) are both the double-voiced sounds (*dvirephāḥ*) and the curly locks of hair (*cūrṇakuntalāḥ*) situated upon the forehead; [the phrase] "by the multitude of those" refers to them. Here, within the locus delimited by the universal of "face," the object delimited by the universal of "lotus" is superimposed through identity. In this case, the cause for this [superimposition] is stated to be the universal consisting of the "multitude of bees" which rests upon the non-difference produced by the pun (*śleṣa*).
An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a genus (*jāti*) arising from the cause of an acquired quality (*guṇa*) is as follows:

"O Mother, I recognize your teeth as bright pearls, which, having been ejected by your sighs, have reached the state of being arranged in rows upon the obstruction of your lower lip, and have descended from the region of your throat. (391)

"By the breath"—that is, by the wind of exhalation—"thrown upward," meaning propelled upwards; "by the obstruction of the lower lips," meaning having attained a state of being arranged in rows (*paṅktibhāva*), that is, standing in a line. The compound is formed according to the rule *dvitīyā śrita* and so forth. The sense is: just as grains blown by the wind stand in rows due to the resistance of some intervening object, so too [do these teeth].

Here, things delimited by the universal of "pearl-ness" are poetically imagined (*utprekṣyante*) as being identical with those delimited by the universal of "tooth-ness"; in this regard, the quality of "purity" (*viśadatva*) is employed as the ground for the figure.
As in the following example:

O Lord of the Mountain, in your face—an ocean of loveliness—the white pearl-forehead ornament (mauktika-lalāṭikā), joined with the Yamunā-like musk-tilaka, shines like the Gaṅgā. [Verse 392] The word *lalāṭikā* means "on the forehead" (*lalāṭe bhavā*). The suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "from *karṇa* and *lalāṭa*, when used in the sense of an ornament" (*karṇalalāṭātkanalaṅkāre*). It refers to a specific kind of ornament called *patrapāśyā*, which is fastened to the forehead by hanging down; as Amarasimha states: "The *patrapāśyā* is a *lalāṭikā*.

In this verse, the nature of being the Gaṅgā (*gaṅgātvajāti*) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being identical with the nature of being a pearl-forehead ornament (*mauktikalalāṭikātvajāti*), which is delimited by its own class. In this context, the quality (*guṇa*) of "whiteness" (*dhavala*) is presented as the basis for the poetic fancy.
Just as she who was born from the sun might become the daughter of the cool-rayed moon, so has this dark streak of tilaka been produced upon your moon-like face, like the Yamunā.

Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that [the river] is "like the Yamunā," the quality (*guṇa*) of "blackness" is employed as the cause. It should be understood that if the intention were to represent the Gaṅgā and Yamunā as substances (*dravya*), these two examples would instead constitute poetic fancies of substance (*dravyotprekṣā*).
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a genus (*jāti*) characterized by an action that has been undertaken (*upāttakriyānimitta*) is as follows:
"In the palace-heart of the Lord of the Bull-Mountain (Śiva), the rays of the central gem, firmly embraced by the pearl necklace, shine forth like horripilation. (394)

Here, there is a poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) based on identity between the universal of "rays" and those [beams] delimited by the universal of "gooseflesh"; in that context, the action of embracing serves as the cause.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a genus (*jāti*) caused by an appropriated substance (*upāttadravyanimittaka*) is as follows:

“Your face, O Lord, we fancy to be a blossoming lotus upon the peak of the serpent-mountain [Śeṣa], where Lakṣmī herself sports incessantly. (395) The meaning is this: we fancy your face to be a blossoming lotus because of its beauty and splendor (*suṣamā-śrī*), due to the fact that it serves as a constant abode for the sporting of Lakṣmī; thus, we fancy it to be a full-blown lotus on account of being the refuge for the incessant play of Lakṣmī.

Here, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the identity of that which is delimited by the universal "mouth-ness" (*mukhatva*) with that which is delimited by the universal "lotus-ness" (*ambhoruhatva*). In this case, the cause (*nimitta*) employed is the substance (*dravya*) consisting of the form of Cupid (*rāma*), whose distinction from [the actual] beauty is produced through *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Here, the word *lakṣmī* denotes a single individual, and thus possesses the nature of a substance (*dravyatva*). By this, those who do not acknowledge that both universals (*jāti*) and substances (*dravya*) can serve as causes in a poetic fancy should be disregarded. As it is stated in the *Citramīmāṃsā*: "Since even universals and substances can function as causes in a poetic fancy, we consider this enumeration of causes to be incomplete."

Thus; the meaning is that this enumeration of causes was stated by the ancients. And therein two types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*) have been illustrated.
An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the essential nature of a genus whose cause is unappropriated (*anupātta-nimitta*) is as follows:

"The musk-tilaka on the forehead of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu), fixed upon the bridge of his nose which serves as the string of the bow of his pair of eyebrows—surely it is the shield for the arrow of Love, who desires to conquer the world. (396)

Here, in the poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) regarding the identity between that which is delimited by the universal "being a tilaka-mark of musk" and that which is delimited by the universal "being the fruit of the arrows of Love," the grounds for such identity—namely, its blackness, its fine point, and so forth—are not explicitly stated. However, in reality, the attribute established in the first half-verse has already been employed, having been made common to both the object and the subject through the metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the manner to be described below.

Since [qualities] such as blackness (*asitatva*) and so forth are not explicitly mentioned, this verse must be considered an illustration of a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the nature of the object itself) based on both expressed and unexpressed causes, according to the method to be explained hereafter; it is not an illustration of one based solely on an unexpressed cause. An example of a pure *svarūpotprekṣā* with an unexpressed cause is as follows: "The forehead-mark (*tilaka*) is victorious, appearing like the upward-tipped eye of Viṣṇu held upon his own ploughshare, as if he intended to sustain the bodiless Smara (the God of Love) by means of that very [ploughshare], using the eye from the forehead of Śiva. (397)

With the very same third eye by which he had rendered the bodiless Smara (Kāma) formless and devoid of body, Hari Śrīnivāsa, desiring to restore him to life, placed [the seed] upon his own forehead; for they say that "for poets, the Kali age is a wish-fulfilling cow."

That whose upper border (*añcala*) or tip (*agra*) is directed upwards is described as such; it is the *tilaka*—the decorative mark of musk—that triumphs in the world. By observing that the eyes have rounded bases and fine, curved tips, the term "eye with an upward-pointing border" is employed so as to evoke the possibility of the *tilaka* being identical to them. For indeed, without the upward-pointing border of the eye, the identification with a musk *tilaka* characterized by a rounded base and a fine, curved tip would not be possible.

Here, by means of the two words *hara* and *hari*, which have "the act of taking away" (*haraṇa*) as their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), a rivalry based on the equality of both is illuminated. It should be noted that this rivalry serves to embellish the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that has been established. In this case, regarding the imaginative identification (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*) with that which is delimited by the universal of "being an eye," the ground for such identification—namely, blueness (*nīlatva*) and so forth—is not explicitly stated.

Or rather, the garland of moon-patterns formed by the tips of the peacock feathers atop the mountain where Lakṣmī dwells shines forth like a row of eyes opened to proclaim its status as a king among serpents. 398.

The state of being a hooded mountain (*phaṇibhūbhṛttva*), the state of being the king of serpents (*bhujagarājatva*), and the state of being the Śeṣa-mountain (*śeṣādritva*)—here, in the *candrakamālā*, the genus [of the moon] is imagined as being delimited by the genus [of the eye-ornament]. The grounds for this, such as its dark-red color and so forth, are not explicitly stated. Thus, the various types of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature of a genus have been demonstrated: those that are pure, those where the ground is explicitly stated, and those where the ground is not explicitly stated.
Now, those mixed figures are illustrated:
"The two arms of Śauri, extended by the delight residing in his heart to lift up his own son situated at the navel-lotus, shine indeed like a supporting staff. (399)
A *yaṣṭi* is a single-string necklace (*ekāvalī*) of whatever length desired, measured by the span of the hand, fashioned with gems;
that which has a gem joined in its center is called a *yaṣṭi* by those learned in ornaments.

Thus, this particular kind of pearl necklace—named *ekāvalī*, though also known by the name *muktāhāra*—is defined by Varāhamihira. The word *ālambā* means "hanging down" (*ālambamānā*). Here, the two arms belonging to Lakṣmī—who resides upon the Lord’s chest—are poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being identical with the two [pearls] born upon the Lord’s string of pearls, as delimited by the universal property (*jāti*) of being "arms."
