In that context, for the purpose of establishing the causal status (*nimittatā*) of the attributes residing in the pearl necklace—namely, their being spread by beauty (*lāvaṇya*), their being pervasive, and their being suspended—it was necessary to ensure that they reside within the pair of arms belonging to the Goddess Lakṣmī. Among these, for the attribute of "beauty" (*lāvaṇya*), which was not explicitly mentioned, its residence within the pair of arms was established precisely because it belongs to the divine body of Lakṣmī. For the other two attributes as well, the bearing of her own son, the four-faced Brahmā, who resides in the Lord’s navel-lotus, is imagined as the result.

This is because the knowledge of its being a means [to that end] generates an effort conducive to extension and support. And thus, when the commonality is achieved through the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) of the natural extension and support residing in the object with the extension and support residing in the object—which result in the aforementioned carrying away—the state of being the cause [of the poetic figure] comes into being. Nor is it correct to say here that this is a "poetic fancy of the result" (*phalotprekṣā*), since the result itself is also fancied.

Since the aesthetic charm (camatkṛti) comes to rest upon the *svarūpotprekṣā* (identification based on essential nature) itself—which is intensified by a cause brought about by the very fruit being imagined—and since the particle *kila*, which expresses the sense of *utprekṣā*, has no syntactic connection with the "fruit," it is appropriate to designate this figure as that very type of *utprekṣā*. Furthermore, this is an *utprekṣā* of identity (*tādātmyotprekṣā*) whose object is not swallowed up (*anigīrṇaviṣayā*), which possesses a cause consisting of both an expressed and an unexpressed action and quality, and whose distinct body is yet to be accomplished (*niṣpādyaviśiṣṭaśarīrā*).
This is because, although the pair of Lakṣmī’s arms is established by its own nature, they are brought into existence by the poet specifically as characterized by their being outstretched.
Or rather,

I consider them to be the necklaces of Śauri, hanging down in various ways, appearing like streams of tears falling from the Kaustubha gem as it overflows with joy at being caressed by his own sister Kamalā.

Here, in the case of the pearl necklace (hāra) produced from the ocean (śauri), there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) identifying it with the drops of tears of joy belonging to the Kaustubha gem resting upon his chest, as delimited by the universal property (*jāti*) of being such tears. For that [fancy] to be established, it is necessary to ensure that the attributes of being in the form of a stream (*dhārākāratva*), not hanging down (*anābhilambitatva*), and being shimmering (*thālathalya*)—which serve as the grounds for the fancy—are attributed to the object of the fancy, namely, the drops of tears of joy belonging to the Kaustubha. Among these, while the attribute of "shimmering" (*thālathalya*) was not explicitly mentioned, its presence in those drops is established precisely through its connection to the tears of joy.

In order to establish the two qualities of having the form of a stream and being suspended—which belong to the other two [the eyes] as well—the state of overflowing with joy from fondling the lotus (her sister) is postulated as the cause. Thus, when there is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on the identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) between the natural form of a stream and the state of being suspended belonging to the objects [the eyes], which are caused by such overflowing occurring in the subject [the face], the attainment of commonality (*sādhāraṇyasampatti*) constitutes the basis for [the figure of] *nimitta*.

This is a *jātyutprekṣā* (genus-based poetic fancy) based on the causes of action and quality regarding both expressed and unexpressed elements, characterized by a body (*śarīra*) produced [by the poet]. This is because the drops of tears from the Kaustubha gem were produced by the poet himself.
Or, for example:

"O Lord, the necklace shines like a pair of arms suspended as a heart-ornament upon the Kaustubha, for the purpose of lifting out the hearts of your own sister Lakṣmī submerged in the lake of your navel. (401)

Here too, in the *Hāralatā*, that which is delimited by the universal of "having two arms" (the subject) is superimposed through identity upon the universal of "being a pearl necklace. In that case, in order to establish the status of the two attributes—length and luminosity—as the grounds for this superimposition, their presence within the object of superimposition (the *kaustubha* gem and the pair of arms) must necessarily be established. Of these two, while the possession of length is already established as residing in the pair of arms, the possession of luminosity—which has not been explicitly mentioned—is established as residing in the pair of arms precisely through its connection with the *kaustubha*.

In order to establish that even slowness belongs to that [lotus], its lifting of its own sister Ramā’s mind—which was submerged in the lake of the Lord’s navel—is imagined as its fruit. Thus, through an *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) based on the identification of the natural slowness residing in the object with the slowness residing in the subject (the lotus) which has such lifting as its fruit, once commonality is achieved, the status of being a "cause" (*nimitta*) is established. Everything else is exactly as in the previous examples.

This too is indeed a *jātyutprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on genus), having as its cause the nature of actions and qualities—both acquired and unacquired—and resulting in a distinct body produced [by the poet]; for it is the poet alone who has brought about the two arms of the Kaustubha gem.
Or, for example:

"The musk-paste tilaka on Mādhava’s lotus-face remains motionless, as if it were a bee drawn there by the lure of its boundless fragrance and fearing the touch of his nose, which resembles a campaka flower. (402)

"Nibhālanaṃ" means seeing. Here too, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting in the identification (*tādātmya*) of the bees—characterized by immobility—with the caste-mark (*kastūrītilaka*) of Śrīnivāsa, which is likewise characterized by immobility. In this context, since the identity between the mark and the bee cannot be easily established unless the immobility residing in the mark is attributed to the bee, it must be proven that this [immobility] resides in the object (the subject of the fancy).

In this instance, since the blue color (*nailya*)—which is not explicitly mentioned—is established in the subject of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣyamāṇa*), two factors—the greed for boundless fragrance and the fear of being scrutinized by the nose—are fancied as the causes for the production of its immobility. Here too, as before, there is commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) due to the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the natural and the imagined. One should understand that just as previously, even when the fruit was fancied, it was not a "fancying of the fruit" (*phalotprekṣā*), so here too, although the cause is fancied, it is not a "fancying of the cause" (*hetūtprekṣā*).
Or rather, O Mother, the rays of the pearl necklace spreading across your chin shine like the fingers of that [necklace] stretched out as it rises to lift your modestly downcast face. 403.

Here, there is a poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) consisting of the identity of the universal "rays" (of the necklace) with the universal "finger," as delimited by the finger-form. In that case, because of the non-difference between the unmentioned attribute of brilliance (*ojjvalya*) and the two mentioned attributes—namely, "spreading forth" (*visṛtvara*) and "extended" (*prasārita*), which have entered into the state of being the primary object (*vastu*) and its counterpart (*prativastu*)—there is a commonality between the subject (*viṣaya*) and the object of fancy (*viṣayin*). Everything else is exactly as before. This should be inferred in other cases as well.
Thus has the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of birth and its essence been illustrated by way of example.
An example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of a subordinate quality through identity is as follows:
"O Śauri, upon your golden-hued body occupied by the quality of blue, I perceive the bright yellow quality that has emerged externally in the form of a golden garment. (404)

O Śauri! I perceive—that is, I imagine—the yellow quality (*pīta-guṇa*) to have issued forth from your golden garment. For you, who are golden-hued, whose entire body down to the very tips of your nails is described as being of golden color by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "He is entirely golden down to his nails" and "Resplendent like gold, accessible through the cognition of dreams," your body has been overtaken by the quality of blueness (*nīla-guṇa*). Consequently, the yellow quality, finding no room there, has overflowed and emerged externally; this is the meaning. Here, the yellow quality is imagined through identification (*tādātmya*) with the golden garment, which is its genus (*jāti*).

In this case, since "brilliance" is the quality (guṇa) that has been adopted [as the basis for the superimposition], this is a figure of speech consisting of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of the state of being a quality, caused by an adopted quality.
O Lord, O Śrījāna, I know your compassion to be like a lotus pond belonging to you—most sweet for all and perfectly fit for the immersion of even the greatest sinners. (405)

"Extremely sweet" means very dear and exceedingly delicious; according to Amara, "the words *madhura* and *svādu* denote both 'sweet' and 'dear'. "Those whose great *āgas*" refers to those who possess great sin or transgression; according to Amara, "*āgas* denotes both 'sin' (*pāpa*) and 'offense' (*aparādha*). "Of all" means by all people; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule "the genitive may optionally be used for the agent of kṛtya-derivatives. "For the purpose of bathing" means for the sake of immersion; elsewhere, it means for the disappearance—i.e., the non-appearance—of great *āgasas*, that is, offenses.

The meaning is: "by all people," that is, by every single person who has committed an offense; "suniṣevyām" means easily accessible for service. Herein, the specific point is that while there is a poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) regarding the identity between the substance in the form of Svāmipuṣkariṇī and the quality in the form of compassion, the quality of sweetness (*mādhurya-guṇa*) is supported by paronomasia (*śleṣa*), and the action of being "serviceable" (*sevyatva*) is employed as the underlying cause.

In this manner, examples of *svarūpotprekṣā* (imaginative identification of the essential nature) based on qualities (*guṇa*) having birth (*jāti*) and other factors as their cause (*nimitta*) should also be cited.
An example of *svarūpotprekṣā* where the cause is not explicitly mentioned (*anupātta-nimittaka-guṇabhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"From anger at the gaze of the kinsman of the lotuses [the Sun], which obstructs its upward expansion, the multitude of gems upon the crest of the serpent-king seems to have burst forth with redness and shines. (306) Here, "gems" (*maṇayaḥ*) are intended to mean rubies (*padmarāga*). In this instance, the quality of redness (*āruṇya-guṇa*) is imagined through identity (*tādātmyena*) within the genus of rubies; the cause, such as brilliance (*aujjvalya*), is not mentioned.

Or rather, O Mother of All, we perceive your measured smile as a white quality that has emerged from your tongue, which, finding no space to remain within the row of teeth due to being overtaken by the redness of the tongue, has risen up from there. 407.
Here, there is a poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) identifying the smile with the quality of whiteness; however, no cause for this is mentioned therein.
Or rather, O Mother of the World, may I place within my heart that pair of shimmering lotuses which, like a redness vomited from the hands due to inner pride, has been cast up high. 408.
Here, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the quality of redness arising from the lotus, where the cause is not explicitly stated.
Or rather,
I think that the Kaustubha jewel is a fresh effort on the part of the Creator toward the chest of the Lord of Śrī, placed there as a mass of loveliness remaining from the creation of Śrī’s own body.

In this case, within the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the Kaustubha jewel as having the nature of a mass of loveliness (lāvaṇya), the quality of "beauty" (darśanīyatva) and so forth has not been explicitly mentioned.

Thus I meditate upon his good character as if it were incarnate, and his affection as if it were manifest; he is an ineffable abode of profound luster, equal to the one who dwells upon the peak of the glorious serpent-mountain.

In such passages as well, one should understand that there is a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) in which the cause is not explicitly stated. "Good character" (*sauśīlya*) is the inherent nature of being closely united even with the dull-witted. "Affection" (*vātsalya*) is the state of possessing a love that overcomes faults. "Extreme blackness" (*atinaiilyam*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Thus has the nature of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the state of qualities (*guṇabhāva*) been illustrated by way of direction. Now follows the *utprekṣā* regarding the state of action (*kriyābhāva*).
Among these, an example of *utprekṣā* regarding the state of action based on an expressed genus (*upāttajāti-nimittaka*) is as follows:

"With masses of spray from her own waterfalls falling from the tips of her peaks, driven forth by the spreading wind, the celestial Gaṅgā offers, as it were, a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Lord of the Mountain of the Serpent-Kings. (411)

Here, in this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the nature of the action consisting of the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), the cause (*nimitta*) employed is the genus (*jāti*) consisting of the mass of spray driven by the spreading wind. In the expression "he offers a handful of flowers," because the act of offering is precluded (*bādha*) in relation to the palms joined as an *añjali*, its connection shifts to the qualifiers, namely the flowers—just as in the case of "the heavenly being has perished" (*svargī dhvastaḥ*). The meaning is that he scatters the flowers situated within the *añjali*. For those learned in logic maintain the principle: "When a prescription or a prohibition applies to something qualified, if it is obstructed in the qualified object, it transfers to the qualifier."

For this very reason, such usages as "the monkey heard those rākṣasīs threatening Sītā" are consistent. Other points to be discussed have been explained by us in the *Lakṣmīsahasraprādurbhāvastabakaratnaprakāśikā*.
An example of a figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting in the nature of an action caused by an apprehended quality (*upāttaguṇanimittaka-kriyābhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"By means of the whiteness of its peaks, which abound in crystal slabs as pure as the exceedingly bright moon, Mount Sphaṭādharagiri, bearing other mountains, clearly mocks Lord Hari. (412)
Here, in this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the nature of the absence of the act of laughing, the quality of the whiteness of the peak of the crystal rock is employed as the cause.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the nature of a state that serves as the cause for an action involving something appropriated is as follows:
"Indeed, the Vṛṣādri mountain, emitting magnificent waterfalls from its lofty peaks, seems to weep tears out of joy at the dwelling of Mukunda within itself."

"He emits vapor" (*bāṣpam udvamati*) or "he becomes vapor" (*bāṣpāyate*), according to the rule *abāṣpoṣmabhyām udvamane* which prescribes the suffix *kyaṅ*. Here, in this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the nature of the action of emitting vapor, the action of the gushing forth of waterfalls is employed as the cause.
In this way, examples based on the signs of appropriated objects (*upāttadravyanimitta*) may also be cited. For instance:
"O Mother, I think that the orb of the moon, having been split in two by your hand-lotus out of anger and threaded upon your forearm, is crying out, its jeweled bracelets jingling. (414)

Here, for those who maintain that the verbal cognition has a term ending in the nominative case as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) in which the property of being the agent of crying is imagined; this is preceded by the imagining of identity with the white lunar orb, which is itself imagined as being non-different from the act of stringing—occurring in the region of the forearm, following the boring through of the middle [of the pearls], caused by hatred directed at the lotus-like hands, and applied to the pearl bracelets characterized by tinkling sounds, through the relation of non-difference.

In that regard, it is established that when there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on identity (*tādātmya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) is the cause; and when there is a poetic fancy based on another relation (*saṃbandhāntara*), the property co-located with it (*tatsamānādhikaraṇo dharmaḥ*) residing in the object (*viṣaya*) is the cause. Thus, since we have here a poetic fancy concerning the property of being the agent of weeping (*krandanakartṛtva*) within the context of what is being described (*prastuta*), the property of being the object of driving (*pravayanakarmatva*), which is co-located with that [weeping], must be established as residing in the object by way of being the subject of restatement (*anuvādyatayā*).

The identity between the pearl bracelet and [the moon] is imagined (utprekṣyate) based on the unstated cause of whiteness. In this regard, just as in a qualified simile (viśiṣṭopamā) there is an implied similarity between the qualifiers of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, so too here, there is an implied non-difference between the "spreading" (pravayana), which is the qualifier of the pearl bracelet—the subject of the figure—and the "spreading," which is the qualifier of the lunar orb—the object of the primary imagination (mūlotprekṣā). Consequently, once the "spreading" having the lunar orb as its object is established, the primary imagination is fully realized.

Even between the weeping (*krandana*) and the tinkling (*siñjana*), there is non-difference by way of the relation of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). Therefore, the mode of cognition is as follows: the pearl bracelet, which is non-different from the tinkling [sound] strung upon the forearm, is non-different from the white hand-reflection strung upon the forearm, and thus it possesses the activity conducive to the act of weeping. However, when the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) emphasizes the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of the act of crying as being non-different [from the tinkling].

In that verbal function (*śābdavṛtti*), although the tinkling (*śiñjana*) is perceived as a qualifier of the bracelet, it remains an object of poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) by virtue of the process of identification (*adhyavasāna*). Furthermore, such a bracelet is the qualifier of the act of weeping; and upon such a bracelet, the disc of the white-rayed moon [is superimposed] through non-difference (*abheda*). However, the disc of the white-rayed moon itself is not directly [the qualifier] of the action; for if that were the case, the bracelet would fail to be syntactically connected (*ananvaya*).

Thus, as before, the apprehension of non-difference between the object of comparison and its counterpart (*viṣayin* and *viṣaya*) occurs through the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*).
Thus has been demonstrated the path of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the essential nature of action and non-existence.
An example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) whose nature consists in the absence of action caused by an unperceived sign (*anupāttanimittaka-kriyābhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"Recollection of that certain abode, whose residence was established upon such a mountain-peak of serpents, bestows upon my mind—as if with adamantine cement—the memory of its very form. (415)

In this instance, within the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the act of applying adamantine glue (*vajralepa*), the cause—the bringing about of proximity through non-separation—is not explicitly stated. Now, as for the poetic fancy of substance (*dravya*) and state (*bhāva*):
therein, an example of a poetic fancy of substance and state based on an expressed genus (*jāti*) as the cause is as follows:

"O Consort of the Lord who slew Madhu, who would not conjecture in their own heart that the moon is melting away before your face, which stands directly opposite it? (416) [In this verse, the moon's disappearance is fancied as its melting due to its proximity to the face, which is of the genus "face."]

By means of this face—which stands directly before him, facing him; which is liquid, moist with compassion, or else, in the alternative sense, dripping with water; and which is a moonstone (*vidhukānta*), for the Blessed Moon himself is the beloved (*kānta*)—thereby, in the alternative sense, that which instantly exudes nectar from the touch of the rays of the nectar-rayed one, and is called a "moonstone," which is difficult to find in the Kali age.

Thus, by means of the moonstone (*candrakāntamaṇi*) characterized as described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, there is here a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the identity between the substance in the form of the moon and the genus in the form of the face; the cause for this is the genus in the form of the moonstone, whose non-difference is established through punning (*śleṣa*).
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the existence of a substance caused by qualities that have been assumed [as attributes] is as follows:
"I recognize the risen Brahman, which the Upaniṣads call infinite, as the dark-blue Mahendra mountain, its vast expanse shimmering with limbs such as hands and feet. (417)

Here, in the case of Śrīnivāsa, who is the Supreme Brahman as a substance (*dravya*), there is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) of his identity with the substance that is space (*ākāśa*), caused by the qualities of blueness and infinity. Because space is one, this [Supreme] Substance is [compared to it]. The "concluding portions of the Vedas" (*nigamāntāḥ*) refers to Upaniṣads such as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. "Infinite" (*anantam*) means Brahman devoid of the three kinds of limitation. In the alternative sense, "infinite" (*anantam*) refers to the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), according to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word 'ananta' is neuter when meaning the sky, and masculine when meaning Keśava or Śeṣa. In this context, the quality of blueness and so forth is what has been employed.
An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the state of a substance caused by an action that is itself apprehended is as follows:
"O Daughter of the Ocean, because it bestows such abundant showers of joy due to its own brilliant luster, I consider this gem upon your nose to be the planet Venus."

Because this pearl ornament (*maṇi*) on your nose—the *Amara-kośa* stating that "the word *maṇi* refers to two kinds of gems born from stone as well as pearls and the like"—is shining brightly in the constellation Svāti due to its not having set; for that reason. In the alternative sense (of the cloud), because of its own extreme brilliance (*atyujjvalatva*), that which has bestowed sufficient joy (*pramoda*)—where the word *datta* is elided according to the rule "after words such as *pra*, the verbal root is optionally expressed, or there is elision of the subsequent member"—gives rain (*varṣa*).
Moving in the direction of Varuṇa under the asterism Svātī, the Sun,
never setting, spreads a full rain that bestows joy upon the world.

This is the intended meaning of the statement "because it is so said. In this context, "a shower of joy" means uninterrupted bliss; [the nose-jewel] "gives" this. For that reason, I consider your nose-jewel to be Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu. Here, Śukra—the substance—is superimposed through identity upon the nose-jewel, which is the locus (*jāti*). And in this regard, the cause has been employed, consisting of the act of giving a shower of joy, based on the reasons of its own brilliance and the non-difference constructed by the established *śleṣa* (punning). This is an example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) whose nature consists in the state of being a substance, caused by a substance that has been employed as the reason.

O Infinite One, that which shines as your Śārṅga bow while you sport upon the peaks of the serpent-mountain, I perceive that very bow as the infinite Śeṣa resting upon its head. (419) Regarding this: the word *śiras* refers to the head, the front, the vanguard of an army, the top of a tree, and the summit—according to the *Ratnamālā*. It is "mounted" (*adhirūḍha*) by the *jyā*; for *jyā* means the bowstring, the earth, and a mother—according to the *Ratnamālā*. I perceive—that is, I imagine—that infinite Śeṣa [resting] there.

In this instance, regarding the substance *śārṅga* (the Śārṅga bow), the [remaining] substance is conceived through identity (*tādātmya*). Therein, by means of the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the two objects—the earth and the bowstring—which are conveyed by the word *jyā*, the substance consisting of the earth resting upon the head is employed as the cause (*nimitta*). This is an example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) concerning the state of being a substance where the cause is not explicitly stated, as in:
"O Acyuta, your arm, encircled by a jeweled armlet, shines like Rāhu emerging from the center of the sun’s orb after piercing it out of enmity."

Here, Rāhu—having emerged from the solar disc after first piercing its center—is imagined as being identical with the Lord’s arm encircled by an armlet; yet, no cause whatsoever for this identification has been stated.

Thus, about sixty varieties of *svarūpotprekṣā* (imaginative identification) based on positive entities such as birth and so forth have been presented. Now, a mere indication of the varieties of *svarūpotprekṣā* characterized by a sense of negation (*abhāvābhimāna*) is being illustrated.
Among these, an example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the very nature of the absence of birth is as follows:
"Upon that mountain of the Lord of Serpents, Śauri delights Ramā day and night, making the forest appear as if devoid of the sun by means of the dark masses of his own radiance. (421)

The meaning is "in that forest. Here, the absence of the sun is poetically imagined as a generic non-existence (*jātyabhāva*). In that case, the quality of its blue luster serves as the cause [for this poetic fancy].
Or, for example:
"The entire surface of the earth, shrouded by the weight of the majesty of the Kañcuki mountains, appears as if utterly devoid of mountains, even though thousands of mountains are visible. (422)

Here, in the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the absence of the genus "mountain" (*niśśailam*), the cause (*nimitta*)—namely, the state of being pervaded by the greatness of Śeṣādri—is explicitly stated. In this same manner, examples of poetic fancies concerning the nature of the absence of a genus (*jātyabhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*), where the causes are respectively a genus (*jāti*) or a substance (*dravya*), should also be cited.
Or rather,

behold how this majesty unfolds for Him who is adorned by the mountain that rests upon the head of the serpent-king— He who, though performing every activity in the world, is indeed devoid of any other deity.
In this case, the cause for the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the absence of the genus [of divinity], namely that it is "devoid of other deities," has not been stated.
An example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on the absence of a quality (*guṇābhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"The jewel upon the head of the Lord of Serpents became, as it were, divested of its own blackness, turned tawny by contact with the mass of stainless, unimpeded, and spreading rays of the lotus. (424)
Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the absence of the quality of blueness, the quality of being reddened by contact with the mass of the lotus's luster is employed as the cause.

In this manner, examples of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on qualities (guṇa), absence (abhāva), and essential nature (svarūpa)—whether their causes consist of genus (jāti), action (kriyā), or substance (dravya) that are apprehended, or those whose causes are unapprehended—should be cited.

An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consisting of the absence of action (*kriyābhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows: "Beholding the bull-bannered Lord of Mountains, whose divine form and beauty equal ten million times ten million times ten thousand Cupids, the entire world became, as it were, motionless. In this instance, the cause for the poetic fancy of the absence of action—expressed by the word "motionless" (*niṣpanda*)—is the act of gazing intently (*nirvarṇana*). Regarding the form *niṣpanda*, there is no substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. This is because the rule does not apply since the root is not taught with an initial *s* (*aṣopadeśa*). Thus Vāmana states: "The substitution of *ṣ* in *niṣpanda* is to be considered doubtful, as no such grammatical rule is observed. Here, "rule" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the technical treatise (*śāstra*).
This was explained by us on the occasion of the commentary on the verse beginning with "dattanispandadṛṣṭiḥ" in the *Haṃsasandeśarasāsvādinī*.

In this manner, examples of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the nature of action (*kriyā*) and non-existence (*abhāva*), which have as their causes forms consisting of appropriated genus, quality, and substance, as well as unappropriated causes, should also be cited.
An example of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the nature of the absence of a substance (*dravyābhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"O Lord who dwells upon the peak of the mountain that is the King of Serpents, by illuminating the entire world with your glory, you shine like a sky without the moon; for the sky, being free from stain, does not appear stained. (426)

The construction is: "While the stainless and spotless [moon] shines, the spotted one does not shine. Here, in this poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the absence of a substance—namely, the moon—the genus (*jāti*), "fame," is presented as the cause. It should be understood that if fame is intended to be expressed as a quality (*guṇa*), then this is an instance where the cause is presented as a quality (*upāttaguṇanimitta*).

Or rather, just as that which is eternal, consisting of truth, knowledge, and bliss, and motionless upon the peak of the bull-bannered mountain— the supreme abode and the dwelling place of Ramā— is surely not non-Brahman.

Here, the absence of Brahman is imagined in the Supreme Abode; thus, this is an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) consisting of the nature of the absence of a substance (*dravyābhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*). It is one where the cause is explicitly stated (*upāttanimittā*), because it takes as its basis the action of sporting (*pariramaṇakriyā*) located on the bull-hill (*vṛṣaśaila*). Brahman is a substance because of its oneness. While [the Lord] sports—that is, while He wanders about—without moving or making any movement from the peak of the bull-hill, [the Supreme Abode appears devoid of Him]. The *ātmanepada* ending is used according to the rule: "The root *ram* takes the *parasmaipada* after the prefixes *vi*, *āṅ*, and *pari*."

Or rather, O Lord of the Mountain, the world became as if it were the sky itself, because of the dust rising upward from the earth—dust resembling that which arose from the impact of the feet of countless people gathering for service to Your majesty. 428.

*Maha* means a great festival; according to Amara, “*maha*, *uddhava*, and *utsava* [are synonyms]. This word ends in a vowel (*adanta*). “*Reṇunibhāt*” means by way of the pretext of dust. “*Khagagiri*” is another name for Śeṣādri itself. Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the absence of substance (the sky being empty), the earth, which is spreading out under the guise of dust, is presented as the cause (*nimitta*).
This [verse] can also exist in the form of a *mālā* (garland), as follows:
"Like a wandering emerald gem, charming with hands and feet like the ocean, like the god of love with his limbs quivering, the prince of the Yadu clan sported in the land of Vraja. (429)

In this case, for the sake of pacifying the contradiction between the qualities residing in the Blessed One—such as his being a wanderer—and the emeralds and other objects (which are incompatible with such qualities) through their identity, there is a process of universalization (*sādhāraṇīkaraṇa*) by superimposing those qualities onto the subjects, namely the emeralds and so forth. Nor can a simile (*upamā*) be established here, because it would result in the futility of mentioning qualities such as "wandering" and the rest.

Nor can their commonality (sādhāraṇya) serve as the producer of the simile, because even in its absence, the simile is accomplished through perceived qualities such as blueness; furthermore, it lacks aesthetic charm and was not intended by the poet as the producer of the simile. For here, the similarity of the Blessed One to emeralds and the like, by means of qualities such as "wandering about" (vicaratva), is not the object of the poet’s creative intent. Likewise, the superimposition of "wandering about" and other such qualities onto the emeralds and so forth would be entirely purposeless once the simile has been established.

However, when the non-difference [between the object and the subject] is to be established, there is indeed a utility for superimposing qualities such as "moving about" (vicaratva) onto the subject—such as [the face], which is not actually moving about, nor has hands and feet, nor is it a limb—in order to dispel the contrary notion that "how could non-difference be possible between this [face] and that [moon]? In this very context, if the word *iva* is absent, it is *rūpaka* (metaphor) with a firm superimposition; if the qualifiers belonging to the subject are absent, it is *upamā* (simile); and if there is the absence of even one of either the word *iva* or the qualifiers, it is *śuddharūpaka* (pure metaphor). This is the distinction.

Thus, the poetic conceits (*utprekṣā*) regarding the existence and non-existence of entities such as birth and so forth have been illustrated merely by way of direction. Now, the conceit of cause (*hetūtprekṣā*). Among these, a conceit of cause regarding the existence of a genus (*jāti*) is as follows:

By means of the jeweled palace of the Lord of the Bull Mountain, as it were, the daughter of the Ocean-King was made to forget her dwelling in the lotus, which is thick with the mud of nectar and pollen. (430)

Here, by means of the word "palace" (*saudha*), the genus (*jāti*) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the forgetting of dwelling in the lotus; that very [genus], being thus imagined, serves as the ground for the cause. Thus, this is a case of *bhāvahetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of a cause consisting in a genus) where the ground is the quality (*guṇa*) that has been explicitly mentioned. When either the cause or the effect is the object of poetic fancy, the ground must necessarily be mentioned, not left unmentioned. For instance, if the thing to be established (*sādhya*) is not mentioned, its designation as a means (*sādhana*) does not sustain the logical connection (*anvaya*); likewise, if the means is not mentioned, its designation as the thing to be established also fails to do so.

Because these two are mutually dependent, in the case of the *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of cause), the effect is the motive; if that [effect] is not mentioned, with reference to what would the causality be consistent? In the case of the *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy of effect), the means is the motive; if that [means] is not mentioned, with reference to what would the status of being an effect be established? Thus, since the full development of the connection (*anvaya*) is lacking when either the motive or the motivated is omitted, it must be noted that when there is a rule requiring the mention of both, the mention of the motive is necessarily required.

Thus, in this cited verse, if the cause of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā)—namely, the forgetting of the residence in the lotus—were not mentioned, the fancy regarding the reason (*hetūtprekṣā*) expressed by the word "saudhena" would not be striking. This should likewise be inferred for the fancy regarding the result (*phalotprekṣā*) that will be discussed hereafter. Therefore, it should be understood that the mention or non-mention of the cause applies only to the fancy regarding the essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*), and not to the fancies regarding the reason or the result.
An example of the poetic fancy based on a quality (*guṇahetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"Surely, out of joy that 'this [Lord] is my true disciple because of his spotless beauty,' the thousand-rayed sun enters the Kaustubha gem when the Lord turns his face toward him. (431)

"Acchāccharuciḥ" means possessing a luster that is exceedingly clear due to its extreme transparency, and also because of its non-crooked affection; this is a qualifying epithet containing a reason (*hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇa*). The sense is that when the Lord Śrīnivāsa turns his face toward him out of joy, thinking, "This Kaustubha gem is my true disciple," the thousand-rayed sun surely enters the Kaustubha gem and attains a state of oneness with it regarding its welfare (*yogakṣema*) and other matters. Alternatively, the literal meaning is that [the sun] becomes reflected therein.

The expression "facing him" (*svābhimukhe*) is used because the reflection of the thousand-rayed sun is possible only when the Lord is present and the Kaustubha gem is situated upon his chest. Here, the joy caused by the possession of excellent scriptures is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the Kaustubha’s entry; that very entry is the stated motive (*nimitta*).
An example of *utprekṣā* based on the cause of an action (*kriyāhetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"As if from serving the moonlight of the moon-like face of Hari night after night, the pair of lotus-eyes of Ramā became perpetually blossomed, ignorant of closing. (432)

In this case, the action "because of being sprinkled" (*secanāt*) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the state of being perpetually in bloom; that very state of blooming is the occasion [for the figure]. Or, for example: "O Lord, as if from the intense humiliation caused by the splendor of the moonlight of your face, why indeed does that swarm of lotuses, trembling at the loss of its life-force, bear such worthlessness? (433)

O Master! Your face alone is the moon (himaruci). The word *himaruci* (cold-rayed) is used to indicate that the moon is its own adversary, possessing the very instruments for the destruction of the lotus-rows. By its *dhāmnā*—meaning by its luster, brilliance, and power (according to Amara: *dhāma* refers to house, body, luster, and power)—the lotus-rows became as if devoid of essence (*arasatām*) due to being humiliated. Here, the phrase *sā arasatām* is to be analyzed as *sā arasatām* (she [the row] became sapless); *sā* refers to the lotus-row (*padmapaṅkti*), which is renowned for its extreme loveliness.

"Vilolā" means especially attached to the breaking of life—that is, having formed the resolve to abandon life according to the maxim, "When the honor of the virtuous has faded," and so forth. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), she is "vilolā," meaning restless or fickle due to the breaking of water—its waves; for Amara states, "Lola means moving or thirsty. She bears "arasatām," which is a distaste for all objects of the senses. The sense is that for those who are pained by the humiliation of others and have set their sights on abandoning life, there arises a total lack of interest in everything.

The word *anyatra* is a compound meaning "elsewhere than," specifically "other than being essence" (*sārasatām*), though its literal sense is "other than being a lotus" (*sarojatām*). Here, the action consisting of contempt is conceived as the cause for bringing about the state of being essence-less; that very [contempt] is the motive there. This is an instance [of the figure] mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
An example of *utprekṣā* based on a material cause (*dravyahetu*) is as follows:

“Though he is powerful, though he has many feet, and though he is rich with great mountains, he is unable to move even a single step while dwelling upon the All-Sustainer (the Earth), for she truly bears him. (434) [Commentary: “Powerful” means possessing strength; in the alternative sense, it means possessing bulk, for Amara states: “*Bala* [is used] in the senses of bulk, power, and army. Even if strength exists, how can movement occur in the absence of a means? To this, he says: “Though he has many feet,” meaning many legs; in the alternative sense, many peripheral mountains.

Therefore, his "great departure" (*mahāgata*) is praiseworthy; here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). He is also "endowed with that" (*tenāḍhyaḥ*). Alternatively, it refers to one who possesses "great mountains" (*mahānto 'gās taravo yasmin*), and he is endowed with the state of being such, which is "great-mountain-ness" (*mahāgatā*). By this, he is also "endowed. Furthermore, the term "serpent-mountain" (*ahibhūbhṛt*) suggests both Śeṣa and the mountain [Śeṣādri]. Just as Viśvambhara (the Sustainer of the Universe), residing within himself, does not desire—even for a step—to move, so too [the mountain] cannot move even a foot. Here, Viśvambhara, residing within himself, is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the substance (*dravya*) that serves as the cause for the immobility of the serpent-mountain. That very immobility is the stated motive (*nimitta*).
Or, for example:
"The thick mass of darkness issues forth from Śauri, as if from another moon, through his own majesty which is skilled in creating the obstruction of the expansion of pure vision. (435)

Stainless and far removed from the possibility of delusion, deception, and the like—on one hand, "vision" (dṛṣṭi) refers to knowledge (*jñāna*), and on the other, according to Amara, "vision" (*dṛk*) means the eye or the act of seeing; she is one whose own majesty and greatness consist in being skillful in obstructing the diffusion of that [vision]. The "mass of darkness" (*tamastati*) is a succession of ignorance (*ajñāna*), as well as a collection of physical gloom (*dhvānta*). Here, the moon is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the substance acting as the cause for the dissolution of the mass of darkness; the dissolution of the mass of darkness itself is the occasion [for this poetic conceit].
This is an instance of *śleṣottambhitā* (poetic fancy supported by paronomasia). By this, those who claim that it is impossible for a substance (*dravya*) to be fancied as a cause are refuted.

Just as when you, O Murāri, dwell upon the mountain of silver (kaladhautagiri)—which is rich with beautiful cardamom plants (suśrīka-elā) [and in the other sense, which is opulent (ṛddha) and beautiful (suśrī), namely Kailāsa]—the northern quarter was adorned by another Śrīdāman (the Giver of Fortune). O Murāri! [The mountain is] "rich with beautiful cardamom plants" (suśrīka-elābhiḥ samṛddham); in the other sense, it is "opulent" (ṛddham) and "beautiful" (suśrī), that is, Kailāsa. That mountain of silver (kaladhautagiri)—the Golden Mountain, which we have stated more than once is merely another name for Śeṣādri—or in the alternative case, the Silver Mountain. Amara states: "Kaladhauta refers to both silver and gold."

By you, Śrīda (the bestower of fortune), dwelling [there], that northern direction—the most excellent quarter characterized by the thirst for the objects of human endeavor (puruṣārtha)—has been made sufficient, that is, fully satisfied, for those who hope [for it]; the word "of those hoping" (āśāsānānām) is to be supplied. In the alternative sense, the northern direction (uttarāśā) has been adorned and embellished; since the term *alaṃ* is designated as a *gati* when meaning "ornamentation," the compound is formed according to the rule *kugati*. The sense is that this was done because he is the sovereign of that region.

Here, the fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) that wealth (*dravya*) is the cause for the ornamentation of the northern quarter by "Śrīda" (the Giver of Fortune) is supported by *śleṣa* (punning). According to the opinion of the ancients, if the word "another" (*apara*) were not used here, it would be merely *śleṣa*, because there is similarity only at the level of the words. In the view of the moderns, however, since there is similarity of meaning and "Śrīda" is an established fact, it is simply a simile (*upamā*). But when that word ["another"] is employed, the subject at hand—the Blessed Lord—is identified as "another Śrīda"; since his status as such is understood through the word "as if" (*iva*), it is indeed a fancy (*utprekṣā*).

However, when the word *iva* is not employed, since the identification (*adhyavasāya*) is already established, it is Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). When neither *iva* nor any other [synonymous] word is employed, it is Metaphor (*rūpaka*); such distinctions should be inferred as they occur.
These two examples are according to the view of Vidyānātha; for he [states]:
"The expansion of the wings of King Pratāparudra has been uprooted from its very foundation, as if by another wielder of the thunderbolt."

Thus, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the cause as a substance (*dravyahetūtprekṣā*) has been illustrated. Although this verse ought to be an illustration of the poetic fancy regarding the very nature of a substance (*dravyasvarūpotprekṣā*), it is beyond dispute that here, upon the removal of the word *iva*, there exists only a metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting of the identity between Pratāparudra and the "other thunderbolt" (*aparavajra*). This being the case, when the word *iva* is added therein, the word *iva* would convey nothing other than the poetic fancy regarding the very nature of the substance—the form of the "other thunderbolt"—with respect to Pratāparudra.

Since it is observed as a rule that where a word such as *iva* is absent, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the nature of one object in relation to another occurs only when that same word *iva* is present for that very object, [one might object]. Nevertheless, if here—in the phrase "by Pratāparudradeva, who is like the other Indra" (*aparavajriṇeva*)—there is a desire to express the grammatical connection (*anvaya*), and if one intends to establish that the uprooting of the kings' wings (which has Pratāparudra as its cause) is the object of a probability regarding its having the other Indra as its cause, then this may somehow be considered an example even of the poetic fancy of a causal substance (*dravyahetūtprekṣā*). This is the intention inferred from the author's perspective.

The authors of the *Citramīmāṃsā* and the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, cite the very same verse—which is far removed from even a scent of such poetic fancy regarding the nature of a substance—as an example of fancy regarding the cause of a substance (*dravyahetūtprekṣā*). In accordance with that, we have already demonstrated an unambiguous example earlier in the verse beginning "Though powerful and though many-footed. Enough of this prolixity.

Now, regarding those [poetic figures] characterized by the conceit of non-existence (*abhāvābhimānavatī*), there is the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) of the cause consisting in the non-existence of a genus (*jātyabhāvahetu-utprekṣā*), as in:

"Surely, because the sun is absent from the surface of the sky covered by its own radiance, the Lord of the Serpent-Mountain bears upon his chest the Kaustubha gem, which possesses the dense luster of a multitude of moonbeams. (437)

Here, the absence of the sun’s birth is poetically imagined (utprekṣyate) as the cause for his wearing the Kaustubha gem; thus, this is a poetic fancy (hetūtprekṣā) based on the absence of a genus (jātyabhāva) caused by an action already mentioned (upāttakriyānimitta).
Or, for instance:

When the celestial river was repeatedly swallowed by the vast masses of dust raised during Śauri’s victorious expeditions, it is certain that the winds attained the state of Marut (wind) in their own domain due to the absence of water. 438.

In its own sense (*svapada*), its own location (*svasthāna*), and as its own expressive word (*svavācakapada*), there is the state of being *marut*—that is, the state of being a desert (*marubhūmi*) and the state of being the word *marut*. In the first case, the doubling of the letter *t* occurs according to the rule *anaci ca*. Amara states: "The two words *marut* denote the wind and the god [Indra]; *marut* and *dhanvan* are synonyms. Here, the absence of the universal property (*jāti*) of being water is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the attainment of the state of being *marut*. This figure is enlivened by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the cause being the absence of qualities (*guṇābhāvahetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:
"While I dwell in bliss together with Ramā, what else need I desire from Hari? Because of this state of undisturbed composure, the serpent-mountain [Śeṣa] is for the most part motionless. (439)

The word "prāyeṇa" (mostly/usually) here functions as a suggestor of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). In this instance, the state of being "unperturbed" (*anākulabhāva*)—which is a quality (*guṇa*)—is fancied as the cause for immobility. This is a fancy based on the absence of a quality as the cause for the absence of the action of moving. In the same way, fancies based on genus (*jāti*) and other such factors should also be inferred.
An example of *utprekṣā* based on the cause being the absence of action (*kriyābhāva-hetu*) is as follows:

"O beloved of the Lord of Mountains, though your middle part (waist) heated its head downwards in order to abandon its middleness, it surely attained leanness because that [middleness] could not be obtained. (440)

In order for your middle [syllable] to abandon its middleness—that is, its state of being devoid of excellence or deficiency and its attachment to a particular side—it would have to undergo the heat of penance with its head downward; even by performing such "head-downward" austerity (*adhaśśirastapaḥ*), it remains in a state of contrariety (*vilomatva*). Because that [middleness] is not attained—that is, because the abandonment of middleness is not achieved—it is said "because that is not obtained," since even when the sequence of letters is reversed, it still remains as "middle. Thus, it attained thinness (*kraśimāna*).

Here, the absence of the action of gaining is poetically imagined (utprekṣyate) as the cause for the attainment of emaciation; thus, this is a *kriyābhāvahetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of the absence of an action as a cause) based on an action, reinforced by *śleṣātiśayokti* (hyperbole through punning). In this same manner, poetic fancies of the absence of an action based on genus (*jāti*) and other factors should also be inferred. An example of a *dravyābhāvahetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of the absence of a substance as a cause) is as follows: "While the body of the Lord of the Serpent Mountain was darkened even in its right half by the rays of Hari’s splendor, Kālī became exceedingly fair, as if due to the absence of Śarva. (441)

Kālī is naturally blue in color; Pārvatī, who occupies half the body of Hara, takes the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule "jānapada" and so forth. She is "residing on the serpent-mountain" (ahigirigā), meaning she has gone to Śeṣādri for the sake of serving the Blessed One—this is the sense. She is dark with the luster of Hari (Viṣṇu); the sense is that she is dark-blue. Even in her own right-hand portion of the body—that is, even in the limb constituting the right half of her husband’s form—she is darkened (*mecakite*), because Pārvatī occupies the right half of the body of Ardhanārīśvara. Thus, when [the mountain] is made dark-blue.

The word "api" (even/also) conjoins the blackness of her own body. The sense is that as the blackness settled without distinction upon both the right and left halves of the body—just as it would upon the absence of Śarva or the absence of her own beloved—the Goddess, suspecting the absence of her husband because she perceived the presence of another half of his body within her own, fell into despondency; thus she became exceedingly *gaurī* (pale).

The sense is: otherwise, how could she, who is naturally dark-complexioned (*kālavarṇā*), possess a fair complexion (*gauravarṇatā*)? This contradiction between the dark and fair complexions of the same Pārvatī must be resolved by means of different births. Here, the absence of the substance "ashes" (*śarvarūpadravyābhāva*) is imagined as the cause for Kālī’s fairness, which is preceded by her despondency; thus, this is a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of a cause) based on a quality (*guṇanimittā*).

In the example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding a substance, namely, “another Ardhanārīśvara as if produced from the two halves of another,” it is stated in the *Citramīmāṃsā*: “Since, in reality, Ardhanārīśvara is a single entity, this is a poetic fancy regarding a substance. Therefore, the status of Ardhanārīśvara as a substance remains unchallenged.

"Just as the Creator, due to the absence of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) on earth, produced the Lord of Mountains (the Malaya range) upon the ground—which bears the burden of granting all desires—as a substitute wish-fulfilling gem. Here, the absence of the wish-fulfilling gem on the earth is imagined as the cause for the creation of the mountain of wish-fulfilling gems. This is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the non-existence of a substance (*dravyābhāvahetūtprekṣā*) with respect to the occasion for an action. We have already stated that "Cintāmaṇigiri" is merely another name for Śeṣādri; this should not be forgotten. Thus ends the section on poetic fancy based on cause (*hetūtprekṣā*), and so forth.
Now, regarding *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a result): therein, an example of *jātiphalotprekṣā* (fancy based on a genus as the result) is as follows:
"When the Enemy of Mura desires to sport with Ramā upon the bull-crested mountain [Kailāsa], the clouds, swelling with vigor, surely expand themselves to serve as a clothed pavilion. (443)

Here, the nature (jāti) delimited by the state of being a cloth-pavilion is poetically imagined as the fruit of the expansion of the clouds; thus, this is an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) where the fruit is a genus (jāti) caused by an action (*kriyā*). Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of the act of "producing" (*saṃpādana*), a pure genus cannot be a fruit and therefore the action itself must be the fruit; for since "producing" functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*), it is precisely through that medium that the genus and so forth can appropriately function as the fruit. Otherwise, the dative case used to express "fruit-ness" would be untenable.

For this very reason, such usages as “Viśvāmitra performed most severe penance for fame, for those desiring victory, for progeny, for householders, and for the status of a Brāhmaṇa” become intelligible. In this manner, instances of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on genus (*jāti*) and other factors, where the genus itself is the fruit [of the action], should also be cited.
An example of *utprekṣā* based on quality and result (*guṇaphalotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"The Vedāntas have proclaimed Hari to be named 'One who resembles me' because he possesses the luster of a dark cloud; does the moon, therefore, bear a spot upon its own body for the sake of such a deep blackness? (444)

In this context, the words *hari* and *vidhu* denote both the Lord and the moon. The phrase “possessing the luster of a dark cloud” (*asitaghanaruciraḥ*) means “charming like a blue rain-cloud. This was proclaimed and extolled by the Upaniṣads through such passages as “standing in the midst of a blue water-cloud,” and “from the dark I attain the variegated, and from the variegated the dark. Here, the quality of blueness (*nīlimā*) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the fruit, while the bearing of the spot (*kalaṅka*) is the cause; thus, this is a case of “poetic imagination of a quality as a fruit caused by an action. In the same way, poetic imaginations of qualities as fruits caused by genus (*jāti*) and other factors should also be inferred.

Just as those who practice the three-strided stride of Viṣṇu, the clouds— possessing supreme lightning and unrestrained— manifest one above another over the mountain of the serpents at the onset of the rainy season.

"Abhyasyanta iva" means "as if practicing. The suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) is used here according to the rule "lakṣaṇahetvoḥ. In examples such as "arjayan vasati" (dwelling while earning), the cause is treated as the result; here, too, the cause is the result. "Ahigirim uparyupari" means "in the vicinity of Mount Ahiga," that is, in the regions surrounding the mountain. The reduplication occurs according to the rule "uparyadhyadhasassāmīpye," and the accusative case is used in connection with these words according to the rule "dhiguparyādiṣu triṣu. Here, the action expressed by "abhyasyanta" is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being the result.

"Because the act of yawning is the cause [of the comparison], this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on an action as the cause, resulting in an action as the fruit. Those based on genus (*jāti*) and other such factors are also to be understood in this same manner."
An example of the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on a substance and its fruit (*dravyaphalotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"Does the Slayer of Madhu (Viṣṇu), bearing bees clinging to his navel-lotus because of the swarms of bees gathering upon his fragrant garland of *lavanga* flowers, perhaps prepare himself for the sake of the infinite Creator (Brahmā)? (446)

"From the swarm of bees clustering upon his forest garland"—that is, clinging to or attached to the lotus of his navel; by this, the transfer of their redness to him is illuminated. "Madhudalanaḥ" means the slayer of Madhu. "To the Creator Ananta"—meaning, in order to create many four-faced Brahmās. Here, the Creator (dhātṛ) is poetically imagined as the fruit (*phala*) of the substance (*dravya*). The act of holding the bees is the cause (*nimitta*); thus, this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) where the fruit is a substance caused by an action.
In this same manner, poetic fancies where the fruit is a substance caused by genus (*jāti*) and so forth should also be illustrated.

Now, there are poetic conceits (*phalotprekṣā*) involving the misconception of non-existence (*abhāvābhimāna*). Among these, an example of a conceit regarding the fruit of the non-existence of a genus (*jātyabhāvaphalotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"Having observed that the twin *arjuna* trees attained liberation through contact with the lotus-feet of Hari, I believe that even other trees on the mountain of the Serpent (Śeṣa) dwell there for the sake of ceasing to be mere trees. (447)

Here, the absence of the genus "tree-ness" (*jātyabhāva*) is imagined as the fruit for the purpose of "not growing on the earth. Since the act of perceiving liberation is the cause, this is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) wherein the fruit—the absence of the genus—is caused by an action. In this manner, fancies based on genus (*jāti*) and other categories should also be inferred. "For the sake of not growing on the earth" means for the sake of not being a tree, and for the sake of the absence of birth upon the earth; that is to say, for the sake of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
The contemplation of the fruit arising from the state of being a subordinate quality is as follows:

"Since sharpness is unbecoming here for the Friend of the World, the Kaustubha gem has become the Sun; surely, therefore, the stream of Hari’s compassion, cool as a cascade, resorts to his heart to remove that sharpness. (448)

Here, the state of being a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) is poetically imagined as the fruit for the sake of "lack of sharpness" (*ataikṣṇyāya*). The action of taking refuge in the heart of Hari, which is cooled by a torrent of compassion, is the cause. In this same way, those [poetic figures] based on genus (*jāti*) and other such factors are also to be understood.

An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of the non-existence of an action as a result is as follows: “As if unable to behold the presence of their own most beloved [husband] within the hearts of all [women], the Goddess Lakṣmī veils their eyes with her own splendors, which resemble flashes of lightning. (449) The word “of all” (*sarveṣām*) here connects with the word “eyes” (*dṛśaḥ*). Here, the non-existence of the action of looking is fancied as the result, while the action of veiling serves as the cause. In this same manner, [fancies] based on genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and substance (*dravya*) as causes should also be discerned.
An example of the poetic fancy of the non-existence of a substance as a result is as follows:

I suspect that the playful fame of the one whose crest is the serpent-mountain spreads through the quarters of the world in order to destroy the snow-capped mountains, the celestial river, the jar-born ocean, the mountain-dweller Śiva, and the moon. 450.

In this instance, the absence of substances such as the snowy mountain peak is imagined as the result, for the purpose of the act of distinguishing wealth. In the same way, other cases should also be inferred.

Here, the varieties such as *jāti* (genus) and so forth have been illustrated merely out of deference to the ancients; in reality, however, these possess no distinctiveness in their aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), and thus they are not worthy of being illustrated at all. It should be understood that the distinctiveness of aesthetic charm belongs only to the three types consisting of essence (*svarūpa*), cause (*hetu*), and result (*phala*).
I think that poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is manifested by words such as *evaṃ*, *manye*, *śaṅke*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, and *nūnam*; the word *iva* is also of that same nature.

Thus, the varieties of expressed *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) consisting of words expressing the aforementioned modes have been demonstrated. When those [expressive words] are not employed, there occurs implied *utprekṣā*.

Among these, an *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on a thing (*vastu*) is as follows: "O Mother, your pair of breasts, possessing desirable pearls (*sara*), attaining a state of being devoid of strings (*sarahitatā*), and reaching a state of extreme upward-turning, became a pair of lotuses. (5.1) The term *sarojayugī* means "possessing a pair of lotuses. *Īpsitasarā* means "by whom desirable pearls (*sara*) [were possessed]. In the alternative sense, it means "by whom a desirable lake (*sara*) was possessed. This word ends in a long vowel (*sānta*). "Attaining a state of being devoid of strings (*sarahitatām*)"—meaning, in one case, "devoid of pearl-strings (*hāra*)," and in the other, "devoid of the letter *sa*" (*savarṇa*). The suffix *śatṛ* is used here according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*.

In this context, "cause" (hetu) means the fruit (phala); elsewhere, it means the sense of cause. For this very reason, *alaṃ* [is used]. *Atāntā* means "unfaded" (*amlānā*). It refers to *unmukhatām*, meaning "eagerness," or in the alternative case, the compound *atāntonmukhatām*. *Atāntaḥ* means the final portion [of the word] is devoid of the letter *ta*; *ut* means the letter *u*. This is because when the letter *ta* is removed from *ud*, only *u* remains.

That state of being "uninterrupted eagerness" (atāntonmukhatā)—belonging to that [autumn] which has such eagerness as its beginning or opening—[is expressed here]; in this case, the neuter gender is used for the general abstract quality (as in the phrase *śaradaḥ kṛtārthatā*), followed by the suffix *tal*. Having attained that, your pair of breasts (*urojayugī*) came into existence; the meaning is that they were born as such. In the alternative sense, according to the aforementioned method, the word *sarojayugī* (pair of lotuses) was transformed into the word *urojayugī* (pair of breasts). Here, since the expressive word for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) identifying the pair of breasts with the pair of lotuses is not explicitly stated, this is an implied (*pratīyamānā*) fancy.
In that very context, an illustration of the poetic fancy of cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:

"Because of its constant association with the mass of radiance spreading from the blue-lotus-like eyes, the dark splendor of Brahmā himself shines forth visibly upon the mountain peak of the eye and the ear. (452)

Here, since the word expressive of the "poetic fancy regarding the cause" (*hetūtprekṣā*)—namely, "because of familiarity"—is not employed, this [fancy] is also "suggested," as it is to be determined through the power of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*).
An illustration of the poetic figure *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result) is as follows:
"O Mother, surely your pair of ears attains its true significance by virtue of contact with the naturally radiant jeweled earrings. (453)

Indeed, O Mother, your pair of ears—the agent—has, through the contact—that is, the bestowal—of those innate and radiant jeweled earrings (in the alternative sense, through the touching of them), rendered its own state as "ears" and its designation by the word *karṇa* meaningful; for according to the *Ratnamālā*, "the word *karṇa* applies to both the organ of hearing and the son of Rādheya. The compound *sahajenojjvalam* means "brilliant by birth," or in the other sense, "shining intensely by its very nature. This is due to the contact—or, in the alternative sense, the grasping—of that [jewelry].

Regarding the word *sahaja*, the *Medinīkośa* states: "The term *sahaja* refers to that which is innate (*nisarga*) or produced simultaneously (*sahottha*), like [the natural color of] gold; it is masculine when meaning 'wind' or 'man,' and neuter when meaning 'touch. The passage praises the excellence of his generosity by noting that he attained a state of joy (*pratītatām hṛṣṭatām eti*) even after cutting off his own earrings—which were born together with his body—and giving them to the king of the gods who had assumed the guise of a brahmin; furthermore, he did not feel remorse after giving them, but remained truly joyful. This is a eulogy of the extraordinary nature of his magnanimity.

Alternatively, regarding the act of giving (*dāne*), the suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamyāḥ*) because it belongs to the *ādyādi* group; the meaning is "regarding the state of being well-known" or "regarding the state of being treated with respect.
One who bestows more than what is desired takes away the joy of the supplicant;
yet you follow [the petitioner] and speak kindly to him—therefore, your ear is superior.

The sense is: "because of this statement. In the present context, "attained renown" (pratītatām) means being adorned by the touch of the aforementioned jeweled earrings. As the *Medinīratnamālā* states: "The word *pratīta* is used in three senses: with respect, known, and joyful; it denotes what is famous, joyful, well-known, and adorned. It "attains" (*eti*) [this renown]. Therefore, the sense is that the name "Karṇa" is truly etymological (significant).

In the *Mahābhārata*, the name Karṇa is etymologically derived from the very act of cutting off the natural armor and earrings for the sake of giving them away; thus, it is explained that he is called Karṇa because his [earrings] were cut (*kṛntati*). Here, in this poetic fancy (*phalotprekṣā*) intended to make the state of being "Karṇa" meaningful, the expressive word (*vācaka*) is not explicitly mentioned. Likewise, in the verses previously cited, when the expressive word is omitted, all those [figures] become merely suggested (*pratīyamāna*); therefore, their specific varieties are not detailed here.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding the essential nature of a thing (*dharmasvarūpotprekṣā*) is as follows:

"O Moon on the peak of the king of serpents, I believe that through your grace, which bestows the highest welfare even upon a most sinful creature quite unexpectedly, [your] delusion is boundless. (454)

The meaning is that this applies even to a most wicked creature, such as a vulture and the like. Here, in the second half-verse, the bestowal of sudden and unsurpassed excellence is employed to establish the quality of delusion (moha) imagined in the first half-verse.

The following point should be noted here: even when several possible subjects (*viṣayin*) for a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) are being considered, the designation [of that fancy] is made according to the subject in which the fancy appears as the primary thing to be predicated (*vidheya*), because of its predominance. Therefore, in the verse "acchāccharuciḥ," although the joy residing in the sun (*sahasrāṃśu*) is the object of the fancy, it is not correct to designate it by that fancy; for that [joy] is a subordinate element and thus merely restated (*anuvādya*). Rather, it must be designated by the fancy regarding the meaning of the ablative case (the "as if" sense), since that alone is what is to be predicated, as it is made known by the word *nūnam*.

Likewise, in the verse "tathā ‘traivikramamiva vikramam’," the designation [of this as *utprekṣā*] based on the imaginative conceit (*utprekṣā*) of practicing the three-striding gait of Viṣṇu is not appropriate; rather, it is by way of the imaginative conceit of the fruit for the enemy. Similarly, in verses such as "hṛdayāspadayā" and "nātha tava nābhisarasi," the designation by way of the imaginative conceit of the fruit is not tenable.

Nor is there [such a figure] in the verse "karapadmena," either through a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of identity with the orb of the moon, which is manifested by that [first fancy], or through a poetic fancy of identity with the forearm being the object of the action of knitting—preceded by the hollowing out of the middle [of the hand] caused by hatred, with the lotus-hand as the agent; for the very same reason stated previously. In this way, in all cases, designation occurs solely by means of the primary poetic fancy, according to the maxim: "Designations are made by the principal."

In this context, *dharma* (the common property) is also twofold: that which is common by its very nature, and that which, though uncommon, has been made common through the means of making it so. And that means may, in some cases, be metaphor (*rūpaka*), in some cases paronomasia (*śleṣa*), in some cases concealment (*apahnuti*), in some cases the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), in some cases the relation of object and counterpart as combined with that [metaphor], in some cases figurative attribution (*upacāra*), and in some cases the poetic intensification (*atiśaya*) consisting of the identification of two things as non-different.

In this regard, a common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) exists by its very nature in the previously cited verse, “*anīlaguṇenākrānte*,” where the brilliance of both the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*)—namely, the golden garment and the yellow quality—is inherent. However, in the previously cited verse, “*bhrūyugaladhanurlastakasaṃhitanāsākarīrasaṃlagnam*,” the attribute occurring in the first half-verse is rendered common to both the object and the subject through the medium of a metaphor (*rūpaka*).
An example of [the ambiguity] being rendered common through *śleṣa* (punning):
"O Lord of the Mahendra Mountain, since you refresh the entire world with the playful touch of fragrant breezes, we know that because you are Mādhava, you are indeed Vasanta (Spring). (455)

"Surabheḥ kāmadhenoḥ svairasparśanam" means the spontaneous touching or the voluntary granting [of boons] by the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu); the sense is that it is like a gift equal to the gift of a wish-granting cow. In another sense, "surabhi" means that which gratifies the sense of smell, i.e., fragrance. As it is said: "The word *surabhi* is recorded as denoting the Campaka flower, gold, nutmeg, and spring; it is also used for that which is fragrant and for that which is charming, functioning as an adjective."

Thus says the *Viśvakośa*. Regarding *svaira*, Amara states: "The word *svaira* means 'slow' (*manda*) or 'self-willed' (*svacchanda*). The term *sparśana* refers to the Malaya breeze; as the *Medinīkośa* states: "In the masculine, *sparśana* denotes the wind (*māruta*); in the neuter, it denotes a gift (*dāna*) or touch (*sparśa*). By its *līlā*—that is, by its playful movement or diffusion—the entire world is nourished; the meaning is identical in both cases. Since you are *Mādhava*—both Śrīnivāsa [the Lord] known as Mādhava and the season of spring—we recognize you as the Spring (*vasanta*).

This [quality] is indeed *upātta* (expressed) and not *anupātta* (unexpressed), because it is not well-known [otherwise]. However, that which is other than *śleṣa* (punning) may also be *anupātta*, as in the case of "moving like an emerald" (*marakatamaṇiriva vicaran*), where qualities such as blueness are unexpressed. Nor should it be argued that here the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*) in the form of "moving-ness" (*vicaratva*) is indeed expressed, for the superimposition (*āropa*) upon the object of comparison (*viṣayin*) is intended precisely for the sake of establishing commonality. Even if commonality were established through such a superimposition, it would lack the power to evoke *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) due to its lack of aesthetic beauty (*asundaratva*). We have already stated that the act of making [the attributes] common serves the purpose of removing obstacles.

Just as the foot of Mukunda— dark blue like a dense cloud, with excellent jasmine-white nails, and containing lotuses, conchs, tortoises, and sea-monsters— I consider you to be the great treasure-store Mahāpadma.

O Ghananīla! O you who are dark as a cloud (in one sense); in the other sense, "Ghana" refers to a particular treasure (*nidhi*) that is "blue" (*nīla*), and this is his address. O Mukunda! O bestower of liberation (the word is grammatically correct by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class); in the other sense, O treasury of the Mukunda-treasure! Your foot—meaning your foot which possesses the lotus, conch, tortoise, and crocodile [marks], that is to say, it is endowed with lines in the form of a lotus and so forth; in the other sense, it means possessing the specific treasures named Padma and the rest.

I consider you to be composed of treasures—specifically the treasures called Mahāpadma and Padma—as stated in the phrase "Mahāpadma and Padma. [This is because] your nails are like excellent *kunda* flowers (or, in the alternative sense, you possess the two excellent *kundas*, which are specific types of treasures); and because of that, you possess great lotus-gloriousness (or, in the alternative sense, you possess the great treasure Mahāpadma). Thus, I regard you as being made of such treasures.

Here, by means of the *śleṣa* (punning) of the lotuses and other [treasures]—which serve as qualifiers of the various treasures that constitute the object of the imagination (*utprekṣyamāṇa*) and qualify the Lord’s attributes such as having His feet resting upon lotuses and other treasures—the commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) of those respective attributes is achieved through the establishment of identity (*tādātmya*).
Or, for example:

"Here shines the difficult-to-access valley of Sarasvatī, enriched by the lineage of Bhṛgu; and this Vṛṣādri mountain, upon which the Lord of Dhātrī (Brahmā) rests, blazes as if composed of the three forms [of the gods]. (457)

On this mountain, the daughter of Bhṛgu (Bhārgavī), connected with the precipice—Amara states, "prapāta means the slope or cliff" (bhṛgu)—shines forth as prosperity (samṛddhiḥ). In the alternative sense, she is "Samṛddhi," meaning one whose wealth (ṛddhi) is continuous; that is, she possesses great majesty. Thus, Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, shines. The foothill region is the *upatyakā*. She is called *Sarasvatī* because she possesses lakes (*sarāṃsi*) upon her; the suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of abundance. Because the rule "tasau matvarthe" prescribes the designation *bha*, the word does not undergo the phonetic changes of *rutva* and *utva* characteristic of a *pada*. In the alternative sense, the meaning is *Bhāratī* (the goddess of speech).

She is difficult to traverse and inaccessible; in the alternative sense, she shines as Gaurī. He lies—that is, stays—upon the *dhātrī*, meaning the earth, in such a way that he remains unswerving (*acyuta*); the suffix *kta* is used here in the active sense of the root *śī*. In the alternative sense, *acyuta-dhātrī-īśaḥ* refers to the Lord Acyuta (Viṣṇu), the Creator Dhātṛ (Brahmā), and the Ruler Īśa (Śiva). This is the accusative plural form. It has been obtained from this place; the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense of the root *i*. Alternatively, *itaḥ* means "on this mountain," where the suffix *tasi* is used for all case endings after the locative.

*acyutadhātrīśaḥ* is the nominative plural; the meaning has already been stated. The connection [of the word] is with *bhānti* (they shine), by changing the verbal form. In the case of *dhātrīśayita*, when *dhātrīśa* and *ita* stand together, after the application of the rules for *rutva* and *yatva*, the elision of the *yakāra* does not occur here because the elision of *yakāra*—by the rule *lopaśśākalyasya*—is optional. For this very reason, this Vṛṣādri shines as if consisting of the three forms (*trimūrtimaya*), as if consisting of Hari, Viriñci, and Hara.
