Here, through the *śleṣa* (pun) of the attributes—such as "being the locus of prosperity, Bhārgava, and so forth"—belonging to the object of comparison (*viṣaya*), namely Vṛṣādri, which are themselves qualified by the terms "Bhārgava" and so on, with the attributes—such as "possessing prosperity related to Bhṛgu"—belonging to the subject (*utprekṣyamāṇa*) consisting of the three forms (*trimūrti*), the attainment of commonality (*sādhāraṇatā*) among those attributes is achieved by way of establishing their identity (*tādātmya*).
Or rather:

"O Acyuta, just as a great sapphire—possessing the luster of pure flowers and gold and set in lapis lazuli—is certainly recognized as being composed of jewels, I perceive that you are likewise established in the state of a ruby."

It nourishes what is auspicious, thus it is called *śubhapuṭ*; in that [place] so described—[a place] where those who are free from passion (*arāga*) and detached (*virata*) possess delight (*rucijuṣi*) and partake in joy (*prītibhāji*). In the alternative sense, it is a place possessing the luster of auspicious *puṣyarāga* gems (specific jewels), meaning it possesses a superior splendor. It is *sumahānīla*, exceedingly dark-blue; in the alternative sense, it refers to a specific kind of gem. It is frequented (*kalite*) and served by those for whom existence (*bhava*)—the cycle of saṃsāra—is far removed (*vidūra*), namely those such as the eternally liberated ones (*nityamukta*) who have not even touched the scent of saṃsāra.

In one sense, I perceive that You, O Acyuta, possess the nature of a jewel—meaning You are composed of gems—insofar as Your two feet have a luster like that of a ruby (*padmarāga*), being set in a base of *vaidūrya* stones (lapis lazuli) from distant lands; in the other sense, You possess the nature of a jewel because You are the very abode (*pada*) of rubies. Thus, I conceive of You, who are of such a form, as being made of precious gems.

Here, through the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) of the qualities—such as being a nourisher of virtue—which qualify the Blessed One’s teachings, with the corresponding qualities—such as possessing the luster of the auspicious Puṣya-rāga gem—that qualify the imagined jewel-like nature of those very teachings, an identity is established between them.

In the first of the two previous examples, in the verse beginning with "asatpadma," there is a commonality [of the subject] through *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (unbroken punning); in the second, the verse beginning with "iha bhārgavī," there is both commonality through *sabhaṅga-abhaṅga-śleṣa* (mixed punning) and a mixture with the *rūpaka* (metaphor) to be described in the *Ratnāvalī*. However, in this verse beginning with "śubhapuṣyarāga," the distinction is that there is merely a commonality established through both types of *śleṣa*.
Just as Mount Hemakūṭa, being under his own control, is generally honored by Mahendra, are these remaining mountains— such as this Prasravaṇa which he frequents— not his servants?

In this context, the words *hemakūṭa*, *mahendra*, and *prasravaṇa* denote specific mountains; their other meaning, however, is quite clear. According to Amara, *utsaḥ* means *prasravaṇam* (a spring). Thus, the meaning is "these mountains. Here, regarding the objects—the Hemakūṭa and other mountains—there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) identifying them with Śeṣādri and Dāsa. The attribute of the object of fancy (*viṣayin*), characterized by dependence and so forth, is made common to the objects (*viṣaya*) through the device of *śleṣa* (punning), by effecting an identity between the objects themselves and the things dependent upon them—namely, the golden peaks, Vṛtrāri (Indra), and the waterfalls.
Concealment leading to universalization is as follows:
"O Beloved of the Jewel of Śrīparvata, I believe that your compassion, which resides in your heart and rises from your face with a smile-like luster, surveys its entire object upon the earth. (460)

The sense is this: just as a great queen residing in the inner apartments, rising out from within her lofty palace out of a desire for diversion, beholds her entire domain, so too does the compassion dwelling in your heart, having ascended to your lofty face, seem to survey all people within its range.

Here, in the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) of the observation of one's own objects being attributed to compassion, an emergence from the internal region to the exterior is required; however, since that—consisting of a connection with the external region—is impossible for compassion, which exists merely as the radiance of a smile, the [internal] location of compassion is transferred to the radiance of the smile by means of the concealment (apahnava) of the smile’s radiance.

Or rather, O Lord, as if Your two eyes, having attained diversity all around through the guise of the jewels in Your crown and other ornaments, were looking about in every direction for the sake of illuminating the universe, You are called "the one with eyes on all sides" (viśvataścakṣus). || 461 ||

O Lord! O Sovereign of all! Your two eyes are the agents [of this act]. The construction is: "He, the Blessed One, the Lord of all, who has eyes on every side and faces on every side," is as if looking in order to manifest Himself. Here, the meaning of the Śruti, "Having eyes on every side and indeed faces on every side," should be kept in mind.

In this context, when there is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) regarding the simultaneous perception of all directions by the two eyes, their functioning in all directions is required as the basis for that conceit; however, since such functioning belongs to the gems situated in the crown and so forth, and not to the eyes themselves, the presence [of the function] in the eyes is extended [to them] through the concealment (apahnuti) of the gems.
O Lord, as the form of Your deeds enters within my ears, it seems to reveal to me a certain perfected ointment that clarifies my pure inner vision.

O Lord! Some ineffable *siddhāñjana* (magical ointment) in the form of Your life-story, having entered through the cavity between our ears, reveals—that is, illuminates—the internal vision and knowledge within us, making it pure, faultless, virtuous, and capable of directly perceiving all things. Here, in this poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) regarding the magical ointment that purifies the inner vision, the interior space is required as the destination for the ointment, as opposed to the exterior region which serves as its point of origin.

Furthermore, that [identification] consisting of a connection with the internal region—which exists only within the context of the Lord’s life-story—is not possible in the case of *siddhāñjana* (the magical eye-salve); therefore, by means of the negation of the Lord’s life-story, it is made to reside in *siddhāñjana*. However, the process of universalization through the relationship of original and reflection has already been explained in the verse beginning with "With his lotus-hand out of hatred... (*karapadmena dveṣāt*).
Or, for example: "The Lord’s heart, its necklace-stones veiled by the luster of the sapphires above, shines like a seed planted in a field, as if to yield abundant fruit. (463)

It is so described because its pearls—the gems of the necklace—are covered or enveloped by the luster of sapphires above; the sense is that the pearls shine within the radiance of the sapphires. By that [necklace], the heart of the Blessed One [is adorned]; the ellipsis "of people" is to be supplied. It bears many fruits in the form of grain, or in another sense, all the goals pertaining to this world, the next world, and liberation.

For the sake of giving them, [the land] was "seed-ploughed" (*bījākṛtam*), meaning it was ploughed together with seeds such as *yava* (barley) and *nāla*; that is to say, having first sown the seeds, the black soil was leveled above them by the drawing of a specific type of plough. According to the rule "after the words *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *śamba*, and *bīja*, the suffix *ḍāc* is added when used with the verb *kṛñ* in the sense of ploughing," the suffix *ḍāc* is applied here after the word *bīja* in connection with *kṛñ* to convey the sense of ploughing. As Amarasimha states: "That which is seed-ploughed is called *uptakṛṣṭa*. It shines like a field (*kedāra*).

Here, in the poetic fancy (*saṃbhāvanā*) that the chest of Hari is identical to a field (*kedāra*), the commonality is established through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of two things that have entered into the relationship of original and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*): namely, the dark luster of the sapphire and the appearance of the seed-pearls of the necklace covered by it.
The same applies to cases such as "having pierced the sun" (*bhitvā bhānoḥ*) and so forth.

Through the state of object and counterpart, intensified by the relationship of the original form and its reflection, this Kaustubha gem, encircled by the radiance of Lakṣmī, shines all the more; is it even covered by the yellow garment itself, as if to mock the gait of his own sister? 464.

"For the mockery"—that is, for the sake of derisive imitation—of the Lord who is the husband of his own sister (the Sun), the husband of his own sister (Viṣṇu). Here, there is a relationship of original and reflection between the lotus and the yellow garment; and because they are both "filled with his rays," there is a relationship of thing and counter-thing (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*) between the two being "surrounded" and "covered. Thus, there is a commonality [between the two similes].

"By means of metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), we consider your narrative to be like the Gaṅgā—the ornament of the peak of Mount Garuḍagiri—for those who plunge into it; [the Gaṅgā] which is sweet, profoundly deep, clear, and cool. (465) In this instance, since the primary qualities of sweetness, profundity, clarity, and coolness cannot literally exist in the Blessed One’s narrative, there is a metaphorical identification of these primary qualities with secondary ones—namely, the tasting [of the narrative], its undisturbed immersion, its easy accessibility, and its removal of the heat of suffering—through the process of figurative transfer. This occurs because, through *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function), the indicated meaning is understood as non-different from the literal meaning. An example by means of mere determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) alone is as follows: [The verse continues: "O King, you are the sun; you are the moon; you are the fire; you are the ocean; you are the mountain; you are the earth; you are the wind; you are the sky; you are the quarters; you are everything. (466) Here, the primary meanings of the words "sun," "moon," and so forth, being impossible in the case of the king, are metaphorically transferred to secondary meanings such as "dispeller of darkness," "bestower of joy," and so on. Through the determination of non-difference, the primary and secondary meanings are made common to one another. Because the secondary meaning is understood as non-different from the primary, the primary meaning is not entirely abandoned. Therefore, this is not *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Furthermore, since the primary meaning is not intended here, it does not constitute *samāsokti* (condensed expression). Nor is it *apahnuti* (concealment), because the primary meaning is not denied. It is not *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) either, because the object of comparison is not explicitly mentioned. Thus, it is established that this is indeed *rūpaka* (metaphor). Alternatively, this may be considered *samāsokti*, because the primary qualities of the subject (the king) are suggested by the description of the qualities of the object of comparison (the sun, etc.). Or, it may be considered *apahnuti*, because the primary meanings are concealed by the secondary meanings. Or, it may be considered *atiśayokti*, because the identity between the two is asserted despite their difference. However, since all these figures are present simultaneously, they do not form a single, unified poetic figure. Rather, they are merely combined. Just as when one says, "This is a beautiful woman, and she is a lotus," both the quality of beauty and the genus "lotus" are expressed, yet they do not constitute a single poetic figure. Similarly, in this case, although multiple figures are present, they do not coalesce into a single figure. Therefore, it is established that this is indeed *rūpaka*. Or again, it may be considered *samāsokti*, because the primary qualities of the subject are suggested by the description of the qualities of the object of comparison. Or, it may be considered *apahnuti*, because the primary meanings are concealed by the secondary meanings. Or, it may be considered *atiśayokti*, because the identity between the two is asserted despite their difference. However, since all these figures are present simultaneously, they do not form a single, unified poetic figure. Rather, they are merely combined. Just as when one says, "This is a beautiful woman, and she is a lotus," both the quality of beauty and the genus "lotus" are expressed, yet they do not constitute a single poetic figure. Similarly, in this case, although multiple figures are present, they do not coalesce into a single figure. Therefore, it is established that this is indeed *rūpaka*. Or, it may be considered *apahnuti*, because the primary meanings are concealed by the secondary meanings. Or, it may be considered *atiśayokti*, because the identity between the two is asserted despite their difference. However, since all these figures are present simultaneously, they do not form a single, unified poetic figure. Rather, they are merely combined. Just as when one says, "This is a beautiful woman, and she is a lotus," both the quality of beauty and the genus "lotus" are

O crest-jewel of Nārāyaṇa Hill, your necklaces seem to laugh as if out of joy, saying, "How could our dwelling be anywhere other than on the chest of Hari, the abode of the daughter of the lord of rivers? 466.

In this case, the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between "manifesting" (*prakāśaprakaṭana*) and "causing laughter" (*hāsakaraṇa*) is the very seed for the commonality of "causing laughter"—which has been adopted as the ground for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the cause of joy—between both [the laughter] produced by the manifested light and the laughter itself. Thus, we have stated more than once that in every instance of fancying a cause or an effect, that which is fancied as the cause or the effect is made common (*sādhāraṇīkṛta*) in this manner and serves as the ground (*nimitta*).

Thus, in some cases, a property (*dharma*) that has been employed—whether because it lacks commonality between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*), or because it is aesthetically unpleasing (*acārutva*)—may, though unable by itself to directly sustain the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), nevertheless prove useful by bringing about the necessary conditions through the employment of another property capable of sustaining it.
For example:

"The quarters of the sky were pervaded by the sounds of the kettledrums of the victorious expedition against Madhu; the entire world seemed to have become as if distant from the very report of the creation of the sense of hearing. (467) In this verse, the property of "being distant" (*dūratva*) is not common to both the sound and the world, nor is it inherently charming; yet, by being supported by the property of "having become as if [distant] from the report of the creation," it successfully sustains the poetic fancy.

In this context, the attribute consisting of the pervasion of the quarters by the sound of the drum, although irrelevant due to its lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) with respect to the possibility of imagining the world's remoteness in the narrative of the creation of the sense of hearing, is nevertheless useful; for it serves to provide favor by reinforcing the cause of such a possibility—namely, the general absence of auditory cognition resulting from the filling of the entire cavity of the ear-entrance produced by that [sound].
The object [of comparison] (*viṣaya*) has also been taken up and demonstrated in the previous examples. In some cases, the object is even concealed (*apahnuti*). For example:
"This face, which shares the lineage of the moon, is being honored by a blue lotus; indeed, one of its petals has been offered upon the face of Hari in the guise of a *tilaka* mark. (468)

In this case, it should be understood that the negation of the object in the form of a forehead mark is for the sake of strengthening the imaginative identification with a single petal of a blue lotus.

The author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, in demonstrating that this very [figure] is *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (poetic fancy with concealment), cited only the *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the essential nature). However, in the *Kuvalayānanda* and the *Citramīmāṃsā*, both *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy regarding cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (fancy regarding effect) are also shown to be *sāpahnavā*. Among these, *svarūpotprekṣā* has been illustrated immediately above. Or, for example: "The mountain-king, bearing the belly of the wind, truly shines like the breast of the Jewel-wombed Earth; from his own mouth, he gives forth nectar as dark as a peacock’s throat, like a nipple, out of fear of Viṣṇu. (469)

[He bestowed] nectar, milk, and supreme bliss from his own mouth—meaning from the upper part of his face; in another sense, by his own means, the implication being that it was situated in the place of the means (*upāya*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *mukha* [is used] in the sense of exit, the face, as well as the beginning and the means. Indeed, the Teachers have accepted this: "The Blessed Lord is the means (*upāya*) for attaining one's own goal, who has been studied as the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*). Where the state of being a parrot (*haritva*) is denied, and there alone the possibility of it being a nipple is conceived, it possesses the nature of pure *apahnuti* (concealment). Through the power of the word *iva*, the conceiving is understood, while through the use of the word *kapaṭa* (deceit), the concealment is implied. As in the following example:
O Mother, I believe these two neem leaves, which have clung to Your moon-like face out of a desire to avoid the bitter taste of the nectar-flavor, are actually Your two eyebrows in disguise.

Here, by means of the concealment of the pair of eyebrows, there is this *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding essential nature) concerning the two neem leaves. Although the reason for the neem leaves being attached to the moon-like face of the Mother of the World is also fancied as being caused by a desire to abandon their bitterness for the sake of tasting the flavor of nectar, nevertheless, this [second fancy] is composed as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the aforementioned *svarūpotprekṣā*, and thus it does not possess primacy.

For we have already stated that where two poetic fancies are composed in a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), the designation should properly be made according to the principal fancy; that must not be forgotten. As for example:

I know, O Mother, that the diamonds have themselves been born within the cavity of your mouth-shell in the ocean of the luster of your face, assuming the name "pearl" under the guise of your rows of teeth.

The term "muktā" (pearls) refers to both the designation and the luster. Here, by means of the concealment of the row of teeth, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) identifying them with diamonds; furthermore, this is a "fancy regarding the result" (*phalotprekṣā*), as expressed in the phrase "to obtain the designation of pearls," while the metaphor (*rūpaka*) beginning with "in the ocean of the luster of their mouths" is composed as a subordinate element.
O Moon among the kings of mountains, I believe that the smile on your face was under the pretext of saying, "The lotus-feet of the purifier of Brahmā and the other gods are not worthy of me. (472)

The Gaṅgā, under the guise of a smile, appeared upon your face, as if to say: "For me, who purify Brahmā and the others, as well as the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, and who am born from the four-faced one, it is not fitting to be called 'born from the feet' (pādajatā) or 'Śūdra-ness' (śūdratā). The sense is that since her birth from the mouth of the Lord establishes her status as a Brāhmaṇī, the restriction implied by being "born from the feet" falls away. Or, for example: "These streams flowing everywhere on the Golden Mountain (Meru), which cleaves the favorable mountain, are surely not born from the arrows of the conqueror of Tāraka; rather, they are undoubtedly the gods (nirjarāḥ). (473)

*Anukūlam* means "on the bank. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending. Those who break—that is, uproot—the *nagas*, which are trees, are so described. Those for whom the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*) is favorable toward their foothills (*pade*), and who are so [favorable] toward the golden mountain (*kanakādri*), the Śeṣa mountain, and Sumeru, are so described. Spreading, flowing, and moving everywhere; those in whom there are clusters (*jātāni*) of arrows—that is, of *kāśa* flowers—which surpass the stars (*tārakāṇi*), are so described.

In one sense, those who possess the six-faced Śarajanman—who is so called because he conquers Tāraka, a specific demon—are these visible objects; they are not merely waterfalls or streams of water, but are surely *nirjaras* (immortals). This is a pure *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the nature of a genus (*jāti*), wherein the commonality is established through paronomasia (*śleṣa*) and which contains within it a simple *apahnuti* (concealment).
Or, for example:

"The Mountain of Serpents (*Ahi-giri*) seems to disregard other mountains—those which are not the abode of Śrīnivāsa, which do not take refuge in all sacred waters (*sarvatīrtha*), which are not composed of the Vedas (*avedamaya*), and which are not immovable (*acala*)—under the pretext of the lowing of Hari. (474)

"Under the guise of the roar of lions and tigers"—this is a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy) consisting of the act of concealment (*apahnava*). The Dīkṣitas maintain that this may also involve a concealed denial (*paryastāpahnuti*), as in the following example:
"It is fitting that he alone is Viṣṇu; I know him to be the Moon because he causes the entire world to flourish. Yet, it is clear that the Moon is inferior to him, for he serves at his feet. (475)

The sense is that it belongs to the entire world and its waters, and not merely to the waters of the ocean. In the alternative meaning, because he increases, nourishes, and expands the universe, I know it is fitting that this Viṣṇu alone is the Moon; yet it is clear that the Moon’s inferiority—that is, its lowness—compared to this Viṣṇu is manifest. For (hi) that Moon serves (paricarati)—that is, attends upon—the feet (pada) of this Viṣṇu (the locative singular form). Thus, there is no room for the suspicion of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original vowel quality) when the vowel *a* follows.

Therefore, the meaning is that its "inferiority" (adharatva) is manifest. In this context, "from this" means from the reason that will be stated hereafter. Its "inferiority"—the state of being devoid of connection with the earth—is clear. To the question "Why?", he says: "For he... Because "he," the moon, "waits upon" (paricarati)—meaning he moves around—"in his footsteps," that is, in the footsteps of Viṣṇu, which is to say, in the sky. Here, by denying the conventional status of the moon through the negation of its nature as a moon, and based on the cause of its increasing all the worlds, there arises the conceit that it is the Blessed Lord; thus, this is an instance of *paryastāpahnuti* (disguised denial) containing within it another *apahnuti*.
O Acyuta, I consider the venerable Vṛṣagiri to be the sole abode of the gods, and not Mount Meru; for if Meru were the sole abode of the gods, it would surely not be variegated in nature.

The compound *śivabhāgavatavat* is a *samāsa* (compound) that is the sole support (*ekādhāra*) for certain wise ones (*vibudhānām*), namely the devotees of Śiva. In the alternative sense (*pakṣe*), it means the sole primary support for the gods (*vibudhānām*). If Meru were the sole support for the wise, then it would not be composed of variegated [spots] (*karburamayaḥ*)—that is, full of demons (*rakṣomayaḥ*)—but rather its actual state is that it is composed of gold (*suvarṇamayaḥ*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "The word *karbura* refers to water and gold; *karbura* [as an adjective] refers to sin and demons.

In this verse, by way of concealing (*nihnava*) Meru’s status as the sole support for the wise, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the glorious Vṛṣagiri, which contains a "reversal-concealment" (*paryastāpahnuti*) and is preceded by the reasoning (*yukti*) in the form of an argument stated in the second half of the verse.
As in the following example: [Example omitted per instructions.]

The moon is indeed the king of the twice-born, yet it is surely only your horse who is truly the king of the twice-born; for while the former harms those separated from their lovers, O lotus-eyed one, this [horse] brings joy to the brahmins.

O lotus-eyed one! The moon is not the king of the twice-born (*dvijarāja*)—in the sense that "therefore the Brāhmaṇas have Soma as their king" according to the Vedic statement—but rather, Garuḍa alone is called the king of the twice-born; this is the intended meaning. Indeed! The reason for this is expressed by the words "he" (*sa*) and so forth: that moon (*induḥ*) destroys those very ones who are both Brāhmaṇas and Yogins; therefore, how could he be the king of the twice-born? This is the underlying thought. The literal meaning is that he destroys those separated from their lovers.

This vehicle of yours brings joy to the Brahmins, and on the other hand, it brings delight to birds (*vīnām* = *pakṣiṇām*) because he is their lord; thus, the sense is that this [moon] alone is the "king of the twice-born" (*dvijarāja*). Here, by means of the concealment (*apahnava*) of the moon’s status as the king of the twice-born, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding Garuḍa, which contains within it a "perverse denial" (*paryastāpahnuti*) supported by a reason.

Or rather: Just as the thousand-rayed sun is considered a mere jewel of light, whereas the Kaustubha gem alone I consider to be the true sun; for while that [sun] illuminates the infinite [world] only by day, this [Kaustubha], however, does so both by day and by night.

That thousand-rayed one (the sun) adorns the infinite mid-air as if it were the sky; however, the actual meaning is that this Kaustubha gem adorns the infinite mid-air as the Blessed Lord (Viṣṇu). The statement "it adorns [it] night and day" provides the reason for this. Here, by denying the status of the "sky-jewel" (dyumaṇi) to the thousand-rayed one, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding the Kaustubha gem, which—as before—is characterized by a concealed denial (apahnuti) with a reversed perspective and accompanied by a reason. In all these examples, there is an intermixture with paronomasia (śleṣa).
An example of concealment (*sāpahnavatva*) in the poetic fancy of a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) is as follows:

"Surely the crest-jewel of lovers, eternally youthful, dwells forever on Mount Abhi [Aghora], his heart a friend to the breasts of Kamalā; this statement is merely a pretext for the desire to uplift the world. (479)

Here, by removing the cause for the Lord’s desire to uplift the world—which is His eternal residence on Śeṣādri—and instead imagining that it is caused by His friendship with the breasts of Kamalā, there occurs a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of a cause) containing a *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment).
An example of the concealment of identity (*sāpahnavatva*) in the poetic figure of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) is as follows:
"O Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, you bear the Śrīvatsa mark upon your chest surely only to indicate that you have taken refuge in the Kāmadhenu; it is certainly not for the sake of adorning yourself."

The *śrīvatsa* is a calf endowed with beauty; in another sense, it is a name for a mark. It is "upon the calf," that is, upon the chest—Amara states, "the chest is called *vatsa*. Here, regarding the wearing of the *śrīvatsa*, there is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) wherein the actual result—the adornment of the chest—is concealed, while the suggestion of his being a "wish-fulfilling cow" (*kāmadhenu*) for those who have taken refuge in him serves as the intended result. This is further characterized by an *apahnuti* (concealment) in reverse. Enough of this prolixity.

The authors of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* and others, however, maintain that "in certain cases, although a simile (*upamā*) is initiated at the time of the syntactic connection of the word-meanings due to the expression of similarity, it culminates in a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) by virtue of the overall purport of the sentence-meaning. Following this view, we previously stated in the section on the figure of speech 'Description' (*ullekhālaṅkāra*) regarding the verse "mṛgamadatilakati" that the simile, though initiated there, culminates in a poetic fancy due to propriety (*aucitya*). An example is as follows:
O lotus-eyed one, your two calves are the quivers of the God of Love who desires to conquer the world; your body is like a grove, with your youth and beauty acting as the trunks of elephants.

O lotus-eyed one! Your body is itself a grove, and within it, youth and loveliness are two elephants; the meaning is that their trunks act like those [two legs]. Here, although at first sight there is a perception of a simile (*upamā*) due to the suffix *kyaṅ*—prescribed for the sense of "acting like" (*ācāra*) after a noun (*subanta*) serving as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the expression *karikarāyete*—the result ultimately culminates in a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) because the qualifiers such as "your body is a grove" would otherwise be redundant according to the requirements of propriety (*aucitya*).

Thus, it should be understood that even when words such as *nibha* and others expressive of comparison, as well as suffixes such as *kalpa* and others, are employed, they ultimately culminate in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) due to the propriety of the totality of factors.

Just as the rays from the tips of the claws on the peaks of Nara’s lion-like arms shone upon the hearts of the sons of Diti, so too did they resemble tongues of fire spreading rapidly from the hoods of serpents whose breath had been snatched away by his fangs.
O Mother, this smile of yours is like a wave of nectar offered by the sweetness of your speech; it is like the tender moonlight falling upon the lap of the moon of your face. 483.

The line of hair on Acyuta’s chest, resembling the trunk of the elephant of Love as he emerges from his immersion in the lake of the navel, possesses the luster of the Yamunā flowing from the lap of the Kaustubha gem’s radiance. However, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādharā* has stated that even suffixes such as *kyaṅ*, as well as *ācārakviP* and others, serve to convey *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Even for him, the ultimate intent lies in their conveying *utprekṣā*. Alternatively, those [suffixes] may themselves be expressive of *utprekṣā*. As it is said in the *Kalpataru*: “Words such as *kalpa*, *deśīya*, and *deśya*;
words such as *spardhin*, *pratibhaṭa*, and so forth;
and also words such as *nibha*, *vat*, and others—these, in certain instances, have the purpose of expressing *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic probability/fancy).”

Thus [it is said]. The detailed exposition has been provided by us on the occasion of commenting on the verse beginning with "From the dwelling of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇorvāsāt*) in our *Haṃsasandeśarasāsvādinī*. Likewise, it is established in the *Citramīmāṃsā* that even in instances where there is the perception of metaphors (*rūpaka*) and the like, the ultimate resolution lies in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). For fear of prolixity, the examples thereof are not presented here; enough of this.

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to speak of *gamyotprekṣā* (suggested metaphorical fancy) as an ornament (*alaṃkāra*), since it is actually a case of 'ornament-suggestion' (*alaṃkāradhvani*)? To this, let it be heard: where the locus (*viṣaya*), the correlate (*viṣayin*), and the cause (*nimitta*) are all expressed, and the metaphorical fancy is understood merely through the non-employment of words such as *iva*, that [fancy] attains the status of an ornament precisely because it is rendered manifest by its extreme clarity. This is illustrated by the example beginning with "īpsitasarā nikāmam. However, where even the correlate (*viṣayin*)—the object of the fancy—is not expressed, and the fancy is understood through a stated fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṃkāra*), there alone resides the suggestion of metaphorical fancy (*utprekṣādhvani*).
Just as the forest does, upon seeing on Mount Vṛṣabha the Goddess Śrī embraced by Kṛṣṇa’s chest like a doe, the female deer constantly gaze toward Kṛṣṇa, their own beloved. 485.

Having seen Śrī, the Goddess of Fortune, embraced by the chest of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa—the one who is known as "harīṇī" (golden-hued) because of her greenish-yellow color, where the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *varṇādanudāttāt* and the substitution of *n* for the *t* is prescribed by usage, while the change to *ṇ* follows Amara’s definition: "A *hariṇī* may be a doe, a golden image, or anything that is green"—the forest doeses (*vanahariṇyaḥ*) [mistook] Kṛṣṇa for a black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*).

"Even without an explicit suffix, there is the elision of both the preceding and following words"—according to this rule, the word *sāra*, which constitutes the latter member of the compound, is elided, as in the case of words such as *bhīmasena*. For this very reason, usages such as "covering with a black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇājinena saṃvṛṇvan*) are beyond doubt. The sense is that they behold their own beloved; they perceive that just as we are denoted by the word *hariṇī* (the female deer), so too our beloved is to be designated by the word *kṛṣṇa* (the Lord). Thus we are like Śrī [to him].

Here, by means of the factual matter (vastu) of the gazelle-eyed woman’s act of gazing at the black antelope, there is suggested a poetic fancy (utprekṣā): that she herself, like Śrī—who is embraced by the chest of Śrī-Kṛṣṇa and designated by the word "hariṇī"—desires to become just like Him.
Just as when,

with a well-disposed mind desiring to bow, the heads were bent down, the flowers situated upon them fell even before that, and further down, at the feet of the one who bears the crest-jewel of the mountain that supports the serpents.

Of the *sumanas* gods; those situated upon it—situated on their crowns—are the *sumanas* flowers. Here, by means of the fact of the falling of the *sumanas* flowers, there is suggested a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): as if, through a rivalry occasioned by the identity of name, they themselves are bowing down even before the crowns of the Thirty Gods.

"O Enemy of Mura, men who are overwhelmed by a heat other than [ordinary] smallness, caused by the intense forest fire of worldly existence, gaze again and again toward the ocean of nectar that is your face. (487)
Here, by means of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "as if to dive in" is suggested. Or, for example:
"O hero of the Raghu dynasty, as you set out upon the path to conquer your enemies in this ocean of worldly existence at an exceedingly late hour, men behold you from the shore like monkeys. (488)

The sense is: "having long ago [plunged] into the ocean of worldly existence like the ocean [of milk]," and "of enemies" such as desire (kāma) and others, or like the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and his ilk. "While the path"—meaning the way or the means—is "not being granted" (avitīryamāṇa), that is, not being given, for the sake of victory; while you remain thus, people look upon you as monkeys would look upon one standing on the bank—both situated on the shore and indifferent—and they observe, wondering: "Why does he not strive to dry up even this ocean of worldly existence with his arrows, or to build a bridge across it? This is the underlying meaning.

For this very reason, there is the address "hero of the Raghu dynasty. Here, through a simile enlivened by metaphor (rūpaka), there is suggested (dhvanita) a poetic fancy (utprekṣā): that he dried up even the ocean of worldly existence just as [he dried up] the ocean; or that his arrows were as if desiring to bind it, or as if desiring to obstruct it.

Just as the moonlight does not leave the moon for even a moment when it has risen high above the ocean, so too, the moonlight of your fame does not leave the moon that is the sun upon the earth (the serpent-king Śeṣa) once your ocean of glory has surged even more exceedingly.

The moonlight, the *kaumudī*, and the moon itself—she does not abandon her boat; for the implication is that women are exceedingly timid. Here too, through the metaphor (*rūpaka*), there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that she acts as if out of fear of drowning.

If it is asked, "Since the basis of *adhyavasāya* (determination) is equal for both *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), how is there a distinction between these two?", listen: *Adhyavasāya* is defined as appearing as non-different. It is of two kinds: established (*siddha*) and to-be-proved (*sādhya*). Where, due to the connection with qualities being characterized, the superimposition of the *viṣayin* (the subject of attribution) onto the *viṣaya* (the object of attribution) occurs such that—despite the *viṣayin* being distinct—the cognition arises as non-different because it functions by encompassing the *viṣaya*, there *adhyavasāya* is established.

Based on this [distinction], the first variety of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) will be demonstrated immediately below. However, where the object of comparison (*viṣaya*) is explicitly mentioned, the subject of comparison (*viṣayin*) appears as distinct; in that case, because the perception of their identity is being brought about through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), it is "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). Since the activity based on this [identity] constitutes *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy)—which has synonyms such as "possibility," "conjecture," and "reflection"—this constitutes the difference between these two figures.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Chapter on Poetic Fancy (Utprekṣā), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Hyperbole (Atiśayokti):
Where, having swallowed up the object of description (viṣaya), the subject of description (viṣayin) alone is firmly established.
The experts in poetic figures know that as *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor).

The "swallowing" (*nigaraṇa*) of the object (*viṣaya*)—such as a face and so forth—is its apprehension by means of words denoting the correlate (*viṣayin*), such as "moon" and so forth, even without the specific employment of words expressive of that [object] itself. Where there is a determination (*adhyavasāna*) of the object as having the form of the correlate, preceded by that swallowing, there exists the hyperbolic metaphor (*rūpakātiśayokti*). In the phrase "as having the form of the correlate," "form" (*rūpa*) refers to either non-difference (*abheda*) or identity of nature (*tādrūpya*).

Thus, the definition should be understood as follows: *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) is that which becomes the object of a superimposed certainty (*āhāryaniścaya*) whose subject matter (*dharmin*) is an unexpressed object (*anupāttaviṣaya*), and which consists in either non-distinction (*abheda*) or identity (*tādūpya*) between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). The term "unexpressed" (*anupātta*) is used to exclude *rūpaka* (metaphor), for in that case the object, such as the face, is expressed. Indeed, this very distinction—this "excess" (*atiśaya*)—is what is stated to differentiate it from *rūpaka*. The term "superimposed" (*āhārya*) is used to exclude *bhrāntimad* (error), and the term "certainty" (*niścaya*) is used to exclude *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).

Furthermore, in this case, because the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*) are conveyed by a single word, the relationship of the topic (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is not possible; for that relationship occurs only between those conveyed by distinct words. For example:
"The radiant friend of the lotus, who is exceedingly capable of dispelling darkness, who brings great fragrance to the lotuses, and who utterly crushes the difficult-to-subdue mud... (489)

For here, in the swallowing of the Kaustubha gem by virtue of being the "kinsman of the lotus" (the sun), two qualifiers found in the first two quarters—namely, "dispelling darkness" and so forth—are directly presented as common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) between the object and the subject for the sake of favoring that [swallowing]. The third [qualifier], situated in the third quarter, is likewise [present] according to the view of those who do not accept it as a verbal expression (*aśābdika*).

For the grammarians (Śābdikas), however, the agency identical to that of the "friend of the lotus" (the sun), which is inferred from the act of trampling the mud (*kardama-mardana*) already expressed [in the compound], exists as a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) between those two—the object and the subject. In the first quarter-verse, there is a swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) of ignorance by means of its identification with darkness; in the second, of the eyes of people by means of their identification with lotuses; and in the third, of sin by means of its identification with mud. This swallowing serves as a supporting factor (*anugrāhaka*) for that very [hyperbole]. Thus, this is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) possessing subordinate parts (*sāvayavā*).
Or as she shines, perceiving a pair of lotuses there in perpetual bloom beneath a moon eclipsed by cataracts—such is the inscrutable and wondrous power of illusion belonging to the Lord. (490)

In this instance, the objects—the beauty of the hair, face, and eyes—are swallowed by their subjects, which take the forms of darkness, the moon, a lotus, thick clouds, and illusion (*māyā*). Here, the verse “Born in the lineage of Janaka, she was fashioned like divine illusion (*devamāyā*)” should be kept in mind. *Māyā* is a power (*śakti*) that produces diverse effects.
Where there is no further act of swallowing by the subject, but rather a pure common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) and so forth, that is the partless (*niravayavā*) [type of *apahnuti*]. For example:
Plunging into the sweet streams of nectar, cool as the moon, yet difficult for the ignorant to fathom, I dispel the entire mass of delusions and abandon all forms of confusion.

These [meanings] are difficult to fathom for ignorant people, those lacking knowledge, and even for those other than gods; herein, the manifestations of Śrīnivāsa’s compassion have been swallowed up. In the first example, by means of the term *ambhojabāndhava* (the kinsman of the lotus), which functions through *sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā*, the Kaustubha gem is presented—preceded by the quality of its excellence in dispelling darkness, which is common to both the primary meaning (*śakya*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*). Therein, that which is presented through primary denotation (*śakti*), namely the one qualified by being the "kinsman of the lotus," is construed with the Kaustubha via the relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*).

For there is no obstacle to accepting the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between two word-meanings presented through *śakti* (direct denotation) and *lakṣaṇā* (indication), just as there is none for the connection between "capacity" and "being a means to a desired end" when both are presented by their respective powers. Thus, in the case of [the verse], the cognition arises that "[the moon] is non-different from the friend of the lotus and possesses the quality of being capable of dispelling darkness, etc."; therefore, this is called "Hyperbole of Non-difference" (*abhedātiśayokti*). The same applies to the two examples immediately following. If it is asked, "If this is so, what is its distinction from Metaphor (*rūpaka*)?", do not say so.

In *rūpaka* (metaphor), because there is the manifestation of the delimiting property of the object (*viṣayatāvacchedaka*), which is pervaded by the difference from the subject (*viṣayin*), the distinction [from other figures] is clear. However, when the intention is not on the manifestation of non-difference, but rather on the manifestation of difference, then because there is the cognition of identity (*tādrūpya*) itself, it will be called *tādrūpyātiśayokti* (hyperbole of identity). In this definition, since it is stated in general that "having swallowed up the object, one determines only the subject," even when there is a metaphorical treatment of non-difference through pure *sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā* (indicative function based on identification), it is indeed *atiśayokti*.

In that [type of *adhyavasāya*], there is the determination of non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*), as in: “The mature merit of the lotus-eyed one, foremost in all the world—may that beauty, which is a refuge for those like us and truly wondrous, shine forth! (492) Here, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of beauty upon the Blessed Lady Lakṣmī, who is the locus of that beauty. In cases such as “This is the moon,” there is a figurative (*gauṇa*) nature because similarity is the cause of the determination. However, when a relation such as being the locus (*āśrayatva*) is the cause, it is pure (*śuddha*). This is the distinction. Furthermore, these two types of difference [between the two forms of *adhyavasāya*] arise from similarity and, likewise, from other relations.

This is because of the statement in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*: "The two [types of] superimposition (*adhyavasāna*) are to be understood as qualified (*gauṇa*) and pure (*śuddha*). The meaning is that these two divisions consist of the forms of superimposition with attribution (*sāropa*) and superimposition without attribution (*sādhyavasāna*). Therefore, it should be understood that when there is an imposition of identity upon one thing in another by means of a relation other than similarity, that is "pure superimposition without attribution" (*śuddhasādhyavasāna*).
The identification of the effect with its cause is as follows:
"I beheld a certain body that was like the nectar-juice of speech, which surpassed the bees by its dark luster; it was a source of joy for Vinatā and a host of gods who paid homage to it. (493)

In this instance, there is a superimposition (*adhyavasāya*) of identity between the effect—the joy of Vinatā—and its cause, the Lord. However, since the specific figure of speech called *hetu*—defined by the statement, “Some declare *hetu* to be the identity of cause and effect”—is rooted in *śuddhasāropalakṣaṇā*, its scope consists of examples such as, “The glances of Lord Veṅkaṭa are the play of Fortune for the learned. Therefore, this [present case] is not rendered redundant by that [figure of *hetu*], which is rooted in *śuddhasādhyavasānalakṣaṇā* consisting of the identity of cause and effect.
Superimposition (sāropā) occurs where both the object and the subject are expressed;
this superimposition is of two kinds, distinguished as metaphorical (gauṇī) and pure (śuddhā).
That which consists of a relationship characterized by similarity is called *gauṇī* (secondary);
that which consists of a relationship other than that is declared to be *śuddhā* (pure).
The moon-like face of the slender maiden, which brings joy to the eyes, triumphs most exceedingly;
for therein the object is swallowed up and only the subject remains fixed.
In that regard, the secondary (gauṇī) [metaphor] is of two kinds: that which involves identification (sādhyavasānā) and the pure (śuddhā).
[Examples are given with] a lotus, a trumpet, a plantain tree, a sandy bank, the sky, and a mountain.
A creeper created from conchs, the moon, and darkness, it is a festival for those possessed by desire.

Thus, in the *Kāvyadarpaṇa*, the definitions of *sāropā* (superimposition) and *sādhyavasānā* (identification) have been demonstrated with examples. This illustration from the *Kāvyadarpaṇa* is intended for the clear comprehension of the meaning of the verse from the *Kāvyaprakāśa* cited immediately above. By this, it should be understood that the example provided by Viśveśvara, the author of the *Alaṃkārakaustubha*, in the verse "By this, proximity to the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) triumphs—the one with the eyes of a trembling deer"—which is characterized as an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on the identification of cause and effect, is not well-formed.

In this case, because the figure is one where the object of comparison is swallowed up (*viṣayanigaraṇa-pradhāna*) through the employment of the object itself—namely, "one whose eyes are like those of a trembling deer"—it cannot be an instance of *atiśayokti*. Since, according to the method already stated, it necessarily constitutes a distinct figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*) called *hetu*, it is more appropriate for this to serve as its illustration; therefore, it is proper to demonstrate another example [of *atiśayokti*].

This is indeed not inconsistent with the definition of the figure *hetu* (cause) as stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*: “The cause [is the figure] when there is a statement of non-difference between the cause and the effect,” and with the definition of *candrāvaloka* presented [therein]: “The identity of the cause and the effect is *hetu*. For its meaning is that *abhidhā* (utterance) occurs through non-difference—that is, through the superimposition of non-difference.
As for the verse: “It is the grace of youth, the laughter of the abundance of supreme loveliness;
it is the ornament of the earth’s surface and the subjugation of the minds of young men.”

Such is his example; however, it should be disregarded because it contradicts well-established examples such as "The charms of Lakṣmī [belong] to the learned. For here, the cause of subjugation is stated as the subjugation of the heroine, and thus, being explicitly expressed (*vivṛta*), it is fit to be an example of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) based on the figurative indication of identity (*sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā*). The author of the *Kaustubha*, however, remarked that the figure of speech called "Cause" (*hetu*), as defined in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* as "the cause for expressing [two things] as non-different," is actually included within hyperbole itself.

The meaning of this [verse] as stated in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa* regarding the figure of speech *hetu* (cause) is as follows: in its illustrative example, “the subduing of the minds of young people,” there is a perception of identity between cause and effect based on *sādhyavasāna-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication where the primary sense is subordinated). From this, it is understood that the definition of that [figure] is intended specifically for such an identity between cause and effect; therefore, such a *hetu* ornament is included within *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) alone, and not even within the identity between cause and effect based on *sāropā-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication where the primary sense is superimposed).

As for the inclusion of *ullekha* and other such figures within this very *atiśayokti* by the author of the *Kāvyakaustubha*, it is not particularly elegant; let the connoisseurs understand this for themselves, so I shall desist from further elaboration for fear of prolixity.
Even in the form of a garland, this is seen:
the good governance of the worlds, the auspiciousness of the fair-browed goddesses, the fortune of the Lord of the Mountain, and—alas!—the accessibility [of Him] to the eyes. (494)
In this case, there is an identification (adhyavasāya) of the effects, such as good governance, with their cause, the Blessed Lord.

In this *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), the qualification "a particular kind of *rūpaka*" (metaphor) is intended to demonstrate that the varieties shown under *rūpaka* are also possible here by virtue of similarity. Since the non-difference (*abheda*) characteristic of primary *rūpaka* is impossible in *atiśayokti*, the word *rūpaka*—like the term *agnihotra* in the expression "he performs the *agnihotra* for a month"—refers by extension (*atideśa*) to something similar to it. Consequently, even here there are two types: *abhedātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-difference) and *tādrūpyātiśayokti* (hyperbole of identity). Furthermore, within these, one should discern all the divisions such as superiority, inferiority, and the absence of both. This is everything that must be considered.
In this regard, an example of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) consisting of the figure of speech *rūpaka* (metaphor) with an excess [of attributes] is as follows:

"This wondrous collyrium, shining upon the peak of the mountain of ointment (*añjanagiri*), always reveals its own treasure to those whose eyes have once been touched by it. (495) Here, the "excess" is to be understood as follows: while ordinary collyrium—which is well-known to reveal a treasure distinct from itself—only does so when it is occasionally applied to the eyes, the Blessed One (the Lord), who is here identified through metaphorical superimposition (*adhyavasita*) with that collyrium and is perceived by the eyes, is said to constantly reveal a treasure that is non-different from Himself. Thus, there is an excellence [of power].

And just as this most wonderful Jambū tree has arisen upon the peak of Mount Jāmbūnada; for there is never observed any loss of its fruit’s efficacy—on the peak of Mount Jāmbūnada, the "remaining mountain," this most wonderful Jambū [tree] has arisen, meaning that the Blessed One is determined to be the Jambū tree itself. "Arisen" means descended. He explains its state of being most wonderful with the words beginning with "na" (not): "of which Jambū tree, the loss of the 'pratyaya'—that is, the renown—of its fruits, meaning the absence of the established reputation for its fruitfulness, is never seen."
The word *pratyaya* is used in the sense of being well-known, as well as in the two types of knowledge beginning with *sanātana*;
it also denotes conduct, an oath, a flaw, and the causes dependent upon trust.

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. In the case of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), however, the meaning is that of the "loss" (*lopa*) of the "cognition of fruit"—that is, the loss of confidence regarding the attainment of one's various desired objectives. Such a loss is never observed here. While the loss of the manifestation of fruit might occasionally occur for a well-known *jambu* tree, it is not so with this [tree]. The sense is that there is never, at any time, a loss of confidence due to doubt as to whether the desired fruit will be attained by those who rely upon it or not.

In this context, the word *jambū* involves the superimposition of the feminine gender, which resides in the object, onto the word itself; thus it is most wonderful. He explains this very point with the words "not" (*na*). This is the nominative singular of that [word]; the elision of the suffix denoting the fruit is never observed.

Although the optional elision (*lup*) of the suffix is prescribed by the rule *jambvā vā* when the meaning is the fruit-form derived from the word *jambū*, the sense is that for this particular instance of the word *jambū*, the elision of the suffix—that is, the elision of the suffix *aṇ* prescribed for the sense of the fruit—is never seen; such is its wonder. The actual meaning, however, has already been stated.

In this context, the superiority of the Blessed One—who is determined to be a *jambu* tree both in relation to the well-known *jambu* tree and in relation to the word "well-known *jambu*"—should be understood as being based on *śleṣa* (punning) in the manner described; and the second meaning of the word is intended for the sake of producing an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
An example of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) based on a deficiency [of attributes] is as follows:

"O Hari, these beasts, not perceiving the hundreds of virtues declared by the Vedas—foremost among which is your excellent character—are crying out in vain in all directions, though they are not four-footed. (497)

Here, there is a deficiency because it is stated that those things determined as non-different from the cattle are not four-legged. However, the *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of the metaphorical identification of both [the subject and the object] with something else is to be seen in the two previously cited verses: "capable of dispelling darkness" and "streams of sweet nectar."
An example of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of *adhikatādṛpya-rūpaka* (metaphor based on excessive resemblance) is as follows:

"This other [moon], a source from the mountain peaks of the ocean, is a different kind of blessed white gem, strung upon the thread of dense virtues; it illuminates the vast expanse with its own rays of nectar, making me fortunate. (498)

It is woven—that is, interlaced—with dense and compact qualities such as omniscience and the like. Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound of two adjectives: "without holes" (meaning free from cavities) and "woven" (meaning sewn together) with a "thread" (meaning a strand). This "black jewel"—the great sapphire (*mahānīla*)—is not produced in the mines of Śikhari (Ceylon), but is something else entirely, distinct from the world; it is, in truth, determined to be Śrīnivāsa.

Making me blessed, fulfilled, and a recipient of wealth, He—by His own splendors, that is, by His particular affections toward His devotees (and elsewhere, by His physical radiance)—clarifies, that is, reveals, the nectar consisting of self-realization and the sovereignty of liberation. In the alternative sense, He clarifies, that is, makes white (pāṇḍura), and not blue, the nectar which is milk. Here, the meaning of the Śruti passage—"He whom this Self chooses, by him He is attained; to him this Self reveals His own form"—should be kept in mind.

For instance: "This Supreme Self is to be attained by the seeker whom He chooses; the meaning is that He is attainable by the person who is chosen [by Him]. And the state of being chosen by Him belongs only to the person who is most dear to Him. And the state of being most dear to Him belongs only to one who possesses love for Him. Consequently, the love of the worshipper directed toward the Blessed One becomes the cause of attaining Him by generating love in the Blessed One for the worshipper."

It was said: "To that devotee, this Self—the Supreme Self—reveals its own body, its own essential nature; it manifests itself and bestows its own direct experience. Even with the reading *vṛṇute*, the meaning is the same.

Here, by the word *anyat* ("other"), its distinction from a well-known blue gem is shown; and by the words *nīrandhra* ("dense") and so forth, its superiority over that [gem] produced in the Siṃhala mines—which is strung on a porous thread, born from a mountain peak, and rendered white by contact with nectar—is demonstrated through its being strung on a dense thread, its origin from a mine at the foot of a mountain, and its clarification by nectar.
Thus...

I shall resort to certain pastimes that dwell upon the lordly mountain of lions, which are servants to the side-glances of Lakṣmī and possess smiles like the moonlight of the lovely autumn moon. (499)
In such cases as well, one should recognize the presence of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) characterized by an excess of that very nature.
An example of Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the figure of Deficiency (*nyūnatādrūpya-rūpaka*):

"Those who are called 'demons' (*piśācakāḥ*) by the gods, whose eyes are fixed upon the serpents [of the underworld], even though they do not utter that name with their speech—what lowly creatures are these that are visible? (500)

The construction is: "even their name is speech. By the statement "those by whom the Vedānta-śāstra has been mastered (sannaya) and investigated (vinna)," [it is implied] that the *ṇatva* of the preceding *da* and the following *ta* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs according to the rule "radābhyām" (*Pāṇini* 8.2.42), as Amara states: "vinna and vitta mean 'investigated'. Because the class beginning with *āhitāgni* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *niṣṭhā* is placed at the end of the compound. In this context, by indicating that "who are these Piśācas?"—thus showing they are unknown—their distinction from those Piśācas who are well-known is shown; and by the word "visible" (*dṛśyāḥ*), their inferiority to those [other] invisible ones is demonstrated.
An example of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) where the object is neither identical to nor different from the subject is as follows:

"I perceive upon the mountain of serpents a certain cloud, which has been attended by the Blue-Throated One (Śiva), whose majesty is celebrated for its unimpeded touch, and which is visible at the end of the rainy season. (501)

I perceive an indescribable cloud—[the Supreme Being] who is attended by the blue-throated Mahādeva and by peacocks; whose touch is unimpeded and unrestrained (or, in the other sense, by the irresistible wind—for the *Medinī* states: "The word *sparśana* refers to the wind in the masculine, and to giving or touch in the neuter"); whose glory is celebrated; and who is to be characterized or known through the dense conclusions of the scriptures, namely the Upaniṣads (for the Śruti says: "Him, however, one knows through the Upaniṣads"). In the other sense, it is visible in the midst of the end of the thick season of rain. I perceive such a cloud.

Just as the appearance of a cluster of *sumanaḥ* flowers brings relief to one distressed by heat, and the emergence of moonlight dispels the fear of the sun's scorching heat, so too, perceiving this certain rain-cloud, I shall surely attain revival.

Regarding *sumanasām*, *mālatīnām*, *kadambānām*, and *nīpānām*: in this context, they refer to hosts of gods (*devanivahānām*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *sumanas* denotes a flower and jasmine (*mālatī*)," and "The word *kadamba* may denote a cluster, the *nīpa* tree, or the *siddhārtha* [mustard] plant, as a masculine noun. *Tānta* means the alleviation of exhaustion. It is called *udbhava* because it arises (*udbhavati*) from the sun (*tapanāt*); the suffix *ap* is added according to Pāṇini’s rule *pacādyac*. That which is *ūṣma* (heat) is the source of fear; its *damana* (subduer) means one who causes the cessation of the heat of the summer sun. This is the meaning.

In this context, *tapana* refers to a particular hell; as the *Ratnamālā* states: "The words *tapana*, *grīṣma*, *bhallātaka*, *naraka*, *antara*, and *bhāskara* [are synonyms]. From that [hell] arises a heat or fever; the alleviation of the fear of that is the meaning. Alternatively, *tapana* is that by which one is tormented, i.e., the cause of suffering. That which is both *uddhata* (exalted/arrogant) and *bhava* (existence/transmigration)—in that [cycle of existence], there are heats such as the internal (*ādhyātmika*) and other afflictions; the meaning is the alleviation of the fear of those. [He is] some *ghanāghana* (cloud-bursting thundercloud), that is to say, Śrīnivāsa.

"Kalayan" means serving; "ujjīvanam" refers to excellent water, or in another sense, crossing over (uttaraṇa). "Labheya nūnam" expresses a possibility. Here, one should recall such verses as "If you have a desire for your own livelihood... In both examples, by the word "kamapi" (some kind of), a distinction from ordinary clouds well-known in the world is shown, but neither superiority nor inferiority; thus, this is an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) of the form of "neither-nor" (*anubhayatādrūpya*), enlivened by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

All of this is in accordance with the *Kuvalayānanda* and other such works. Jagannātha, however, holds that the determinant of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is the state of being a cognition whose qualificandum is the indicated object (*lakṣya*) and whose mode is solely the delimitant of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), [arising] from the word denoting the superposed (*viṣayivācaka*) when there is a transference of function (*sādhyavasānalakṣaṇā*) onto the object (*viṣaya*).

Thus, since it has been established that in every instance of "swallowing" (nigaraṇa), the object appears solely in the form of its property as the delimitor of the objective domain (*viṣayitāvacchedaka-dharma*), and not as non-different from the subject (*viṣayin*), [the author] stated: "The two-fold division into *abhedātiśayokti* (hyperbole of identity) and *tādrūpyātiśayokti* (hyperbole of similarity of form) is therefore untenable. Regarding this, Vaidyanātha remarked: "This is a display of overweening pride; for since the delimitor of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is not previously perceived in the indicated object (*lakṣya*), a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) qualified by that [delimitor] is impossible."

He stated: "Because the cognition of the object (*lakṣya*) as qualified by a property (*dharma*)—in which the relation with the primary meaning (*śakya*) can be grasped—is the cause of a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) that possesses the same mode (*prakāra*); and because the logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) that necessitates *lakṣaṇā* remains as it was. Even if such a cognition is admitted on the strength of *tātparya*, there is no obstacle to a cognition where the non-difference from the primary meaning is also the mode, precisely because of that *tātparya*; for the word 'only' (*mātra*) excludes only the delimitors of the objective domain (*viṣayatāvacchedaka*)."

If it be asked, "In the examples cited such as 'shining upon the peak of Mount Añjana,' since the object (*viṣaya*) is presented by the word 'this' (*idam*), how can there be hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)?", listen: if this [word 'this'] is intended as a qualifier of the superimposed object (*viṣayin*), there is hyperbole; but if it is intended not as a qualifier of the object, there is merely metaphor (*rūpaka*). This is likewise the case in expressions such as "this man is a bull" (*gaura* is a pun for both 'white' and 'bull'). For this very reason, the statement of the ancients that in hyperbole the identity (*abheda*) is merely a restatement (*anuvādya*) and not something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is consistent.

For this very reason, the author of the *Prakāśa* has appropriately provided the example of the fusion (*saṃkara*) of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the verse: "This orb of the moon, which bestows joy upon the eyes, is brightening.
This is the direction [for further study]. Hyperbole with concealment (*sāpahnavātiśayokti*) is that same [hyperbole] when it is infused with concealment (*apahnuti*).

If that very same *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor) is infused with concealment (*apahnuti*), it is called *sāpahnavātiśayokti* (hyperbole with concealment). Thus, it should be understood that *atiśayokti* is of two kinds, distinguished by the presence or absence of concealment.

Just as the peak of the king of mountains, who bears the hood of the serpent, possesses an inexhaustible treasure that is the livelihood for all, everyone considers it a "treasure" in the abode of Kubera; how great is this ignorance! 503.

Here, the statement "the crest-jewel of the lord of mountains is a treasure" (*nidhi*) is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*); yet, because it resides in the abode of the Giver of Wealth (*Dhanada*), it contains a concealment (*apahnuti*) in that it is not [merely] a treasure. Here, the denial (*nihnava*) is established by the sense itself through the presentation of innocence.

Just as the sun, the eye of the world, truly dispels the blindness of the world by roaring from the mountain peak of the lord of beasts, it would not be the "eye of the world" if it were to create some who are blind while leaving others in darkness. (504)

The blindness of the worlds means ignorance. "Katicana" refers to a few [beings], such as those blind by day. "Indhām" means "may they shine"; from the root *ñi indhī* in the sense of "to shine," this is the first person singular imperative in the active voice (*kartari*). Here, the phrase "the eye of the world roaring on the mountain peak of the lord of beasts" is an instance of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), while the underlying conceit (*paryastāpahnuti*) consists in the negation that the sun is the eye of the world.
Or, for example:

"This very thing is indeed the gārutmata [emerald], which is the jewel found upon the peak of Mount Gārutmata; those who are ignorant call it 'gārutmata,' while it is renowned as 'aśmagarbha' (emerald). (505)

This belongs to Garuḍa, thus it is *gārutmata*; and that mountain is indeed Śeṣādri, for its names are listed as "Vedādri and Garuḍādri. That which is the jewel on its crest—that is, on its peak—is the Lord Himself. Because it originates from the peak of the Garuḍa-mountain, this alone is the *gārutmata* jewel. However, the ignorant say that the *gārutmata* is that jewel which is renowned as *aśmagarbha*—meaning "having stone as its womb" or "born from stone"—and thus produced solely from rock.

The meaning is that those who claim that what is produced solely from stone possesses the nature of the *gārutmata* gem are indeed fools. Here, because the attributes of the *gārutmata* are denied in favor of an identification with the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), there is a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) containing a concealment (*apahnuti*). By the phrase "the ignorant say," the denial is rendered implicit. It should be noted that in the first example, there is a concealment consisting of pure *apahnuti*, whereas in the other two, because the denial of being the "eye of the world" and the "nature of the *gārutmata*" is supported by the presentation of a reason, they contain a concealed *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment) accompanied by a cause.
Thus, even in the case of *apahnuti-atiśayokti* (hyperbole with concealment), a twofold division must be accepted.

*Bhedakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of differentiation) occurs when that which is presented (*prastuta*) is described as something else. The meaning is that *bhedakātiśayokti* is where the "otherness" of the subject is described—even though there is no actual difference—in order to convey its world-transcending nature. This description of difference where there is no difference should be understood as being imposed (*āhārya*). The same applies to what follows. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the figure of *bhrānti* (error).

O maiden, this innocence of yours is one thing, while the wisdom of the ocean is quite another; for by it, the Lord whose banner is the king of serpents—the very cause of the world’s birth—has surely been purchased.

*Maugdhyam* (innocence) refers either to beauty or to a specific stage of life characterized by the definition: "A *mugdhā* is one whose youth is dawning and who has surpassed the god of love with her modesty"; *vaidagdhyam* (cleverness) is skillfulness.
Or rather,
this creation of yours is some kind of nectar-filled one, since the person who praises your virtues never tolerates even the slightest scent of an ordinary person, even if encountered by mere chance.

That person who recites and praises your description—this is some kind of creation consisting of nectar and consisting of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). The feminine gender is used here in accordance with the word *sṛṣṭi* (creation), which is the predicate. Therefore, this person who praises your qualities never, even by chance, tolerates the "fragrance"—that is, the association—with those who are *prākṛta*, meaning products of *prakṛti* (or, in another sense, commoners); as Amara states: "The *vivarṇa*, the *pāmara*, the *nīca*, the *prākṛta*, and the *pṛthagjana* [are synonyms for a low-born person]. They do not tolerate contact with them.

If this creation were merely natural (prākṛtī), how could it not tolerate even the scent of ordinary people? Therefore, I consider that this is not a natural creation, but rather something else entirely, composed of nectar—this is the intended meaning. Here, the distinction of those who praise the Lord from the common creation is described, even though they are included within the well-known natural creation. Or as another example: "O Lord, the mental state of Your venerable devotees is of a different kind; for it never, under any circumstances, partakes in the nature of egoism. (508)

"Āhaṃkārikatām" means being a transformation of the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*). Alternatively, that which "deserves the ego" is *āhaṃkārika*; its state is expressed by the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule "tadarhati. The meaning is "the state of being possessed of ego" (*ahaṃyutva*). Here, even though it is *āhaṃkārika*, the distinction of the mind devoted to the Lord (*bhāgavata-manas*) is described. The first [verse] is pure; the others are mixed with puns (*śleṣa*).
When a connection is asserted even where no connection exists for the sake of exalting the qualities of the description,
those who know the ornaments call that *saṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of connection).

The relation (saṃbandha) should be understood as that which, while being distinct from non-difference, cannot be defined as "otherness" (*anyatva*) and so forth. By this, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to varieties such as *rūpaka* or *atiśayokti*.
For example:

"I contemplate the crest-jewel of the mountain that feeds on the wind (Śiva), who has made the world dark with the abundance of the mass of light from his own most beautiful body, and whose forehead shines with moving locks of hair. (509)
Here, although there is no actual connection between the entire world and being darkened by the luster of the divine form of Śrīnivāsa, there is a statement of such a connection.

"Or rather, even we [the rocks] shall, in a few days, shake off our dullness by the dust from the feet of the milkmaids' eyes and manifest our womanhood"—thus do the rocks of the Lord of the Serpent Mountain rejoice. (510) "Dullness" (*jaḍimā*) here means insentience. Regarding the form *dhutajaḍimā*, the suffix *ḍāp* is applied according to the rule "ḍābubhābhyām."

Let us now clarify femininity: while the grammatical gender of "femininity" (*strītva*) residing in its own designating word is accessible only through the treatises on grammar, hereafter we shall gradually manifest the worldly femininity residing in the object itself—defined by the statement "a woman possesses breasts and hair"—as those [stones] have shaken off their stony nature through contact with the dust of the Lord’s feet. The sense is that they are like Halayudha’s wife, who attained the state of stone due to Gautama’s curse. Here, although the stones of the Ahi mountain lack a connection to such joy as described, the attribution of that connection is for the purpose of enhancing the excellence of the subject being described.
Or, for example:
"O Hari, as the splendor of the sun-like Kaustubha gem radiates all around you, the crest-jewels of the gods bowing in your presence become nothing more than common glowworms. (511)

O Hari! The supreme, most excellent crest-jewels became mere *kīṭamaṇis*—that is, glow-worms; the meaning is that in the presence of the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, which resembles the sun, they became obscured in their luster like glow-worms. This is according to the *Tiryakkāṇḍa* of the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇipariśiṣṭa*, which states: “In the sense of a glow-worm, the word *kīṭamaṇi* refers to the *yotirmīlī* (glow-worm) and the *tamomaṇi* (jewel of darkness). In the alternative interpretation, the word division is *aparāḥ*; thus, the crest-jewels, with the letter *ra* removed (*apagata-repha*), result in the form *kīṭamaṇayaḥ*. This is the meaning.

The pronunciation of the letter *a* after the letter *r* is for the sake of ease of articulation; the point is that when the consonant *r* itself is removed, one observes that the vowel *i* following the letter *k*—which is heard as being followed by *r*—and the vowel *ī* [following *k*] undergo the rule of *savarṇadīrgha* (lengthening into a homogeneous long vowel). Here, although there is no actual connection between the jewels on the crown and the status of being "jewels of insects" (*kīṭamaṇi*), such a connection is imagined. Furthermore, this other meaning is intended to produce an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
Even when there is a connection, the absence of that connection is declared to be the hyperbole of non-connection (asaṃbandhātiśayokti).
The meaning is that *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consisting of non-connection (*asaṃbandha*) is the conceptualization of non-connection even where a connection exists. For example:

"By serving the Lord of All, who dwells on the peak of Mount Girīśa and is like a hooded serpent, certain wise ones have become most fortunate; they do not at any time desire [anything else] for the sake of escaping rebirth. (512)
"For the sake of non-rebirth and for the highest good. Here, although there is a connection with the longing for liberation (*mokṣa*), it is described as being without such a connection.
Or rather:

"Just as men worship him who has descended from the peak of Mahīdhara after the exhaustion of the ascent, so do the immortals here worship him together with their consorts, free from the fatigue of descending."
Here, despite the connection between the descent and fatigue, there is a description of their lack of connection.
If there were simultaneity of cause and effect, this [sequence] would be preceded by a lack of succession.
When cause and effect are simultaneous, this hyperbole (atiśayokti) preceded by the word "akrama" would be "hyperbole of non-sequential order" (akramātiśayokti).
Just as they draw their bows, they draw the eyes of their enemies; and when they leave the earth in the hand of the Lord of the Collyrium Mountain (Śiva), they abandon even their songs.

When the Lord, whose hand rests upon Mount Añjana, takes up his bow—that is, when he strings it—his enemies take up their bows; in the alternative sense, the word is split as *ā-pam*: their eyes shed a flood of tears (*āp*). When that blessed hand releases the arrow (*gāṃ*), those enemies likewise abandon the earth (*gāṃ*); in the alternative sense, they leave the ground. The meaning is that they shed tears due to extreme distress. When that blessed hand releases the arrow, those enemies also abandon the earth; in the alternative sense, they leave the ground.
