In the phrase "saṃdadhati jahati," the form is the third person plural present indicative (*laṭ*) derived from the roots *dhā* (with the prefix *sam-*) and *hā*. According to Amara: "The word *go*—when viewed in its various senses—denotes heaven, water, cattle, speech, the thunderbolt, direction, the eye, the sun, the earth, and a woman; it is masculine when referring to a cow. Here, the simultaneity of cause and effect is described: at the very moment the bow is strung, the enemies shed tears; at the very moment the arrow is released, the earth is abandoned [by them]. Or, for example:
In agitation the host of enemies stirs forward, and in agitation they flee; O jewel upon the crest of the mountain-king who is the lord of beasts, they abandon their circle and abandon their circle.

When you move forward—whether out of agitation, haste in destroying the enemy, or with great earnestness—the host of enemies also moves forward; "agitation" (saṃbhrama) here conveys the aforementioned meaning, or in this context, refers to impetuosity or fear, as Abhara states, "saṃbhrama is haste," and the Ratnamālā says, "saṃbhrama [occurs] in earnestness, fear, or impetuosity. "Forward" (puraḥ) means ahead, and from his own city.

The meaning is this: when you employ the *sudarśana* discus, even the multitude of enemies abandons the *sudarśana* [city] and the kingdom, relinquishes them, and departs for another world. According to the *Ratnamālā*: “*Cakra* refers to a collection, a whirlpool, the wheel of a chariot, a kingdom, and an army.

Here, the simultaneity of cause and effect is expressed: at the very moment the Lord moves forward to subdue his enemies, the enemies abandon their city; and at the moment the *sudarśana* is employed, they abandon the kingdom.
O Lord of Veṅkaṭagiri, just as you enter into your armor for the sake of victory over enemies, even your foes are filled with great agitation, thinking, "Which fortress shall we ourselves enter? 516.

O Veṅkaṭagirinātha! When you put on your *kaṅkaṭaka*—that is, your armor (*kavaca*; "armor is called *uraśchada* or *kaṅkaṭaka*" according to Amara)—even your enemies are greatly agitated, thinking, "Let us too enter the *kaṅkaṭaka*"; in this alternative sense, they think, "Let us enter the mountain slope (*kaṭaka*; "the non-feminine *kaṭaka* is the mountain’s *nitamba*" according to Amara). Here too, the simultaneity between entering the armor and entering the mountain slope is demonstrated.
If an effect is bound [to its cause] by the mere fact of its attachment to that cause, it is declared by the skillful to be an *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) of extreme mobility.

The meaning is that *capalātiśayokti* (hyperbole of instability) is the description of an effect based merely on the possibility of a cause, even when that cause is absent. "Possibility" (*prasakti*) here means cognition.
For example:

"Some playful women, adorned with lotus garlands, sport about, restless in the lotus groves; for at that time, they were eager to serve Śrī [the Goddess of Fortune] in the dwellings of those [lotuses]. (517) In this verse, the women are described as being eager to serve Śrī in the abodes of the lotuses, even though the presence of Śrī—the cause for such eagerness—is not actually established. This is because the lotuses are merely the objects of their play. Thus, it is an instance of *capalātiśayokti*.

In this context, even in the absence of Śrīnivāsa’s personal service, it is described how his mere will brings about the activity of the Lord’s pastimes within the dwellings of his devotees; here, Śrī is identified as being of the nature of divine play (līlā).

Just as when you, O Enemy of Mura, ever desire battle and wish to enter into armor (*jāgara*), the host of enemies themselves enters into a state of wakefulness through constant anxiety, as if they were your foes. O Enemy of Mura! When you are at some time or other eager for battle—ready for combat—the word *raṇa* takes the third case ending according to the rule *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca*. For this very reason, *jāgara* refers to armor, as Amara states: *jāgaraḥ kavacostriyām*.

He desires to enter—that is, he wishes to penetrate—but once he has actually entered, the host of enemies, due to the agitation of fear (*raṇaraṇaka*), always—and not merely occasionally—attains wakefulness, armor, and the loss of sleep. Here, even in the absence of the actual cause consisting of being armored for battle, the effect consisting of the enemies' loss of sleep is described by the mere desire [to enter].

In these two examples, even in the absence of well-known causes such as the service of Śrīnivāsa or being prepared for battle, there is the emergence of an effect—namely, the desire to serve and the attainment of wakefulness by the enemies while [the Lord] sports in His abode. Since this aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*) arises solely through the figure of speech *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect in the absence of its cause), it is not *capalātiśayokti* (hyperbole of fickleness); therefore, no other distinct figure of speech should be postulated. This is just as in the verse: "Though not sprinkled with lac-dye, Your two feet are red," where the effect of redness appears despite the absence of the cause, which is the application of lac-dye.

This is because there is no lack of distinction [from *vibhāvanā*] in its description as the manifestation of an effect characterized by the absence of its cause. For this very reason, the ancients did not treat it as a separate figure. However, the Dīkṣitas maintain that while in *vibhāvanā* the absence of the cause must be explicitly stated (*vācya*), here the absence of the cause is merely implied (*gamya*) by the mention of the presence of the cause; nevertheless, perceiving the existence of a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) based on this alone, they declare it to be a distinct ornament (*alaṃkāra-antara*).
If there should be a reversal of the sequence between cause and effect,
those skilled in poetry call that *atyantātiśayokti* (hyperbole of extreme excess).

Just as for men, sins become more distant and greater blessings appear right before them, only afterwards does the connoisseur of flavors—the one who knows the nectar-flavor of the name of Veṅkaṭanātha—appear.

Or, just as the excessive dust and heat that pervades all paths are pacified beforehand, and only afterwards does the cloud rain as desired; so too is Kṛṣṇa, who dwells upon the peak of the Hill of Virtue (Vṛṣādri).

It pervades all paths; thus it is *sarvapathīnaḥ*. By the rule beginning with "tatsarvādeḥ pathi," the suffix *kha* is applied in the sense of "pervading. The meaning is "facing in all directions" (*sarvatomukha*). In such a state, where the excessive *rajas*—both as a specific quality and as dust—is present, the heat, whether internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth or seasonal (graiṣma), is pacified beforehand.

Afterwards, the Lord Kṛṣṇa—who resides upon the peak of Vṛṣādri, who is dense with all auspicious qualities, and who is "Kṛṣṇa" (dark) in one sense and a "Kṛṣṇa-ghana" (black cloud) in another—sheds rain at will, bestowing desired objects; in the other sense, he rains or sprinkles sufficiently, as the case may be.
Just as first the circle of darkness dissolves for those who are humble, afterwards the shimmering light, the friend of the lotuses, spreads among them.

Of the *tamas* (darknesses), which are both ignorance and physical obscurations; and of the *padminī*, which refers to Śrī (Lakṣmī), the lotus plant, and its friend—the Lord Sun—its "light" (*āloka*) being both his sidelong glance and its radiance. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *padminī* is used for a female elephant, a woman, Śrī, a lake, and the lotus plant."

In these three examples, the posteriority of the causes—the utterance of the Lord’s name, the raining [of clouds], and the spreading of the light of the sun—and the priority of the effects—the removal of sin, the allaying of heat, and the dissolution of darkness—are described; thus, there is conformity with the definition [of *paurvāparyaviparyaya-atiśayokti*]. The first is pure (*śuddhā*), while the second and third are mixed with *śleṣa* (paronomasia); this is the distinction. All three of these *atiśayoktis* are intended to convey the swiftness of the effect.

If it is asked, "Since the individual causes for the application [of the term] are absent among the aforementioned varieties, how can they be designated by the term 'hyperbole' (*atiśayokti*)?", the ancients reply: "The state of being any one of those varieties is itself the cause for the application of the term 'hyperbole' that is common to all; and that alone constitutes its general definition."

Others, however, maintain that there are not two distinct varieties of *atiśayokti*—namely, "non-connection where there is connection" and "connection where there is non-connection"—because such an exaggeration (*atiśaya*) exists almost invariably in all figures of speech other than *svabhāvokti*, such as metaphor (*rūpaka*), illuminator (*dīpaka*), simile (*upamā*), and concealment (*apahnuti*). For there is no aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) in the mere narration of things as they actually exist; furthermore, since even the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect is already encompassed by this very [figure], it cannot be established as a separate variety.

Therefore, they say that *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) consists in any one of the following: the swallowing (*nigīrya*) of the object (*viṣaya*) by the subject (*viṣayin*) and its subsequent determination (*adhyavasāna*); the attribution of otherness to that very [subject]; the conceptualization of an impossible thing through words such as "if" (*yadi*) and so forth; and the inversion of the sequence between cause and effect. However, let it not be so; rather, *atiśayokti* is simply the swallowing of the object by the subject through identification. As for the other modes, it is more appropriate to conceive of them as distinct, separate figures of speech.

Indeed, this definition of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) as a unique excellence common to these four types is not possible, on the basis of which they might be called a single figure of speech by virtue of being delimited by a single property (*dharma*). Nor should it be argued that "being any one of these" (*anyatamatva*) is what is common to all of them; for when there exists a distinctness in their aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*), "being any one of these" is not a determining factor. Otherwise, it would be easy to establish a definition of *atiśayokti* as "being any one of a few [figures] such as simile (*upamāna*) and metaphor (*rūpaka*)" or "being any one of all [figures]," and thereby one could easily subsume even similes and other figures under its varieties.

Nor should it be argued that there is a burden of complexity in postulating an additional ornament (*alaṃkāra*), for you too must accept that the nature of an ornament consists in its enhancing the excellence of the primary element; furthermore, I do not postulate any other category of entity [beyond the poetic figure itself], and the enumeration of the defining properties (*upādhi*) that subdivide ornaments is merely a human convention—so they say.

In reality, however, the general definition of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is: "being the object of a determinate cognition of a superimposition that is both voluntary (*āhārya*) and productive of aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*), while being distinct from metaphor (*rūpaka*). The phrase "while being distinct" (*satyantam*) excludes metaphor; "voluntary" (*āhārya*) excludes error (*bhrānti*); and "determinate cognition" (*niścaya*) excludes poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

In the first variety of *rūpaka-atiśayokti*, there is the non-difference (*abheda*); in the second, otherness (*anyatva*); in the third, relation (*saṃbandha*); in the fourth, non-relation (*asaṃbandha*); in the fifth, simultaneity (*sahatva*); in the sixth, the state of being produced by the application of a cause (*hetuprasaktijanyatva*); and in the seventh, the state of being the object of such a superimposition (*tathāvidhāropaviṣayatva*) regarding priority and posteriority (*pūrvāparatva*). Since these exist in all cases, the definition is consistently applicable throughout. Nor should it be argued that this leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because such a superimposition generally exists in figures of speech other than *svabhāvokti*, for we accept that as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Even when hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) exists as a subordinate element to another figure that constitutes the primary source of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), it is not appropriate to designate the poem by that [hyperbole], because only the predominant figure merits such designation. For this very reason, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, in the section on the figure of "Distinction" (*viśeṣa*), states: "In all such cases, hyperbole alone stands as the vital principle (*prāṇa*), for without it, there is generally an absence of the status of a poetic figure. Therefore it has been said:
'This is everywhere the "crooked expression" (*vakrokti*); by means of it, the meaning is brought to life.'"
"Poets should exert effort in this [poetry]; for what ornament is there without it? Thus [it is said].
Daṇḍin also said:
"They declare this utterance, honored by the Lord of Speech, to be the sole ultimate resort even for other figures of speech; it is that which is called *atiśaya* (hyperbole)."
Thus they also say: "It has been so stated."
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on Hyperbole (Atiśayokti), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Equal Pairing (Tulyayogitā):
"Whether it be the attributes of the objects under description alone, or of others alone, a single attribute [is common]."
Where [a quality] is described as being possessed [by both subjects], there *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) may occur.

The word *vā* (or) signifies an optional alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). Thus, *Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) occurs where there is a connection with a single attribute either among the subjects under discussion alone, or among those not under discussion alone; for the etymological derivation is: "that wherein there is *yogitā*—the state of being connected—with a single attribute of things that are 'equal,' meaning they possess a similarity based solely on being either contextual or non-contextual. In the phrase "of the subjects" (*varṇyānām*) and so forth, the plural number is indicative of both two and more. Furthermore, it should be understood that the attribute (*dharma*) here must be one that produces aesthetic charm (*camatkārin*).

Thus, the definition should be understood as follows: it consists in being either (1) a single striking property connected with multiple relevant [objects] alone, or (2) a single property connected with multiple irrelevant [objects] alone. The term "multiple" (*aneka*) is included to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as "The face has blossomed with a smile," where there is not a single property connected with multiple subjects such as the face, glances, and so forth. The term "alone" (*mātra*) is used to exclude the figure *dīpaka* (the Illuminator). The inclusion of the term "either/or" (*anyataratva*) is for the sake of ensuring that the definition applies equally to both the relevant and the irrelevant varieties.

In this context, *dharma* (the common attribute) generally occurs in the form of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*). Thus, it has been stated in the *Kuvalayānanda* that *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) consists in the connection of qualities or actions—whether they belong to the subject under discussion (*prastuta*) or not—with a single attribute. This is merely an illustration of any attribute whatsoever; this will become clear at the time of providing examples. Furthermore, the comparison here is implied (*gamya*), because the common attribute which serves as its basis is expressed, yet there is no word for "comparison" (*upamā*) itself.

For this very reason, it is understood that even for the Alaṃkārikas (theorists of poetics), similarity (*sādṛśya*) is a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*), and not merely the nature of common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*). Otherwise, the statement that comparison (*aupamya*) is here to be inferred would be untenable. Some, however, maintain that the state of similarity itself is an additional entity, whereas similarity consists precisely of those respective common attributes.

Furthermore, they also maintain that while the delimitor of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka) for the primary words is indeed that [similarity], even when words expressing those respective common properties convey that common property in the form of their own respective delimiters of denotability, the cognition of it in the form of a state of similarity is achieved solely through suggestion (vyañjanā).

Just as tears well up in the eyes, horripilation arises on the body, and agitation stirs the mind— so too does the añjali gesture arise upon the head for those who remember You, O Lord whose splendor is like the mountain of collyrium.

In this verse, because the Bhāgavatas are the subject of description, the action of pouring out (udañcana) of tears and so forth belonging to them—the agents under discussion—is employed as a common attribute (*sāmānadharma*) [for comparison], as are the eyes and other sense organs, which serve as the loci (*adhikaraṇa*). This is because all grammatical factors (*kāraka*) are equal in their connection with the action. Thus, although there is a unity of the attribute consisting of the action among all eight [elements], a comparison is perceived only between pairs, not mutually among all eight. This is because the general property culminates in the specific forms of being the locus and being the agent.
In that context, in the word *smaratām*, the genitive case is used according to the rule *adhīgartha* (Pāṇini 2.3.52).

O Mother, in your feet which remove the pride of the lotus, in your mind which tolerates the bowing of sinners, and in your speech composed of sweet syllables, a world-transcending softness shines forth most brilliantly.

In this context, "softness" is the quality (*guṇa*), and its possession by the feet and so forth constitutes the poetic figure; for the action of shining does not directly connect with the substrata themselves.

Just as the whiteness [of a conch] which was its refuge has been made its opposite by that [blackness], so too, in that very conch and in the discus, the indescribable majesty of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva) blazes forth.

By which conch (*śaṅkha*) whiteness (*dhavalimā*) was attained—that is, a pale state—and by which discus (*cakra*) whiteness was made "inverse" (*viparīta*), that is, overturned or cast aside; such is the apparent contradiction (*āpātato virodha*). Through the inversion of the sequence of the word *dhavalimā*, the form *mālivadha* is produced. One must also assume that the term *mālivadha*, though consisting of only a verbal root (*prakṛti*), functions as a nominal stem (*subanta*). Although there is a prohibition stating, "A mere root should not be employed," this does not constitute a fault in certain types of ornate poetry (*citrakāvya*).
As it has been said in the *Kāvyārthacintāmaṇi*: [text follows].
For even in cases of reversal or other such variations, the employment of the base form itself is not a fault in certain instances, just as one says "nadī dīnaḥ" (the river is wretched).

Thus [it is said]. However, the actual meaning is that by which discus the slaughter of the Rākṣasa named Māli was performed. One must not forget the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārtha-tādātmya*). The construction is: "In the conch and also in the discus of the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents, there is *maha*. Here, the two qualities of being a conch and a discus share a single common attribute in the form of the quality (*guṇa*) of *maha*. And if the second half-verse is read as: "Those two hands of the Lord of the Śeṣa-mountain illuminate the Pāñcajanya-conch and the discus," then the attribute is in the form of an action (*kriyā*).

And if it were said, "Those two [the conch and the discus] bear a wondrous radiance upon the five-fold people and the wheel of the Lord of the Bull-mountain," then there would be an action qualified by attributes, because there is no direct connection with the attribute alone, and because a bare action is unpleasant [as a subject]. In this case, however, both [attributes] are connected with the property [of radiance].

O Mother, neither your face, nor your pair of eyes, nor your heart is anything but serene; neither your pair of hands, nor your bimba-like lower lip, nor even your pair of feet is anything but crimson.

Here, in the case of the property (dharma) consisting of a negation—namely, "neither unpleasing nor reddish"—there is a co-occurrence (*anvaya*) of the face and other features, as well as the pair of hands and so forth, which are the subjects under discussion. For this very reason, in the definition, the term "property" (*dharma*) was introduced in its general sense alone, rather than being specified as being of the nature of a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*). This [definition] follows the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*. For he, while refuting the statement in the *Kuvalayānanda*—"Tulyayogitā is the co-occurrence of a single property, whether of the nature of a quality or an action, among subjects that are either relevant (*prastuta*) or irrelevant (*aprastuta*)"—argues that the mention of "being of the nature of a quality or an action" is merely superficial.
O King, while you rule the entire circle of the earth,
there is not even the slightest anxiety in the realm regarding either enemies or friends.

In this regard, he stated that it is because only a property (dharma) consisting of a negation (abhāva) is the logical concomitant (anvaya). Others, however, maintain that in the verse "śāsati," the distinction from "niścinta" (free from anxiety) is presented as a property belonging to the circle of enemies and friends; thus, it is indeed of the nature of a positive quality (guṇasvarūpa), because the distinction of one who possesses the absence of anxiety is not distinct from the anxiety itself. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the absence of the absence of anxiety would have to be something distinct.

Now, even if we grant that this is acceptable there, they say: how can non-existence (*abhāva*) be excluded from the category of qualities (*guṇa*), since both the grammarians—who maintain that "the application of words is fourfold" (referring to genus, quality, substance, and action)—and their followers, as well as the rhetoricians, admit its status as a quality? For this very reason, the examples cited by the author of the *Prakāśa* in the case of a contradiction between genus and quality—namely, “even mountains are devoid of loftiness” (*girayo 'py anun-nati-yujaḥ*)—and that cited by Vidyānātha—“even the sovereign emperor is without pride” (*amadaḥ sārvabhaumo 'pi*)—become consistent.

If the absence of such qualities as "lack of loftiness" were not itself a quality (*guṇa*), then the citation of that example would be clearly inconsistent. Therefore, since even an absence can be a quality, there is no fault whatsoever in stating that a *dharma* (attribute) takes the form of a quality or an action. Thus, it should be understood that even in this example, in cases such as "not un-clear," the *dharma* is indeed of the nature of a quality. In reality, however, we have included the *dharma* in the definition under that very form; therefore, there is no defect at all.

For him, there was both the goddess Ramā, who is as unswerving as the ocean on the crest-jewel of Mount Adhiphaṇi, and sovereign power; and his mental disposition, as well as his compassion, were vast in their forbearance.

The Lord, the jewel of the serpent-mountain (Śrīparvata), was like a rain-cloud; [the compound *adhiphaṇigirimaṇinīradam* is an *avyayībhāva* used in the sense of a case-ending]. *Ramā* was unshakable (*acañcalā*), yet she acted as if she were fickle (*cañcaleva*); the meaning is that she shone like lightning. From the word *cañcalā*, with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of habitual action, the feminine gender is formed and the augment *aṭ* is added. Her sovereignty (*vibhutā*)—that is, her majesty (*aiśvarya*)—was also unshakable, meaning steady. This is derived from the root *as* (in the sense of "to exist") in the *laṅ* tense. The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *astisico’pṛkte*, and because the elision of *śna* and *as* is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *abhīya*, the augment *āṭ* is applied.

The mental disposition (*mānasavṛtti*) of that Blessed One was, through his forbearance (*kṣamā*) and patience (*kṣānti*), not narrow but acted as if it were vast; the meaning is that it was equal to the earth (*bhūtulyā*). From the word *vipula*, by adding the suffix *kvip* to denote habitual action and applying the *luṅ* (aorist) as before, [the form *vipuleta* is derived]. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *vipule* [and *ita*]. And his compassion (*karuṇā*) was vast—that is, great. The sense is that for Śrī-Śrīnivāsa, sovereignty, forbearance, and mercy are rooted in his abiding with Śrī-Lakṣmī. Here, because of the absence of both qualities and actions common to both [the Lord and the earth], the meaning—either the verbal expression alone or the object unified through the superimposition of non-difference based on the root-word pun (*śleṣa*)—is the poetic figure (*dharma*). Or, for example:
O Murāri, your neck, adorned with a string of pearls, has surpassed a row of teeth; yet, O lotus-eyed one, your chest and mind have never once been surpassed by pride.

O Murāri! The analysis of the compound is *tava dantālī muktālyā* (your row of teeth [is] like a string of pearls). Regarding the term *asitā*, there is a compound with the negative particle *na*; the meaning is that it is not "not black" (*asitā*), but rather "white" (*sitā*). Furthermore, *grīvā api ca muktālyā* uses the third case singular; the meaning is that the neck is not "unbound" (*asitā*)—that is, not tied—by the pearl-string (*muktālyā*), but is indeed "bound" (*sitā*). As Amara states: "The words *baddha*, *saṃdānita*, *mūta*, *mudrita*, *saṃdita*, and *sita* [are synonyms for 'bound']."

O lotus-eyed one! Your chest and your mind are "not lacking in joy" (*apramadam*); the meaning is that they are not devoid of prideful women (*avidyamāna-māninīkam*) nor devoid of Lakṣmī (*avidyamāna-lakṣmīkam*), but rather possess Lakṣmī and are full of joy. Here, even the possibility of negating whiteness and the presence of joy is excluded by the two *nañ*s. As Vāmana has stated: "In the case of the exclusion of a negation that was merely possible, there are two prohibitions.
Here too, as in the previous example, it is a quality (*dharma*); the difference, however, is that its nature here is that of an absence.
In some cases, even a word denoting a property (dharma) that is supplied by ellipsis (adhyāhṛta) brings about the figure *tulyayogitā*. For example:

"O Acyuta, your form is most divine, this prosperity of yours is most auspicious, and this garland of forest flowers is most worthy of praise; what need have you for the objects of the senses, since you are transcendent? (528)

The meaning is that if there were *paratva* (remoteness) in you, there would have to be an object of doubt; the point is that doubt does not exist at all. Here, the divine form and other qualities under discussion are connected with the verb “exists” (*asti*) by virtue of their function as the basis for the doubt regarding *paratva*. This is according to the grammatical rule: *“The root *as* exists even when the term *bhavanti* is used instead. In this context, *bhavanti* is a designation for the present tense (*laṭ*). The suffix *jhic* is added to the root *bhū* by the Uṇādi rule *“bhuvo jhic”*; then, by the rule *“jho’ntaḥ”*, the *jha* of *jhic* is replaced by *anta*. Thus, the form *bhavant-ī* is derived.

Even when a verb (*ākhyāta*) is not explicitly employed, it is implied because of its rapid presentation. If it is asked, "In that case, why is it not supplied in every sentence?", the answer is no; for, on the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more logical that what has been supplied in one place should be supplied by way of ellipsis (*anuṣañjana*) elsewhere. An example of this kind is demonstrated in Viśveśvara’s *Alaṃkāra-kaustubha*.

Just as the entire host of humans and the entire host of demons bow down to that which is worthy of being bowed to, how could there be any talk of non-distinction here regarding the crest-jewel of the serpent-king and the mountain? (529)

In accordance with the statement, "He who is to be bowed to is the Supreme Residue," the entire host of humans and the host of demons bow to the crest-jewel of the mountain-king of serpents, who is worthy of being made the object of salutation as the Residue of all. Herein lies the point: how could there be any talk of non-difference between the groups of humans and demons who bow, since, despite the lack of distinction in their act of bowing, there remains a mutual difference between humans and demons?

Alternatively, regarding this Lord who is to be saluted, how could there be any talk of non-difference with those who salute Him? The sense is that non-difference is impossible between the saluter and the one saluted, or between the subordinate (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin). Or else, "here" refers to the two groups—the humans and the demons—who are saluting; there is no talk of non-difference regarding their pride (*mada*). Pride is a particular mental affliction caused by the conceit of one's lineage, character, and so forth, which leads to the contempt of others, and it is reckoned among the group of six internal enemies (*ari-ṣaḍ-varga*).

The sense is: how could there not be news of his division—that is, the account of his being split—among those who bow to the Blessed One, since all defects such as desire have been removed? In the alternative sense (pakṣe), here, how could there not be news of the difference between the two words *mānava* and *dānava*—that is, the report of the distinction between the letters *ma* and *da*? For the difference between them is clearly visible to that extent. Here, there is a commonality of the attribute consisting of the act of bowing (*namana-kriyā*) between the two groups, *mānava* and *dānava*, which are not the primary subject. Or, for example: The sense is: how could there not be news of the difference between the two words *mānava* and *dānava*—that is, the report of the distinction between the letters *ma* and *da*? For the difference between them is clearly visible to that extent. Here, there is a commonality of the attribute consisting of the act of bowing (*namana-kriyā*) between the two groups, *mānava* and *dānava*, which are not the primary subject. Or, for example: [Example: "O Lord, the moon has risen; the night-lotuses have blossomed; and the bees are humming. Here, the commonality of the attribute of "humming" (*guñjana*) exists between the bees (*alīnām*), which are the primary subject, and the quarters of the sky (*diśām*), which are not the primary subject. Or, for example: "O King, your fame has ascended to the peak of Mount Meru, and the sun has descended into the western ocean. Here, the commonality of the attribute of "ascending" (*ārohaṇa*) exists between the fame (*yaśasaḥ*), which is the primary subject, and the sun (*raviṇaḥ*), which is not the primary subject. Or, for example: "The lotus-faces of the women of the city have blossomed, and the night-lotuses have closed their eyes. Here, the commonality of the attribute of "closing the eyes" (*nimīlana*) exists between the faces (*mukhānām*), which are the primary subject, and the night-lotuses (*kumudānām*), which are not the primary subject. Or, for example: "The sun has set behind the western mountain, and the moon has risen from the eastern mountain. Here, the commonality of the attribute of "rising" (*udaya*) exists between the sun (*raviṇaḥ*), which is the primary subject, and the moon (*induḥ*), which is not the primary subject. That which shines as the supreme form within the intellect of the wise indeed shines even in the sun; I understand that the Veda and the verbal testimony declare it to be the one Supreme Being, whose nature is eternally worthy of praise.
That form of the Supreme Brahman which flashes forth in the intellect— the contemplative insight— of the virtuous yogis,
this Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth.
But it is seen by those of subtle vision through a sharp and subtle intellect.

The intended meaning is that, according to the method stated in the Śruti, the essential nature (svarūpa) remaining after the internal ruler’s (antaryāmin) divine form is perceived by those with subtle vision through a subtle intellect endowed with one-pointed concentration. For the word "hi" signifies both cause and emphasis, according to Amara. The "supreme form" (pararūpa)—the form of the Supreme Brahman described in such Śruti passages as "This golden person who is seen within the sun"—which is characterized by a divine, auspicious body, shines and blazes even within Mārtaṇḍa, the sun.

To the question, "How is their identity known by you?", he says, "He said. The Śruti states: "That which is here in the person and that which is there in the sun, that is one. This means that the Supreme, whose nature is Being (*sat*), is to be reckoned by its true form (*ākṛti*)—that is, by its glorious manifestation; the sense is that it is characterized by a divine, auspicious body. The meaning is that the Supreme, which is the very nature of the Paramātman, exists in both places. "One" means non-different; "I say" (or "I know")—therefore I understand; this is the sense of the sentence, with the act of knowing as the object.

And the verbal expression conveys this very meaning; for instance, "that which is correct" (*sādhu*) means that which is properly taught (*samyaganuśiṣṭa*), namely, a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) consisting of the subsequent form—the attainment of the status of the following phoneme by the preceding phoneme—within the word *manīṣā*. It "shines forth" or manifests in the word *manīṣā*. The sense is that this is because, in the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) of *manasa īṣā*, the attainment of the form of the subsequent phoneme *ī* by the *as* (the syllable *as*) occurring immediately after the letter *n* is clearly evident.

For that very same *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent vowel) manifests even in the word *mārtaṇḍa*. The point is this: in the derivation of *mārtaṇḍa*—meaning "born from a dead egg" (*mṛte aṇḍe jātaḥ*)—one observes the *ekādeśa* (single substitution) of the vowel *a*, which follows the letter *t* in the base word *mṛtaṇḍa* (the source of the secondary suffix), with the vowel *a* that follows it. However, between these two words, only one—the word *mārtaṇḍa* as read later—is [included]; not even the word *manīṣā*, because its inclusion is seen in a different list to be mentioned later. This is the intended meaning.

"Always to be counted by its form" means to be included, by way of its external form (*ākṛti*), within the *śakandhvādi* group; "having obtained the 'wealth-group'" refers to the suffix *-yat* [in *gaṇya*]. By the word *labdha*, ending in the suffix *-tṛn*, the habitual nature of obtaining is indicated. This means it is fit to be recited in the aforementioned group. The "verbal statement" refers to the Vārttika of the science of grammar which states: "In the case of *śakandhu* and others, the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) should be prescribed. I say this—that is, I understand and consider it so.

I consider that, because the word *mārtaṇḍa* is not included in the list [of words] like *manīṣā*, this word should be read in the *śakandhvādi* group by way of its having the aforementioned *pararūpa* (substitution of the subsequent vowel). The implication is that otherwise, in the absence of another rule prescribing *pararūpa*, this word would incur the status of being ungrammatical (*asādhutā*). For this very reason, the statement at the end of the *śakandhvādi* list—that "this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class), as in the case of *mārtaṇḍa*"—is consistent.

The meaning of the Vārttika is that, for the sake of deriving the forms of words such as *śakandhu* and others, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) for the *ṭi* [the final vowel and following consonant] must be stated in those words. Here, the two unrelated terms, "hearing" (*śruti*) and "verbal expression" (*śābdokti*), are connected with the verb "says" (*āha*). This [verse] is embellished by the figure of speech *śleṣa* (punning).

Or rather, O jewel of the Bull-hill (Śrīśaila), both the excellent jewel of the gods (Viṣṇu) and the excellent jewel of the gods (Indra) surely resort to your splendor; for these two are indeed equal, being undivided from Lakṣmī.

O Lord of Vṛṣādri! [The assembly of] the *gaṇikās*—meaning the multitude of courtesans (*gaṇikā*) of the best of gods (*suravara*), [expressed as] *gāṇikyam* according to the rule "the suffix *yañ* should be stated after the word *gaṇikā*" (Pāṇini 4.2.39)—and the sapphire jewel (*indranīla-ratna*), which is the *māṇikya* (ruby) among the best of gods, [both] [attain] your splendor (*lakṣmī*), meaning beauty; in another sense, [your] fortune (*śrī*). By the phrase "your *lakṣmī*," the well-known state of being eternally and permanently devoted to another as a wife, as in "Viṣṇu’s *Śrī* is inseparable" (*viṣṇośśrīranapāyinī*), is suggested. *Amara* states: "From *gaṇikā* and others, the form is *gāṇikya*. (Amara-kośa 3.5.10). (Note: The commentary explains that the *gaṇikā-s* of the gods and the *indranīla* jewel both acquire the *lakṣmī*—the beauty or fortune—of the Lord.)

The phrase "by your own appropriate splendor" is to be understood here as referring to this. They both serve and honor [you]. The sense is that even the luster of sapphire utterly fails to surpass the beauty of your divine form. In the alternative sense (the allegorical), the multitude of Apsarases such as Rambhā, having become your handmaidens, attend upon your divine queen—this is the intended meaning. Do not think, do not consider these two—the jewel of the best of gods and the courtesan of the best of gods—to be distinct or mutually different; for "those roots which have the sense of 'going' also have the sense of 'knowing'."

Why [is this so]? These two are indeed equal to one another in their possession of the quality (*dharma*) consisting of the act of serving the fortune (*lakṣmī*) of Your Lordship. In this context, the compound *suravaramāṇikyasuravaragāṇikyarūpe pade* is a single term; the meaning is that they are distinct from each other, possessing differentiation solely through the letters *mā* and *gā*. They are indeed equal in having the same sequence of other phonemes.

Here too, as before, there is a connection (*anvaya*) between the two non-subjects—the *māṇikya* (ruby) and the *gāṇikya* (courtesan)—and the action of serving performed upon the Fortune of the Blessed One.

In those whose inner hearts were distressed by anxiety over the weight of the humiliation inflicted by Hari’s splendor, a state of insensibility appeared, as if they were blue lotuses, clouds, and sapphires.

In this case, it is a *guṇa* (quality), because the action of manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) does not directly connect with the subjects (*dharmi*). If one were to compose the second and third quarters as “The inner organs, distressed by anxiety, became utterly withered,” and the fourth quarter as “Indīvaras, clouds, and sapphire gems,” then it would be an *kriyā* (action). If the third quarter were instead made “They assume insentience,” then it would be an *kriyā* qualified by a quality (*guṇa*). Thus, in subsequent cases, one should infer [the distinction] as appropriate.
O hero of the Yadu clan, by your greatness, the minds and faces of the asuras have become soiled, while the faces of the women of the gods and the quarters of the sky have become stainless.

In this instance, "stainedness" (*malīmasatva*) is a quality (*guṇa*) in the first half-verse; in the second half-verse, according to some, the property consisting in the absence of stainedness—expressed as "spotless" (*nirmalāni*)—is [the subject], but in reality, that too is indeed a quality.
Or rather,
O Blessed One, when the gods, asuras, kinnaras, or even humans adorn Vṛṣagiri because of you, those who lack devotion and those whose desires have not been fulfilled shall never exist there.
In this case as well, as in the previous example, it is indeed a merit (guṇa).
Or rather, just as at first they were of opposing colors and generally avoided each other's sight, now they both delight in me, who am of their own color— just like the bee and the white lotus.

O Rāme! That bee (*cañcarīka*), renowned for its dark-blue color, and the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*)—both of which were previously described as having mutually contradictory colors due to their being black and white respectively (the neuter form remaining according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*); then, subsequently, at some point... [the rest of the sentence follows].

By your glance—that is, by your side-long look (*kaṭākṣavīkṣaṇa*)—those two [the eyes] become *savarṇe*, meaning they possess an identical color (*samāno varṇo yayos tau*). The sense is that through the blackness or whiteness of the side-long look, they become either black-colored or white-colored. This is because the duality of color in side-long glances is established by poetic convention (*kavisamayasiddha*), as seen in such passages as: "The side-long glances have the luster of seizing the dark Yamunā and the blue water-lilies," and "The line of the side-long glances is a companion to the streams of the bride's rays. The word *prāyaḥ* is used here in the sense of probability or possibility.

In the case of the two words *cañcarīka* and *puṇḍarīka*, in their first parts—which consist of four syllables each—they possess letters (*akṣara*) that are mutually contradictory. The sense is that this is because the initial segments, namely *cañca* and *puṇḍa*, have mutually opposing forms. Then, after the two syllables, there is the word *īkṣaṇe*; the word *na* is to be separated [as a distinct particle]. This *na* connects with what follows. "Upon seeing" (*īkṣaṇe*) means when there is a correct investigation (*samyag-vimarśe*).

The word division is *rame asavarṇe*. In this interpretation, *te* is the nominative dual. The sense is that the bee (*cañcarīka*) and the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) are "not of the same color" (*asavarṇa*) mostly—that is, for the most part, but not entirely—because at the end [of the words], their dissimilarity is seen through the presence of the visarga and the bindu respectively; thus they do not become non-dissimilar, but rather remain similar. Alternatively, let *īkṣaṇena ete* be a single inseparable compound ending in the instrumental case.

Let it simply be "they sport with one of their own kind" (*savarṇe*). Thus, by observation and reflection, the meaning is that they generally [sport] only with one of their own kind—that is, with one whose sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is identical. The sense of "in both places" is due to the identity of the sequence of phonemes in the word *rīkā*. Here too, there is only a quality (*guṇa*), because the action of "becoming" does not directly connect with the two subjects; rather, the connection of the mentioned quality is with the bee (*cañcarīka*) and the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), which are not the primary subjects of the sentence. And this [figure] is distinguished by its being a mixture with the *tadguṇa* ornament to be described hereafter, and by its being embellished by a specific charm consisting of the description of the phonemes as the secondary object.

Just as the cloud and the blue lotus, though they contain the world within their bellies and are themselves eternally insentient, appear here clearly within the world— O Blessed One, even these two external things have become mere metaphors for You.

Here too, as in the previous example, it is indeed a *guṇa* (poetic excellence). The sense is this: although the cloud and the blue lotus are respectively compared to the Lord through their capacity to support the world within their bellies and their entry into the interior of the world, they are excluded from that comparison because of their eternal insentience (*nityajaḍatva*). This [figure] is established through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) based on the pun (*śleṣa*) between the words *bhuvana* (world) and *jaḍa* (insentient). "O Lord, O you who protect the worlds with your splendor, shining upon the mountain of the lord of serpents, the mass of the splendors of your enemies does not shine even within its own home. (537)

By your great splendor (*maha*), the multitude of enemies was seized within your own home; this is the *liṭ* (perfect tense) in the passive sense from the root *grah* preceded by the prefix *ni*. For this very reason, you "shone" (*abhāsi*)—the sense being that you shone because of being the subduer of enemies. This is the *ciṇ* (passive suffix) in the *luṅ* (aorist) for the sense of the verb *bhās*. The particle *api* is used as a conjunction (*samuccaye*). Even the multitude of their splendors—their own fires—did not shine (*abhāsi*); that is, they lacked luster (*bhāsa*), which means appearance or light. The word *bhāsa* is derived from *bhās* with the suffix *ghan*. That which possesses such luster is *bhāsi*; the negative form of that is *abhāsi*.

The sense is: "If it is not manifest even in its own home, how much less elsewhere? The word *khalu* is used for well-known fact (*prasiddhi*). Here, since the two subjects under discussion—the enemy and the sun—lack common qualities or actions, the *dharma* (attribute) is either the word alone or the meaning based on the identification rooted in *śleṣa* (punning).

O Mother, just as a person who has attained supreme sovereignty, when looked upon by you, finds peace even if neglected— so too does one whose thirst was roused by the great Amarāvatī find relief once the letter has been delivered.

O Mother! The person beheld by you attains *param-śreṣṭham*—the state of being most excellent, that is, the status of Maghavan (Indra); in another sense, the word *param* is split [as a separate adjective], meaning "extremely. He is one who experiences *aghavattvam*—the state of suffering, sinfulness, or addiction; as Amara states: "*aṃhaḥ* [is used] for sorrow, calamity, and sin (*agham*). He is so called because he is one by whom the *lekhās*—the gods—have been *abhyudūḍhāḥ*, meaning lifted up or rescued from all misfortunes.

In one sense, he is so called because he has carried (*abhyudūḍha*)—that is, made the subject of his transport—the *lekhās*, or royal writs; the meaning is "a messenger. (The *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *lekha* refers to a written document or a god"). In the other sense, he is so called because he possesses a great and surging thirst (*udīrṇa-tṛṣṇā*)—a desire for ever-increasing advancement—in that great *amarāvatī* (the city of the gods). In the alternative sense, he is one who has a great thirst in the vast desert (*mahatī marau*), for the *Amara* lexicon states: "The words *maru* and *dhanvan* are synonymous" (referring to arid land).

He is so described because his *tṛṣṇā*—meaning both longing and thirst—is exceedingly aroused and excessively increased. As Amarasimha states: “*Tṛṣṇā* has two meanings: desire and thirst. He is exhausted; the sense is that in one case by activities such as lifting the gods, and in the other by carrying documents and the like. Here too, as before, the figure of speech (*dharma*) is to be understood in the same way.

O Mother, the fish, the cakora birds, and the deer, conquered by your eyes, have fled to the forest; even the coral, sprouts, and bimba fruits have been cast away by your lips.

In the word "vana" (forest), the meaning should be understood as either the forest or water, as appropriate. Since corals are born from the ocean, their presence in a "forest" is possible. It should be noted that because of the perception that "the cakora bird is like a fish" and "the deer is like a cakora bird," they take the form of a girdle. In reality, however, this is simply the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing), consisting of the connection of many unrelated subjects with a single common attribute; for in its definition, the plural term "of the subjects" (*varṇyānām*) or "of others" (*anyeṣām*) is used.

And where there is the connection of actions—whether they be only those under discussion (*prakṛta*) or only those not under discussion—with a single grammatical factor (*kāraka*), that is *sākārakatulyayogitā*, according to Jagannātha and others.

Who else besides the Lord of the Mountain of Kākoda is capable of sustaining the worlds, uplifting the earth, removing the calamities of those who have sought refuge, and bestowing infinite spiritual welfare?
According to another opinion, however, this is simply the figure of speech called *samuccaya* (accumulation), which will be discussed hereafter.
This is an example of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*):
"O Murāri, where there is talk of your splendor blazing day and night, who could possibly be the sun or even the fire playing there at any time?"

Here, by the phrase "who knows?", the impossibility of counting anything other than the expressed (vācya) and the indicated (lakṣya) meanings is suggested through its connection with the moon and fire, which are themselves non-contextual (aprakṛta).
The second type of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) is considered another [variety], wherein there is equality of behavior toward both the beneficial and the harmful;
the meaning is that this other *tulyayogitā* consists in the equality of conduct regarding objects that are either beneficial or harmful.
Just as you granted an identical station to the Caidyas and others who cursed you, and even to the yogis who chanted your name—tell me, O Yadu prince, what is this skill of yours? ||442||

Here, the Lord is addressed as a scion of the Yadu lineage in order to make known that the intended subject matter pertains to His incarnation; even therein, the address "O Youth" (kumāra) is used with the intention of implying His innocence regarding the distinction between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Just as you have made the son of the Ocean (the Moon) a friend and the enemy (Rāhu) an adversary, yet you say, "There is no one hateful nor dear to me"— this is not at all surprising to you.

A friend, such as Arjuna and others, has been made to attain *śam*, meaning happiness; likewise, even an enemy has been treated similarly—on the other hand, the meaning is that he has been *śamita*, i.e., destroyed.

Or rather, O Lord of the Serpent Mountain, though [the sun] is turned away from you there, you cause it to partake in the fullness of your majesty as it faces your feet; what indeed is this maturity of yours?

The term *vaibhavasya* refers to the pervasion (*abhivyāpti*) of majesty (*vibhutva*). This is derived from the verbal root *mūrch*, meaning "to faint" (*moha*) and "to rise up" (*samucchrāya*), with the suffix *lyuṭ*. In the interpretation where [the word] is directed toward the [divine] presence (*sammukhīna-pakṣe*), it means "possessing that. However, regarding the remote object (*parācīna-viṣaya*), the indeclinable *vai* signifies "well-known"; thus, the meaning is: "In this worldly existence (*saṃsāre*), you extend [your power] to those who possess absorption (*saṃmūrchanabhājaṃ*)—that is, those who possess delusion (*mohabhājaṃ*)."

O Acyuta, just as the multitude of beings—though always subject to birth and death—is rendered free from fear by you, so too is this great wonder of mine even greater, since even my own mind was once full of doubt. (545)

O Acyuta! By you, the people (janatā) are made both *vinatā* (bowed down) and *vimatā* (devoid of pride). She is one whose *āsthā* (steadfastness or faith) is always directed toward those who are *vinata-pakṣa* (of humble disposition) and who are knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*); or rather, she is one whose *āsthā* is excellent (*praśasta*) because it rests upon such persons. Furthermore, she is made one whose birth (*janman*) is *vara* (supreme or excellent). Because the word ends in the suffix *man*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is not applied. In another sense, they are made *sadā-sthāvara-janmā*—that is, constantly possessing births as immobile things such as trees and the like. The particle *hi* indicates well-known fact. The rest is clear. O Kṛṣṇa, you have thoughtlessly arranged for the consumption of black fruits by the well-nourished calves and the young palm trees alike, thereby violating the established order.

O Kṛṣṇa! And this address [“O Kṛṣṇa”] is intended to indicate that the unique deeds of His incarnations are what is meant here in this verse. Those by whom the cows (dhenavaḥ) have been well-nourished are *paripuṣṭadhenukāḥ*; the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule “*śeṣādvibhāṣā*”. In the alternative sense, those among whom the demon named Dhenuka—who took the form of a donkey—was well-nourished; these are the *savayasām*, meaning companions (*vayasyānām*), as Amara states: “*snigdhaḥ vayasyaḥ savayāḥ*. In the other sense, it means “of those having wings” (*sapakṣiṇām*).

The *Viśva* lexicon states: “*Vayas* [means] bird, childhood, and so forth. In the first case, where the analysis (*vigraha*) is "those whose age (*vayas*) is the same (*samāna*) at the beginning," the substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs according to the rule *jyotirjanapadādi*. In the second case, where there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with *saha-* as the prior member—"that which exists together with birds (*vayas*)"—the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* occurs according to the rule *vopasarjanasya*.

Without considering the difference—that is, the disparity—between the childish cowherd boys and the *tāla* trees, the kings of grass, you [the demon] imagined the consumption of fruits by means of fruits; or, in another sense, you brought about the falling down of the fruits. "Batā" expresses wonder. Here, the story of the slaying of the demon Dhenuka from the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata* should be well-recollected.

The phrase "without considering the difference between the sounds of *bāla* and *tāla*," meaning without disregarding the distinction between the letters *ba* and *ta*, also nourishes an extraordinary aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). Here, it should be understood that the non-beneficial nature of the *tālas* is due to their being the refuge of the demon Dhenuka, who was harmful to others.

Or rather, O Lord whose crest is the mountain of serpents (Śiva), it is a marvel that you treat as beneficial that which is harmful—[a person] who is characterized by hatred for the virtuous, who is inclined toward a path that is not the true way and is contrary to the scriptures, who is beset by misfortune, and whose mind is utterly empty and void; for [the word] *ahita* means one who has hatred for the good, and such a person is described as being prone to an improper path, accompanied by ill fortune (*ariṣṭa*), and possessing an extremely empty (*atirikta*) or trivial intellect (*ātman*). [The Amarakośa states: "The words *vaśika*, *tuccha*, and *rikta* mean empty. The meaning is that he is devoid of intelligence. [Such a person] is treated [by you] as beneficial. 547.

And thus, what is beneficial is performed. On one hand, his dress is excellent; on the other, he is inclined toward that path which is delightful due to its conformity with the scriptures. The sense is that his dress and so forth are in accordance with his age, occupation, and purpose, according to the rule: "of age, action, and wealth. He is endowed with *ariṣṭa*, meaning auspiciousness—Amara states, "the word *ariṣṭa* refers to both the auspicious and the inauspicious. His nature (*ātman*) is *atirikta*, meaning exceeding or superlative; the meaning is that his character is extraordinary.
Amara states, "*atirikta* means exceeding. Thus, a marvelous thing is being accomplished.

Just as a clear jewel, O Acyuta, bestows its luster upon the kingdom that rests upon it, so do you—though unworthy of being a mere ornament for your lineage—bring welfare, and even harm, to people. 548.

O Acyuta! You fashion even an unfriendly person in such a way that he becomes like one whose splendor and beauty are as manifest and clear as the luster of jewels—using the suffix *ka* according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*. You make him one who is resorted to by a preeminent and supreme radiance, meaning one who bestows prosperity upon the entire kingdom; indeed, you make him worthy of being an ornament for his lineage. It is truly a marvel that you fashion even an enemy in this very same manner.

In reality, however, he is one who has near him even harmful people—clearly visible jars made of clay; for Amara states, "A *maṇika* may be a *alañjara*. He is making the kingdom into a frying pan (*bhrāṣṭra*), meaning he is fashioning it into a vessel for roasting; that is, by prefixing the letter *bh* (the third case singular) to the syllable *bhā*, which stands for the foremost (*prāgryeṇa*) or best part of the kingdom. This is because, by attaching the consonant *bh* alone to the beginning of the word *rāṣṭra*, the form *bhrāṣṭra* is produced.
Therefore, he is a potter (*kulāla*), and for that very reason, he is unfit and unworthy for the performance of good deeds (*satkarma*).
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the basket-maker,
the fisherman, the Meda, the Bhilla, the goldsmith, and the tailor.
The woodcutter, the oil-presser, the butcher, the wheelwright, the banner-bearer,
the barber, and the artisan— these sixteen are the outcastes (janaṅgama).
The meaning is that, according to the statement of Parāśara, he is included among the village-caṇḍālas.

Just as Your power, O Acyuta, perceives both friend and foe when You have assumed the office of a domestic priest on earth and attained the lordship over Puloma’s daughter, so indeed does it perceive them now.

O Acyuta! Your power and prowess perceive that your friend—Yudhiṣṭhira and the others—who has attained a state of benevolence and favor toward the citizens and townsmen (the compound being formed according to the rule *caturthī tadartha*), have obtained the status of the Lord of Pulomajā’s husband—that is, the sovereignty over Śacī, or rather, the lordship over the earth, meaning universal sovereignty—upon the surface of the earth; yet they perceive their enemy in exactly the same way. Alas, what a marvel!

In reality, in the case of the enemy's side (*amitrapakṣe*), the state of being the Lord of Pulomajā (*pulomajāteśvaratva*)—meaning the state of being the Lord of Lomajā (*lomajāteśvaratva*)—has reached a state of being devoid of or separated from the letter *pu*. This is because such a form is produced by the removal of the letter *pu* [from *puloma*]. The sense is that it is utterly base, like a person who buys and sells sheep and the like.
Or, for example:

"Alas, O Mother! You bestow upon both him who has sought refuge in you and him who has opposed you an unchanging sovereignty that is enjoyed by the entire world, O Sovereign of the Universe (bhuvaneśvari). O Bhuvaneśvari! This is an address to the consort of the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe (bhuvaneśvara). Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is simply "the sovereign (īśvarī) of the worlds (bhuvanānām). According to the rule *aśnoteḥ āśukarmaṇi varaṭ ca*, the suffix *varaṭ* is added to the root *aś* (to pervade/attain), and by virtue of the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied. Thus, the meaning is: "She who swiftly grants boons to the worlds."

For this has been explained as “the swift bestowing of boons and so forth,” and it has been elaborated upon in the *Prādurbhāvastabaka* of the *Lakṣmīsahasra-ratnaprakāśikā*, during the commentary on the verse beginning with “O Sovereign of All. You bestow sovereignty that is entirely unchanging and fit to be enjoyed by the universe upon both him who has taken refuge in you and him who is opposed to you. Alas! In one case, "unchanging" means indeed immutable—fit for enjoyment, worthy of being experienced, and beneficial to the entire world.

You ordain sovereignty. Elsewhere, that which is "avi" means that whose "vi"—meaning variegated—is non-existent; thus, it is made such that the enjoyment of the universe (*viśvabhogya*) becomes the enjoyment of dogs (*śvabhogya*). The sense is that it is utterly trivial. There is an identity between the word and its meaning: you ordain sovereignty.
Just as the two feet of yours bestow splendor upon both the gods and the Daityas, for that divine essence, O Blessed One, is common to both of them.

"O Blessed One! Your two feet bestow splendor even upon the gods and the Daityas. How is it fitting that they grant equal fruits to both the beneficial and the harmful?"—anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution with the word "teṣām. For those two groups alike, those two feet of yours are indeed the common deity (*sāmānya-daivata*). The sense is that because they are the common deity for both, it is entirely appropriate that they grant equal fruits to both. Indeed, as it is said: "The presiding deity is common to both the gods and the Dānavas."

The phrase "the pair of feet at all times" indicates the well-established authority [of this usage]. Regarding the term *prabhāsana*: in the context of the deity, it is so called because it bestows (*dadāti*) illumination (*prakāśam*); elsewhere, it is so called because it bestows (*dadāti*) the removal (*asanam*, i.e., *nirāsam*) of radiance (*prabhāyāḥ*). Among these examples, the first is pure (*śuddha*), while the others are mixed with puns (*śleṣa*) and, as appropriate, mixed with other poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*).
This has been shown through an eagerness to describe the Blessed One;
therefore, the wise should not entertain the notion of fault regarding the many examples therein.

This is the *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) as described in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*. Regarding this, some maintain: “This is not a distinct variety of *tulyayogitā* from that previously mentioned, because it falls under the definition: ‘of the subjects of description or others. For in the phrase ‘supreme prosperity is bestowed,’ there is a unity of the attribute—either through the fact of being the recipient of the act of giving whose object is the thing indicated by the identical word-order, or through such a word itself.”

Regarding the verse beginning with "And he who [cuts] the neem tree," they say that here too, it is possible for the neem tree—specifically as characterized by its bitterness—to possess, through a traditional succession, the status of a property belonging to the cutter, the waterer, and the worshipper. Others, however, maintain: "This is not well-founded; for instance, the aforementioned method applies only where a property is known to be common to many [subjects], and by serving as the indicator of their similarity, generates aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*)."

However, where there is a single conventional usage—consisting of both auspicious and inauspicious forms—pertaining to both beneficial and harmful objects, which produces aesthetic charm by indicating either praise or censure on the part of the speaker, that is the "other" (apara) type; thus, there is a distinction. For in this case, it is not the case that the word *parābhūti* (defeat) or its referent—the act of giving—is perceived as residing in the enemy or the friend through a secondary process; rather, by the power of *śleṣa* (punning), such an act of giving, determined as a single entity, is perceived as residing in the king alone. Therefore, how could it fail to be covered by the previously stated definition?

By this, the view that in the verse "And he who [cuts] the neem tree," the quality of pungency—which belongs specifically to the neem tree—is indirectly a property of both the cutter and the worshipper, is refuted. This is because, in reality, such a property does not constitute the realization of the figure of speech (alaṃkāra). Otherwise, the mere statement "The lotuses close" would result in the undesired consequence of it being *tulyayogitā* (parallelism).

Rather, it is the status of being a property known to reside in multiple entities that is the determinant of *tulyayogitā*. Therefore, they say that to claim its inclusion [within *tulyayogitā*] in the absence of that [determinant] is entirely improper.
The third type, Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing), is considered another [figure] where there is a statement of equality with those possessing superior qualities.

Another form of *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) consists in the description of common attributes through the disregard for equality with those possessing superior qualities. This differs from the previously mentioned type because the attribute pertains to both the subject under description (*varṇya*) and the non-subject (*avarṇya*). It should be understood that the term *tulyayogitā* is etymologically appropriate, as there is a perception of equality with those renowned for superior qualities in the object of description, in accordance with the maxim favored by experts in grammar: "Whatever is heard as being prevalent, that is understood to be such."
O Śauri, it is said that even the king of jewels, the forest garland, the *śrīvatsa*, the milk-ocean-born maiden, and a flower-garland made of clay attained the state of being your ornaments.

Here, the subject of description—a garland of clay flowers—is described by being equated with ornaments such as the Kaustubha gem, which are not the primary subject. Since it is the garland of clay flowers alone that is intended to be described, the definition [of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*] is consistent. The word "kila" indicates tradition; the Puranic story should be recalled here: "Once, on the mountain of Śiva (Phaṇigiri), the Blessed One placed upon his head a garland of clay flowers offered by a certain devotee."

As for the statement, "He wore upon his crown a clay garland of flowers given by no one," since there is an intention here to present the Kaustubha gem and other jewels as belonging to the Lord, this is merely an instance of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) based on priority; thus, this is not a pure example [of *samāsokti*]. This, however, is a pure example:

"O Acyuta, the wish-fulfilling tree, the cow of plenty, and the jewel of thought—when they take refuge in you, they shake off the miseries of the world through your magnanimity and provide joys. (553) Or, for example:
The lord of tortoises, the leader of the multitude of serpents, and the mass of green rays [of the sun]—even so does Veṅkaṭagiri support this entire earth exceedingly well.

In these two examples, there is a description of common attributes by equating the two subjects under discussion—the Lord and Mount Veṅkaṭa—with non-contextual entities such as the Kalpavṛkṣa and the Lord of Kamatha, who are superior in their respective qualities.
Thus, O Blessed One, even the moon, though its light is bestowed by you, possesses great radiance; and likewise, even a human being who follows you dispels the darknesses of the worlds.
This should also be understood in the case of such passages as the above.
Just as the mental state of one who is averse to you, O Mother, and like the final night of the dark fortnight, both become entirely shrouded in darkness due to the loss of the light of Hari.

O Mother! Due to the absence—meaning the lack—of the glance and the radiance of the light of Hari, the Blessed Lord; in the other sense, due to the absence of the light and the side-glances of the two *haris*, namely the sun and the moon, she becomes thoroughly *tāmasī* (enveloped in darkness). In the other sense, she becomes possessed of *tamisra* (thick gloom).
Or as it is said:

"O Lord of Vṛṣādri, a learned man who does not study, a protector who does not protect the wretched, and a wealthy man who does not give—such a man becomes a burden to the earth. In the first three examples cited above, there is praise; in the final two examples, there is censure. Thus, in the definition [of *pratīpa*] as "by means of superior qualities," the word "superior" (*utkṛṣṭa*) is also indicative of the "inferior" (*apakṛṣṭa*), because there is no difference here in the principle of "contextual proximity" (*prāyapāṭha*) which serves as the basis for understanding equality. This has been shown in the *Kāvyakṣadarśa*.
Some have designated this *tulyayogitā* as *siddhi*. Thus Jayadeva states in the third chapter (*mayūkha*) of his work on poetic characteristics:
"When names are mentioned among the famous for the sake of expressing equality, it is *siddhi*:
'You two alone are renowned—you by your armies, and the ocean by its waters.'"

Thus, according to the views of Sarvasvakāra and others, because the two—the description of the subject and the description of the non-subject—possess a common attribute in that both become "dark" (tāmasī) like the night of the moonless day for one whose mental state is turned away from the Blessed One, this is indeed the *dīpaka* (illuminator) which will be explained hereafter, due to the connection with a single property.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Chapter on Tulyayogitā (Equal Pairing), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Chapter on Dīpaka (Illumination):
Dīpaka occurs when there is a single attribute shared by both the subject under description and that which is not.

The *dīpaka* (illuminator) is the connection of a single common attribute between the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*). Here, the dual number is not intended [to be restrictive], since the *dīpaka* is observed even when many subjects share a single common attribute, as in the verse beginning with “*maṇiśśāṇollīḍhaḥ*” (*the gem polished on the whetstone*). Just as in *tulyayogitā*, here too the comparison is implied. It is called *dīpaka* because the attribute employed for the relevant subject, by occasion, illuminates—that is, reveals and beautifies—the irrelevant subject as well.

Alternatively, *dīpaka* means "like a lamp" (*dīpa iva dīpakam*), using the suffix *kan* according to the rule *saṃjñāyāṃ ca*, which falls under the governing heading *ive pratikṛtau*. It should be understood that its similarity to a lamp lies in its capacity to illuminate both the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) and that which is not (*aprakṛta*). For example:

"The speech of the ancients, overflowing with the grace of the Teacher, is as sweet as honey and profound; and that devotion to the feet of Acyuta is indeed the full fruition of their meritorious deeds. (558)

The word *vāc* here ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. In this instance, there is a connection through a single common attribute—namely, the nature of being a quality consisting in the ripening of past meritorious deeds—between the subject at hand (*prastuta*), devotion to the feet of Acyuta, and the subject not at hand (*aprastuta*), such as being overwhelmed by the grace of the Teacher. Here, since only one [of the two] is the subject, it is *dīpaka*; otherwise, it would simply be *tulyayogitā*.
Just as a woman devoid of passion does not shine, nor does sovereignty without power, nor poetry without logic, nor even intellect without devotion toward You, O Śauri. (559)

In this case, non-existence (*abhāva*) is the common attribute; however, according to another school of thought, even non-existence is indeed a quality (*guṇa*), as we have stated on the occasion of defining *tulyayogitā*. Here too, it should be understood that when only some [of the subjects] are contextual (*prakṛta*), the figure is *dīpaka*, whereas when all are either contextual or non-contextual, it is *tulyayogitā*. But where action is the common attribute, then for as many factors of action (*kāraka*) such as the agent (*kartṛ*) as are present, there occurs *tulyayogitā* or *dīpaka* with respect to each of them alongside another of its own kind, because the comparison (*aupamya*) appears quite distinct [in these cases].
O jewel of the Bull-hill, just as beauty adorns the crest-jewel of a woman, redness adorns coral, and skillfulness adorns a lord of men, so does compassion perfectly adorn you. (560)
In this context, [the rule applies] to the agent and the object.
Just as a golden earring and that beautiful circle of refined gold, both possessing a distinctive saffron hue, color even the infinite [space] they occupy.

"Ruciram" means beautiful. "Tapanīyakuṇḍalam" refers to an ear-ornament made of gold (*tapanīya*); since *tapanīya* is derived from the name *tapana* (the sun), the term *vṛddha* is applied by the rule *vā nāmadheyasya*, and then the suffix *cha* is added in the sense of "belonging to that" (*tasyedam*) according to the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ*. "Maṇḍalam" means the orb or disc. "Kuṅkumasya varṇaviśeṣa iva varṇaviśeṣo yasya" means that which has a specific color like the specific color of saffron (*kuṅkuma*) produced in Kashmir; that is to say, it is reddish in hue. "Tad vayam api" means even we, and even the infinite Lord.

The sense is that even the sky is dark like a *tamāla* tree on one side. It "delights" (*abhirañjayati*), meaning it reddens. Furthermore, that which is a golden earring (*tapanīyakuṇḍala*) and that which is a golden orb (*tapanīyamaṇḍala*)—the only distinction between them being their shape and color—that pair also delights the earth (*kuṃ*) and the infinite intermediate space (*anantam antarikṣam*). The meaning is that by the spreading of its own color, it makes them red.

In the alternative where *ku* is treated as a separate word (*pṛthakpada*), it should be understood that the *parasavarṇa* (the following sound) applies according to the rule *vā padāntasya*. Here too, the distinction lies in the fact that it is intermingled with *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

"Your majesty shines naturally like that of the wish-fulfilling tree, your profundity like that of the ocean, the abode of Śrī; and your coolness like that of the snowy mountain—such is your sovereignty. (562) Here, there is only the agent [of the comparison].
Speech devoid of truth, the home of householders devoid of wealth, a birth devoid of good conduct, and even a mind devoid of devotion to Hari are all to be lamented.
In this case, [it refers] to the action.
O lotus-eyed one, by the digit of the moon that is your chin, the sky constantly attains beauty; and by the line of your navel, the lake does so as well. (564)
In this context, [the rule applies] to the agent and the instrument.

O Lord, by your poetry you have purchased the hearts of the connoisseurs; by your beautiful appearance, the minds of the youth; and by your excellent character, O All-pervading One, the entire world has been bought.

In this context, the distinction is that of the agent, the instrument, and the object. Good character (*sauśīlya*) is the nature of an intense and continuous union with the great by those who are humble.

The cloud gives nectar to the cātaka birds, the moon to the flocks of cakora birds, and the Lord of the Serpentine Mountain (Śiva) bestows nectar even upon those who bow before him, all without any expectation of reward.

In this context, the meanings of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the recipient (*sampradāna*) are, respectively, nectar (*amṛta*), water (*salila*), ambrosia (*pīyūṣa*), and supreme bliss (*niśśreyasa*). It should be understood that by the repetition of the word *amṛta*, the object (*karman*) is also included. "Entirely without expectation" means being devoid of any desire for a reciprocal benefit. From the lotus one obtains nectar; from the mango tree, a cluster of sweet-tasting fruits; from the jasmine, fragrance; and from Mukunda, a person attains the bliss of liberation. (567)

In this context, regarding the [distinction between] the ablative and the object: that which has a sweet mode of being or state is "sweetly disposed" (*madhuravṛtti*); the meaning is that its very nature is sweet.
Just as darkness fears the dawn, herds of rutting elephants fear the lord of monkeys (Hanuman), and fevers fear the moon, so do sins, O Mother, fear you because they have sought refuge in you.

In this case, there is [the application] of the ablative (*apādāna*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). Furthermore, here the genitive case, characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix according to the rule "the sixth case [is used] for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows," is to be understood.

A multitude of rays shines upon the sun, the friend of the lotus; a multitude of jewels shines in the great ocean; and a multitude of virtues shines upon the Lord who is the kinsman of all, bringing joy to the entire universe while resting upon the king of serpent-mountains.
In this context, [the rules apply] to the agent and the locus.

Daṇḍin and others have included even *kārakadīpaka* within *dīpaka* itself. On this point, some maintain that *dīpaka* is also subsumed under *tulyayogitā*, because there is no difference between the two cases regarding the aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) rooted in the single occurrence (*sakṛdvṛtti*) of a property (*dharma*). Furthermore, while distinctions such as being "contextual" (*prakṛta*) or "non-contextual" (*aprakṛta*) may establish internal subdivisions, they do not establish the status of a separate figure of speech.

Otherwise, in the case of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), since there exists the distinction of the subjects being either exclusively contextual or exclusively non-contextual, it would follow that there is a duality of figures of speech; likewise, in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), such a twofold division would result, and furthermore, all figures of speech would suffer from a lack of distinction due to their differences in subdivisions.

Therefore, since the "concomitance of a single attribute" (*ekadharmānvaya*) belongs only to those that are relevant (*prakṛta*), only those that are irrelevant (*aprakṛta*), and those that are both relevant and irrelevant (*prakṛtāprakṛta*), it is appropriate to speak of three subdivisions of *tulyayogitā* alone. Thus, they say that the claim of the ancients—who maintain that *dīpaka* is a figure of speech distinct from *tulyayogitā*—is merely a stubborn prejudice. Others, however, define it thus:
"When words situated in various substrata are joined by a single sentence as illuminators, that is called *dīpaka*."
Just as lakes are made non-empty by swans, trees by flowers, lotuses by intoxicated bees,
and garden groves by social gatherings, so too are they always kept from being desolate in that place.

Since the sage Bharata and Daṇḍin also acknowledge only *dīpaka*, it is considered inappropriate for them to include *tulyayogitā* within *dīpaka*; rather, they maintain that *dīpaka* is actually included within *tulyayogitā*.
