Rudraṭa and others, however, declare this ornament to be threefold, according as the common attribute (*dharma*)—consisting of qualities, actions, and so forth—is situated at the beginning, middle, or end [of the sentence].

According to that view, as illustrated by the very verses cited here, the attribute (*dharma*) is indicated at the beginning in “*aruṇāt trāsas tamasām*,” in the middle in “*raktivihīnā vanitā*,” and at the end in “*lāvaṇyaṃ lalanāmaṇim*. However, in reality, although the attribute occurs at the beginning, middle, and end there, the statement of its threefold nature is merely superficial, as it lacks any particular strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of varieties, because a property (*dharma*) would have to exist in the beginning, middle, or end of its substratum, and furthermore, because it would subsist in regions that are slightly more or less extensive than those. In the examples shown immediately below, the *Dīpaka* is demonstrated when the common property is purely pervasive (*kevalānugāmī*). It was also shown in such cases as "a woman devoid of passion" (*raktivihīnā vanitā*), where it occurs through the relationship of the original and the reflected (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). Or, for example:

"The Lord of the learned shines, endowed with statesmanship; the Indra of warriors shines, endowed with victory; the king of birds (Garuḍa) shines, endowed with speed; and the lord of the Veṅkaṭa mountains also shines, endowed with loftiness. (570)

We have already shown that this [principle] is possible even in the case of *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing). Here, in the relationship of *bimbapratibimba* (original image and reflection), the cause of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is not merely the commonality of action as a form; rather, as illustrated by the examples given, it is permeated by the state of being reflections of the river and so forth. However, there is this distinction: the accomplishment of figures such as *upamā* (simile) can also occur through the mere relationship of original image and reflection, as was previously exemplified in the simile with the words "adorned by the pair of arms like lotuses," and so on.

In the present case, however, it is not so; for without a common substratum (anugāmin), the very nature of the property (dharma) cannot be established. Indeed, the simultaneous occurrence of a property cannot be possible through the mere relation of the original object and its reflection. This [simultaneous occurrence] is also possible through paronomasia (śleṣa).
Indeed,
O Lord of Śeṣa Hill, for those who know the science of grammar as well as those who know the Supreme Brahman, their goal is invariably one that leads to a state of pure movement.

For one who knows the science of grammar (*śabdavidyāvit*), that is, a knower of etymology (*vyākaraṇavettṛ*), and for one who knows the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmavit*), the term *gati* necessarily occurs in the sense of "towards" (*accha*). In the first case, *accha* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) meaning "towards"; when used in conjunction with a verb having the sense of motion (*gatyarthaka-dhātu-yoga*), it becomes a *gati*, that is, it receives the technical designation *gati*. The point is that, while the rule "and *gati*" (*gatiśca*) is being carried over, the rule "towards in the sense of verbs of motion and the like" (*accha gatyarthavadeṣu*) prescribes the designation *gati* for the indeclinable *accha* when it is joined with a verb signifying motion.

In the second sense, *accha* means that which releases one from the connection with *prakṛti*; *gatiḥ* refers to the journey by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*). For that purpose—according to the rule “when two words denote the same object, they are designated as indeclinables”—*gatiḥ* means knowledge; the meaning is that it is accomplished. Here, through the device of *śleṣa*, there is a commonality of attributes between the person under discussion who knows the science of grammar and the person under discussion who knows the Supreme Brahman: for both, the *gati* (knowledge/attainment) occurs for the sake of the *acchagati* (the clear path/release).
In this regard, the following should be noted:

although both shine forth as capable of shattering the darkness of difficult-to-subdue poverty—the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) and the crest-jewel of the gods (śikharimaṇi)—the one who is the jewel of the gods is indeed the wish-fulfilling gem itself.

In this case, the simultaneous connection of the relevant (prastuta) and the irrelevant (aprastuta) with the common attribute appears. In the previously cited verses such as "A woman devoid of passion," etc., the connection with the attribute occurs first for the irrelevant subject alone; nevertheless, its status as incidental (prāsaṅgika) is not lost, because the description—which was actually undertaken with the relevant subject as its objective—ultimately connects with the relevant subject as well.

For the lamp does not lose its incidental nature simply because it simultaneously benefits both the street and the palace, nor does soup cooked for the sake of a son-in-law lose its incidental nature by being served first to guests; however, the distinction in *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) is that since no distinction is perceived—because one thing is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*) while the other is not—the stated attribute applies to all subjects without exception.

Furthermore, this is another distinction between these two: although there is no difference in the fact that the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) is implied (*gamya*) in both cases, here the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) is fixed—where the non-contextual is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the contextual is the object of comparison (*upameya*)—whereas in the other case, because no such distinction is perceived, it is optional. All of this is clear in the *Kuvalayānanda*. Some, however, have subsumed *mālādīpaka* (the lamp-chain) within this very category; that is incorrect.

In such instances as “By Smara [the god of love] she was placed in his heart; by him, however, you were established there,” and so forth, there is an absence of connection through similarity (*sādṛśya*). This point will be elaborated upon during the discussion of the *mālādīpaka* (the lamp-in-a-garland) figure.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter on *Dīpaka* in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the chapter on *Āvṛttidīpaka*:
when there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of both the word and its meaning, either collectively or individually.
The most excellent of the wise have declared that *āvṛttidīpaka* (the illuminator by repetition) is of three kinds.

The meaning is that *āvṛttidīpaka* (the lamp of repetition) is of three kinds when there is a repetition of both the word and its meaning—whether combined or separate—acting as a "lamp" by providing manifold assistance. There is one variety when there is a repetition of both the word and its meaning; and two varieties when there is a repetition of the word alone or the meaning alone; thus, it has three modes. This is a literal designation (*anvarthābhidhāna*), for just as a single action connects with multiple factors of action (*kāraka*s), so too does this "lamp of repetition" consist in multiple factors of action connecting with a repeated action.
The examples are given in their respective order:

when men perceive the great manifestation of Hari, who dwells upon the mountain of Hari (the sun), the multitude of their lotus-eyes blossoms, and the multitude of the lotuses of their hearts blossoms as well. (573)

Veṅkaṭagiri is the mountain of Hari; it is called "Udaya" (the Rising) because it belongs to Him. When there is an acquaintance with the manifestation of the splendor—that is, the manifestation of the festival of light—of that very Lord Hari who possesses the sun, [the following occurs]. Here, there is a repetition of both the action of blossoming and the words expressing it; thus, this is an instance of *ubhayāvṛttidīpaka* (the illuminator through the repetition of both).

"O Murāri, just as my eye drags me in one direction, this sense of hearing drags me elsewhere; and that virtuous tongue drags me yet another way—what can my devotion do in such a case? (571) The underlying sentiment is: "Me, who desires to see You, to hear Your stories, and to utter Your name. The word *dṛk* refers to the organ of sight (*cakṣurindriya*), and its meaning is "in one direction," namely toward its own object. The same applies to the subsequent senses. The rest is clear. Here, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of both the action of dragging (*karṣaṇa*) and the words expressing that action.

This [verse] is intermingled with a *samāsokti* (poetic suggestion by ellipsis) consisting of the superimposition of the conduct of a virtuous wife tormented by a rogue and many co-wives; whereas the preceding [verse] was characterized by *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).

Just as sin would attach to us [if we were to commit it], so too would Hari be compelled to grant its fruit; and compassion would likewise attach to Lakṣmī, who would then be compelled to propitiate her own beloved.

Just as the roar of the noble elephant resounds, so too does the roar of the noble lion resound on all sides; and it echoes within the interior caves of the remaining mountains, reverberating back toward them.
Just as the cakravāka birds warble, the parrots and cuckoos warble, and even the cranes warble, bestowing delight upon the ears on Mount Pṛdākugiri. (577)
These three examples are pure. Here too, in the first two examples, the "garland of causes" (kāraṇamālā) is suggested; however, the final example is the most purely [pure].
An example of *padāvṛtti-dīpaka* (repetition of words as an illuminator) is as follows:

"By the light of the moon on the mountain of the supreme serpent, darkness flees far away; likewise, even the stone of the hearts of those who have sought refuge melts at the nectar-rayed [light] of Him."

In this case, there is a repetition of the word *dravati* itself, but not of its meaning, because there is a difference between the meaning of the first instance, "he runs," and that of the last, "it becomes moist."
O Śauri, just as your smiling fame spreads at will, so too the vast fame of your enemies is shaken far, far away in all directions.

Here too, because there is a difference in meaning between the two instances of *vidhūyate*—namely, "acting like one who is separated" (*vidhur ivācarati*) and "trembling" (*prakampyate*)—this is also a *padāvṛtti-dīpaka* (an illuminator through the repetition of a word).

Just as [the serpent] repeatedly drinks from the mountain of the Lord (Śiva), so too, O Lord born from the ocean-jar (Agni), this blessed one indeed purifies that sacred ford of yours many times over.

"O Master! On Mount Ahi, the fortunate and meritorious one indeed drinks repeatedly—that is, he drinks much—your *tīrtha*, meaning the *tīrtha* for your ablution. [The root] *ghaiṭ* means 'to drink. He purifies—that is, makes pure—this person who maintains the *tīrtha*, so that it may become a great *tīrtha*; the meaning is that he extends [the state of being] free from the entire mass of sins. Here too, there is a repetition of individual words (*padāvṛtti*).

Just as my mind runs in many directions toward that certain wonder born of the Wind-eater’s Daughter (Pārvatī)—that wonderful Lord Śrīnivāsa, the treasury of all marvels—it likewise protects me in many ways as I remember Him, the abode of the great ocean, dark as a massive cloud. [The meaning is: My mind, acting as the agent, "runs"—that is to say, remembers—that certain wonder born of the Wind-eater’s Daughter (Pārvatī), namely Śrīnivāsa, the repository of all wonders. It also "protects" me in many ways as I remember that wonder, the Blessed Lord, who is the abode of the great ocean, meaning He is as dark as a vast water-bearing cloud.

It protects, pleases, and guards me as I remember it in many ways. Here too, there is the repetition of even a single word. This [figure] has been established through *abhaṅga-śleṣa* (uninterrupted pun) in the first two examples, and through *sabhaṅga-śleṣa* (interrupted pun) in the two examples cited immediately following.
Just as he who conceals the sun, the beloved of Kamalā, from the serpent-mountain [Rāhu], for him indeed the profound darkness consisting of worldly existence (bhava) is utterly concealed.

That person who holds [the Lord] within the mind—that is, meditates upon Him—for that person, the Blessed One conceals the dense darkness consisting of worldly existence; that is to say, He covers it over and brings it to an end. Here too, there is a repetition of the word itself.
An example of *dīpaka* based on the recurrence of meaning (*arthāvṛtti-dīpaka*) is as follows:
"The nectar of the name of the Lord of Veṅkaṭācala instantly washes away sins; it also cleanses even the powerful wickedness acquired here through association with evil people. (583)

In this case, although there is a difference in the verbal forms (*kriyāpada*), because their meaning—purification—is non-different, this is an instance of *arthāvṛttidīpaka* (illuminator through repetition of meaning).

"Just as where the forest garland blazes and the Kaustubha gem shines with glory, how much greater would its fortune be if even a garland of lotuses were to shine there? (584) In this instance too, although there is a difference in the words expressing the actions such as "blazes" (*indhe*) and so forth, one should understand that there is no difference in their meaning, which is "illumination. Furthermore, this should be analyzed as being mixed with *samāsokti* (poetic implication), which consists in the superimposition of a worldly transaction characterized by praising the good fortune of an inferior individual who is shining in a rank equal to that of a superior individual worthy of an exalted position.

Just as this world, by taking refuge in you, O Lord of Śrī, certainly attains victory, gains prosperity, finds modesty, resorts to right policy, and even achieves what is dear, so too does it find its goal. || 585 ||

One finds shame (*hrī*) regarding improper acts; this is a great virtue. As it is said here and there, "one who cultivates shame" (*hrīniṣevī*). The distinction is that in the first two examples, the agents are connected with repeated actions, whereas here, they are connected with objects such as "victory" and so forth.

One might object: "Since the instruction of attributes (*dharmopadeśa*) here lacks the quality of having both a relevant (*prastuta*) and an irrelevant (*aprastuta*) subject, how can it be designated by the term *dīpaka*? This is not so, for its validity is established through its similarity in being a benefactor to many. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kuvalayānanda*: "Even though the repetitions lack the quality of having both a relevant and an irrelevant subject, they are designated as *dīpaka* merely by virtue of attaining the shadow (*chāyā*) of *dīpaka*. By employing the word "merely" (*mātra*), the author Dīkṣita indicates that this is a distinct ornament and not a sub-variety of *dīpaka*. Therefore, it was said by Daṇḍin: [text follows]
The three ornaments— namely, the repetition of meaning (arthāvṛtti), the repetition of words (padāvṛtti), and the repetition of both (ubhayāvṛtti)—
are likewise desired as instances of the figure *dīpaka*.
Thus; the meaning is that this threefold ornament is similar to the *dīpaka* (the illuminator).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the Section on Illumination by Repetition (*āvṛttidīpaka*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*; now begins the Section on Simile by Corresponding Objects (*prativastūpamā*).

Since the meaning of a sentence is composed of the meanings of its constituent words, the discussion of figures of speech residing in the sentence-meaning follows immediately after those residing in the word-meanings. Among these, when a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is expressed once through the employment of particles such as *iva*, it is *Upamā* (Simile). It is the same even when there is a single expression of the attribute through the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (the thing and its counterpart). When the particle *iva* and so forth are not employed, but the attribute is expressed once, it is *Dīpaka* or *Tulyayogitā*. However, when it is expressed more than once, there are two possibilities: either it takes the form of a pure common attribute or it constitutes the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection). The first type is *Prativastūpamā*.

An illustration will now be stated based on the second type [of *prativastūpamā*]. Thus, in this way, *prativastūpamā* is indeed based on comparison (*aupamya*). Accordingly, its definition is as follows: "If, when two sentences have been concluded through similarity, a single attribute is employed twice, that is called *prativastūpamā*."

*Prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism) occurs when, for the sake of achieving a single unified sentence between two statements that culminate in a relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*), a single common attribute in the form of a quality or action is mentioned separately by different words through the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding subject and counterpart). The meaning is that this is so because of the etymological derivation: "it is a *upamā* (simile) in every instance (*prati-vastu*) regarding the relationship of standard and object of comparison," and it is characterized by that common attribute which serves as its cause. The term "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is included to exclude the figure *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general proposition).

In that case, however, it is merely the relationship between the capable and the capable (the prover and the proven) that is intended to be expressed, not similarity. Even in the case of an illustration based on the relationship of the original and its reflection (*bimbapratibimba*), the word "one" (*eka*) is used to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because in that instance a distinct property (*dharma*) is indeed employed. Thus, there is no fault.

"Just as Nārāyaṇagiri alone indeed bears extensive fame among mountains; Airāvata alone indeed possesses supreme splendor among the elephants of the quarters. Here, the single attribute "bears" (*bibharti*) and "possesses" (*dadhāti*) is indicated by two distinct words in the sentences concerning the object of comparison and the standard of comparison. This very phenomenon is called *vastuprativastubhāva* (the relation of thing-to-thing correspondence).
O Hari, how indeed can a minor deity attain equality with You, the Great One, by those who worship You? Can a glass trinket, held in low esteem, ever be equal to a diamond of supreme excellence? 587.
The form "bhajatām" is the imperative (loṭ).

O Hari, just as fools do not find You, O Brahman, even though they travel day after day; for those who lack knowledge of the Field (akṣetrajña) do not discover the treasure, even while walking over it again and again. 588.

In this context, the meaning of the scriptural passage occurring in the Dahara-vidyā has been kept in mind: "Just as those who do not know the location might pass over a treasure of gold deposited beneath them again and again yet not find it, even so all these creatures, though they go to this world of Brahman day after day, do not find it, for they are held back by untruth."

The meaning of this is as follows: just as those who lack knowledge of the nature of the field containing a treasure—such as a hoard of gold deposited beneath—do not find it even though they pass over it again and again, even so all these creatures, going day after day into deep sleep and becoming unified (avibhāga) in that state according to the scriptural statement, "Having attained [the Self] which is Being, they do not know," do not find, do not obtain, and do not know this world whose nature is Brahman and which is called the small ether (daharākāśa). This is the meaning.

The two words *brahma* and *loka* are in apposition according to the *niṣādasthapati* maxim. He states the reason for this: "for they are veiled by untruth" (*anṛtena hi pratyūḍhāḥ*). By "untruth," that is, by ritual action (*karman*), they have been led away from their true nature and brought to a different state; in other words, they are covered over.

Alternatively, the phrase "going day after day" does not refer to movement occurring at the time of deep sleep; rather, it means that although they go higher and higher day after day—referring to the space within the heart (*daharākāśa*) which exists eternally as the inner self and constitutes the supreme human goal like a hidden treasure—they do not know it and thus do not find it, meaning they do not attain it. In the illustrative example, the term "deluded" signifies being "obstructed by untruth. In these two statements, the common attribute consisting of the absence of attainment is presented through different words.

If it is asked, "What is the distinction between this and the *arthāvṛttidīpaka* exemplified by the verse 'He washes Veṅkaṭācala'?", we say no; for *arthāvṛtti* consists in the mention of a single attribute residing in multiple subjects that are either all relevant (*prastuta*) or all irrelevant (*aprastuta*), whereas this [present figure] consists in the mention of such an attribute residing in both relevant and irrelevant subjects. Thus, because of the existence of this distinction, there is indeed a difference between the two.

Furthermore, *arthāvṛttidīpaka* occurs only when there is a repetition of the meaning (*artha*) between two sentences, and that [repetition] occurs only through similarity (*sādharmya*), not through contrast (*vaidharmya*). This [figure], however, occurs even through contrast; thus it differs from that as well. This has been stated in the *Kuvalayānanda*: “*Arthāvṛttidīpaka* pertains to things either both relevant (*prastuta*) or both irrelevant (*aprastuta*); whereas *prativastūpamā* pertains to both relevant and irrelevant things—this is the distinction. Moreover, this is another distinction: *āvṛttidīpaka* is not possible through contrast, whereas *prativastūpamā* is seen even through contrast.”
For only those who are exclusively devoted to it recognize the fragrant excellence of the virtues of the Lord of the Hill of the Serpent; village pigs never perceive here the heavy scent of musk.
O Lord, just as a multitude of my great sins sinks deeply into your forbearance, so indeed does mud never rise again from the Ganges with its exceedingly pure waves.

Or rather, it appears to me that my lotus-heart, while holding you within—O daughter of the ocean—is like a pearl-oyster shell from which the pearl-jewel has been extracted; it shall never again shine with luster.

Now, it may be argued that this is contradictory, since an *upamā* (simile) consists of similarity (*sādharmya*). This is true; however, there is no fault because what is intended as the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is not the sentence-meaning "the fragrance of musk" and so forth—which is presented by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—but rather the sentence-meaning "only those who know [it] know [it]. Although there is an initial perception of dissimilarity, the final conclusion rests upon similarity; thus, the term "by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa*) means "through the medium of dissimilarity."

In this instance, by describing the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) through the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (subject and counter-subject), the intention is to convey the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflection) among the other constituent elements, as well as the structural symmetry (*ānurūpya*) of the composition. Otherwise, [the verse would read]: "Indeed, the wicked are skilled in the act of obstructing their own welfare; likewise, serpents are expert at taking away the lives of the innocent."

Thus, even in this case where the meaning of the sentence is not clearly unified, there may be a *prativastūpamā* (point-by-point simile). For here, although there exists a relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) between the chaff and the serpent, and between those who harm life and those who create obstacles—both of which ultimately resolve into destruction and prior non-existence respectively—there is no relationship of prototype and reflection due to their lack of correspondence (*anānurūpya*).

Alternatively, let there be a *prativastūpamā* (parallelism) here; however, because the meanings of the nouns, case-endings, and so forth contained in the first sentence—namely, "the acts of promoting welfare and creating obstacles"—are absent in the phrase "to take away the life-breaths" within the second sentence, the general defect of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmānya-doṣa*), characterized by a lack of coherence, remains present. Thus, it is indeed unpleasing, like a defective simile (*duṣṭopamā*).

For the meaning of a sentence composed by great poets—whose inner faculties have been refined by profound mastery and who are skilled in the arrangement and transformation of various word-meanings—possesses an indescribable charm, whereas that of others does not.

Therefore, regarding such figures of speech, they say that one must consult the hearts of connoisseurs (sahr̥dayas) alone, for it is expected that the subsequent sentence-meaning should be constructed with noun-meanings corresponding to the noun-meanings constituting the preceding sentence-meaning, with case-endings corresponding to those case-endings, and with a grammatical relation corresponding to that relation.

Viśveśvara, the author of the *Alaṃkārakaustubha*, however, states that this [figure] is also seen in the scope of other figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*). Among those, regarding the scope of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), he gives the following example:
"O Mother, before you, even the lake seems tasteless, the moon seems as if thick with darkness, the sprout seems to possess a rhythmic beat, and indeed, the coral seems to have melted away. (592)

The sense is: "of you, whose eyes, face, hands, and lips are exceedingly beautiful. Here, a single attribute in the form of inferiority—namely, tastelessness (*nīrasatva*) and so forth—is expressed through different terms in each clause regarding the cranes and the rest. It should be noted that this is a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) mixed with poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

This [simile] is also seen in the form of a garland (*mālārūpa*), as follows: "The mango tree bears incomparable fruit; Hara wears the moon, the treasury of digits; the sovereign bears a crown; and the mountain of serpents harbors Hari within its caves. (593)
For example:

"The sage shines with his formidable brilliance; the friend of the lotus-bed [the sun] shines with his radiance; the lord of the earth glows with the splendor of sovereignty; and Hari gleams with eternal glory. (594) Here, because the acts of carrying, holding, supporting, and bearing in the first verse, and the acts of kindling, shining, ruling, and gleaming in the second verse are in fact identical in nature, this is a *prativastūpamā* (parallel simile) in the form of a series (*mālā*).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the Section on Simile by Corresponding Objects (*prativastūpamā*), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Section on Illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*):
[An illustration consists of] two things possessing the status of the original image (*bimba*) and the reflected image (*pratibimba*), such as their respective attributes and so forth.
If a comparison between the meaning of a sentence and its referent is intended for the sake of illustration, it is called a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustrative example).

The meaning is that a *dṛṣṭānta* (illustrative example) is an implied simile (*aupamya*) between two sentence-meanings based on common attributes that have entered into the state of being an original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). As it has been said: "Furthermore, the *dṛṣṭānta* among all these [figures] is their reflection. This refers to all [figures] beginning with the simile (*upamā*). It is so named because its meaning is as it is expressed (*yathārtha*), since in this case, a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding a matter that was doubtful in the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) is observed.

Just as poetry devoid of poetic figures is praiseworthy if it is polished with the name of the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śrī Śaṅkara), so too a woman is truly desirable if she possesses full beauty, even if she lacks ornaments. 595.

In this instance, there is a relationship of "original and reflection" (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) between the two subjects of comparison—the poet and the woman—and between their respective attributes: being praiseworthy and being desirable. This very point is what distinguishes this ornament from *prativastūpamā* (parallelism): in the latter, the attribute does not function as a reflection but exists merely as a pure universal; here, however, it functions as a reflection. Or, for example:

"The three worlds have become more auspicious solely through the grace of the moon on the serpent-king’s peak [Śiva]; the day has become radiant solely through the splendor of the sun, the friend of the lotus. (596)
Just as this earth is purified by the river born from the feet of the Lord of Śrīśaila, so too is the splendor of heaven enriched by the Mandāra tree through its great generosity.

Just as the Lord of Mountains and others shine by Your side-glance, O Blessed One, while You Yourself are the Sovereign by Your very nature; a glass gem reflects light from the rays of the sun, whereas this [gem] shines by its own luster.

Just as one who is devoted to you is worthy of honor even if destitute, while another is not, despite possessing great wealth; or as even the bodiless Cupid is praiseworthy for his beauty, while one who is not like him is not, even if he possesses a large body. (599)

*Anaṅgaḥ* (bodiless) means *alpāṅgaḥ* (having small limbs); here, as in the expression “a girl with a small belly” (*anudarā kanyā*), the meaning is "smallness. The intended sense is "even one whose body is thin. One should also supply the word *kāmaḥ* (the God of Love). *Mahāṅgaḥ* (large-limbed) means even one with stout limbs; in another sense, it means a camel. Amara states: "For a camel: *kramelaka*, *mayūra*, and *mahāṅga*. An example by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*) is as follows:
"O Wind! It is only through the boon granted by the Lord of Mountains that embodied beings possess wealth. Without the arrival of autumn, who would be a payer of tribute to the Moon? (600)
Of the favor of Vidhu—that is, of the clarity of the moon—he was a giver of tribute, one who offered the support of his hand.

Or rather, O Blessed One, may you remain as our protector for as long as you are not merely the object of our gaze; when the syllables of the Suparṇa mantra are uttered from the ear, there is no longer any fear of serpents.

In the first example here, the granting of a boon and the manifestation of power—two elements pertaining to the meaning of the contextual sentence—and in the second example, the state of being the creator of existence and the state of being the object of the Lord’s sidelong glance—these two, by way of contrast (*vaidharmya*), were presented as reflections in the subsequent sentences: namely, the absence of the granting of clarity by the moon at the arrival of autumn and the absence of fear for the serpent due to the mantra of Suparṇa reaching the ear, respectively.
Or rather, just as you grant every supramundane fruit to all those who worship you, O Jewel among Wives of the Mountain-King of Serpents, surely the jasmine flower does not produce fragrance. (602)

In this case as well, an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) should be understood. Regarding this, the author of the *Ekāvalī* states: "By the very power of the figure of speech known as the Example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object compared (*upamānopameyabhāva*), which is already apprehended through the relation of the original image and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), should not be disregarded and expressed again by the poet using such terms as 'example' (*dṛṣṭānta*), 'illustration' (*udāharaṇa*), or 'exemplification' (*nidarśana*), for that would result in redundancy.
For this very reason, there is no further satisfaction for the greatest of things even through a superior excellence;
here, the great ocean, longing for the rise of the full moon, serves as the example.

Thus, on the occasion of commenting on *Māgha* 1.3, Mallinātha stated: "This is not the figure of speech *Dṛṣṭānta* (Illustration), because that arises when a comparison is implied through the relation of the original (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). Rather, since the word *dṛṣṭānta* denotes a similar object, it is the figure of speech *Upamā* (Simile). Having said this, he cited the passage from the *Ekāvalī*. In reality, however, we consider that in such instances composed with words like *dṛṣṭānta*, *udāharaṇa*, and so forth, it is precisely the figure of speech *Udāharaṇā* (Exemplification) as previously defined [by Mammaṭa] that applies. And since that was correctly characterized earlier, it is not further elaborated upon here.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the Lake of Simile (Dṛṣṭāntasara), in the Alaṃkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Lake of the Figure of Speech Nidarśanā:
"If the non-difference between two meanings that have been presented is proclaimed [through a single sentence]," [that is Nidarśanā].
When it culminates in a comparison, this is *nidarśanā*.

The meaning is that *nidarśanā* (illustration) consists of an implied non-difference (*abheda*) between two objects that have been explicitly mentioned, which culminates in a comparison. The term "of two [objects] that have been mentioned" (*upāttayoḥ*) serves to exclude *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) and the like, while the term "implied" (*ārtha*) excludes *rūpaka* (metaphor) when it is expressed as such. Furthermore, this "implied" nature (*ārthatva*) means not being the object of the initial syntactic cognition (*prāthamikānvayabodha*).

If it is argued that in a qualified simile (viśiṣṭopamā) the non-difference between the two qualifiers is what is perceived, then the qualifier "belonging to those whose subordinate status is determined by the primary [elements] which have not entered into the relation of prototype and counter-image" must be adopted for the two objects. For in a qualified simile, since the primary upamāna and upameya do enter into the relation of prototype and counter-image, there is no over-extension even when the non-difference of the qualifiers—whose subordinate status is determined by them—is apprehended through implication.

In the case of *nidarśanā*, however, in the examples to be mentioned later, although there exists a relationship of original and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*) between the two subordinate actions such as "recognizing" (*abhijānan*) and "knowing" (*vetti*), the two agents—who possess primary status as defined by those respective actions—do not themselves enter into a relationship of original and reflection. Consequently, because the two subordinate actions of "recognizing" and "knowing," as defined by those respective agents, are perceived as identical through implication (*ārtha*), the definition will be satisfied. This is the definition of *nidarśanā* based on direct expression (*śrautī*).
The common definition for the implied (*ārthī*) variety, however, will be demonstrated in the section on the *lalita* ornament.

Just as one who constantly recognizes You, the eternal Supreme Self, as non-different from his own inner self, knows the Emperor as the Truth through his identity with the servant, O Lord of the Serpent Hill. (603)

In this case, the cognition based on similarity is that which regards the knowledge of the Supreme Self as non-different from the knowledge of the individual self—as one regards the knowledge of a king as non-different from the knowledge of his servant. (603)
Or rather, one who desires to know Your infinite majesty, having measured it with the heart, alas, longs to encircle the entire intermediate space within his armpit and cast it therein.
When men shall roll up the sky like a piece of leather, then,
having realized Śiva, one attains the end of suffering.

Thus, the shadow of the Vedic text is grasped. Here, the desire to know the infinite majesty of the Blessed One by delimiting it with the mind, and the desire to wrap up the intermediate space like a mat and tuck it under one's arm, are not distinct [in their impossibility]. 604.
Or rather: he who, disregarding you, would resort to another deity whose eyes are like lotuses, is like one who, shaking his crest-jewel, carries instead a lump of iron upon the head of a serpent.
O Lord of Ramā, he who would offer another manifestation of You, whose divine glory is limitless, is like one who offers an ornament made of lead to the Golden Mountain.
O Murāri, he who wishes to describe your infinite greatness is like one who desires to cover the entire expanse of the sky with the palm of his hand. (607)
O Lord of Śeṣagiri, he who wishes to speak another esteemed discourse while abandoning yours, is like one who desires to eat the dust of a salt-flat while discarding sugar.
He who considers himself a scholar yet speaks of the Lord of the Serpent Hill as equal to other gods, he indeed calls a jewel a clod of earth and darkness the likeness of the scorching sun. (609)

Among these seven examples, in the first two, the non-difference (abheda) resides within a single sentence; in the latter ones, however, it resides across distinct sentences. Even among those, in the four beginning with "tvām avigaṇayya," the non-difference is based on the similarity between two mere facts (vastumātra). In the final verse, "phaṇigiri," the distinction is that the non-difference is based on the similarity between two poetic figures (alaṅkāra).
Just as one who might be able to measure the entire water of the ocean with a single jar would likewise be capable of delimiting the entirety of Your glory with the mind. (610)

Here, the distinction from the previous examples lies in the fact that the non-difference between the meanings of the sentences expressing the standard of comparison and the object of comparison occurs in reverse order, and there is a commingling with *mithyādhyavasiti* (false attribution).
Or for example:
"For he alone is able to recount the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who adorns the peak of the Vṛṣagiri mountain—he who is capable of measuring all the particles of dust upon the earth. (611)

In this context, the distinction lies in following the meaning of the Vedic scripture: "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms. Everything else remains exactly as before. This [example] is intended to demonstrate the presence of such a figure of speech (alaṅkāra) even in the Śruti. The same should be understood regarding the verse previously cited beginning with "tava mahimānam" ("your greatness"). This is called *vākyārthanidarśanā* (illustration by means of the sense of a sentence), because it is accepted that *nidarśanā* occurs when there is a semantic non-difference between two distinct objects residing in a single common subject.
Furthermore, in this figure, the relationship between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) among the constituent word-meanings is necessarily present.
This [figure] is also seen in the form of a garland (*mālārūpa*), as in:

"He scatters nectar all around, he hurls forth the stream of the autumn moon’s radiance; he bestows the anointing of sandalwood—he who propagates the story of Hari. (612) Furthermore, this other point should be understood: "That this leader of the great mountains, whose nature is like the wind, has departed from my heart—that, I believe, has caused my sin to transcend its bounds and take on the form of a spear. (613)

"Śūlākārṣīt" means he cooked with a spit (śūlena apākṣīt). The suffix *ḍāc* is applied to the word "śūla" by the rule "śūlātpāke. Here, according to the view of those who maintain that verbal cognition has the action as its primary object—following Yāska’s dictum "the verb denotes the action"—there is a verbal superimposition (*śābda abhedāropa*) between the two actions; thus, as in "The face is the moon," a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is appropriate. However, for those who maintain that verbal cognition has the nominative subject as its primary object, this is a conceptual superimposition (*ārtha*), and thus the distinction is that it is an "illustration" (*nidarśanā*).
An illustration based on the meaning of the words (*padārthanidarśanā*) is as follows:

"May the beloved of the Daughter of the Ocean of Milk be victorious for a long time—he who possesses a white luster shimmering like a circle of fresh blue water-lilies blooming at the hour of sunset. (614)

Here, although the splendor of the blue lotus petal and the splendor of the Blessed One are distinct due to the difference in their substrata, there is either a superimposition (*āropa*) or a conceit of identity (*tādrūpyābhimāna*) based on their similarity, [consisting in] the attribution of the splendor of the blue lotus to the Blessed One.

O Hari, just as one tormented by the heat of worldly existence, when bathed today in the nectar of your compassion, attains the bliss of an elephant submerged in the cool pools of the Gaṅgā while suffering from the scorching sun.

In this instance, the shadow of the authoritative source (pramāṇa) is followed by the statement: "I have entered this Brahma, as one enters a cool lake in the summer heat. Here, through the immersion in the Ganges lake—which is afflicted by contact with the intense heat of the sun—there is a reflection (*pratibimbana*) of being scorched by the forest fire of worldly existence and being drenched by the nectar of the Lord's compassion. Thus, there is a distinction from the previous example, as well as a blending with *rūpaka* (metaphor). However, the identification (*tādrūpyābhimāna*) based on similarity between two pleasures that are distinct due to their different substrates remains exactly the same. As in another example:
O Mother of All, your pair of eyes, shimmering like the moon over the forest of moving locks of hair, bears the beauty of a pair of fish darting in a vast reservoir of water.

Here too, there is a relationship of original and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*) between the trembling locks of hair and the spreading net, as well as between the face and the moon and the pool of water; however, the distinction is that the pair of restless eyes and the pair of moving fish constitute a relationship of object and counterpart (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*). The rest is the same.

In this [type of *nidarśanā*], there is an apprehension of the identity between the attributes residing in the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) through the sense of the words; therefore, it is called *padārtha-nidarśanā*. Furthermore, in this *padārtha-nidarśanā*, the relationship of reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*) between the standard and the object of comparison occurs when they possess qualifiers (*saviśeṣaṇatva*), as in the two immediately preceding examples. Otherwise, however, it does not; such is the distinction. Now, one might object: "In *vākyārtha-nidarśanā*, since the qualifiers are also included by means of words denoting the qualified entities, let there be an identity between the expressed [qualifiers] through the sense of the words."

If it is argued that in *padārthanidarśanā* (illustration of a word-meaning), only one of the two—either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) such as "desire" (*ruci*), etc., or the object of comparison—is actually mentioned, and not both, [we reply: this is not so, because by the word "desire" (*ruci*), both are indeed mentioned in their capacity as "desire-ness" (*rucitva*). For what is intended here is not mention by way of the specific forms that delimit the status of being the standard or the object of comparison, which would result in an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*). Alternatively, the previously stated definition applies only to *vākyārthanidarśanā* (illustration of a sentence-meaning), not to *padārthanidarśanā*. However, let the definition for this latter be as follows: "That other [type] is *padārthanidarśanā*, where there is the superimposition (*āropaṇa*) of the property of one thing onto another. This is another form of simile (*upamā*) where the property of either the standard or the object of comparison is attributed to the other.

The meaning of *padārthanidarśanā* (illustration by a word-meaning) is the superimposition of a property belonging to either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object of comparison (*upameya*) onto the other. Now, one might object: "Even so, since *vākyārthanidarśanā* is already covered by *rūpakadhvani* (suggestion of metaphor), and *padārthanidarśanā* by *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) consisting of the swallowing-up of the object and its identification with another, these two figures are redundant. This is not the case. For in *vākyārthanidarśanā*, the metaphor is subordinate; therefore, it cannot be considered a suggestion (*dhvani*) of that metaphor. Otherwise, the metaphor would also be rendered superfluous by subordinated simile (*guṇībhūtopamā*).

Furthermore, the body of this [figure] consists merely of the mutual non-difference between two such objects, which rests upon both. However, in *rūpaka* (metaphor), the non-difference of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) resides in the subject of comparison (*upameya*), whereas in *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), the distinction between the two lies in the swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) or not swallowing of that [non-difference]. This is another matter. Thus, its distinctness from both *rūpaka* and *atiśayokti* is quite evident.

For this very reason, there is no loss of aesthetic charm (*cārutā*) even when the sequence of the meanings of the two previously cited verses—“With a jar, [he desires] the entire water of the ocean” and “[He desires] to adorn the Vṛṣagiri mountain”—is reversed. It should be understood that the same applies to verses such as “Your infinite majesty,” where, although the word *kāṅkṣati* (he desires) is restated as *kāṅkṣan* (desiring), it is prescribed as *icchan* (wishing) or *icchet* (may he wish).

In this context, when a suggested metaphor (*vyaṅgyarūpaka*) and the like are being discussed, even the relationship of subject and predicate (*uddeśyavidheyabhāva*) at the level of the suggested meaning must conform to the relationship of subject and predicate at the level of the expressed meaning (*vācyakakṣyā*). Consequently, in such instances as "He who is indeed able to measure the entire water of the ocean with a jar," since one must perceive the non-difference between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—consisting of the capacity to measure the entire water of the ocean using a jar as the instrument—and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—consisting of the ability to delimit the entirety of the Lord’s manifestations using the mind as the instrument—it follows that [the suggested meaning is subordinate].
This must be considered by the sovereigns among the theorists of poetics, lest an inconsistency arise regarding the nature of metaphorical representation (*rūpaka*).

Thus, regarding the illustration of the categories, although there is a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the examples already shown previously are to be applied according to the different modes of coordination (*samanvaya*). This too should be inferred by the wise in the manner that will be explained hereafter.
O Blessed One, it is true that he who, having failed to praise you, composes hymns for others, is cast out by the virtuous and bears the reputation of being a "forest crow. (617)

By the virtuous who know Brahman, he has been cast out and rejected; from where else could he come but to the state of a forest crow (*vanakākatām*), the term "forest" being used as a qualification to indicate extreme degradation? He bears this state. In the alternative sense, the word "praise-maker" (*stavanakāraka*)—being "cast out," meaning having its *repha* and *takāra* letters removed—results in the form "forest crow" (*vanakāka*). The rest is easy to understand. Here, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon the object of comparison (the praise-maker) of the quality of being a forest crow, which belongs to the standard of comparison.

And this results in a comparison: the sense is that praise of anyone other than the Blessed One is as useless, unpleasant, and unmelodious as the cawing of a crow in the forest. Here, the description of a different meaning for the word serves to heighten the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
O lotus-eyed one,
he who is talkative for no reason even when you— the treasury of joys— are present, truly reveals his own harsh nature as being devoid of essence.

The sense is: [O Lord] whose eyes are like those of a crane, who is a treasury (*nidhāna*)—that is, a storehouse—of joys (*mudāṃ*), meaning the bearer of the burden of bestowing every kind of bliss up to the sovereignty of liberation. Even though Your name exists, the meaning is that he who disregards Your name and remains merely talkative (*mukharaḥ*) for no purpose whatsoever—that man, being deficient in joy (*mudā nyūnaḥ*), is deprived of the utterance of the name which is a treasury of bliss; this is the sense. In the alternative sense (the pun), he is "deficient in gold" (*muvarṇena nyūnaḥ*), meaning separated from it.

In this view, it should be understood that the optional doubling of the letter *n* in the word *nyū* (in *nyūna*), according to the rule *anaci ca*, is for the sake of conforming to the intended meaning of the alternative reading. Regarding the word *bhāvam*: it means the state, nature, or movement of a donkey (*khara*). As Amara states: “*Bhāva* [is used] in the senses of existence (*sattva*), nature (*svabhāva*), intention (*abhiprāya*), movement (*ceṣṭā*), soul (*ātman*), and birth (*janman*)”. He “proclaims” this; the sense is that by being devoid of the aforementioned practice of uttering the Lord’s names, and by wasting his time with excessively harsh, unhearable, and meaningless chatter, he is indeed equal to a donkey.

In this context, the word *mukhara* signifies the manifestation of harshness (*kharatva*) through the displacement of the letter *m*. Here too, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the quality of a donkey (*khara*), which serves as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), onto the subject of comparison (*upameya*), namely, one who engages in vain chatter devoid of the utterance of the Lord’s name. Furthermore, the distinct aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) remains exactly as before.

Just as this Himavat mountain, possessing a form as pure and delightful as the moon and being the cause of Śiva’s exaltation, assumes the character of the great mountain Himavat; so too does that king of serpents.

*Sumanoramaḥ* means "exceedingly charming. *Ramaḥ* is derived from the root *ram* with the suffix *pacādyac*, meaning "one who delights. Alternatively, in the case of the Śeṣādri (the Hill of Śeṣa), it may mean "the delight (*rama*) of the wise (*sumanasām*). In the case of Himavat (the Himalayas), however, he is so called because his wife was the beautiful Manoramā;
for in ancient times, there was a daughter of Sumeru named Manoramā, and by her alone did that mountain-king become a householder and a sovereign among rulers.

Because of this statement: he is so described as one whose stainless form (*mūrti*) is honored by serpents (*ahi*), the sense being that his form is that of the sovereign of the *bhujaga*s (serpents). Alternatively, the word *hi* is a separate term meaning "well-known"; thus, he is so described as one whose stainless form is honored. In the other [metaphorical] sense, he is one whose form is stainless—that is, clear—due to the mass of snow (*himāni*). He is the cause of the prosperity, increase, and birth of the auspicious (*śiva*), of blessings, and of Śivā (Umā).
Here too, as before, there is the superimposition of the attributes of the standard of comparison onto the object of comparison, and this is reinforced by paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
Or rather:

"O Vṛṣagiri-māṇikya, your excellence of dark luster sports at will upon the emerald waters of the sky and the sapphire slabs of the youthful tamāla trees. (620) "O Vṛṣagiri-māṇikya" is the address. "Suṣamāyā asitimā" refers to the blackness of your supreme beauty.
Or, for example:

"The Veda appropriately calls this lotus 'the jewel-foot of the one with beautiful teeth' (acyuta-sudatī-maṇi-pada), since here the splendor of her feet is seen to be soft, smiling, and charming. (621)
The foot of Śrī, the jewel of the teeth of Acyuta, is her abode; "padalakṣmī" refers to the beauty of her feet.

O lion of the Raghu dynasty, even now the night-stalkers of the city of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa are bewildered upon beholding the luster of your compact frame, just as they were before the mass of jewels produced from the mines of Siṃhala.

In the first six examples here, beginning with "at the time of the day’s departure" (*adinavigamasamaya*) and so forth, there is the superimposition of the attributes of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) onto the subject of comparison (*upameya*). Even therein, in the first triad, the figure is pure (*śuddha*), whereas in the final triad, beginning with "having not praised you" (*tvām astutvā*), it is mixed with paronomasia (*śleṣa*). Subsequently, in the three examples beginning with "the young tamāla tree" (*taruṇatamāla*), there is the superimposition of the attributes of the subject of comparison onto the object of comparison. Furthermore, it should be understood that in the distinction of this last verse, "the sword-blade of Sihaḷa" (*sihalakhaṇi*), the ornament of illusion (*bhrāntimad-alaṃkāra*) is suggested by means of the figure of illustration (*nidarśanā*).

In both cases, however, the ultimate result is identical: through the impossibility of a property belonging to one thing existing in another, there is an implication of a similar property, which culminates in a simile. Jayadeva designated this type of *nidarśanā*—which functions on the basis of word-meanings—as *lalitopamā* (the charming simile).
The author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, however,
says: "That which is the cleansing of the jewels of your toenails of red lac is itself the whitening of the moon by the application of sandalwood paste."

Thus he cited this verse as an illustration of *vākyārthanidarśanā* (illustration by means of a sentence-meaning). He further stated: "But where another sentence-meaning is superimposed upon the primary sentence-meaning through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there it is proper that only *nidarśanā*—rooted in the impossibility of a [literal] connection—should apply. This is not correct, because it would result in the total abandonment of *vākyārtharūpaka* (metaphor by means of a sentence-meaning). Nor is this a desirable consequence, for the objection remains equal: "Let *vākyārthanidarśanā* alone be discarded, and let *vākyārtharūpaka* be accepted!"

And this is logical, as in cases such as *mukhaṃ candraḥ* ("the face is the moon"), where there is a superimposition of identity (*abhedāropa*) that is established through direct expression (*śrauta*). For it is appropriate to consider such a superimposition as the very life-force (*jīvātu*) of the figure of speech *rūpaka*. However, in instances of *padārthanidarśanā* (illustration of a thing), such as *induśobhāṃ vahatyāsyam* ("the face bears the beauty of the moon"), there is no superimposition of identity; therefore, it is impossible for [superimposition] to be the life-force of that [figure]. To claim that "there is no reflection (*bimbana*) in *rūpaka*" is merely a matter of oath, as there is a lack of reasoning [to support it], and because our aforementioned examples leave room for the existence of *vākyārthanidarśanā*.

As for the definition formulated by that same [author]—namely, that "Nidarśanā is a comparison understood through a connection with a real object, whether possible or impossible"—that too is not correct, because it over-extends to *rūpaka*, *atiśayokti*, and other such figures. For example:
"He who dyes your toe-nails with lac-dye makes the moon white with an application of sandal-paste."

Thus, when a verse is composed in this manner, the figure of speech *nidarśanā* (illustration) is appropriate. It should not be argued that the *nidarśanā* we have described is merely "expressed" (*vācyā*), whereas this one is "implied" (*pratīyamānā*). For it could equally well be said that "the face is like the moon" is an expressed simile (*vācyopamā*), while "the face is the moon" is implied; yet this [latter] is not a different figure of speech altogether. Therefore, the very life of *nidarśanā* is an implied non-difference (*abheda*) that exists outside the paths of both superimposition (*āropa*) and identification (*adhyavasāna*).

And that [simile] is established by means of demonstrating the non-difference between the agent and so forth, for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of the sentence. Others, however, claim that in the verse "tvatpādanakharatnānām" (of the jewels of the nails of your feet), there is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). That too is incorrect, because *dṛṣṭānta* consists precisely of two independent sentence-meanings composed of objects that have entered into the relationship of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

Therefore, it is established that in the phrase "your toe-nail," there is only a metaphorical sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-rūpaka*) and not an illustration (*nidarśanā*); this was demonstrated in the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, which follows the *Vimarśinī*. Thus, the illustration based on the connection of an impossible relation between things, occurring at the level of both the sentence-meaning and the word, has been shown.
If there were an illustration of the true meaning, it would be the awakening to what exists and what does not; otherwise, it would be a different kind of illustration.

The meaning is that "another" type [of simile], based on a possible connection between real entities, is that which is composed as the communication—by means of its own action—to others, of some object, whether existent or non-existent, characterized by a certain activity.

Just as the lotus-eyed Lord, who is constantly honored by those desiring greatness with bowed heads, makes this great serpent-mountain his crest-jewel while awakening it—so too does he [the king] act. 623.

*Mahattva* means worthiness of worship. *Sumahān* means exceedingly worthy of worship and also very vast. Here, because the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of "favoring"—just as in the expressions "the fire of dried cow-dung teaches" or "alms provide lodging"—and because it is possible for the serpent-mountain (Śeṣa) to perform an action conducive to the realization by people desiring greatness that the Lord is an object of head-worship, and because there exists a comparison such as "the Lord is honored on the head by me just as He is by another," this [poetic figure] is based on a relationship between possible entities (*saṃbhavadvastusaṃbandhamūlā*).

An instance [of this figure] is possible. Nor should it be argued that, because [the sun] does not actually awaken [the householder], this must be a mere *gamyotprekṣā* (suggested fancy); for since awakening is indeed possible in reality, there is no occasion for such a fancy to arise. For example:
"He who bears the divine Sun arrived upon his crest-jewel, thereby informing the householders that hospitality must be rendered to the virtuous."

Regarding this, they say: This [definition] is consistent with the view that "agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in being the substratum of the operation expressed by the verbal root," as stated in the rule: "When the action has been expressed by the root, agency is always intended for the *kāraka*. However, if one holds that the meaning of the suffix *tṛc* after the root *kṛ*, which signifies effort (*yatna*), is such that the word "agent" (*kartṛ*)—which follows a root whose meaning involves an object—denotes the substratum of effort through a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, when it is considered according to the principle that "the primary meaning of agentive suffixes is [the conscious agent], whereas the insentient is secondary," then it is said that even in the expression *bodhayan* ("awakening"), a suggested metaphor (*gamyotprekṣā*) is indeed possible; one should understand that a similar metaphor is possible here as well.

Just as one becomes illustrious through complete success by having one's feet worshipped by the heads of kings, so too did Śauri place his foot upon the peak of the mountain of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) to demonstrate this very truth.

The term *saṃsiddhi-prakṛti* means "those whose very nature is perfection," according to Amara. *Pada* means either a foot or a place. Here, the Blessed One, by the very act of placing His feet upon the site of the peak of Phaṇigiri—His own abode—naturally becomes one whose station is worthy of worship by the heads of kings; thus, as He conveys this true meaning (*sad-artha*), this is an instance of *sad-artha-nidarśanā*. The same applies in the subsequent verses as well.

Just as Fortune does not abandon a man of great merit even when he is clad in a forest garland, so too does Fortune dwell eternally upon the chest of the Wearer of the Forest Garland on the Bull-Flagged Mountain. 625.

The meaning is: "one who possesses exceedingly great merit" (atiśayita-puṇya), that is, one endowed with supreme virtuous deeds. In the context of the Blessed One (Bhagavat), he is called "atipuṇya" because he has transcended merit; for according to such scriptural passages as, "Neither good nor evil [affects him]; all evils turn back from him; his name is 'Ud' (risen); he has risen above all evils," and so forth. It has been established in the authoritative sources (Ākaras) that the word *pāpman* here refers to both types of karma, namely merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*). The remainder is clear.

In the first example, the awakening is expressed by the verbal suffix (*śānac*) in the word *vibodhayan*; in the second, it is expressed by the word ending in the suffix *tumun* (*darśayitum*). Here, however, that [awakening] is merely implied. Furthermore, the distinction is that the first is pure, while the others are mixed with paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
An illustration of an unreal object is as follows:

"Even though he is the most eminent of those with a noble lineage, the Lord is indeed greatly deceived and humiliated by many"; thus Hari demonstrates this by making the mountain of the serpent-king (Śrīparvata) inferior to a mere jackal.

*Gotra* and *pravara* mean lineage and noble ancestry; he who possesses these two is so described, meaning one born of a noble family. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), it means even the best of excellent mountains. A "deceiver of many" (*bahūnāṃ vañcakaḥ*) refers to one who outwits others. In the alternative sense, it refers to that [mountain] where there are many deceptors, namely jackals. He is "brought low," "humiliated," and "subordinated."

In this instance, by means of the action of being cast down—which has the Lord as its agent and the Hill of the Serpent (Śrīparvata) as its object—serving as a simile for His own self, another person who, though belonging to a noble lineage, is a great deceiver, is likewise understood to be cast down by the Lord; thus, because it conveys an unreal matter, this is an example of *asadarthanidarśanā* (illustration of the unreal).
As if demonstrating to the people that such would be the fate of those who cannot endure the serenity of the Blessed One’s countenance, the moon approached, trailing a mass of deep gloom.

The secret is this: the moon’s inability to endure the splendor of the Lord’s face culminates in its very likeness to that [face]. It attains (*upait*) an excessive connection (*anubandham*) with Raurava—that is, with the hell of that name. However, the actual state of affairs is that *raurava* means "belonging to the *ru* (deer)," from which the suffix *aṇ* is applied; and being both that and a connection, it refers to a stain or blemish.

Here, the moon is described as partaking in a connection with Raurava, thereby communicating a false idea: that those who cannot endure the splendor of the Lord’s face, like the moon itself, will suffer the fate of falling into Raurava. As in another example:

O Murāri, Vaiśvānara (the Fire-god), proclaiming his departure from those who rivalled Your splendor, turned away from his own color (red) and entered the midst of dogs, thereby attaining the status of a low-born person. 628.

Vaiśvānara, proclaiming that he shall indeed be the refuge for those who rival him with their splendor, turns his face away—that is, becomes averse—from his own *varṇa*, meaning from his own caste and from the collection of syllables that denote him; the singular number is used here with reference to the genus (*jāti*), meaning he has fallen from his own *varṇa*. In the alternative sense (the wordplay), the meaning is that he possesses the primary *varṇa* (syllable) "vai" which resides at the beginning (of the word).

For this very reason, in the middle—meaning in the interval between these two—he became a dog (*śvā*); in the alternative sense, he is one whose middle consists of the syllable *śvā*, thus "having *śvā* in the middle" (*śvāmadhya*). Then, immediately thereafter, he attained the state of a low-born person (*antyajana*), that is, the condition of a Caṇḍāla, according to the scriptural statement: "Having passed through a hundred births as a dog, one is born among the Caṇḍālas. In the alternative sense, he attained the state of that which has *na* and *ra* as its final letters in its birth (its formation), being thus called "one having *na* and *ra* at the end" (*antyanaravat*).

In this context, Vaiśvānara—who is characterized by aversion and so forth—is composed [in this verse] to demonstrate the false conclusion that such is the fate of those who rival the splendor of the Blessed One.

Or rather, like a diamond that has lost its luster, having become worthless and fallen into the state of being an object of "mine-ness," it spreads the grasp of "I" and "mine"—the cause of misfortune—at the very beginning [of existence]. (629)

*Masāra* means sapphire (*indranīla*), according to the statement, "One may use *masāra* for sapphire," and there is also the usage in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "having a face like *masāra* and *galvarka*" (*masāragalvarkamukhaḥ*). "Devoid of *tvadruci*" means devoid of *ruci*—that is, affection or love—for you; in the alternative sense, it means inferior to your luster, that is, possessing less radiance than you. "At first" (*ādau*) means initially. "The notions of 'I' and 'mine'" (*ahantāmamatayaḥ*) refers to egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*). Both *ahaṃ* and *mama* are indeclinables functioning as substitutes for case endings; the suffix *tal* is applied to them.

Having attained the state of being a locus— that is, a substratum— it becomes, for that very reason, essence-less and devoid of substance, yet it spreads the grasping of "I" and "mine," which is the cause of misfortune.
That notion of self in what is not-self, and that thought of "mine" in what is not one's own—
this twofold state is the seed from which the tree of ignorance grows.

The intention is that, according to the manner described above, [the verse] makes one understand how [this world] is the cause of misfortune characterized by worthlessness, preceded by wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), the word *masāra* means "devoid of Your splendor" (*tvadrucihīna*). The statement regarding the word *masāra* being devoid of the Lord’s splendor arises from the conceit of identifying the word with its meaning. The reading should be split as: *hanta amam atāspadatām iti*.

In the beginning, in the first part, "ama" becomes "ata" by being deprived of its *m* (i.e., through the elision of the letter *m*). "Atāspadatām" means the state of being the locus (*āspadam*) or support (*āśraya*) of *at*, that is, the state of being the vowel *a*. Having attained that state—meaning having reached the nature of the vowel *a* in that very place through the elision of the letter *m*.

"Just as in the injunction, 'One should not say "girā girā," but having made it "aira," one should chant,' the word *airā* prescribed after prohibiting the word *girā* occurs in the very place of the word *girā*, so too here, it should be understood that the vowel *a* (avarṇa) prescribed after prohibiting the vowel *m* (mavarṇa) also occurs in its very place. This should be observed in all such instances."

Therefore, having become "insubstantial" (*asāra*), by extracting the *ma* from that word according to the aforementioned method and placing the letter *a* [in its stead], the form "Masāra" is produced; this is the intended meaning. The rest is clear. Here, one who feels aversion toward the Blessed Lady because she has become the locus of the notions of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "mine-ness" (*mamattā*) becomes "insubstantial" (*asāra*). Thus, he is bound [to suffering] while spreading an unreal object—the grasping at "I" and "mine"—which is the cause of the aforementioned misfortune. This [figure of speech] is brought to perfection through an identification based on the foundation of *śleṣa* (punning), which relies upon the identity between word and meaning.
The same should be understood in the previous example as well. For instance: [Example follows]
Even those born of high status who follow the path of dull-witted beings fall lower and lower; thus, waterfalls descend from the peaks of mountains inhabited by self-indulgent lords of the wind.

Here, although one ought to say "falling lower and lower," the term "making [others] understand" is not employed because its meaning is already implied. Consequently, even though the waterfalls originate in high, elevated regions, they fall characterized by the act of falling themselves due to their following after dull-witted creatures; thus, by means of their own falling as an illustrative example, they cause others of a similar nature to understand the sense that they too are falling lower and lower—a sense that culminates in an undesirable outcome.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is an instance of *asadarthanidarśanā* (illustration with an unintended result), supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Chapter on Nidarśanā (Illustrative Simile), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra. Now begins the Chapter on Vyatireka (Distinction):
"If some distinction is stated between the object of comparison (upamāna) and the subject of comparison (upameya)..."
The wise call that the poetic figure known as Vyatireka (Distinction).

Now follows the description of figures of speech (alaṅkāra) where difference is predominant. Among these, *vyatireka* (distinction) is the description of some kind of difference between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*). Therefore, it should be understood that this figure occurs even when there is a mere point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), provided that the excellence of the subject, the excellence of the object, or the perception of both being superior or inferior is not intended. Regarding the excellence of the subject (*upameya*), an example is as follows:
"The mind of the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents (Śiva) appears deep like the middle of the ocean; the latter was once agitated by Mount Mandara, but the former has never been so at any time. (631)
"Agitated by the slow [pace]": that which has a slow rhythm (*manda*) and a slow sentiment (*rasa*) is "agitated" (*saṃkṣubhita*), meaning disturbed. The rest is clear.

Just as the Yamunā, dark-hued like the body of the Lord of Añjana Mountain and beautiful with its waves, shines forth; yet while the former dispels the heat, the latter is born from the son of Tapaṇa (the Sun). 632.

*Tapana* is a specific hell. Regarding *tapana*, the Medinī lexicon states: "The word *tapana* may refer to the sun (*bhāskara*), to a difficult task (*duṣkara*), or to a particular hell (*nirayāntara*). Thus, she is the daughter born from the body of Tapanabha, the Sun.

Just as the sun possesses lotuses made radiant by its rays and a form shimmering with the light of its spokes, so too is this Sudarśana; yet while the sun is difficult to behold, this Sudarśana is easy to behold.

The Lord of Weapons of Hari, the Blessed One, is the King of Discuses (Cakrarāja); he is so called because his lotuses are "sphuṭa" (blooming) with rays, like the sun. In another sense, he is so called because he "finds" (vindati) the "aras"—the spokes, those rods fixed around the hub—as they are clearly manifested (pravyakta) by his rays; for the *Medinī* lexicon states, "Ara means 'swift' and the mark on a wheel. [The suffix] *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). [He stands] within the "prabhāvitāna," the circle of splendor.

Alternatively, "prabhāsa" refers to luminous beings such as Agni and others who possess intense light (*prakṛṣṭā bhāḥ*). He is so described because his form flashes forth in an immeasurable (*amitam*), that is, unlimited (*aparicchinna*) manner within their *vitāna*, which is their collective assembly. Elsewhere, it means one who is a protector (*avitā*) of light, or one who has attained (*prāpta*) it. [The suffix] *tṛn* is applied to the root *av* in the sense of protection or attainment to denote habitual action.

With his form shimmering due to the rim (*nemi*)—the circular edge situated all around him—the Sun is difficult to behold; whereas this Lord of Weapons, Sudarśana, is "of beautiful aspect" (*sudarśana*), meaning he whose appearance is excellent. The word *sudarśana* is prescribed as masculine as well; thus the *Medinī* lexicon states: "Sudarśana is the discus of Hari and the *jambū* tree on Mount Meru; [it is] masculine. And the *Nāmanidhāna* states: "*Sudarśana* is [used] for the discus, not in the feminine.
Furthermore, Māgha employed it in the masculine: "This Sudarśana is the kinsman of the worlds."

O Mother, your face—with its locks of hair trembling from your sighing and its radiant forehead—is like a lotus; yet here, the latter shines even more intensely with the auspicious light of your lotus-like hands.

In one sense, it refers to him whose *cūrṇakuntala* (curled locks) are "moving" (*vicalantaḥ*) due to "sighing" (*niśvasanena*). In the other sense, it refers to that whose "petals" (*dalāni*) are "moving" (*vicalāni*) due to the "wind" (*nitarāṃ śvasanena*, i.e., *marut*), formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134; the suffix *ka* is added according to Pāṇini 5.4.154. It is further described as having a "shining forehead" (*lasad-ālīkam*), for Amara states that *alika* is a synonym for *lalāṭa* (forehead). In the other sense, it refers to that in which "bees" (*alayaḥ*) are "shining" (*lasantaḥ*), with the suffix *ka* applied as before.

However, your face shines most intensely with the auspicious glances—meaning the beautiful rays—of the moon; in the alternative sense, it belongs to the Lord (Bhagavān), who holds the conch (abja) in his hand, and it shines with his auspicious, benevolent side-long glances (ālokaiḥ). Or as another [verse] says: "O Hari, the king of the outcaste hamlet (*pakkaṇa*) becomes a king of the city (*rāṭ*), while yours becomes a king of the city (*rāṭ*). Between these two, a difference in form arises merely from their intense conjunction. (635)

He who is devoted to another [deity] than you becomes a *pakkaṇarāj*, a king of a *pakkaṇa*—a mere wretched village that serves as a dwelling for Śabaras. In the analysis of the compound (*vigraha*) "one who rules over a *pakkaṇa*," the suffix *kvip* is applied; thus Amara says, "*pakkaṇa* is the abode of the Śabaras. But your devotee, one who worships you, becomes a *paṭṭaṇarāj*, a king of the capital city (*rājadhānī*), according to Amara’s rule: "*rāṭ* [is used] for a king."

Vācaspati and others, citing the rule "paṭṭaṇaṃ puṭabhedanam," maintain that just as there is the word *pattana* with the letter *ta* (tavargya) as its middle-final consonant, there also exists the word *paṭṭaṇa* with the letter *ṭa* (ṭavargya) as its middle-final consonant. For this very reason, the usage "aṭṭaśūlāḥ katipaye paṭṭaṇe’smin pratiṣṭhitāḥ" is appropriately consistent with the established tradition.

This word is conventional (rūḍha), and one should not dispute this here. By the mere fact of the intense—that is, excessive—contact or association between these two, namely the *pakkaṇa* and the king of cities (*paṭṭaṇarāj*), a distinction in the form of those people who associate with them is established. The sense is that, according to the maxim "faults and virtues are born of association," even great men become base through association with a *pakkaṇa*, while even base men attain greatness through association with the king of cities; thus, a distinction of this nature is established.

The "excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*) conjunction of the two consonants *ka* and *ṭa*—defined by the rule "a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) consists of consonants that follow one another"—is intended here, by virtue of propriety, as the conjunction of *ka* with *ka* and *ṭa* with *ṭa* alone. From this very "intense conjunction" (*utkaṭasaṃyoga*), the distinction between forms is established. The point is that the difference between the words *pakkaṇarāṭ* and *paṭṭaṇarāṭ* arises solely from the conjunct *ka* and *ṭa*, and not from other phonemes.

In the first four examples cited, the simile (upamā) is verbal and rooted in contrast (vyatireka); here, however, the distinction is that it is implied (gamyā), being brought about by the act of worship and so forth. Or, for example: "Śiva causes fear to elephants; Viṣṇu wards off the fear of elephants. Between these two, Hara and Hari, what difference is there in their color—white and black? (636)

Giriśa (Śiva) is Dhūrjaṭi, the instiller of fear in the elephant Gajāsura; Phaṇādharagiriśa (Viṣṇu), however, is the warder-off of fear for the elephant, the protector from the terror of the lordly elephant. Regarding their respective colors—white and black, or white and blue—what indeed is the identity between these two, Hara and Hari? There is no identity at all; rather, the distinction is clearly evident. This is the meaning.
