Regarding the syllable (*pakṣe varṇe*), the meaning is that in the case of the words *kāva-bhida* ("splitting the *kāva*") and *kāva-bhaya-kāri* ("causing fear to the elephant"), the difference lies solely in the syllables *kāva*, and not in other phonemes. Furthermore, regarding *hara* and *hari*, there is some kind of identity (*kāva-abhidā*) through the letter *kā*; the distinction lies only in the letter *a*, as there are two *a*s in the word *hara* but only one in the word *hari*. This is the sense.

In this instance, the superiority of the remover of fear over that which causes fear—considered in relation to the effect of fear—is witnessed by all the world, since between the two who bestow both fear and fearlessness, it is the bestower of fearlessness alone who is more excellent. Here, although the word *hari* ought necessarily to be placed first in accordance with the rules "in a *dvandva*, a vowel-ending [word] precedes" and "the more venerable is placed first," one should note that its position at the end follows the observation that the section beginning with the rule "in the sense of a characteristic or a cause" (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*) is non-mandatory, as it conforms to the desired aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*).
Furthermore, here too, as in the previous example, the comparison is implied by the fact of being denotable by the word *īśvara* and so forth.

O Mother of mine, O Goddess, your row of teeth and your row of girdles are both richly endowed with the splendor of the tongue; the former is preeminent, the latter is intermediate, and between these two, O Goddess, there is only a slight difference. O Mother of mine, O Goddess, that well-known row of your teeth is "richly endowed with the splendor (*abhikhyā*) of the tongue (*rasanā*)," meaning it shines with a pale-red hue like the seeds of a ripe pomegranate due to its resemblance to the tongue, which is the "knower of flavors" (*rasajñā*). And there is also the "row of girdles" (*raśanāli*), the series of waist-bands. [The distinction is merely that the teeth are superior.]

Alternatively, *raśanāli* means "a row of girdles," as in the *Amara-kośa*: "The word *ālī* is feminine, while *setu* is masculine. The meaning of the lexicon is that when *ālī* is feminine, *setu* is masculine. It is "rich" (*āḍhyā*) by its designation, namely its name *sārasana*; for the *Amara-kośa* states: "Likewise, *saptakī* and *raśanā* [are synonyms]; *sārasana* is neuter; and *abhikhyā* refers to both name and beauty."

Between these two, the first *daśanāli* is the primary (*mukhyā*), the best (*śreṣṭhā*), and that which pertains to the face (*mukhe bhavā*); the other, *raśanāli*, is situated in the middle (*madhyasthā*), intermediate (*madhyamā*), and located at the waist (*avalagnasthā*). Between these two, there is a distinction (*bhidā*)—a difference (*bheda*)—of only a slight degree (*daramātrī*). The analysis of the compound is: "that distinction is of only a slight degree. The meaning is that the difference between them consists solely in being primary and being situated in the middle, and nothing else. In the alternative sense (the pun), the distinction is merely by the two letters *da* and *ra*; the point is that the words *daśanāli* and *raśanāli* differ only by those [two phonemes], as they are identical in their sequence of other letters.

Just as, through your grace, the two Indras were liberated and endowed with their true essential nature—one became a self-sovereign (Svarāṭ) and the other a self-ruling (Svārāṭ), yet remained lacking in full manifestation; such is the difference between them.

"O Blessed One"—this is understood from the context. By your grace, the person (pumān) is liberated, meaning released from the bondage of primordial nature (prakṛti); and Indra and Śakra are "liberated Indras," endowed with their manifested true forms (āvirbhūtasvarūpa).

In the state of liberation (*muktapakṣe*), he is endowed with that essential nature which has become manifest—an essential nature characterized by Brahmanical attributes such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth. Previously, his freedom from sin and other qualities were concealed due to his connection with a body initiated by past karma; the meaning is that he subsequently manifests his own true nature in the manner described in the text: "Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own form. Here, the meaning of the *Sampadyāvirbhāvādhikaraṇa* (the section on emerging upon reaching) should be kept in mind.

In the case of Indra, he is "manifested," meaning appeared or shining forth. That *svaru*—which, according to Amarasimha, is a sacrificial wooden splinter called *śatakoṭi*, *svaru*, or *śamba*—with which [Indra] was endowed; the sense is that even Indra’s acquisition of his thunderbolt weapon (*vajrāyudha*) depends solely upon the grace of the Lord. Of these two, the one first mentioned is the liberated *svarāṭ*; *svarāṭ* means "shining by himself," signifying one who is not subject to karma, as stated in the Śruti: "He becomes a *svarāṭ*."

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For this very reason, he has no other lord" (*ata eva cānanyādhipatiḥ*). Because of the scriptural revelation that "he is free from evil and his resolve is true," the meaning of the Sūtra is that he is not subject to karma. As for the "other"—Indra, who was mentioned immediately prior—he is *svārāj* (self-sovereign), meaning he does not rule by himself; thus, he is dependent on karma. Alternatively, *svaḥ* means the king of heaven (*svargasya rāṭ rājā*). *Svar* is an indeclinable ending in the letter *r*.

In the word *rori*, due to the elision of the *repha* (visarga), there is a lengthening according to the rule *ḍhralope pūrvasya*. Amara states: *svārāṇṇamucisūdanaḥ*. Between those two—the one from whom Mahendra has been liberated and the other—there is a difference that is *āsphūrtimān*, meaning possessing slight manifestation (*īṣat-sphuraṇavān*). The prefix *āṅ* is used here in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadarthe*). Thus, the meaning is that the difference is extremely small. Alternatively, *ā* means "on all sides" (*samantāt*), used here in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). The sense is that there is a great difference between the two: one who is independent of karma and one who is dependent on the power of karma. Amara states: *āṅ* is used in the senses of "slight" and "pervasion" (*abhivyāptau*).

Alternatively, although these two are equal according to the manner stated above, he—deliberating on whether some distinction might still exist or not—recalls [it] and says: "Āḥ! It has become manifest. The meaning is that the distinction between those two—the liberated one and Mahendra—namely the difference that one is a *svarāṭ* (self-ruling) and the other is a *svārāṭ* (ruler of his own domain), has now been clearly manifested as he remembers it. The particle *āḥ* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) designated as *pragṛhya* used in the sense of recollection; as Amara states: "The *ā* used in recollection is *pragṛhya*."

The meaning is that in one case it possesses manifestation, being radiant through the forms of shortness and length; for it is by that alone that a difference is observed between the words *svarāṭ* and *svārāṭ*.

Or for example: "O Hari, you are lotus-faced; your son was born as the very one seated upon a lotus (*kamalāsana*). No distinction between the two should be reckoned in this world, since you both are known as the Lords of the World (*lokeśau*). (639) O Hari! You are *kamalānana*: the *anana*—the animator or life-giver—of *kamalā*, that is, Śrī. [The word] *anana* is derived from the root *an* (to breathe or animate), meaning "by which one is animated"; thus, you are the one whose face is like a lotus. Your son is Brahmā, who is *kamalāsana*. [He is so called because he] rejects (*asyati*) Śrī; thus the analysis of the compound is "the one who rejects (*āsana*) Kamalā. He is also described as "seated upon a lotus" (*padmopaviṣṭa*).

The distinction or difference of the kind described should not be counted—that is, it should be disregarded—because such a slight difference is of no consequence; this is the intended meaning. For what reason? Because "you two" (*yuvām*) refers to him and you, where, according to the grammatical rule *tyadādīnāṃ mithassahoktau yatparaṃ tacchiṣyate*, there is a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of the word *yuṣmad* as the subsequent term. You are both known as "Lords of the World" (*lokeśau*). The sense is: "What is this difference between you two who are both recognized as Lords of the World?"

For even the status of being the Lord of the World (Lokēśa) is well-established for the Four-faced One (Brahmā), as it is said: “Hiraṇyagarbha is the Lord of the World. In this context, the distinction between the two [the face and the seat] should be counted by means of the *nas* sounds and the *na-sa* sounds; the sense is that the difference between the lotus-face and the lotus-seat is perceived through that much alone. Here, in the three examples beginning with “rich in the name of the girdle” (*sārasanābhikhyāḍhyā*), the specific feature is that the figure of contrast (*vyatireka*) is enlivened by the similarity (*tulyayogitā*) manifested by the suggestion of the pun (*śleṣa*) in the word *sārasana* and so forth.
O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents, your fame and the female hawk are both winged; yet while the former is renowned as a "devourer of rabbits," the latter devours the moon by its own power.

O Lord of Phaṇigiri! There was a certain bird named *pattriṇī*, a female hawk (*śyenī*) or one called a hawk (*śyenā*). According to Amara: "Now, *śaśādanaḥ*, *pattrī*, and *śyenaḥ* [mean] a hawk. And according to the *Amaramālā*: "*Śyena*, *pattrin*, and *śaśādana* [are synonyms]. And Śāśvata says: "*Śyena* is the name of a bird; *pattrī* and *pattriṇau* refer to an arrow and a winged bird. From the word *pattrin*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied because it ends in *n*, or the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it denotes a genus (*jāti*). Your fame, likewise, was a female hawk; this is the meaning already stated.

In this context, she was white-colored (*śvetavarṇā*); as Amara states: "clear, white, pale" (*viśada-śyeta-pāṇḍuraḥ*). When the feminine gender is intended from the word *śyeta*, the suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "from a non-udātta vowel, with *t* as its penultimate, *naḥ* [is substituted for *t*]" (*varṇādanudāttāt topadhāt to naḥ*), whereby the *t* is replaced by *n*. However, from the Medinīkośa—“*śyenaḥ* [is used] for a bird and for what is pale"—it is understood that there is also a form *śyena* with a nasalized penultimate (*nopadha*) used in the masculine.

Therefore, because *pippalī* and others belong to the class of words known as *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is to be understood [to form the feminine forms]. Of those two, the first is *patriṇī* (the winged one), which is renowned by the name *śaśādanī* (the devourer of rabbits), being well-known by that appellation. But the latter—your own fame—by its own vigor, that is, by its own splendor, devours, that is to say, swallows up or eclipses, the moon, meaning the one possessing a rabbit (*śaśavat*), or the moon itself; such is the actual sense.

Just as the crow scratches at the heart while the cuckoo is dear to you because of its servitude to your voice— O Mother, there is some difference between these two birds even in their plumage and their tone.

O Mother! The crow—the *vāyasa*, meaning the son of Indra (*aindri*)—has "scarred" (*rarāda*), that is, scratched, your chest (*vakṣas*); [the root] *rada* means "to scratch," [the form being] the perfect tense (*liṭ*). Alternatively, the crow—the ordinary *vāyasa*—has "scarred" your heart, the minds of those who hear you; that is to say, it has caused agitation through the harshness of its voice. As for the cuckoo (*pika*), however, in your speech it has attained the status of a servant (*dāsa*); as in the verse beginning "Even in service to your mouth, the autumnal [cuckoo] has not attained the right to authority," the comparison culminates in this very likeness.

"He became dear to your heart"—that is, he became beloved to your heart; in the alternative sense, the meaning is that he became charming to those who heard him due to the sweetness of his voice. Although they were two *dvijas*—meaning both were twice-born as Brahmins, yet in reality, they were two birds, a crow and a parrot—there exists an indescribable (*kāpi*) distinction (*bhidā*) between them, both in their *vyañjana* (external marks such as the beak and wings) and in their *svara* (sound or tone). According to Amara, "the word *vyañjana* refers to a mark, a mole, a mustache, spittle, or a limb."

In this alternative view, the distinction existing between the syllables *kā* and *pi* in the words *kāka* and *pika* exists in the consonants (*hal*)—namely the forms *ka* and *pa*—and in the vowels (*svara*)—namely the forms *ā* and *ī*—even though these do not belong to the *ava*-group; it exists in both types of phonemes (consonants and vowels), but not in the final *ka*s of both words, because in those cases both are seen to be identical in form. The specific point in these two examples is that the figure of speech is *vyatireka* (contrast), which is enlivened by *dīpaka* (illumination) and stimulated by the flash of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

And it should be understood that this [simile], from the verse beginning with "equal in mind to the lord of the mountain of serpents" up to the end of these eleven verses, culminates in the exaltation of the object of comparison (upameya).
An example of the excellence of the object of comparison (*upamānotkarṣa*) is as follows:

"Mount Meru and the serpent-mountain [Śeṣa] are both enriched by the celestial Gaṅgā; yet of these two, the former supports the entire world, while the other has himself become the support of the earth."
He holds the earth, the sustainer of the universe, beneath him; that is, he places it below. Alternatively, he has become inferior to the Lord, the sustainer of the universe.

Just as you possess an infinite capacity for support, so too do I, O cloud; yet there is this much difference between us: you dispel the heat caused by the arrival of the summer, while I, a fool, carry this very heat.

Of the infinite intermediate space and of the Blessed One. "Heat" refers to the fever born of the summer season, arising from the arrival of warmth; alternatively, it refers to the heat—the internal and other forms of suffering—arising from existence (*bhava*), which is characterized by a sharp onset (*āgama*) of warmth. The rest is easy to understand.

Just as the acquisition of prosperity (*śrī*) from your side-glance is equal for both the lords of the quarters (*diśāmpatīnām*) and the lords of the people (*viśāmpatīnām*), yet there is a distinction (*bhidā*) regarding their residence in heaven (*divi*), O Beloved of the Lord of the Great Mountain of Serpents (*phaṇigirīndramaṇidayite*). Regarding "residence in heaven": while there is a distinction in their station—namely, that the lords of the quarters have a residence in heaven (*svarga*) whereas the lords of the people do not—on the other hand, in the case of the words *diśāmpatīnām* and *viśāmpatīnām*, there is a distinction only in the presence of the two syllables *di* and *vi*, since all other syllables are identical.
The other [type] is indeed explicit (*vyakta*). In these three examples as well, there is the excellence of the object of comparison (*upamāna*); everything else is exactly as before.
When neither excellence nor deficiency of both is perceived, as in:
"O Lord, Your form and Your fame are known through hundreds of scriptural traditions to be as white as camphor"—since these two are impossible to praise, silence is here considered superior.

O Lord! O Śrīnivāsa! Your form and your fame are like *ghanasāra*. According to Amara, *ghanasāra* means "strength," "firm part," "just," or (neuter) "excellent"; in this sense, it is "excellent. Like that, [your form] is *śiti*, meaning blue. In the other case, *ghanasāra* refers to camphor—Amara states: "Now, camphor is *astrī* (not feminine), it is *ghanasāra*. Like that, [your fame] is *śiti*, meaning white—Amara states: "*śiti* refers to both white and dark."

She is known through hundreds of scriptural passages (*śruti*) as being "not blue" (*anīlata*), for in such texts as "From the dark I go to the variegated; from the variegated I go to the dark," she is celebrated as being as dark as a dark-blue cloud. In the case of her fame (*kīrti*), the meaning is that she is known or understood by hundreds of scriptures—that is, by the thousands of ears of those who hear her—or alternatively, that she is celebrated for her whiteness. Or else, her form (*mūrti*) is celebrated because of its non-material nature and other qualities; whereas fame (*kīrti*) is celebrated for its greatness, according to the statement: "His name is great glory."

The sense is this: who has the power, with their limited speech, to describe these two—the form and the fame—which are beyond praise and renowned through hundreds of Vedic texts? Here, the "silence" (*mūkībhāva*) regarding these two, form and fame, is specifically characterized by the very presence of the phonemes *mū* and *kī*; because all other phonemes are equal [in this regard], this alone is the distinction and nothing else. The identity between the signified and the signifier (*tādātmya*) is the recourse here; otherwise, the intended distinction could not possibly reside in the object itself.

Furthermore, in this matter concerning its praise, silence is specifically enjoined; the meaning is that for those in our condition, remaining in silence alone is better. Here, because excellence and deficiency are not distinguished due to being permeated by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is an "exclusion of both" (*anubhayavyatireka*). This should be understood in the same way in the subsequent examples as well.

Just as you are indeed the mother of the world and the protector of the world, O Daughter of the Ocean, so too is your beloved; for while you two are equal in all virtues, there remains only this distinction between you: that he is your husband.

The sense is that there is only a slight difference—merely a trace, an indescribable and insignificant distinction—and not a difference in every respect; as Amara states: "In the feminine, *mātrā* and *truṭi*; in the masculine, *lava*, *leśa*, *kaṇa*, and *aṇu*. In the alternative sense (the pun), the meaning is that the difference consists solely of the letters *mā* and *trā*.

Just as desire afflicts me here, and Yama there in the next world— though these two times are distinct from one another, their difference being merely that of the body— therefore, O Mukunda, bestow Your compassion upon me.

By its very nature (*svataḥ svabhāvata eva*), the agreement (*samaya*) is equal in its capacity to subvert [the opponent] in both cases; that is, when these two—*kāma* and *yama*—are accompanied by the letter *ma*, the distinction between them is merely physical (*kāyamātrāt*), meaning the difference lies only in their form (*śarīra*) and not in their qualities (*guṇa*). Alternatively, the meaning is that *kāma* has no body (*kāya*) while *yama* does possess one, and thus the difference is due to that alone. Furthermore, it should also be understood that the distinction lies simply in the letters *ka* and *ya*. As in the following example: [Example omitted per instructions]

Formerly, those two wicked ones, Muru and Khara, whose heads were severed by your swift discus—which was suited for the hells—were indeed killed by you with their flaws exposed, through a mere breach of their faces.

The sense is that they are "consonant" (*anuguṇau*)—that is, suitable—with Naraka, Narakāsura, and Niraya: because of their friendship with him in one case, and because of their own sinful deeds in the other. They are "accompanied by Dūṣaṇa," meaning they exist together with the demon named Dūṣaṇa due to his fault (*doṣeṇa*). The ellipsis is that those two previously had their heads severed by you with the swift *sudarśana* discus—that is, by the multitude (*cakra*) of swift arrows (*āśuga*).

Between those two, Muru and Khara—the Daitya and the Rakshasa bearing those names—there is a distinction only in their faces: Muru has three heads, resulting in a three-facedness due to his being three-headed, while Khara has a single head, resulting in a single-facedness; this is the only difference, as their aforementioned qualities are identical. Furthermore, there is another sense: the distinction lies solely in their golden and donkey-like complexions.
Or, for example:

"O Govinda, those who, under the sway of immense misfortune, revile you—the teacher of all—these people's speech is nothing but the barking of dogs; the difference between these two lies only in their outward form. (649)

*Bhāṣaṇa* means speech, derived from the root *bhāṣ* with the suffix *lyuṭ*. *Bhaṣaṇa* means the barking of a dog; as it is said, "the root *bhaṣ* [is used] in the sense of threatening," and here "threatening" refers to the sound of barking. From this [root], the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied. Between these two—*bhāṣaṇa* and *bhaṣaṇa*—there is a difference only in their form, consisting merely in whether they are uttered from the mouths of humans or dogs; otherwise, there is a difference only through the short vowel *a* and the long vowel *ā*. The sequence of other phonemes, however, is exactly the same. Or, for example: * **Example:** * *bhāṣaṇa* (speech) * *bhaṣaṇa* (barking) In these cases, the distinction lies solely in the vowel (*a* vs. *ā*), while the rest of the syllables remain identical.

Śveta-dvīpa and Dvīpa are indeed equal, both being composed of the syllables *para-bala-hara-hari* and *kha-la*. What difference could there possibly be between these two, since they are identical in their phonetic form in every respect? (650)

Śvetadvīpa, Śvetadvīpa, and Airāvata. In the case of Śvetadvīpa, it means "held by Hari, the Blessed One, who is the remover (hara) of the strength, power, or army of enemies (para-dviṣ). In the case of Airāvata, however, it means "held by Hari, that is Indra, who is the remover (hara) of Bala—the enemy (para) known as the demon Bālāsura. [The two words] are formed by the elision of one of the pair (ekaśeṣa). For this very reason, they are identical.

"In every way" means in every respect; the sense is that only when two things possess the same color—both being white, for instance—is there a question. In the alternative sense (pakṣe), it refers only to those whose syllables have identical sequences (*samānānupūrvīka*). What difference could there be between these two, Śvetadvīpa and Śvetadvīpa? The meaning is that since they are entirely equal, even the existence of some indefinable slight distinction between them is of no consequence. In the alternative sense, the word division is "kiyatī ībh idā."

The meaning is that the difference between the long *ī* and the short *i*, as well as between the long *ai* and the short *e*, is very slight; the sense is that even though there is some slight difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), it is not worth taking into account.

Or rather, I consider these two to be equal, for both possess a sweetness of voice learned from that [same source]. Therefore, O Madanma, let the distinction between the cuckoo and the parrot always be made in your heart. (551)

O noble lady! I consider these two—the cuckoo and the parrot—to be equal, for they have both been trained in the sweetness of sound by your own words. The point here is that the distinction between these two, the cuckoo and the parrot, lies solely in the difference between the syllables *pi* and *śu*, and not in any other phonemes; let this be kept in mind. It should be understood that even this distinction between the syllables *pi* and *śu* residing in the sound is actually caused by the misconception of identity between the word and its meaning.

"And another meaning: 'O auspicious one! is the vocative address. 'Ada' is the word division. Here, regarding these two—the cuckoo and the parrot—let that mutual similarity always be kept in mind; you should reflect that there is an equality between them due to the sweetness of their voices, which have been trained by your speech."
Or, for example:

"Vāsudeva and Vāsuki are both served by the gods who desire immortality; they are equal, yet there is indeed a distinction between them—namely, that one is Devakī's son and the other is her brother. (552)

He is renowned as Vāsudeva, and Vāsuki is likewise; they are both to be served by those gods who are seekers of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*) and by the wise who know Brahman, and for that very reason, they are equal. The distinction between these two, however, lies solely in their mother—namely, Devakī. For while Vāsudeva’s mother is well-known as Devakī, Vāsuki does not have such a mother; this alone is the difference. The sense is that their status as being served by the gods seeking the nectar of immortality is indeed identical.

In this case, between the two words *vāsudeva* and *vāsuki*, there is only a slight (*mātra*) difference. The sense is that the only distinction is that in the first word there are the syllables *deva*, while in the latter there is the syllable *kī*; for the first two syllables are identical in both. (The word *mātra* is used here in the sense of "slight," as Amara states in his list of synonyms for smallness: *striyāṃ mātrā truṭiḥ puṃsi lavaleśakaṇāṇavaḥ*). Furthermore, *mātrā* [is defined] as an ear-ornament, wealth, a measure, a covering, a part of a syllable, a small amount (neuter), entirety, or emphasis.
Thus says the Medinī lexicon. Or, for example:

"That kingdom which is naturally to be given by one, and that body which is naturally to be abandoned by the other—between Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, there is no difference between them other than this very distinction. (653)

The kingdom of that Rāma—which was *sahajadeya*, meaning it was to be given to his co-born brother Bharata—*āsa* (was). *Āsa* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) resembling a verbal form; it is used here like the expression “this was the sign” (*idamāsa cihnam*). It is not the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *as* (to be), for if it were a verbal form, the rule *asterbhūḥ* would require the substitution of *bhū* in the perfect tense. Alternatively, it is the perfect tense of the root *as* in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*). The suffix *yat* is applied in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*) by the rule *aco yat*. Thus, the meaning is: "the kingdom, which was to be given to the co-born, shone forth.
Indeed, [he gave] Sītā, the kingdom, his life-breaths, and dear wealth.

"Unprompted, I shall give [the kingdom] to my brother Bharata"—from this statement [of Rāma]. Or rather, the meaning is that it was "to be given" (*deyam*) by the "innate" (*sahajena*) Bharata; for Bharata said: "I shall give back to him that which you gave to me. That kingdom was also to be "abandoned" (*heyam*)—meaning "to be given" (*deyam*)—by Lakṣmaṇa as well, toward his innate brother or by his innate brother. [The root] *ohāk* means "to abandon"; [the suffix] *yat* is applied according to the rule *aco yat*; and Amara states: "Abandonment (*tyāga*), relinquishment (*vihāpitam*), and giving (*dānam*) [are synonyms]. In reality, however, the meaning is that it was to be abandoned or renounced by the "innate" (*sahajena*), that is, by nature itself (*nisargeṇa*).

Regarding the term *sahaja*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *sahaja* refers to that which is innate (*nisarga*) or born together (*sahottha*), like [the word] *anya*. Here, one should reflect on such passages as: "When the son of Sumitrā, though exhorted with all his soul, did not enter into yoga... The sense is that because his sole delight was in service (*kaiṅkarya*), the kingdom had to be relinquished by him. Between these two—Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa—the difference between what is to be accepted by nature and what is to be abandoned by nature exists only in their physical bodies (*vigraha*); there is no difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or in the aforementioned qualities.
Then, the lotus-petal-eyed one, having divided himself into fourfold...
Then he chose King Daśaratha as his father.

Because of this statement, the word *ātman* here denotes the body. In this context, the meaning is that between the two terms *sahajadeyarājya* and *sahajaheyarājya*, the difference lies solely in the two syllables *de* and *he*, and not in any other letters. In these nine examples, beginning with “*ghanasāraśitiḥ*,” one should observe the *anubhayavyatireka* (neither-excess-nor-deficiency), since there is no perception of either superiority or inferiority.

Thus, the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) has been demonstrated in accordance with the *Kuvalayānanda*. Now, the *vyatireka* according to the method of the ancients will be shown in accordance with the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, *Rasagaṅgādhara*, and other such works:
"When the object of comparison (*upameya*) [is distinguished] from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) by a particular quality..."
When excellence is described, the wise call that *vyatireka* (contrast).

*Vyatireka* (distinction) is the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*) by virtue of its possession of specific qualities over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). The inclusion of the word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) is intended to exclude *pratīpa* (the inverse) and other figures; furthermore, it refers to a point of contrast (*vaidharmya*). In that context, the superiority of the object of comparison arises solely from its being the subject of comparison rather than the standard, and not from the contrast itself, because only similarity (*sādharmya*) is perceived. Merely possessing superior qualities or merely the inferiority residing in the standard of comparison does not constitute the nature of *vyatireka*, for those two lack aesthetic beauty unless they imply the superiority of the object of comparison.

For this very reason, it is not merely the absence of similarity; for that [absence] could occur even when the object of comparison (upameya) is inferior to the standard of comparison (upamāna), and since such an object of comparison—possessing inferior qualities—is in reality unsightly. Furthermore, if the absence of similarity were qualified by the excellence of the object of comparison, then since that excellence of the object of comparison alone would be appropriate as the poetic figure (*alaṃkāra*), the additional element [the absence of similarity] would be purposeless. As in: "Even though this face of the one whose abode is the lotus is always possessed of unfading splendor, how could it ever take recourse in a comparison with the lunar disc, which possesses faded splendor? (654)

"It does not wither, therefore it is *amlānā* (unfading); it is stainless (*nirmalā*)," such is the actual state of things. Hemacandra states: "*Amlānaḥ* [is used] for *jhaṇṭī* and *bheda* when [the word] *amala* [is present]. That which possesses such splendor (*śrī*) is described as "that" (*tathoktam*). The suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule "*śeṣādvibhāṣā*" (Pāṇini 5.4.154). In some instances, the construction is *mlānaśriyā*. Furthermore, this [type of simile] is fourfold: based on the presence or absence of both the points of contrast (*vaidharmya*)—one which enhances the object of comparison (*upameya*) and one which diminishes the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—and based on the non-mention of either one of those two.

The ancients maintain that this [simile], being twelvefold through its divisions into *śrautī* (verbal), *ārthī* (objective), and *ākṣiptā* (implied), becomes twenty-four types when further distinguished by the presence or absence of *śleṣa* (punning).
"O King, let the talkative ones say whatever they wish; yet your hand, like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadru*), bestows abundant prosperity—why then does it give so little? (655)

Is your hand like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadru)? The sense is that it should not be like that [the tree]. Why? To this he says: "This. This refers to your hand. The rest is easy to understand. Here, there is the mention of both [the object and the standard of comparison], and the simile (upamā) is verbal (śrautī). In this very context, if the second half were composed as "How is it that this [hand] never gives even small fortune, like the wish-fulfilling tree? or if it were composed as "Is this like the wish-fulfilling tree, which always gives only very little fortune?", then there would be the non-mention of one of the two.

This is also a verbal simile (*śrautī upamā*). In the verse, "To whose satisfaction could the words 'like the wish-fulfilling tree' (*kalpadruriva*) be imagined by a wise man?", it is a verbal simile because the common property (*hetu-sāmānya*) is not explicitly stated. For when two causes [of excellence or deficiency] are present, that one which is not explicitly stated is understood through implication (*ākṣepa*). When neither of the two is explicitly stated, it is the same; there is no lack of understanding, because contrast (*vyatireka*) consists of superiority and inferiority, and these cannot be cognized without knowledge of their respective causes.
Thus, does that outward-flowing stream—which is constantly pure in nature yet occasionally becomes turbid at certain times—deserve your impartial compassion? (656)

In this case, both [the simile and the standard] are explicitly mentioned (*ubhayopādāna*), while the simile is implied (*ārthī*). When the first half-verse is read as "O girl, like the ocean of nectar, sometimes attaining turbidity," and the second and third quarters are conceived as "sometimes enjoying clarity at any time; the outward-flowing stream," there is the non-mention of either one, and the simile is implied. When the second quarter of "O girl, like the ocean of nectar" is composed as "having its foundation established in the heart of the Lord of Mountains (Śiva)," there is the non-mention of both, and that [simile] is likewise implied.
Dwelling in the presence of the Lord of the Mountain, who is the source of limitless bliss, surpasses the residence of men within the worlds of Brahmā and others, which yields only limited joy.

In this case, because there is an absence of words such as *iva*, which possess the power of denoting mere similarity, or words such as *sadṛśa*, which possess the power of denoting that qualified by similarity, the simile (*upamā*) is merely implied (*ākṣiptā*) by the act of disparagement (*adharīkaraṇa*), thereby deviating from the path of direct expression (*śruti*). In this very context, there is an omission of one of the two [terms] either in the composition of the first quarter, beginning with "attainable through boundless merit" (*niravadhikasukṛtasulabhe*), or in the composition of the second half, beginning with "it surpasses the abode of the Lord of Wealth, the Moon-crested Lord, and the inhabitants of the world of men" (*adharayati vidhinidhīśvaravidhuśekharalokanivasatiṃ nṝṇām*). And thus, the simile remains implied.

When the first half [of the verse] was composed as "His dwelling is in the proximity of the lotus-feet of the Madhumathana, the lord of mountains who bears serpents," there was a non-mention of both [the common and the specific qualities], and that is [an example of non-mention]. Thus has the direction of *niḥśleṣa-vyatireka* (non-allusive contrast) been shown. Now, the direction of *saśleṣa-vyatireka* (allusive contrast) is demonstrated. For example:
"Is the Blessed One, whose sins are destroyed, not like the sun—since he, by the touch of his hand, brings joy even to the lotus-plant which is devoid of beauty? (658)

Is he perhaps the Lord Bhāskara (the Sun), who—like the sun—bestows joy (*āmoda*), which signifies both delight and fragrance, upon the *kamalinī* (lotus plant) by the touch of his hand (or rays)? This lotus plant is "destitute of splendor" (*niśśrīkā*) because she has not been bathed and her luster is faded; the suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. She is "soiled" (*malinī*), meaning she is menstruating (*puṣpavatī*), as Amara states: "*malinī* also means *puṣpavatī*. In the alternative sense, [the lotus] is "devoid of Lakṣmī" (*niśśriyaḥ*) because it has not blossomed and is thus bereft of the abode of Fortune. Is he, therefore, the radiant Sun who imparts fragrance and joy through the contact of his rays?

To the question "Why should this not be so?", he says "yataḥ" (because). Because this [Self] is "free from evil," according to the Śruti: "Neither good nor evil deeds [reach it]; all evils turn back from it, for this world of Brahman is free from evil. Here, both [the literal and metaphorical senses] are employed; there is a scriptural simile (*śrautī upamā*), and the pun (*śleṣa*) is indeed evident.

How indeed could the world describe the mountain of the serpent-king as being like the Golden Mountain? For that [Golden Mountain] is known as the abode of the gods, while this [serpent-mountain] dwells at a sacred ford that removes all impurities.

The holy ford (tīrtha) known as "the remover of turbidity" and "the destroyer of sin" is situated on Śeṣādri. Here too, both [epithets] are employed; thus, there is both a simile based on the Vedic tradition and a pun (śleṣa).

O Veṅkaṭanātha! You are indeed not like the rain-cloud; why? Because you have not failed to bestow the intense, thick essence—that is, the affection—upon the virtuous. Furthermore, you possess the manifestation of accumulated asceticism and the gait of a pure swan. O Veṅkaṭanātha! You are certainly not like the rain-cloud. Why? To this he says: "Because" (yad). Since you have not failed to bestow (*tyāga*) that which is "intense" (*ghana*), meaning thick, "essence" (*rasa*), namely affection (*anurāga*), upon the "virtuous" (*sādhu*), meaning the good—thus he is so described.

Alternatively, "sādhu" means praiseworthy; "ghana" means full; and "rasa" means bliss. Thus, the meaning is that by him the abandonment of such unsurpassed bliss was not ordained. In the other sense (pakṣe), the meaning is that the abandonment of pure water was not ordained. He is so described because he possesses the manifestation of both austerity (*tapas*)—meaning ascetic practice—and the summer season (*grīṣma*). [He has reached] the state (*gati*) of the stainless (*vimala*), clear (*viśada*), and pure—both the *haṃsas* who are wise men and the *marālas* who are swans. The word *gati* is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ktin* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*), meaning "that which is reached. [Note: This passage is a double-entendre (*śleṣa*) describing a spiritual figure while simultaneously describing the summer season.]
Here, there is no mention of anything that would detract from the standard of comparison; furthermore, there is both a verbal simile (śrautī upamā) and a paronomasia (śleṣa).

O Mother, how can they understand your eye to be like a blue lotus, when that [lotus] first attained a bad color, was then disrespected in the middle, and finally met its destruction, whereas yours remains ever thus? 661.

The *kuvalaya* (blue lotus) has already at the very beginning—that is, from the outset—attained a "bad color" (*ku-varṇa*), meaning a contemptible color, or rather, the syllable 'ku' (as the suffix *kta* denotes the agent). In the middle—that is, during its intermediate stage—it was "despised" (*avamānita*) by your eyes; the sense is that it was treated with contempt. In the alternative interpretation, it was "despised" within its own denotative word, meaning it was joined with the letter 'va'. For this very reason, at the end—that is, in the final conclusion—it has reached "dissolution" (*laya*), a state of merging into something else; here too, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent.

The meaning is that the two syllables "la" and "ya" have arrived in the [word] *pakṣe*. Here, there is no mention of the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*); the simile is verbal (*śrautī*), and there is also a pun (*śleṣa*).

O fair-faced Śrī! Just as gold, though carrying a beautiful color externally, always possesses a base color within; so too may your deer-like body be equal to Hari’s behind, but never before. O fair-faced one! O Śrī! "Antaḥ" means either inside or hidden within. "Suvarṇam" means gold.

On one hand, although she carries—that is, possesses—the syllable *su* (the form *su*) within her own name, situated between the words denoting her; and although she always bears the syllable *ku* (the form *ku*), which is an ill-favored letter (*ku-varṇa*), at the beginning of her face (*mukha*, i.e., her mouth); yet she bears a flower (*kusuma*). By this [description], it is shown that her entire body is gold, unrevealed [by clothing]—referring to a golden statue of a deer (*hariṇī*), for the Vedic scripture states: "The golden-hued, the deer-like" (*hiraṇyavarṇām hariṇīm*). And [she is so called] because she is green-colored (*harita-varṇā*).

According to Amara: “*Hariṇī* may mean a female deer, a golden image, or that which is green. Let [your beauty] be equal—meaning, equally esteemed—behind your body, that is, out of sight; but not so in front, meaning it would not be equal when face-to-face. The sense is: let one indeed boast that it is equal when out of sight, but how could one say it is equal when directly perceived? Alternatively, let it be equal in the rear—the back part of the body—but in the front—the forepart—it is certainly not equal.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "later," that is, at some time in the future, let it be equal—that is, similar—if it so happens; however, this is said with disregard [for such a possibility]. But "at first," that is, initially, it would not be equal. The core intention is that it is never equal even throughout the three periods of time. In the alternative interpretation, the meaning is that after the two syllables *ku* and *su*, there is a "similar" one, namely one accompanied by the letter *ma*, because the word *kusuma* is seen to be exactly like that. But "in front," that is, at the beginning, it is not so; the meaning is that it is not accompanied by the letter *ma*.

The sense is that the word *ukta* (spoken) is not [applicable] in that way. Here, both [simile and paronomasia] are employed; for the simile is semantic (*ārthī*), since it is expressed by the word *sadṛśa* (similar), and there is also paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
Or as follows:

"O glorious Lord, King of the Golden Mountain! Let the deluded—who do not know the truth—say that the sky is of a form similar to yours; but how can that sky, which has resorted to a smithy (*vyokāra*), be equal to you who are of such noble form (*sujātarūpa*)? (663) "O glorious one, O King of the Golden Mountain! The meaning is this: let the deluded (*mugdha*), those who do not know reality, say that the sky (*vyoma*, *gagana*) is "of a similar form" (*sarūpa*) to yours; however, those who know the truth do not say so. Why? To this he replies: "Which has resorted to a smithy" (*vyokāram*). That sky, acting as the subject, has resorted to a smithy (*ayaskāra*).

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Amara states: “A *vyokāra* is an iron-worker (*lohakāraka*)”; the *Ratnakośa* says: “A *vyokāra*, an *ayaskara*, an *ayaskāra*, and a *lohakāra* would be [synonyms]”; and Hemacandra also says: “A *vyokāra*, a smith (*karmāra*), and an iron-worker (*lohakāra*)”. The etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: “one who makes (*karoti*) *vya*. There is also the usage in the *Harṣacarita*: “by *vyokāras* who collect firewood for charcoal” (*aṅgārīyadārusaṃgrahair yokāraiḥ*), where the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇyaṇ*. However, the actual meaning is that the syllable *vya* is resorted to as a letter (*varṇa*). The suffix *kāra* is added according to the rule *varṇāt kāre*.

Of "well-born form" (*sujātarūpa*), meaning beautiful gold; in the alternative sense, it means of lovely appearance. How could it be similar to you? It is simply not equal. The sense is that a similarity is impossible between well-born gold and one who relies on a blacksmith (an ironmonger). Here too, everything is exactly as before. The distinction, however, is that while there was one cause for the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in the previous case, there are two here.

O God of gods, can the splendor of the Yamunā, dark as a swarm of bees, ever equal your body which purifies all, with its complexion measured by the radiance of your face? Or rather, can it even rival the Yamunā itself?

O God of gods! Your body, possessing a most brilliant luster that shines in every direction, has its facial color—where "color" (varṇa) refers to appearance, form, or radiance—measured as being inferior to [the sun’s]; that is, it is said to be measured as being slightly less than the face [of the sun].

[Note on the term *varṇa*: it denotes the four castes beginning with the twice-born (*dvija*), white and other colors, fame, qualities, praise, various types of women, distinctions, forms, syllables, and ointments.]

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. "Born of a *milinda*" (*milindajā*) means born from a bee; that is to say, it has the nature of a bee. "Luster" (*ābhā*) means radiance. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. "Is she not similar?"—the meaning is "is she indeed similar?"—for a similarity between one possessing excessive brilliance and one possessing limited brilliance is impossible. In the alternative sense (the word-play), regarding the color of the face, it is so called because its initial syllable possesses the letter *i*, as the word *milindajābhā* itself begins with that letter.

Likewise, by your very body which is so purifying, she is called *saraka-pānā*—one whose drinking vessel (*pāna*) is a *saraka*, meaning a vessel for sugarcane liquor (*ikṣu-madya*). The sense is that she was exceedingly impure. Amara states: "The word *caṣaka* is not feminine; it denotes a drinking vessel, and *saraka* as well. And Medinī states: "*Sarakā* is not feminine; it refers to the drinking of *śīdhu* (spirituous liquor), the vessel for *śīdhu*, and sugarcane liquor. The word *agre* ends in the vowel *e* and is an indeclinable. In the alternative interpretation, the truth is that she is one whose initial letter (*agra*) is the letter *ka* (as in *agresaraḥ*), because the word *kalindajābhā* likewise begins with that letter.

The identity between word and meaning must not be forgotten. [Is she] like the luster (*ābhā*) of the Yamunā, the daughter of Kalinda? The sense is that she is not like it, because equality between the purifying and the non-purifying is impossible. Here too, the mention of both the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*), as well as the implied simile (*ārthī upamā*) and the pun (*śleṣa*), is all the same. The distinction, however, is that there are two standards of comparison, which are intermingled according to their respective order (*yathāsaṃkhya*).
Or rather, is a swan terrified by the roar of a thundercloud comparable to the conch Pāñcajanya of Hari, which produces only a single sound in the mind yet possesses a sharp resonance? 665.

The phrase *ghananirghoṣaḥ* means one whose sound is deep; the sense is that [the enemy] was terrified by anyone possessing such a voice. From that [fear], he was struck with terror regarding even a single battle (*janya*), for Amara states: "Battle, combat, and war are synonyms. Furthermore, that battle was merely mental—that is, conceived only in the mind and not accomplished through physical action—which is what is meant by the term. Alternatively, the literal meaning is "born from the Mānasa lake. By means of the *pāñcajanya*, which has a sharp resonance, he has endured five kinds of battles (*pañcajanya*); thus he is called *pāñcajanya*.

In the sense of "he has endured that," the suffix *aṇ* (applied according to the rule *prāgdīvyato’ṇ*) is used; this means "one who has conquered five battles. Alternatively, it means "by the conch named Pāñcajanya. Here too, both [meanings] are employed, resulting in both implied simile (*ārthī upamā*) and paronomasia (*śleṣa*). The distinction from the first example cited is that here the object of comparison (*upameya*) itself is also characterized by paronomasia. Or, for example: "May there be a noble lineage (*santāna*) that is expansive (*udāra*) and endless (*nanta*). But when encountering an adversary, may there be someone else who is 'endless' (*anantā*); what use is such a lineage? Let him be equal to the Slayer of Kaiṭabha (*kaiṭabhahantā*). (666) [Note: In the verse, *santāna* (lineage) is paronomastically linked to *santāpa* (torment), *udāra* (noble) to *udāra* (vast), *nanta* (ending) to *pratīpa* (adversary), and *anantā* (endless) to *anantā* (the goddess Lakṣmī).]

May the lineage—the noble *devataru* (divine tree) par excellence—be all-pervading (*sarvamahān*) through its designation as being free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhikanirdeśena*). If one were to say "may he be all-pervading," the form *bhavatāt* would imply a lack of respect; however, the actual state of affairs is that he is a giver (*dātā*). As Amara states: "The word *udāra* is used for a donor and for the great. Furthermore, upon the approach—that is, the arrival—of adversaries (*pratīpa*), that lineage [is so called]; here, one should understand that the *parasavarṇa* (the following sound) for the anusvāra is optional according to the rule *vā padantasya*, for the sake of achieving a correspondence between the word and its meaning in this other sense.

*Nantā* would mean "one who performs bowing"; that is, one should bow down out of reverence. Therefore, the sense is that he is indeed not noble (*anudāra*). In the alternative sense, regarding the arrival at the opposite view—that is, when there is a movement in the reverse direction—the word *santāna* would become *nantāsa*. This is the meaning. Regarding the first sense, in the phrase "there would be *s*," the doubling of the second *s* occurs optionally by the rule *anaci ca*.

Otherwise, since the word *saḥ* ending in the nominative singular would undergo elision of the suffix *su* according to the rule *“etattadoḥ sulopaḥ”* (Pāṇini 8.2.103), doubling of that *s* would be impossible. Thus, by such [a form], he is one who does not bow to anyone at all—an infinite non-bowing agent; for the suffix *tṛc* is used here from the root *nam*. The sense is that, according to the principle stated as *“The Supreme Śeṣin is to be bowed to,”* there can be no other object of obeisance for Him, who is the one to be bowed to by the entire world. In this regard, the meaning of the Vedic text *“Like a tree, He stands firm”* (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9) should be reflected upon.

"May this slayer of Kaiṭabha be equal"—the meaning is: "How could he not be equal? Here, both factors are employed: the quality of being a slayer (*nantṛtva*) as the cause for the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and the quality of not being a slayer (*anantṛtva*) as the cause for the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*). Furthermore, because the word *tulya* (equal) is used, the simile (*upamā*) is expressed through implication (*ārthī*). The distinction, however, is that the pun (*śleṣa*) applies only to the inferiority of the standard of comparison. "O river of intense salt-water, you are by no means equal to Mādhava; indeed, you are far inferior. For even though you have your head cast down (*adharita-śīrṣa*), you do not become one who observes the vow of protecting the wretched (*dīna-rakṣā-vratī*). (657)

"O Tīvrakṣāra!"—meaning "O merciless one," though the literal state of affairs is "O you who are excessively salty. Hemacandra states: "The word *tīvra* is used in the sense of 'intense,' 'pungent,' and 'excessive'; *kṣāra* [is used] for glass, taste, molasses, ash, salt, and a rogue. Alternatively, the meaning may be "O you who are exceedingly crafty (*atidhūrta*)," while the actual situation remains as before. "O Nadīna! O Lord of Rivers! You are not equal to Mādhava, the Blessed One Śrīnivāsa."

The sense is that although you are a river-dweller (*nadīna*), you are not equal [to the ocean] because of your intense saltiness. He states another reason for this: since you have lowered your head—meaning you have bowed down—in a distinguished and superior manner, you would not be one whose vow (*vratin*) is the protection of the wretched (*dīnarakṣā*). The sense is that in one who is merciless or exceedingly deceitful, a singular devotion to protecting the wretched is impossible.

In this context, the word *nadīna* is "qualified" (*viśeṣyate*), meaning it is differentiated (*bhidyate*) by something; thus, *viśeṣa* (in the sense of the instrument) is a *ghañ*-derivative, meaning a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*). The phrase *saviśeṣam tīvrakṣāraḥ* means "along with its qualifier," that is, accompanied by the qualifier "intense alkali. The term *adharitaśīrṣaḥ* means "recited in reverse order," that is to say, possessing the sequence [of the syllables] as in *nadīnarakṣāvratī*. This is the intended meaning.

Here, the causes for the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—namely, its intensely salty nature and its being the constant protector of the river—are presented; however, the qualities that cause the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*)—namely, its being an infinite ocean of compassion and its singular vow to protect the people who have once sought refuge—are not presented. Furthermore, the simile (*upamā*) is based on the sense (*ārtha*), and there is also a pun (*śleṣa*).
O daughter of Bhṛgu, just as the bee Makaranda first worshipped her lip with the nectar [he won from it], and then, shaking his hands, became dull-witted, how could he ever be equal to her?

O Bhārgavī! Makaranda was initially honored—that is, esteemed for its sweetness—in the state prior to contact with the nectar of your lips. Subsequently, having been surpassed by the nectar of your lips, he now shakes his hands; this is a description of the physical manifestation (anubhāva) of his humiliation. He is "manda," meaning deprived of the fortune of such sweetness; as Amara states: "The words *manda* denote one who is foolish, small, unskilled, or unfortunate. In the alternative sense [of the word-play], he is "mahitaḥ" at the beginning—that is, that in which the syllable *ma* (the letter *m*) was placed (*hita*).

The meaning is that it is distinguished by the letter *ma*. Thenceforth, "shaking his hands" means emitting the letters *ka* and *ra*; [the result is that] "Makaranda"—the word *makaranda*—became "manda. The meaning is that once the middle syllable *ka* is emitted, the word *makaranda* results in the form *manda*. The rest is easy to understand. Here too, as before, there is the employment of a mere attribute that detracts from the object of comparison; furthermore, there is both an implied simile (*ārthī upamā*) and a pun (*śleṣa*).
How could the primordial Being, the Lord of the Mountain who possesses eyes of auspicious peaks and a form that emits the intense brilliance of a thousand vajras, be equal to Indra? (669)

He is so described because he possesses eyes—countless, auspicious, and beautiful organs of vision. In the alternative sense, he is the "leader" (*nayana*) who brings about millions of blessings (*kalyāṇa*), for it is by him that people are led; this is the implied meaning. He is one whose form possesses a hand whose radiance surpasses thousands of *vajras* (thunderbolts).

"He whose form produces radiance" (*dīptikarī mūrtiḥ*) means he who creates the brilliance of thousands of diamonds and thousands of tigers; the sense is that because his body is dark-hued, it acquires a secondary luster (*parabhāga*) from the thousands of diamonds set as ornaments, thereby producing radiance. Here, only the quality that enhances the excellence of the object of comparison (*upameya*) is mentioned; the simile (*upamā*) is implied (*ārthī*), and there is also a pun (*śleṣa*). An example where the simile is suggested (*ākṣipte aupamye*) is as follows:
"O Acyuta, O Ananta, by you—who, by removing poison, restored life to the wielder of the Pināka bow—the cloud was surpassed when it drank poison and released water [instead of life]. (679)
The two names of the Perfectly Awakened One, Acyuta and Ananta, contain the intention of His power to restore Śiva to life by removing poison.
By reciting the supreme Anuṣṭubh mantra of Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda,
encapsulated by "Oṃ" and "Namaḥ," even Hara becomes a bearer of poison.

This is because it is stated in the injunction regarding the three names [of the Lord]. The construction is: "Having drunk poison, [he] was abandoning his life. Here, since words such as *iva* or *sadṛśa* (meaning "like") are absent, the simile (*upamā*) is implied by the word *parābhūta* ("defeated"). By the removal of poison, the restoration of life serves to elevate the object of comparison (*upameya*), while by the drinking of poison, the abandonment of life serves to debase the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); thus both are employed, and the pun (*śleṣa*) is manifest.

Just as the king of serpents, bent by calamities that have approached him, might at times contract his coils, he has been utterly cast down by Your arm— which shakes away misfortune and whose coils are eternally uplifted.

"O Blessed One"—this is understood from the context. "The King of Serpents" refers to Vāsuki; as Amarasimha states: "Vāsuki, however, is the king of serpents. "Bent" (bhugna) means afflicted by the calamity (vipad) arising from the attacking adversary (abhiyātinaḥ); as Amarasimha states: "the words *rugṇa* and *bhugna* [mean 'bent']. For this very reason, he is one by whom there has been assumed (ātta) a contraction of enjoyment (bhoga), that is, of pleasure (sukha). In the alternative interpretation, *abhiyāti* is a separate word consisting of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*).

In some places, he is so called because his *bhoga* (hood) has its contraction seized; the sense is that his hood is never expanded. Amara states: "The word *bhoga* refers to pleasure, a serpent, a king, a snake’s hood, and the body. He is called "footless" (*padbhirvihīna*) due to having hidden feet (*gūḍhapāt*), for Amara says: "The word *pada* means a foot. He is "crooked" (*bhugna*), meaning curved; Amara states: "The words *āviddha*, *kuṭila*, *bhugna*, *vellita*, and *vakra* all mean crooked."

"He approaches" means he goes toward; for his crookedness (*jihmagatva*) is well known. The rest is clear. Here, two [qualities] each are mentioned: *vidagdhaghnatva* (the state of being a destroyer of the clever) and *kvacidāttabhogatva* (the state of having enjoyment grasped only occasionally), which cause the inferiority of the object of comparison (*upamāna*); and *dhutavipattva* (the state of having shaken off calamity) and *anityocchritabhogatva* (the state of having enjoyment that is not constantly elevated), which cause the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*). The distinction from the previous [example] is that the paronomasia (*śleṣa*) is both with and without word-splitting (*sabhaṅga* and *abhaṅga*). But the implied simile (*ākṣiptopamā*) is exactly the same.

O Lord of All, although even the Lord of Wealth has been surpassed by You through the boundless abundance of Your majesty, they do not call him "the Protector" (Pān) nor indeed "the Sovereign" (Adhipa). 672.

O Lord of All! By You—who are thus described as possessing an infinite abundance of majesty and a preeminent power—the Lord of Wealth, Vaiśravaṇa, has been surpassed; that is to say, he has been reduced to being merely a wealthy man and rendered devoid of the letter "Dha" (due to the identity of word and meaning). Nevertheless, even so, he has not attained—that is, has not reached—mental anguish (*ādhi*). [The compound is formed with the negative particle *na*: "he has not gone to mental anguish."

Therefore, "pāntam" means protecting or guarding wealth. People say that he is "not a lord" (*anadhipam*), "not a master of wealth" (*adhanādhipam*), or indeed "without sovereignty" (*anīśvaram*). The sense is this: even though his wealth is being guarded, people who know his vital secrets call him "not a lord," because despite being disregarded by the Blessed One, he remains shameless and, ignoring even the pain in his mind, continues as before to proclaim himself the master of his own wealth.

In this context, [the word] *nādhi* has not been understood; it has neither reached the form *nādhi* nor the syllable *dh*. By the rule "the second member is compounded with words such as *śrita*," a compound is formed. That which has the letter *pa* at its end (*pāntam*)—that is what is so described. They call this Lord of Wealth (*dhanādhipam*) "Nādhipa" alone. For when the syllable *dha* is elided from the word *dhanādhipa*, and there is the presence of the two syllables [remaining], together with the letter *pa* at the end, the form *nādhipa* is indeed produced.

Here, the lordship over all and the state of possessing boundless abundance are presented as the grounds for the excellence of the object of comparison (the subject), while the status of being the lord of wealth and the lord of heaven are presented, as before, as the grounds for the inferiority of the standard of comparison. By the word *adhaḥkṛta* ("cast down"), there is a negation of the simile (*upamākṣepa*), and the pun (*śleṣa*) is also as before. However, the distinction is that the pun also resides in the very word *adhaḥkṛta*, which serves to negate the simile.

O Hari, is either Agni or even Indra worthy of being called "Sakalāda" (the eater of all) as a mere title of friendship for one like you—a pure-born person who eats only what remains after you have eaten? 673.

O Hare! [I salute] him who eats what remains after you have eaten (*tvadbhuktaśeṣabhoktuḥ*), who eats only that which has been offered to you (*tvanniveditaśeṣameva bhoktuḥ*), whose birth is pure (*viśuddhajananasya*), and whose lineage is holy (*pavitragotrasya*)—or rather, whose birth is holy (*pavitrajanmanaḥ*). He belongs to you (*tāvakasya*), meaning he is your devotee (*tvadbhaktaḥ*). He is called *sakalādaḥ* because he eats everything (*sakalam atti*); the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of an action. The meaning is "one who eats all food" (*sarvānnīnaḥ*). In reality, however, based on such statements as "by whom Agni was made an eater of all things" and "just as Agni is the consumer of all," the meaning is "an eater of everything" (*sarvabhakṣakaḥ*).

Agni is the *vahni* (the carrier); he is the *kalāda*, meaning a goldsmith (*kalādaḥ rukmakārakaḥ*—Amara). However, the true meaning is that he is called *kalāda* because he takes away the *kalās* (digits) from the sun. Alternatively, according to the statement "Agni drinks the first [digit]," since the digits are given to Agni and others during the dark fortnight, he is called *kalāda*. Is even the moon (*indu*) worthy of friendship? No, he is not worthy. This is the sense.

In this case, the distinction is that there is an employment of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), whereby the qualities of "eating only what is offered by the Lord" and "producing purity"—which serve to elevate the object of comparison—are presented alongside the qualities of "eating all kinds of food" and "being a goldsmith," which serve to devalue the two objects of comparison, fire and the moon, respectively. However, the *upamākṣepa* (the denial of a simile) remains exactly the same.

Or rather, O Mother, even if the ripened mango were to fall headlong into a skull-cup, it would possess the essence of that vessel; yet it is not able to rival or even approach the service of the sweetness of Your words, which surpasses all sweetness.

"O Mother! The ripened *rasāla*—the *rasāla* being a specific variety of sugarcane, its product being either jaggery or sugar—is such that even if one falls with one's head downward, the implication is that one attains a state equal to your words. It possesses a pith (*sāra*) like that of a skull (*kapāla*), meaning a head-bone or a potsherd; thus, it would have a flavor exactly like that essence. Here, the word *sāra* (essence) is used by way of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (contrary indication) to mean 'worthless' (*asāra*).
The eating of a cow's horn is useless and detrimental to life:
'Even the teeth are worn away, yet no juice is obtained.'"

The sense is that, according to the maxim stated in the *Śrī-Bhārata*, he would indeed become tasteless (*nīrasa*). Hema states: "The word *kapāla* refers to a type of leprosy, a fragment of a jar or similar object, and a collection of skull-bones"; and "The word *sāra* refers to marrow and the solid part of a substance; it also means strength, excellence, wealth, justice, and water. In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), the compound *rasālapāka* results in the form *kapālasāra* when its syllables are read in reverse order; the rest is clear.

In this instance, the quality of being as hard as a skull-cup (*kapāla-sāratva*) is presented as the cause for the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), while the quality of possessing sweetness exceeding that of all [other things] (*sakalādhika-madhurimatva*) is presented as the cause for the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*). The implied denial of the simile (*upamākṣepa*) is exactly the same; however, the distinction lies in the fact that the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is accomplished through the identity of the meaning of words when read in reverse order.
O you whose emblem is the best of birds, how indeed shall your face become the friend of the moon—even though it follows the path of truth—since its hands are like blue lotuses? 675.

"Utpalabhujaḥ" means one who eats raw meat (*udbhūta-āmiṣa*); in the alternative sense, it refers to one who enjoys or protects blue lotuses (*utpala*, *kuvalaya*). The rest is clear. Here, only the quality of being a consumer of lotuses is mentioned as a cause for the inferiority of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), but not the quality of purifying all the world, which is the cause for the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*). The simile (*upamā*) is merely implied by the use of the word "friend" (*mitra*); the pun (*śleṣa*), however, is manifest.
O Daughter of the Ocean, though it is said by people that even what shines within is vomited forth as refuse, your hand here eclipses the sprout [of the mango] which seeks its own victory.

O Abhisute! The sense is that [the light] shines forth and is manifest within, but not without; in the alternative sense (pakṣe), it means "excellent" (santaṃ) because of being joined with the letter *la* (lena)—that is, the letter *la* combined with the letter *la*—in such a way as to be preeminent within (*antaḥ*).

Although one would expect three *l*-sounds to be heard due to the substitution of *l* for the *t* of the word *uccha* by the rule "for *t*, *l*" (*tor li*), nevertheless, because of the optional elision of the second *l* by the rule "there is elision of *yam* [consonants] before a *yam* [consonant]" (*halo yamāṃ yami lopaḥ*), only two *l*-sounds are heard; this should be noted so that the word may maintain its uniformity as a two-*l* form in its other meanings. The term *pādya* means "for the feet" (*pādārtha*), that is to say, it is worthy of being like the feet; the sense is that it is not worthy of being like the hands.

In the phrase “*pādārghābhyāṃ ca*,” the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of being for the sake of that (*tādarthye*). In the alternative [interpretation], it is that which has the letter *pa* as its initial; thus it is so described. According to the *Medinī* lexicon: “*janaḥ* [means] people in the world, the Maharloka, the next world, and also a commoner (*pāmara*). By virtue of being "vomited" (*vāntatayā*), that is, having been cast out, it means it is excluded from all the world; in the alternative, it means it is stated to end with the letter *va*. "Pallava" means a sprout; in the alternative, it refers to the word *pallava*. The rest is easy to understand. Here too, there is the employment of only that which degrades the object of comparison.
And that [suggestion] as well as *śleṣa* (paronomasia); its distinction lies in its being rooted in the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthatādātmya*).
Who could say that the lotus is even capable of performing the service of a servant to the eye of the Lord of Veṅkaṭagiri, which is so skillful at uprooting the mud? || 677 ||

Here, only that quality which enhances the excellence of the object of comparison (the upameya)—namely, its skill in wiping away mud—is mentioned; whereas that which detracts from the excellence of the standard of comparison (the upamāna)—namely, its being smeared with mud—is not mentioned. By the phrase "servitude" (*kiṃkaratām*) and so forth, the simile (*upamā*) is indeed implied, as is the paronomasia (*śleṣa*).
O Mother Turmeric, you who attain such extreme brilliance through the touch of Hari’s hand—how could even your shadow possibly serve as a pupil to that very Śrī? 678.

O Mother! O Śrī! You who, through the touch (*avamārśa*) of the rays—both the beams of the sun and the hands of the Lord Hari—attain such extreme brilliance, such intense luminosity, and such an abundance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*). [As Hemacandra states: "The word *ujjvala* refers to that which is blooming, to the erotic sentiment, to the pure, and to the radiant. Of you, even by the mere shadow—that is, even by the color (*varṇa*), and not by some other quality—the sense is that even by a slight degree (*leśataḥ*) [of your hue], [the world is transformed]. This is the intended meaning. The word "even" (*api*) implies "even by a small amount."

The meaning is: "What [fault] would there be for those who resort to the state of being a student (*chātratva*) or a resident pupil (*antevāsitva*)? Rather, they ought certainly to resort to it. Alternatively, the construction may be joined as: "What [fault] would there be even for those who resort to the state of being a student by means of their shadow (*chāyayā*)? The sense is that even that is unworthy of being resorted to, let alone equality. Here, only the possession of extreme brilliance caused by contact with the hand of Hari (Viṣṇu)—which serves to elevate the object of comparison—is mentioned; however, the lack of luster caused by contact with the hand of Hari, which would serve to debase the standard of comparison, is not mentioned. This involves both *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *sāmya* (equality).

Just as the light of Brahman—which transcends the Lokāloka mountain, is not unmanifest, and does not dry up the nectar—is beyond description, how could even the Sun (Bradhna) be capable of perceiving it? The term *jyotis* refers to Brahman, the Supreme Brahman, endowed with unsurpassed radiance as heard in the Śruti: "Now, that light which is beyond this heaven... It transcends the Lokāloka, the Cakravāla mountain; the compound is formed according to the rule *dvitīyā śrita* etc., meaning it is all-pervading. Alternatively, it transcends the *āloka*—the vision or perception—of the *lokas*, meaning people; thus, its sense is that it cannot be grasped by the eye.

"It is not grasped by the eye; the eye does not go there—that which is invisible," according to such scriptural passages as "in the invisible, the bodiless. It is not "unfamed" (*avikhyātam*), meaning it is celebrated in all the Vedāntas as the cause of the entire universe and so forth. There are two negative particles (*nañ*) to negate the absence of fame that might otherwise be imagined.

It is not the case that it does not dry up the nectar (*amṛta*), meaning the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); for its attainment of the supreme good is heard in the scripture, "This is the bridge to immortality" (*amṛtasyaiṣa setuḥ*), and its state as nectar is heard in passages such as, "This is the nectar. In the alternative sense, the meaning is that it is not known as a sheep (*avi*) nor is it a dryer of water; for Amara and Medinī state: "The words *avi*, *śaila*, and *meṣa* mean 'ram'; *amṛta* may refer to the remnant of a sacrifice, nectar, water, or clarified butter."

The sense is this: can even the sun—the radiant form of Brahman—be capable of perceiving or beholding it? Or rather, he certainly cannot. Here, only the qualities that enhance the excellence of the object of comparison (the upameya)—such as its being beyond the Lokāloka mountain and so forth—are employed; whereas qualities that would detract from the standard of comparison (the upamāna), such as its not being beyond the Lokāloka, its lack of renown, or its being dried up by nectar, are not mentioned. Furthermore, the figures of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *upamākṣepa* (the denial of a comparison) are evident here.

This is what must be noted here: in this particular variety of *vyatireka* (distinction) based on *śleṣa* (punning), since neither [the common property nor the object of comparison] is explicitly mentioned, it is difficult to establish the threefold division of simile (*upamā*)—namely, the verbal (*śrautī*), the objective (*ārthī*), and the implied (*ākṣiptā*)—based on those distinctions. If the point of contrast (*vaidharmya*) is not stated, upon what basis would the *śleṣa* manifest?

Nor should it be argued that an example of this [Vyatireka] is easily established only in cases where the standard of comparison and the object compared are understood through words such as *dvijarāja* (the moon), *ratnākara* (the ocean), *prabhañjana* (the wind), or *mātariśvan* (the breeze)—where the *śleṣa* (punning double entendre) is conveyed by its own word and serves to manifest the *vyatireka*—because in those instances, the point of contrast (*vaidharmya*) is indeed cognizable through its own word. Thus, the statement of the ancients that there are twenty-four varieties must be somehow justified by those who observe a much larger number of examples.
Furthermore, since all varieties of *upamā* (simile) are possible here, enough with this enumeration of twenty-four types.

Now, one might object: "Is it not more appropriate for this figure of speech—which is rooted in dissimilarity—to be considered an opponent to simile (*upamā*) rather than having simile as its internal essence? For simile is rooted in similarity (*sādharmya*), whereas this [figure] proceeds precisely by way of negating that [similarity]. Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion, as it would result in the collapse of established doctrine. This is true; however, when the negation of the similarity of one thing to another—based on the prominence of certain qualities—is intended to culminate in the excellence [of the former], then even if the similarity of that thing to the other is not established through those specific qualities, it may still be established through other qualities.

This is because the cognition of similarity is unavoidable. Furthermore, if the intended meaning were a negation of the universal of "similarity to that," then the mention of specific qualities would be purposeless; for there is a universal human experience expressed as: "When it is said, 'He is superior to him in lineage,' [one understands] 'he is equal to him in form, age, learning, and wealth.

Thus, the intention of the ancients was that even though similarity is perceived, its luster is eclipsed and it is rendered as if bound by the excellence arising from the negation of other qualities, such that it is unable to produce aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*).

In this figure of speech (alaṃkāra), sometimes the excellence of the object of comparison (upameya) and the inferiority of the standard of comparison (upamāna) are implied by the verbal negation of similarity; sometimes the absence of similarity and the inferiority of the standard of comparison are implied by the verbal excellence of the object of comparison; and sometimes the excellence of the object of comparison and its absence [of inferiority] are likewise implied by such an inferiority of the standard of comparison, producing aesthetic charm (*camatkṛti*). Among these, the first variety has been illustrated with its subdivisions according to the method of the ancients. The second and third varieties also generally possess the same number of subdivisions. Of these, only a mere indication is provided here as an illustration.

"O Moon (vidho), you, whose heart is eternally serene, are superior to the Moon (vidhu) whose heart is dark; for while you are the object of meditation for yogis, that [dark] moon causes suffering to those separated from their lovers. (680) [Commentary: "O Moon (vidho)" and "O Viṣṇu (vidho)" constitute the vocative address. Here, in the first half-verse, the excellence of the subject of comparison (upameya) is expressed directly (śābda); the inferiority of the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the absence of similarity are implied (ākṣipta). In the second half-verse, the inferiority of the standard of comparison is expressed directly; the excellence of the subject of comparison and the absence of similarity are implied.
Thus, although it is possible for two or even all three of these elements to be expressed directly in certain cases, such instances are not cited here as they are not particularly striking.
In some places, the Creator fashioned even all three together;
yet in this vast expanse of the world, He established seven oceans. O Mother, Your eyes, which are the limit for vision, create worlds that are oceans of jewels beyond counting.

The meaning is that a *kaṭākṣa* (side-glance) is the limit of vision. Brahmā (*vidhi*) created only the oceans, which are mines of jewels, upon the surface of the world; but O Mother! Your side-glance, however, creates countless worlds themselves as oceans that are mines of jewels—that is to say, it creates repositories for the most excellent things. The sense is that it ordains all forms of prosperity.
Just as the ocean is deep yet not high, and Mount Meru is lofty yet not deep, so too is the one who bears the crest-jewel of the serpent-king both deep and lofty.
The sun is radiant but not cool; the moon is ever serene yet never warm here in this world. But you alone, O Lord, are simultaneously glorious, ever-pleasing, cool, and warm.

*Śiśira* means cool and moist with compassion; *uṣṇa* means sharp and capable—according to the *Medinī*, "the word *uṣṇa* denotes summer, a man, and the capable, while it has other genders when meaning heat or cold. Alternatively, following the maxim, "A king who is both sharp and mild is highly esteemed," he is neither too mild nor too sharp; rather, his nature consists of both restraint and favor. Otherwise, there is the recollection of the faults of mere sharpness or mildness: "The world trembles before the sharp, while the mild is indeed despised.
The rest is clear. As for example:
O Śauri, you are pure both within and without, whereas the moon is foul within; O lotus-eyed one, you are indeed most noble, while he is the crest-jewel of the greedy.
