O Lord, with a face free from stain, you bestow the nectar of truth even when thundering; whereas the rain-cloud, thundering with a soiled face, pours down nothing but poison in this world.
By means of touch, he causes the succession of bonds that have reached full maturity to fall away; Mādhava alone leads another to his own supreme state through that very [touch]. 686.

The single Mādhava—the spring season—causes that succession of *sumanas* (flowers) to fall downward; it causes them to become ripe, transformed, and facing destruction, as well as their stalks (*vṛnta*). The other Mādhava—the Blessed Lord—does the same for the succession of *sumanas* (wise men), whose bonds to worldly existence are fully ripened. This is the meaning. [Regarding the word *sparśana*: Medinī states, "In the masculine, *sparśana* refers to the wind; in the neuter, it refers to giving and touch. By means of the wind through its contact, and by means of the granting of fearlessness, he causes them to fall. Thus it is said.

By that touch, one attains a high and exalted state worthy of worship—“*mahatyuccaiḥ*” (high and great), according to Amara; indeed, one reaches one’s own very place, the station upon the branch of the tree where one resides. In another sense, one attains the supreme state itself. O Mother, through association with your devotees, a person attains the status of the Lord of the Kukuras (Kṛṣṇa). Another, however, attains the status of the Lord of the Kukuras even without the contact of hands [i.e., without physical effort]. (687)

O Mother! By association with your people—that is, by contact with the devotees (bhāgavatas)—even a common person (*jana*), meaning even a low-born one, attains the feet of the Lord of the Kukuras, the sovereign of the Yadu clan; that is to say, he becomes a refugee at the Blessed One’s feet. Alternatively, it means he reaches the abode of the Blessed One. As for "another," it refers to a person distinct from your followers; a "person" (*jana*) who is low-born (*pāmara*). According to the *Medinī* lexicon: "In the world, a 'person' (*jana*) is [one who is] low-born (*pāmara*), even in the higher worlds such as Maharloka."

"Antare" means among those who are base and contemptible; according to Amarasimha, "kheṭa," "garhya," and "aṇaka" are synonyms. "Kukurāṇām" refers to dogs; according to Amarasimha, "kukkura" and "mṛgadaṃśaka" are synonyms. An "adhinātha" is a master of dogs—a dog-keeper—who, as stated in such Smṛtis as "the dog-keeper and the falconer," is censured for being unworthy of receiving offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya). The sense is that he "attains" (aśnute)—that is, reaches—the "pada," meaning the station or the feet of such a person, thereby becoming a frequenter of despicable places.

In this context, there is a word-break as *antareṇa*, meaning "in the middle. As Amarasimha states: "Now, *antara*, *antarā*, and *antareṇa* may signify 'in the middle' (*madhye*). [The term] "attains the status of being the Lord of the Kukuras" (*kukurādhināthapadam aśnute*) means that by the aforementioned method, when the letter *ka* situated in the middle of the word *kukurādhinātha* is joined with another *ka*, the status of being the word *kukurādhinātha* is produced; this is the intended sense, because the letters *ka* and *va* are conjoined—that is, they exist without being separated by vowels.

In this context, the word *antareṇa* should be understood as referring merely to the glance of the sound "kukku-ra," for only when that is the case is it possible for the conjunction of the letter *ka* to occupy a middle position. Alternatively, let it be taken with reference to the word *kukkurādhinātha-pada*; for in that word, just as with the letters *ra* and others, the intermediate position of the letter *ka* between the first and last letters is undeniable. This is how it should be understood. Here, a certain stainless king of birds (the moon) holds Puruṣottama (Viṣṇu) within himself; another soiled king of birds (a crow), though constantly holding [something], does not hold *antareṇakaṃ* (the innermost essence). (688)

A certain king of the twice-born (dvijarāja), the foremost among those born from the mouth [of Brahmā], bearing the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) within his mind—that is, meditating upon Him—is pure and stainless. Another "king of the twice-born," namely the moon, bearing some contemptible thing (aṇaka) within—namely, some despicable object while meditating—is soiled; elsewhere, the meaning is that he bears the deer (eṇaka) within his own orb.

In these examples, one must never be deluded into thinking that the *vyatireka* (distinction/superiority) is merely suggested (*ākṣipta*) by the force of employing the standard of comparison and its qualifiers, rather than being the actual expressed meaning (*vyaṅgya*). This is because the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) does not manifest unless there is even a slight degree of incongruity (*anupapatti*). And here, although the qualifiers of the Blessed One may somehow serve the purpose of praise, the incongruity of employing the standard of comparison and its qualifiers remains active, as it cannot be accounted for except through the excellence of the Blessed One.

However, where there is no employment of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or its qualifiers, but rather the excellence of the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is perceived—through the manifestation of the actual state of things by means of its own qualifiers (as in "Devadatta is handsome," etc.), which have already fulfilled their function—by virtue of a specific intention relative to another property characterized by distinct qualifiers of its own, that is the domain of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
Just as you grant life to the worlds, you do not become sapless even after a hundred autumns; nor do you turn pale, but rather you always maintain a flourishing splendor. (689)

"Of autumns"—that is, of the autumnal seasons and years. This is a suggestion of *vyatireka* (distinction) based on the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) arising from the difference between the cloud and the Blessed Lord. Regarding this, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* states: "As for the claim of the author of the *Alaṃkārasarvasva* followed by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda*, who maintains that *vyatireka* occurs even when the object of comparison (*upameya*) is inferior to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), because distinction alone constitutes *vyatireka*, and cites as an example of such inferiority:
'Thou art red with fresh sprouts; I too am red with the praiseworthy virtues of my beloved.

To thee come the arrows released from the bow of Smara; to me likewise [come those same arrows]. [In this case, the lover is not actually inferior to the cloud; rather, the distinction lies in the excellence of his own qualities.]'"
The kick from the foot of a beloved brings you joy; likewise, it does for me.
O Aśoka tree, everything is equal for us both; the Creator has made only me sorrowful.

In this case, it might be argued that by means of the presence of sorrow (*saśokatva*), an inferiority (*apakarṣa*) in comparison to the *aśoka* tree is ultimately established; however, even that is questionable. Just as the removal of some ornament from a limb may lead to a particular excellence of beauty because it is conducive to the sentiment of love (*rati*), so too here, the mere exclusion of the figure of simile (*upamā*) is charming due to its conformity with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), not the figure of contrast (*vyatireka*). For this very reason, the ancients did not highly regard the figure of "unequal" (*asama*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to accept it as a distinct figure of speech altogether. As in the example:
"Even though the three worlds are filled with suns, gods, and demons..."
O King, he who attains the state of equality with you will not exist in the future, does not exist now, and did not exist in the past.

Thus [it is said]. For this very reason, the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*, that foremost among connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), having stated that "a true poet should, in accordance with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), sometimes employ figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*) and sometimes dispense with them," cited the verse "raktas tvam" as an example for the removal of similarity (*sādṛśya*). And for this same reason, Bhaṭṭa Mammaṭa stated that "vyatireka (distinction) consists merely in superiority," thereby excluding inferiority from the definition of vyatireka.

Therefore, it is established that the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) consists solely in the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*) over the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and not in its inferiority. However, if there is a persistent insistence that inferiority also constitutes *vyatireka*, then this example should be cited:

"O King, you who have undertaken the vow of protecting the three worlds, yet protect only the surface of the earth—alas, how do you, possessing but two eyes, ascend to the equality of the thousand-eyed Indra?"

In this case, because it produces a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) through the cognition that "you are inferior by two qualities, yet equal by another quality," it constitutes a figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*). Thus, in the definition, a deficiency (*apakarṣa*) of this same kind should also be included.
Furthermore, as for the example of *vyatireka* (distinction) culminating in actual experience which was stated by the author of the *Kuvalayānanda*:
"Between the miser and the sword— both of whom have their fists firmly clenched, who reside within a sheath, and who are naturally dark— there is only a difference in outward form."

Thus, that has not been scrutinized with precision by your long-lived self. For instance, in this case, is the *vyatireka* (contrast) of the nature of superiority, culminating in actual experience, derived from the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)? Or is it of the nature of inferiority, according to the direction stated by the author of the *Sarvasva* and others? It cannot be the first, because the property that serves as the cause for superiority is not present here. Nor should it be argued that the presence of the long vowel (*dīrghākṣara*) is indeed established through *śleṣa* (punning), for that [long vowel], existing in the standard of comparison, does not effect the superiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*).

This is because [the city] is made common [with the moon] through an identification based on *śleṣa* (punning) with another object in the form of its generic shape; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total elimination of *upamā* (simile) rooted in *śleṣa*. Even in cases such as "The city, like the orb of the nectar-rayed moon, is *sakalakala*," the possession of clamor (*kalakala*) and the perfection of digits (*kala*) are in fact states of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Nor should it be mistakenly thought that the poet’s intent lies solely in the simile in the phrase "*sakalakalam*," while in the present case, because of the mention of the word "difference" (*bheda*), there is a distinctiveness [that precludes simile].

If, in this case, the *vyatireka* (distinguishing contrast), consisting in the disruption of the simile, were intended to be the primary focus, then the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *ākāra* would be useless. One should simply have said, "The difference between the wretched man and the sword arises from the long vowel alone. For here, the pun is not favorable to the *vyatireka*; on the contrary, it is actually detrimental to it. However, it is favorable to the simile (*upamā*), because it makes common the dissimilarity consisting of the long vowel, and because there remains a difference in form between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.

"Indeed, the poet's intention is as follows: 'There is an identity between the miser and the sword, owing to the similarity of their qualifiers such as "extremely firm" and so forth. The difference in syllables, however, is not contradictory, as it arises from a difference in form. This should be discerned by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*). The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it lacks coherence even in its mere expression and is unpleasant to the heart. Therefore, let it suffice to say that the implied simile (*gamyopamā*) alone is well-established here; let us cease this investigation into counterfeit coins and return to our subject," he said.
And thus, in this view, the examples of non-exclusion from both (anubhayavyatireka) previously demonstrated by us should be understood accordingly along this very same path.
An example of deficient negative concomitance (*nyūnavyatireka*) is as follows:
"The lordship over the entire universe belongs to Him; yours is the lordship over all but one. O Mother of the World, how then can you ascend the scale with the Creator of the World? (690)

However, this must be considered: in the *Kuvalayānanda*, the *vyatireka* (distinction) is divided into three types—namely, that which results in the superiority of the object compared (*upameya*), that which results in its inferiority, and that which results in neither. Among these, the reading "resulting in neither" (*anubhayaparyavasāyī*) is the result of a scribe’s error; for it is more appropriate to establish the third variety of *vyatireka* precisely as "resulting in neither," as in the case of *anubhaya-tādṛpya-rūpaka* and other such figures.

Even in the example cited, in the phrase "of one with his fist firmly clenched," there is clearly seen an absence of any conclusion regarding either the superiority or inferiority of the object of comparison (*upameya*). However, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, considering the reading in the *Kuvalayānanda* to result merely in an experience [of the figure], and determining that *vyatireka* consists in either superiority or inferiority, refuted the third variety of *vyatireka* as presented by the *Kuvalayānanda*.

However, if the reading is *upadarśite 'nubhayaparyavasāyī* ("shown as not culminating in either"), then all these aforementioned criticisms are entirely irrelevant. Furthermore, if the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* intended for the *vyatireka* (contrast) to consist in either the excellence or the inferiority [of the subject], then its division into "culminating in the excellence of the subject" and "culminating in its inferiority" would be untenable; for it is improper to speak of a contrast consisting in excellence as "culminating in excellence."

Therefore, the intention of the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* is precisely this: that *vyatireka* (distinction) consists solely of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and it is of three kinds—namely, that which culminates in the excellence of the object compared (*upameya*), that which culminates in its inferiority, and that which is devoid of both culmination in excellence and inferiority. It is with all this in mind that Vaidyanātha states in the *Candrikā*: "The essence of *vyatireka* is the difference between two things perceived as possessing similarity due to the application of some common attribute, caused by the application of some other attribute."

"However, it should be understood that the distinction [between the two types] results in either the excellence of the object compared (*upameya*) or its inferiority; yet in some cases, even in the absence of such a conclusion regarding either of those, it rests solely upon its own unique charm. By this, one should know that the refutation of the latter two varieties and their examples by a certain critic—which might appear superficially plausible—is answered. Since it is utterly worthless, it does not even merit further discussion; thus, I shall desist. So he said.
This [simile] can also occur when it is reinforced by another poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*). For example:
"Two beautiful birds, close companions and friends, embrace the same tree together; one of them eats the sweet fruit of this pair, while the other looks on without eating. (RV 1.164.20)
This verse: "Two birds, united and friends, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating."

This is a restatement of the meaning of the Śruti: "Yuk" means that which is joined (*yujyate*). The word *yuk* refers to qualities, because Vyāsārya has explained it as "one who possesses similar qualities is a *sayug*. Thus, the two *sayujau* (joined ones) are those possessing identical qualities, being mutually equal in qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth. The two *sakhāyau* (companions) are associates; the two *suparṇau* (birds) are like birds. They have taken refuge in a *samānam* (common) tree—that is, a single tree, meaning a body fit to be cut down like a tree.

"Between those two, one—the individual soul (jīva)—enjoys the sweet, fully ripened fruit of the *pippala* tree, which is the fruit of karma; the other, however, the Supreme Self (paramātman), shines forth while remaining non-enjoying," so say the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni. This [verse] is supported by the figure of speech *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor). In this manner, its intermingling with other figures of speech should be observed according to the specific context. Furthermore, since this figure of speech contains within it a sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), and since similarity is manifested through three types of common attributes, the application of those same varieties [of similarity] should also be traced here.

In that regard, O Hari, your charming conduct, manifested by the non-inert [the wise], surpasses the nectar manifested by the inert [the dull-witted], which, though desired by all, is merely to be tasted. (692)

That which was spoken by those of dull intellect and feeble minds is said to have "arisen from the ocean"—this is the actual state of affairs. That which was spoken by those of non-dull intellect and subtle minds is said to have "not arisen from the ocean. Here, the qualities of being praiseworthy, being delicious to taste, and being charming are the common attributes. The states of being spoken by the dull-minded and the non-dull-minded, conveyed through the device of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), serve as the causes for inferiority and superiority respectively.

O beloved of the Lord of the Mountain-Kesarin, your neck— adorned with a necklace of pearls as familiar to it as a reflection in a mirror— surpasses, O Mother, the conch shell which has mastered the waves of the ocean of milk.
Here, between the pearl necklace and the waves of the milk-ocean, there is a relationship of original and reflection; and between the familiar and the pervasive, there is a state of pure generality.
Thus has *vyatireka* (distinction) based on similarity been described. This same figure can also exist as one based on non-difference (*abheda*), as for example:

O Lord with wide eyes, you have shaken off the multitude of *palāśas* (crows/carnivorous beasts) and dispelled all strife; you always possess the state of blissful joy. How then could we say that you are merely a *mandāra* tree? [Commentary: He by whom the multitude (*kula*) of *palāśas*—meaning either leaves or carnivorous creatures (*kravyāda*)—has been shaken off, is thus described. He whose "wide vision" (*viśālekṣaṇa*) consists of the sight (*īkṣaṇa*) of *śālās*—meaning branches (*śākhā*)—is so called. The sense is: even the mere sight of his branches does not exist [in the case of a tree], much less its being adorned with them. According to Amara, *śākhā* and *śālā* are synonyms.

Otherwise, you possess expansive eyes (*vipulanayana*); by whom the buds and flower-clusters (*kalikāḥ korakāḥ*) have been shaken off. In the other sense, he by whom the Kali age (*kali*) has been shaken off is so described—that is to say, one who has cast away the defects of the Kali age, as stated in such passages as: "The Lord of All, the destroyer of the mass of Kali's impurities. [The suffix] *kap* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*. You constantly partake in the state of being non-delighting (*sadā-anandanatām*), that is, the lack of connection with the Nandana grove; in the other sense, you are *ānandana* (one who gladdens), and thus *sadānandana* (one who eternally gladdens the virtuous).
This being so, how could we call you a *mandāra* (the celestial coral tree)?
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the Section on Contrast (Vyatireka), in the *Alaṅkāramaṇihāra*.
Now begins the Section on the Ornament of Joint Description (Sahokti):

When there is a description of a relationship involving the word "together" (saha) between two objects, both of which possess the status of being either subordinate or primary, that is known as Sahokti.

*Saḥukti* (conjoint expression) is the connection between two objects delimited by the relationship of subordinate (*guṇa*) and principal (*pradhāna*), based on the sense of "together" (*saha*). This figure also occurs only when there is predominance of distinction (*bhedaprādhānya*). Here, the predominance of distinction is grounded in the relationship of subordinate and principal; and this relationship of subordinate and principal is necessitated by the sense of "together," according to the grammatical rule: *sahayukte'pradhāne* ("when joined with 'saha', that which is not the principal [is called the second case]"). Furthermore, the status of being the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*) here is determined by intention (*vaivakṣika*), since both may be either contextual (*prākaraṇika*) or non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*).

For their status as equals is established by the force of the sense (*arthabala*), since the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is impossible between things of unequal status. In that context, because the word ending in the third case is invariably subordinate, it possesses the status of the standard of comparison; by implication, the remaining word has the status of the object of comparison. Furthermore, the relationship of primary and secondary here is purely verbal (*śābda*), not semantic (*ārtha*), because in reality the reverse is also possible. And it should be understood that "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) here consists of various distinctions such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

And "loveliness" (*hṛdyatva*), which is included in the general definition of an ornament (*alaṃkāra*) and is common to all ornaments, occurs here when it is vitalized by hyperboles (*atiśayokti*) consisting of either (1) an inversion of the sequence of cause and effect, (2) based on a metaphorical identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) supported by a pun (*śleṣa*), or (3) a simple metaphorical identification. So they say.
O Enemy of Mura, for those whom you behold, their faces and their joys bloom simultaneously; likewise, their enemies and their hells alike vanish instantly from them.

Thus, the phrase ending with "of the two delimited [meanings]" is included in order to avoid over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to cases such as *tulyayogitā* (equal conjunction). For in that case, both meanings are indeed primary (*pradhāna*) and are connected with the sense of "together" (*saha*). Here, however, because there is a rule that what is joined with the word "together" must necessarily be subordinate (*aprādhānya*), the connection with the sense of "together" occurs only between two meanings delimited by the relationship of subordinate and primary; hence, there is no over-extension.
O Blessed One, just as you swiftly descended from the earth along with its burden, pervading the entire world that had been shattered by the crushing of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa and others.

"By one desiring to protect" (aviviṣatā) means by one wishing to guard. Here, there is a simultaneity (sahabhāva) animated by the reversal of the sequence between the Lord’s descent and the removal of the earth's burden.
Or for example:

"The people, their curiosity greatly increased by serving Your pair of feet which are so purifying, ascend the lion-throne together with Siṃhācala. (697) In the previous instance, there was a co-utterance (*sahokti*) of the agent; here, however, it is of the object. *Siṃhācala* is Śeṣādri. Here too, the co-existence (*sahabhāva*) is animated by the reversal of the temporal sequence between the two actions—the ascent of Siṃhācala and the ascent of the throne—whereas in reality, the cause must exist at a fixed prior time and the effect at a subsequent time. It should be noted that even an expression of these two as being simultaneous is itself a reversal of that [actual] order.
O Lord, when the sound of your Pāñcajanya spreads abroad, surely the lotus-faces of the asuras wither away along with those of the goddesses, according to their desire.

The lotus-faces of the goddesses (amarīs) are blossoming and opening; however, the lotus-faces of the demonesses (asurīs) are "vidalanti"—that is, they act like those whose petals (dalāni) have fallen away, appearing like petal-less lotuses, devoid of beauty. Here, through the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *vidalanti*, there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasiti*) [between the two meanings].
Just as Your deeds, having entered the sinews of the ears of the wise, thoroughly cleanse their hearts along with their misdeeds, O Lord of Śrī. (699)

Here, through the verbal pun (*śabdaśleṣa*) in the word *dhāvayanti* ("they cause to run" / "they purify"), there is an identification (*adhyavasiti*) between the acts of causing to run and purifying. The former [example] was a co-expression with the agent (*kartṛsahokti*); this, however, is a co-expression with the object (*karmasahokti*).
Or as follows:

"Upon hearing the cries of the distressed, you raised your discus together with the crocodile; by that very [discus] he was released from you, for there is no difference between these two in their natural state. (700) The word *uddhṛtam* should be applied by changing its gender (*liṅgavipariṇāmena*) to mean "raised," "lifted," and "uprooted. By that very discus, the crocodile was released—that is, abandoned—by you. The use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is justified by the rule for forming compounds such as *apeta-apoḍha-mukta*, which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In the alternative sense, it means he was released from the curse of Devala.

As it is stated in the *Śrī Bhāgavata*: “Hūhū, the best of Gandharvas, was released from the curse of Devala. To the question of how the lifting [of the crocodile] and the releasing [from the wheel] can be equal, he says: “In their primordial nature,” and so forth. For (*hi*) because there is no difference (*bhidā*)—that is, no distinction at all—between these two, the crocodile and the wheel, in their primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is their own inherent state (*svabhāva*), therefore the equality of their lifting and releasing is appropriate; this is the intended meaning.

In this context, regarding these two words *nakra* and *cakra*, when they serve as the subject (*uddeśya*) in a rule prescribing an affix (*pratyaya-vidhi*) in their original form (*prakṛti*)—that is, in the forms *nakra* and *cakra*—there is no difference between them based on the letters *na* and *ca*; for the phoneme *kre* is identical in both cases. The point is that although there exists a distinction between these two words in the masculine and neuter genders when followed by an affix beginning with *s* (such as the visarga or anusvāra), the distinction in the mere base (*prakṛti-mātra*) consists solely of the letters *na* and *ca*.

This too is a simultaneous expression of action (*karmasahokti*), based on an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) founded upon paronomasia (*śleṣa*). Although here there exists a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) characterized by the inversion of the sequence of cause and effect, it is precisely the identification rooted in paronomasia that imparts the excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). The distinction here is that in the first half-verse, the relationship between the two is one of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) between the crocodile and the wheel, whereas in the second half-verse, this is reversed between the wheel and the crocodile.
An example based on the identification [of two things] rooted in the wall of pure *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:

"O Blessed One, by you—the boundless treasure-house of compassion—who are bowed to and who do not bow [to others], all that is undesirable has been cast aside along with the desirable, even as you were bowed down by the heat of worldly existence. (701)

The undesirable and inauspicious was cast out along with the desired object. In the case of the "desired" (iṣṭa) side, that from which [the undesirable] has gone out, set, or become invisible is "cast out" (nirasta). The word *asta* is an indeclinable ending in *m*; thus, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with it. According to Amara’s list of indeclinables, *asta* means "invisibility. The meaning is that he made it shine forth, as if it had not set. In the case of the "undesirable" (aniṣṭa) side, "cast out" means thrown away or destroyed. Here, the identification of the difference occurs solely through the pun (*śleṣa*), and not by any other means. In this instance as well, there is indeed a conjunction with the object (*karman*).

The heads of the enemies fell along with the arrows of Murāri, together with the streams of tears of the enemy women, their earrings, and the flowers of the gods—all bearing the marks of victory. || 702 ||

"By the marks of victory" (vijayāṅkaiḥ) means by those things that serve as signs of victory. Here, although the act of falling is diverse due to its various substrates such as arrows and so forth, it is rendered non-different by being delimited by the single common attribute of "having fallen. Consequently, there is a connection with a single action. For this very reason, this is not *śleṣa* (paronomasia), since *śleṣa* is admitted only when there is a difference in the delimitors of what is to be expressed (*pratipādyatāvacchedaka*). In these examples, the relationship of subordinate and principal is governed by the instrumental case used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*).

When there is a connection with an action (*kriyā*) based on predominance, however, it becomes either *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) or *dīpaka* (Illuminator), as the case may be. This [figure] is possible even without the use of words such as *saha* (with), because the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) can proceed without obstruction by the rule "an old man [is compared] with a youth" (*vṛddho yūnā*). Nevertheless, it is to be understood as being devoid of the use of words such as *iva* (like), similar to *utprekṣā* (Poetic Fancy); its subordinate status, however, is purely verbal. Although the states of being contextual (*prakṛta*) or non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) generally determine the roles of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), [this distinction is not absolute].

Nevertheless, in this case, the determination of those two [the subordinate and the principal] is not made by those two [the qualities of being subordinate and principal], because even in the case of the two subjects under discussion, their coexistence is possible. Rather, it is determined solely by their relative predominance and subordination. And we have already stated that the charm of this [figure] is produced by hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). However, where that [hyperbole] is absent, there is the example: "The father has come with his son."

"Beyond the sky, shining in the world beyond that supreme divine realm—the Lord, the Filler of the World (Lokaṃpṛṇa), dwells together with Lakṣmī alone on the Vṛṣādri mountain. In such passages, the figure of speech *sahokti* (conjunction) is not present. [The word] *lokaṃpṛṇaḥ* means "one who fills (*pṛṇati*) or pleases (*prīṇayati*) the world (*loka*). The root *pṛṇati* has the sense of "pleasing. From this root, the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *mūlavibhuja* (Pāṇini 3.2.5). The augment *mum* is inserted by the rule "lokasya pṛṇe. (Pāṇini 6.3.98).

In this regard, it is argued that it is not correct to claim that in examples such as "by the destructions of the ten-faced one [Rāvaṇa] and others," there exists the figure of speech *sahokti* (concomitance) animated by the inversion of temporal sequence. This is because, in this case, it is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) alone that brings about aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), while *sahokti* is merely a name. For, when comparing the *atiśayokti* verse, "O King, your anger and the destruction of your enemies arise simultaneously," with the verse, "O King, your anger arises together with the destruction of your enemies," no specific distinction in charm is perceived despite the difference in grammatical status (the former being primary and the latter secondary). And it is precisely this distinction that serves as the differentiator between figures of speech.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence that figures such as *rūpaka* (metaphor), which are vitalized by similarity, would become redundant; for in instances such as "He resembles a fresh cloud" (*navanīradasadṛśo’sau*) versus "This is a fresh cloud in person" (*eṣa navīnāmbudaḥ sākṣāt*), a distinct aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*) is clearly present. Otherwise, there would be the logical impossibility of the emergence of *vyatireka* (contrast), which is itself prompted by similarity.

Furthermore, just as in metaphors (*rūpaka*) and the like—which are occasioned by similarity—the similarity itself occupies a subordinate position and thus does not deserve a separate designation from the metaphors and so forth, which are the actual loci of aesthetic repose; likewise, it is appropriate that this *sahokti* (simultaneous expression) should not be distinct from *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which is manifested through the coexistence of factors and consists in the reversal of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.

If this were the case, one might object that there would be a lack of a distinct subject for the *sahokti* (simultaneous mention), since even another form of *sahokti* is swallowed up by the poetic excellence (*atiśaya*) consisting of the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*). To this we say no; for in a *sahokti* rooted in the determination of non-difference, it is the *sahokti* itself that is embellished by that very determination of non-difference. Thus, following the principle stated as "the subordinate is not eclipsed by the principal, but rather the subordinate by the principal," the *sahokti* finds its proper scope. Furthermore, the relationship between the subordinate and the principal must be discerned with a subtle vision and without dogmatism.

Furthermore, the mere determination of mutual non-difference is simply an *atiśaya* (exaggeration); it is not *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because that [mere exaggeration] exists even in cases such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia). *Atiśayokti*, however, consists in the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object by means of the standard of comparison. And thus, in examples such as “they burst open” or “they fell,” since there is no swallowing up of one thing by another, there is not even a trace of *atiśayokti*. Yet, mere *atiśaya* generally enhances most poetic figures (*alaṃkāra*) in the aspect of their common attributes.

For indeed, in such instances as "The face shines like a lotus," the simile does not manifest without the identification (adhyavasāna) of the lotus and the beauty of the face, which are in reality distinct. Therefore, the claim of the author of the *Sarvasva* and others—that one variety of *sahokti* has its root in the reversal of the sequence between cause and effect—is based merely on dogmatism. However, let it be granted that the variety rooted in identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) may indeed be the province of *sahokti*.

If, however, it is considered that while in *dīpaka* and *tulyayogitā* there is a connection of attributes such as action between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) primarily, whereas here (in *samāsokti*) there is such a connection only by way of a subordinate and primary relationship—and thus, although this distinction exists, because it does not produce a specific striking effect (*vicchitti*), it does not necessitate a separate figure of speech, but rather constitutes a sub-variety thereof; and if, casting aside the courtesy of looking toward the faces of the ancient *alaṃkārika*s, this [view] is accepted, then let this [figure] also be included among those already established.

It is argued that a mere slight distinction is sufficient for the differentiation of figures of speech, lest the infinite variety of verbal expressions lead to the undesirable consequence of an infinity of figures. True; however, the ancients themselves are the authority for regarding *sahokti* as a distinct figure, for they perceived a specific aesthetic charm (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*) in the coexistence of elements when that coexistence is characterized by a relationship of subordinate and predominant factors, as distinguished from other figures. Otherwise, there would be great confusion due to the proliferation of such similar cases.

We do not at all accept as authoritative those ancients whose eyes were closed by falsehood; that this poor woman should be cast into the prison-chamber of the harem amidst other ornaments is a matter of mere power, not of aesthetic sensitivity—enough of this long digression!

Thus have examples been shown regarding the commonality of attributes (sādhāraṇadharmatā) in the case of action (kriyā). Regarding the same in the case of a quality (guṇa), for example: "O Lord of the World, even your mind attains depth along with your navel; O Enemy of Kaṃsa, even your greatness attains great loftiness along with your fleshy shoulders. (704) In this instance, although action also shares a common attribute with the quality, nevertheless, because it is subordinate (nāntarīyakatvena) and lacks aesthetic charm, in the final analysis, it is the quality alone that bears the full weight of the poetic effect.

Here, there is a coexistence [of qualities] through the superimposition of non-difference upon profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) and loftiness (*unnati*), which are otherwise distinct in their substrata. This should be understood to apply to *śleṣa* (punning) as well. Furthermore, where a single object of comparison (*upameya*) serves as the basis for a coenunciation (*sahokti*) with mutually distinct counterparts, that is "garland-like coenunciation" (*mālāsahokti*) by virtue of its being like a garland (*mālātulyatayā*). For instance, in the verse beginning "The heads of the enemies fell," although the companionship is manifold due to the diversity of the points of comparison—such as with Murāri and Bāṇa, with the streams of tears of the enemies' wives, with their earrings, and with celestial flowers—[it remains a single instance of this figure].

There is no difference [between this and other types of simile] because of their falling together and being mentioned simultaneously; or, even if there were some kind of difference, there would be no distinction [from other similes], since the attribute is the same. For it is intended here that the distinction be made by the attribute, the object of comparison, and both together.

"May the side-glances of the Daughter of the Ocean protect you—glances which fall upon the lotus-eyed one, spreading forth along with the drops from the ocean tossed up by churning and the flowers of the gods. (705)

In this instance, although there is a difference in the attributes (*dharma*), the figures of speech *sahokti* (concomitance) and *upamā* (simile) are not of the nature of a "garland" (*mālārūpa*), because the jars, the oceans, the drops, and the flowers—which serve as the objects of comparison (*upamāna*) manifested by the attribute of spreading—also function as constituents of the *sahokti* manifested by the attribute of falling. Here, the qualifier "daughters of the ocean" (*payodhikanyāḥ*) is intended to suggest that the side-glances possess the character of being like the descent of the Ocean of Milk.
But this is an illustration:

blooming together with the fortunes of the worlds, expanding along with their splendors, and reaching its limit only with their wonders—blessed are those who enter the festival of the Lord of the Serpent Hill.

In this verse, it should be understood that because of the distinctness between the attributes such as "unfolding" (unmiṣitatva) and the objects of comparison such as "fortune" (bhāgya), and because the object of comparison—the festival of Śrīnivāsa—is a single entity, the *sahokti* (concomitance) takes the form of a *mālā* (garland). "O Lord of the Raghus, the red dawn was created by you along with the corner of [Rāvaṇa’s] eye; and his body, along with his life-breath, was rescued by you along with your arrow. (707)

O Lord of the Raghus! Simultaneously with the corner of Your eye, the body of the Ten-faced one was rendered red with wrath. (In the alternative reading, there is a word-break as *aruṣā*). The meaning is: the corner of the eye became red with wrath (*ruṣā śoṇaḥ*), while the body of the Ten-faced one became red (*śoṇaḥ*) with a wound (*aruṣā*); for Amara states, “*vraṇaḥ*, *īrmaḥ*, and *aruḥ* are used for a wound, and are not feminine. Along with the arrow, the life-force (*prāṇaḥ*)—the primary breath consisting of five functions—of this Ten-faced one was also carried away; that is, the arrow extracted and uprooted his life.

This is because the root *dhṛ* preceded by the prefix *ut* possesses the capacity to convey both meanings [of "lifting up" and "eradicating"], as Hemacandra states: "The word *uddharaṇa* may mean 'lifting up' (*unnaya*), or it may mean 'that which has been discarded after being eaten' (*bhuktojjhita*) and 'uprooting' (*unmūlana*). In this case, even though there are two distinct types of *sahokti* (concomitance), the quality of being a "garland" (*mālā*) certainly exists; for even so, examples of "garland-like concomitance" (*mālāsahokti*) are found in works such as the *Rasagaṅgādhara*.

In the first half [of the verse], there is a coexistence of qualities (*guṇasāhitya*), while in the second half, there is a coexistence of actions (*kriyāsāhitya*). These are enlivened by a *śleṣa*-based hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and a hyperbole consisting of the inversion of sequence (*paurvāparyaviparyaya*). However, one should observe the distinction that in the previous example, the coexistence was supported by a quality that follows along (*anugāmi-dharma*). Thus, the differences should be noted.
Just as the host of night-stalkers,

together with their cruelty, was inflicted with pain by the Lord of the Raghus, so too was their lack of joy, along with their exhaustion, removed by him for the sake of the gods who enjoy the oblations.

The Lord of the Raghus, together with his twanging bowstring, inflicted *ārti* upon the host of night-stalkers; that is to say, he placed the bowstring upon the tip of the bow and inflicted suffering (*pīḍā*) upon the multitude of demons. According to Amara, "ārti" means both "suffering" and "the tip of a bow. By that infliction of *ārti*, the Lord of the Raghus, along with the exhaustion of the gods who partake in sacrifices, extended a limit to their joy—that is to say, he brought an end to their distress and bestowed joy upon them.

According to Amarasimha, the term *sāti* is used in the senses of "giving" (*dāna*) and "conclusion" (*avasāna*). Here too, as in the previous examples, its nature as a *mālā* (garland-like) figure and so forth should be understood according to the specific requirements of each case.

Just as your service toward your elders shines forth in your conduct, O Acyuta, so too does the fame arising from your charity spread through the courtyard of your home along with the entire circle of the directions.

O Acyuta! Among your own people—your devotees—a desire to hear (*śuśrūṣā*) your life-story shines forth together with their elders and teachers. The meaning is that regarding the elders, there is service and attendance (*paricaryā*), while regarding your life-story, a longing to hear it (*śravaṇecchā*) is manifest. Hemacandra states: "Now, *śuśrūṣā* [denotes] both service and the desire to hear. Alternatively, the word *diśām* ends in the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; thus, the meaning is "together with the courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*) of the quarters (*diś*) of the directions (*kakubh*)."

In their very courtyard, in the precincts of their palace, fame—arisen through giving (*dāna*)—shines; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. In the courtyard of the quarters (*diśāṅgaṇe*), fame (*kīrtiḥ*), meaning glory (*yaśaḥ*), which has arisen and risen through giving—that is, through bestowing—is shining. Alternatively, in the courtyard of the house, fame—which has arisen and been produced by the gift of the ichor of elephants (*dviradamadasalila*)—shines as mud (*kardamaḥ*) or as an expansion (*vistṛti*); such is the meaning. For the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *dāna* [is used] for elephant-ichor and for renunciation; *kīrti* for favor and for glory; and *kardama* for mud and also for expansion."

Here too, forms such as a "garland" (mālārūpa) should be understood according to the possibility of their occurrence; however, the distinction lies in the coexistence of loci (adhikaraṇasāhitya). In the first half, the term *carite* denotes a locus in the sense of a sphere of activity (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*), whereas in the second half, *gṛhāṅgaṇe* denotes either an immediate proximity (*aupaśleṣika*) or a pervasive locus (*abhivyāpaka*); this is the difference. Furthermore, the pervasion (*abhivyāpti*) here should be understood as relative.

In this context, the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that has entered into the state of being an original and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) is also possible. For example: "May Hari, the bestower of boons upon elephants, purify you—he who, while suddenly releasing his serpent-king’s hood, simultaneously releases his chariot, which is encircled by the rays of the jewels on the hoods and surrounded by a garland of flames. (710) Here, there is the relation of original and reflection between the rays of the jewels on the hoods and the garland of flames. However, between "encircled" (*parivīta*) and "surrounded" (*āvṛta*), there is the relation of thing and counter-thing (*vastuprativastubhāva*). Regarding the release of the chariot and the discus (*cakra*), there is a reversal of sequence; this is a *sahokti* (simultaneity figure) enlivened by the *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based upon that [reversal].
This [figure of speech] can also occur when it is commingled with another figure of speech, as for example:

"Alas! Just as a whole block of camphor dissolves instantly in the presence of a flame, so too has my extensive sin dissolved in a single moment before the mountain-crested Lord who possesses two tongues (Śiva). (711)

Like a fragment of camphor situated within a block of ice, [which is singular in number] by virtue of its noble nature; from Śrīnivāsa, the crest-jewel of the Śeṣācala mountain—the peak of the mountain of the double-tongued [serpents]—my sin has spread out, [which is likewise singular in number] as before. "In a single step" (ekapade) means in the mere placement of a single foot, that is, very quickly. Alternatively, the indeclinable ending in "ekapade" is listed among the words beginning with "ca" in the sense of "from one," meaning unexpectedly.

"Extremely quickly" means: it dissolved along with the mind. In the case of camphor, "dissolved" (vilīna) means melted (*vidruta*); as Amara states: "The words *vilīna*, *vidruta*, and *druta* [mean melted]. In the case of sin (*durita*), it means it became beyond the range of sight. In the case of the mind, however, from the phrase "from the peak of the mountain of the double-tongued one" (*dvirasanagiriśekharataḥ*)—referring to Śrīnivāsa—the suffix *tasi* is used in the ablative sense according to Pāṇini 5.4.44. The meaning is that my mind, in a single moment—that is, in a single resolve, specifically the resolve to attain Him—became absorbed (*līna*), meaning it became fixed upon Him.

The sense is that, according to the manner stated in [Bhagavad Gītā 10.10], "I give them that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me," their attainment depends solely upon Him. Alternatively, the suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*); the meaning is that He is merged in a single state or reality, namely Śrīnivāsa. Or else, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*); the meaning is that He is fixed upon a single station or foot of Śrīnivāsa. According to Amarasimha: "The word *pada* is used in the senses of resolve, protection, place, mark, foot, and object.
Here, the figure of speech is *sahokti* (conjunction), enlivened by the figures of *upamā* (simile) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia) based on hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). As in another example:
O jewel of the Bull-mountain, how could you, the granter of fearlessness to the gods, so violently have caused great terror among the host of deities in the face of this assembly of asuras? (712)

O jewel of the Vṛṣa mountain, how is it that you are the bestower of fearlessness upon the gods? Why is it that [the demons] say, "I am not [here]"? To this, he says "asura" and so forth. By you, along with the host of Asuras, the host of Suras was "vyatāni"—that is, having violently overcome the host of Asuras, the host of Suras was made to tremble intensely. The compound *susādhvasam* means "that which has intense *sādhvasa* (trembling/fear). In the case of the *surakadamba*, the division of the word is *su-sādhu-asam*.

The construction is by way of inversion: "susādhu asaṃ atiprasabhamatānīti. [It means: "Very well, indeed; *asaṃ* (that which lacks the letter *sa*), very correctly; *atiprasabhaṃ* (exceedingly brilliant), meaning *atiprabhaṃ* (of extreme luster). One must not forget the identity between word and meaning (*śabdārthayostādātmyaṃ*). The intention is that it was composed (*atāni*) as something exceedingly radiant (*atitejasvi*). It should be understood that this is a *sahokti* (conjoined expression) animated by *tulyayogitā* (parallelism)—characterized by the equality of the conduct of the beneficial and the harmful—by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), and by *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), which is the manifestation of praise through censure.

Indeed, how great is your wondrous magnanimity, O Lord of the gods on the mountain of serpents! Even toward your enemies, you swiftly bestow that which is dearer than your own beloveds: the extreme suffering of hell. 713.

O Lord of Ahicchatra, this [statement] contains the intention of Your supreme magnanimity. Your generosity is wonderful and distinct from that of the world. He establishes this very point with the word "together" (sākam): You bestow upon those who are hateful together with even those dear to You—those who are objects of Your affection according to the teaching "he is dear to Me," namely the knowers of truth—even the most terrible hellish suffering, which is devoid of the interval for discerning between the beneficial and the harmful; thus is the reproach.

"To those who hate you, you bestow hell"—a hell that causes excessive agony; as Amara states: "Nāraka is indeed hell" (*nārakastu narakaḥ*). "You grant [this]" means that, according to the saying, "Those deluded ones who hate me, I cast them into hell," you bestow upon them a miserable rebirth. Regarding the phrase "but to those dear to you, quickly" (*priyebhyastu satvaram*), the word division is *saḥ* *tu* *aram*. The construction is: "He, you. "Exceeding suffering" (*atiduḥkha*) means that which has transcended (*atikrānta*) suffering; thus it is so described.

The compound is formed according to the rule *atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). Following the direction stated in the verse *yanna duḥkhena saṃbhinnaṃ*, the meaning is "unmixed with suffering. *Aram* means devoid of the letter *ra*; thus, *nārakam nākam* means "the heaven that is not hell. As in passages such as *te ha nākaṃ mahimānaḥ*, the word *nāka* here refers to the supreme ether (*paramavyoma*). The sense is that you grant this, because it has been stated by yourself [in the scripture] in such phrases as *nayāmi paramāṃ gatim*.

Here too, as in the previous example, the figure is enlivened by *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing), *śleṣa* (paronomasia), and *vyājastuti* (ironical praise). However, the distinction [from the previous case] should be noted as follows: it is enlivened by the sprout of *parikara* (poetic circumlocution) characterized by an intentional subject (*viśeṣya*) mixed with *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of *ahigirisuradro*, and it possesses the aesthetic quality of *saṃpradāna-sasāhitya*.

In this way, even in the previously cited example of *sahokti* (joint description) involving the phrase “service together with the elders,” one should recognize that it is enlivened by *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), characterized by the connection of a single attribute—namely, the act of serving—and so forth.
All these examples of *sahokti* have been demonstrated using words expressing the sense of "together" (*saha*). An example where it is implied rather than expressed by such a word is as follows:
“O glorious Trivikrama, formerly in the forest of Bali, the head of the city-demon was pressed against the surface of the earth by your lotus-foot, and thus rendered motionless. (714)

O Trivikrama! This [address] is intended to illuminate the unique character of that incarnation regarding the matter about to be expressed. "With the forces" (balaiḥ) means with the armies of Virocana at the sacrifice (savane); "with the surface of the earth" (dharāṇitalena) means together with the ground—though we have already stated that the third case ending occurs even without the use of the word "saha. The head (uttamāṅgam) of Śiva, the destroyer of the cities, was touched by the lotus (kamalena)—meaning by the water—of your foot (tvatpadasya), which is the Gaṅgā.

*Stimitam* means moistened, made wet, or prepared; it existed (*asti*) or was (*āsīt*) in the past—this is the sense. Regarding the form *purā*, the rule *“puri luṅ cāsme”* prescribes the *laṭ* (present) tense for the remote past (*bhūtānadyatana*). In the case of the "surface of the earth" (*dharaṇitala*), however, it refers to your lotus-feet (*tvatpadakamala*), your lotus-like feet; as Medinī states: *“kamalaṃ salile tāmre jalaje”* (a lotus is in water, copper-colored, or born in water). That which is *stimita* is such that the phonetic cluster *sti* does not exist (*avidyamāna*) within it; thus, it means measured (*mita*) and subjected to the act of measuring.

Thus, it should be understood that in all the examples previously shown, if words expressing the sense of "together" (saha) are removed, those [examples] likewise become illustrations of implied *sahokti*.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the Chapter on Sahokti (Simultaneity), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now, the figure of speech called *vinokti* (description by absence):
if the beauty or even the lack of beauty of the subject under discussion is depicted as being [only] in the absence of something else,
then that is the ornament *vinokti*.

The figure of speech *vinokti* (description by absence) consists in the description of either the beauty or the lack of beauty of the subject (*varṇya*) as being caused by the absence of something. For example:

"Whether one follows the system of the Lord of Serpents [Patañjali] or even the system of Kaṇāda [Kaṇāda], no person deserves to be counted among the wise without devotion to the Lord of the Mountain [Śiva]. (715)
In this context, there is the worthlessness of that which is devoid of devotion to the Blessed One.

O Acyuta, even if one were to wander through all the immovable mountains or undergo hundreds of hardships such as the performance of austerities, the multitude of people would not have attained the fulfillment of their purpose without the sight of you.
In this case, there is a state of despondency for one who is deprived of the sight of the Blessed One.

Just as song does not shine without the cymbal, so knowledge does not shine without virtuous conduct; as a housewife does not shine without a child, so the earth, O Hari, does not shine without you as its protector.

Here too, the lack of charm in that which is deprived of rhythm and so forth is like this: as a forest shines without the delusion of fire, as the ocean shines without a crocodile, and as a good person shines among the wicked without their affection. (718)

"One who resorts to Acyuta" is *acyutabhāk*, meaning a devotee of the Lord; the suffix *ṇvi* is applied according to the rule "bhajo ṇviḥ. *Jaladhiḥ* means a lake (*saraḥ*), based on the analysis "that in which waters (*jalāni*) are held (*dhīyante*)," as stated in the *Ratnamālā*: "The words *abdhi*, *saras*, and *sarasvant* [denote a lake]. Here, there is beauty in being free from delusion and the like. The first [example] is purely [an instance of *śleṣa*], while the others are favorable to *dīpaka*.

"O Goddess, just as your splendor never shines without leanness, yet your pair of eyes does not shine in the heart without flickering—here, the beauty of two things deprived of leanness and flickering is [simultaneously] perceived; thus, this is a 'Mixture' (miśratā) that is favorable both to the *Prativastūpamā* and the *Parisaṃkhyā*."

The multitude of virtues of the Lord of the Mountain, who is the king of serpents, possesses perfect beauty, being free from even the slightest fault, like the digit of the moon which is without a blemish. (720)

When the inner self is constantly turned toward the Lord of the Mountain of Serpents through the surrender of its own burden, it shines like a gem in the heart that has been polished, freed from its tarnish.

*Pratyaṅ* means the inner self (*ātman*), that is, the individual soul (*jīva*). According to the rule *ṅamo hrasvādaci ṅamuṇṇityam*, there is always the augment *ṅamuṭ* after the letter *ṅa* before a vowel in *saṃhitā*. Like a gem [which becomes bright] through polishing such as rubbing on a whetstone, the inner self, by surrendering its burden to the Blessed One, shines forth as *hṛllekha*—that is, heart-pleasing (*hṛdya*)—being free from the soiled state caused by contact with mud and the like. It is called *hṛllekha* because it "scratches" (*likhati*) the heart; the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the root *likh* with the word *hṛdaya* as an upapada.

In accordance with the rule *‘hṛdayasya hṛllekhayadaṇlāseṣu’*, the word *hṛdaya* undergoes the substitution *hṛt*. In the alternative sense, being free from the impurity of ignorance created by *avidyā*, he shines—meaning he blazes with eternally uncontracted knowledge—becoming one who reaches the heart (*hṛdayaṅgama*) of the Lord, according to the manner described in such passages as *‘maṇivara iva śaurernityahṛdyaḥ’*. Of these two [interpretations], the former is favorable to a pure simile (*śuddhopamā*), while the latter is favorable to a simile based on *śleṣa* (punning).

A creeper may flourish even without roots; a pond of mossy water may exist even without a bank; yet, O King, Lakṣmī can never abide anywhere without the Lord who is the protector of the mountain that is the king of serpents. This is an example of *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) in the form of a *dīpaka* (illuminator).
Just as a woman without passion, just as a river without the flow of water, and just as prosperity without renunciation, so too is wisdom without union with Śauri.

Previously, a connection based on action, quality, and so forth was necessary; here, however, that [connection] is understood through the very power of the simile, and thus it is not required in that manner.

And this [negation] occurs not only when the word "vinā" exists, but also when there is the existence of words expressing the meaning of "vinā. Thus, it occurs even in the presence of such usages as *nañ*, *nira*, *vi*, *antareṇa*, *ṛte*, *vikala*, *viyukta*, *rahita*, *dūrita*, *vidhura*, and so forth. For example:
"If a tree should appear without fruit, if the ocean should appear without water, if even a king should appear without power, or if the earth should appear without Mount Mahendra... (724)

The grammatical connection is: "If even a king should fear [his enemy] without strength. Here, the word *antareṇa* is employed in the sense of "without" (*vinā*). This is an instance favorable to the figure of speech *dīpaka* (the illuminator) based on false attribution (*mithyādhyavasiti*).
The orb of the sun in the sky, the orb of the sun whose eyes are lotuses—could even the lotus-eyed one, the son of the ocean, not shine by virtue of his own splendor? 725.

Here, the negative particle *nañ* is employed in the sense of exclusion (*vinārthaka*). "Not having lotus-eyes" means being devoid of those lotus-eyed ones who are celebrated in the Veda as "his eyes are like a blooming lotus with petals like a monkey's buttocks. "Not the son of the ocean" means one who is separated from Śrī (Lakṣmī). The intended meaning is that he possesses great splendor and a golden complexion. Why should he shine? The implication is that such a state is difficult to attain when one is separated from Śrī.

For this very reason, the Teacher specified in the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali* that [the Lord] "possesses eternal splendor within the solar orb. Here, the scriptural text stating, "He is entirely golden, even to the tips of his nails," should be kept in mind; this is consistent with the subsequent *Mālādapikā*.
Those whose inclination toward the Śeṣācala mountain has not been raised even slightly will not attain orientation toward the Śeṣyacala mountain even in a thousand births.

The "unwavering" (acalam) and "immovable" (niścalam) "facing toward" (abhimukhatvam) of the Lord, who is the Sovereign of all and the one to whom others remain subordinate (śeṣiṇaḥ), means, in effect, being within the range of His side-long glance (kaṭākṣagocaratvam). They "will not attain" (naiṣyanti)—that is, they do not reach—the fruit consisting of the Lord’s own orientation toward them, because of the absence of the means consisting of being oriented toward the Lord, who is the Remainder (Śeṣa). The sense is that such a result is difficult to obtain in the absence of this specific means. Here too, the word *vinā* (without) has not been employed to express the meaning of the word *na*. This [verse] is conducive to the poetic figure *ullāsa*, which consists in the emergence of a defect in one thing due to the excellence of another.
Free from the touch of fear, like pearls abandoned by the scent of defects, these excellent qualities, headed by brilliance, blaze forth like the jewels upon the immovable hoods of serpents.
In this case, the word *saṃtyakta* (abandoned) is used; and this [simile] is favorable to the comparison (*upamā*).

The auspicious qualities of Śrīnātha, such as knowledge and bliss, which have cast far away all defects, are like the rays of the sun; they delight the heart, dispel darkness, and are always to be savored. (728)
In this case, the word *sudūrita* is employed; this too is entirely conducive to the simile.

The author of the *Alaṅkārabhāṣya*, however, states: "Vinokti is the statement of non-connection regarding things that possess an eternal connection. According to his view, the aforementioned examples do not qualify; instead, he offers this as an example: "O Slayer of Madhu, by the hosts of the enemies of the gods who were experiencing the heat of Śiva’s majesty, two suns were seen, yet they were perceived as being devoid of heat. (729)

"Citrabhānu" refers to the pair of the sun and fire; as Amarasimha states: "The sun and fire are called Citrabhānus. Here, although heat is invariably concomitant with both the sun and fire, their absence [of heat] is depicted.

Just as in this world, when Your fame—rich with unsurpassed clarity—shines forth on all sides, Mādhava, the moon, the Creator, and the celestial damsels are seen to possess no whiteness apart from it. 730.

The Sarasvatī [states]: "Vidhivanitā. Here, although there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with whiteness, its absence is shown. Its charm arises solely from its embrace by another figure of speech (*alaṃkāra*), and not inherently; therefore, they say that its status as a distinct figure of speech is indeed tenuous. Others, however, maintain that since the emergence of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) occurs without obstacle simply through the cognition of charm or lack thereof induced by a slight *vyatireka* (contrast), and since its charm—unembraced by any other figure of speech—is witnessed solely by the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), its status as an independent figure of speech remains entirely intact.

"Then what would be the use of that birth in which the Infinite One (Ananta) was not contemplated within one's heart? Or what would be the use of that action which is not offered to the Infinite One at its conclusion? (731). Here, by means of an objection or a question regarding the result—asking "what [is the use]?"—the worthlessness of a heart without contemplation of the Blessed Lord and of an action without its offering to the Blessed Lord is suggested (*vyajyate*). And although this [suggestion] serves as a subordinate support (*anugrāhaka*) for the suggestion of the aesthetic emotion (*bhāva*) directed toward the Blessed Lord, its status as a *dhvani* remains entirely unimpeded.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of destroying the very definition of "support," which is characterized by such subordination.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on Vinokti (Peculiar Allegation), in the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra.
Now begins the Chapter on Samāsokti (Condensed Expression):
"When, due to similarity, the unmentioned subject (*aprastuta*)—consisting solely of its distinguishing features—is implied, the ancient masters who know the ornaments call this *samāsokti*."

A differentiator is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). *Samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis) is a description of an unmentioned subject (*aprastuta*) that is understood through the similarity of its qualifiers alone; it is called "by ellipsis" (*samāsena*) because it expresses both the mentioned (*prastuta*) and the unmentioned subjects in a concise manner.
"He has ascended the mountain of sunrise, he is radiant, his orb is crimson;
this king captivates the hearts of the people with his gentle rays."

Thus, in the case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) between the contextual and the non-contextual, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to that [type of *śleṣa*], because the non-contextual account of the king is also understood through the word "king" (*rāja*), which is the substantive term (*viśeṣya*) used in the pun.

May my mind, uplifted by devotion, embrace the crest of the mountain of the serpent-king with a grace that is languid due to tears of joy, choked speech, the bristling of hair, trembling, and fainting. (732)

In this context, while the account of one’s own mind being intent upon devotion is being described, due to the similarity of the adverbial qualifiers such as "with joy" (*sāmoda*) and so forth, the narrative of a heroine engaged in a spontaneous embrace with her beloved is perceived.

With its blossoming breasts and face of radiant color, this exceedingly deep river of the poet’s speech, possessing incomparable circularity, bestows supreme joy upon Hari through the embrace of its graceful words. 733.

She is so described because her letters—those phonemes whose initial sounds are *ku* (the *ka*-group) or *cu* (the *ca*-group)—are distinct (*sphuṭāni*). Alternatively, she is so described because her "colors" (*varṇāḥ*), namely the colors of her breasts and face (*kucamukhavarṇāḥ*), are clear and radiant. She is one for whom there exists no comparison (*avidyamāna-tulanā*), meaning no equality. This means she is incomparable through verses (*vṛttaiḥ*)—that is, through poems composed in various meters (*chandaḥ*) distinguished by measures and syllables—or through the conduct (*vṛttena*) of the Blessed One; the sense is that she has no peer.

The sense is that she is highly praiseworthy because she is composed of *vṛtta* (verses) that transcend the world (*lokottara*). According to Amara, "the word *vṛtta* means a verse, conduct, past, firm, or round. The term *abhitaḥ* means on all sides; thus, she possesses the quality of profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), defined as "the state of being free from sound" (*adhvanimattā*). In the alternative [interpretation], *vṛttā* means round like a whirlpool; she is one whose navel (*nābhi*) is incomparable (*atulā*)—that is, unlike any other—and by that navel, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case. Thus, the meaning is: she possesses a navel that is exceedingly deep, round, and peerless.

That [poetic speech] in which the words (*padāni*)—consisting of nominal and verbal suffixes—are graceful (*lalitāni*); and she who has graceful feet (*lalite pade caraṇe yasyāḥ*) is likewise described. By means of *śleṣa* (punning), in the alternative sense, the word is split as "by an embrace" (*āśleṣeṇa*), meaning by a hug. Here, while the context concerns the poet and the Goddess of Speech (*Bhāratī*), an account of a longingly expectant heroine (*utkaṇṭhitā nāyikā*) is perceived due to the similarity of qualifiers such as "with manifest breasts and face," and by the power of the feminine gender inherent in the word *vāṇī*. In the former case, the qualifiers are common to both.

In this case, however, the distinction is that the words are "punned" (*śliṣṭa*). Furthermore, "commonality" (*sādhāraṇatva*) consists in the fact that the events concerning both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) subjects are applicable even without a formal pun. For example:

"O Acyuta, at first I was soiled with pride and had set my foot upon the lake; then I was seized by a most terrible crocodile; today I cry out with my hands upraised! (734) [Note: This verse is an instance of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), where the words apply simultaneously to a literal sense (the speaker's physical plight) and a metaphorical sense (the soul's spiritual state).]

O Acyuta! At first, he was defiled by intoxication, pride, and the water of his liberality; then, having set foot—meaning both his resolve and his physical step—into reservoirs of dull-witted people and receptacles of stagnant water, he was consequently seized by a most treacherous and wicked crocodile, that is, by a stubborn persistence (or, in the other sense, by a specific aquatic creature), for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *grāha* denotes both seizing and a crocodile (*avahāra*)."

He by whom the trunk—the hand, the arm, and the proboscis—is tossed up and raised, being thus described, now, at the stage of the ripening of his karma, cries out; that is, he weeps. Here, within the context of the account of one weary of saṃsāra, through the similarity of the shared epithets, the story of an old elephant seized by a crocodile is understood.
This [similarity] is also seen through resemblance (*sārūpya*), as for example:

"O Sarasvatī, your dwelling is upon the shining chest of the Lord of Serpents and the Lord of Mountains; you shine like the Kaustubha gem. Blessed is your peerless splendor! Who else is there like you? (735)

In the verse beginning "Sarasvatī in the ocean," while the description of Śrīnivāsa’s Kaustubha gem is the subject at hand, the account of a fortunate man—or perhaps a great scholar—who has attained imperial sovereignty after being born in some most praiseworthy foreign land is understood; thus, this is an instance of *sārūpya* (similarity) as the basis for the poetic figure.

Just as the pair of eyes rejoices, the heart expands, darkness dissolves, and a beautiful luster gathers upon beholding the supreme Kaustubha gem in the chest of the Lord of the Serpent Hill (Śrīnivāsa). 736.

Here, by means of the contextual narrative of beholding the Kaustubha gem, the contextual narrative of beholding the rising sun is implied. In the phrases "the pair of eyes rejoices" and "the heart expands," through similarity (*sārūpya*), the joy of the cakravāka couple and the blossoming of the lotus are respectively understood. In the phrases "darkness dissolves" and "lovely luster appears," through paronomasia (*śleṣa*), the disappearance of darkness and the attainment of splendor are understood; this constitutes its distinction from the previous examples.

Regarding this, the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* states: "The communication of an irrelevant (aprastuta) occurrence—whether by the power of qualifiers common to both the relevant (prastuta) and the irrelevant, or through similarity—is for the purpose of superimposing it upon the relevant subject (*viśeṣya*), since that which is in no way connected to the relevant cannot be the object of a poet’s creative intent. Consequently, in *samāsokti*, the superimposition of the irrelevant mode of behavior (*vyavahāra*) is the source of its charm; however, as in *rūpaka*, there is no superimposition of the form of the irrelevant upon the relevant."

In the case of "the moon-face" (*mukhacandra*), there is the co-occurrence of the word "moon," which serves as the cause for the superimposition of the nature of a moon upon the face. However, in examples of *samāsokti* (speech of compounding) such as "the red moon kisses," there is an absence of the co-occurrence of a word expressing that [loverhood] which would serve as the cause for superimposing the nature of a lover upon the moon and so forth; furthermore, unlike the example of *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifesting) *rūpaka* such as "having gazed with lightning-eyes," there is likewise an absence of anything that could lead to the understanding of the superimposition of the form of the non-contextual (the lover) upon the contextual (the moon).

For in that case, in the verse beginning with *vidyunnayanaiḥ*, because of the suitability for the act of gazing, and in accordance with the requirement for the connection with the eyes—which constitute the meaning of the second member of the compound established as a *mayūravyaṃsaka* type where the sense of the second member is predominant—the metaphorical representation of the cloud as a beholding person, though unstated, is understood as implied. However, in the present instance, there is no such thing as the act of gazing; nor is there, as in the verse "When you arrived, why does this ocean tremble?", any mention of a unique, contextual event belonging to the subject under description, such as the building of a bridge.

Nor is there, in the case of two occurrences—one relevant and one irrelevant—presented by qualifiers that are either *śliṣṭa* (double-entendre) or *sādhāraṇa* (common), any predominance for the irrelevant occurrence such as that of lightning for the eyes; for if there were, we might admit the superimposition of the form of the irrelevant even when unstated upon the relevant, as in the verse "You are the maker of the bridge. Therefore, in this case, the cause of charm is merely the superimposition of the behavior of the irrelevant as presented by the qualifiers.

Although there is equal prominence here because the contextual and non-contextual narratives—presented through shared epithets that possess double meanings—are connected directly with the subject itself, just as they would be with distinct words expressing their attributes; nevertheless, one must not accept the superimposition of the non-contextual form upon the contextual subject merely out of deference to the connection with the non-contextual narrative.

For instance, just as there is no fitness for the connection of an irrelevant occurrence with the subject under discussion, likewise there is no fitness for the connection of the relevant occurrence with the irrelevant subject. Thus, since one must necessarily admit the superimposition (āropa) of either the relevant or the irrelevant occurrence when both are of equal prominence, it is logical to say that the superimposition of the irrelevant upon the relevant—which is already heard—is the cause of aesthetic charm (*cārutā*). So they say.

The author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara*, however, has stated the definition and other characteristics of *samāsokti* as follows: "Where a discourse concerning the subject at hand appears as non-different from a discourse concerning a non-contextual subject, which is evoked solely by means of common adjectives—that is *samāsokti*. Furthermore, it may be defined in a single statement as: 'the state of being a discourse concerning the contextual subject appearing as non-different from a discourse concerning a non-contextual subject, which is evoked solely by the hearing of common adjectives.'"

The word "only" (*mātra*) is used to exclude *dhvani* based on the power of the literal meaning (*śabdaśaktimūla*), because even the substantive (*viśeṣya*), being itself punned (*śliṣṭa*), brings to mind another subject (*prakṛtetaradharmin*) through its capacity to evoke a conventional usage regarding such a subject.
Even so, [the verse reads]:
"You bind the *ālaka* [locks of hair], you cast away darkness, you clothe yourself with a *cola* out of a desire for flavor, and you create a wound upon the forehead of the shanks."
O King, alas, you mercilessly rub each and every limb; your audacity regarding the objects of women is truly marvelous!

In this context, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a case of *śleṣa* (punning) where the subject matter concerns the conventional behavior (*vyavahāra*) of both the contextual (*prakṛta*) and the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), the states of being "contextual" and "non-contextual" are presented as qualifiers of the substratum (*dharmin*). However, if those two were presented as qualifiers of the specific behavior itself, then—since the contextual heroic narrative would remain established as non-different from the non-contextual amorous narrative (*śṛṅgāra-vṛttānta*) brought to mind merely by the hearing of common qualifiers—this very over-extension would indeed occur.

Nor should it be argued that because the description of the king is the subject at hand here, both incidents occurring within that context must also be considered the subject, and thus how could there be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)? There would be no such over-extension if only the description itself were the subject; however, in the case of a description of mere fortitude during a battle or similar occasion, there would indeed be an over-extension.

O bee, how is it that you do not abandon the lotus plant, which is full of passion even when soiled, with its face in bloom even when there is much chatter, and full of nectar even though you are fickle?
