In such cases of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because the non-contextual activity is directly expressed, it is indeed presented by the substantive (*viśeṣya*) as well; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to that figure. However, if in the context of a water-sport or similar scene the account of the bee itself is what is intended to be contextual (*prastuta*), then this is certainly *samāsokti* (speech of compression).
There,
at dawn, the sun, overflowing with passion, triumphs as he awakens with the touch of his rays the lotus-plant whose face was closed.

In this context, the meaning of the sentence—"The Sun, who is non-different from that which possesses an activity conducive to the blossoming of lotuses (the object) by means of the contact of his rays (the instrument), is victorious"—is first apprehended through *śakti* (denotative power) alone. Furthermore, another meaning—such as "non-different from that which possesses an activity conducive to the conciliation of a particular heroine (the object) by means of the touch of the hand (the instrument)"—is apprehended in both cases either through that same *śakti*, through another *śakti*, or through *vyañjanā* (suggestion); in this matter, the connoisseur (*sahṛdaya*) alone is the authority.

And thus, if these two sentence-meanings were entirely unrelated—like the left and right horns of a cow—then the belovedness of the Lord Sun and the heroinehood of the lotus-creeper, which are established by universal consensus, would be contradicted; furthermore, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result due to the presence of two primary subjects.

If another meaning were superimposed upon the subject at hand (the sun), then the resulting cognition would possess a dual objective domain—namely, that the sun is both the agent of the blooming of the lotus and the agent of the heroine’s conciliation—which would result in the fallacy of "two things in one" (*ekatra dvayam*). This, however, does not resolve the aforementioned logical inconsistency. Furthermore, even if the perception of the heroine and so forth in the lotus and other objects is established through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) rooted in punning (*śleṣa*), the Blessed Lord, as presented by the non-punned words, remains entirely untouched by the role of the hero (*nāyaka*).

If, in place of the word *padminī* (lotus-lady), the word *nalinī* (lotus) were employed, how could she ever become an object of cognition as a *nāyikā* (heroine)? Therefore, by the power of the similarity of the qualifiers, the meaning of the sentence under discussion (*prakṛtavākyārtha*)—having evoked a corresponding object such as a heroine—remains non-different from the sentence-meaning, its body being completed by that [evoked] object; it thus becomes an integral part of that [sentence-meaning], its own parts becoming identical with the parts of that [object]. And this [superimposed entity], like a transformation (*pariṇāma*), serves the purpose of the action precisely through its identity with the original subject.

And by its own nature, it serves as the enjoyment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth. Here, because the non-contextual meaning (*aprakṛtārtha*) is not expressed by a separate word, this differs from *rūpaka* (metaphor) based on the connection between sentence meanings; it differs even more clearly from *padārtharūpaka* (word-meaning metaphor). Furthermore, because it is constituted by an implied meaning, it differs from *vākyārthaśleṣa* (sentence-meaning paronomasia). Thus, the view of ancient authorities such as Bhāmaha and Udbhaṭa is that in this case, all meanings are sustained through both direct denotation (*śakti*) and implication (*ākṣepa*).

In such instances as “This moon kisses the face of the night,” since the words *niśā* (night) and *candra* (moon) are not *śliṣṭa* (punned), and because the mere act of kissing the face is common to sons and others, how can there be an implication (*ākṣepa*) of a specific lover? Furthermore, even if a lover is implied, how could he be construed with the night and the moon through identity (*abheda*), rather than through difference (*bheda*) in acts such as kissing? For if that were the case, the two would remain in a state of neutrality (*tāṭasthya*) as mere lovers, which would result in the failure to evoke aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

Therefore, in instances such as “This moonlight kisses the face of night; the fierce sun kisses the face of day,” the suggested status of being a *nāyaka* (hero/lover) is manifested within its own substratum by means of the femininity and masculinity inherent in the bases (*prakṛti*)—which are conveyed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp* and the nominative case endings respectively. And thus, the establishment of the status of *nāyaka* for the Night and the Moon is achieved through the use of *śliṣṭa* (double-entendre) adjectives. The cognition of the non-contextual meaning occurs solely through the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), because the primary denotative power (*śakti*) is restricted by context and other factors.

Thus, by the very power of the suggestive word (*vyañjana*), the contextual meaning of the sentence remains established through its identity with the non-contextual meaning of the sentence; and this is a variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion)—this indeed is the delightful path. All else should be sought therein by those desiring detail; enough, therefore, of wandering at length beyond this point.

Now, its exclusive varieties are explained. The identity of qualifiers occurs either through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) or through pure commonality (*sādhāraṇya*). Each of these is again twofold—based on the presentation of another attribute (*dharma*) or based on the presentation of an effect (*kārya*). Among these, an example of the identity of qualifiers through the presentation of another attribute based on *śleṣa* is as follows: "Adorned with various painted patterns, possessing beautiful shade, removing the intense heat from the sun, and full of joy through the service of the Beloved of Śrī—the forest on the slopes of the Serpent Mountain [or: the forest on the slopes of the Mountain of Serpents, i.e., Śiva]. (737)

"Vilikhitāni" means especially fashioned; "vibhilikhita" means scratched by the beaks of birds (vi-bhiḥ, pakṣibhiḥ, likhitāni). "Citrāṇi" refers to various forms such as the shapes of sea-monsters (makarī) and so forth; "patrāṇi" refers to decorative line-drawings in the form of leaves. In another sense, it refers to one whose foliage (palāśāni) consists of various colors. "Succhāyā" means possessing beautiful shade and a charming luster. "Harā" refers to that which removes the "atanu" (not small, i.e., intense) heat of the "bhāsvataḥ" (the shining one), namely the sun (bhānu).

Elsewhere, the sun has risen; [yet] the feverish torment of the bodiless Madana is taken away by him. This is because of his attendance upon the Beloved of Śrī (Viṣṇu), through his constant movement around her and his service to her—[the sun] being full of joy, radiant, and full of delight. Here, the contextual matter (the description of the moon) stands as non-different from the matter concerning an excellent woman who has received attentions from a southern lover (*dakṣiṇanāyaka*), by means of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) based on shared attributes such as "possessing good shade" (*succhāyatva*) and "being full of joy" (*sollāsatva*).
The same should be understood in the verse previously cited, "sphuṭakucamukha," and so forth.
An example of the similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) by means of presenting a connected action (*śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa*) is as follows: "O Śauri!

Having first cast down those who were equal and middling heroes at the time of battle (*vigrahakāle*), yet afterwards not casting down even a single step (*ekaṃ padam*)—you manifest the state of being well-spoken (*suśabdatā*) in the world. (738) O Śauri! "At the time of battle," meaning during the occasion of combat; "without casting down even a single step," meaning without withdrawing even one foot. "Equal" (*samāna*) means similar, that is to say, superior ones. "Middling" (*madhyama*) refers to those heroes (*vīra*) who are inferior in comparison to oneself. Alternatively, there is a word-division (*cheda*) as *asamān* [unequal]. In this verse, the word *samāna* (equal) is applied to both the literal sense of "middling" and the figurative sense of "superior"; thus, it is a case of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Furthermore, the word *pada* (step) is applied to both its literal sense of "foot" and its figurative sense of "word" (*pada*); therefore, this is also a case of *śleṣa*. Consequently, because the two meanings are connected through the action of "casting down," this is an instance of *śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa viśeṣaṇasāmya*. Alternatively, the following may be considered an example of *śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa viśeṣyasāmya* (similarity of the qualified through the presentation of a connected action): "Having first cast down the enemies in battle, you have now brought them under your own control; having first made them your servants, you have now made them your friends. In this verse, the word *ripu* (enemy) is applied to both the literal sense of "foe" and the figurative sense of "servant" (*ripu*); thus, it is a case of *śleṣa*. Moreover, the word *vaśa* (control) is applied to both the literal sense of "subjugation" and the figurative sense of "friendship" (*vaśa*); therefore, this is also a case of *śleṣa*. Consequently, because the two meanings are connected through the action of "casting down," this is an instance of *śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa viśeṣyasāmya*. Alternatively, the following may be considered an example of *śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa ubhayasāmya* (similarity of both through the presentation of a connected action): "Having first cast down the enemies in battle, you have now brought them under your own control; having first made them your servants, you have now made them your friends. In this verse, the word *ripu* (enemy) is applied to both the literal sense of "foe" and the figurative sense of "servant" (*ripu*); thus, it is a case of *śleṣa*. Furthermore, the word *vaśa* (control) is applied to both the literal sense of "subjugation" and the figurative sense of "friendship" (*vaśa*); therefore, this is also a case of *śleṣa*. Consequently, because the two meanings are connected through the action of "casting down," this is an instance of *śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa ubhayasāmya*. Alternatively, the following may be considered an example of *śliṣṭakāryapuraskāreṇa viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyasāmya* (similarity of both qualifier and qualified through the presentation of a connected action): "Having first cast down the enemies in battle, you have now brought them under your own control; having first made them your servants, you have now made them your friends. In this verse, the word *ripu* (enemy) is applied to both the literal sense of "foe" and the figurative sense

"Unequal" means those who are not his equals in terms of valor, heroism, and so forth; for that very reason, "not middling," meaning superior. Having first—meaning at the very beginning and not after delay—struck down, that is, having caused to fall and slain, these heroes; by this it is indicated that the repelling of enemies is easy for him. "Suśabdatām" (the state of being well-sounding) means the state of possessing excellent fame or renown. You manifest this. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word 'śabda' [is used] for syllables, fame, song, the sky, speech, and sound."

In the case [of a compound], at the time of analysis—that is, on the occasion of demonstrating the analysis for the sake of understanding the meaning of the compound—one should first employ those words such as *samāna*, *madhyama*, and *vīra* as previously described. This is because their prior placement is regulated by the rule: "The words *pūrva*, *apara*, *prathama*, *carama*, *jaghanya*, *samāna*, *madhyama*, *madhyama*, and *vīra* [are placed first]" (*pūrvāparaprathamacaramajaghanyasamānamadhyamadhyamavīrāśca*). Thus, the meaning is that even a single word—such as the word in the form "one" (*eka*)—should be employed first, rather than being placed later.

Because of the rule *pūrvakālaika* (Pāṇini 2.1.49), which mandates that [the word denoting] the earlier time in sequence must be placed first, you manifest—meaning you display—the state of being well-versed in grammar (*suśabdatā*), that is, proficiency in the science of words. Here, the contextual narrative (the subject at hand) is established through its non-difference from the narrative concerning the grammarian. There is a similarity of adjectives by virtue of the inclusion of the shared effect, such as "having been applied" (*nipātya*) and so forth.

Thus, two varieties of *samāsokti* (condensed expression) have been shown: one through the similarity of an ambiguous qualifier that conveys a property distinct from the subject matter (*kārya*), and the other through the similarity of that [qualifier] which conveys a property in the form of the subject matter itself.
By means of pure commonality (*śuddhasādhāraṇya*) through the presentation of another attribute (*dharmāntara*), as follows:

"O enemy of Kaṃsa, this most graceful glance of yours, which has wandered here in this cycle of existence, now falls upon me with impetuosity, eager to rescue me, possessing boundless affection. (739) The analysis of the compound is *utsukā āpatati* (eagerly approaching). "Approaching" (*āpatati*) means "coming toward" (*āyāti*). Here, the contextual situation (*prakṛtavṛttānta*) exists through its non-difference from the account of a mother and her child. The presentation of another attribute occurs by means of pure commonality, such as "possessing boundless affection" and so forth.

O Lord of the Bull and the Mountain, we feel ashamed to praise you merely by way of your pure universality or by reference to your effects; for indeed, your unrestrained expansion, having shaken the sky in the assembly, devours the ten directions.

"In the assembly" means in the council hall (*sabhā*). "Ambara" means a garment. The sense is: because your twanging of the bow, through its shamelessness, causes the enjoyment of the ten directions even within the assembly by first shaking the very garments [of those present], we ourselves feel ashamed to praise you. However, the actual state of affairs is this: your bow’s twanging in battle pervades the entire sky and the ten directions; thus, we, whose speech is limited and petty, feel ashamed to praise you, who are such a crest-jewel of great prowess.

Here, the incident concerning the sound of the string of the Lord’s bow—the subject at hand—subsists as non-different from the incident concerning the shameless lover—the subject not at hand. The similarity of the qualifiers is established by way of the effect, namely, "he enjoys" (*bhuṅkte*). Moreover, in the present context, "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) is used in a figurative sense. This should likewise be understood in the verse previously cited, beginning with "sāmodabāṣpagadgada."
An example of commonality through the confusion of both the effect and another property is as follows:

"O Lord Maghavan, while spreading forth your auspicious glory, you even create your former form; and here, O wielder of the firm thunderbolt, you possess the quality of one who has firmly applied the sacred scriptures. (741)

O Blessed One! He is so described because the scripture (*śāstra*) and the collection of weapons such as the *sudarśana* discus have been firmly placed in His hand. The sense is that He has taken up the five weapons for the purpose of warding off what is undesirable and attaining what is desired by those who have sought refuge. You, O Maghavan (Indra), are the bestower—meaning the giver—of the expansion of auspicious power; that is to say, the expansion of auspicious, blessing-bestowing power, namely the sovereignty over the three worlds.

"Recalling"—that is, remembering—his very former form, the state of his vigor and other qualities prior to the curse of Durvāsas; the word "recalling" is connected [to the following]. The meaning is "causing [him] to proceed. Therefore, "in that which is auspiciously radiant," meaning in him whose splendor is beautiful, i.e., in him of blazing luster. Here, in this Indra, you also fashion his virtues, such as the excellence of statesmanship and humility.

The sense is that it is solely through your grace that Indra has obtained such prosperity and so forth, you whose knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor are fully perfected. With this very intention, he addresses you as "Bhagavan. In the alternative [grammatical] interpretation, you are one for whom there is a treatise—namely, grammar—which is firm (dṛḍham), well-practiced (svabhyastam), and beneficial (hitam) to Pāṇini. In this interpretation, the word division in the phrase *śubhavibhavasaṃprasāraṇam* is *śubha-vibheti*. Thus, you are one who possesses auspicious radiance (*śubhā vibhā prabhā*).

Its vocative form is *he śubhavibho*, O Blessed One! [The term] *subhe* means "in the auspicious" (*suṣṭhu-bhe*). When the designation *bha* applies—characterized by being followed by a case-ending beginning with a vowel (as stated in the rule *ayaci bham*)—in the word *maghavat* (the vocative *maghavan*), there occurs the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the *va*; that is, the *saṃprasāraṇa* of the letter *va*, which, according to the definition stated in *igyaṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*, is an *ik* vowel (*u*) taking the place of a *yaṇ*. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that, because the rule *‘śvayuvamaghonāmataddhite’* prescribes the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *c* in the word *maghavan* when it bears the technical designation *bha*, [the form is established]. Furthermore, by taking into account the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute of the preceding vowel) according to the rule *‘saṃprasāraṇācca’*—which ordains a single substitute of the *pūrvarūpa* type when a vowel follows a *saṃprasāraṇa*—you produce here, in this word *maghavan*, the *guṇa* (single-substitute of the *guṇa* class) according to the rule *‘ādguṇaḥ*.

Thus, the distilled meaning is that by applying the designation *bha* to the word *maghavan*, you effect the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the letter *va*, the substitution of the prior form (*pūrvarūpa*), and the *guṇa* strengthening, thereby producing forms such as *maghonī*. Here, within the context at hand—the narrative of the Blessed Lord who bestows the majesty of Mahendra and other boons—the narrative of an irrelevant grammarian is presented as non-different [from it]. In this case, the effect—consisting of the acquisition of auspicious prosperity, vocalization, and so forth—is intermingled with the attribute of being firmly established in the science of Pāṇini.

In *samāsokti* (synecdoche), the suggested non-contextual behavior serves merely as an embellishment (*upaskāraka*), not as the primary element. It has been stated that the primary element is the expressed meaning itself, which is embellished by that [suggestion]. In that regard, if the suggested meaning alone were primary and not the expressed meaning, then in the previously cited verse, "We are ashamed to praise you," there would be no culmination in praise through the pretext of censure; for it must be understood that praise and censure are based respectively on the contextual and non-contextual behaviors.
The author of the *Alaṃkārasarvasva*, however, states: "Similarity of adjectives is also possible by virtue of containing a comparison, as for example:
'The deer-eyed woman was well-adorned with a mass of hair like a braid, beautiful with hands like sprouts, and covered with flowers like the luster of her teeth.'"

Here, by the power of the qualifier "well-dressedness" (suveṣatva), which functions solely with respect to the deer-eyed woman, one abandons the construction "the flowers are like the luster of her teeth" and adopts a construction based on an upamita-samāsa (compound of comparison): "the luster of her teeth is like flowers. Once the intended meaning is thus established, that very construction which was previously abandoned is revived through another mode of expression (vṛtti). Consequently, because the creeper is implied by the objects of comparison—the clusters of flowers and sprouts—there arises the superimposition of the behavior (vyavahāra) [of a woman] upon that creeper.

Thus, when "suveṣā" (well-dressed) is abandoned and "parītā" (surrounded) is substituted, since there is an absence of any valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for either establishing or refuting the presence of simile (*upamā*) or metaphor (*rūpaka*), a combination (*saṃkara*) consisting of doubt regarding both occurs upon their conjunction. Subsequently, however, because the creeper (*latā*) is perceived according to the previously stated method, it is indeed *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation). Even though there is a difference in meaning due to the difference in compound, the identity of the adjectives (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) should be understood as being based on the single word, just as in the case of *śliṣṭamūla* (based on a punning root).

It has been stated: "Whether at the beginning or the end, when the application is made that 'the luster of the teeth alone are the flowers' based on a metaphorical substratum, the cognition of the non-contextual object is established by means of a partial *ekadeśavivartin* metaphor—which implies identity with a creeper in the case of the 'deer-eyed woman'—and thus there is no need for a *samāsokti* here."

That [example] cannot withstand scrutiny; for even if one initially applies it as containing a simile—namely, "the luster of her teeth is like flowers"—it would be redundant to employ a *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning), because the sense is already conveyed by the *ekadeśavivartinī* (partially manifest) simile itself, wherein the deer-eyed woman implies the creeper as the object of comparison. Nor should it be argued that such a statement was made because Udbhaṭa’s school does not accept the coexistence (*saṃkara*) of a partially manifest simile and other figures; for he himself accepts that very point immediately thereafter.
Your anger is like *hālāhala* poison, your compassion is like nectar,
your fame is like the moon, and your warriors are as formidable as sea-monsters.

In such cases, since there is no other alternative and because that very [author] has accepted this as nothing but a *samāsokti* (synecdoche) where the comparison is partially manifest (*ekadeśavivartin*), it is inappropriate to postulate a different variety when the phenomenon can be accounted for by what is already established. Therefore, the mode of *samāsokti* suggested by an adjective containing a comparison within its meaning does not cohere. However, where an adjective containing a comparison within its meaning is accompanied by either a punning (*śliṣṭa*) or a purely common (*śuddhasādhāraṇa*) adjective, there *samāsokti* indeed exists.

Nevertheless, this cannot be considered a third variety [of *dīpaka*] arising from a qualification containing a simile (*aupamya*), because it lacks the status of being an independent subject. For example:
"Autumn triumphs most exceedingly—she who possesses the lovely beauty of the stainless sky, in whom a few stars are revealed, and who is adorned with a necklace of swans."

In this case, the *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning) is indeed evoked by the double-entendre (*śliṣṭa*) adjectives occurring in the first half; it is then approved by the fool who follows it, just as a logical argument (*yukti*) formulated by a wise man in the second half—containing adjectives pregnant with comparison—is approved by a fool following him. This is so when the first half is composed as: "She bestows joy upon all, wearing a garland of blossoming blue lotuses. Here, the figure is evoked solely by the purely common (*śuddhasādhāraṇa*) adjectives.
With eyes like full-blown lotuses, smiling with the beauty of moonlight,
and adorned with a necklace of rows of swans, the autumn season reigns supreme.

In this case, since there is neither a probans nor a sublater for either the simile (*upamā*) or the metaphor (*rūpaka*), according to the school that accepts the figure of *saṃkara* (commixture), there is indeed the figure of *saṃkara* consisting of doubt regarding both, which is "partially manifest" (*ekadeśavivartin*). However, according to the school that does not accept it, when the *upamitasamāsa* (compound of comparison) presents itself, there is a "partially manifest" simile;

and when the *viśeṣaṇasamāsa* (attributive compound) presents itself, there is likewise a metaphor. Since the non-contextual meaning is understood through the first interpretation alone, the second interpretation—which contains a simile such as "the eyes are like full-blown lotuses"—is redundant and thus fails to arise at all.

However, when the fourth quarter is composed as "babhau śaradvarṣāsakhī" (she shone like a friend of the autumn rains), then, because the status of being a "friend of the rains" applies only to autumn, an *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison) must necessarily be employed—having lotuses, moonlight, and swans as its primary elements. Consequently, the comparison is sustained solely by the simile that first appeared [in the first quarter], which has the beloved woman (implied by the "swan-like eyes") as its object of comparison; for this very reason, it is a case of *ekadeśavivartinī* (partial metaphorical) simile. This point, though already established, is restated here for the pleasure of the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*), as it is stated in the *Rasagaṅgādhara*.

This superimposition (samāropa) occurs in four ways: of a worldly thing upon a worldly thing, of a scriptural thing upon a scriptural thing, of a scriptural thing upon a worldly thing, or of a worldly thing upon a scriptural thing. Among these, although the first was already illustrated previously, it is illustrated again here for the sake of clarifying the understanding of those with dull intellects.
Just as the army of your enemies, shedding blood from the agitation of a wound, became distressed, loathsome, withered, and filled with great uncertainty because of the scion of Raghu.

O descendant of Raghu! [The word] *asram*—meaning tears or hair—is used in the singular by virtue of the genus (*jāti*). It refers to the agitation caused by the *pradara*—which, in one sense, means a piercing arrow, a breaking, or a rout; and in another sense, refers to the agitation caused by *pradara*, a specific female disease characterized by the flow of blood. As Amara states: "The words *pradara*, *bhaṅga*, *nārī-ruk*, and *bāṇa* [share the same meaning]. And Medinī states: "The word *pradara* may denote a type of disease, a fissure, or the breaking of an arrow. *(Note: The term *pradara* is a pun, functioning both as a weapon/act of destruction and as a medical condition.)*

Elsewhere, "rudhira" means blood; the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *asra* is masculine when it refers to a corner or hair, and neuter when it refers to tears or blood. "Pramuñcamānā" means emitting or shedding. The root *muc* is marked with the *svarita* accent; hence the suffix *śānac*. In one sense, the meaning is that she has disheveled hair due to being weeping from the distress caused by either the tearing [of her body] or the breaking of her arrows; in the other sense, it means she is bleeding from a particular disease.

She was pained, tormented, loathsome, and deformed—serving as the objective basis for the sentiment of disgust (*bībhatsa-rasa*), according to Amara’s definition: "The words *bībhatsa* and *vikṛta* have these two meanings in the three genders. She was seized by excessive doubt (*ativicikitsā*), meaning she had fallen into a state where her very life was in peril. In the alternative sense, she was one whose medical treatment (*cikitsā*) for her ailment had ceased; thus, being characterized by excessive doubt (*ativicikitsā*), she was utterly distressed by the lack of remedies for her intense illness. Furthermore, she became withered, her joy having faded away.
In this context, regarding the subject at hand—the activity of the army of enemies struck down by the Blessed One—there is the superimposition of the activities of worldly women afflicted by disease.

In the context of scriptural practice, by means of superimposing scriptural practice upon it according to the literal injunctions, [the Veda] is a mantra-attainer that joins together various root-meaning explanatory passages (arthavādas). O Acyuta, you have certainly known that this is the eternal Dharma of the wise.

O Acyuta! By one who has "heard the injunction"—that is, by one who has heard and understood the injunction traditionally taught as "He is to be seen, He is to be meditated upon"—and for that very reason, by one who is "mantric," meaning possessed of the habit of reflection; for "reflection" (manana) consists of contemplating through logical reasoning, "It is exactly thus," in order to establish the meaning of what has been heard.

"By the one who reconciles the various discourses concerning the fundamental meaning"—this is the analysis [of the compound]: "various" (nānā) means manifold in the manner that will be described; "fundamental meaning" (mūlārtha) is a *karmadhāraya* compound, where "root" (*mūla*) refers to the primary cause, and "meaning" (*artha*)—according to Amara's lexicon—"is used for the first [cause], a root, an object, wealth, purpose, and explanation"; thus, it refers to the reality in the form of the cause of the universe, which was declared as the object of meditation in the passage, "But the Cause is to be meditated upon. The term "discourses" (*vādāḥ*) refers to the various doctrines regarding that subject, and the compound is formed with a genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Amara states: "Root (*mūla*) is used for the first [cause] and a fibrous root (*śiphā*); meaning (*artha*) is used for the denoted object, wealth, purpose, and explanation."

In passages such as, “O dear one, all these actions have their root in Being, they have That as their root; when one is weary of the root of roots,” the word *mūla* (root) is employed in the sense of a cause. The underlying point is this: since various types of causal statements—such as “In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone”; “In the beginning, Brahman alone was this”; “In the beginning, the Self alone was this”; “Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning”; and “Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone existed”—must necessarily have a single referent, [the principle of] the goat (*chāga*)... [is applied].

According to the principle stated as "on account of the wording of the mantra," general terms such as *sat*, *brahman*, *ātman*, *hiraṇyagarbha*, and *śiva* are made to terminate in the specific form of Nārāyaṇa, based on the Śruti passage: "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed. [The word] *āptrā* means "by the attainer. By this, the state of being the attainer of the Supreme, mentioned in the passage "the knower of Brahman attains [It]," is made manifest. For the knower, it is said: "Two sciences are to be known: the higher and the lower."

O Great Sage, it has been stated that both knowledge and action are the causes for attaining that [liberation]. Knowledge is likewise said to be twofold: that arising from scripture and that arising from discernment.
The Brahman of Sound consists of scripture; the Supreme Brahman is born of discernment.

The meaning here is "by one possessing knowledge arising from the scriptures mentioned therein," because the knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*), which is supported by the seven means beginning with discrimination (*viveka*), will be explained separately later. "Sanātana" means eternal; "dharma" refers to the nature of perfected duty. For dharma is indeed the means to supermundane well-being (*alaukika-śreyaḥ*). And that [dharma] is twofold, distinguished as "perfected" (*siddha*) and "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). The application of the word "dharma" to a perfected entity is also seen in the *Mahābhārata*, as for example:
"Those Brahmins who know the Vedas and those people who know the supreme self (*adhyātma*)—they call the Great-Souled Kṛṣṇa the eternal Dharma."

The meaning is that You are the one who has become the perfected means (*siddhopāya*). "That You" refers to You as the object to be attained (*prāpyarūpa*). "It was known" (*avedi*) means You were meditated upon (*upāsya*) in such a way that [the knowledge] was certain and unshakable by other arguments; for in the *Āvṛttyadhikaraṇa*, it has been stated that the terms "knowing" (*vidi*) and "meditating" (*upāsi*) have the same meaning. Meditation (*upāsana*) is defined as a form of contemplation (*dhyāna*) that is uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, which acquires excellence through daily practice, which takes the form of love, and which is identical in character to direct perception (*darśana*). By this, the sense of the scriptural injunction "He is to be seen, He is to be meditated upon" (*draṣṭavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) is followed.

"In the [relevant] context, the injunctions heard—those injunctions which are divided into the categories of *apūrva* (original), *niyama* (restrictive), and *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive)—are such by whom; that is to say, by one who has a thorough knowledge of the nature of such injunctions. Among these, that injunction which brings about an object that is absolutely unestablished is an *apūrvavidhi*. As it has been said: 'An injunction [is operative] when there is absolute non-attainment [of the object]'."

For example, in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), regarding the injunction "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*): in the absence of this injunction, the sprinkling would not apply to the rice-grains used in the New and Full Moon sacrifices by any means whatsoever. However, when this injunction exists, the sprinkling certainly applies to those grains. Because it brings about a sprinkling that was absolutely unestablished (*atyantāprāpta*), this is an *apūrvavidhi* (an original injunction). An injunction that restricts an object already established as an alternative option is a *niyamavidhi* (a restrictive injunction), as it is said: "A restriction (*niyama*) occurs when there is an option (*pākṣika*)."

For example, in that very context, there is the injunction: "One threshes the rice. In the absence of this injunction, regarding the rice used in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one might occasionally resort even to scratching with the fingernails—just as threshing is performed for the purpose of producing the dehusking (vaituṣya) that is conducive to the preparation of rice grains for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), as understood from the originative statement (utpattivākya)—rather than threshing alone. In that case, since threshing would not necessarily be obtained, the performance of threshing would be merely occasional (pākṣikī prāptiḥ) due to the impossibility of otherwise accomplishing the required purpose.

And since this rule exists—that dehusking must be accomplished by threshing alone—threshing is excluded by implication; thus, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). An injunction whose fruit is the exclusion of one alternative when both are obtained through simultaneous application is an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*). As it is said: "An exclusive injunction is proclaimed [to apply] when [an action] is obtained both there and elsewhere."

Just as in the section on the *cayana* sacrifice, there is an injunction for a mantra—namely, "imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya" (They have grasped this rein of Order)—as an auxiliary to the taking of the horse’s bridle: "He takes the horse’s bridle with [the mantra] 'imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya'. For in the absence of this injunction, the mantra, which reveals the act of grasping a rein, would necessarily apply to the taking of both the horse’s bridle and the donkey’s bridle due to its *liṅga* (indicative power), namely its capacity to reveal the act of taking a rein. But when this injunction exists, one should take the horse’s bridle specifically with this mantra.

But it is not the donkey’s rope; rather, that [rope] is to be grasped in silence. Thus, since there is a possibility of both [the mantra and the silent grasping] being combined, this is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) whose fruit is the exclusion of the other. This is the summary. Let us return to the subject at hand: "attained by means of the mantras. The meaning is: attained (*āpta*) by the mantras, i.e., understood through those mantras. The compound is to be analyzed as before. Mantras are those which cause one to remember the objects associated with the ritual performance.

And their purposefulness consists solely in their being reminders of such meanings; however, their recitation is not for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), because when a visible fruit is possible, it is improper to postulate an unseen fruit. Nor should it be argued that the recitation of mantras is useless since the visible remembrance of meaning can occur through other means as well; for one must resort to a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that "the meaning must be remembered by means of the mantras alone."

"By one who synthesizes explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) based on various roots" means by one who, having joined the explanatory passages—that is, the sentences of explanatory passages—which have various roots and many causes, with the injunctive sentences (*vidhi-vākya*) as a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), thereby establishing them as authoritative (*pramāṇa*). An *arthavāda* is a sentence intended for either praise (*prāśastya*) or censure (*nindā*); its purposeful meaning is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For instance, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—since there is no purpose in conveying its own literal meaning—conveys by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) the excellence or the lack thereof in that which is to be enjoined or prohibited; for if it were restricted to its own literal meaning alone, it would result in pointlessness, since the Veda has action as its purpose.

Nor is this an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the injunction for study, "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied," establishes that the study of the entire Veda is a duty; and since it indicates that the whole Veda culminates in a purposeful meaning, its inclusion [in the canon] precludes the possibility of its being meaningless. Furthermore, that [meaning] is of two kinds: that which is supplementary to an injunction (*vidhi-śeṣa*) and that which is supplementary to a prohibition (*niṣedha-śeṣa*).

In this context, a passage such as “Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity,” which is supplementary to the injunction “One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu,” possesses purposefulness by making known the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the matter to be enjoined. A passage such as “He wept; because he wept, that is the origin of Rudra’s name ‘Rudra,’” which is supplementary to the prohibition “Silver must not be given on the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),” possesses purposefulness by making known the censurability of the prohibited object.

Nor should it be argued that the arthavāda lacks purposefulness because the communication of praise and so forth serves no practical aim; for such communication is useful as it generates activity and the like in a person who might otherwise fail to act due to laziness or other causes. Furthermore, that [arthavāda] is threefold. As it has been said: "In case of contradiction, it is a figurative statement (guṇavāda); when [the fact] is already established, it is a restatement (anuvāda); and when those [two conditions] are absent, it is a statement of fact (bhūtārthavāda). Thus, arthavāda is considered to be of three kinds."

This is the meaning: when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is a figurative description (*guṇavāda*). For example, "The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the sun" and so forth. Since the identity of the sun with the sacrificial post is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this statement conveys—by way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—the quality of being as radiant as the sun. A restatement (*anuvāda*) is that which makes known an object already understood through another means of valid cognition. For example, "Fire is the remedy for cold. Here, the fact that fire is opposed to cold is already understood through direct perception.

A *bhūtārthavāda* (a statement of an existing fact) is a discourse that conveys a meaning not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and which does not result in the attainment [of some further goal]. An example is: "Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra," and so forth. Enough of this digression following upon a digression. A wise person—one who knows the injunctions (*vidhi*), the mantras, and the *arthavādas*—should understand that this is the eternal Dharma, as it has been handed down through the tradition of the Śruti, Smṛti, and other sources, according to the maxim: "This is the eternal Dharma."

Dharma is that which has the nature of being an object to be accomplished; it was known—that is, understood by you—in such a way that it became certain and free from doubt through the principles of Mīmāṃsā. "Dharma" is defined as a purposeful matter propounded by the Veda, and that is specifically sacrifice and the like. The term "purposeful" is used to exclude over-extension to the [mere] purpose itself. The term "propounded by the Veda" is used to exclude over-extension to eating and so forth. The term "matter" (artha) is used to exclude over-extension to acts such as the Śyena sacrifice, which, because they result in harmful consequences, are themselves non-matters (anartha).

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the definition of Dharma given in the Sūtra, "Dharma is a purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo ’rtho dharmaḥ*), because the word *codanā* refers only to that portion of the Veda consisting of injunctions. For even there, the word *codanā* refers to the Veda as a whole; since the entire Veda possesses the purport of Dharma, it is the means for the comprehension of Dharma. Enough of this elaboration. Here, in the context of the present discourse belonging to the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* Śāstra, there is a superimposition of the discourse belonging to the *Karma-mīmāṃsā* Śāstra, which is not under discussion.
Or rather, O Blessed One, although many qualities were previously attributed to you even before [attaining realization], elsewhere it is not possible to attribute even a single quality. (744)

O Blessed One! This [title] contains the intention that He possesses the fullness of the qualities to be described hereafter. *Pūrva* means before creation; *aprāpta* means having reached the waters (*apaḥ*). In that which is thus stated, there is a compound according to the rule beginning with "dependent on a second case" (*dvitīyāśrita*), meaning "lying upon the water of the great ocean. This is supported by such authorities as: "The seers worship Him within the ocean," and "Lying in the great ocean, in the waters. By this, it is said:
"The waters are called *nārāḥ*; the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara.
Since they were His abode (*ayana*) in the beginning, He is remembered as Nārāyaṇa."

Thus, the etymological derivation of the word *Nārāyaṇa* as stated in the Smṛti has been shown. By this, the causality mentioned in the Śruti—“In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; neither Brahmā nor Īśāna, nor these two, heaven and earth”—is also established. The sense is that in You alone is the supreme [state]; and although there are many, even innumerable, auspicious qualities conducive to causality—such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), omnipotence (*sarvaśaktitva*), and so forth—they are ordained by such Śruti passages as “He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving.”

But in any other deity besides You, it is impossible to enjoin even a single quality, let alone many; for not even a single auspicious quality of the aforementioned kind is mentioned regarding other deities by even a single scriptural passage—this is the intended meaning.

It should be understood that by this, the very point stated in the previous verse—that words such as *Hiraṇyagarbha* and *Śiva*, which are composed of causal statements, refer exclusively to Nārāyaṇa through some partial etymological power (*avayava-śakti*), conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), or the function of non-literal extension (*paryavasāna-vṛtti*) according to the logic of the *aindrī* mantra—has been further stabilized by the analogy of "driving in a pillar" (*sthūṇānikhana-nyāya*).
When a ritual action has already been established elsewhere, it is not possible to enjoin more than one accessory;
however, when it is not so established, even many accessories may be enjoined with a single effort.

Thus, the meaning of the first and second halves of the Mīmāṃsaka kārikā has been described in reverse order relative to the latter and former halves of this verse. To explain: prior to the injunction of the qualities (*guṇavidhāna*), that is, before an action (*karman*) has been established by another scriptural authority (*śāstrāntara*) as being otherwise unestablished (*aprāpta*), there occurs here the optional doubling (*vaikalpikaṃ dvitvam*) of the letter *pa* containing the letter *ra*, according to the rule *anaci ca*. Furthermore, many qualities (*bahavo’pi guṇāḥ*), which are subordinate meanings (*apradhānabhūtā arthāḥ*), are enjoined—that is, they become prescribed—by means of a single effort alone (*ekayatnenaiva*).

And thus says the Sūtra: "But those [qualities] should be enjoined for it, because there is no division [of the action], provided they are taught by another [text] for the purpose of enjoining [them]. However, when an action has already been established elsewhere, it is not possible to enjoin multiple qualities [for it].

For this very reason, with reference to the passage, “Curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain, water, and rice—these mixed together constitute the *prājāpatya*,” the statement “one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā*” is an injunction of two qualities—variegatedness (*citrātva*) and femininity (*strītva*)—by way of restating a rite already established by another means of knowledge; thus, because there would otherwise be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the word *citrayā* is a name (*nāmadheya*). This is unlike the case of the passage, “When there is the *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds, which is never omitted on the new-moon and full-moon days,” where the rite is not already established by another means of knowledge.

It has been established in the authoritative treatises (*ākaras*) that a sacrifice—characterized by multiple qualities such as a single deity and a cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*), and occurring on the new moon or full moon days—is enjoined as inferred through the relationship between the substance and the deity; thus, because this is an injunction of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭakarman*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This principle should be understood to apply elsewhere as well; this is the summary. Here too, just as before, a scriptural convention is superimposed upon a non-scriptural usage.

Or rather, may Brahman grant victory—He through whose very presence even the unprecedented instruments and other factors attain their capacity, and whom the gods, such as the Sun and others, follow. (745)

*Apūrva* means that which is devoid of any other cause, in accordance with the statement "And there is no creator of this [Brahman]"; it is the cause of all effects, as per the statement "The cause is prior. May that Lord Brahman be victorious! By the *anvaya*—that is, by the impulsion—of that Brahman, even the *karaṇas*, such as the sense organs (the word *ādi* including the vital breaths and so forth), attain their capacity for their respective objects and functions. As it is said: "By whom impelled does the mind fly forth? By whom sent does the first breath proceed? (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.3).
By whom impelled do they utter this speech? And which god yokes the eye and the ear?
Thus, regarding the inquiry into the nature of the Supreme Brahman:

"That which is the hearer of the ear, the thinker of the mind, the speaker of speech, and the breath of the breath—that is the eye of the eye. Having transcended these, the wise, departing from this world, become immortal.

Thus, the Śruti in its affirmative form is here kept in mind: "The gods, such as Prabhākara and others, headed by Sūrya, are his followers"—that is to say, they do not transgress his command. This is known from such scriptural passages as: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable One, the sun and the moon stand held apart; through fear of him the wind blows, and through fear of him the sun rises."

In this context, *apūrva* refers to a certain entity accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas. Once it is understood through their respective scriptural injunctions and prohibitions that specific prescribed and forbidden actions are the means for attaining their respective fruits, they postulate an intermediate entity called *apūrva*—also known as the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)—which consists of merit and demerit. This is necessary to explain how actions that perish instantly can serve as the means for producing fruits that occur at a later time. This *apūrva* is of various kinds, such as the "originative *apūrva*" (*utpattyapūrva*), the "fruit *apūrva*" (*phalāpūrva*), and so forth.

This applies even to the collection of words denoting *kārakas* (factors of action), such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth, which is defined by the rule "the most effective means is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*). It is precisely because they are connected with that *apūrva*—that is, because they are already associated with it—that they attain their capacity and their primary meaning. For, since these words denote what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitva*), the primary meaning of words denoting *kārakas*—which denote what is connected to the unique effect (*apūrva-kārya*)—is indeed that which is connected to it; they maintain that if one abandons this connection, there is merely figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The "Prabhākaras and others" refers to those scholars and wise men whose leader is the foremost of tantric masters named Prabhākara; they are called "those who follow him" because they follow that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*), meaning they are devoted to the exposition of the unprecedented. Here too, as before, there is a superimposition of conventional usage.

Or rather, O Blessed One, it was surely by you alone that the glory of the arrival of Umā was firmly established as half the body of Mṛtyuñjaya, through the analysis of various words, names, and forms. O Blessed One! By him who is so described—namely, one who performs (*vyākaraṇam*) the analysis (*vibhāgaḥ*) of various words (*padānām*), things, and of names and forms (*nāmarūpayoḥ*), such as the diverse creations consisting of the designations of gods and so forth—as stated in the Vedic scripture: "Entering with this living self, let me manifest names and forms. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

By you alone was the glorious union with Umā—the Goddess Gaurī—most excellently established as the half-body within the half-body of the Pināka-wielder, the Conqueror of Death. The sense is this: who else indeed, apart from you, the creator of the manifold world of names and forms, could have fashioned the status of being the half-woman for the Enemy of Tripura?

"By one who has spoken thus": [this refers to] the grammarian who provides the grammatical analysis—the explanation of stems, suffixes, and so forth—of the various forms of words other than those consisting of nominal bases ending in *kṛt* suffixes, as well as nouns consisting of nominal and verbal endings (*suptiṅanta*). "In the half-portion of the word *Mṛtyuñjaya*": since that word consists of four syllables, two syllables constitute its half-portion; the meaning is: "in the latter part of the first two syllables."

The sense is that [the word] is exceedingly and excessively delightful because it achieves softness in pronunciation. Regarding the *mum*-augment: the meaning is that the augment *mum*—in the form of the suffix *mum*—is applied by the rule "after *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, *vṛj*, etc., when a *saṃjñā* is to be formed" (*saṃjñāyāṃ bhṛtṛvṛji*), followed by the rule "the augment *mum* is added to a word ending in *aru*, *dviṣat*, or a consonant" (*arudviṣadajantasya mum*). It was "performed" (*vyadhīyata*), i.e., prescribed. Here, within the context under discussion—the discourse of the Vedānta system—there is the superimposition of the discourse of the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), which is not the subject at hand.

Or rather, just as the verb is predominant in its expression of successful action by which the universe is governed, so too, O All-pervading Lord, your names shine forth, bearing the predominance of pure being (sattva).

O All-pervading Lord! By You—who were heard [in scripture] as the one who sets beings in motion with the words "He is the impeller of beings"—the entire universe (*viśvam*), whose primary focus is virtuous action (*sādhukriyāpradhānakam*)—that is, that which has excellent deeds as its principal duty to be performed—was instructed, characterized, and, in short, brought back to life. Or rather, it should be construed as: "it was instructed in such a way that virtuous action became its primary focus."

The meaning is that this has been declared and established by the aforementioned method through such scriptural passages as: "For He alone causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds. Other scriptures such as "This entire universe is indeed the Puruṣa; He lives upon that universe; He is the Lord of the universe" should also be considered here. Of You, who govern the universe in the manner described, the names—that is, the designations—possess *sattva-pradhānatām*, which means the predominance of the quality of *sattva* (purity), or rather, the fact that they have *sattva* as the basis for their application.

The meaning is that [the name] is derived from reciting the *Sahasranāma* as "the one possessing *sattva*, the *sāttvika*. Alternatively, *sattva* is the state of being (*sat*), and [the name refers to those] who possess its predominance, because it is recited in that very same text: "Being and non-being, the perishable and the imperishable" (*sadasatkṣaramakṣaram*). And because it is said: "The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*. Regarding the form *dadhati*, there is an absence of the *num* augment due to its optionality by the rule "vā napuṃsakasya. They shine forth.

Alternatively, according to the aforementioned method, the meaning is that the divine names of You, the ruler of all worlds, flourish—that is, they shine forth—nurturing the quality of sattva in those people who proclaim them as their creators.

In this context, it is understood that by Yāska [it was taught]: "The entire *ākhyāta*—that is, the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) whose primary element is action—has been correctly instructed so that it may be grammatically sound. In examples such as "Devadatta cooks rice," the verbal understanding (*śābdabodha*) takes the form: "Cooking which has Devadatta as its agent and rice as its object. Thus, the primacy of action in the *ākhyāta* is what was instructed by him in the rule: "The *ākhyāta* has action as its primary element" (*bhāvapradhānamākhyātam*). Here, *bhāva* means action (*kriyā*). And they say:
"The verbal root (*dhātu*) is traditionally held to denote both the result and the operation; however, the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) are remembered to denote the locus (the substratum).
The result is the primary [meaning], while the operation is subordinate; but the meaning of the verbal suffix itself is the qualifier."

Thus, it is understood that this refers to Yāska. Names—namely nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in *kṛt* suffixes and so forth—are "predominantly substance" (*sattvapradhāna*), meaning they shine as having substance (*dravya*) as their primary referent. The sense is that in the cognition of a name such as "cook" (*pācaka*), there is a predominance of substance in the form of "the locus of cooking" (*pākāśraya*), because he [Yāska] has taught that "names are predominantly substance. Here too, in the context under discussion—the discourse of the Vedānta system—there is a superimposition of the discourse of the unrelated science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*).

O Protector, even when one who has committed evil deeds becomes truly devoted—just as you recognize a doer of good—you, being well-disposed, manifest yourself before him, appearing not in your own form but in a likeness of yourself. (748)

O Lord! You are a "doer of evil" (*pāpakārī*) because you perform evil even for one who performs evil; this term is formed with the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action according to the rule *supyajātau*. You are a "doer of good" (*sādhukārī*), a performer of virtuous deeds, because you make a person who worships you well—meaning one who worships you perfectly with undivided devotion—good; here too, the suffix *ṇini* is applied as before.

Knowing that which is equal to that—namely, that one who acts rightly becomes good and one who acts wickedly becomes evil—the Śruti is reaffirmed by the two terms "one who acts rightly" and "one who acts wickedly. Recognizing that even a man who has previously been a doer of evil, if he devotes himself properly to Me, is like one who acts rightly: "Even if a person of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion, he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved."

The sense is: because it was sung by him himself. You shall extend that protection to that man who is "without conflict with his own feet"—that is to say, he for whom no conflict (vigraha), meaning quarrel or dispute, exists with his own two feet [the Ganges].
As it is said: "O King Vaivasvata Yama, if you have no dispute with him who resides in your heart, then let him go neither to the Gaṅgā nor to the Kurus."

The meaning is: "In the manner described, cause him to be without dispute with You Yourself, who are the inner controller of all and the Lord of all. Here, the dispute between the individual self (pratyagātman) and the Blessed Lord—expressed in the manner of "You are mine" and "I am mine"—is stated figuratively (*aupacārika*) in those two words for the purpose of demonstrating His greatness, as in the expression "favor of the feet" (*caraṇānugraha*). It should be understood that in this cited statement, the terms "Yama," "Avivastrata," and "Rāja" refer to the Blessed Lord; however, the word "non-dispute" (*avivāda*) refers to the entrusting of the burden of protecting the self to His feet. This has been explained by Varadaguru as follows: [text follows].
In this matter, the Lord of the Southern Quarter does not hold the primary place in my heart;
for he who has entered within is the Teacher who even restrains all people.

Remaining within himself, he dwells in the heart of that Death-of-Death; by surrendering his very self at the feet of that sovereign lord of all, who resides within the solar orb, he remains free from dispute.

Thus, the sense is: "May You place the burden of protecting my self upon Your own lotus-feet. Now, after thus entrusting the burden of self-protection—meaning immediately at that moment when distress is excessive; or, if one is arrogant, at the end of that body—the meaning is: "You make that surrendered soul like Yourself," that is, You cause them to attain supreme equality in accordance with the teaching, "The stainless one attains the highest equality. Intending to state the reason for what has been said, He says: "sumanāḥ" (well-disposed), meaning one whose great and noble mind is filled with compassion.

In this context, *sumanāḥ* means "learned. Knowing that the word *subhajantam* is like the word *sādhukārī*—that is, equivalent to the term for one who performs good deeds—you construct it as having no analysis of its own constituent parts (*asvapadavigraha*), being devoid of an analysis involving all the words that compose it. This is because the formation of compounds for the words *pāpakārī* and *sādhukārī* is prescribed by the rule *upapadamatiṅ*, while the formation of the word *subhajantam* is prescribed by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*.

Furthermore, because of the recurrence of the word "nityam" (always) from the rule *nityaṃ krīḍā*, the compound prescribed by that rule is obligatory (*nitya*). For this very reason, there is no analysis using its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*), as it is stated: "An obligatory compound is either without analysis (*avigraha*) or has an analysis not using its own words (*asvapadavigraha*). Analysis (*vigraha*) is defined as the presentation of the compounded words in their separated form, according to the statement: "That which is grasped by being divided is proclaimed as analysis (*vigraha*)," and according to the *Ratnamālā*: "Analysis (*vigraha*) [occurs] in battle, in the body, and also in expansion."

The construction is: "you expand [the compound] *svanibham* and *svanibhaśabdam*, which do not have their own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). The sense is that this too is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*). This is because of the grammatical rule: "These [terms] occur when they are the final member of a compound (*uttarapade*): *nibha*, *saṃkāśa*, *nīkāśa*, *pratīkāśa*, *upama*, and so forth. Since the rule teaches that the word *nibha* has the meaning of "equal to" only when it functions as the final member of a compound, and since the term *uttarapada* is conventionally used for the final constituent of a compound, here too—as before—there is a superimposition of conventional usage.

Just as, in this world, a quality that is beautiful due to its renown in the scriptures shines forth incessantly beyond [the object], so too for this wise man who abides not at the end of a word, the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) form occurs. (749)

In the scriptures, such as the *Aupaniṣada* and *Dahara-vidyā*, there is well-known renown (*prasiddhi*) for His auspicious and delightful qualities, as stated in the Śruti: "Free from evil, ageless, deathless, a mass of pure consciousness," and so forth; [the singular number] is used here with reference to the genus (*jāti*). "From the Supreme" (*parataḥ*) means from that which is beyond, from Nārāyaṇa who is denoted by the syllable *A*, according to the statement: "The syllable *A* is the primary designation of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa. This means from the Supreme Brahman, or rather, through His grace.

When [the Self] shines forth without interval—that is, unimpeded through the complete cessation of all ignorance—then [it shines]. Alternatively, "ataḥparataḥ" may be understood as having the sense of the genitive case; the suffix *tasi* is used here to denote any case ending. Thus, the construction is: "in the quality of that which is beyond this," namely, in the quality of the Supreme Brahman. The meaning is: "in the divine qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth. "Shines forth without interval" means while [these qualities] are eternally manifest.

The "pada" (abode) of this Nārāyaṇa—who is denoted by the letter 'a' and whose state of being resides at the end of the word "apada"—is the station traditionally taught as "that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Within that, or in its midst, is the indeclinable [word] ending in the letter 'r', which primarily possesses the power of the locative case.

For this wise knower of Brahman, who abides in that state and whose qualities of Brahman have been manifested through the grace of the Supreme Brahman, there arises—that is, he attains—the supreme form, which is the form of the Supreme Brahman; that is to say, the "supreme equality" mentioned in the scripture: "The stainless one attains the highest equality. In this regard, the meaning of the *Brāhma-adhikaraṇa* located in the *Phala-adhyāya* (the fourth chapter) should be kept in mind.

In this regard, concerning the doubt as to whether that which is described as "attaining manifestation in its own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*) consists solely of qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), or solely of knowledge, or both—since qualities such as freedom from sin are mentioned with reference to the liberated soul, Jaimini’s view is restated by the Sūtra: "By his [own] form, according to Jaimini, because of the introductory passages and so forth" (*brāhmeṇa jaiminirupanyāsādibhyaḥ*). However, since texts such as "He is indeed a mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana eva*) lead to the understanding that his essential nature is knowledge alone, [the conclusion follows].

Furthermore, because terms such as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*) refer to the absence of sorrow and so forth, [the soul] manifests with the nature of pure consciousness alone. Having thus presented the view of Auḍulomi in the sūtra, "It manifests by means of pure consciousness, because its essence is that [consciousness]," [the author] rejects both positions on the grounds that each contradicts one of the scriptural texts. Since the restrictive statement, "It is indeed a mass of consciousness," aims to dispel the suspicion of partial insentience rather than to exclude other attributes, [the soul] manifests in both forms. Thus, the sūtra, "Even so, because of the mention [of both], and because of the prior state, there is no contradiction—Bādarāyaṇa [thinks this]" (BS 4.4.5), refutes both views.

In this alternative view (*pakṣe*), when there exists subsequently after a short vowel (*hrasvākārāt*) another letter—a sound well-known in the treatises (*śāstraprasiddhyā*) or established in the science of grammar (*śabdavidyāprasiddhyā*)—namely, a "fortunate" (*subhaga*) phoneme termed a *guṇa* beginning with the vowel *a*, and when that [short vowel] shines forth without interval (*nirantaram*) in *saṃhitā* (i.e., appearing without separation), then a word (*padam*) consisting of a nominal or verbal suffix (*suptiṅanta-ātmakam*) does not have its end (*antaḥ*)—the final portion (*caramabhāgaḥ*)—at that point; thus it is "not at the end of a word" (*apadantaḥ*). In that which is distinct from the end of a word (*padāntabhinnē*), there resides this [short vowel] previously mentioned as the limit (*avadhi*) for *guṇa*.

The meaning is that the *pararūpa* (subsequent form) of the short vowel—that is, the form of the subsequent phoneme designated as a *guṇa*—is the single substitute (*ekādeśa*). One should understand the sense according to the grammatical procedure stated in the sūtra "ato guṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.97). Here too, the superimposition is exactly as before.
Or just as,

in this world, even one who is dull-witted, though he may be like an ox following the path of the virtuous, becomes an object of Your vision— you establish him at the end of Your own state as a wise man and a destroyer of evil.

A man who, like an ox (*anaḍvān*) or a bull, is devoid of consciousness (*acit*)—lacking knowledge (as Amara states: *citsaṃvitpratipadjñapticetanāḥ*), and as it is said, "one devoid of knowledge is equal to beasts"—and thus falls away from the path of the virtuous (*sanmārgasrad*), may nevertheless become the object of Your glance, that is, Your side-long look, by virtue of some accidental merit; this is the sense. The word "may he be" (*bhavet*) is to be supplied.

That man is "tamed" (*damita*) or "self-controlled" (*dānta*). From the root *dam* (meaning "to pacify") with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *kta* is applied; because the rule "optionally *dānta*" (*vā dānta*) is optional, the augment *iṭ* appears in one alternative. Amara states: "But *dānta* means tamed. According to the expression "peaceful and self-controlled," the meaning is that he is endowed with the means of accomplishment.

Now, [the Lord] dwells upon the wise knower of Brahman; for this very reason, he is called *aghadhvas*, meaning "the destroyer of evil" (*agha*)—that is, he destroys both future and past evils consisting of merit and demerit. The sense is that he is one whose future and past evils have been rendered non-adherent and destroyed, according to the established principle stated in the aphorism: "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-clinging and destruction of future and past evils, because of the scriptural declaration thereof. The form *aghadhvas* is derived from the root *dhvaṃs* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the *kvip* suffix, resulting in the elision of the *ṇic* by the rule *ṇer aniṭi*.

By these two verses, "vidvāṃsamaghadhvasam" and so forth, the meaning of the scriptural passage, "Then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin," is explained. The sense is that You place [the devotee] at the end of Your own abode, in the midst of Your supreme state, or in the proximity of Your own feet.

In this context, the word *acit* is derived from the root *cit* (meaning "to perceive" or "to know") with the suffix *kvip*, following the rule for the *saṃpadādi* group; thus, this word *cit* ends in *-t*. From that, the negative compound *nañ* is formed. That which exists like the word *anaḍvān* (ox)—namely, the word *sanmārgasraḥ*—becomes the object (*viṣaya*) or range (*gocara*) of your vision or knowledge. [O Lord,] place at the end of Your own feet that one who is like the word *anaḍvān*, namely the learned man (*vidvān*) whose name is like the word *vidvat*, and the destroyer of sin (*aghadhvaṃs*), whose name is like the word *aghadhvac*.

Regarding the word *svasvarūpa*, which possesses the technical designation *pada* as prescribed by the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne*: at its end—that is, in the final phoneme consisting of *t*, *h*, or *s*—you ordain *daṃ*, meaning the substitution of *d* for *t* and so forth. This is because, in the case of the word *aci* ending in *t* at the end of a *pada*, the substitution of *d* is ordained by the rule *jhalāṃ jaśo’nte*; and in the case of words such as *anaḍut*, the substitution of *d* is ordained at the end of a *pada* by the rule *vasusraṃsudhvaṃsvanaḍuhāṃ daḥ*.
The intention is that this is because it is prescribed as such. Here too, as before, there is a superimposition of scriptural usage upon a non-scriptural usage.

Or rather, does not Hari himself assume the nature of a pronoun through internal and external connection? For among the wise, when establishing a system, he is known as both "prior" and "subsequent" when not used as a proper name. (751)

This Hari himself is the Inner Controller (*antara*); according to the manner stated in such passages as “He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth,” he is by nature one whose mode of being is to pervade from within as the Inner Controller. Through external connection—that is, through external pervasion—he possesses the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*), meaning the status of being designated by all pronouns; and according to the manner stated in “both within and without, that is all,” because of his all-pervasiveness, he is denotable by the word “all” (*sarva*). This is the meaning.

One attains [this truth]: "Nārāyaṇa is both within and without; Nārāyaṇa alone is all this; the Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be; indeed, all this is Brahman; from every side, he is everything"—such authorities (pramāṇas) should be remembered here. For this very reason, it is recited among his names: "He is Sarva, the All."

Furthermore, "designation" (*saṃjñā*) refers to a convention (*saṃketa*); the meaning is that it is not established by mere convention, but rather by being produced through the very path of the scriptures. This occurs within the "establishment of the wise," which is to say, within the settled position of those who know Brahman.

"Prior" (pūrvaḥ) means that he is the cause of the entire universe according to the manner stated in such passages as, "This is the eternal [nature] of the primordial God, the creator of the world," and he is the supreme (paraḥ), the highest of all, as heard in such scriptural texts as, "The highest of the high, the supreme Great Lord among lords. "Known" (viditaḥ) means understood. Alternatively, [it refers to the verse]: "Brahman indeed is this immortal [reality] in the east; Brahman is behind, Brahman is to the south and to the north."

The meaning is that, according to the manner stated in such passages as, "Brahman alone extends below and above; this entire universe is Brahman, the most excellent," every object perceived in the directions of east, west, and so forth, is known to be this very [Brahman]. It should be understood that here, in the root text, the words "east" (pūrva) and "west" (para) are indicative of all the directions mentioned in the Śruti, such as south, north, and the rest.

In this context, the word *antara*—being internal (*antara*)—attains the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatām*), that is, the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāmasaṃjñām*), because it possesses an external form due to its connection with what is outside. This is understood by the wise (*dhīmatām*), that is, by the learned, in the sense of a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*) distinct from a proper name (*asaṃjñāyām*), which consists of a restriction regarding a limit relative to its own denotation. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the present tense according to the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca*, and the genitive case is employed in connection with it according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*. The construction is as follows: the word *pūrva* and the word *para* attain the status of a pronoun.

In this context as well, it should be understood that the words *pūrva* (prior) and *para* (subsequent) are indicative of the terms *sthāvara*, *dakṣiṇa*, and so forth, which appear in the sūtras to be cited later. The intention is that for the word *antara*, according to the rule *antaraṃ bahiryogopasaṃvyānayoḥ*, its meaning is "external" (*bāhya*); and for the words *pūrva* and *para*, by the rule *pūrvaparāvara*, their status as pronominals (*sarvanāmatā*) is taught when they do not denote a technical name (*asaṃjñā*) and when they signify relative position (*vyavasthā*). Here too, the superimposition (*samāropa*) is exactly as before.

Or rather, just as for you, who have the internal state [of Brahman] as your very self, everything external remains unestablished for us; so too, the postulation of externality for you could never occur in the absence of the "non-born" (ajānantarya). (752)

"O Acyuta! While you are present within our inner mind—that is to say, while we are meditating upon you—all external things, including the collection of limbs such as hands and feet, are 'unestablished' (asiddha). The sense is that because of the absence of cognition directed toward external objects, all the limbs appear as if they do not exist. By this, the one-pointedness of meditation is demonstrated. He states the reason for this with the word 'na': 'No, O Unborn One; immediately,' is the division of the words."

O Aja! O Blessed One! [The term] *aja* refers to Śambhu and Viṣṇu, according to the *Ratnamālā*. "In your state of immediacy" (*ānantarye*) means in that state of being immediate, which signifies inseparability; by implication, this refers to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*). Furthermore, the "postulation of externality" (*bahiṣṭvaklūptiḥ*)—that is, the conceptualization of external existence, or what amounts to separation—can never occur. Therefore, the meaning is that nothing external ever becomes an object of knowledge.

The sense is this: if the mind fixed upon you were to turn outward, then it would be as ineffective as an external means that has not attained perfection. It is with this very intention that the Lord is addressed as “Acyuta” (the Unswerving). For it is etymologically defined thus: “He from whom those who have reached him do not fall away is Acyuta. The meaning is that for anyone whose mind is fixed on the Blessed One, there is no falling away from whatever object [of devotion] they may have.

In this context, the first half [of the verse] demonstrates the *paribhāṣā*: "That which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)," while the second half shows its exception: "There is no application of the status of being external when there is immediate sequence of vowels (*nājānantarye bahiṣṭvapraklṛptiḥ*). The meaning of the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* is that when an internal operation is to be performed, the external one shall be considered as not having taken effect.

The meaning of the *ajānantarya-paribhāṣā* is not that there is no application (*praklṛpti*) or attainment (*prāpti*) of the status of being "unestablished" (*asiddhatva*) caused by the fact of being *bahiraṅga*, when an *antaraṅga* operation is to be performed on account of another immediate cause; for the word *bahiḥ* denotes the *bahiraṅga*, its state is *bahiṣṭva*, which is *bahiraṅgatva*, and it is the non-application of the *asiddhatva* resulting from that which is intended here. The details are elsewhere. Here too, the superimposition is exactly as before.
Or, for example:

O Lord of the worlds, having attained You—the true cause who are renowned for Your pervasiveness, uncontradicted, without rival, and established on the side of the virtuous—the wise accomplish their desired goals. (753)

O Lord! O Blessed One! The wise and intelligent perceive You as one whose affliction—meaning suffering (for *pīḍā*, *bādhā*, *vyathā*, and *duḥkha* are synonyms according to Amara)—is non-existent, owing to Your pervasion (*vyāpti*) as declared by such scriptural texts as “all that is within and without is That. Here, such scriptural passages as “neither old age, nor sorrow, nor death” should be considered. You are without rival, according to the scripture: “Who is worthy to vie with Him?”

One who stands on the side of the virtuous and the wise is called *sādhupakṣastha*; for it is said in scripture, "The man of knowledge is indeed My very Self; that is My opinion, and he is dear to Me. You are the true cause, meaning the cause of the entire universe, according to the manner stated in such passages as "Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning. Having attained You—that is, having worshipped You—people accomplish their desired goals, such as liberation and sovereign powers.

The two words "anyatra" and "sādhu-pakṣastham" [are explained as follows]. "Jagatām-īśa" is an address. "Vyāpti" refers to the rule of concomitance well-known through such [formulations] as "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. "Bādha" (sublation) means a subject that possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*). That which does not have this is "abādha" (unsublated).
