"Pratipakṣa" (counter-position) means a subject possessing a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) that establishes the absence of the probandum, which is contrary to one's own probandum. That from which this has departed is "niṣpratipakṣa" (free from counter-position).

The term *pakṣastha* means that which "resides" (*tiṣṭhati*) in the *pakṣa*—that is, in the mountain or other locus possessing the doubtful probandum (*saṃdigdhasādhyavat*). Therefore, the meaning is that they establish desired objects such as fire by "attaining," that is, by knowing, a valid reason (*saddhetu*) such as smoke. In this context, where the discourse of the Vedānta system is under discussion, the superimposition (*āropa*) of the discourse of the Nyāya system—which is not currently under discussion—is the distinction from previous [commentators].

Or rather, as it is said, "Where you are, there is Śrī"—there is a rule of concomitance between you two; and this pervasion (vyāpti), O Acyuta, is established by that [rule], for your Śrī resides in the same locus as you.

"O Acyuta! Wherever you are, there also is Śrī, Lakṣmī. Thus, between the two of you and Śrī, there is a rule of grammatical co-occurrence (*sāhacarya-niyama*) based on the principle "the pronouns beginning with *tyad* [and others] are always retained when combined with all other words," resulting in the retention of the word *yuṣmat* alone. She exists as a celestial being when in a divine body, and as a human being when in a human state;
indeed, she makes her own form conform to the body of Viṣṇu.

The sense is that there exists an invariable concomitance according to the method thus stated. One should also consider such passages as: "This Mother of the World is eternal, the inseparable Śrī of Viṣṇu. And this pervasion is as follows:
"Just as the world is pervaded by me through my own form and nature, so too is all this pervaded by her; likewise, she is the sovereign controller."
Just as she was pervaded by me, so too am I, the Lord, pervaded by her.

Thus, it is connected [to the previous statement] that the pervasion (vyāpti) spoken of in the *Lakṣmītantra* also exists. Therefore, those who belong to the side of the virtuous—those who take the side of the knowers of Brahman—are indeed considered by Me to be My fourfold devotees alone.
Among them, the single-minded (ekāntin) are the best, and they have no other deity.

The sense is that this has been stated by Him Himself; or, it means "one who sides with the virtuous," because of His statement, "The Pāṇḍavas are indeed my very life-breaths. [The phrase] "from you" refers to You, whose fortune never departs. [As it is said:
"O Jātavedas, bring to me the golden Lakṣmī who dwells in the moon;
O Jātavedas, bring to me that Lakṣmī who does not depart."
In which [place] I might find gold, cattle, horses, and men.

The sense is that, according to the manner stated in such passages, all kinds of prosperity—pertaining to this world, the next, and liberation—are accomplished from you alone, who possess great majesty (*mahāvibhūti*). The word *jātavedas* has been explained as referring to the Blessed Lord in the *Śrīsūktabhāṣya*: "For Viṣṇu is the bestower of all fruits; what is unattainable when the Blessed One, the abode of Śrī, is pleased? Such authoritative texts should be kept in mind here.

In your view, there exists a rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*)—as in "where you are, there is prosperity" or "where there is smoke, there is fire"—and this is indeed pervasion (*vyāpti*). This very thing is pervasion. For every sentence implies restriction; the meaning is that it is precisely a rule of concomitance. Indeed, the definition of pervasion is: "pervasion is a rule of concomitance. The word "this" (*iyam*) refers to the gender of the term *vyāpti*, which is the predicate (*vidheya*).

Therefore, precisely because of the existence of the pervasion (vyāpti) as previously described, [the reason] resides in the subject (pakṣa)—that is, in the mountain and so forth, which are defined as "the subject is that which possesses the probandum (sādhya) in a state of doubt. Thus it is so called. From you, who are such a valid reason (saddhetu), prosperity (śrī), that is, Lakṣmī, is established, just as fire and the like are; this is the intended meaning. Here too, as in the previous example, the superimposition (āropa) is to be understood.

Or rather, O Lord of the mountain of the hooded serpents, he who has within him that certain, infallible goal—the supreme good—residing there, being your devotee, shall be a partisan among those who know the right path. (755)

O Lord of the mountain-king of hooded serpents! O Acyuta! In which person that supreme good—liberation—is to be attained, as it were certainly established within the mind; or rather, the construction may be "that which is to be attained is certain," meaning it dwells there as something determined to be accomplished. By the maxim "when a qualified [subject] is mentioned," this implies that there exists in the mind a certainty regarding liberation as an object to be achieved. [Tell us] that about which they have doubts, O Death, concerning the great hereafter.
This boon which has entered into the secret [of the Self]—Naciketas chooses nothing other than that.

The sense is that, according to the manner stated above, this resides in the mind of Naciketas. This designation—that the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) dwells within—is to be understood as being like the expression: “Does the performer of the sacrifice, who gives the earth as a sacrificial fee, perhaps dwell within [the heart]? He—your devotee—is a *sapakṣa*: one whose side (*pakṣa*) is similar (*sadṛśa*), meaning he belongs to the same class as those who know logic (*nyāyavidām*), those who know the method of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā-nayavidām*), and those who know the Nyāya system of Gautama.

The sense is that, according to the manner stated in the passage, "May you become like Naciketas, a questioner such as this," he should be accepted as a student. Here too, within the context of the Vedāntic treatise under discussion, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of a non-contextual (*aprastuta*) logical-philosophical convention, namely: "A *sapakṣa* is that which possesses the established probandum (*sādhya*). The meaning of this is that a kitchen (*mahānasa*) or similar locus, which possesses the established probandum—such as fire—is designated as a *sapakṣa*.
Or rather,

O Bestower of Boons, just as you, the Puruṣa, are the witness who undergoes the state of being both the primordial nature and its transformation, so too must you indeed become the unchanging primordial nature of another, even greater than Mahat.

O Varada! You are *avikṛtiḥ*, the unmodified, the changeless primordial nature (*ādyaprakṛtiḥ*), who has become the primary material cause of all worlds. The word *prakṛti* is eternally feminine; passages such as “Vāsudeva is the supreme nature (*parā prakṛtiḥ*)” and “And [He is] the nature, because there is no contradiction with the promise and the illustration” should be considered here. By the qualification *avikṛtiḥ*, it is stated that this Nature is devoid of any alteration in its essential form (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*), unlike the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) which, according to the teaching, “is insentient, exists for the sake of another, is eternal, and is subject to constant transformation.”

The point is this: although the Supreme Brahman is the material cause by virtue of having both consciousness and unconsciousness as its body, the fact that modifications (vikāras) reside within the body has been established in the *Śrībhāṣya* and other works; therefore, since Brahman is devoid of modification—as demonstrated by such scriptural authorities as "partless and actionless" and "to the changeless and pure"—the possibility of those modifications applying to It does not arise. For this very reason, the Puruṣa [says]: "I was indeed here before."

The Supreme Person, who is the subject of the etymological definition "the state of being a person (puruṣatva) belongs to that person (tatpuruṣasya)," is the witness, the eternal seer of all, according to such scriptural passages as, "He is the witness, the conscious one, solitary, and devoid of qualities. You do not undergo the state of being a modification of Prakṛti—that is, the state of being a transformation of Prakṛti, which is to say, a change in the nature of your own essence such as consciousness, bliss, and so forth. The sense is that since such a state is produced by karma, there is no contact with it for you.

According to the *Medinī* lexicon: “*Prakṛti* occurs in the sense of equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*), in the nature of ministers and so forth, in the womb, and in the sexual organ. In this lexicon, the word *yoni* denotes *prakṛti*. But for another—that is, for anyone other than You, such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā) or others—even for the Great Inner Self (*pratyagātman*) who is venerable in comparison to others—that state of being both material cause (*prakṛti*) and effect (*vikṛti*) must indeed exist. For all of them, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, living beings situated within the world are subject to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) produced by their own karma.

The meaning is that, by demonstrating dependence on karma in this way, a change in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anyathābhāva*) necessarily occurs. The particle *khalu* indicates what is well-known in the treatises (*śāstra*).
But elsewhere it is said: "The root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), are both nature and modification;
the group of sixteen is modification only; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification."

Thus the system of the Sāṃkhya school has been set forth. To explain its meaning: that which is called *mūlaprakṛti* (the root-nature) is the nature consisting of the equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Accordingly, the *Kāpila-sūtra* states: "The state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is *prakṛti*. This [root-nature] is one, non-conscious in itself, intended for the experience and liberation of many conscious beings, eternal, omnipresent, constantly undergoing transformation, and not a modification of anything else. Thus says the *Sūtra*: "Because there is no further root below it, the root is rootless."

Rather, there is the supreme cause alone. The seven beginning with the Great One (mahat) are: the Great One (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the five subtle elements (tanmātra) starting with sound—these constitute the seven. The sense is that these possess both the nature of being a "prakṛti" (material cause) relative to their own effects and the nature of being a "vikṛti" (evolute/derived effect) relative to their own causes. For example, the Great One possesses the nature of being an evolute relative to its material cause and the nature of being a material cause relative to the ego-sense; the same should be understood for the others as well.

And as in the previously cited fragment of the Sūtra: “From *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-sense, the five subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*). The pentad of elements beginning with space, the pentad of cognitive organs beginning with hearing, the pentad of active organs beginning with speech, and the single mind—these sixteen are exclusively modifications (*vikāra*). They are not, however, the *prakṛtis* of anything else. And there is another fragment of the Sūtra: “The [remaining] sense-organ is both; from the subtle elements come the gross elements.”

The *puruṣa*—the person described in the Sūtra as "the male distinct from the body and so forth"—is, by virtue of being changeless (*niṣpariṇāmatva*), neither the material cause (*prakṛti*) of anything nor the modification (*vikṛti*) of anything. As for the meaning of the illustrative verse: the *puruṣa* is the witness (*sākṣin*), existing solely as a witness.

The Puruṣa exists because the aggregate is for the sake of another; because there is a reversal of the three guṇas and so forth; because there must be a presiding controller; because there is the state of being an enjoyer; and because of the activity for the sake of liberation.
And from this absence of error, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established,
as well as his isolation, neutrality, state of being a seer, and lack of agency.

Such indeed is its process. According to the manner described, the relationship of cause and effect (prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva) does not apply to anything being either a cause or an effect. The primordial nature (ādyaprakṛti), the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), is unevolved (avikṛti) and changeless (nirvikārā). The word "api" (also/even) is to be construed with a different order [of words]. Indeed, that relationship of cause and effect—both causality and effectuality—must necessarily belong even to the others, namely the six categories beginning with the Great Principle (mahat/mahattattva) and ending with the subtle elements (tanmātra), including the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) and so forth.

This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), including the statement that "the sixteen are modifications" as well; such is the summary. The distinction from previous [commentators] is that here, within the context of the Vedānta system under discussion, there is the superimposition of a discourse established by the non-contextual Sāṃkhya school.

Just as you bestow length upon the entire universe in its manifestation, so too do you do for every other line of words; surely, O descendant of Raghu, you do not entertain doubt in this matter, for you possess knowledge of every word.
"O delight of the Raghus!
Even if he is capable of providing protection, that man in this world who, out of greed or fear, abandons one who has come for refuge,
incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin."

The meaning is that even Raghu experienced joy while instructing the Rākṣasa through such words as these, by way of contrast, regarding how the protection of those who have sought refuge is the pinnacle of dharma. Furthermore, by this vocative term, it is illuminated that he has descended into a lineage suited for the practice of dharma such as the protection of those who seek refuge, and that he holds the preeminent position among such protectors.

One who knows the state of all—that is, one who knows the resolve regarding the seeking of refuge by the entire world—or alternatively, one who knows all things, being omniscient; or one who knows the state, that is, the protection, of all—meaning he is the protector of all beings by granting them freedom from fear.
He who speaks thus:
"To one who has surrendered even once and entreats, 'I am yours'..."
"I grant fearlessness to all beings; this is my vow."
Thus [it is said]. Amarasimha states: "The word *pada* is used in the senses of resolve, protection, place, mark, foot, and object.
Whether you be Vibhīṣaṇa, Sugrīva, or even Rāvaṇa himself, O best of monkeys, bring him here; I have granted him my protection.

The sense is: "one who speaks thus. The sense is that even though Vibhīṣaṇa was suspected by Sugrīva and others as belonging to the enemy's side (*para*), he is nonetheless [trusted]. Or rather, the sense is: even toward Rāvaṇa and others who are *para*, how much more so toward Vibhīṣaṇa? Here, the word *api* expresses possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). In this context, "possibility" refers to the manifestation of one's generosity (*dānaśauṇḍatā*). He is called *padarāji* because he shines (*rājate*) upon the two feet (*pada*). Thus it is said.

The sense is that he has taken refuge at the lotus-feet of Rāghava by renouncing everything—wife and children—in accordance with the expression: "Having abandoned wife and children, he has gone for refuge to Rāghava. This meaning is suggested by the word *rājī* (king). Furthermore, the word *tathā* here indicates the ineffable nature [of the state], as in the phrase *tathāgatāṃ tām*. The meaning is: having placed his trust in the universe in such a way as to be ineffable. [Grammatical note: The suffix *lyap* is applied to the root *śvas* preceded by the prefix *vi-* after the gerundive suffix *ktvā*.

Regarding "vasuni," which signifies wealth, you bestow—meaning you grant—sovereignty over the objects of the senses, longevity lasting until the end of the kalpa, or perhaps boundlessness; in this matter of conferring such sovereignty, you do not entertain doubt—that is, the various hesitation as to whether it should be given or not—but rather give it without any uncertainty whatsoever.

"In one sense," it means one who knows all words—that is, one who understands the entire science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*). Alternatively, it means one who knows those words that have attained the state of compounds (*samāsa*); that is to say, one who knows the rules governing all types of compounds. When *vasu* (the word "wealth") and likewise *rāj* (the word "king")—which possesses the designation "word" (*pada*)—follow [the preceding term], then for *viśvasya* (the word "of the universe"), there is lengthening (*dairghya*), i.e., the long vowel (*dīrgha*); the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).

In the sūtra *viśvasya vasurāṭoḥ*, you ordain [the lengthening]; that is the meaning. The meaning of the sūtra is that the vowel of the word *viśva* becomes long when followed by the word *vasu* or the word *rāṭ*. They say that in the term *rāṭ*, the substitution of *ṭ* for *t* (*cartvam*) is not intended to be significant, as it serves merely to indicate the end of the word (*padāntopalakṣaṇārtham*). With this very intention, it should be understood that in the expression *padarājī*, the word *rāṭ* is qualified by the word *pada*. In this matter—namely, this rule prescribing the long vowel—you do not extend an option (*vibhāṣām na tanuṣe*).

The sense is that [the word] is prescribed as being eternal. In this historical account of the Blessed One, the distinction from the previous set of examples is the superimposition of grammatical usage.

Or just as you, O Hari, Lord of the Mountain and Serpent, though appearing dense, formerly fashioned the entire host of Daityas so that they lacked their own abodes and bodies, and thereby accomplished the nectar; || 758 ||

O Lord of the Mountain! O Hara! "Desiring to commit a sin" means even desiring to commit malice toward the gods; for in such passages as "another does not incur the sin of others who have committed sinful deeds," the word *pāpa* is seen to signify malice (*droha*). By the rule "the suffix *kyac* is prescribed after the words *sattrāt*, *kakṣāt*, *kaṣṭāt*, *kṛcchrāt*, and *gahanāt* when there is a desire to perform what is denoted by them," the suffix *kyac* is applied to the word *gahana* ending in the accusative case—here signifying 'sin'—to express the sense of desiring to do (*cikīrṣā*).

They say that *pāpaṃ cikīrṣati* is an *asvapadavigraha* (an analysis where the constituent words do not appear in the compound). [The term] *samastaṃ sarvam api ditijam* refers to all the sons of Diti, the Daityas; *asvapadavigraham* means without conflict (*avigraham*) with those who do not sleep, namely the gods (*asvapantaḥ asvapnā devāḥ*). According to Amara, "strife" (*kalaha*) and "conflict" (*vigraha*) are synonyms. The sense is that he was establishing a peace treaty between the gods and the Asuras regarding the churning of the ocean.

"In former times you accomplished the nectar of immortality (*sudhā-amṛta*)," meaning you achieved it during the Kūrma incarnation. By the rule "puri luṅ cāsme," the present tense (*laṭ*) is optionally used in connection with the word *purā* to denote the remote past (*bhūtānadyatana*). Here, the account of the Kūrma incarnation from the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam should be consulted.

Except for the word *gahanāyamāna*, which is a compound (*samāsa*) formed from the word *gahanāyamāna* itself, and the word *ditija*, which is an *asvapadavigraha*—meaning a sentence that conveys the meaning of its formation without using its own constituent words—the author composes [the rest] in such a way that the word *gahanāyamāna* lacks an *asvapadavigraha* according to the method previously shown, while the word *ditija* has the analysis: "born of Diti" (*dityāṃ jātaḥ*), with the suffix *ḍa* applied according to the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ*.

Since this is an *upapada* compound, it must be understood as a mandatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), and thus its analytical expansion (*vigraha*) cannot consist of its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*). This connects with the phrase "constructing the word *sudhā* and the word *sudhāśabda* [as an] *asvapadavigraha*. He "accomplished" or "produced" it. It is called *sudhā* because it is "well-sustained" (*suṣṭhu dhīyate*). From the root *dheṭ* (meaning "to drink") preceded by the prefix *su-*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. Regarding the rule *ātaścopasarge*, the suffix *ka* would have been more appropriate; this is stated in the *Amarasudhā*.

This too, according to the method previously stated, is a case of *nityasamāsa* (eternal compound) with an *asvapadavigraha* (non-analysis in its own constituent words). It should be noted that the distinction from the examples of the ancients lies in the fact that here, within the context of the Puranic usage under discussion, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the linguistic usage of grammar, which is not the subject at hand.

Just as the earth attained auspiciousness through the quality of being placed under your control during your state as Upendra, so too it was improper for its downfall to occur at the conclusion of those deeds while you were the performer of the gift of the land, O destroyer of Bali.

O Destroyer of Bali! This is intended to indicate that the unique deed performed during the Vāmana incarnation is what is meant here. "Upendrabhāve" means in the state of being Vāmana; "yataḥ" refers to that sacrificial act of giving (*yajñiya-dāna-kṛtye*), where the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings (*sārvavibhaktika*).

“Partaking of the act of making [the earth] yours” means that she partakes in the act of placing the object to be given under your control; thus she is so described. Regarding the suffix *sāti*, following the rule *“vibhāṣā sāti kārtsnye”* (Pāṇini 5.4.52), when the word *sāti* is in effect, the optional suffix *sāti* is applied after the root *kṛ* in connection with the word *deya* (to be given), according to the rule *“deye trā ca”* (Pāṇini 5.4.55). The sense is: “The earth was given to you by the powerful one. The earth (*bhūḥ*) [arose] from merit (*guṇāt*), meaning from the virtues of the giver, the receiver, and so forth. As stated by Devala:
“The giver, the receiver, faith, the object to be given endowed with righteousness, the place, and the time—these six they know to be the constituent parts of gifts.”
Free from disease, righteous in soul, desirous of giving, pure,
and blameless in livelihood and action— a donor is praised for these six qualities.
One who is pure in the three respects, lives a pure life, is compassionate, has his senses restrained,
and is freed from the defects of birth— such a Brāhmaṇa is called a worthy recipient.
"Triśukla" means pure by virtue of having been instructed by three—namely, one's mother, father, and teacher.
Purity (śauca) is cleanliness; likewise, it is great joy upon seeing those who seek [his help].

Honor, freedom from envy, and faith in giving are declared to be the qualities of a donor; wealth that is acquired by one's own effort, without violating proper conduct, without causing harm, and without distress [is fit for giving].
Whether it be very little or even extensive, it is declared that "it is to be given," provided that the substance is not difficult to obtain at that particular time.
The place and time for giving are both excellent when they are appropriate, and not otherwise;
this depends on the state of the place, time, and circumstances, as well as the excellence of the recipient and the donor.
Even that which is inferior may become superior, or that which is superior may otherwise become inferior.

Thus: "Bhavyatva" means auspiciousness or fitness; as the *Medinī* lexicon states, "the word *bhavya* [is used] in the senses of auspicious, fit, and true. That is to say, the state of being conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskaratva*). "He attained" (*agāt*) means he obtained it. "In the giver of the earth" (*kṣmādānakartari*) means in Bali, the lord of the Dānavas, who performed the act of bestowing the world. "The fall at the conclusion of that ritual act" (*tatkṛtyāntanipātaḥ*): "at the conclusion" (*anta*) refers precisely to the end of that aforementioned act of giving, and not at some other time. "Fall" (*nipātaḥ*) refers to his being cast down into the subterranean realm (*adhobhuvana*).

In the phrase "nipāto ’yuktaḥ," the word division is *ayukta* (unfit). *Ayuktaḥ* means inappropriate. The essential meaning is this: when a gift has been given by a donor to a recipient for a particular act of giving, and that gift would have resulted in great fruit according to the principle stated—"By the abundance of qualities such as the worthiness of the recipient, and by all six limbs being complete, a gift becomes one of vast outcome"—then it is improper for the recipient to cause the downfall of that very donor at the conclusion of that act. This same point is expressed in the verse: "The man of steady intellect, having offered water with lotuses and having performed true worship even with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass... (and so forth).
If even he attains the highest state throughout the three worlds after giving with an undaunted mind, how could he possibly fall into distress?
Thus, it should be understood that this was described with reference to the meaning expressed by Brahmā to the Blessed One from a worldly perspective on the occasion of the subduing of Bali.

In the verse, the words *kṣmādāna* in *kṣmādānakartari* and *upendra* in *upendrabhāve* are distinct words ending in the vocative case (*saṃbuddhi*), and not compounds. *Ādāna* means "one who takes" or "one who accepts"; the suffix *lyu* (equivalent to *ana*) is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule for the *nandivṛṣi* group. *Kṣmādāna* is "the taking of the earth" (*kṣmāyā ādānaḥ*); its vocative form is *kṣmādāna*.

Alternatively, in the term *kṣmādāna* (giver of the earth), the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the past tense (*bhūta*) with respect to the agent (*kartṛ*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*; this is because the mention of "variously" (*bahulam*) allows for such usage, as explained in the *Tattvabodhinī* and other commentaries on the rule *tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena* and so forth, where it is stated that "one who has spoken of a quality is a *guṇavacana*."

Alternatively, the word *kṣmā* (earth) takes the locative case by the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayośca*, meaning "that in which [something] is given," thus signifying the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This is similar to expressions such as *tadasmin vṛddhyāyalābhaśulkopadā dīyate* ("in this, interest, profit, gain, tax, or tribute is given") and *samam abrāhmaṇe dānam* ("a gift is equal when given to one who is not a Brahmin"), where the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is intended to be expressed as the locus. Thus, the meaning is: "she who has become the recipient of the act of giving the earth. O Upendra! O younger brother of Indra! O destroyer of Bali! *Tvatsātkṛtiḥ* means being made subject to you, being dependent on you, or, in other words, being under your command.

He is so called because he resorts to that (bhajati tām). The suffix *sāti* is applied according to the rule “*tadadhīnavacane ca*” [Pāṇini 5.4.54]. “*Bhūḥ*” means the verbal root *bhū*. It is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), because of the grammatical injunction: “*tayor eva kṛtyaktakhalarthāḥ*” [Pāṇini 3.4.70], which means that these suffixes are used only for the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Since the suffix *yat* is prescribed by the rule “*aco yat*” [Pāṇini 3.1.97], the meaning is “having obtained the suffix *yat*. The ablative case is used here with respect to the object (*karmani*), following the principle of ellipsis regarding the gerund suffix *lyap*.

From the quality (*guṇa*)—that is, from the quality prescribed by the rule *asārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* [Pāṇini 7.3.84] due to its being an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix—the form *bhavyam* attains the state of being fit (*bhavyatvam*). The sense is that because the root *bhū* is intransitive, when the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*), and the *guṇa* substitution occurs, the form *bhavyam* is established. Regarding the agent (*kartari*), there is the irregular derivation (*nipāta*) of that very root *bhū* ending in a *kṛtya* suffix; the meaning is that it is irregularly formed as ending in a *kṛtya* suffix by the rule *bhavyageya* [Pāṇini 3.4.68].

A *nipāta* (irregular form) is the utterance of words in their own specific form by the author of the Sūtras for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) in the absence of any [standard] defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The word “*yukta*” is the division [of the compound]; its meaning is “appropriate. Under the governing rule “*kṛtyāḥ*,” the *kṛtya* suffix *yat* is established after the root *bhū* by the rule “*aco yat*. The distinction is that this [form] is irregularly prescribed (*nipātita*) as denoting the agent by the rule “*bhavyageya-etc.*. Here too, the superimposition (*āropa*) is exactly as before.
Or just as,
O Lord, the water from your voice, through contact with even a single drop of another's speech, manifests itself perfectly in its entirety according to the instruction that arises.

O Lord! Your mountain Veṅkaṭādri—its water, from the region [indicated by] ‘ā’ (up to), pervading all regions; [the use of] ‘ā’ here is according to the rule ‘āṅ maryādāvacane’. Since it bears the designation of *karmapravacanīya*, the ablative case is employed according to the rule ‘pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ’. Because the rule ‘āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ’ falls under the heading of the *mahāvibhāṣā* (optional application), there is no compound formation.

Having risen and emerged in the form of rivers such as the celestial Gaṅgā and others, at some time—meaning through contact with even a single supreme (para) drop (bindu), that is, a single spray (śīkara)—it causes its entire self, which is in contact with it, to become fully manifest as pure, awakened, and cleansed of all evil. The summarized meaning is this: a waterfall issuing from the moist peaks of Veṅkaṭa purifies the entire multitude of sentient beings merely by the touch of its own single spray.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: "The water of your speech, having arisen (*udetya*) from your command, truly manifests itself as pure through its contact with even a single drop of [the teachings on] self and others. Having "arisen" means having attained emergence, that is, having attained excellence by such names as Svāmitīrtha and so forth; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *udaya* refers to a man, the eastern mountain, and elevation. All else has already been explained. In another sense, it means "situated in your mountain," that is, situated in your speech, meaning uttered by you.

"Water" (*udaka*) and "the word water" (*udakapada*); that is to say, when there is a desire to express a compound. Due to the conjunction of a single *bindu* (anusvāra) with itself and what follows it—from "itself" meaning from the word *udaka*, and "what follows it" meaning existing after it, being singular (*eka*), that is, alone and not separated by another word—due to the conjunction (*saṃsarga*), that is, the connection, of that *bindu*, namely the word *bindu*; [this occurs] "by receiving the substitute *uda*" (*udetyādeśāt*), meaning having obtained the substitute in the form of *uda*. [The ablative case here is used] in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) when the suffix *lyap* is elided.

Alternatively, the word *jātu* is connected here; its meaning is "having attained some form of modification (*ādeśa*) at some time. By this, it is indicated that this substitution of *u* for *o* is optional, as prescribed by the sūtra which will be cited immediately following. It makes itself—its own self—which has reached a state of total integration (*samasta*), manifest as excellent (*sādhu*).

The word *udaka* (water) is compounded with the word *bindu* (drop), which is not separated by any other word; in that case, as the final member of the compound, it undergoes the substitution of *uda* according to the rule "in the case of *mantha*, *odana*, *saktu*, *bindu*, *vajra*, *bhāra*, *hāra*, *vīvadha*, and *gāha*. Thus, the fully established meaning reveals its own grammatical correctness. Here too, in the Puranic usage, there is a superimposition as before. For the greatness of the rivers and sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*) born on Mount Veṅkaṭa is well known. As it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Veṅkaṭagiri-māhātmya*:
"On that lord of mountains, Veṅkaṭa, who is saluted by gods and demons..."
There is indeed a most excellent sacred site (tīrtha) known by the name Viyadgaṅgā.

Thus it is said. In that very place, elsewhere, there is the auspicious Kalyā, the best of rivers, born from Mount Vṛṣabha, resplendent with rows of sacred bathing places (tīrthas), and the destroyer of the flood of impurities.
Thus it is said; and in the Vāmana Purāṇa: "All these holy fords (tīrthas) exist together upon this best of mountains;
all the rivers are destroyers of sin, and their number is not known."
And thus it is said:
"The Svāmitīrtha is of great merit and the destroyer of all sins;
on its bank the Lord of the World (Jagannātha) sports together with Ramā."
It is renowned throughout the three worlds, O prince, especially so.
Thus it is said.
Because it is the lordship over all sacred fords, it is called Svāmitīrtha.
And so forth; enough of this long digression.

Or rather, O Acyuta, your name, whatever it may be—even if it consists of a derivative suffix or a kṛt-suffix—is indeed a complete nominal stem (prātipadika); for this alone shines forth when followed by case-endings (sup), whereas anything else does not.

Indeed, O Acyuta! That [name] is well-known in all the Purāṇas and other scriptures as *hitakṛd-antam*—meaning that which has a beneficial conclusion (*antaḥ*) or end (*antaḥ*), i.e., it bestows ultimate welfare; or alternatively, that which has a beneficial essence (*antaḥ*) or nature, meaning it is auspicious by its very own character. As the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *antaḥ* is used in the senses of certainty, destruction, essential nature, front, proximity, and interior. In this regard:
"If Govinda is praised or even merely heard of in any way whatsoever, even sinners shall become purified, and the pure shall attain liberation."
Govinda, even when remembered but once, quickly burns away the heap of sins accumulated by men over hundreds of years, just as fire consumes a pile of cotton.
He has girded his loins for the journey toward liberation;
by whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" have been uttered even once—
even if that name was chanted involuntarily— one is freed from all sins.
A person is instantly liberated, like deer terrified by a lion.
Hari removes sins even when remembered by those with wicked minds;
even fire burns simply by being touched, even against one's will.

Thousands of such authorities are to be cited. Whatever name or designation you possess—entirely and in its totality—that indeed is your name. "Pada-pade" means at every step; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of "according to the object. *Prātipadika* means that which exists at every step (*pratipada-bhavam*); the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied in the sense of "belonging to" (*bhava-arthe*), as the *adhyātma* group is an open-ended class (*ākṛti-gaṇa*). "Repeatedly" (*paunaḥpunikam*) means in such a way as to be done again and again. It should be employed by the virtuous—that is, by those who know Brahman—and should be properly utilized and glorified; this is the meaning.

Alternatively, according to the stated method—"and that naming [of the child], this quartet is servitude"—the meaning is that it should be properly applied to one's son, disciple, and so forth, as an indicator of servitude. It "shines forth" (prabhāti) or manifests. Or else, "prātipadika" is an adjective qualifying the name itself; the construction is: "this prātipadika [name] should be employed among the virtuous. *Pratipat* means knowledge; as Amara states: "citsaṃvit, pratipat, jñapti, and cetanā [are synonyms for consciousness]."

The suffix *ṭhak* (ika) is applied here according to the rule *prāgvahatīyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.1), with the sense that "the means of practice" (*pratipādaka*) is its purpose (*prayojana*). The meaning is: that which has knowledge as its fruit. And here, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is defined as that by which [reality] is perceived—that which is free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single nature;
or rather, that which is clearly seen or attained—that is knowledge.

It should be understood that what has been stated consists of worship (*upāsanā*), which serves as the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). It should be noted that because the word *pratipat* is derived from the verbal root *pad* preceded by the prefix *prati*, it ends in the letter *d*; therefore, the substitution of *k* for the suffix *t* (by the rule *isusuktāntāt kaḥ*) does not apply here. As for other names—that is, names other than those of the Lord—they are not to be employed among the virtuous. The sense is that such names do not belong to them, as they are not subordinate to anything else. As it is said in the *Bharadvāja-saṃhitā*:
"One should avoid designations that are characterized by *tamas* and *rajas*."
Even a devotee surely departs [from the truth] through insincere designations.
By designations, that is, by names:
the name of pure [beings] is *sāttvika*, while that of impure ones is *rājasa*;
but the name of deities established in external tantras and the like is *tāmasa*.

Thus [it is said]. "Pure" means those who sacrifice to no other; "impure" means those who sacrifice to others—this is the meaning. Alternatively, even in the first half-verse, the construction is: "Whatever name of yours exists, that has 'the maker of welfare' (hitakṛt) as its end. The meaning is exactly as stated before. The distinction in this alternative view is that "having 'the maker of welfare' as its end" is the predicate to be enjoined.

Except for that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix or a *kṛt* suffix—meaning any word-form ending in a *taddhita* or a *kṛt* suffix—and also that which is a compound (*samasta*), meaning any word-form that is a compound; and where the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*) or the abstract state (*bhāva*); that indeed is a "noun" (*nāman*), for it is designated as such by convention. For the word "indeed" (*hi*) signifies both cause and restriction, according to Amara. It is called a "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), being designated as such; for the words "noun" (*nāman*) and "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) have the same referent, since the designation "nominal stem" is prescribed for nouns by the rule: "And those ending in *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compounds."

This previously mentioned nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is "to be properly employed" (*supprayojya*), meaning it is to be employed with the case-endings included within the *sup*-pratyāhāra; for in common usage, their employment is observed only through the specific qualification of case-endings (*subvaiśiṣṭyena*). *Sat* means "good" (*sādhu*); according to Amara, "the word *sat* [is used] in the senses of truth, good, existing, excellent, and venerable. It shines forth. The other [nominal stems] are "not to be properly employed," meaning they are not qualified by case-endings.

It is not good, nor does it shine forth, because of the statement that "prakṛti alone should not be employed"—this is the intended meaning. Here too, there is a superimposition (āropa) of the unmentioned technical usage of grammar onto the mentioned worldly practice well-known from the Purāṇas.

Just as the supreme station, which is the Brahman devoid of all attributes (*nirguṇa*), dwells in bliss—O Blessed One, you are that very reality—so too, by resorting to the figure of speech known as *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā*, [the word "Brahman"] here applies to this mountain, the abode of serpents. 762.

O Blessed One! O Śrīnivāsa! That which is the supreme state of Brahman, celebrated in such Vedic texts as "That of Viṣṇu," that divine, blissful, and glorious abode—having taken up a divine, auspicious form for the sake of showing grace to His devotees, You have occupied it; the construction is: "In this world, You are that very Brahman, resting upon the mountain of the serpent-king (Śeṣācala). The meaning is indeed clear.
Beginning with the words, "Śrīnivāsa also [resides] on the Śeṣa-mountain, and then on the banks of Svāmisaaras... [the text continues].
The ancient Puruṣa, the Ordainer, the Puruṣa beyond darkness—
having abandoned his former abode, Vaikuṇṭha, he indeed now dwells here.

Thus ends the statement regarding the majesty of the Padma-Veṅkaṭādri; here, statements such as "the master of illusion, supreme bliss," etc., are also to be kept in mind. For this very reason, there is the light (*bhā*) of that supreme state (*paramapada*). This word ends in a long vowel (*ā*). From the abode of Brahman, His supreme station shines forth—that divine, effulgent place which the gods themselves do not behold.
O King, that abode of the high-souled Viṣṇu blazes more intensely than the sun and fire;
by its own radiance, it is difficult for even gods and dānavas to behold.

Thus is described the divine radiance mentioned in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts. Having come from the supreme abode (*paramapada*) and arrived upon this earth, it "continually goes to" (*atati*) that which is the "resort characterized by the serpent" (*agalakṣaṇāśrayaṇāt*)—that is, the support whose form is the aforementioned Śeṣācala mountain. [This is derived] from the root *ata*, meaning "to go continuously," with the suffix *kvip*. It comes to be so. The meaning is that when the Supreme Brahman has descended from the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*) to the Serpent Mountain (*phaṇigiri*), the divine radiance of that supreme ether likewise constantly resorts to the Serpent Mountain alone.

The point is that, in this context, the two words *tat* and *tvam* convey their meaning by resorting to the *bhāgatyāgalakṣaṇā* (indication through partial renunciation), which is the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*. It should be understood that since the Supreme Brahman, who is characterized by a divine, auspicious form, previously possessed a specific spatio-temporal qualification, but now lacks that same spatio-temporal qualification, there is a renunciation of the literal meaning in the aspect of *tattā* (that-ness) within the word *tat*, while there is no such renunciation in the aspect of *tvattā* (you-ness) within the word *tvam*; thus, this constitutes the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*.
Depending on the distinction of its parts, a word both abandons and does not abandon its own meaning,
if it possesses the characteristic of *jahadajahatsvārthā* indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Such is its definition. Here, within the context of the Puranic discourse under discussion, there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of the discourse of the science of poetics (*alaṃkāraśāstra*), which is not itself the subject at hand.

Alternatively, because the words “That thou art” (*tattvamasi*) here evoke the recognition of the Vedic statement “That thou art, O Śvetaketu,” the discourse of the Advaitins—who establish the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman—is perceived as the unmentioned subject; this is then superimposed upon the Puranic discourse that is actually being discussed.

For they describe it thus: in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), by discarding the contradictory portions—namely, omniscience and limited knowledge—of the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, and by retaining the non-contradictory pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), a single, undivided reality indicated by both is established through the figurative indication known as *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā*. This alone is the difference between these two [views].

For instance, the rhetoricians maintain that in expressions such as "This is that Devadatta," since the aspect of "that-ness" (tattā) is currently impossible, it is abandoned; however, since the aspect of "this-ness" (idaṃtā) is currently possible, it is not abandoned. Thus, they describe this as the "partially renouncing and partially non-renouncing" (jahadajahatsvārthā) indication (lakṣaṇā).

The proponents of non-dual Brahman (*advaitabrahmavādin*), however, in order to ensure consistency between the illustration and the illustrated, have established that even in the case of "This is that Devadatta," one must employ the *jahadajahatsvārtha* (partially inclusive) mode of signification. Here, by abandoning both the mutually contradictory aspects of "that-ness" and "this-ness," yet without abandoning the underlying nature itself, the pure essence indicated by both is pointed out. Likewise, in great statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), they maintain that by discarding the contradictory portions inherent in the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*, and by retaining only the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), [the identity is realized].
Thus, it is established that a single, indivisible reality, characterized by both [aspects], is indicated through the aforementioned type of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). As they say:

"Where one part of the primary meaning is abandoned and another part alone is indicated, that is *jahadajahatsvārthā* (indication where the word abandons and does not abandon its own meaning); this is to be seen in instances such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*)."
Thus, enough of this excessive over-extension.

O Infinite One, whose power is well-known, who possesses the defining marks, who shines with the splendor of Mount Añjana, who has attained excellence through literature, and who resplends with glory— I take refuge in You, the one of auspicious renown.

"Ananta" means one who is unlimited by space, time, and substance, according to the Vedic revelation: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. Its vocative form is "O Ananta! O Lord! O Residue of All! [I salute] Him whose power is well-known—that is, perfectly established through all the Vedas.

*Śakti* (power) is a specific quality consisting of universal material causality (*sarvopādānatva*), which is described in such passages as: “That state of being the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of the universe, by virtue of which I am called *śakti*,” and which carries out all capacities other than itself. Alternatively, it is the capacity to bring about that which others cannot accomplish and which thus appears as if unachievable. In this regard, the scriptural text, “His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold,” should also be considered.

"Kṛtalakṣaṇam" means recognized for its auspicious qualities, according to the stated manner beginning with "He consists of all auspicious attributes" (*samastakalyāṇaguṇātmako’sau*). According to Amara, "the terms *kṛtalakṣaṇa* and *ahitalakṣaṇa* denote one who is recognized by his qualities. It refers to Him whose joy (*ullāsa*)—meaning delight or radiance—is upon Mount Añjana; or, it is so called because He is made to shine forth (*ullāsya*) by Mount Añjana. Having attained association (*sāhitya*), that is, distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*), with Śrī (Lakṣmī), He shines; the sense is that Your manifestation occurs precisely because of the distinction of Śrī.

In this context, the following should also be considered: "He rejoices with Ramā on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī. For this very reason, you—who are celebrated in the Śruti as the Lord of Lakṣmī in the words, "Modesty and Lakṣmī are your two wives"—are heard to possess great fame in the words, "His name is great glory. Furthermore, for you alone, who are introduced as the cause of the universe in the words, "He milked forth these two worlds," there is the renown of being the playful agent of the creation and so forth of the entire world, as well as its universal protector. You are one of "beautiful renown" (suśloka), meaning one of auspicious fame. It is precisely of such a person that this glory is proclaimed.

The meaning is "not of another. Regarding the word *nāma* (name), the *Upaniṣad-bhāṣya* states: "In the sense of what is well-known. I take refuge in You. Since the first section (*anuvāka*) of the *Nārāyaṇīya* reads, "From the waters He was born as Hiraṇyagarbha—these eight [verses]," and since that same section contains the scriptural statement, "Hrī and Lakṣmī are Your two wives," one should understand that the glorious renown mentioned in that section—"His name"—belongs to the Lord of Lakṣmī alone and not to anyone else.

*Śakti* (denotative power) is a synonym for *abhidhā* (primary signification); it is the primary function residing in the word, which is the cause of the cognition of the object that is the direct referent of the convention. This is according to the definition: "The primary function residing in the word, which is the cause of the cognition of the denoted meaning, is called *abhidhā*. He by whom this is well known is [described as such]. He is likewise described as one by whom *lakṣaṇā* (indication) has been examined. *Lakṣaṇā* is defined as follows: "That function, distinct from *śakti*, which is the cause of the cognition of a meaning based on the impossibility of the connection of the intended sense with the literal meaning, is called *lakṣaṇā*."

The function of a word (*śabdavyāpāra*) has been defined as such. Since the root *kṛ* signifies action in general, it should be understood that in the expression *kṛtā*, it carries the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇā*). For this very reason, in expressions such as *kṛtahastaḥ* (skilled-handed) and *kṛtadhīḥ* (wise-minded), the root *kṛ* is seen to signify "training" (*śikṣā*) and so forth. *Añjana* is a specific function of a word, synonymous with *vyañjanā* (suggestion), whose definition is stated as: "the operation that produces a cognition of a meaning distinct from both the expressed (*vācya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*). [The compound refers to] one whose *ullāsa*—meaning joy—is *acala*, or steady, in that [function].

By these epithets, his unimpeded skill in employing expressive (*vācaka*), indicative (*lakṣaka*), and suggestive (*vyañjaka*) words is illuminated, owing to the emergence of intuition that thoroughly masters the three functions of language—denotation, indication, and suggestion. "Sāhitya" refers to all the sciences taken together; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). As it is stated in the *Bhāvaprakāśa*:
"In comparison with logic, grammar, Mīmāṃsā, astrology, and so forth, 'Sāhitī' is said to arise from 'Sāhitya'; the suffix *ṣyañ* is declared by the wise to be used in its own sense."

"The synthesis of all sciences is called *sāhitya* (literature/colligation). This also accords with the meaning already stated. "Having approached" (*etya*) means "having known. "By *śrī*" means by the power of speech suitable for composing poetry, which corresponds to the knowledge of the instruments [of composition] as demonstrated. Hemacandra states: "'*Śrī* [is used] in the sense of Lakṣmī, the Sarala tree, attire and its implements, the arrangement of dress, intellect, speech, beauty, and the attainment of the three goals of life (*trivarga*)."

For this very reason, he possesses "endless" (*anantāḥ*)—that is, unlimited—"well-praised verses" (*suślokāḥ*), meaning poems whose form consists of words and meanings endowed with the characteristics of poetry, such as being free from defects, possessing excellences (*guṇa*), and being adorned with figures of speech (*alaṃkāra*). The sense is that, by virtue of his mastery over speech, he is skilled in the composition of abundant excellent poetry. Here, as before, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon the subject matter expounded in the Vedānta and Purāṇas.

Just as a single name of the lotus-eyed one pacifies the forest fire of poverty, so here the pure, secondary metaphorical indication (*gauṇī lakṣaṇā*), consisting of both superimposition (*sāropa*) and identification (*sādhyavasāna*), is characterized by its excellence.

In this world, *sāropāsādhyavasitiḥ* refers to that which has a firm resolve (*adhyavasitiḥ*)—a certainty—regarding the object of worship (*upāsanā*). The meaning is that the firm resolve concerning the object of worship is called *sāropāsādhyavasitiḥ* because its fruit is necessarily realized and is thus most excellent (*śreyas*). Furthermore, it should be understood that "worship" (*upāsana*) here refers specifically to recitation (*japa*), as in the expression "one who worships the mantra *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*. It is *gauṇī* (secondary) in the sense described by the statement "those names which are secondary" (*gauṇāni*); that is, it is derived from qualities (*guṇata āgatā*).
It is so called because it destroys (*śrṇāti*) all defects and nourishes (*śrīṇāti*) the world with virtues.
It is eternally resorted to by all, and it itself resorts to the supreme state.
Resorting [to it], being resorted to, hearing, and even causing to hear.

The sense is that this follows from such etymological explanations (*nirukti*). For this very reason, she is so described as one whose *lakṣaṇa*—meaning the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—is "good" (*sādhu*). Alternatively, *lakṣaṇāḥ* means those by which things are characterized; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Thus, she is one whose *lakṣaṇās* (characteristics) are good. The meaning is: she by whose name good people (*sādhavaḥ sajjanāḥ*) are characterized—that is, made known—as being virtuous. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *sādhu* [is used] in the sense of a usurer, a handsome man, and a virtuous person, like any other term denoting its referent."

"Śuddhā" means purifying; according to the *Medinī* lexicon, "aśuddhaṃ syāt triṣu kevale nirdoṣe ca pavitre ca" (the word *aśuddha* is used in three senses: as a mere [neuter] quality, as faultless, and as pure). The meaning is that she is the fortune (*bhāgadheya*) of the lotus-eyed Śrīnivāsa—that is, she is determined to be the very fortune of Him. The single name "Śrī" and so forth, having but one referent, extinguishes the forest fire of poverty; the point is that this is because her names are recited as "the destroyer of all poverty."

In this context, in the phrase *dāridryadavam*, there is a metaphorical (gauṇī) indication based on superimposition (*sāropā*); however, in the phrase *abjākṣabhāgadheyasya*, there is a pure indication based on identification (*sādhyavasānā*). According to the sequence of the text, the correspondence follows the respective order. The meaning is "excellent, excellent" (*sādhu sādhvī*). It is used in the neuter gender for the sake of the general category (*sāmānya*), as in the example *śakyamaravindasurabhiḥ*. Alternatively, the indication itself is qualified by its excellence (*sādhutva*). Or rather, it should be understood as an adverbial modifier of the verb "it is" (*bhavati*), which is supplied by ellipsis.

The intended meaning is as follows: in the phrase "the forest fire of poverty" (*dāridryadava*), because of the coreferential indication (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words *dāridrya* (poverty) and *dava* (forest fire), which denote the object and the subject respectively, there is the metaphorical function (*sāropā lakṣaṇā*). And that [metaphorical function] is secondary (*gauṇī*), because the word *dava* operates through similarity with the quality of causing heat and so forth.
This superimposition (sāropā) is of two kinds, distinguished as figurative (gauṇī) and pure (śuddhā). That which consists of a relationship characterized by similarity is called figurative.

"However, that [indication] which consists in the relation with something other than that [primary object] is called 'pure' (śuddhā)," according to the definition. In the phrase "of the fortune of the lotus-eyed one," however, having suppressed (nigīrya) the "fortune" (śrī), which is the object of superimposition (āropaviṣaya), there is indication based on the primary object (sādhyavasānā-lakṣaṇā) because it is based solely upon the "fortune" (bhāgadheya), which is the subject of superimposition (viṣayin). The distinction is that it is "pure" because, while taking the relationship of cause and effect between "fortune" and "beauty" as a basis, it employs only the word for the subject of superimposition. And thus its definition is: "Where, having suppressed the object (viṣaya), the subject of superimposition (viṣayin) alone is established."
In that regard, the secondary (gauṇī) [metaphor] is divided into two types: the one based on complete identification (sādhyavasānā) and the pure (śuddhā).

Thus: what is called *adhyavasāya* (determination) is a cognition that is intense (*utkaṭa*) regarding one aspect; and the intensity of a cognition consists in its having as its object a substratum possessing many properties associated with various alternative possibilities (*koṭi*), and so forth. That which proceeds by virtue of a relationship of similarity is the "secondary" (*gauṇī*); that which proceeds by virtue of a relationship other than that is the "pure" (*śuddhā*). One should observe that a distinction exists here, just as it does in the case of the definition of *sāropā* (superimposition with the source).

Here too, while the worldly usage concerning the glory of the name Śrī Lakṣmī is the subject at hand, there is a superimposition of the terminology of the science of poetics (*alaṃkāra-śāstra*), which is not the subject at hand.

Or rather, just as those who understand the characteristics of secondary indication (gauṇa-lakṣaṇā) resort to that very same function (vṛtti) in the Supreme Abode, and not to another "cow-like" (goṇī) function appropriate for poetry, so too does the devotee [resort to it] in Prabhākara and others. 765.

Those for whom the intellect (*buddhi*) is *kāvyā*—meaning appropriate and consistent—are called *kāvyocitāḥ*. This refers, in effect, to those possessing subtle intellects in the manner described by the statement: "It is seen by those of subtle vision with a subtle and foremost intellect. Regarding the word *kāvyā*, Viśva, Medinī, and Hemacandra state: "The word *kāvyā* may mean a female demon (*pūtana*) or intellect (*dhī*). Regarding *ucita*, the *Ratnamālā* states: "'Ucita' may mean measured, suitable, known, practiced, or consistent (*samañjasa*)."

In the Supreme Abode, the Lord Śrīnivāsa—who is determined to be "splendor" (tejas) by virtue of possessing qualities such as brilliance, loveliness, and the dispelling of darkness—devoted men who possess devotion [approach]. The word *agauṇa* is to be split [as *a-gauṇa*]. Being recognized as true devotees (*bhāgavata*) by means of the primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*), namely the insignia of the conch and discus (*śaṅkhacakralakṣma*), they are known as such. This is derived from the root *jñā* preceded by the prefix *abhi*, with the suffix *aṅ* added in the sense of the object according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*; it is a feminine noun like *upajñā*. By its very nature, this word is feminine.
Furthermore, because the marking with the conch and discus alone is primary even among the marks of the five weapons, they are said to be "conversant with the primary characteristic.
And thus says the Śruti:
"O Viṣṇu, [be] before Your two purifiers, the lotus and the discus..."
To cross the ocean of birth,
those ancient lords of men place your emblems upon the roots of their arms; others offer them as sacred images.
Thus it is said in the scripture of the Blessed One, and Bharadvāja also states:
"Agni and Soma are indeed the two lotuses of the wheels; all things whatsoever consist of them.
Whether deficient or complete, one who honors even one of them attains the fruit."
For the conch and the discus are primary; all other items, such as the mace and so forth, are secondary.
One who is marked with the conch and the discus is indeed considered marked by everything.
Thus; or else, having begun with:
"Understand those who are devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa to be sāttvika."
O sages, learn the characteristics of those who are devoted to all beings:
their fruit is solely the service of Viṣṇu, and they abide in the conviction that He alone is the means.
Delight in carrying out His commands, proclaiming the virtues of His deeds,
having one's body marked with His signs, and taking pleasure in His worship.

Detachment from contact with anything other than that, lack of greed regarding the objects of the senses, living under the authority of the teacher, and dedicating one's own life to the service of the teacher.
Freedom from anger, greed, pride, laziness, arrogance, and delusion;
and being endowed with truthfulness, purity, compassion, fortitude, forbearance, and contentment.
Those Vaiṣṇavas who are endowed with these characteristics and are free from impurity should be honored merely by the sight of them; they should never be treated with contempt.

Thus, the meaning is that they are those who know the characteristics of the primary mode of life (mukhyabhāgavata) as stated in the *Bhāradvāja-pariśiṣṭa*. The suffix *ka* is applied to the root *jñā* preceded by the prefix *abhi* in the sense of the agent, according to the rule *ātaścopasarge*. For this very reason, they follow—that is, they resort to—that very same primary mode of life (*vṛtti*), which is characterized by the qualities about to be described, such as having no delight in anything else. As it is said in the *Bhāradvāja-saṃhitā*, a scripture of the Lord:
"Just as surrender (*prapatti*) to the lotus feet of the Lord is prescribed, so too must one's conduct therein be performed according to the instructions of the Guru."
Livelihood, prescribed conduct, avoidance of what is forbidden,
vision, devotion, and likewise service to the virtuous— these are the sixfold characteristics.

Having thus demonstrated the sixfold nature of conduct, one who knows the truth of the Vedas and Vedāntas, having no other recourse, should practice what is enjoined and avoid what is prohibited to the utmost degree.
Worshipping Viṣṇu in images and other forms while marked with the signs of Hari,
and serving one's gurus with devotion— this is considered the highest mode of conduct.

Thus, the meaning of the previously cited verse has been explained. Here, by the qualification "para" (supreme), the preeminence of this very function is stated. By the restrictive particle "eva" (only), the exclusion of others is indicated; he explicitly shows this exclusion with the words "na cānyām" (and not another) and so forth. Being devotees of Prabhākara and others—namely Bhāskara and the rest—they do not go to, nor do they resort to, another—that is, a secondary (gauṇī)—function. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "but" (tu).
Now, constantly performing this function, free from affliction, one casts off the body and attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, because it is the cause of unimpeded supreme liberation, compared to the Bhāgavata conduct described in the Bharadvāja-saṃhitā,

that twice-born man who is devoted to the duties of his caste and stage of life and remains a single-minded devotee of the Sun for seven births— he, indeed, is a true Brāhmaṇa throughout those seven births.
Then, by the greatness of that merit, he will become a devotee of Rudra;
likewise, for seven births, he will be solely devoted to Śiva.
By that great merit, he shall attain the state of a Vaiṣṇava.
Likewise, a human being who is devoted to Viṣṇu for seven lifetimes,
a Brahmin who performs sacrifices solely for the Lord within the lineage of the Bhāgavatas;

"Then he attains liberation, which is extremely difficult even for the gods to obtain. Thus it is said in the *Vārāha-purāṇa*: "A devotee of Prajāpati [attains it] in three [births], but that of Śaṅkara in five."
Through twenty births as Agni, Indra, Sūrya, and others, one becomes a Vaiṣṇava.

The meaning is that [the devotees] do not favor a secondary mode of devotion—such as exclusive attachment—to Bhāskara and others who, according to the *Bharadvāja-saṃhitā* and other texts, are described as means to liberation only after the intervention of many births.

In the alternative sense (pakṣe), they are those accustomed to poetry, namely, literary critics (*ālaṃkārikas*). And "figurative" (*gauṇī*) is that which is "indicative" (*lakṣaṇā*); those who are experts in this are those who understand such cases as "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*) or "Fire studies" (*agniradhīte*).
Figurative indication is declared to be a relationship consisting of similarity.

Recognizing that the secondary (gauṇī) indication (lakṣaṇā) has the characteristics thus described, for this very reason, even in the case of the word *dhāmnidhāmani* [in the verse], they apply that same function—namely, the verbal operation known as secondary indication (*gauṇalakṣaṇā*)—just as in the previously cited example; so they believe. As they have said:
"Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is defined as a cognition that is inseparable from the primary meaning (*abhidheya*).
However, the state of being secondary (*gauṇatā*) is held to belong to that function (*vṛtti*) due to its connection with the qualities (*guṇa*) of the thing being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*)."

Thus [it is said]. And here, "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*) refers merely to a relation, and not to necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*); for if that were the case, since there is no spatial or temporal inseparable connection between a bed and those situated on the bed, it would follow that there is no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the expression "the beds cry out. The meaning is that the "metaphorical nature" (*gauṇatā*)—that is, being prompted by a quality (*guṇa*)—of the function (*vṛtti*), namely the operation called secondary indication, is accepted because of its connection with the qualities being indicated. By the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "that very [function]," he shows what is excluded by saying "and not another," and so forth.

Prabhākara was the foremost of the Tantrikas; those who begin with him are the Bhaṭṭas and others. Among them, the devotees—meaning those who follow their doctrines—do not resort to, nor do they accept, another function (vṛtti) distinct from indication (lakṣaṇā), namely the secondary (gauṇī) function, which arises from qualities (guṇata āgatā) and consists in a relation of association. For they hold that in expressions such as "The boy is fire," the purport of the word "fire" refers to the boy as qualified by qualities such as tawny color (paiṅgalya), precisely because of the use of words in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa).

In cases such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), where there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the intention of the word "Ganges" refers to its correlate, the bank, even without the employment of the word "bank. Thus, the distinction between figurative indication (*gauṇī*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*) arises from the specific or non-specific nature of the intention, which is determined by whether or not another word is employed. Even in cases where no other word is used, such as "Agni studies" (*agnir adhīte*), the intention of the word refers specifically to that which is qualified by similarity (to the priest). This is because the determination of the intention occurs in exactly the same way in instances where the employment of another word is present.

Just as in cases such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," where the indicative force (*liṅga*) and other markers have their purport toward the *apūrva* (unseen potency) by virtue of the connection between the object of desire and the person enjoined, so too do they describe it in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*) such as "One should perform the twilight worship daily. This is the underlying idea: the Alaṃkārikas maintain that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is considered to be fivefold—based on connection with the expressed meaning, similarity, inherence, contrariety, and connection with action.

Thus, because similarity (*sādṛśya*) is also accepted as a type of relation, even in cases such as "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*) or "Fire studies" (*agniradhīte*), since no such relation would otherwise account for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the like, and because the purpose of producing a cognition of non-difference—the very seed of *lakṣaṇā*—is fully present, they include even the figurative function (*gauṇī vṛtti*) within *lakṣaṇā* itself, rather than accepting it as a separate function. Here too, there is the superimposition of the terminology used in the scriptures of the Blessed One.

Or rather, O Acyuta, since this assembly of wise men sacrifices to you with golden-mouthed [spoons] solely out of a desire to please you, how could it not be a *sallakṣaṇā* (one possessing good characteristics) that abandons its own primary meaning? 766.

O Acyuta! It is solely out of a desire to please you—that is, out of a wish to gratify you, and not with any other motive in view—that the multitude of Buddhas, the assembly of the wise, worships you with sacrifices (makhaiḥ) on the golden-mouthed river (kanakamukharī), that is, on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī at Veṅkaṭādri. For it is your own teaching that "I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices"; thus, the sense is that they worship you as the enjoyer of all sacrifices. He worships; he propitiates.
Having realized the Lord, the imperishable inner self of all beings who is to be worshipped,
the wise practice the dharmas solely for his supreme pleasure.

The meaning is that, according to the method described in the *Bhāradvāja-pariśiṣṭa*, she performs sacrificial rites and other duties solely for the sake of pleasing You. She is called "sallakṣaṇā" because she possesses the *lakṣaṇas*—the marks or characteristics—of the virtuous (*sat*). The suffix *-ac* is used here in the sense of possession, as the group beginning with *arśas* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. In this context, the characteristic of both the virtuous and those possessing the marks of the virtuous is stated as follows:
"A husband’s conduct consisting of knowledge is said here to be dear to Viṣṇu;
those who are devoted to that which exists [in him] are proclaimed as the virtuous (*santaḥ*)."
Thus,
there shall be a branding on their limbs with the heated divine weapons of the Lord,
and they shall always wear the vertical *puṇḍra* mark made from the earth extracted from the field of Hari.
Having begun thus:
"The wise know the designations by name and the characteristics of Viṣṇu, as well as of those sentient and insentient beings who take refuge in Him."

Up to this point, that which is stated in the *Bhāradvāja-pariśiṣṭa* should be understood. This assembly of wise ones, sacrificing to you solely for the sake of pleasing you, in this act of sacrifice—how could she not be one who "abandons her own purpose" (*jahatsvārthā*)? That is to say, she would indeed be one who abandons her own purpose. [As it is said:
"Having renounced all actions in Me with a mind centered on the Supreme Self..."
Having become free from desire and free from the sense of "mine"...

The sense is this: for this assembly of wise ones who, in accordance with your teachings, perform all actions solely as a form of worship to you, considering them to be for your gratification, no desire for any other purpose can possibly arise. By this it is shown that: "That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits, having composed the mind with the thought 'the sacrifice must simply be offered,' is characterized by goodness (sāttvika)."

By the manner stated above, the sattvic nature of the sacrifices performed by him is illuminated. By this very epithet *jahatsvārtha* ("one who has abandoned his own self-interest"), her status as a supreme *ekāntin* (exclusive devotee) is demonstrated. For those who are supreme *ekāntins*, because their sole delight is in the service of the Lord (*bhagavad-dāsya*), they do not desire even the slightest personal goal apart from His propitiation. As it is said in the *Bharadvāja-saṃhitā*: "That man who, seeking some fruit, takes refuge in Hari, the Supreme Lord of all, while being averse to other [goals], is a supreme *ekāntin*."

He who has entrusted his entire burden to the Lord of Śrī and whose sole life-purpose is service—such a person is a supreme exclusive devotee (paramaikāntin); these two are indeed remembered as Vaiṣṇavas.

Thus [it is said]. In the first half of the verse, the meaning is indeed not additional. However, in the second half—specifically in the phrase "he worships here at Kanakamukharī"—if that indication (*lakṣaṇā*) were to abandon its own primary sense (*jahatsvārthā*), how could it not be a "good indication" (*sallakṣaṇā*), that is, the operation of a word known as indication? The point is that, just as in the case of "the hamlet on the Ganges," there must certainly be indication here as well through the abandonment of the primary sense.

It may be *jahallakṣaṇā* where, having abandoned its own primary meaning (*svārtha*), there is an application to another [meaning]. This is according to the definition: "Where there is an application to the meaning of another through the abandonment of one's own primary meaning, that is *jahallakṣaṇā*"—this is its sense. And here, in the phrase "in the Kanakamukharī," because the literal object—the flowing current—is unfit for connection with the act of performing a sacrifice, the word *Kanakamukharī* abandons its own primary meaning and functions in reference to the bank, which is related to its own primary meaning; thus, it should be understood that this is *lakṣaṇā* that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*).

Here, within the context of the practice established by the Gītā, the Bhagavad-śāstra, and other such works, there is the superimposition of the practices found in unrelated treatises on logic (nyāya) and so forth.

Just as one who has resorted to the mountain of the serpent-king (Śeṣa) to attain the supreme goal of man—what person here would doubt that this middle course of action achieves its own purpose without abandoning it? (767)

The term *madhyamavṛttiḥ* means a middling way of life (*madhyamā vṛttiḥ*). That surrender (*prapatti*) whose characteristics are about to be described is so designated; that is to say, persons characterized by surrender, just as in the expression "the spearmen enter," one refers to persons characterized by spears. To attain—that is, to obtain—the supreme human goal, which consists of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), she dwells upon the mountain of the Serpent-King (*phaṇādharagiri*); thus she is called "she whose own purpose is the supreme human goal" (*avijahatsvārthaḥ paramapuruṣārtho yāṃ sā*).
One who has abandoned both the [excessive] means and the [extreme] avoidance relies upon this middling way of life.
Having resolved, "He will protect me," and having relinquished one's own sphere of concern,
one should awaken to that God of gods, the Protector, the Supreme Person.

Thus, according to the path taught in the Lakṣmītantra, a person who has taken refuge in the Blessed One, established in a state of conduct that stands between means and the avoidance of means, [should know]:
"Where the divine Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self, resides—
that is the supreme holy Brahman, that is the sacred ford, that is the grove of asceticism."

The distilled meaning is this: on the Venkata mountain—which, according to the manner stated in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, is fit for the residence of those who have taken refuge, and where all the celestial sages (*devarṣis*), perfected beings (*siddhas*), and those whose wealth is austerity (*tapodhana*) dwell—he, having made his abode, accomplishes the supreme human goal he desires. Regarding this matter, who indeed would doubt? The sense is that even a common person (*pāmara*) would not entertain any uncertainty concerning the attainment of such a supreme human goal. [Grammatically,] this is the third person singular imperative (*loṭ*) in the active voice derived from the root *diha* (meaning "to increase") preceded by the prefix *sam*.
Regarding the nature of means (*upāya*) and non-means (*apāya*), it is stated in that very *Lakṣmītantra*: "O Ambikā, what is the state between means and non-means?
All ritual action (*kriyā*) indeed relies upon the very nature of means and non-means."
Whether in the case of acceptance or rejection, the scriptures of injunction and prohibition clearly reveal that action consists of means and ends.
To Śakra, who asked thus, [the Lord said]:
"O Lord of Gods, behold the threefold, profound course of karma; learn from me that threefold nature as it is set forth in the treatises on prohibitions and injunctions."
Some action accomplishes what is not beneficial, while some accomplishes what is beneficial;
certain action is taught for the purpose of avoiding what is harmful.
Thus, the threefold classification of actions should be understood by one whose eye is the scripture;
however, one should set aside the first two categories, which are designated as "misfortune" and "means."
The third category is twofold: one heap consists of the avoidance of misfortune, while another consists of expiation, which destroys misfortunes that have already arisen.
A wise person should not even consider that portion [of the gift] as belonging to the previous owner, just like the rest of the mass;
for that which is being given does not accrue to anyone else’s purpose.
One should perform that action which does not lead to harm even if it results in non-action;
for this is the Vedic steadfastness consisting of the means, the avoidance, and the middle way.
Abiding in this, one should take refuge in Janārdana, the Lord of the World.

Thus it was spoken by the Blessed Śrī Lakṣmī herself. And this has been explained by the venerable teacher Vātsyavarada: "In this context, acts such as violence and theft are means for achieving what is harmful, whereas optional rites (kāmya) are means for achieving what is beneficial."
Likewise, the construction of shrines and so forth; likewise, the practice of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth;
likewise, the means consisting of ritual action, Sāṃkhya, and so forth; and likewise, penance and so forth.
One should never perform rituals such as the Cāndrāyaṇa,
even if they are prescribed for the purpose of averting a future misfortune.
The twilight worship, the five great sacrifices, and so forth, are honored by those seeking liberation;
as are the occasional rites such as the Agrayana sacrifice and the Sīmantonnayana ceremony.
