When there is eligibility, twice-born men should perform the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna);
they should not perform other acts known as prohibited or optional (kāmya) means.
One should perform those specific expiations that are prescribed for one who has sought refuge, as taught by Kamalā in the Lakṣmītantra regarding the sacred occasion.

By such [statements] as these: here, in the word *prapatti* (resort) within the context (*pakṣe*), there occurs the middle function (*madhyamavṛtti*) known as *ajahatsvārthā* (non-abandoning of its own primary meaning). Among the functions enumerated in sequence as *abhidhā* (denotation), *lakṣaṇā* (indication), and *vyañjanā* (suggestion), the middle one is the function called *lakṣaṇā*, which is the operation of the word. In the phrase "the resort was inhabited" (*prapattir adhyuṣitā*), the word *prapatti* functions with respect to the person possessing the resort, in order to bring about the accomplishment of the residence on the mountain of the Serpent-King (*phaṇādharagiri*), which is the locus of the resort. Here, because the resort itself is connected to the action through its association with the person, it is *ajahallakṣaṇā*.
When another [meaning] is implied for the sake of establishing one's own [meaning], it is called "non-abandoning indication" (ajahallakṣaṇā).

This is because of the definition [of *lakṣaṇā*]. Where that which is related to its own expressed meaning (*svavācya*) is indicated (*lakṣyate*) for the sake of establishing the connection of its own expressed meaning, there it is *ajahallakṣaṇā*; such is the meaning. Here, in the usage belonging to the Bhagavat’s scripture, the superimposition of the usage belonging to another scripture is exactly as before.

In this regard, the following must be noted: the verses beginning with "He occupied the supreme station" (*paramaṃ padamadhyavasat*), excluding the verse "O Lord, whose power is well-known" (*suviditaśaktiṃ svāmin*), have been treated as examples of *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis) merely on the basis of the presence of a manifestation of that specific function known as *lakṣaṇā* (indication), which is considered by rhetoricians and others to be necessary for the comprehension of various meanings residing in those respective words, through the medium of a description of something irrelevant (*aprastutavyavahāra*).

However, when the manifestation of the treatment of the non-contextual subject (aprakṛtadharmī) is rooted in the employment of a qualifier common to both the contextual and non-contextual subjects, that is the very form of *samāsokti* (condensed expression); and this [form] does not easily find scope in the verses under discussion. This is because the non-contextual subject, in the form of the *tattvamasi* principle and so forth, is denoted by the words *tat* and so on themselves; and furthermore, because no qualifier whatsoever is employed that is common to both the contextual subject—such as the Lord situated upon the peak of Śiva’s serpent-couch—and the non-contextual subject in the form of the *tattvamasi* principle and so forth.

Although, by resorting to the *lakṣaṇā* known as "abandonment of a portion" (*tadbhāgatyāga*), the meanings of the two words *tat* and *tvam*—namely, the one who resorts to the peak of the serpent [Śeṣa] after traveling as far as the Supreme Abode (*paramapada*), and the splendor of the Lord residing in that Supreme Abode—may be determined as non-different through paronomasia (*śleṣa*) because they possess the capacity to convey meanings caused by resorting to such *lakṣaṇā*, so too are those two respective meanings present in the other words as well.

Nevertheless, these two [the object and the attribute] are not perceived as qualifiers of anything at all, much less of both the relevant (prakṛta) and the irrelevant (aprakṛta); thus the subtle truth will be clarified. In that case, these examples will once again belong exclusively to the domain of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) concerning both the relevant and the irrelevant.

Alternatively, because of the recourse to the *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (the indicative function consisting in the abandonment of a portion of the literal meaning), there arises—by implication within the context at hand—the cognition of a non-contextual usage characterized by two words. This cognition occurs with the intention that [the subject] is the possessor of its own radiance, acting as the agent who, after traveling as far as the supreme state (*paramapada*), takes refuge on the peak of the serpent-king’s hood; and thus, while being a qualifier of the contextual Lord, it possesses the quality of conveying a meaning based on the recourse to the *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* accepted by the proponents of non-contextual figures of speech such as *alaṃkāra*. It is with this intent that [the word] "supreme" (*paramam*) is used here.

The word *padam* refers to the verse (*padya*) which has been presented as an illustration of *samāsokti*. However, if one were to accept the rule that the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), when it enters into the body of *samāsokti*, must necessarily be expressed by words (*śābdatā-niyama*), then, according to the reasoning stated above, this would instead become an illustration of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). This same principle should be inferred for other verses as well.

O Lord of the mountain of the serpent-king, just as the utterance of Your name—which brings joy to the world—automatically entails the utterance of the word "pūrva" (the former), which effects a faultless state for a person. (768)

O Maker of the stainless state! Bestower of divine destiny! Lord of the mountain that supports the serpents! When there is the grasping—that is to say, the utterance—of Your names, such as Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, Hari, and so forth, [the following occurs]: the word "of You" (tava) is to be supplied here as well, referring to the Supreme Person (puṃsaḥ puruṣasya) who is the cause of the entire universe, according to the manner stated in the verse, "The First-born even of the ancients. The sense is: "even of You, who are difficult to grasp even for yogis."

The grasping [of the self] should occur spontaneously, independent of any further effort, as a process of subjugation by making oneself the intended object for the offering of the self, according to the method stated in the mantra: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee for the Great Brahman; Om—thus one should unite the self."
The single syllable "Om" is the direct designator of Vāsudeva;
by the mere utterance of "Om," the Supreme is brought into manifestation.
Through the yoga of the twelve syllables, that which is far away is here at hand;
as soon as it is remembered, O subtle twelve-syllable great mantra.
Hari is perceived with great ease when reflected in the mirror of the mind;
therefore, Janārdana [is attained] through the self-study of the twelve-syllable mantra.
"Swiftly one whose mind is dedicated to Brahman attains proximity [to Him];
thus,
that man who utters the name 'Hari' even involuntarily..."
What need is there for other means? Hari will become subject to his control.
The meaning is that this is because of the statement in the *Bhagavat-śāstra*, which is the supreme Dharma-śāstra of Śāṇḍilya.

In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), the word division (*cheda*) is as follows: in *jagadānandakṛtaḥ*, it is *jagadānanda* [with a vocative ending], and in *anaghagatiḥ*, it is *anagha*. "O Jagadānanda! O cause of the world's bliss! O Anagha! O one whose sins have been destroyed! Here, by the inclusion of the *kṛt* suffix, the inclusion of even that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or an agentive case-factor (*kāraka*) occurs; thus, the meaning of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—namely, "when a *kṛt* suffix is mentioned, that which is preceded by a prefix or an agentive factor is also included"—is demonstrated.

Therefore, it should be understood that according to the rule prescribing compounds—*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32)—the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] implies that a compound occurs even with a *kṛdanta* word preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*, just as in *nakhabhinna* ("split by the nails") from *nakhair bhinnaḥ*, so too in cases such as *nakhanirbhinnaḥ* ("pierced by the claws of a lion") from *nakhair nirbhinnaḥ*. Here, a *gati* is a word listed in the group of *prādi* prefixes, synonymous with *upasarga*, based on the grammatical injunction: *upasargāḥ kriyāyoge gatiśca* (Pāṇini 1.4.59).

The grammatical factors (kārakas), such as the object (karman) and the instrument (karaṇa), are well-known. Here, the linguistic conventions of grammar are superimposed upon the conventional usage found in the Blessed One’s teachings.

Just as the *visarjanīya* at the end of a word placed after the head (*śiras*)—even when it is unaccented (*asamasta*)—attains the status of a *sattva*, so too, alas, O Blessed One, a human being is reckoned among those who have transcended the *yoga-vāhas*. (769)

O Blessed One! Those who carry out yoga are *yogavāhas* (active practitioners); those by whom [yoga] is not carried out are *ayogavāhas*, meaning those devoid of meditation upon You. Even if such a person is counted among them, at the end—meaning even if he is excluded from the assembly of the virtuous—that man (*manuja*), being equal (*sama*) to all [others], [should place his devotion] at Your feet (*pade*). Here, the word division is *samaḥ te*. At Your feet (*tava pade caraṇe*), "beyond the head" (*śirasaḥ parataḥ*) means above the head (*śīrṣād ūrdhvam*), that is, upon the crown of the head (*śīrṣe*).

For instance, in the sense of "a hawk on the treetop," one also observes the usage "a hawk beyond the treetop. When [the mind] is placed or fixed, he is "samaḥ" (equal/even), meaning "good"; for the *Medinī* states: "In the case of words meaning 'all,' 'good,' or 'equal,' the term *sama* may function like its referent. Or, according to the direction stated in "equal toward both friend and foe," he is "sarvasamaḥ" (equal toward all). Alternatively, there is a word-break as *asamaḥ*; the meaning is that he is "asadṛśaḥ" (unequaled). He resorts to *sattva*. For it is said: "The Great Puruṣa is indeed the Lord; He is the instigator of *sattva*."

The meaning is that, according to the manner stated in the Śruti, by the power of placing one’s head at the lotus-feet of the Lord who impels the quality of goodness (sattva), one attains the state of goodness (sāttvikatā) or the nature of being (sat-bhāva), just like Bali, the lord of the Dānavas. In the alternative [grammatical] sense, when the word *pada* is placed—that is, employed—after the word *śiras*, following the word *śiras* (i.e., in the compound *śiraḥpada*), and having entered into a compound (*samasta*), otherwise the *satva* (the substitution of *t* for *d*) to be mentioned would not occur, because of the governing rule: “In a compound, [the substitution occurs] for [the *d* of] *pada* when it does not stand as a final member.”

The *ayogavāha* sounds—namely the *anusvāra*, *visarga*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya*—are so designated by the venerable Patañjali because he has prescribed those technical names for them. Among these, the *visarjanīya* (the *visarga*) occurring at the end of a word ending in the word *śiras* also attains *satva* (becomes the letter *s*). The sense is this: although the rule "the *visarjanīya* becomes *s*" (*visarjanīyasya saḥ*) would normally apply when followed by a hard consonant (*kharparka*), that rule is set aside as an exception; instead, by the rule "in the case of the words *adhas* and *śiras*, [the *visarga* becomes *s*] when followed by a vowel or a soft consonant" (*adhaśśirasī pade*), the *visarjanīya* is specifically ordained to become *s*. This applies here as well.
Even a sinner, by receiving upon his head the sandals of the God of gods, becomes pure in essence (sāttvika) and goes to that very abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, linguistic conventions derived from the science of grammar are superimposed upon the reality established by the teachings of the Blessed One.

Just as the noble *Bhāgavatagītā*, narrated by Vaiśampāyana, which Kamalā herself proclaims, pacifies the fear of living beings, being intent upon the instruction of beloved peace; so too [is this work]. 770.

The word *vai* is a separate particle. It means she is to be described as being like lightning (*vidyut*) because her color is celebrated in such Vedic texts as “of sun-like hue” and “of golden hue,” which describe the path or course of lightnings (*śampā*, i.e., *śatahradā*). Alternatively, *śampā* means the thunderbolt (*dambholi*); she is the one who has attained its path, or she who is reached by the thunderbolt. In either case, the meaning is that she is the wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra. According to the *Anekārthadhvanikośa*: “*Śampā* [means] lightning, the thunderbolt, and *śampā*. By that [term], she is to be described:
“Obeisance to you, O you who are born from the ocean; obeisance to you, O you who are born from the lotus.”
Obeisance to you, whose abode is the lotus of the heart, the consort of Nārāyaṇa.

The meaning is that she was praised by the king of the gods (Indra) with such verses as, "I bow to the mother of all worlds, born from the ocean," and so forth, in the *Lakṣmītantra*, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, and other texts. Alternatively, she is so called because the *Lakṣmītantra* and other works were to be told—that is, taught—to Śampāyana, who is Indra; the sense is that the *Lakṣmītantra* was taught to Indra by Lakṣmī herself.

In this context, *vaiśampāyana* is a single word. It means "to be told" (*kathanīyā*), derived from the root *kath* with the suffix *anīyar* in the sense of the object, according to the rule *tayoreva*. Thus, the meaning is that it was taught to Janamejaya by the supreme sage Vaiśampāyana. The term *udārabhāgavatagītā* refers to those noble *bhāgavatas*—the devotees of the Lord—who have been praised by the Lord Himself as "all these are indeed noble" (*udarāssarva evaite*). These are the generous devotees of the Lord, namely the four types of virtuous people mentioned in such passages as "O Arjuna, four kinds of people who have performed meritorious deeds worship Me": the distressed (*ārta*), the seeker of knowledge (*jijñāsu*), the seeker of wealth (*arthārthin*), and the man of wisdom (*jñānin*).

For whatever those [devotees] receive from the Blessed One, they give it all back to Him; such is their generosity (*audārya*). By them this *Gītā*—in one sense, the *Bhāgavatī Gītā*, meaning the *Bhagavadgītā Upaniṣad*—has been sung. It is so called because it is generous (*udārā*) toward those who recite and listen to it. Its generosity consists in its bestowing the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) upon those who study and hear it, or alternatively, in its greatness among the narratives existing within the *Mahābhārata*. As Amarasimha states: "The word *udāra* applies to a donor and to something great."

She is so described because she has applied her effort toward the instruction—that is, the command issued out of an excess of affection—for the sake of the peace of her beloved Lord, which consists in the calming of the surge of anger provoked by the description of the transgressions of those who have taken refuge in Him.
"O Mother, like a father, your beloved is ever intent on the flow of welfare toward a person whose offense is complete; yet, at times, he may become clouded in intellect."
"Who in this world is so free from fault that you, our mother, would cause them to forget their own kin through such appropriate means? You are indeed that for us."
The sense is that, according to the manner described above, [the devotee's] sole activity is the propitiation of the Lord's mind.
In this regard:
"For men who are long occupied solely with offenses and are thus unworthy..."
In seeking refuge with her husband, she herself first took up the role of active human effort.
Acting out of affection, she nurtures her husband with maternal love and other virtues; at the time of his spiritual practice, she increases his power of knowledge and other faculties.

And such things as these should be remembered. It is so called because it contains two sections (*parvan*): *Śānti*, which produces joy for those who hear it when it is dear to them, and *Anuśāsana*. And it is so called because it contains the section *Udyoga*, which is beneficial and bestows the highest good (*śreyas*). Kamalā (Lakṣmī) pacifies the fear of worldly existence (*bhava-bhaya*) for *bhavins*—those wandering in *saṃsāra*. Here, the distinction lies in the superimposition (*āropa*) of the usage of the *Bhārata-saṃhitā* upon the context of the usage found in scriptures such as the *Pañcarātra*.
Or, for example:
O Acyuta, in you—whose splendor is most renowned, who are the foremost in the worlds, and whose nature is divine—shines forth exceedingly your eternal state, which is not common to all.

O Divyasvabhāḥ! (O You whose nature is divine!)—addressing Him whose radiance is of the kind described by such passages as “There the sun does not shine” and “By His light all this shines. O Acyuta! In that one of “suprathatejasi” (splendidly renowned luster)—that is, in Him whose splendor is thus designated. For “tejas” (luster) means independence from auxiliary causes. As it has been said: “Luster is the state of non-dependence on another.
Indeed, that which is the lack of dependence on auxiliaries in the performance of all effects [is luster].
Those who know the truth declare this sixth quality to be fire.
And thus: "Or rather,
O King, like the sun, you shall cover the Kurus with your splendor"—
by this, the capacity for overcoming enemies has been demonstrated.

"Tejas (splendor) is defined by some as the capacity for overcoming others," so it is said; the meaning is "the primary cause of the worlds. By these epithets, such passages as "The one of great power, of great luster; the one of great splendor, the great serpent; the bearer of vigor, splendor, and radiance; the perfection, the beginning of all, the infallible (Acyuta)" are recalled. Therefore, in You—who are not common to all and are distinct from the entire world—there is a "constant" (nitya), eternal state; "vaśī" means one who possesses mastery (vaśa), that is, sovereignty; the meaning is that existence (bhāva) or being (sattā) persists through the distinction of such sovereignty.

The phrase "the controller of all" (*sarvasya vaśī*) is what is intended here. Alternatively, *vaśī* means a state (*bhāva*), an action (*kriyā*), or a manifestation (*vibhūti*) characterized by mastery (*prābhava*). Or else, *vaśa* means birth; that which possesses this is *vaśī*. *Vaśībhāva* is the state of one who was previously *avaśin* (lacking mastery) becoming *vaśin* (possessing mastery); the suffix *cvi* is used here to denote the transition from not being something to becoming that thing. The word is split as *anitya* [iti]. The sense is that it is "impermanent" (*anitya*), meaning it occurs only occasionally because it is not subject to karma but is instead governed by will. Alternatively, the construction is *bhāvo vaśī*; here, *bhāva* means birth.

"Vaśī" means one who possesses *vaśa*. *Vaśa* signifies desire (*icchā*), meaning "subject to will. The intended sense, however, remains as explained previously. In this regard, passages such as "He assumes at will a body of vast proportions according to his desire" should be kept in mind. For this very reason, the previously mentioned meaning [of being subject to change] is not applicable here. Alternatively, the word "jagatām" (of the worlds) is connected directly with this term: "the state of being under the control (*vaśībhāva*) of the worlds," that is, dependence. Hemacandra states: "*Vaśa* is used in the senses of birth, longing, dependence, and sovereignty. Consequently, he shines forth—that is, he manifests—most intensely. In this interpretation, the meaning of the first [term, *ādya*] is precisely "the cause of the entire world and so forth."
"This world, including all things moving and unmoving, exists under the control of Kṛṣṇa"—
this is what must be remembered here.
*Bhāva* refers to existence, essence, intention, activity, self, and birth.
In the objects of ritual play and among those beings who are wise regarding his manifestations.
Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. The intended meaning is that the entire world is dependent upon you in the manner described.

In the alternative interpretation (*pakṣe*), the word division is *suprathate* and *divyasvabhāva*. O *divyasvabhāva* (O one of divine nature)! O *acyuta* (O Imperishable One)! It shines—that is, it is manifest—in the first [word], the word *prathama*, which is not common to all (i.e., not found among all words), even though it is non-existent [as such] due to its equality with the word *sarva*. Amara states in his list of synonyms for "equal" (*tulya*) that "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) and "same" (*samāna*) are equivalent. The word "even" (*api*) is understood here by implication, as in the verse "not even a slight pain of duality exists here. This means: even though [the word *prathama*] is not listed in the *sarvādi* group [of pronouns].

In the case of *jas* (the nominative plural suffix), there is the substitution of *śī*; that is, the replacement by the form *śī*. The word "anitya" (non-eternal) is the division [of the compound]. It is "non-eternal," meaning it is optional; thus, it is proclaimed—that is, well-established—among the worlds. The sense is that, according to the rule *prathamacaramataya* (Pāṇini 1.1.33), even for the word *prathama*, which is not a pronominal (*asarvanāman*), the substitution of *śī* is taught as being optional specifically in the case of *jas*. Here, there is a superimposition of a usage established in grammatical treatises upon the well-known usage found in such works as the *Sahasranāmādhyāya*.
Just as a thief who has been repeatedly caught in a multitude of villages may, even when forbidden, compel me to perform some necessary auspicious act for his own sake— so may Śauri [Viṣṇu] do so.

He who is Śauri, possessing many abodes and immeasurable splendor, was once born in Vraja; though born in the cowherd settlement of Nanda and forbidden—though restrained by Yaśodā and others—he became a *malimluca*, a thief of milk, curds, butter, and the like. [The word *malimluca* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that resembles a verbal form. That Śauri, regarding his own domain, performed what was necessary and mandatory, for there is no auspicious Vedic action more meritorious than the worship of Viṣṇu.

"May [He] cause me to perform the worship and other rites described above. The verbal root *kṛ* takes two objects according to the rule *hṛkroranyatarasyām*. In one sense, "in many ways" means "many times"; or rather, it means "in various modes," that is, without restriction during the months beginning with Caitra and ending with Āśvina. This is because an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) may occur within those very months. A "troop of months" (*māsavraja*) refers to a collection of lunar months; Amara states: "A cow-pen, a path, or a multitude are called *vrajas*. That which exists in such a troop is "born in the troop of months" (*māsavrajabhū*).
[This occurs] when thirty-two months and sixteen days have passed.
An intercalary month occurs every four ghaṭikās.

Because of this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*): "That which is *malimluca*—this month of sixty days—is the *malimluca* in its first half. The meaning is that it is an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), characterized as described above. And its state of being *malimluca*...
The evil occurring within the year destroys the fruit of sacrifices;
it is beset by Nairṛtas and Yātudhānas who bring about destruction.
"One should know that month to be *malimluca* (intercalary), which is devoid of the *saṃkrānti* of the Sun and is overcome by thieves; it is censured in all ritual acts.
According to this statement of Śātātapa, it should be understood that [the month] is "overcome" because it is seized by thieves and *yātudhānas* (demons).
The word *malimluca* refers to a specific month, a thief, or fire;
thus says the *Medinī*. That month which is *malimluca*, even though it is prohibited, is designated as a sinful month.
Having abandoned that [impurity], one should perform the rites for the ancestors, gods, and others on the following day.

"Because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa): 'That month which is excluded from the ancestors and the gods is designated as sinful,' the sense is that this occurs only occasionally, when such a possibility exists.

May he cause me to perform the auspicious and propitious rites—such as the *sīmantonnayana* and others—which are mandatory within his own domain and must necessarily be performed at their fixed times."
In matters prescribed for a month-long duration, there is no impairment caused by the retrogression (moḍhya) of Jupiter or Venus;
nor do defects such as the intercalary month (adhimāsa) apply, due to the power of the rules governing time.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Here, while a Purāṇic narrative is the subject under discussion, there is the superimposition of legal procedures from the Dharmaśāstras upon that which is not the primary subject; this constitutes its distinction from the previous types [of figures].
O Lord,
just as all auspicious qualities shine forth without pride within You, so too does auspiciousness and conduct such as prosperity shine for those who abide by Your command.

Here, within the scriptural discourse of the Śruti, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth, there is the superimposition of the technical terminology of the science of prosody (chandaśśāstra). To illustrate: the analysis (*cheda*) is *sakala-śubha-gaṇā asmayā iti*. Thus, *asmaya* means "one who possesses no *smaya*"—that is, pride (*garva*). As the *Medinī* and *Viśva* lexicons state: "The word *smaya* occurs in the senses of wonder and pride; *smaya* [is used] in the sense of pride and wonder. Furthermore, as stated in the *Śrī Rāmāyaṇa*: "He was neither arrogant nor envious; the wise man was one whose mind was free from haughtiness."

The analysis of that term is as follows: it is one whose *smaya*—meaning pride or wonder—is non-existent; for it is stated in that very same [text]: "He is possessed of vigor, yet he is not amazed by his own great vigor. Alternatively, it is a genitive *bahuvrīhi* compound, like the word *anuttama*, meaning "one from whom no marvelous thing (*smaya*) exists";
as in: "O Brahman, for me who beholds you, in whom all wonders on earth, in the sky, or in the water reside, what here could be considered a marvel?"

The meaning is: “O treasure-house of all wonders,” in the manner spoken by Akrūra. Alternatively, having split the word *smaya* as *smaya iti*, it is an address: “O Smaya! The meaning is exactly as stated; furthermore, the passage beginning with “the beholding of many wonders” should also be considered here. O Īśa! O Lord of All! For the Śruti says: “The one God rules over the perishable self... the Lord sustains the manifest and unmanifest universe... He is the Lord of All. etc.

"Upon you rest all the hosts of auspicious things"—meaning she in whom the entire multitude of blessings is interwoven. She is thus described as "the Mother of these worlds," and so forth. Alternatively, because the power of the word is not restricted by any limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in this designation, the meaning of "Mother" (mātā) itself is "the progenitor of the entire universe. One may also read the word as *ābhā*; that which shines everywhere (*ā samantāt bhāti*) is *ābhā*. From the root *bhā* with the suffix *kvip*, it means "pervading the universe."
Just as the world is pervaded by me through my own form and nature, so too is all this pervaded by her; she is likewise the sovereign controller.

Thus it is stated in the *Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā*. Alternatively, she is "Ābhā" because her radiance (*bhā*) shines everywhere (*ā*); that is to say, her splendor faces all directions. This is according to such Vedic passages as: "The moon-like, radiant, blazing, and satisfied one. She is "Na-sajarā" (not co-existing with old age), meaning she does not possess old age. The compound "na-sajarā" is formed by the rule *sup-supā* (joining nouns with other nouns). For, in accordance with the manner described in Vedic texts such as "He transcends old age and death; he is free from old age, free from death," she—like the Lord—is beyond old age, and thus her state of being the opposite of all that is to be rejected is unimpeded. Therefore, it is said in the *Lakṣmī-tantra*:
I am the beloved goddess of my beloved god of gods, Viṣṇu, who is endowed with excellent qualities; I am eternally the supreme one, consisting of knowledge and bliss.
Blameless and possessing blameless limbs, she was always devoted to his dharma.
Thus,
I am that supreme Vaiṣṇava reality named Nārāyaṇī, endowed with eternal, faultless, and boundless auspicious qualities.

And so forth. Alternatively, the analysis of the verse is: *mātā abhā na sa-jarā* (the mother is not lusterless, nor is she with old age). The particle *na* follows both [parts] according to the "middle jewel" (*madhyamaṇi*) maxim. She is not *abhā*—that is, not lusterless—but rather possesses radiance (*saprabhā*). By means of the double negation, even the possibility of her being occasionally lusterless is excluded; for Āmanasimha states: "Two negations serve to exclude a suspected negation. Nor is she *sajarā*. The meaning is exactly as stated. The verb *bhavati* ("she is") is to be supplied.

The meaning is that you are distinguished by unimpeded great majesty (*mahāvibhūti*), because even when not explicitly employed [by others], you exist as the object of their speech. For this very reason, the term *tvacchanda* refers to those who abide in your *chanda*; according to Amara, "the two terms *chanda* and *abhiprāya* signify intention. Thus, "those who abide in that" means those who do not transgress your intention, as in the expression "those who follow your profound mind. Alternatively, it means those who possess a state of dependence upon you.

The sense is: "of those people who have become nothing but skin [remaining]. *Śubham* means auspiciousness; *śrīḥ* is prosperity; *prabhā* is luster; that which has these as its beginning—by the word "beginning," fame and so forth are included—is what is meant. *Vṛttam* is conduct corresponding to that [virtue], and this shines forth or becomes manifest. The underlying idea is: "What is unattainable when the Blessed One, the abode of Śrī, is pleased? For Viṣṇu is the bestower of all fruits. Thus, for those who follow the will of the Blessed One—the giver of all fruits—such a distinction is not difficult to obtain.

In this context, the division of the verse is: *sakala-śubha-gaṇāḥ sma yam-ātā-bhā-na-sa-jarāḥ*. O Lord! Regarding you, the groups (*gaṇas*) consisting of *ya*, *ma*, *ta*, *bha*, *na*, *sa*, *ja*, and *ra*—even though there are long vowels among these initial letters (*mādi-varṇeṣu*), they are pronounced as short *a*-vowels (*akāra*) for the sake of ease of pronunciation when followed by letters beginning with *yādi*. These groups, designated as *yamatabhanasaja-ra*, are entirely auspicious. The eight three-syllable groups (*trikāḥ*) here are as follows: 1. *sarva-guru* (all heavy): ***sss** 2. *mukha-anta-laghu* (light at the beginning and end): **sIs** 3. *ya-ra-anta-guru* (heavy at the end, light in the middle): **IsS** 4. *madhya-ādi-guru* (heavy in the middle and at the beginning): **SI** 5. *ja-bha* (light in the middle and heavy at the beginning): **IS** 6. *tri-la* (three lights): **III** 7. *na* (all light): ***II** 8. *aṣṭau* (the eighth): **SI** Thus, these are the eight three-syllable groups that occur here.

Thus, the groups (gaṇas) well-known in the treatises on prosody (*chandaśśāstra*), consisting of three syllables each, "adhere"—that is, they come to be fixed—within your intellect; that is to say, they became present in your mind. In this sequence, within the triad of syllables beginning with *ya*, the *ya*-group is produced such that it has a light syllable at its beginning.

Thus, by the successive removal of one syllable at a time from the sequence beginning with *mā*, eight *gaṇas* are produced within each triad of syllables: the all-heavy *magaṇa*, the final-light *tagaṇa*, the initial-heavy *bhagaṇa*, the all-light *nagaṇa*, the final-heavy *sagaṇa*, the middle-heavy *jagaṇa*, and the middle-light *ragaṇa*. These are designated by their respective names based on their initial syllables. It should be observed by those with attentive minds that in the phrase "ending in a light" (*laganti*), both the light and the heavy syllables are indicated.

"Of those abiding in Your will": "Your wills" (*chandāṃsi*) refers to the prosodic meters such as *uktā*, *ayuktā*, and so forth; "of those abiding in them" means of those possessing knowledge regarding that [will]. "Auspicious" (*śubham*) means auspicious by its very name, referring to the *vṛtta* (meter) *Śrīprabhā* and others. *Śrī* is the meter defined in the *Uktā* [section] as "gśrīḥ," and *Prabhā* is the meter in the *Jagatī* [section] defined as "svaraśaraviratir nanau rau prabhā"; that which has these as its beginning is [the compound]. The word *vṛttam* refers to verse (*padya*), used in the singular by way of genus (*jāti*). The particle *ca* serves to aggregate what was mentioned previously. For example: [The original Sanskrit verse follows here. ...as in the above.

O friend, having reached the feet of all heavy syllables at the beginning of a guru’s position, by placing light syllables beneath them, you should show the remainder as if above; thus, that which is entirely light becomes perpetually so.

O friend! Having reached—that is, having taken refuge at—the feet (the singular number is used for the class) of all gurus, beginning with one's own preceptor and extending up to the Lord; specifically, beneath the feet of the primordial guru, the Lord, as stated in the injunction: "Salute some primordial guru. The phrase "beneath the feet" means at the base of the feet, according to the manner expressed in such passages as "I take refuge at the root of Your feet.
One should do this quickly and without delay through *nyāsa*—that is, by surrendering the burden of self-protection; one must not hesitate in this matter.
This boat of a body has been purchased by you with the great merchandise of merit;
hasten to reach the far shore of the ocean of suffering before it is shattered.

The sense is that this is because of what has been stated. Alternatively, from the *laghunyāsa* (the easy exposition), meaning by means of *prapadana* (surrender) as a simple expedient in comparison with devotion; the meaning is "having performed *prapadana*. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*) when the suffix *lyap* is elided. It should be understood that the same applies to the previous meaning as well. Here, the meaning expressed in the verse “Having approached the Lord Śrī through the mouth of the Guru” is being kept in mind. The sense is that, as if on top, [it refers to] the feet of the first Guru, just like the feet of the Guru previously shown. The word “his own” (*svam*) is to be supplied; the meaning is “himself” (*ātmānam*).

Show the remainder—that which is residual, whose very nature is to be accepted with the desire to bestow excellence upon another—or rather, show it as being toward the Blessed One, the Lord of the entire universe, who exists above all worlds; the sense is that it is just as it would be toward the feet of the Guru, who is the teacher of all. Thus, "show the remainder" is to be construed. Alternatively, the meaning of "above" (upari) is "as if toward the feet of the Blessed One, which are to be borne upon the heads of all the world. The rest is the same. As it is said: "He who has supreme devotion for the God, and for the Guru as he does for the God..."

According to such scriptural passages as these: "When there is a deficiency"—that is, when a possible deficiency in the limbs (aṅgas) and other factors that ought to be present at the time of practicing the means is suspected—"constantly see the Guru," meaning one's own teacher; this phrase is connected here as well by the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*).
[The disciple says: "Having beheld the Grandfather, Nāthamuni, be gracious, disregarding my conduct."

The sense is: "In the manner described above, show the Teacher so as to propitiate the Blessed One. Therefore (*tat*), from practicing in the aforementioned way, everything that is both complete and easy (*akhilalaghu*)—that is, every desired goal culminating in the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—comes to be, or is accomplished. As Amarasimha states: "The word *laghu* is used for three things: a friend, the small, and the light. And there is the usage: "By means of a brief [vision] of the desired object, both ascetics attained joy toward them. This is explained as "by a brief [means] of the desired [goal]. Or, when:

*Laghu* is a neuter noun meaning black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*) and *śīghra* (quick); it is a masculine adjective meaning light (*laghu*), weak (*nissāra*), or charming (*manojña*); and it is a feminine noun meaning *pṛkkā* (a fragrant plant).

If one accepts that the word *iṣṭa* found in the *Amarakośa*—beginning with "it is desired" (*ityādi*)—denotes "pleasing," based on its singular consistency with the *Abhidhānacintāmaṇi*, then the phrase *akhilalaghu* means "entirely pleasing. The underlying sense is that all this—including the taking of refuge in the lineage of gurus and the surrender at the lotus feet of the Lord—is captivating to the minds of all those who are proficient in the science of Nyāsa.

In this context, the method of expansion (*prastāra*) according to the science of prosody (*chandaśśāstra*) is demonstrated. To explain: O friend! having reached—that is, having written down according to the aforementioned lines—that quarter of the verse (*caraṇa*, the fourth part of the *padya*) which is "all-heavy" (*sarvaguru*), meaning that in which all the heavy syllables are indicated by specific curved lines; [one should place] beneath the first heavy syllable—that is, beneath the first mark indicating a heavy syllable, meaning beneath the specific curved line that denotes it.

According to Amara, "pada" refers to a position, protection, a place, a mark, a foot, or a thing. "Adhas" means below. By the "placement" (nyāsāt) of a short [syllable]—that is, by drawing a specific straight line indicating a short vowel—one writes that [line]. As before, the fifth case is used. "The remainder" (śeṣam) means the rest; "as if above" (uparīva) means as if in the upper row. The sense is: when there is an absence of the lines indicating long vowels above, and the presence of the lines indicating short vowels—that is, in the case of a deficiency [of long marks].

The phrase "show the guru" connects here as well, meaning "show the specific curved line that indicates a heavy syllable. Likewise, "constantly" means again and again, show it thus. This being the case, that "foot" becomes "entirely light," meaning it is that in which all the "lights"—the specific curved lines indicating light syllables—are present. [The procedure for constructing the *prastāra* is: When the foot consists entirely of heavy syllables, place a light syllable under the first heavy syllable;
then, as above, perform the remainder of this method repeatedly.
In the deficient [cases], one should add only heavy syllables until all [syllables] become light;
this is called "prastāra" by those who know the science of metrics (*chandaḥśāstra*).

Thus, the entire meaning of this verse should be investigated as follows: the first meter among all meters has all heavy syllables (sarvaguru) and the last has all light syllables (sarvalaghu); therefore, a quarter-verse (pāda) is likewise of that nature. This being so, when a quarter-verse consisting entirely of heavy syllables is written with curved lines in the shape of a half-moon to conform to the requirements of the meter—this is the sense.

Below the first heavy syllable (āder guroḥ), that is, beneath the initial curved line in the second row, one should place and write a light straight line (laghuṃ ṛjurekhāṃ). Then, just as there are lines indicating heavy and light syllables on the right side of the upper row following the position of the light line above, in that very same manner, one should place the remaining heavy and light lines until the end of the previous row. Furthermore, below that, at the beginning of the third row, one should again apply this same procedure beneath the first heavy syllable.

One should perform [the procedure] beginning with these words and write [the sequence]. In the second row, because there is no preceding *guru*, the first *guru* occurs precisely at the second position. Likewise, in the third [row] and so on, it should be understood that the first [element] occurs precisely at the third position and so forth. Where there is a deficiency—that is, where the writing according to the sequence is lacking—one should place or write only *gurus*, namely curved lines (*vakrarekhā*), in the position to the left of the short-line (*laghurekhā*). To the question of how far one should write in this manner, he says: "as long as" (*yāvat*).

The meaning is that this procedure applies for as long as there may be a foot consisting entirely of light syllables (*laghu*). Thus, in this illustrative verse, it should be noted that the entire expansion (*prastāra*) of the *atyuktā* meter has been demonstrated; for therein there are four metrical patterns (*vṛtta*): first, all-heavy (*dviguru*); second, light-then-heavy (*laghuguru*); third, heavy-then-light (*gurulaghu*); and fourth, all-light (*sarvalaghu*). Here too, the superimposition (*āropa*) is exactly as before.

O Blessed One, may he who, through the vision of you, attains the true essence of his own inner being— such a person is a master of speech, proficient in the Vedic hymns and also skilled in usage within the world.

O Blessed One! By Your vision and by Your glance, whatever person may find within his own mind an innate—that is, natural and not to be abandoned—quality of *sattva* (the quality of purity), that person is indeed to be known as *sāttvika*.
For it is said: "Whatever person Madhusūdana beholds at birth, him one should know to be *sāttvika*; he is truly one who contemplates the goal of liberation."

The meaning is that this follows from the statement in the *Mokṣadharma*. That person is a master of speech (*vācaspati*), being eloquent; as Amara states, “*vāgīśa* and *vākpati* are synonyms. Alternatively, he is equal to Bṛhaspati; as Amara states, “*jīva*, *āṅgirasa*, and *vācaspati* [are synonyms]. He is “virtuous in his desire” (*chandasi sādhuḥ*), meaning his aspirations are noble; the sense is that he does not desire trivial objectives. Or else, he is “virtuous in the *chandas*,” meaning in the Veda; the sense is that he is venerable because he has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*aṅgas*) and appendages (*śiras*).

The word *chandas* takes the seventh case-ending when used with the word *sādhu*, according to the rule: "When *sādhu* and *nipuṇa* are used in the sense of worship, the seventh case is employed provided *aprati* does not follow. Thus, the seventh case is used after the word *chandas* in connection with the word *sādhu*.

*Chandas* refers to meter and the Veda, as well as to one's own conduct and desire—so says the *Medinī* lexicon. From *prayoga*, meaning "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*), and *yoga*, meaning "meditation" (*dhyāna*) because it is not mixed with heterogeneous cognitions (*vijātīyapratyayāsaṃvalitatayā*), [the term] *prayogayoga* is formed. Therefore, even in the world, he is a virtuous person (*sādhu*) and a refined gentleman (*sabhyas*), meaning he is to be venerated for his contemplation of the goal of liberation (*mokṣārthacintaka*). He becomes such a one. He knows that supreme abode of Brahman (*brahmadhāma*), wherein the universe is established and shines forth, radiant.
Those wise ones who, being free from desire, worship the Puruṣa, they indeed transcend this pure light.

The sense is that this is because it is heard [in scripture] that those who know Brahman and those who worship [it] are exempt from rebirth. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The word *sādhu* is used in three senses: for one who is fit, for one who is virtuous, for a refined person, and also for a usurer."

In your view—that is, according to the treatise on grammar (vyākaraṇa)—the word *vācaspati* has its final syllable (*sva*) devoid of the *visarga* (meaning it occupies the position where a *visarga* would normally be). One should find the state of that [word], namely its quality of having the letter *sa* instead of the *visarga*. This is according to the *Ratnamālā*, which states: "The term *darśana* refers to a mirror, a dream, cognition, a treatise, and the sight of the eyes. Thus, one should realize the nature of that [term] as being characterized by the presence of the non-*visarga* *sa*.

The meaning is that, according to the rule *‘ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputrapārapadapayaspoṣeṣu’*, the visarga of the genitive case is prescribed to be replaced by the letter *s*. That term *vācaspati* is correct (*sādhu*) and fit for usage in the *chandas*, that is, the Veda; for it is only in the Veda that the substitution of *s* is prescribed by the aforementioned rule. Even in common worldly usage (*loka*), it becomes correct due to its frequent occurrence in authoritative employment, such as in the phrase *‘vaktā vācaspatiryathā’*; the point is that just as words like *paripanthin* are correct even though they belong exclusively to the domain of the *chandas*.
In this context, within the scriptural discourse of the Vedas, Itihāsas, and so forth, there is the superimposition of the technical usage of grammatical science (*śabdaśāstra*). For example:

"If the Self (*ātmā*), which consists of many verbal roots (*dhātu*), were to find even a slight difficulty in obtaining a suitable suffix (*supapadatā*) [in its expression], it would surely not fail to be resorted to by the wicked; yet, through your vision, it becomes truly trustworthy (*pratyayita*). (776)

O Lord! The *ātman* is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). It is called *sūpapada* because it is easily approached (*sukhenopapadyate*) even slightly (*īṣat*) or minimally (*alpaṃ*) by evil (*durita*) or sin (*vṛjina*). The suffix *khal* will indeed be mentioned later; its state (*bhāva*) being "if" (*iyāt*), the meaning is: "if it should happen to be possessed of some slight evil. "In many ways" (*bahudhā*) means in many modes, that is to say, generally (*prāyeṇa*). That it would not be "resorted to by the wicked" (*khalāśrita�*)—meaning associated with the base—is certainly not the case; the sense is that it would indeed be so.

The word *tu* is used for emphasis; *khalu* is used either to express inquiry or as a poetic ornament (*vākya-alaṃkāra*). As Amara states: "The word *khalu* is used in prohibition, as a poetic ornament, in inquiry, and in conciliation. Indeed, association with the wicked is rooted in evil. As it is said:

"Alas! Association with the wicked is the great fruit of sins. Even he—though thus defiled by association with the wicked—became "convinced" (*pratyayita*) by the sight of you, that is, by the vision of you which is easily obtained through the ripening of accidental or other merits; the meaning is that he became possessed of knowledge, having gained conviction. The particle *iti* is to be connected here as well with the word *syāt*.
The meaning is as stated in the saying: "Ignorance perishes and knowledge arises from the vision of Hari.

In the alternative sense (pakṣe), [the word *īṣaddussūpapadatām*] means: *bahudhātūnām* (of many verbal roots) such as *bhū* and others; *ātmā* (nature/form); *īṣat-dus-śabdābhyām* (by the words *īṣat* and *dus*); *itaḥ* (followed by); *suḥ* (the suffix *su*); *upapadam* (an accompanying word)—that which is designated by the rule "that which stands in the locative case is called an *upapada*"; *tasya bhāvaḥ* (the state of being that). Thus, it means "the state of having *īṣat*, *dus*, and *su* as *upapadas*. Alternatively, the meaning is "having *īṣat* and *dus* as the *upapadas*."

The word *sūpapada* refers to that which has *su* as its preceding member (*upapada*) when joined with *itaḥ*. The compound *īṣadduritasūpapadaḥ* is a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇobhayapada-karmadhāraya*). From that [compound], the suffix *tal* is applied; thus, one might say "the state of being such" (*tattām*). In the phrase *sopi*, the word *api* heard there is displaced in order; it is connected with the word *pratyayita*. Thus, it means "even one in whom confidence has arisen. The word *cet* (if) is also supplied here; the meaning is: "even if he should be one ending in a suffix. It is not the case that he would not be "resorted to by the suffix *khal*" (*khalāśritaḥ*).

The point is this: if any verbal root (*dhātu*) were to have the suffix *khal* prescribed after it with the prefixes *īṣat*, *duḥ*, or *su*—in accordance with the rule "after roots preceded by *īṣat*, *duḥ*, or *su* in the sense of difficulty or ease, the suffix *khal* is applied"—then it would necessarily end in *khal*, just as in the examples *īṣatkaraḥ*, *duṣkaraḥ*, and *sukaraḥ*. It should be understood that the example provided here is merely illustrative, like the one given for the term *sūpapada-tām*. In this case as well, the superimposition (*āropa*) is to be understood in the same manner as before.
O Moon of the Serpent King, do not ever think, "This is a clenched fist," for having seen its incapacity here, this fist is indeed clearly grasped by me.

"O Lord of Serpents! Do not think that this *añjali* (gesture of reverence) made by me is 'contracted'—meaning diminished or incomplete because it was not performed according to the scriptures—and thus do not disregard it; such is the sense. Having seen my incapacity here—the inability to perform the *añjali* correctly—this [gesture] is 'manifest' (*sphuṭaḥ*), meaning it is evident as being performed improperly; the sense is that even here, it has been done in whatever way [possible]."

"Añjali" refers to a specific type of mudrā (hand-gesture) that quickly propitiates the gods, as stated in the verse: "Añjali is the supreme mudrā; it swiftly pleases the deities. It is characterized by two extended hands joined facing one another. As Amarasimha states: "An extended hand is *prasṛti* when the fingers are bent inward; when those two are joined together, it is called *añjali* (masculine)."

By the use of the singular number, it is illuminated that you must not remain indifferent—even though this [request] has been made but once—by you, who are devoted to your dependents in the manner expressed as "I am your servant with joined palms," and who, as the sovereign of supreme compassion, consider even such a small gain as a most significant acquisition. The word *grāhyāḥ* (to be accepted) is used; *hi* is for emphasis, meaning "it must indeed be accepted by you with respect. *Aho* expresses either joy or wonder born from reflecting upon your own incapacity and the supreme compassion of the Blessed One.

This *añjali* gesture, for one who has other purposes, accomplishes those respective purposes; however, it should be understood that for one who has no other purpose, it bestows the supreme human goal culminating in liberation (*niḥśreyasa*). In this regard, even if performed by anyone at any time, in whatever manner, or even just once, directed toward Your feet—
At that very moment, it steals away all inauspicious things without exception,
nourishes auspicious things, and never declines.

O Lord of Elephants, since our union with you— whose fruit is followed by the poison of the suffering of being an elephant— is unimpeded even for those as lowly as worms who have not attained Brahman,
and since it is difficult to overcome due to the force of our accumulated evil karma, this salutation with joined palms is our counter-weapon against your weapon of restraint.
The power of the *añjali* (the hollowed palms joined) described in such passages should be reflected upon.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *homā*, it is *sphuṭaḥ*," the word division is *sphuṭaḥ* and *home*. In the context of *homa*—referring to the *homa* performed with the *añjali* as prescribed by the rule "one should offer oblations with the *añjali*"—this enjoined *añjali* is not to be understood as "contracted" or "closed like a bud. Rather, this is an instruction for someone who might have such a doubt: one should understand that this enjoined *añjali* in this *homa* is *sphuṭaḥ*, meaning "open" or "expanded," having observed its efficacy here. As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *sphuṭa* [means] manifest (*vyakta*) and blossomed (*praphulla*)."

Herein, the meaning of the final *sāmarthya* (capacity) section of the first chapter of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* has been set forth. For in that context, regarding the injunction "one should offer groats with joined palms (*añjali*) into the forest fire," it is considered whether, as in the case of a prayer for the favor of a deity, the mere joining of the hands is to be understood as the *añjali* in this oblation, or whether it must be opened according to its functional capacity.

Having thus raised a doubt and reached the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position that there is no fixed rule because no specific distinction is heard in the scripture, [the Siddhāntin argues as follows]: Since an injunction for an impossible matter cannot exist, one must necessarily admit that capacity (*śakti*) is a concomitant factor for that which enjoins. Therefore, it is the injunction itself—assisted by capacity—that determines the object to be enjoined according to its capability. Consequently, the Siddhānta is established: the restriction of the grinding (*vyākoca*) to the flour-meal (*saktu*) occurs by virtue of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Capacity (*sāmarthya*) means causality;
capacity is indeed causality, as in: "This cuckoo sings from me because of honey."

Thus, from the definition provided with its illustration: just as the denotative power (*abhidhā*) of the word *madhu*—which commonly refers to nectar and other such things—is restricted by the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting in being the cause of the cuckoo’s intoxication to the month of Caitra, which is a single part of spring; so too here, it should be understood that the denotative power of the word *añjali*, which is common to both the contracted and the expanded forms, is restricted to the expanded *añjali* by the functional capacity consisting in being the means for performing the oblation (*homasādhanatā*). Here, the conventions of the Karma-Mīmāṃsā are superimposed upon the usage found in the Pañcarātra Āgamas and similar texts.

O Supreme Soul, the multitude of devotees—whose nature is skilled in the yoga of the sinless, who are fortunate through their service to the venerable guests of the [divine] days, and who approach You with the five-limbed prostration—approaches You. (778)
O Supreme Soul! The virtuous, who are like the fruit of sacred pilgrimage sites, must be served, must be served by those seeking the highest good;
even a moment’s practice of attending upon them shall not be fruitless.

Thus, by serving guests—who possess the qualities described in the dialogue between Cyavana and Nahuṣa—one attains through the worship and honoring of their turns (or arrangements) a state of good fortune, meaning either excellent splendor or excellent renown.
One should recognize as a guest him who has arrived from a long journey, who is weary, and who appears during the Vaiśvadeva offering; one who arrives before that time is not [yet] a guest.
One should never accept as a guest a resident of one's own village;
because he arrives at irregular intervals, he is therefore called an *atithi*.

The meaning is that she has attained good fortune through the hospitable treatment of guests, as defined by Parāśara and others in such passages as: "One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other courtesies."

In this context, *sevyā* is a separate word, meaning "to be served" by those desiring to know the results of their birth [horoscopes] (*jātaka*) and so forth. *Tithayaḥ* refers to the lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*), and *vārāḥ* refers to the days of the week beginning with the Sun and the Moon. *Arcā* is derived from the root *arca* with the suffix *ac*; thus, it means "one who worships the lunar days and weekdays. This also is a separate word. According to the *Ratnamālā*: "The term *vāra* denotes the days of the Sun and others, as well as the two *bṛndāvasaras* (the full and new moon). She is called *Subhagā* because she goes to (*gacchati*) or knows (*jānāti*) the auspicious asterisms (*su-bhāni*), such as Aśvinī and the rest.

"O sinless one," [referring to] the Lord as his sole object; "faultless" (*niravadya*); "one whose self is skilled in the performance of *yoga*, that is, meditation (*dhyāna*), and who possesses a wise mind. Alternatively, "O sinless one" is an epithet of the Lord. *Yogas* are the *viṣkambha* and others; *karaṇas* are *bava*, *bālava*, and so forth. "One whose self is skilled in them" means one whose intellect is trained in discerning their essential nature, qualities, and so on. Regarding *yoga*: "In the attainment of a new object, in conjunction, meditation, and reasoning;
in the steadiness of the body, in application, in the *viṣkambha* and other [astrological] configurations, and in medicine. Thus it is said.
The word *karaṇa* here [refers to] the *bava* and other [lunar-day divisions], the cause, the primary field, the body, the chariot-formation (*rathabandha*), action, the Gītā, and the senses;

thus says the *Medinīratnamālā*. By these three adjectives, his expertise in the *pañcāṅga-karaṇa*—characterized by the determination of lunar days, weekdays, asterisms, yogas, and *karaṇas*—is indicated. Such a multitude of devotees (*bhaktatati*): here, by the word *bhakta*, those established in either the devotion of means (*sādhana-bhakti*) or the devotion of fruit (*phala-bhakti*) are intended, since the Teacher has granted that both are designated by the term *bhakta* in the verse: "Both [types of devotion] have been shown as 'devotion' through the devotion of fruit and the devotion of means."

The five limbs have been described as "the resolve for conformity" (*ānukūlya-saṃkalpa*) and so forth—namely, the resolve for conformity, the avoidance of opposition (*prātikūlya-varjana*), great trust (*mahā-viśvāsa*), the acceptance of [the Lord] as protector (*goptṛtva-varaṇa*), and self-surrender (*kārpaṇya*). By means of that surrender (*prapadana*), which consists of these limbs or exists as an independent form, one approaches You as the means; this is the "entrustment" (*nyāsa*), synonymous with "depositing" (*nikṣepa*), endowed with these five limbs. One should employ that surrender, which is encompassed by its five constituent parts.
As stated in the teachings of the Blessed One:
"The resolve for favorability, the avoidance of unfavorability,
the conviction that [the Lord] will protect, and likewise the seeking of His protection."

Regarding the statement that "the sixfold taking of refuge consists in the wretchedness of self-surrender," this description of the sixfold nature of *prapatti* (surrender) is intended to show the combination of both the subordinate and principal limbs (*aṅga-aṅgin*). This is similar to the designation of "eight-limbed yoga" (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*) despite there being more than eight elements involved; otherwise, it would contradict the scriptural authority shown immediately following in the passage beginning with "endowed with five limbs. Furthermore, the teachers have established that the principal element here consists in the entrusting of the burden (*bhara-nyāsa*), as determined by the statement: "The entrusting of the burden of oneself and one's own is indeed called 'self-surrender' (*ātmanikṣepa*)."

He is characterized by the attainment (*prapadana*)—that is, the acquisition—of the *pañcāṅga*, which is another name for the *tithipatra* (almanac) and reveals the essential nature of the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth; he approaches, reaches, or honors you. Herein lies the distinction: while the context concerns the divine activities prescribed in the Bhagavata scriptures, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the practices belonging to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), which is not the primary subject at hand.
Just as a woman who approaches a man before Hari might attain equality with the virtuous, so too a person, though their state may be lowly, shall never again fall into a base condition.

"Whether dull-witted (*manda*) or even of little capacity (*alpa*," or "unskilled in devotion and so forth"—according to Amara, *amūḍha*, *alpa*, *apaṭu*, *nirbhāgya*, and *manda* are synonyms). By this, the absence of capability in devotion and so forth, as well as the attainment of the aforementioned qualifications and the necessity of taking refuge through human effort (*puruṣakāra*), are indicated."

If, prior to taking refuge in the Blessed Lord—before seeking refuge in Hari—one should first take refuge in and attain the protection of the Goddess, the beloved of the Blessed Lord, namely Śrī, and thereby attain equality (*tulā*) with the perfected ones who have surrendered, then his "attainment of the Blessed Lord" (*bhagavati gatiḥ*) would be even higher than that of Lakṣmī herself. The meaning is that by first taking refuge in Śrī, thinking, "May all be accomplished for you through her alone," one becomes graced by Śrī and subsequently takes refuge in the Blessed Lord.

Alternatively, he may be so called because his movement is directed upward toward the higher worlds—that is, his course follows the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and so forth. At any time whatsoever, he shall never have a lowly course, nor an downward descent.

For one who has reached the supreme ether by way of the path beginning with light, and who has taken refuge at the lotus feet of the venerable Vallabha, how could there ever again be an involvement with the cycle of worldly existence? This is the sense, based on the scriptural declaration: "This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool."

In the case of Hari (the Sun), immediately after [passing through] the sign of Leo (*siṃha*), that is, directly following it; having reached the maiden (*kanyā*) sign—that is, having attained it—if he should find Libra (*tulā*), meaning the sign of Libra, "properly," that is, without deviation; then Saturn (*mandaḥ*)—as Amara states, "Śani and Manda" [are synonyms for Saturn]—would also be in his exaltation (*uccagati*). This is because Libra is his place of exaltation. The intention of the word "also" (*api*) is that he is not only situated in a friendly sign, but is also in his exaltation.

In this way, Saturn situated in the sign of Libra can never, at any time, be in its state of debilitation (nīcagati); it simply cannot be so. This is because Aries is traditionally remembered as its place of debilitation, and therefore, for Saturn located in Libra, that condition does not apply. Here too, as before, there is a superimposition of astrological conventions onto the divine scriptural practices of the Lord’s tradition.

When one perceives the life-force (jīva) of the Slayer of Madhu as being gentle (saumya), then that [perception] has arisen; they call such a person a seeker of the highest good (śreyas-cintaka), and he is to be honored by the foremost among those endowed with sattva. *Saumya* means ever-serene due to being composed of pure *sattva*; it is also understood to mean "wise" (*budha*). As the *Medinīkośa* states: "The word *saumya* applies to a wise man (*jña*), in the masculine; in three genders, it means fierce, charming, or having Soma as its deity. *Madhumathana* refers to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān). By this, his proficiency in dispelling the quality of *tamas* is illuminated.

Indeed, the demon named Madhu is well-known in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts as being the very embodiment of the quality of darkness (*tamaḥ*). When—at which time—one should thoroughly behold the *jīva*, the inner self, who is the lord of speech; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *jīva* refers to a living being, a tree species, and Bṛhaspati. At that time, one should regard that *jīva* who has arisen as a seeker of the highest good (*śreyas*), one who contemplates the goal of liberation.

At that time, during the period when Mercury was being aspected by Jupiter, he begot a son who was a seeker of the highest good (*śreyas*)—one who contemplates the welfare of all and reflects upon righteousness (*dharma*). According to the *Medinīkośa*, "the word *śreyas* is used for liberation, auspiciousness, dharma, and what is most praiseworthy. Therefore, [the son] became the leader of those possessed of *sattva*—that is, of *sāttvika* persons; otherwise, [the term refers to] kings who are powerful, resolute, or wealthy.
As the lexicon states: "The word *sattva* denotes a quality, a piśāca, strength, substance, and nature;
it signifies the self, resolve, and impurity; and when not feminine, it refers to living beings."

Thus says the *Medinī* lexicon. They say that the word *śiraspadaiḥ* (by the head-places) means "worthy of honor. According to the rule *adhaśśirasī pade*, the visarga of the word *śiras* becomes *s*. Alternatively, the construction may be: "They say that for those possessed of goodness (*sattvavatām*), [the sight of] the head-places is honorable and brings about the consideration of what is beneficial (*śreyaḥ-cintakam*). In this interpretation, there is an exceeding correspondence with the meaning of the statement that will be cited immediately below:
"For Madhusūdana gazes upon the man who is being born..."
For one who is sattvic and worthy of being known, there is indeed the contemplation on the goal of liberation.
Thus, when the legal proceedings of the *Mahābhārata* have been set forth,
Bṛhaspati is either joined with or regarded as equal to Candraja;
for the lords of the earth carry his command upon their heads.
Thus, there is the superimposition of an irrelevant astrological convention.
Just as a virtuous person, having been given the essence of the Lord of the World by a physician who was himself taught by a teacher, becomes free from all ailments upon partaking of it; || 781 ||
Having cast aside and abandoned those who are unlearned and ordinary, one who is himself unlearned and ordinary is called "unlearned," whereas a Vaiṣṇava is called "learned.
A learned person should not perform even the slightest action with anyone who is unlearned.

The sense is that this is because of the statement of the Blessed Teacher (Bhagavacchāstṛ). By the physician (*vaidya*)—one who knows the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) as stated in the words, "That is true knowledge (*vidyā*) which leads to liberation. The suffix *aṇ* (forming *vaidya*) is applied here according to the rule for derivatives meaning "one who knows that" (*tadveda*), falling under the *prāgdīvyatīya* category. By the teacher (*guru*)—that is, by the preceptor (*ācārya*). By these two terms, the meanings of the words "one learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*), "established in Brahman" (*brahmaniṣṭha*), and "teacher" (*guru*) as spoken in the Śruti, "For the sake of knowing That," are recalled.

A person who partakes of the essence of the Lord of the World—which is given and bestowed, and which consists of the bliss of experiencing the Blessed One—becomes one whose every ailment has departed; thus it is said. According to Amara, "strī, rug, rujā, upatāpa, roga, vyādhi, gada, and āmaya" are synonyms for disease. The meaning is that all afflictions have dissolved away. Such a person becomes a holy soul (puṇyātmā), one of blessed nature; according to Amara, "puṇyavān" and "dhanya" are synonyms. In this state, the seer does not see death, nor disease, nor even suffering.
The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every respect.

Thus, the meaning of the scriptural passage from the *Bhūmavidyā* has been recalled. In this context, the sense is that a person who is ill—having cast aside and rejected those physicians who are not learned—and who partakes of the medicinal elixir known as *Lokanātha-rasa*, which was bestowed by the preeminent physician, the Guru, becomes free from all ailments, with every disease pacified. Having thus elaborated upon the nature of the *Lokanātha-rasa* in the *Vaidyacintāmaṇi*, [the author concludes]: "This *Lokanātha-rasa* shall conquer all diseases."

This is the intended meaning of the statement "because it has been so said. For this very reason, one whose soul is meritorious (*puṇyātman*) becomes beautiful in body through freedom from disease.
