There are five stages of the mind: the distracted (*kṣipta*), the deluded (*mūḍha*), the scattered (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*niruddha*).

The meaning of that [sūtra] is that it is "known" in all those stages (*bhūmi*s); as Bhojarāja said: "And that cessation is a property of all mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) of all living beings; it manifests at some time or other on some stage of development. This is the intention: when a particular cognitive fluctuation (*buddhivṛtti*) arises in the mind, then the cessation of other fluctuations is observed therein.

Just as in the state of the "thrown" (kṣipta) there is the cessation of the state of "deluded" (mūḍha), so too this cessation is understood to occur in all stages of the mind (*cittabhūmi*) in the manner described. Vācaspatimiśra, however, states: "The one-pointed mind has three stages: the 'Honeyed' (*madhumatī*), the 'Honey-like' (*madhupratīkā*), and the 'Sorrowless' (*viśokā*). But for the suppressed mind, there is only one stage, consisting of nothing but residual impressions (*saṃskāraśeṣa*). In all four of these stages, the cessation of the other fluctuations (*vṛtti*) such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is understood. It is with this meaning that he speaks.

And this is logical: among the five stages beginning with the "distracted" (*kṣipta*), the distracted state is always characterized by *rajas*, being tossed about among various objects and thus extremely unstable. The "deluded" (*mūḍha*) state, however, possesses sleep and so forth due to the predominance of *tamas*. The "distracted-and-diffused" (*vikṣipta*) is distinguished from the "distracted"; the distinction lies in the occasional stability of that which is otherwise predominantly unstable.

In that regard, although there is a cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-nirodha*) between the *kṣipta* (distracted) and *mūḍha* (infatuated) states in relation to one another, they lack even an indirect cause for the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and, moreover, are detrimental to it; therefore, they do not even qualify as forms of *samādhi*. As for the *vikṣipta* (distracted) mind, its occasional *samādhi* does not belong to the category of Yoga; rather, like a lamp tossed by a violent wind, it perishes of its own accord.

One-pointedness (*ekāgra*), however, is the capacity for a continuous flow of mental modifications directed toward a single object. Due to the predominance of *sattva* and the dissolution of lethargy and other states caused by the quality of *tamas*, the modification becomes uniform in form. Furthermore, because of the absence of distraction in the form of instability caused by the quality of *rajas*, it is restricted to a single object; thus, when *sattva* is purified, the mind becomes one-pointed. On this stage, there is "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) concentration, wherein even the modification in the form of the object of meditation is manifest. When that too is restrained, the restrained mind reaches the stage of "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi; such is the sequence.

Therefore, since *samādhi* is impossible in the states of the distracted (*kṣipta*), the stupefied (*mūḍha*), and the occasionally distracted (*vikṣipta*), Vācaspati Miśra has established the "universal sovereignty" (*sārvabhaumatva*) of yoga by taking the four intermediate stages beginning with the "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*), which belong exclusively to the remaining two stages known as the one-pointed (*ekāgra*) and the restrained (*niruddha*). Indeed, this is precisely the position intended in this illustrative verse, because it rejects reliance on the three stages of the distracted, the stupefied, and the occasionally distracted, and demonstrates the universal sovereignty of yoga solely through its abiding in the two stages called the one-pointed and the restrained. Enough of this.
Or rather,
O Śauri, as the dust of Your army rises up— free from the distress of proximity— I believe it has touched the entire sky through contact with the waters of the celestial river.
O Śauri! Your army’s dust has reached the sun and the woman in her courses.
*Aviḥ* means a mountain, the sun, a ram, a mouse, a woolen blanket, a wall, a house, or light; as for the word *avi*, it refers to a woman or the earth.

Thus ends the *Ratnamālā*. "Sannidheḥ" means from proximity; "sātaṅkaḥ" means possessed of distress (*tāpa*) and possessed of the apprehension of injury (Amara states: "Sātaṅkaḥ" is used for pain, distress, and apprehension). "Ullalan" means rising upwards; in the alternative sense, it refers to the expression of his character and disposition as one who leaps up. "Upasparśāt" means from contact with, or from touching, the water of the celestial river (*abhrasarit*); in the alternative sense, it means having performed bathing and sipping water (*ācamana*). We have already stated in the commentary on the preceding verse that in the speech of males, the presence of multiple meanings is not a fault.

Regarding the ablative case in *lyablope*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The ablative is used in the sense of mere contact (*upasparśa*), including both bathing and sipping water. He touched the entire sky, that is, the atmosphere. I think—and thus infer—that he merely touched it, for otherwise contact with the Mandākinī would have been impossible; this is the intended meaning. In the alternative sense (the allegorical), he touched the entire sky, meaning he contacted the senses such as sight and so forth.
One should avoid outcasts (*caṇḍāla*), those who have recently given birth (*sūtikā*), women in their courses (*udakyā*), and the fallen (*patita*) from a distance;
therefore, by mere proximity to them, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on (*sacela-snāna*).
Thus, having bathed, drunk, eaten, slept, or sneezed, the best of the twice-born,
having sipped water properly according to this rule, attains purity.
And thus, according to the Saṃvarta-smṛti:
"Having sipped water three times with water that is natural, free from froth and bubbles, and having wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the cavities of the head with water."

Thus, following the sipping of water (ācamana), Yājñavalkya prescribes the touching of the sense organs, such as the eyes, and so forth; Amarasimha states, "The word *kha* [also means] an organ of sense. Here, within the worldly context of the dust from the Lord’s army, there is the superimposition of the legal terminology of the Dharmaśāstras.

Or, victorious is Hari, who wears a pearl necklace upon his chest, who is exceedingly beautiful with the luster of his dark throat, and who possesses a supreme radiance through his association with the light of the great crest-jewel. 790.

He is so described because he possesses a pearl necklace (*muktāvali*)—a *muktāhāra*—that resides in his heart, stays upon his chest, and dwells in his mind; the suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*. He is also beautiful (*subhaga*) by virtue of an excessive passion (*ativelā ruciḥ*) for the *Śitikaṇṭhīya*, which relates to the peacock (or, in the alternative sense, the *Śitikaṇṭhīya* is a specific treatise on Nyāya); he is beautiful by virtue of an intense devotion (*āsthā*) toward that work.

The term *prauḍha* means mature. *Śiromaṇi* is a crest-jewel; from its *dīdhiti*—that is, its radiance—or in the alternative sense, from contact with or study of the *Śiromaṇidīdhiti*, a specific treatise on Nyāya, he became *parabhāgavān*, meaning possessed of an excellence of qualities (the lexicon states: "the word *parabhāga* refers to an excellence of qualities"). Here, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the technical terminology of the Nyāya system onto the worldly description of the divine form of Śrīnivāsa.
If the intention here were that even this non-contextual (aprakṛta) description is worldly, then this would be an illustration of the first variety [of *samāsokti*].
Just as it is said:

"Indeed, your exceedingly high bow is fixed upon your hand in the [position of] Rājya; and it stretches forth you—who bear a gentle friend (the Moon), who possess great beauty, and whose rising is self-accomplished. (791)

O Ananta! O Blessed One! [The bow], having become attached to Your hand—which is high, excellent, or elevated—thereby attained an exalted state; the sense is that it is like Vibhīṣaṇa and others who have reached eminence. And [it is like] a gentle king, whose governance is gracious, established in the position of supreme sovereignty; for the *Medinī* lexicon states: "The word *saumya* refers to Mercury (*jña*) or is used in three genders for 'gracious' (*anugra*), and *ina* refers to a lord (*pati*), a king, or the sun."

The meaning is that he establishes [the kingdom] in a state free from obstruction, nourishing and supporting it. "Suśrīkam" means possessing beautiful splendor; "svakalito-dayam" means one whose rise or power (*prābhavam*) has been acquired through his own wealth—according to Amara, *sva* in the feminine gender means wealth. The word *tu* is used for emphasis, meaning "exactly as described above. The sense is that there should be no doubt in this matter. Thus he "spreads" [it].

"Otherwise, indeed"—this is an address to someone. When the hand-asterism (hasta) is at its maximum altitude in the infinite sky (ananta), and when the observer is situated at a point equal to the middle of the eyebrows, the bow (dhanu)—meaning the ascendant known as Dhanus—has arisen, having reached its rising; thus it is said in the *Jyautiṣopakaraṇa*: "Facing the south, at night, having observed the yoga-tārā situated at the middle of one's own eyebrows, the wise man should declare the time, which is the zenith."
Based on the numerical sequence of the syllables such as *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*,
and *ya*, the movement of the ascendants when each respective asterism is in its exaltation is described.

Having begun with these words, it continues: "The hand, the bow, the house, the girl. If the asterism Hasta is situated in its exaltation and the sign Sagittarius (Dhanu) is the ascendant, the meaning is that three *nāḍikās* and three-eighths of a *nāḍikā* have elapsed.
In every sentence, the first letter of the pair of syllables being recited indicates the *nāḍikā* at the ascendant, while the subsequent letter indicates one-eighth of that *nāḍikā*.

This is because it is stated right there [in that very text]. "In the tenth house of the kingdom" means in the sign of Virgo (*kanyārāśi*), "exalted" meaning situated in its exaltation. This connects specifically with the word "Saumya" (Mercury), for Virgo is the exaltation sign of Mercury alone, and not with the word "Ina" (the Sun), for Aries is the exaltation sign of the Sun. Thus, by holding both Saumya (Budha) and Ina (Bhānu), it extends great prosperity (*suśrīka*)—meaning excellent sovereignty—to you, who have attained birth (*kalitodaya*) in its own sign, Sagittarius (*dhanurlagna*).

The meaning is that because the Sun, as the lord of fortune (*bhāgya*), is situated in its exaltation along with Mercury, the lord of the kingdom (*rājya*), in the house of royalty; for Sagittarius ascendant, Leo and Virgo are the houses of fortune and royalty, since the ninth and tenth signs are designated as the houses of fortune and royalty respectively, according to the rule: "The ninth is fortune and dharma, and the tenth is action and royalty. In this worldly convention regarding the Lord’s bow, if both the lords of fortune and royalty should be present in the house of fortune or in the house of royalty, and if even one of them is in its exaltation, it bestows a great kingdom.
Thus ends the application of astronomical conventions. Or, for example:

"O Lord of the Mountain of Serpents (Śiva), though You dwell in some corner [of the world], You are worshipped by the gods; whoever beholds Your rising shall become wise, illustrious, and possessed of a beautiful body. (792)

O Lord! O Master! [The locative case is used here according to the rule *svāmīśvarādhipati* etc. You, who are worshiped by the gods (*surapūjya*)—in the alternative sense, meaning Bṛhaspati—reside somewhere in a corner on the Crest of Serpents (*phaṇiśikhariṇi*), that is, on the Śeṣa mountain (*śeṣādri*), in some particular region; in the alternative sense, while residing in the so-called trine (*trikoṇa*) position, either the fifth or the ninth from the ascendant (*lagna*), at the rise—that is, the prosperity—of a certain man...

In this context, the word *udaya* (rising) indicates one's own place of observation (*svadraṣṭavyasthāna*), namely the ascendant at birth (*janmalagna*) and the other trines (*trikoṇa*) indicated by it. One whose "sight" (*dṛṣṭi*)—meaning intention (*abhiprāya*)—is thus directed toward that [place] will become wise, prosperous, and handsome. The underlying sense is: "What is difficult to obtain for one who is glanced upon by you?"

Regarding the second alternative: if Jupiter, situated in the fifth or ninth house from the birth ascendant—that is, in a trine—aspecting the ascendant with a trine aspect, that person becomes wise, prosperous, and handsome. Because the fifth house is the seat of intellect (*buddhi*), when Jupiter is located there, he is wise; because of the aspect on the ninth house from that fifth-trine, he is prosperous; and because of the aspect on the ascendant—the seat of the body—from the ninth-trine, he is handsome.

Thus, because the ninth house is the locus of fortune (*bhāgya*), when [the lord] is situated there, one becomes illustrious (*śrīmān*); from there, by aspecting the fifth angle (*pañcamakoṇa*) and looking at the ascendant (*lagna*), as before, one becomes embodied (*vapuṣmān*); and by aspecting the fifth house through the ninth angle (*navamakoṇa*), one becomes wise (*dhīmān*). This is the distinction. In this worldly context of the conduct of people favored by the Lord’s glance, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars all aspect the seventh houses;
furthermore, they especially aspect the third, tenth, and fourth houses.
Whichever house is aspected by or conjoined with its own lord,
or with benefics, there will be an increase in that very matter.
Thus ends the superimposition of astrological conventions and terminology.

Or rather, do not bow your head; for when you stand upright, a certain *mālinī* indeed becomes perfected—a woman radiant with the beauty of a noble lineage, resplendent with the *atiśakvarī* meter, and possessing stainless fortune. (793)

This verse is the speech of someone addressed to a certain wise man (*kṛtin*). "O wise man! Do not bend—do not lower—your head. For what reason? Because regarding your conduct (*vṛtta*), that is, your character, no *mālinī*—meaning *mālinya*, or impurity—exists. [The word *mālinī* is derived from *mālinya* with the suffix *ṣyañ* in the sense of an abstract quality (*bhāva*), and the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by virtue of the rule for words ending in *ṣit*. The particle *nu* is used here in the sense of entreaty (*anunaya*). According to the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *nu* occurs in the senses of conjecture (*vitarka*) and contempt (*apamāna*); and in the senses of deliberation (*vikalpa*), entreaty (*anunaya*), question (*praśna*), and statement of reason (*hetvapadeśa*)."

If there were even the slightest stain upon your conduct, then you would have to bow your head; for that is the cause for bowing the head, yet such is not seen in you—this is the sense. He states the reason for this with the word "sādhu": O sinless one! For [you are] "sādhu-anvaya-guṇa-ruci," meaning those whose lineage (*anvaya*)—that is, their kinship—is "sādhu" (virtuous), implying they are eternally connected to virtue.

Such are the qualities—namely truthfulness, knowledge, bliss, and so forth, as well as the auspicious attributes such as freedom from sin—and by these she is radiant and beautiful. She is an *atiśakvarī*, meaning one who possesses exceeding power in both the subduing of evil and the bestowing of grace upon those who take refuge; the suffix *kvanip* is applied to the root *śak* according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well. When the feminine gender is intended, the suffix *ṅīp* is added and the letter *ra* is substituted for the final syllable, according to the rule "after *van*, *ṅīp* and *ra*. Such is Lakṣmī, the Śrī, who is resplendent and luminous within you, in your heart—in other words, she has been meditated upon by you.

The intended meaning is that, because your heart is the abode of the Goddess Lakṣmī in the manner described, there can be no contact with impurity for you. As for the alternative reading "tvayi" (in you), the word division here is "ayi" (O!). Thus: "O wise one! From that which has 'nanamaya' at its head"—meaning that in which, at the beginning (the head), there are two *nagaṇas*, an *agaṇa*, and a *yagaṇa* in succession; from that *yagaṇa* (which is at the head) [comes the meter]. The suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). This refers to the meter, expressed in the singular by way of genus (*jātyekavacanam*).

The meaning is that among the meters (*vṛttas*), this one is also one of them; it becomes *mālinī*, that is, the meter named *mālinī*. This is because of its definition: "This *mālinī* consists of *na*, *ma*, *na*, and two *yas*, as stated by the world of *bhogins* (the serpent-grammarians). He further qualifies that very meter with the word "well" (*sādhu*). The grammatical analysis (*anvaya*) is as follows: That which has no letter *u* is *anu*. In the *nañ-pūrvapada-bahuvrīhi* compound, after the elision of *na* [in *an-u*], the augment *nuṭ* is applied by the rule "tasmānnuḍaci. That [augment] is followed by *a*, and that which goes toward (*yāti*) this [syllable] is *aya*. From the root *yā*, the suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "āto’nupasarge kaḥ. Thus, *an-aya* means that which lacks the syllable *u*. It goes toward this [syllable], hence it is *anayaya*. The *mālinī* is joined (*yutā*) with these [elements]. Therefore, the sense is: "O King, you are indeed a *mālinī* (garlanded one), for you possess a garland (*mālā*) consisting of *anayayas* (those who go toward what lacks the letter *u*). 1.23.15. 1.23.16. 1.23.17. 1.23.18. 1.23.19. 1.23.20. 1.23.21. 1.23.22. 1.23.23. 1.23.24. 1.23.25. 1.23.26. 1.23.27. 1.23.28. 1.23.29. 1.23.30. 1.23.31. 1.23.32. 1.23.33. 1.23.34. 1.23.35. 1.23.36. 1.23.37. 1.23.38. 1.23.39. 1.23.40. 1.23.41. 1.23.42. 1.23.43. 1.23.44. 1.23.45. 1.23.46. 1.23.47. 1.23.48. 1.23.49. 1.23.50. 1.23.51. 1.23.52. 1.23.53. 1.23.54. 1.23.55. 1.23.56. 1.23.57. 1.23.58. 1.23.59. 1.23.60. 1.23.61. 1.23.62. 1.23.63. 1.23.64. 1.23.65. 1.23.66. 1.23.67. 1.23.68. 1.23.69. 1.23.70. 1.23.71. 1.23.72. 1.23.73. 1.23.74. 1.23.75. 1.23.76. 1.23.77. 1.23.78. 1.23.79. 1.23.80. 1.23.81. 1.23.82. 1.23.83. 1.23.84. 1.23.85. 1.23.86. 1.23.87. 1.23.

The meaning is that it possesses the vowel *a* in place of the vowel *u*. "Guṇa" means "gaṇa. This is because, by the aforementioned method, when the vowel *u* is removed from the word "guṇa" and the vowel *a* is substituted in its place, the form "gaṇa" is produced. "Sādhu" means auspicious (*śubhaprada*) according to the method to be described; this refers to the "anvayaguṇas" (lineage-qualities), with the singular used for the genus. Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is made using the plural forms of the two words themselves: "sādhavaḥ" and "anvayaguṇāḥ. The "anvayaguṇas" refer to those previously mentioned *nanamayayagaṇas*; [the Goddess] is beautiful (*rucirā*) on account of them.

*Atiśakvarī* is the meter (chandas) of that name consisting of fifteen syllables. Since it is counted as the fifteenth, beginning from *uktā*, *atyuktā*, and so on, up to the rule "that [śakvarī] preceded by *ati* becomes [atiśakvarī]," the term *ujjvalā* means "shining" or "resplendent. The compound *anaghalakṣmyaḥ* is a genitive *bahuvrīhi* meaning "one whose fortunes (*lakṣmyaḥ*)—meaning prosperities (*saṃpadaḥ*)—are stainless (*anaghāḥ*), i.e., faultless (*nirdoṣāḥ*), within (*antaḥ*) or in the midst (*madhye*) of that [meter]. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The sense is that when this [meter] is employed at the beginning of a composition, the prosperities of both the poet (*kavituḥ*) and its author (*tatpraṇetuḥ*) are surely accomplished. As it has been stated in the *Alaṃkāraśirobhūṣaṇa*:
The *nagaṇa* (the first group of three syllables) consisting of three short vowels bestows all desired objects incessantly upon its deity, the sacrificer;
though he resembles yellow orpiment, he is free from planetary afflictions, and thus no host of enemies exists for him.
A *magaṇa* followed by three *gurus* bestows fortune; such glory arises from its presiding deities, Mercury and the Earth.
Furthermore, when accompanied by a *sagaṇa*, it extends prosperity; however, if joined with malefic planets, it becomes inauspicious.
In the *yagaṇa*, the deity is the Water-god (*Jaladevatā*), who is exceedingly white; he bestows wealth and is the first among the light [syllables], being the planet Venus (*Kavi*).
When joined with a *tagaṇa*, it bestows inauspiciousness upon the poet and his leader, like rice mixed with poison.
Whichever auspicious presiding deity belongs to whichever group, that group possesses gentleness;
for whichever [deity] is otherwise in this world, that group indeed possesses cruelty.

Thus, it should be understood that since this meter begins with a *nagaṇa*, and because the *nagaṇa*—despite its association with all other *gaṇas*—bestows auspiciousness due to its being presided over by a planet (the Moon), there is no room for inauspiciousness arising from a connection with inauspicious *gaṇas* caused by having malefic planets as deities, as is the case with *magaṇa* and others whose deities are enemies or malefic planets. Furthermore, due to the natural conjunction of the two auspicious *gaṇas*, *magaṇa* and *yagaṇa*, it bestows prosperity (*lakṣmī*). This is how it should be contemplated.

In this regard, the following should be understood: although the suffix *kap* is established by the rule *nadyutaśca*, the inclusion of the word *lakṣmī* among the *uraḥprabhṛti* group is stated to serve a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatā*), namely that *kap* is obligatory only for a *bahuvrīhi* whose constituent member is the singular-form *lakṣmī*, whereas elsewhere it is optional according to the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā*. Since the analysis (*vigraha*) here is shown using the plural-form *lakṣmī*, there is no occasion for the obligatory application of *kap*. Furthermore, because *kap* under the rule *śeṣādvibhāṣā* is optional, it is not intended to be expressed here.

Nor does the shortening of the penultimate vowel apply by the rule "gostriyoḥ," because that rule prescribes shortening only for words ending in feminine suffixes; and since the word *lakṣmī* does not end in a feminine suffix, [the rule does not apply]. Here, within this worldly context under discussion, there is the superimposition of the technical terminology of the science of prosody (*chandaśśāstra*), which is not relevant to the subject at hand.

Just as spectators experience joy upon beholding a beautiful form with lovely proportions, charming features, and a rasa that is delightful on every side, so do they find delight in seeing Your exquisite form, Muktunda. (794)
That which has beautiful joints and connections; by this [it is meant] that the arrangement of the major and minor limbs is according to what is appropriate.
That which possesses joints and bonds that are exceedingly smooth is called "beauty" (*saundarya*);

thus, the possession of beauty as defined by that description is illuminated. In the alternative sense (the poetic), it refers to that in which there is a composition (*bandha*) of the five junctures (*sandhi*)—namely, *mukha*, *pratimukha*, *garbha*, *avamarśa*, and *upasaṃhṛti*—which are described [in dramaturgy] as being "delightful" (*ramaṇīya*). Furthermore, it is that which has a mark (*aṅka*)—the Śrīvatsa emblem—situated in the heart (*hṛdaya*), meaning it is dear to the heart. In the alternative sense, it refers to that which has marks (*aṅka*) that are pleasing to the heart.
An act (aṅka) is characterized by the conduct of characters present on the stage, preceded by the manifestation of the seed-plot (bindu);
it is the locus of various types of plot arrangements and aesthetic sentiments (rasa).

That in which there are specific pauses (*viccheda*) characterized as described above; that by which the ground of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-bhū*) is delightful on all sides—that is, possessing the delightful flavors of love (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth—and beholding your beautiful and charming form, your divine body, the virtuous members of the assembly attain joy. Here, the conventions of drama are superposed upon worldly experience.
The sublation of worldly usage by scriptural authority is as follows:
"O Blessed One, you are free from old age, free from death, with evil destroyed, and whose desires are true. Thus, the faultless Śruti, being intent upon You, brings forth every desired object. (795)

In this Vedāntic discourse, there is a superimposition of the worldly behavior of a housewife who has a beloved husband and virtuous children. The meaning of the Śruti, “free from evil, ageless,” is here kept in mind; in the present context, it means that [Brahman] has true desires and is devoted to its own consort (the individual soul). "Desired object" refers both to the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*).

Or rather, O Acyuta, liberation—which is more skillful—now awaits your fortunate [soul], which has abandoned the insentient *prakṛti* (nature) that has already experienced enjoyment and is now longing for its own attainment. (796) The phrase "having experienced enjoyment" (*bhuktabhogām*) means that she has already undergone pleasure; the sense is that the enjoyments were experienced prior to dispassion (*virakti*), and will not be experienced hereafter. "Abandoning the insentient" (*acitām*) refers to her unconscious nature and ignorance. The Vedic scripture is recalled here: "The other, the unborn, leaves her behind once her enjoyment has been experienced. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6).

"Longing" (utkaṇṭhā) refers to the state of being filled with yearning upon attaining one's own nature, characterized by the removal of all evil and other such qualities; in another sense, it is that which poets know as longing accompanied by volition—the desire for the attainment of that [nature]—wherein one imagines there exists the relish of pleasure through all the senses. Upon the attainment of one's own nature, one feels a longing; in the alternative sense, "upon the attainment of one's own nature" means upon the attainment of the Self, wherein one conceives that the taste of happiness from all the senses exists.
Poets understand this longing to be a desire for its attainment coupled with a mental resolve.

Thus it is said, accompanied by a particular desire: "O Acyuta! Liberation awaits—that is, it waits for—your devotee, who is blessed, who has fulfilled his purpose, and who is a man who has obtained wealth; and [it awaits] one who is *kuśalatara*, meaning exceedingly auspicious (*atimātra-kṣemaṅkara*) and most clever (*caturatara*). As the *Ratnamālā* states: 'The word *kuśala* is used in three genders in the senses of sufficiency, merit, and security, as well as skill. Here, in this context of the Vedānta scripture, there is a superimposition (*āropa*) of the behavior of a woman who, having enjoyed her pleasures and being in a state of longing (*vāsakasajjikā*), waits for a lover who desires her, preceded by her abandonment of a foolish husband."
In this way,
that deity is preeminent in victory through the various manifestations of the enemy's array, as well as through her virtuous form, her role as the inner controller within the world, and her renown.

That deity—referring to the deity described in the passage "that very deity thought"—is the deity in the form of the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*). Through the distinctions of the Supreme (*para*), the Manifestation (*vyūha*), and the Incarnation (*vibhava*), He triumphs exceedingly: as the Supreme, He is Paravāsudeva; as the Manifestations, they are Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and the others; and as the Incarnations, they take the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth. Furthermore, in this world, He exists in the form of a beautiful image (*arcā*)—a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "He whose beautiful image resides [therein]"—dwelling in divine sacred sites such as Śrīraṅga and Veṅkaṭācala.

The compound *sādhvī arcā* may be analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa*: "an image that is virtuous. Amara states: "An image (*arcā*) is a likeness (*pratikṛti*). [She] is [present] by way of being the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmitayā*), that is, in the form of the Inner Ruler; the instrumental case here denotes cause. "And also by fame" means: and also by the renown resulting from being the Inner Ruler. Alternatively, she is so called because her fame is distinguished (*viśiṣṭā khyātiḥ yasyāḥ sā*); this should be construed with "and also by way of being the Inner Ruler. The phrase "she triumphs exceedingly" (*vijayatetarām*) is to be supplied.

The distilled meaning is this: the Deity, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, triumphs pre-eminently in the world through her forms as the Paravyūha, Vibhava, Arcā, and Antaryāmin. Alternatively, in the latter half of the verse, the analysis is *bhuvane antaḥ yā amitayā*; "within the world" (*bhuvane’ntaḥ*) means "in the midst of the world."

It should be understood that, because the word *antaḥ* (within) is included in the *śauṇḍādi* group mentioned in the rule prescribing the locative compound (*saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*), the locative case is used when there is a desire to express the locus of the whole in relation to its parts—just as in the expression "the branch in the tree" (*vṛkṣe śākhā*). The meaning is that she is worthy of worship (*pūjyā*), being one whose beautiful image (*arcā*) is characterized by a boundless and immeasurable fame (*vikhyāti*) resulting from the destruction and shattering of the power and military arrays (*vyūha*) of her enemies.
The grammatical connection is: "That deity is most victorious. Here, in the context of the worldly conduct established by the *Pañcarātra-āgama*, this great deity indeed abides in human form;
thus, the worldly conduct of a great king—rendered auspicious by his majesty, valor, and fame as previously described—is superimposed [upon her].
Or rather:
"O Lord, am I not truly fortunate? For, though terrified by a host of eternal robbers and finding no protection anywhere, I have placed my entire being in you; how could I not be blessed? (798)

O Lord! Is it not so that you are terrified—frightened by the group or even by a single one of those eternal and relentless enemies, such as desire and the rest? In the alternative sense, you are alarmed and agitated by the group of thieves; for the *Medinī* lexicon states, "The word *dasyu* applies to a thief or an enemy" in both cases.

Finding no protection anywhere and obtaining no refuge, he has placed—having entrusted—his own self and wealth upon you, relying on the conviction that you will protect the universe; such a person, how could he not be fortunate and one who has achieved his life's purpose? The sense is that for one who has cast the burden of protecting himself upon the Blessed One, there is indeed the attainment of the goal. (Regarding the words *sva* and *dhanya*: Amara states, "The word *sva* refers to a kinsman and to the self; in three genders it means 'one's own,' and in the neuter it means 'wealth'"; this applies to both terms. How could he not be blessed and successful? The meaning is that for one who has surrendered the responsibility for his own protection to the Lord, fulfillment of purpose is certain.

The sense is: having obtained wealth from one who is trustworthy and a sovereign among good people, how could that person not recover the wealth once deposited? Here, there is a superimposition of worldly transaction upon the transaction described in the scripture of the Blessed One.
Or, for example:

"At the end of the rainy season, the body of the Lord of the Serpent-Mountains shines forth, his hands bearing blossoming, stainless lotuses, and having adorned the quarters of the sky with the splendor of his radiance. (799)

He in whose hand the stainless lotus and conch shine forth; he in whom the stainless rays of the moon, appearing like lotuses, shine forth. Adorned with the splendors of light—that is, with preeminent excellences—and with the magnificent beauty of *kāśa* flowers, he has filled the quarters of space. He is the limb—the divine form—of the Lord of the Mountain who bears hoods (Śiva); he resides at the end of the "dense" scripture—that is, in the Upaniṣads of the Veda.

"In the course of" means at the end or conclusion of the arrival of the clouds, that is, the rainy season; "it spreads. Here too, there is a superimposition of the worldly convention of the autumn season upon the technical usage of the treatise.
Those who are proficient in calculation, all-knowing, and for whom aesthetic wonder is their sole life-breath,
must tolerate the abundance of examples provided here, which were composed out of impulsiveness.
And this [figure] occurs most frequently in accordance with other ornaments, as in:
"The bracelet slipped onto the foot, while Hari’s crest-jewel ascended to the head; even when the space between them is very small, the young bride’s conduct becomes unrestrained. (800)

In this instance, the *samāsokti* (condensed expression) functioning as a capacity (*sāmarthya*) imparts a quality conducive to the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth). As in the following example:
"Who indeed on earth can grasp the hearts of women, who are by nature fickle? When the Blessed One is not present before her, fortune abandons a man, even one long acquainted. (801)
In this context, it functions as a means of justification.
I think that the gems within the necklaces, with their spreading rays of light, stretch out their hands to present a gift to the Supreme Gem who has taken His place upon the lotus-heart of Śauri.

Here, the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) regarding the stretching out of hands is rooted in the worldly dealings of a multitude of kings—lords of various provinces—who are intent on offering tributes to a sovereign emperor seated upon the throne of empire. By this very same path, when the behavior of insentient things is introduced, the conceits of nature, cause, and effect pertaining to the behavior of sentient beings are based solely on *samāsokti* (synthetic metaphor); likewise, when the behavior of sentient beings is introduced, the conceits of nature, cause, and effect pertaining to the behavior of insentient things are also based solely on *samāsokti*.

Dīkṣita asserted that this [figure] also becomes *samāsokti* (synecdoche/metaphorical identification) due to similarity (*sārūpya*). However, the author of the *Rasagaṅgādhara* stated that this is untenable because, in the absence of the equality of adjectives (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*)—which is the very life-breath of *samāsokti*—the status of *samāsokti* itself is impossible in a verse such as "purā yatra srotaḥ" (where formerly there was a stream). According to his view, in examples like "purā yatra srotaḥ," there is only *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), since he has established it as such.
We shall demonstrate all of this later, at the occasion of defining the figure of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the Section on Samāsokti (Indirect Description), in the first part of the Alaṅkāramaṇihāra (The Necklace of Jewels of Figures of Speech).
